Aw, poor Josh! Yeah, it can take ages to clear up. Got eeny weeny drops I used to use when my son had that. I’ll bring them over next time I pop in. I swear they worked wonders.      Oh, bless you, that’d be great! You always remember the little things. Didn’t even get round to washing those bottles you brought the other day, by the way—still sitting in the sink.      No worries, that’s what sisters are for, right? Fun left’s week, though! I had the best time in Birmingham, catching up with mum. She screamed when she saw photos of Finley’s new haircut. Poor lad—still doesn’t know half the comments she made in front of his teacher.      Oh no, spare me the details. Good to see her, though. I do miss the old days, though, when we used to drive down there every week with the kids and just be deadly for the day.      Aye, it feels like centuries ago. How’s the marketing work been, by the way?      Honestly, it’s been flat-lining these past few months. Should’ve stuck to proofreading, I suppose. At least that's reliable. Got a big deadline on Tuesday—developing a social media plan for some new boutique. Bit floring, to be honest, but money doesn’t grow on trees.      Oy, I about forgot—your birthday’s in two weeks, right? What’re we doing? Dinner out or staying in with the cabers?      Let’s do something fun! I fancy a proper night out—y’know, like before the kids. The club at The Winter Garden would be a laugh. Do you think we could get a babysitter?      As long as we can’t afford to outstay our welcome with lunches and shots and whatnot! Let me speak to Sian, she’s delivering something around then and might be able to swing it. Oh right, he’s changed course over the summer.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You used to just get on the train and it was sorted when you showed up, innit? Now it’s like more paperwork than when you’re actually flying. I was in Prague a fortnight ago and had the same fanny of a time.      Right? I swear I lost half an hour just queueing at the border checkpoint in Austria last week. I’ve only got so much research money in this grant, and I’m watching every penny now. Still, it’s worth it to be doing fieldwork on the continent when it's possible. You get different perspectives, you know?      That’s the main thing, yeah. You can’t put that into a university budget, but you get it in your head. I did this one survey in Geneva, and these older EUs in the area? Half had never even met a Brit since ‘16. Felt like prime real estate for some folk responses. The funny part was, they all looked at me, saw the lanyard and called me “ah, the bloke from the UK Research Institute”, but I was like—“No, luv, it’s  me , and I’m from Sunderland, thank you very much.”      “Sunderland – Mate, I got a mate in Sunderland who runs a football club!” “You mean he nearly gets blacked out in the changing rooms?”      Honestly, just someone who knows how to get the crowd voting. Anyway, it just goes to show the point—everyone’s got this vague sense of the UK and thinks they know it all, but when you actually speak to most people about it, they’re baffled. “How do the pubs work?” “What’s a  Real ale ? Is that better than a cider?”      I had that in Munich last year. I told them I was doing a PhD based on British pubs, and the first thing they mentioned was the  King’s Cross witches  or some myth about London. We lost two hours down that alley. They kept talking about how English people were all stuck-up or told tall tales. Some lad even said, “Are you serious? You Brits think the weather is a gothic mystery novel!”      You’re just in the middle of it. Going along, bloke chats away, your research’s forgotten. It’s like fluency in small talk’s one of the necessary hours now, innit? It’s not like we talk like that where we’re from anyway—back home it's more like—“Here’s the project, done.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to do a bit of marking tomorrow, but it's such a beautiful evening... What do you fancy for dessert after this game, love? I was thinking maybe we could have a little ice cream? Not too often, you know, as you both know. But it's been a good week and we  are  on Monopoly 'again'.      Can we have sprinkles on top, Mummy? Please! I got to be the bank this time and I kept giving lots of money to Freddie anyway.      Well done, Mollie. You were very responsible with the property deeds and the cash, weren't you? Though I don't know whether Freddie  appreciated  being forced to buy properties left and right. Tenants, London – who are you, Roald Dahl?      It wasn't  so  bad! Wait, Mummy – if I land on Park Lane again I’m just going to shout “GG” again, like Grandad showed me.       Giggle  Oh, you're such a little man now! I don’t think your grandad ever said “GG” in his life, but go on… You can't say "GG" when you win, though. You win normally. Like a fairly normal, cheery human being. Not some dramatic final showdown.      Mummy’s funny when she’s tired. Freddie made me pay rent for Whitechapel Road when I didn’t even own it! That wasn’t fair at  all .      Oh, right, because you  did , Mollie! Look, it’s right here in about five places. That’s the thing about the English, you lot keep buying property and not remembering where you’ve gone. Don’t you trust the documentation?      Well, Mummy, you just keep giving us extra money. I think you're biased.      No, I’m not! I am accurate, missy. I just occasionally reward good behaviour and clever deals. Let’s not forget, you've both spent a little more on hotels than strictly necessary today.      Then can we have two scoops of ice cream? I promise to share if you promise not to shout at me about my dentistry after.      You can have two scoops if we finish the game. But I am  not  promising not to mention your molars, Missy. It's your third consultation in a month and you still eat the ice cream with a spoon that looks like it’s been dropped in a compost heap.      Am I allowed to choose the flavour, Mummy?

Rather annoying this, innit? I mean, I’ve been talkin’ for hours on end 'bout this update to the corpus, an’ now I’ve got to wait for it to process. An’ where is it processin’? No one ever tells yer!      Yeah, I saw the email about the update. It was posted   yesterday  , wasn’t it? You should’ve hit submit earlier if it was that important. Why'd you leave it till last minute?      Well, no one said the submission window was early in the mornin’! I saw the notification Friday, sorted the bloody thing, an’ it wasn’t till I’d submitted that I saw they changed the deadline again. You know how it is. Admin types like to throw yer off with the dates, don’t they? I swear, the more professional they are, the more likely they forgetin’ breakfast, innit?      I suppose there’s a bit of that. You try talkin’ to someone at the top, they just pass it round like a football and tell you it’s “being looked into.” I mean, we did a similar thing with the project last week, and still no confirmation on the client. They say they’re in discussions.      Mate, I’ve heard that one before, an’ it means either “no” or “we haven’t got round to it.” If I could blame somethin’, I’d say the coffee machine someone at the office is also in discussions.      Bloke at the firm said something very similar about a client wants to talk being “prioritised.” I was like, there’s a word about nowhere close to “actioned.”      You’re telling me. I swear, if you speak that lot too clearly they get it twisted. No, I just do what I do for the corpus: format it well an’ submit it. The rest? Well, the rest is a lottery ‘cos it sounds very disappointed if I do complain.      Yeah, and I know what you mean. Even trying to get tech support on site takes weeks. I took the kettle in there for repair, and they said it was a “structure issue.” I was like, right, if that’s not broken then what is?      You might be on to somethin’. Kettles and structure. I’m gonna get me a brand new one, after I wait hours to compile this bloody corpus file. I’ve had it with hidden delays over this job.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp as a cellar all week. Never mind me bones, I say. I can feel it in every joint.      Not to mention the smell o' things round 'ere. We haven’t had a proper window cracked since  Christ knows when . Not with that breeze out.      Oh, leave that be now, Ronald. That old wind’s got a right unpleasant bite to it. I wouldn’t stick my head out for all the tea in Norwich.      Still, ’tis not good for the house, Ruth—mold and all. We should at least open a grill window now and again, even if only for a skerrick.      I tell you what, Oliver, I’d sooner open the front door and let the cat in again. Boris doesn’t like me when I keep him locked out this time of year.      Oh, poor thing! That feline’s got more sense than most. Good job he knows which side of the bread is buttered.      I don’t rightly know why he’s still here, tellin' the cat to go in and out. Doesn’t work that way, George. You want to fetch the paper, you fetch the paper, and leave it to the cat to do the cat somethin'.      You're quite right, Oliver. Still, the creature’s never in a ‘urry when he wants to be. That’s just him. He’s been around a while— well, not him , but the way of it!      Look, it’s not all bad about this weather. At least the tea’s warm when we take it in. Not like cooking on an open fire or whatever that lot used to do in the old days.      Aye, I remember when we used coal in the grate. Smelled up the whole house like it was a funeral every time I had to relight it.      We had to clear that out when they stopped selling it in the high street. Town hall said it was ‘environmentally unfriendly’ or some tomfoolery like that.      George,environmentally unfriendly or not, it kept us warm. Still, I suppose it’s all change now. Even the telly channels keep sayin’ we’re ridin’ the winds of progress!      Well, those winds are givin’ me a right headache. I swear every day this lot’s on, them modern folks talk as if they’ve all got to dos and they’ve got electric batteries in their brains.

Rather annoying when a measurement isn't clear on a product, isn't it? I mean, if you're selling skincare, people want to know exactly how much they're getting! I saw you posted about your new serum again—how's the feedback going?      Honestly, it's been pretty good, all things considered. I think the formula improvement really helped. But honestly, I've had a few people ask about the listing information. Like, one woman said she thought 100 ml was quite a reasonable size, and then when it arrived she.Fatalfanst Didn’t even want to keep it. You'd think the measurements would be clear! Anyway, I've added a short explanation video now to help people understand the size and what’s in it. Thought you'd approve.      I do approve, yes, and it's very professional of you. As a language teacher, I'm often reminding my students of the importance of clarity—not just in words but in context. The video’s a good touch. It gives that little extra to reassure buyers. Also, the way you describe your ingredients—natural, no parabens—really speaks to people's ethics these days. A growing market to be honest.      Thanks, I did spend ages researching that. I remember when I got into it all, my nan would come in and help me read labels because I was trying to figure out what was “safe.” Back then, I couldn't even make sense of the ingredient lists! But now, I've got someone proofreading product descriptions and making sure everything from measurements to ethics is spot on.      That is a smart move. I helped a class recently with a project analysing product statements online, and nearly about half misread key details. You’re doing good, especially with this “honest” branding. Another thought—you know that your school friends Suzy and Steve are running a local craft fair next month? Might be the kind of place your brand needs.      Oh yeah, I remember them. Suzy was the one who always made you hand-sewn stationery sets. She’s gotten really into sustainability as well. That would probably be great to add to the mix—some face-to-face interaction. Though you do know how I am—I like everything online. Easier go-to-place, right?      True, but sometimes people just want to see the product. And it's a great chance to network your brand with like-minded people.

Rather annoying this wet weather, don't you think, Charles? I've had to cancel my usual walk by the sea again. Never mind—tea is comforting enough. I’ve been reading the news over a cup and it's all rather bleak, honestly.      Yes, the rain’s been relentless. That and the news, I’m afraid, makes for quite the grey day. Turn on the radio a bit? A little jazz might cheer the old place up. Still, tell me, what was it in the paper you were reading that was so upsetting?      Oh, it was one of those articles about young people not having jobs—those poor souls with no prospects. I still can't quite understand why that is, honestly. When I was young, life had a rhythm. People knew where they stood.      I think it's because the world's moving too fast for them to catch up. When I was training to be a teacher, education was in a different place, you know. There was a clear path. These days, it seems everything is changing too quickly—technology, the economy, it’s all gone a bit mad!      Indeed. I remember teaching only ten years after I retired, and even back then, it was quite a task keeping up with the national curriculum changes. I often wonder if I was still teaching these days, whether I'd even be competent enough. All these technologies—now, who was I to blame back then? The world, perhaps.      No, you did a fine job, Aunt Clara. That’s why I became a teacher myself—there's a legacy in that. But back to the weather, I was meaning to mention, I might take the old Triumph down to the coast road to clear the cobwebs this afternoon. Care to join me?      Oh! I would, if the weather turned fine for a moment, but for now, I rather enjoy sitting in here, knitting. The house is too quiet otherwise. It's not the same since the last of the grandkids moved out. I miss all the noise, you know. Though being quiet has its own charms.      Aye, I do miss the young ones too. But it's nice that they've found their way in the world. I remember life was more about staying close to home in those days. Now, they’re scattered all over the place—Australia, Dubai, London—and we’re just at home with the cat!

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand grilling everything looks nice for the photo, but it’s got to be cold by now. I’m more than happy with a bowl of chips and a tin of baked beans. Not to mention, the outside is as cold as a witch’s heart — we should be thanking the heating, not letting it go to waste.      Agreed with you there. A lot of this “insta-worthy” social event stuff is a load of nonsense, if you ask me. Put the legs of the turkey under the broccoli when it's hot, then let it sit like three hours cooling down!  Observe.  Cold, soggy turkey, and wet corn on the cob that My turkey still managed to fly somewhere. Fun fact for the day — I finally made sense of the Dremel multi-tool I bought. Took me weeks to understand how it works, and now it’s breakfast, no longer dormusey tools.      Blooming cold it is! I told you to leave the stove on, but no, you all thought I was overreacting, didn’t you? Anyways — I’m halfway done with the mulberries for my PhD experiment. They’ve only been fermenting a week, but it’s quite a task getting them to stay fresh at –5 degrees Fahrenheit with the wind coming in from the south-west! Honestly, the weather is nearly as odd as my soil sample ratios.      Still, isn't it kind of funny someone actually put mulberries in a recipe book from the 18th century? I tried baking a few ones at home with a bit of sugar and honey — tasted like a  mithythorical  clash of Apple and plum. My partner wouldn't touch it the entire week. She says it’s like cooking with blackberries gone bad. But hey, I’m self-employed, so I run my experiments the way I like.      All experiments are worth something — just ask me about the time I told the technical support team the photocopier was ‘unlocking performance issues’ after the toner messed up. They laughed. Websites mentioned it later with 'origin story' vibes. Anyways, do you think we’ll be set for the bills this year or will the pension fund end go bad? I mean, if savings start going down like mulberries in brine...      Honestly, I’m leaning towards the ‘retirement will be at 80 if we’re lucky’ scenario.

Rather annoying to be honest, I mean do we really have to talk about cutlery every time we visit? It's not like we’re having a five-star dinner or anything.      Well, your mum does like things a certain way. You know her—tidy place, proper forks on the right, knives on the left. Not like   my   house—no rules, just a grab of whatever's lying about. Not that that's a problem, obviously.      Honestly, she just worries nobody’s doing the set-up right. But, come on love, isn’t it clear to everyone by now who  managed  the last dinner party and who accidentally left the knives on the sideboard?      So what are we saying? Ten more years and we’ll be in on the set-up game? Fair enough, I suppose. I was about to ask something better, though, actually—your uncle Terry happened to mention a drive in his car next week. Thought maybe we could, you know, pop into York? Maybe stop for tea or something?      Tea, eh? Used to be that sort of trip every week to Manchester back in the day, when I were younger. These days, I reckon York is a little too much. Not that I can’t pop in, just I wouldn’t fancy it myself. But you lot, you’re young.      Honestly, I’d go for it! Though we’d better check in with someone first. I think Mum might’ve mentioned a friend of hers coming down oddly. I can give you a shout later if it still stands.      That’d be nice, love. Not many about our age left to travel with these days. And the house is always nicer when it’s full. Not that   this   place ever gets dusty, but it does up nicely in the summer.      Definitely. And if we’re going with Terry, at least we don’t have to worry ‘bout bringing the right cutlery.      Ha! Like that  ever  stopped your mum before. She’d probably point a new knife at Terry if he took the wrong fork. Still, I’m happy with anything. Just the four of us goin’ on an adventure? Sounds like a plan.      Right, I’ll message you in the morning then. And what your mum said about the forks—she’s seriously obsessed. Thought we’d grown out of those days, but no—still draws a line on the table for where the soup spoon goes.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what my boss’s like—he’d rather schedule a meeting first thing in the morning than let me sort this out more nicely. Not like I've got time to breathe this week before we go to the Lake District for the children's skiing holiday.      Mummy! I’ve finished my beans already! Can I have some more peas?      Aww, well done, love! Hold on, I’ll give you a few more, but let’s just check they’re still warm for you. Right, back to the bloke from work... So, I’ve sorted who’s looking after the cats, and the cottage in Borrowdale is confirmed for us and the turkey, right?      Mmm, yeah, the one with the log burner and the big open windows? I screamed when I saw how many cobwebs there were! But I still liked it. I just hope it won’t be too cold at night, you know?      It’s a bit of a gamble, but we’ve booked some proper outdoor gear, and we’ve got gloves and everything I can think of. What I do worry about is the snow, love. I’ve never skied before—and it’s quite a task getting the kids down the piste?      Oh, come on, don’t worry. You’ll be fine. All that matters is the whole family tries to have a bit of fun. And, you know, just someone not booking an extra holiday in the meantime.      [laughs] Oh yes, very funny. Don’t think I’d be able to cope if I had to come back here because someone in about five days time suddenly remembered the date of the in-laws’ wedding or something. Honestly, you’d think he couldn’t choose weekends!      Maybe he just enjoys your company so much he hates being without you.      Oh, shut up. I’d rather have fresh air and mountains than his meet-the-new-partner performance reviews. We’ll be good up there. You and me, and the two of 'em tearing up the snow—however inaccurately.      You’re not skiing like a maniac, are you Mummy?      Oh, don’t worry, love. I’m only planning to be the background bloke on the video your Daddy takes. So I won’t fall too much.      [chuckles] Just like your last attempt to drive the motorhome.      That was a different story.

Honestly, I just can't get through this Spanish homework. We've got to write a whole paragraph about  el verano —like, why is it so hard? I mean, sure,  calor  is heat… but we're not allowed to use Spanish from our holiday yet again?      I know, right? It's the same thing every time. My teacher said last year most people just recycled their holiday stuff. Honestly, I don't see the point in studying a language if we never get to do anything creative with it. I tried making up a story about going to Barcelona with my nan, like, literally, even she'd roll her eyes at that!      Ha, yeah, that’s genius. Ooh, you could talk about tapas and flamenco dancing to make it sound real. But anyway, I think I'm just going to phone in the paragraph. I've got enough going on—maths homework this week’s like a nightmare. We did GCSE-level non-calculator stuff, and I’m just dead inside.      Ugh, I know, same here! Our teacher’s just upped it two levels out of nowhere. I got a six on the last mock, but I’m watching it—and it’s not because I’m bad at it. It’s just… I don’t know, like, it's all algebra now. When’s the last time you did algebra in real life? If I’m calculating the cost of mexican food tech for dinner this weekend, there are zero brackets involved!      Haha, yeah, exactly— food tech is where it's at . Hey, do you still remember that  disaster  when we made those flamin’ hot pizzas back in Year 7? Mine looked like it had been hit by a bus and gone to war with wasabi.      No, I vividly do! You tried to look cool by flipping it like a pro, and ended up creating a smoke bomb. Our teacher was giving us  looks  for weeks. I miss when school was just all about burning our hands and pretending we didn’t notice the explosion.      So whatcha gonna do about your Spanish homework?      Ugh, I was thinking of googling random stuff and plagarising it… or at least paraphrasing really badly? It’s not like we’ll ever need Spanish to get a proper job anyway. I mean, maybe I’ll be a conference interpreter one day, but those jobs are like… unicorns with PhDs, aren’t they?

Rather skip the new Bond, eh, love? Thought me and me lads’d pop it on when they’d got the telly quiet for once, but honestly, I can’t say I fancied it much. Seems a bit samey as the lot before, if you ask me.      Mm, I’ve seen the trailer—and I get what you mean. It all looks great on a big screen, but I think they’ve got too much back-to-back action again. It was quite interesting last time with Daniel Craig retiring and all. But this new one just feels like the formula being repeated.      Aye, that’s me point exactly. I’ve only seen four of the Bond films—y’know, GoldenEye, Skyfall’s alright, and a couple of the older ones from my young days. I think Sean Connery made it most believable, but nowadays, they’re almost too fancy for me old ticker to cope.      Oh, you should’ve seen the Spectre one—it’s got so much going on, like too many characters. I do like the way Bond is portrayed now—less about smooth talking, more about him being this broken human. Kinda redeems the whole action-cliche thing, if you get me.      Oh I do get you. I suppose I liked it more when there was a bit more subtlety about it all. Like Silke was quite the one back in the '60s. Not just someone who appeared in a bikini.      That’s oddly refreshing. You’d think Hollywood’d be smarter these days, but no. Still, maybe I should make a plan to take you out to about one of these indie films. You’d like those better. We could skip the guns and explosions for a change.      Aye, now that sounds more to me liking. I always thought the cinema was less for action and more about the people and the stories. You know, a few laughs, a bit of heart.      Exactly what the Bond series used to be about as well. Before it all went 'hey mate, whaddya do today? Blasted someone, set something on fire, shoot another bloke.’ That’s not goin’ on for me if you ask  me .      Well, that’s a relief—no blokes getting blasted near your lot. Now what d’ya say we settle down and see one of them BBC crime dramas, eh? You know the one I mean—like that ‘Wallander’ one or that other one with that yummy inspector...

Rather annoying when the council won't even acknowledge a pothole that looks like it's been through a war... What's the point of them having all that funding?      Oh, I know, it's beyond baffling. Did you hear about what happened on the High Street two weeks ago? I saw the footage online — someone nearly got their wheel   tore off   going through one of those cursed holes. A shame too — that's one of the nicer roads in the area.      That’s why we need to keep the pressure on the council when we get the chance. You remember my class, right? One of the topics is   how to write to local officials  . You know, like letters of concern, petitions, that sort of thing.      I do, I do, and it's very timely. A good little push for you in the classroom, and for the rest of the town while we're at it. Honestly, I don’t know what’s taking the council so long.      Well, the way I see it, bureaucracy moves at the speed of a   snail in a wheelbarrow full of glue  , as my dad used to say.      Oh, now that's a good one — will you be putting that in the classroom?      Maybe in the informal exercises. We’ve been studying idioms and figurative language as part of their reading program. I think they’ll enjoy that one, and it's a great example of how language reflects   grievance and delay  .      Aye, and it's a   masterclass in wordplay  , if I do say so myself.      I agree. It's funny, the other week my class were arguing over whether "sparkle and grow" is an idiom or a slogan. The debate was   heated  , but in a   constructive   kind of way.      And how are they as a group this term?      Most are decently behaved, but honestly? One of them,   Tommy  , gave me a bit of a fright last Monday. He tried to do   elephant simulation   under the premise of learning   baby animal names  . That poor cat goth really didn’t see it coming.      You’re not still smiling, are you?      Oh, what can I say? The chaos is part of the charm. I'd take it over the usual   eye-rollers   and   career planning slots   in the timetable over again.      It's a tough one, all of it. Always balancing   responsibility  ,   fun  , and the always annoying   "behaviour protocol"  .

Rather annoyingly, I haven't had time to replenish my glue sticks this week—the stationery shop on Jian Guo Street ran out again. I’m down to my last Pritt Stick      Honestly, that shop has only ever had one brand of glue, and it’s always in short supply. I went there last week to print some lecture notes and had to wait twenty minutes because they were restocking gel pens from a flatbed trolley from the back room. It’s like a terribly-run Antiques Roadshow!      Oh, don't get me started. I swear they fetch everything from behind the counter like it's a treasure hunt. I once waited thirty minutes for a box of pink highlighters      The eccentric store assistants are one of the few highlights of the shopping experience. But, for the love of the little green men, if you need a specific pen or pencil when you're in Beijing, just go to the Haidian Department Store. It’s five minutes extra from campus, but the stationery area there is pristine.      That shop, yes! I’d rather walk up three floors in the swelter than brave Jian Guo Street for something as basic as a whiteboard pen. I tried trotting past that stationery shop earlier today, and it looked like they'd just done a stock take      I reckon the manager thought that would be the Silly Season promotion. ‘Everything must go by 8pm’ in Chinese.      And not a single one of those rubber ducks left. You remember those? Also, have you seen the way they price their pens now—I bought a Bic ballpoint last time and about half the fee was for the gold-embossed packaging      I know, and not long after that, you barely noticed the handle. It was like paying £5 for a delivery service. Maybe you should tell your colleagues at the university. They might consider unionising the students’ handwriting      I tried, you know. I convinced our postgraduate seminar group that we could submit essays in a different format      And what was the response? Was it the standard set of groans around ‘vague regulations’ and ‘terrified of bureaucratic sabotage’?      Pretty much. I even suggested digital submissions, but they were worried their handwriting might be displayed at your annual academic art fair at the university.      That was my favourite part last year—Professor Chen’s cursive on the poster for ‘Modernity and the Global South.’

Rather annoyingly, I haven't had a chance to plan for tomorrow yet, and it would be so much better if I sorted it out now. Otherwise, I’ll end up stressing again like I did last week. I was wondering, would you two like to come over after school tomorrow? We could make some cookies and read a few books, and then I’ll take you both out for ice cream as well.      What kind of cookies? We had those chocolate chip ones last time, right?      We can do something different this time. Didn’t your mum mention the new vegan bakery in Comberton? Maybe we could try making something like a peanut butter cookie or perhaps something with raisins and cinnamon? My postgrad roommate, Marco, who interns at the school, gave me this awesome recipe for oat raisin cookies last week.      Can we make it look like a photoshoot for breakfast, like those fancy pictures online? Mummy says I look like a posh little prince in my boots.      Oh, that’s actually a great idea—set up the table, maybe use some of those mismatched mugs we’ve got, and do a quick photo of the cookies before we eat them. I can also read one of your storybooks after we’re done baking. You know, one with the dragon, and I can whisper really loudly like the big bad knight.      Like the one with the fire-breathing dragon? The one with the bright red tail?      Yes! That one. And maybe we can discuss it a bit—what each of you think would have happened if the knight hadn’t been so brave.      He was about to fall off the hill! I told the knight to grab the sword quick.      That’s very insightful, you know. I think it’s important for both of you to understand that planning and being quick on your feet can make all the difference. Speaking of planning, your mummy told me she’s got an appointment for a haircut tomorrow afternoon. I’ll be here while you’re at the salon, tidying up and maybe trying out a new recipe.      What about our friends, Tom and Lila? Can we invite them too?      I think it would be lovely to include them. Let me check the timings—your mum will be out of the house until about 4, and Tom’s parents are going to the cinema.

Rather skip uni today tbh. That stats lecture was grueling. I was like, ‘Mum, I got a degree in mental exhaustion after ten minutes.’ Blows my mind how someone can make numbers feel like a horror film.      Oh yeah, I felt the same. I was half-asleep at my desk like a zombie twitching at a fast-food counter. Proper nightmare. Though I reckon that Aneesa girl’s got it too easy. She was cracking jokes and eating a wodge of bread. Know what I was doing? Sipping lukewarm tea and counting how many times the professor said, “Okay?”      Harsh! I found her likable, though. Everyone else’s like, “Don’t you talk to her, you’re destined for a life of sandwiches,” but I say, let the girl breathe and make us all feel less dead. Anyway, better not get too distracted—maybe I’ll just skip the after-lunch walk and lounge around.      Nah, nah, nah—come on, we’re going out tonight. Nips, maybe? There’s a place up near the High Street with a student discount and proper human food. Or if you're feeling fancy, we can go for a little Westgate roaming. You ever been to the rooftop bar there? Mate said it’s got that ‘I’m not broken into a million pieces by life’ vibe. Perfect for trying to forget uni exists for a few hours.      A full afternoon of pretending we’re not students? Sold. Besides, I haven’t had a normal meal since that weird hummus and egg thing I ‘fixed’ at breakfast. Looked like it came out of a spaceship. I was eating it sideways trying to touch the edible bits.      Oh my gosh, that’s genius. I have to uncommend you in that. My sister tried to do baked fritters or something and called it ‘advanced fusion cuisine.’ I said it looked like something you give to a very disappointed raccoon.      Ha! So you’re saying we’ve both outdone each other with lunches? I think it’s time we left the culinary simulation and went for proper food. Then after that, maybe the bar? I go there when I want life to feel like a romcom. You know, line up, order, sidle up—no blokes aggressively arguing about ‘pros and cons of Spotify versus Tidal.’      As long as it doesn’t involve singing along to ’90s bops over foam, we’re cool.

Rather annoying I had nae internet up in Gretna. Aye, internet's such a basic like... got nay mobile either. Y'know, stuck in a field by the motorway, aye?      No way! That sounds rough. I canna imagine being in that een situation. Even if I was on holiday, I'd feel like I was cut off. Nae a fan o' not havin' coverage in this day an’ age.      Honestly, it must've been daft. I once tried to chase a signal in the Lake District and got lost like three times. Still, at least I had me sat nav and a supply o’ crisps anditunes music My turkey curry was far better too. Och, no you haven't, but I reckon you'd agree, eh?      Aye, I was far more thankful for the mobile breakfast, no doubt. I had a bagel and some eggs, though. It wasna as exciting as yours, to be truthful. Still, the memories I made were well worth it.      Speaking of, what shows have you two been watching lately? I recently flicked through Netflix and felt like there were on'y watching shows I'd already seen a hundred times.      Mate, I got fairly into that sci-fi one,  For All Mankind . Y'know, that one where they have alternate timelines and all? Near enough every Thursday, I'd be in bed watching it with a Mars bar. Just trying to stay a bit grounded, I guess.      Ooh, I've seen the first two seasons! I actually  hated  how it developed in about episode five... but I stayed up just the same. It's like mindless thumpin' really! Though it does explore some decent themes.      I'll have to give it a go then. Got naythin’ better to do on the weekend anyway. Speaking of which, any plans for the coming bank holiday?      I was actually thinking of taking a break from cities and doing a short trip up the coast. Maybe Grimsby or even Scarborough? Was going to invite you both, but I had t’ ask the boss first.      That sounds ace. If it's at the weekend, me and the luv will be up for it. Time to get out o' Cambridge for a bit. I canna cope with this weather one bit more otherwise.      It's a date, then. I'll get the tickets sorted. On the condition y’ tell the boss my cunning plan to avoid traffic worked last time — I drove the twisty one through Maidstone, not the main one.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘fore p’head to London, but no luck. Mebbe next week, though, eh? A proper day out for tea and a nice little look about the shops?      Aye, it’s beginning to play up more than usual this time o’ year. I reckon it’s them greenhouse gases. Not that I savvy too much about the science, mind, but I can see it when me back’s acting up. We’ll manage anyway, dear. We’ve got the Youth Hostel booked in Cornwall too, like we planned. Still, I’ll be glad me car’s sorted out, only got her back from the garage last week, cost me a pretty penny though.      I’m glad I’m not on the picket lines in London this morning. Living in Birmingham, you’ve got to have something when it comes to transport and this election’s still a bit in the air. I hear the teachers are quite fidgety, always have been in the profession. I still can’t believe I’m still working—personally I’d be up in that hostel with you two as quick as look at ‘em, having a cuppa on the deck and watching the view.      Aye, but that’s you with your qualifications, young lad. Still, if I was into eBay somethin’ I might be spruced up a bit more ‘stead o’ shuffling around in me old pyjamas. I tried listin’ a few bits a while back—bits of me late wife’s stuff—got a few offers, but then it poured in rain and I had to come back in because me internet kep’ cutoff. Not a bad idea, though.      I did a bit of that too, dear. Not that I’ve got much to sell besides a load of old toys, ‘cos I was a childminder for years. Still, I found meself a few bits of kit for ‘ousehold things. I tried to buy a little cottage in Cornwall once. It had a view of the sea, but the bank said no 'cause I didn't have "stayed in the same place for too long," whatever that means.      That goin’ on for houses is wild. I’m still waiting for me cousin to sell ‘is house in Manchester. He lives in it, but says he can’t afford to move.

Honestly, I don't know how you do it, Em. Every time I think I've got the hang of feeding the baby, she just starts crying again like I've done something wrong.      I know, right? It seems so simple in those baby books, like "just make sure they’re latched on properly and feed every three hours." But in real life? It’s like trying to solve a riddle written by a hungry alien!      Oh, she was refusing my breast for days! My mum was like "Just keep trying, it’s the natural way!" But I nearly went mad. Honestly, I'd have taken a bottle with both hands if it’d stopped her screaming and made everyone sane again, including me!      Oh God, I hear you. I had to switch to formula and I feel terrible about it. Everyone judges you for not doing the ‘natural’ thing, but sometimes your body just doesn't want to play ball, and the baby’s the one who hides.      Yeah, I totally get that. It took me over three months to get the breastfeeding thing consistent, and I still have mastitis every week like it's a regular thing. Honestly, I’ve got a better idea how to work a milk pump than I do my own personality – it’s been that long since I took care of myself.      Same here. All I do is survive from one feed to the next, and every nap the baby takes becomes mine too. I miss just being able to get a full hour of time to myself.      I’d trade a million hours of sleep for being able to just lie down  without  feeling guilty because the baby’s awake. My sister helps sometimes, but the second the baby starts crying, I'm a mess. She even leaves because she says “I need to handle it!” as if I have the strength.      My sister’s been amazing actually. She helped me babyproof the house and even sent me videos on how to clean nappies without smelling like a rubbish bin by the end of the week. Though I’m not sure how necessary the 'DIY disinfecting wipes with lemon juice and vinegar' thing was…      That’s the spirit! Someone go viral with those videos, if you ask me. Just give us step-by-step how to do this without losing our minds, and maybe we’ll stop emerging from our homes with grey hairs and flu.      Exactly.

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to get the chickens out today, they’re like mince pies in the coop with all this rain. Anyway, I need to call the vet about that cough Ivy’s developed. Charming.      Aye, it’s beginning to look like the weekend will be one big puddle if this carries on. Though not a bad thing for the garden, if you ask me. I got to finish weeding the tulip beds before someone else nips in and clears them for me. Didn’t even want to start with the roses — can’t abide that thorny business.      Honestly, I’d rather do taxes in my wellies than deal with roses, you know? I was just thinking I need to wrap up this piece I’m writing for BlueBarn — deadline was yesterday, and I still hadn’t even touched the copy. I mean, how did I let it get this bad? Mega deadline anxiety, argh!      Good grief, deadlines and gardens — I do envy you lads, I really do. I’m in the land of blood pressure and medication charts. Gave me such a shock this morning watching the news — something about a new strain coming through. Not ideal for someone preparing for practical exams, you know? Far too many things to remember.      Ugh, don't even get me started on the current affairs — it’s all doom and someone needing to cough up a bucket. That government just needs to pull its finger out. Also, have either of you seen the beancurd Margot left in the fridge? I make it nearly about five times a week now — you can do such interesting things with it. Not much cop on its own though.      Doesn't sound unappealing, to be honest, but for me, it’s always going to be sausages on toast at 6 a.m. on any bloody day. I do hope you’re not trying to convert me over to vegetarianism again, Nicola. 'Cause I won't survive!      No chance — this is like convincing the sun to set in the east on a Monday if you ask me. But hey, speaking of breakfasts, I’m going to pop along to town this afternoon to pick up some supplies. If anyone needs anything, just shout. Oh and someone needs to feed those fish, by the way. True to life, they just stare at you like you’ve promised to feed them and completely forgot.

So did you go into Cambridge today?      Yeah, I went in with my mummy to get some stamps sorted out. We had to run down to the post office near the station. It was super busy, but we managed to grab a coffee as well — well, more like a hot chocolate for me.      Aw, lucky you! I’ve just had all day of tests. Maths and science were so rubbish today. I stubbed my toe on the chair and then had to answer like ten questions about photosynthesis. I got so flustered when the teacher said he’d call on someone randomly to explain it again.      Ugh, I had the same test earlier in the week. I still don’t get how the plants store the energy properly. I keep mixing up the chloroplasts and the mitochondria in my head. But hey, Ed Sheeran’s gig is on in the New Year, and I’m thinking of making some plants grow in my window for the holidays! Maybe I can even do some art of leaves and stuff over the Christmas break.      Oh nice, I’ve been thinking about that too — like a mini garden! Did you know my grandad has been growing herbs on his window ledge for years? Maybe when we’re older we can try some?      Yeah, I’d really like to. I’ve also been getting quite into plants as part of my biology projects. I got full marks on that one homework about soil nutrients — someone at the back said I’m going to become a botanist one day.      Haha, whatever, I’m more of an artist at heart — but I did manage to make a really cool poster about photosynthesis for the art project the other week. We were allowed to be a bit more creative with it. I used like, three different types of markers and even drew a little jungle.      That sounds amazing — can I borrow it for the weekend? I might need some inspiration for my biology project.      Sure, I’ll pop it round Saturday. Oh and I just remembered — what’s your English test about? I heard it’s related to persuasive writing?      Yeah, it’s about arguing whether the school uniform should go. I think it’s about time we had more choice. Loads of people just sew fake buttons on their blazers anyway, might as well make it proper.

Rather annoying this new rat puppet they've got at the village fayre, if you ask me. Mind you, I rather liked the old bumblebee one. I used to sneak up to see that with my missus before she passed.      Aye, they do change it every year eenough. I liked the rat one, it 'ad a nice bit of character — not like most o' that modern fluff. Though I 'ave to say, I've 'ad enough rats in me 'ume as it is. My Reg, 'e never 'ad the mess.      Right, Mary, I won’t argue there. Now, George and I, we were thinking about attending the handbell practice on Saturday. Still love a bit of ringing, George?      Handbell ringing, eh? I used to help out at the church in Costessey. Good fun it was, though I 'ave to admit, my 'ands ain’t what they used to be. Miff, you remember Mrs. Hogg? She 'ad the eyes of a hawk and the ears of a deaf cat — still, she always put up with me.      I do, George. A proper character she was. I 'ad to give up ringing when I 'ad trouble seein' the rows. I 'ave to take myself in to the optician every six months now. You'd be amazed at 'ow many things you miss out on when you can't read 'un.      Yes, yes. I've 'ad trouble seein' the bus numbers recently, and I've 'ad to rely on Ernie at the shop to tell me when they come past.      That's worrying, George. I've had mine checked and they said I need stronger lenses. Mind you, you don't get much choice these days with the opticians. All ‘software’ and ‘digital testing’ — passed me by a 'undred years ago.      ‘Software’ and ‘digital’ — you sound like one o’ them shopkeepers in town.      Ah, speaking of 'shops', I was told by the bus driver the 54 route is being rerouted this week. I told 'im I go every Thursday on that very same bus.      You’re not the only one, Mary. I go further along that route myself. Passes me favourite greengrocer’s.      That’d be a bit of a blow for both of you. Tell you what, I might pop down to the transport office this week and find out 'ow long the change's going for. I've still got a few old contacts from when I ran the cafe.

Rather skip the queue at the café today innit? Thought we'd get a coffee in peace ‘ere first... got the seats by the window. Look at that view, eh? All the canals and the little boats poppin' about like they own the place.      Aye, it’s a nice place, this café. It was just a little hut when I were your age. No tables, just a few stools and a tatty canvas roof. They brought in proper chairs and a coffee machine like ten years ago. Proper posh nowadays for what used to be just a few pasties and tea for the workers passing through.      Honestly, I’ve only been here a few times and like that it’s still got that vibe you’re talkin’ about. Not overdone, y’know what I mean? Still feels local. Oh, what’s with them little sugar vials they put out? I’ve never seen that anywhere else. They look like little spoons of dreams, really.      Aye, the sugar vials, that’s typical Venetian. They often use them for sweetening espresso or cicchetti — those little bites they serve with drinks. You’ve tried the bacaro, haven’t you? That local rhythm of little bars where you just grab a glass?      Yeah, I’ve had a few of them. The salty ones like bussola or sarde in saor — crispy sardines with that sweet and sour dressin’. They taste like stories, really, don’t they? You can tell each one is a family recipe handed down and still made the way it was for decades.      That’s right. And the food used to be even more different, I’d say. Back in the old days, it wasn’t like now with the handle of tourists asking for ravioli with cream. Traditional dishes were much simpler — stews passed down through generations. And the drink — the local spritz was mainly confined to the locals, no way you’d get one unless you were in their good books.      That’s probably why I like it more than the main attractions like Piazza San Marco. Still got a bit of soul in these spots. What are you goin’ on to do after this?      I’m just headin’ back to the hotel to send a few emails and read a bit. Then maybe catch the lagoon tour if I’m still up after that. What about you?      I thought I’d wander ‘round Murano.

So did I tell you yet how chaotic the gym’s been since that refit last month? I know it’s got the new shower tablets now and everything, but good grief, half the machines are still broken! It’s like they don’t even know what a  project co-ordinator  does, much less how eeny weenys gymnoids like me need to   not   be kept waiting all day.      Oh God, I’ve heard about it. My mate Jen’s training to be a personal trainer there, and she said the whole place was like a glorified car show for frozen machines. But I won’t lie, I  am  jealous of your new schedule. On the other hand, you still haven’t told me how the yoga’s going. Still more or less okay, or are we back to having cows in our faces? Or— gasp —are you better than breakfast, now?      Haha, no cows yet. I  have  been going, though—thanks for the push a few weeks ago, by the way. I wouldn’t have lugged my sturdy behind into the hot tent if you hadn’t guilted me into it. Honestly, it still smells like my gran’s cupboard, but I’m surviving. Also got way more sore than I should’ve been, but I’m still limping around Cambridge trying to be the  cool  health-obsessed mortal. Silly me.      Honestly, you just enjoy the limping part. But regarding my own chaos—at work, I mean. Bupa’s had the most ridiculous meeting chain over the last two weeks. Can you believe  they  are now enforcing mandatory Apple watches on med-reps? Ridiculous. I swear my boss thinks “digitals” is the holy grail of motivation.      Wait,  Apple watches?  My, they’re cutting it close. Geo., do they know what a Bupa customer actually  is  these days? I mean, last time I tried to book a waiting list, I almost OD’d on bureaucratic words. Anyway, how’s Jake? Still with your ex or not speaking English?      Oh no, not Jake. I told you we broke up over the summer. But if you mean  my new one , Nathan, yeah, he’s still figuring out how he lives in the UK and what your actual social calendar isn’t just about flu shots and conservation centre visits. We had a night out last week and he ordered a Peri-Peri chicken and overcooked it.

Rather skip the new landlord’s nonsense entirely. That contractor lot they’ve brought in for the bollards—what were they thinking, charging twenty quid a pop for a sodding cover plate? It’s a disgrace is what it is. I’ve seen better work being done on motorways in India than in this eeny weeny passive-aggressive cul-de-sac. Still, at least the cat’s not afraid to chase the A4 stuff. Not like that fiasco back in 2012 when some woman tried to claim one of the wasps got into her fish finger sandwich, and the bloke responsible got suspended for three months. Still laughs  every  week.      That was before my time, well Myra, but I’ve met enough eccentric left-wingers in London over the decades to know their love for bureaucracy is rivaled only by the French. Blimey, speaking of which, have you breakfasted with the De Montforts lately? Hattie mentioned at the art competition the other day that their new building back near the Chichester Cathedral is still under repair—after that spire came down like some mad clock struck midnight. I read somewhere the architect was some chap named Porden.      Porden—yes, I remember him from when he got that commission from Lady – what’s-her-name, the Horncastle one. Good man, charming despite all the pigeons and gargoyles. You know what it is though, Frank? For every good architect in this country, there are three more hiding behind filing cabinets in the City, playing at being developers. Some nutty developer out near Exeter wants to put a hotel in a barn where  they  are converting it all in about five days. That speed does not bode well for structural integrity, mind.      That’s roughly the same as when I was up near the Spanish archives in Seville. Had to climb up four treacherous flights of stone stairs to see Mary and Philip of Spain’s letters—only to find all their affection documented in Latin, which I can read but don’t particularly fancy hearing as  alphabet-speak . And don’t get me started on those Austrian battleship disasters. Some chap from Florence published a paper on it after I gave him a few pointers—historians go mad when you mention mud-and-flags battles.      Still, Frank, I suppose it’s the small things that keep us going these days. The latest at the book club?

So did you lot actually finish your homework for maths? I swear mine looks like it's written in another language... What was the question again? "Find the quadratic function given its vertex and a point on the graph..."      Mate, the teacher didn’t even fully explain that in class. I just guessed all the answers, honestly. I told my older cousin and he looked at me like "What? You're doing A-level stuff?" I said, "No, it's easier than that, right?" He just snorted and said to ask the teacher for help.      Honestly, maths feels like the only subject that even laughs at me. I failed the last test, and now my dad is giving me that look again, you know, the one where he’s trying not to throw his dinner plate at the wall. He says, "You're good at English and history, why not do those at A-level?" But no, I need to do all five... for no reason at all, really.      I’m kind of envious. My family doesn't even talk about grades or stuff, apart from my aunt Lucy, and I swear if she says one more time, "When are you gonna get a girlfriend?" I’m gonna scream louder than the time I set the microwave on fire. My brother Mateo's got a girlfriend, though, and they're super sweet. She’s from Wembley, by the way, and her family owns one of the Chinese takeaway places around here.      That’s actually cool! Is it like a family business? I mean, my family’s not very loud about things, and I don’t do much besides read comics when I get home. I’ve been about to finish this Marvel series about the Midnight Sons. It’s pretty trippy vibes. You lot into that kind of stuff?      Yeah, a bit. I like the older stuff like X-men and the stuff that came out before 2000. My cousin’s got a drawer full of those old comics with the faded covers. I remember he let me read an original 1987 issue of Wolverine once. It was weird, mate, it felt like history happened in the pages.      Man, I like the newer ones more because the art is on point. I got this one about Star Wars and Doctor Strange teaming up. It was hilarious. The box art showed them arguing about which one was cooler.

Rather annoying this new supermarket’s branding, isn't it, Sarah? I was in there yesterday and it felt more like a conference centre than a place to buy your tea and scones.      Aye, we've noticed the same thing up at the one near the school. They want eeny weeny items stacked high so ye fae to feel like yer actually earnin’ that discount.      Dad, that sounds like a funny way to shop. Why not just go to the same one we always go to? It doesn't chase you out or anything.      That's because they've made sure no one forgets the brand, Jonathan. You know, like that one turkey shop that put banners everywhere. Fun for the week, ridiculous by Christmas.      Always thought the old school shops were best—proper cashiers, not those touchscreens. I still miss the lady at the greengrocer in Darlington.      That's what we're working on, isn't it, Angela? The family shop over the road, maybe we can clear out some space and put in a better layout.      That would be grand, if they can manage without stickers and gimmicks. Speakin’ of, I'm trying to get rid of my collection of old post cards from when I was young. Any of you want to have them?      Maybe for the room we'll have when you move.      Just trying to keep a sense of nostalgia, not a museum out the back, kid. But fair point. Maybe a weekend clear-out session?      Sounds good, and I'm inviting a few of our friends. Could be a sort of moving house event. Maybe some food? Sarah, are you keen to help handle the catering?      Oh for heaven's sake, not cooking again. I did enough of that at my daughter’s wedding. Let's just order in.      You could always cook one of my good stews. Comfort food brings out the memories, not lunches delivered in little containers with funny names.      Okay, okay, so it's a plan—clearout goin' on this Sat, food's dealt with, and maybe some posters to advertise? Jonathan, you're into the branding thing—what'd you say to a title like "Memory Lane Makeover Day"?      That's a solid name, dontcha think? Just don't have sound systems installed in the middle of the garage like that game store did.      At our age, soft music and old photographs is enough entertainment, but go on then.

So do you know what GCSEs you're going to do yet? Our teacher said we've got like... three weeks to decide or something. I’m so stuck I can't even.      I know, right? I’ve been stressing about it all weekend. I think I’ve settled on English, maths, double science, history, and maybe drama. What about you?      I’ve got all the main ones done—English, maths, science, but then I was torn between geography and art. My parents are like "Art doesn't do you any favours," but I love it. It's like my only creative outlet.      I get that. My brother did like nine GCSEs and now he's an app developer or something. I dunno, I feel like if I do more, I’ll be set for a proper job in the future. But sometimes it’s like, do I actually enjoy this?      Oh yeah! I watched this YouTube vlog, you know, those bloggers who do college and university stuff, and one of them said she did way too many GCSEs and dropped out halfway. Like, that’s terrifying. I dunno, YouTube has so many life-changing videos. I tried following this one about being a YouTuber yourself – but I’m too shy to make a clip.      Me neither! I don’t reckon I could do that. I’d panic and trip over the camera. But those bogs out there — the big ones with the millions of views — like, how did they start? They must’ve had to work their bally socks off.      Yeah! Look at Louis or something. I did his clarinet covers once — you remember the one where he did “In the Heights”? My teacher was like “Wow that was brilliant!” I mean it helped that we had loads of practice, but I really like the clarinet. Although I passed my ABRSM and all, I don’t really play any more. I dunno, maybe I will take music at GSCE?      Oh yeah, doing music would be brilliant with drama. I think it fits well. I do love going to the theatre and everything. Then again, like you said, my parents go on about careers. My mum says "You can’t be a YouTuber in the long run!" But like, maybe she can?      It's all so confusing. I asked my cousin and he's like, "Look, just choose what you like to do, and if you get over 5 good GCSEs, you can apply to any sixth form."

Rather annoying this new tablet they’ve given me at the library. I tried to download the ‘Natterjar Wildlife Checklist’ the other day—pesky thing won’t cooperate! Kept saying I needed a ‘cloud account’… Not quite sure what the cloud is—do you think it’s a type o’ cheese?      [chuckles] I reckon it’s more like… well, a place where your things are kept on the internet! I got me one of them ‘OneDrive’ boxes—wife clapped me on the back for sorting that out during the lockdown! Still, I don’t use it much. Too much jumbling about on the screen for someone like me, only interested in seeing the birds that Myra keeps attracting to the garden.      Oh, Myra would be proud! We used to birdwatch together back in Harrow. She’d dress up in her better coat when she thought the magpies might notice. "Look at me!" she’d say, ever so proudly, even though the puffins weren’t in the area. Speaking o’ which, I do miss the way the Norfolk birds sing—there’s something in the land here that makes their songs richer.      It must be the landscape, really. West Norfolk has got such a dramatic coastline—those salt marshes are vital habitats. And it's interesting to see how the local history ties in with that. You know, the old Celts and Romans used the same migratory flyways for their own travel. I included a module on this in my environmental studies class last term. Funny thing—while talking about ancient history, the students were all glued to their screens trying to Google whether the Romans used Windows or Apple about five thousand years ago!      Ha! I had a laugh myself once when I thought I was answering the phone and instead accidentally replied to a Facebook ad about vintage Land Rovers. Burgundy colour, 2.5-litre V6. I was tempted to buy it—only trouble was, I had to print the reply, take it to the library, and ask the librarian what I meant.      Aye, and speaking of cars, I took the old Citroën GSA for a spin t’other day—usual grumble and rattle, but she runs like a proper workhorse! You ever owned one, Albert?      Me? Aye, 1978 model. The radiator gave up and I decided it was high time to retire from driving—plus, I prefer a sit down with a good book and the birds at the window.

Rather annoying when the schoolteachers bring up all that modern stuff. I mean, just last week they sent a letter asking us grandparents to teach them about poetry rhyming properly! As if we didn’t have a clue back in our day. I showed the lass what a half rhyme was and she was proper impressed. Right good at spelling I was at Costessey School. Ay, dusty old books and all!      Oh, I know! My孙辈, Timmy, used to come home pulling his hair out! All that “free verse” stuff! Told him the only verse he needed to get through life was “Tomorrow won’t be so bad, as long as I’ve got tea and cake in my hand.”      Ha! That’s a good’un! I tell me pupils the same. But, y’know, the modern system—bloody brilliant at a lot of things, breakfast clubs, laptops, that sort of thing, but I reckon poetry’s being dummed down too much. Proper language is vanishing. I mean, why speak full sentences when a text message with emojis will do?      I agrees with yer, Simon. We still got grief when the deliveryman today asked us if we wanted him to tweet the time of delivery. I said no, I prefer a good old Royal Mail stamp, and he looked at me like I was from Neptune! Now don’t get me started on the tea program on the telly. Half the actresses wear trousers and act like someone who fought in Iraq!      Oh, I love that show. Mary’s hotter than the kettle at ten in the morning and still stays chic! Although I had to ballet away when my great-niece asked me about “para-para-para-bobbly something on the wings.” I said, “What about bog-standard curtains?” and she nearly fell off the chair laughing.      Burgundy curtains! What was her thinking? I did a poem about bad curtains once. Thought it was funny at the time.      You must tell me one day! I’m not that bad at doing poems—though I do specialise in limericks! Know why? Because you can drop a laugh in the last line and get away with it!      Aye, that’s the ticket! But I swear, nowadays it’s all about the binge-drinking, not the verse! My nephew went to a pub at 10 am to get his first pint after work! And now he never even dresses properly.

Rather annoying this, innit? I mean, I grudgingly admit it's beautiful, but when you're trying to pick up bin bags and shovel paths, it's sod all picturesque.      Aye, we had a bit o' snow at our house too. I was trying to get the cat out, and I slipped on the threshold. Still reckon me trousers are dented from where I hit the floor!      Aw, poor Timmy! He alright?      Aye, me more than him! Right, while I’m stuck at home, I thought I’d get some veg growing sorted. Found a few seeds at the back of the shed. You like broad beans yet?      Broad beans are alright. I’m more of a salad kinda person, but I’ve been thinking of doing a veg patch in the summer. Mabe we could plant it together?      Haha, yeah, sounds like planting and then we both fawn over them for a bit before the slug invasion hits and we blame each other for not using slug pellets.      Fair point. What about the garden tools though? Mabey I should buy some good ones. My old ones are basically from the Stone Age.      True. I got a pair from the local hardware shop. They weren’t expensive, but they lasted ages. Silly question, but ‘ave you heard of the Come Dine With Me someone’s booking in for? Gary's trying to get a seat, he said it's an out-of-town-chef lot.      Oh aye, I heard about it! We were nearly about to book our tickets for the same round. I thought it was going to be th’ weekend after next!      Yeah, it is. Gary invited us to do the hen do for 'is sister-in-law. All ready to celebrate with bubbly and me trying not to spill a single bloody cocktail.      Awd, that sounds good. Me mate Charlotte’s got a stag do booked for the same weekend elsewhere, though. She told me the wedding’s gonna be in Liguria.      Liguria? Oh yeah go on then! They’ve already got our number for the hen do, obviously.      Aye, bloomin’ marvellous. Mike’s in at the moment, fetching special cleaning supplies and a first aid kit for the broken glass incident last time.      Haha, fair’s fair, them glasses were 100% blamed on me. Always me, innit.      Mabey we should get a camera for when we try to cook for it.

Rather good this, isn't it, love? That stew of mine sticks to your ribs, if you like... got the recipe from old Mrs. Tilney down the village, back in the '50s, I expect. Not quite like those fancy things the children eat these days.      Oh dear, yes, it's lovely, as always, Arthur. My goodness, I couldn’t resist a second plate before I even got halfway through the first. Still, you’d think she’d have learned her lesson by now—she was the one who tripled the recipe, don't forget.      Honestly, Mary, I can't complain, but the portion sizes are rather generous for someone like me who’s still trying to eat healthy. Though I must say, the rosemary in the potatoes was genius. I might just have to steal the recipe for my evening class, you know, the one on breakfasts and light meals? The students are always after shortcuts in the kitchen.      You can say that again. Cooking isn't what it used to be—everyone's into "wellness" now and "low-carb" nonsense. Like a banana tart without bananas and only ten ingredients. Tell me what on earth is replacing the flour?      Flour's flour – that's what gives the texture, young man. No room for these modern substitutes, no matter how clean their labels look. Silly if you ask me. When I was your age, the only food someone worried about was whether it filled you up before the bread ration ran out.      That is such a different world from the one I grew up in. I was taught as a child to have about five meals a day: breakfast, a snack, lunch, another snack, and tea. My godmother even measured her water to see if I was drinking enough.      That’s overkill if you ask me. All I remember is tea at four, porridge at seven, and something vaguely greasy for lunch. My nan used to say I was spoon-fed the same thing every time. Though to be fair, it probably kept lunches simple.      Some things, no matter how exotic, never change. Pies and puddings still end up on the table most days if you ask me.      I suppose it’s the same with the box sets—whether it’s your mother’s lasagna or something from The Great British Bake Off, someone in every generation thinks they can make it better.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand grilling’s the default for veggies, but when you try to make a salad or something fresh, you run out of herbs in an hour      Aye, we do that in the North as well — throw things on a barbecue if it stands still. Even lettuce gets charred      When I were your age lass, you couldn’t buy any decent provisions before ten! I used to kill for a salad, as long as someone else made it      Funny you say that, Grandma. Mummy just grates frozen kale into a lettuce mostly to justify eating processed meat      That’s Alice for you — always thinks a bit of cheese melanger solves the world’s problems      You're all too picky. If it has cheese on it, I’m already a happy man      You need to expand your horizons — in fact, next week you’re making a salad, Grandad      Good luck with that, I’ve been trying to get Dad into healthy eating since 2015 — no leaves touched to this day      Alice’s got something on us though, we should mix it up more. I’m gonna try that lemon vinaigrette, still needs work      You lot are quite the snobs, you realize that? I grew up in a house that fed me warmed-up cereal at lunch      And you made it a success, didn’t you love? Some of us’d be struggling with a bowl of Choc Pot at 6      True, I about blocked the kettle while warming up my biccies the other day      Maybe next weekend we should all learn to make a proper batch of lasagne? I bet the smell alone would stop everyone from hiding in guestrooms      Aye, I know it’d bring any grump out of hiding — tried it once on your Uncle Fred, he emerged from the airing cupboard      He probably just wanted to keep the heat from the oven      Still remember when I tried teaching your Dad how to cook a stew — he threw it in the microwave and complained there was no meat      Yep, I was 8, ate the whole thing and your face was like you’d just bit into a wasp      And now he eats dry belly pork from a packet on toast — poetry      Family recipes tend to string together the weird and wonderful. Least we’re all sat together, still weird, but all one lot      Just make sure Alice doesn’t want mushroom risotto again, it won’t end well      Like I said, last one to ever do it.

So do you remember that time we worked on that social story project for the primary schools in Wellington? The first one got heaps of attention on YouTube—ended up with over a million views by the time we wrapped it up.      Oh, I  do  remember—my heart nearly dropped when it accidentally went public before we’d finished testing it. But you were right about the concept; it resonated a lot. A lot of educators DM’d us asking about implementing it in universities. We even had some interesting talks with a few private colleges in the UK and Australia.      Exactly. That’s what I’ve been thinking about mostly over the past week. With our start-up focus now, why not push that idea into a university-level tool? Universities are crying out for inclusive learning strategies, especially in fields like psychology, social work, and business studies—places where understanding cultural and social dynamics is key.      Absolutely. You know I’m all for education tech—especially if it’s using modern methods to bridge generational and cultural gaps. We could adapt the storytelling platform for more complex scenarios—real-world case studies presented through interactive video segments. I mean, we even saw that with those viral grief support videos on YouTube. People responded best when watching other people, not just reading about it.      Exactly. Imagine a student walking through a sensitive negotiation, or trying to de-escalate a conflict in a professional setting through their own decision-making. The tool could evaluate their choices, provide feedback in real-time, and then suggest strategies. And because it's a narrative-driven experience, it's not just educational—it's emotionally engaging.      That’s a great point. We could even develop it as a supplement to lectures or seminars—like flipped classroom material. From what I’ve seen in my postgrad studies and teaching experience, that method works particularly well with older students who appreciate autonomy but still crave interaction.      And here’s the kicker—we could partner with universities to run pilot programs. If we land a couple of pilot projects, we’ll have data to back up our claims. It would also help us tailor the platform to different learning styles and specialisations. I’ve already been in touch with an old classmate who’s a learning strategist at UOW in Wollongong. She’s on board.      That’s brilliant. I can reach out to some of my contacts in further education—educators who are always looking for innovative tools.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand things get delayed, but it's been two weeks and everyone's still waiting on one person to send across the budget outline! Honestly, it's driving me a little mad.      That does sound frustrating! You wouldn't think it was too hard just to send an Excel sheet. I totally empathise. I had something similar at work last week with a care plan transcription from a GP—came in too late, and suddenly we had to refer a patient who should have been seen earlier. Stressful business.      Definitely. But at least you get the satisfaction of helping people, right? I don't get that the same way with my job. It’s mostly spreadsheets and chasing emails these days. Fun stuff. How’s your team doing, anyway?      We’ve been swamped, thanks to an increase in referrals. But it’s been a good few of us working together—no complaints there. The placement team are looking for some new support workers, though, so I might get a shift to mentor someone new in the future.      That’d be awesome! I mean, sharing your knowledge as a mentor must feel rewarding.      It does—it always does. But it’s a long-term plan. For now, I’m focusing on the present, like actually making myself eat something today. This kitchen is nearly empty again.      Oh, I blame you for that! What, no leftover Halloween food? I told you to save some of the toffee apples. Those things were magic. Halloween was hotter than the summer—only in London, really. Still, at least we had your colleague’s party last Saturday.      Yes! That belfry bar near Hackney had vibes. I definitely enjoyed that! Going out with work colleagues and pretending not to know each other for most of the night.      Classic guest list disasters. I did see that and refrained from laughing. But I assume you all ended up talking about work anyway.      We did, didn’t we? Though to be fair, it’s the easiest conversation starter. At least we’re not all awkward. I’d be lost in a room with strangers.      I know what you mean. I sometimes think I’m so over planning events, but in the end, it's always the small things that make it what it is. Now, about the planning ahead—five years from now, where do you see yourself?      Honestly?

Rather annoying isn’t it, how cold it's been in Cambridge of late? I swear it’s been like a proper nippy winter already. You’d think more for September!      Aw, it’s probably just the wind, Mummy. It’s not  that  cold — coordinates it on your cocoa! But yeah, it’s been a bit frosty this week. Proper autumnal, I reckon. A lot worse than last year this time.      It was quite a reasonable September last year, bless. I remember picking apples in the garden, don’t you? You were hell frozen to help, even! Sitting in the house with a book the whole morning.      My bad, I was probably working on my dissertation or something. Ten thousand words on environmental policy and sustainability. Drained and sad in the world of academia. But I was about to ask you something else. When are we actually going to visit Nana Hilda in Brighton?      Well, you didn’t have to mention dissertation talk to bring it up! I was just thinking about that today. Wednesday next week maybe — I’ve got a friend round for tea and she might pop off, but as long as she does, we can drive up. Do you think she’d want to come back?      I reckon, yeah. She loves escaping the rain and her flat in Hove. Maybe you should pop her a text and double-check? She tends to forget what day things are on when it’s more than a few days ahead. It’s not age, it’s what you make of it!      Haha! I’ve had enough people tell me that it’s about how I treat it! Although I prefer the good days — watching films, sipping a nice herbal tea, and you coming round to chat. Doesn’t sound too bad for my advancing years.      Definitely not. You passed 60 with style, remember? You looked absolutely stunning in that red dress.      You were there, darling. As good as ever. Though I  still  don’t know what you were on about with your "emoji hierarchy" talk. That sounds like a serious LinkedIn post by some 20-year-old goon.      Well, you don’t know my line of work. I had to survive explaining box trucks and lead times to your 20-something postgrad friends!      Well, you made it sound important, anyway. Smarter than it was, I imagine.      It  was  important! The kind of boring yet vital stuff that keeps the world spinning.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get why they talk fast and all, but when everyone’s shouting over the top of each other in the café, it’s like a right mission to decipher what they’re sayin’. Not to mention they have like, ten different words for things that mean the same in eeny different situation. I swear the menu was like   50%   translations gone wrong.      Aww, don’t stress too much, love. You're used to pickin' up lots of slang from different regions back home, right? Think of it as the same but just in another language. I mean, I  still  don't get why the waitress kept callin' me  Chérie  like it was some nickname! Makes me feel like a cat or summat.      Roight, I think it just means ‘sweetie’ or ‘love,’ but better safe than sorry—still doesn’t mean I want to be called in French at the age of 20! Speaking of which, have you sorted out the uni application details for that lab work module?      Yeah, just cracked it yesterday! Felt a bit like a proper human experiment myself, with all the bloody forms and watching how the proper scientific method is supposed to be applied. I mean, it’s one thing doin’ it, it’s another thing explainin’  the process . All that hypothesis and all?      Tell me about it. I mean, in Sixth Form we just assumed we’d blag through it, but now it's like, ‘no— you need to document every single step .’ Anyways, at least you get to escape the Prime Minister for a few days. I’m stuck trying to bumble through the French library this afternoon. Got a mission to find some local research on how French and English teams handle match-day press ups.      Oh yeah? That’s actually kinda interesting. I did some work on how sport psychology affects performance before. You know, scientists trying to find if there’s a scientifically backed reason why some teams talk more quietly and others just rage. Websites like that are a proper minefield, by the way. I took the liberty of finding you a couple of source articles.      That goon really? You're a star. If I end up in some French line of work, I might need you explaining how bloomin’ everything works one day. Although I swear, sometimes I think they speak in code just to mess with us foreigners.

Rather annoying when a spider turns up in the kitchen when you're cooking dinner, isn’t it? The first thing you do is drop the knife and reach for the tea towel! I saw one the other day, probably thought it was £20 or the tinned tomatoes!      Aye, they’re always there when you don’t need 'em. I’ve got a dachshundButtonDown that’s constantly terrorising spiders—course, every time she goes for one, she misses and manages to knock something off the side. My aunt says I should just chase the spiders myself with a broom. I like to think of them mostly as harmless little mite, though. They eat the flies.      True, I’ve read enough to know that spiders are more scared of us than we are of them, but still—there’s something about the way they move, you know? All slow and deliberate, and then suddenly they’re gone. Reminds me of when I was a child and I’d hides behind the curtain looking for the one in the corner.
