That’s not a pleasant image, listen—there I am with a dog and a brush and you’re talking about crawling behind curtains like a serial killer watching for unsuspecting trotters in dark corners. You’re giving me the shudders, I am not joking. Anyhoo, what about the mice? Now there’s something to be nervous about. If I saw one in the kitchen, I’d be out in five seconds flat.      You’d better rush, then. I’ve got a nutty bat out back that regularly wants to come inside through the cat flap. I’ve come close to stitching it in about five places. That bird does not like the word no.      That’s not a mouse, that’s a bird. Still, if a mouse turned up to have a go at my flour stores, I’d be right on it. Cleaners and pests—they go hand-in-hand, if you ask me.      You must see your fair share of vermin then. Though I’ve seen worse in retail with people trying to stick biscuits in their pockets. Some people, no respect for pricing, no idea of appropriate snack storage.      I’ll tell you what's worse than a mouse in the kitchen line of work—it’s a customer with a box of tissues and a sneeze ready to go at the worst time.

Rather lovely to finally meet in person, Delyth. I've heard so much about you through the family... Our dear cousin James often talks about the side of the family you're on.      A pleasure, honestly! I've not had as close a connection with the Dorchester side of the family as I'd like, but I'm always open to learning about our roots. Have you ever looked into yours?      Of course, I've spent a few years going through my mother's old papers and chatting to aunties and uncles during the holidays. She was born right in Dorset, near Poole, if I recall. I've traced the family back to my great-great-grandmother Myfanwy, who was from a small farm near Bridgwater. I think she came over from Wales, actually. I'm trying to find out if that's accurate.      That would tie in with me! My own ancestors were in Bridgwater, too. I remember my mawn -- that's mother in Welsh -- once telling me stories about her childhood there. My father's family, though, were from near Cardiff. Tricky mixing both to find the full tree, but it's been a labor of love.      That sounds beautiful. I remember my mother's side often spoke about Bristol and the surrounding areas. Unfortunately, she passed a few years ago after a long battle with multiple myeloma. It was a cruel and slow disease, and it feels only fair to talk about it more openly. She was a remarkable woman, full of stories. Some made you laugh, some made you wonder.      I'm so very sorry for your loss, about your mother. That must have been such a difficult time. My own mother passed from a related illness -- not multiple myeloma, but a blood disorder. She was a schoolteacher, just like I was. I left the education sector after retiring, but it was the heart of my career. Teaching was something I lived for.      You must take pride in being a teacher as well. You've clearly taken after your mother with your passion for family history and your profession.      Thank you for saying so, Delyth. I enjoy the work, though it's exhausting sometimes. I think the two roles complement each other in a way, between guiding young minds and exploring the lives of those who came before us. It's all about learning, really.      I couldn't agree more.

Rather annoying power lines just tore across that scenic view, wasn't it? You’d think they'd string them a bit more thoughtfully out here. Otherwise, it’s been a fantastic few days. That walk this morning with the dog was quite invigorating, especially as it picked up pace through those fields. Got a bit of a waddle from the dog, didn’t he?      Yeah, I saw that too from the other trail earlier. Honestly, I’m beginning to wonder if they were even worth building in the first place out here. They disrupt the vibe completely when everything else feels so idyllic. Not to mention, it does complicate photography. That said, the dog’s still got form, hasn’t he? I still can’t get over his eccentric left-right weaving when he sees a hare – like he thinks he can pick one out of the air somehow.      Oh wait, better yet, when he actually chases one and then stops dead for no reason at the edge of the field! No, you didn’t see that one? It’s like he realises he’s overstepped, maybe? Speaking of, I’ve been thinking about the land a bit more lately. Do you remember back when we were camping in Wales—what was it? Two years ago now?      Mate, of course I do, and I barely remember sleeping that whole week. You were set on learning to identify birds through their calls. I ended up naming everything after your surname, just for fun.      Honestly, I wish I’d thought to write them down. I remember being flabbergasted at how many different sounds and types crowded that one valley. I was in a lecture last week and about half the class didn’t even know a field sparrow from a common lark. Honestly, lack of exposure leaves you that blind.      You're not wrong there. My sister had that problem with her kids constantly. All they saw was concrete. I’m actually planning a getaway with them soon, maybe take them to Northumberland or something. You ever been out there?      Once as a student—enough said. But I heard it's incredible. Now, the reason I brought up camping earlier—somewhat by way of the landscape—is because I’ve been thinking about how cheap it's getting to go ballooning lately. There’s a firm that runs weekend packages in Norfolk now—what’s the one near Wells?

Rather annoying isn’t it, how bright it is at this time of the morning. Felt like it was already warming up a bit out there after the class.      Oh, aye, it’s sunnier than I expected for this time of year. Up near Leeds it was still pretty nippy at this hour last week. But you get used to it, I s’pose. Though I reckon that sun should save itself for the afternoons, not be bleedin’ glaring at us first thing.      Isn’t that the truth. It always feels a bit cruel to get the full blast of it when you’re just winding down from a tough class, don’t it? You made that one of the Zumba sessions, then?      Yeah, I did the 9 o'clock one. Hadn't done anything like that in a while, and my legs aren’t too happy with me at this stage. But I’d rather be stiff and tired than the other way round, you know? Managing a few gyms isn’t exactly the ideal way to stay in shape, is it?      I can imagine. You’re bound to spend more time managing spreadsheets and bookkeeping than working out. I tried working at a little language school last spring, and – no disrespect – it’s not much different, sometimes. You spend as much time worrying about staff shifts and funding as you do about lesson plans.      Aye, I know what you mean. Spent my last two weekends trying to sort a problem with one of our franchises. Some nutty kid dropped a kettle in the treadmill and it’s been under repair ever since. End up doing more crying over about £300 a week repair bills than talking to clients, I swear.      That’s tragic. I know barely more about treadmills than I do about astronomy, but I’d be stumped by that. Though at least your job must give you a sense of variety – I assume you travel around the gyms a lot?      We do, we do. I cover as far out as Scarborough and York. Towns and big cities—each with their own vibe. Leeds is proper lively, but this place, Solihull, it's got a nice mix of old and new, don’t you think?      I do. I’ve actually been meaning to read a book on the history of postwar housing developments here. Thought it might give me a bit of local colour for one of my classes.

Rather annoying I though, the pair of yer, coming in with that lorry-load o’ ‘owsehoith and not ‘even telling us! Me and Dobby’ve ‘ad to clear out ‘alf the sittin' room t’ fit it in!      Sorry Gran and een, we thought we’d surprise you both. Me and Lee got this dusty old wardrobe… well, a proper bargain, from a flat clearance in York.      Oh bless me, pulling that stick out! Put it som’un else for ‘eavens sake! That's Mrs. Whates' stick from thirty year back!      What’s all the racket? I was trying t’ turkey on me telly!      Tenr, abbi, you're on! Me and Lee bought it for you. It's in the wardrobe, brand new!      Oh ‘oo’s been a good little eedle, planting the turkey! That's you then, I suppose?      It’s thoughtful o’ ‘em, I’ll give it that. I mean, we did say as ‘owsehoith was on the cards for Xmas…      Well then, best get it polished up – that’s if it’s not broke in, because if it is, I shall be very cross.      Lee was the one who drove the lorry. I was stuck in the back counting the plates. Honestly, I thought my back was gonna go.      ‘elp, I mind the days as I used t’ polish the floor with your ballet slippers when you were about five!      Now now, Ma, we’re trying t’ be civil this weekend. Let’s not bring up the ballet!      Gran, you ‘ad me do ballet for four years before I even kicked a football! I could do the leap before I was ten!      Oh, bless yeh, I just wanted you as not end up as clumsy as your grand-dobby 'ere!      Clumsier than that tom-cat, even!      Oh leave go’, Dobby! The man's trying t’ sit dowwwn!      Honestly, it was bloomin’ marvellous getting that wardrobe in! We nearly popped it on the kitchin door out o’ excitement, I’ll tell ya!      ‘elp, if we start laughing again, Dobby’ll go green ‘gain!      Just make sure yeh put the turkey in by tea. And yeh can ‘elp us, Lee.      Yeah, yeah, I’ll… I’ll ‘elp. Probably. Unless my foot's on fire. Or my back.      Well, that's you sorted then! A bit o’ family, a bit o’ ‘ousehoith, and if we're lucky, a bit o’ turkey!      That’s the spirit, love.

Rather annoying this new satnav eh, love? Thought mebbe we’d know this road by now, like it’s the seventh time we’ve passed this bloody roundabout since we left Cumbria. An’ where is this bridge over the burn they warned us about?      Aye, it’s beginning to grind my nerves more than the miles,   Vicky  . I’ve been trying to resist the urge to swap it for a paper map from one of them charity shops we used to pick up vintage posters from. Know we’d be directions savvy by now, chase through the Dales with a car full of frozen pies.      Aye,   Simon  , I remember the first time we managed that drive without a satnav, back when you were writing that gig book about folk spots in the North. Drove us past three cows in a field and called it an adventure, while I tried to interpret those ancient Ordnance Survey symbols!      Ha! Aye, you ever looked at that map, didn’t it look like a puzzle made by someone who’d imbibed a few kegs of ale and a pint of poetic riddles. Right, as to this bridge grief – off to the right we go, past that bend with that view over Westmorland. You’ll see the –?      Duckboard, that’s the name of it. Fancied telling the staff at the pub last night was what it was called. Smacked the barkeep right in the chuckles when he said “duck boards” are just a bit of gardening oddly named. You’d think a place with a moat and real ale would be au fait with all things biblical in naming.      Aye, well the bridge story's good for a chuckle but let’s not be too cheeky about it. Not with barely enough time to park the car, let alone do your dance warm-up before the ceilidh. Though I must say, that new set you worked on – the one with the snippets of Keats and that song you wrote when Arbroath’s shop lost the queens.      Ah, you've got to keep the folklore whirling in these parts love. Mebbe you remember delivering the poetry set by that old man with the crooked hat? I think he was more of a muse than a man.      I will never forget the box of old jumpers and your insistence it was his spiritual accessory. The man was a walking seminar on metaphor and nappy wool, if you ask me.

Rather annoying isn't it? I mean, I understand grilling everything they know her—the project brief is tight, but still. I'm starting to feel like more of a requirements warehouse than an architect.      Yeah, I hear you. We’ve got our own set of challenges here too. I saw the latest passive design update last night—and trust me, if this is what they're suggesting for a retrofitted university, I would  prefer  a social housing brief for a change. It's pulling teeth trying to get anything past the board. You’d think working in conservation would make them more appreciative of detail, but no.      Honestly, the only way I can stay sane these days is My turkey and avocado on rye. You got your banana porridge by now?      Yeah, I did—though I may need an extra kale latte if this morning goes on much longer. You need to see some of the stuff in Jo’s latest email. She’s been assigned to rework the entire ground floor plan for accessibility, but based on the site visit we did, half of what they’ve listed doesn’t make sense with the existing structure. I feel like I sent her an issue log from Mars and she’s responding as if it’s from the moon.      Oh, Jo? Right, I know her—does she not come over for the weekend poker nights?      She said she’s been too busy, which I suppose is someone’s full-time job—doing everything at once and forgetting to breathe. I told her to email you as well, just in case you can talk her through some of the site constraints.      I’ll do that. I mean, I know she can be a bit headstrong sometimes, but architecture this detailed—you know that learning curve is a steep one.      Definitely, but for someone just starting out, it can be overwhelming. Hey, speaking of headstrong—did you see any of those girls last night?      The ones who asked you about your  pens  of all things?      Haha, come on, I let it drop for  one minute . You know how it is—archi goth girls on the prowl. Not that I'm complaining, mind you.      Honestly, you blokes—and your questionable taste in romantic partners. I’m surprised you didn’t try to sell one of your steel bar graphs as a dating profile.

Rather annoying when people just pull out without indicating, isn't it? I was just in my car when that happened last weekend. Someone just shot out in front of me on the roundabout.      Yeah, it can be pretty dangerous. I think people these days are just too used to rush and don’t care about basic driving etiquette.      I know! It's not a race. A lot of drivers just think they're in a Formula One car instead of a family estate pulling someone to work!      Funny you say that, because the other day I was driving into work near the council offices and this guy behind me was honking like crazy because another driver changed lanes like that.      So what did you do?      You know, I just tried to stay calm and screamed at them with mental imagery about collisions and paramedics. I mean, I actually said to myself, "Just drive in!"      You're not serious?!      I'm dead serious! Sometimes I feel like just pulling over and giving them a driving lesson. I know, quite a rude thought.      Tell me about it! I always feel it. I remember when I got my driver's license – it was a Royal Enfield, and I had to go to Grantham to take the test.      Oh, Grantham! That's where I'm from.      Oh, really? That's a small world then. I passed the test in the main square there. It was freezing and it poured rain the entire time!      I did mine at Sleaford.      Oh, that's near there too. How did you get on?      I passed, but I was so panicked I realized halfway through the test that I had passed the marker for the designated lane without realizing. I had a panic attack, I thought I'd failed for sure.      That sounds tough. I remember being terrified too. Then trying to catch up with friends after that! They had all the best stories from road trips, something I had yet to do.      I know what you mean. I think road trips are such a great way to spend time with friends. Who do you stay in touch with these days?      Oh, a few girls from uni. We usually try to get together for a weekend to catch up and see the country over the summer. We've been planning something in the Cotswolds this year.      That sounds lovely!

Rather than just a LinkedIn profile, you need to make sure that everything presented forms a full, rounded picture. I got the producer to put me through the rounds more than once before I landed the media mentorship a few years ago. Confidence is important, but not in a brash way. You want to show competence and warmth.      It was actually   Vicky   at the radio station who mentioned a position might be coming up. I know that this isn't top-tier BBC but, you know, pulling someone local in can help. Leeds has a very warm media community when it comes to new voices.      That helps! And speaking locally works well with national opportunities, too. Still, make sure you tailor the application properly. You’ve already got solid experience with the documentary team over at the university, yes?      Yeah, the history documentary piece with the Palestine Heritage Angle? They’re still pinching themselves that it got noticed in London. Hitting the right emotional notes, planting the right hook — that’s the magic for media folk, isn’t it?      Exactly, and it’s something I’ve noticed crop up in shortlists quite a bit. You’re human, real, and still professional — that balance is key. You remember when I was applying for teaching modules at the uni?      How could I forget? You were up all night tweaking your cover letter because you wanted them to see  who  you were and not just your ability to teach. Like this someone who could bring a classroom together with a calm energy and a sense of shared purpose.      Exactly. So in your case, being able to weave in that  authenticity  is crucial. I mean, I know a few people who’ve had the misfortune of job interviews ruined because they tried to be someone they were not.      Ugh, I hate the idea of ‘performing.’ I’d much rather someone passed me by than me just pretending for a role. It’s exhausting being all things to all people.      I agree with you there. Just being prepared to show  your  skills in the best light is more than enough. So, do you want me to read through your statement again this evening?      Actually yes, I think it would help. If I can give it to you today, would you mind looking it over with a critical eye?      Of course. We can even go over your live read-through after I’ve seen the written version.

So do you really think it's feasible to start a business together while we're house-sitting? I mean... we don’t exactly have a permanent base at the moment. But maybe this could be the perfect opportunity to make a start with the café idea?      I like the timing, actually. We’ve got a bit of space to think and breathe. And if we use this as a testing phase—it could work. What I'm saying is, this isn't a conventional move, but maybe we don’t need it to be. Less pressure than starting from scratch in either of our hometowns.      You're right. I mean, I’ve been feeling static the last couple of years. Running the IT contracting gig was good, financially, but... it left me emotionally drained. I want to do something meaningful, something I can physically put my hands on. A café feels like it could do that.      And if I step back from teaching... I’m not saying it’s goodbye forever, but I’ve always wanted to have a bit more freedom. I could handle front-of-house and do the menu—personally design it—while you take care of the logistics. We both play to our strengths, don’t we?      Absolutely. I can handle the supply chain, negotiating with suppliers, maybe even handle the finance stuff and business planning. You’ve got the creative flair and the warmth—customers would love you. You know what people need in a community.      Thanks. And in terms of lifestyle, wouldn’t it be a rush to run something like that? To be our own bosses? After years of working for other people’s goals, this  feels  like it could be about our own.      Exactly. But we need to be realistic. We’ll need some kind of funding plan. Could we take out a small business loan? Or maybe do a crowdfunding campaign for local interest?      I did some research while I was on a school break last term. There are some government grants for small enterprises, especially ones that support community. We could frame this as a community café, which would help with that angle. And maybe partner with the local farmer's market?      That’s a solid idea. More than that, it gives it a sense of purpose. If we can give it a name like “The Hub” or “The Crossroads Café,” something that invites your regulars and makes them feel part of it.

Rather annoying this new school situation, isn't it? Seems like we've had to apply for five different primary schools in the last month alone. You'd think with Cambridge being so well-connected, we’d have a little more in the way of resources. Look at the children! They're like jelly on a plate—trembling at every mention of the word ‘placing'.      It’s not just a Cambridge issue, love. I remember when Glasgow was like a pot of jam—too many bumps, not enough jars. We had to send the bus for the most part when the numbers piled up. You'd fetch the children from a temporary school in a neighboring parish, goodness knows the roads taken to get there on a wet day. It still breaks my heart to see it left so unprepared now. I had twenty-two in my class, and now I hear teachers managing over thirty—how in God’s name can they teach?      Mumbled something about "giiirrups." Then, louder: Mummy, can we have pizza again tomorrow? They came early, and that man was wearing a really big beard!      I don’t think your face is quite made for grief, Liam, love. As for pizza… well, tomorrow is tomorrow, and then the day after is Thursday, and somehow it turns into a week, and suddenly it's  again  next week. But yes, pizza tomorrow. Just as long as the delivery man stays in his van and doesn't try to help out. The beard was suspicious—reminded me of that one time your brother came to visit with what he called a '90s hipster revival'. The beard was so big he looked like a coconut with a personality about it.      Ah, touché! We were all trying to be  edgy  in the '90s. I remember the lad up the street—wore a ‘90s treble cord jacket and passed off a chin-length salt-and-pepper as minimal grooming. But I digress. Speaking of revisits, I recently read a book on the migration from Poland and how it’s affected not just the housing but the schools too. They're pouring in like water through a sieve, you know, and the schools are like a sponge—trying to go from dry to saturated all in one wash.      It's not just affecting the education system. The healthcare system is buckling under the pressure too.

Rather annoying really, having to get a car park permit now. I mean, it's not like it's a proper town centre or anything. You'd think they'd make it a bit simpler      Yeah, I feel you. Look, I’ve got one for work now, but figuring it out? A nightmare, honestly. You got one yet?      Yeah, most days I just park on the street or walk in from Fradley. Oh, and you were joking about that local football match we went to? That was when the team won, or was it a draw? I can’t remember now.      It was the draw, only just. I distinctly remember that one of the kids from years ago who played left back is now back as a mascot – I nearly fell over trying not to say hi!      Oh, that’s classic! Wait, you haven’t gone and started going to those after-work gym sessions at the leisure centre again, have you? They were bloody mad. I mean, why would you want that kind of pressure with a child and everything?      Honestly, no. Left it all to grief when the back gave out again. Otherwise I might have considered it – it does seem like the only chance most of us have to get out the house, and actually take our eyes off the telly.      Fair enough. You know what I miss though? Piano lessons. I mean, I used to enjoy music and now it’s just not even on the radar anymore. I should definitely buy some books for the kid.      Beginners books at least. I did ballet as a kid and nearly flunked school because I was off every Friday! But my kids were never into it. My eldest was more into her friends and school plays.      You’re quite the accomplished woman for getting through sixth form education. I passed out of it – just couldn't be bothered. But I was lucky my sister looked after me.      My brother did the same for me. Look, we did our bit trying with lunches and school events and whatnot. Now he's working in sales for some big company around Birmingham and I’m the lunchtime supervisor go-between. I get it if you don’t get it.      It’s brutal. Honestly, with all the sales roles and your part-time gig. It must take its toll. You ever manage to go out?

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what I mean. I was just trying to post a quick update for the conference, and no sooner had I press the tweet, ay, someone had reply with a meme that was… honestly, I donnae ken what it means.      A een? Aye, I understand the frustration. It’s hard to ken if folks actually read what’s goin’ on before they hit reply. But from a social media perspective, it’s alright as it’s gettin’ people engage. Although, I do kinna chase the threads when they get too chaotic.      Still, it’s part of me job. I run communications for a non-profit and like it or loke it, Twitter is still a wee bit prim’ryr tool to reach the folk who are, how do I say, the loud voices in the room, eh?      Aye, and I use it more for education context in me role as Director of Studies. We run a few online courses now and folk takin’ to Twatt for help or discussion forums can be a useful way tae gaither feedback. But, honestly, as much as I like the idea, it still has a wee way to go before it resembles something saner from the way folk use it – especiall when it’s not even in moderation.      Let’s no forget It’s not just Twatt. LinkedIn is a right useful tool for me job. It’s whaur I connect with other professionals, get invited to webinars, and share case studies. I do tend to keep it very professional, mind. No memes and no hillarious sarcastic commentaries.      I do similar on there. I use it quite a touch for professional development as well. And I’ve even found some good research that way. Facebook I only handle it for the family side; the work, I prefer to keep it off that. Though I will admit – sometimes I have me eye on it for a event or twa.      Aye, I could see that. Social media can be a weapon of good if you knows whar to keep the focus whar. It took me a while tae figure that out. There are times I started the day intended go work on my report and I ended up scrollin’ through TikTok for an hour, no seein’ the time go.      Aye, I could have written fluently on that subject. I think I’m startin’ to accept that It’s a right useful tool in moderation.

Rather annoying to be honest. I had a request at six on Saturday morning and it turned out they just wanted to update the project timeline—not even a real change. Blows it all out the water when you're trying to relax at the weekend.      Ugh, that  does  sound awful. My friend went out of town last weekend and didn’t even let me know until Thursday. Left me a voicemail on Sunday when I was halfway through a shift. Still, easier said than done to get time off as a mental health nurse, I suppose.      Definitely. I mean, I get the stress of juggling shifts and everything. I heard you’re the one who brought that new recipe in the other day, by the way? I made it last night and it was  so  good. You're a genius, and I think I turned my stove brown with burnt butter while attempting it.      Oh no! I’m sorry to hear that—sounds dramatic. I didn’t mean to set your kitchen on fire. But the recipe was from my nan, actually—she’s the real mastermind. I’d say try it again, though, because it’s worth it. And tell me what colour the stove is now… brown sounds fun.      It’s still brown, but somehow it matches with the rest of the décor now. Deadpan, I know. Anyways, speaking of friends—did you hear from Anna this week? She’s been MIA and I’m just starting to miss her. We need to book a coffee or something soon.      Yeah, I saw a DM from her Friday and it’s been radio silence since. We should absolutely do something. I’ve been meaning to walk to the coffee shop the other week, but I had two back-to-back 12s. I’m running on three cups of tea a day, to be honest.      That’s not even allowed anymore. You need coffee and friends, not a sugar-free shambles. I’ll reach out to her today and we can sort out a day to meet up. I’ll propose 4pm on Monday? Unless you’ve got another whopper shift coming up?      No, I’m actually off on the Monday. That should work really well for me if you don’t mind walking over? I’ll even bring the recipe again, but this time with detailed instructions—and maybe a video tutorial.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what he's like – always making a schedule and then piling last-minute changes on top of it. I just don’t know how we've found time to manage this meal at all with all the chaos over his visit.      Well, we couldn’t just let him come all the way from London and not host him properly. He  is  family. I’ve only had time to set the table this morning, to be honest. The stew was easier; someone just needs to check the timings so the timing doesn’t run out, or the slow cooker won’t fetch its full game of gentle broiling.      What I found strange is how stressed he’s been about arriving on time. I met his new girlfriend’s mother this morning – I had to visit their home for some pick and mix cake recipe she swears goes with stew, by the way – and she hinted that he was dithering about whether to make the trip at all. I said no chance! No, you didn’t have a choice in the matter, she said politely.      Sounds like he’s surrounded by the occasional drama in his personal life as usual. Did I tell you, by the way, that I’ve finally got rid of that ancient Bezza? You know, the red one I held on to for, like, decades just for memories. I’ve upgraded to an electric car – all done through the council initiative for retirees. No more oil changes, which is a relief.      Honestly, I’m a bit in awe of you, Dad. You outgrew the car before most of us have even thought through whether owning a car  at all  is necessary. I about blocked the milk van a week back trying to reverse the Renault into this drive.      That leaves me with the school van, and it is a  creature  to handle. But I’m managing. The kids at the high school are all buzzing about the new science exhibit. I had a few ask me if the fossil I brought from our trip to Exeter could power the car we’re planning to sprite to the museum for the next visit. Of course not, but I do like their enthusiasm.      You’re teaching them to think, which is more go than most get in life if you ask me. Just don’t expect me to follow the jargon when they return explaining ‘kinetic energy through carbon-neutral motion’ and whatnot.

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been at this Spanish malarkey for months now an' I still got the gist of it no clearer than fog on Blundells Bank on a winter morning!      Aw, don’t be so hard on yerself,Dee. Got eeny idea when  I  last got an 'A' at summat? Proper self-taught me whole life from when I was ten! Proper proud I was of me Latin O-level as well, but that was thirty year ago now.      It's the verbs, innit? Where’s the sense in tener  meaning  tener, but then the past tense comes out like some kind of posh turkey? Tenia? C’mon! I’m not rallyr, I was an English teacher for thirty years and I still get confused between ‘tener’ an’ ‘haber’!      Look, I’d say maybe you need a different system, love. I tried one of them apps, you know the blue one? It’s all that gamify ery thing, you get stars, levelling up an’ that sort of t’ing. Could be worth a ten, innit?      I have it on me phone, but it's too – what’s the word I’m looking for – it's  too  streamlined. Don’t give’en no proper grammar practice. Silly little fill-in-the-blanks! An’ the accent’s all posh-Spanish, like they’re trying to sound like they’ve been to university or summat. Not the real deal.      Right, so maybe speak to someone, eh? Real people about. I mean, I’ve bin trying to teach meself French once in a while and what helps me more than any book is just watching French TV series with subtitles on. Gets to know the rhythm ‘cos they repeat phrases so much.      Aye, I’ve bin watchin’ ‘La Casa de Papel’ with them subtitles on. I could stick the Catalan subs as well. You seen how they speak there? Half of Barcelona speaks Catalan an’ half doan’t an’ no one care really, it's all by context! I mean, can go out of one room speakin’ one language an’ into the next speakin’ another without no clash. Fancy that, innit?      So summat to aim for, innit? We live in a border town, never had to worry about two languages, but in that ‘ole region, everyone just bounces from one to the other like they were playing a game. Proper cleverness, if you ask me.

Rather annoying when a bank won't accept anything but a paper document. I had her fill out a form first... got the email, she scanned it, saved as PDF, uploaded it, and BOOM! Rejected for being low res.      Course they wouldn't accept it — if it's not clear as day, they can print it and   lose   it. They all have that same paranoia with digital transcription now. Like documents are more likely to disappear if they're digital. Imagine what some linguist would do with all that   corpus   of banking nonsense.      That’s the funny thing, Dad! In corpus linguistics, we'd analyse the way they phrase things — like "Kindly submit a high-resolution scan of an acceptable ID..." It’s ridiculous! I had her print the form, scan it again using   Flitscan  — you know, that free app — better quality. She said it worked then.      Oh aye, you ever looked at that flight ticket ordering lark? They make it seem like you need a doctorate in tech just to get on a plane.      Right! It’s like they want to make sure only the people who read   The Guardian   can book flights. Speaking of... have you seen the new Kelly Brook ones on the cover? Horrible choice really, considering she’s into cooking now — don’t you think it undermines the whole message?      What, those airbrushed shots? Oh no, she’s got a new cookery show coming out. Probably a backlash — you know the internet.   She wants to cook and look like Margot Robbie but insists she eats healthy?   Not about to fall for that marketing.      Oh I'm not saying cooking is easy, Dad. Just that she shouldn’t be worrying about   scanning   her face. My students struggle to put their lesson plans together. Though at least they can speak. I remember when the whole class sent me a voice note once with their paragraphs — I had to transcribe   three hours   of that.      Heh, that’s a new one on me. I do the same work, just on a different level. My course on the database is set go live in two weeks. I had to scan all the old forms and convert them into digital templates. You'd be amazed how many old sales reps wrote your address with a   wet finger  !      That is crime! I mean even linguistically, it’s unspeakable. It's like walking into a classroom and nobody's   using the right prepositions.

Rather annoying when the petrol’s out, innit? I had to go all the way down ‘ere like... off the main road an’ everything. It’s not like there’s a pump round every bloody corner where I live. Not like up North, I s’pose.      Yeah, I saw the place wobbled a bit with the wind. Still reckon it’s not as grim as most. I’ve driven through places where there’s no pump for miles, an’ you’re just sat there pulling in to a sodding nothing, like a mobile depot or summat. I once had to pay someone cash at a farm to get fuell—mind yer, it was the Isle of Wight. That’s like posh turkey countryside, innit?      Honestly, I’d sooner stick my fingers in a pastry pipe and hope for the best than go to an island for fuel. Cats ‘n’ buggies and bikers just happened to be wot I saw at the pump today. Proper loaded lot, they were. I mean, shoutin’ over exhaust pipes and taking selfies with the tyres, luv. I swear, every one of ‘em looked like they’ve read  Top Gear  and thought, “Yeah, I’m good at that.”      You’re not takin’ it serious, are you? Bikes take the hassle out of fuel. They’ve got smaller tanks and they know it. You know what I hate though? Folks who ride those two-wheelers an’ then try to race us on the dual carriageways. I had a guy give me the finger at 70 and then hit a hill and nearly dropped his  arse  over the bonnet.      I don’t biff it, but I do mind when they take up the whole lane. One of ‘em barely gave me a blink when I moved in to the left, ‘cos they was playing their Geo., innit? Bit daft when you could be a bin lorry any bloody second.      I dunno, I just stick to my lane and keep calm. Let ‘em speed if they want. Blisters up the road and then they’re gone. Still, cheers for the fuel. Picked up the best price in goon’s map for it if you ask me.      Yeah, I’m just glad it wasn’t a bloomin’ cash-only one. Can you imagine? Me with a debit card and no signal, stuck out in the middle of nowhere with belly full of cripes and no fuell.

Rather annoying when a close friend turns up unannounced, isn't it? Especially when you've got a ton of proofing to do.      I know, I've been over this a thousand times with my parents. They don't understand that being a self-employed marketing consultant means I can’t just drop everything when they drop by. It's like they haven't caught on.      Maybe they just feel too far apart? I mean, social media is easier but seeing each other in person is different. We've all got our own routines now.      That's not it at all. It's more like they still see me as the same Sutton Coldfield girl who needed help moving out of the family house. I’ve proven enough times that I can run my business, but old habits are slow to change.      I get it. My own family often doesn't quite know when it's appropriate to include me in their plans or when to just back off. And I'm 15, not 5. There's still a struggle to assert that I need space.      Yeah, I remember when I moved from South Korea as a kid and tried to fit into British ways. It was like watching a tennis match – rhythm and timing are crucial. One wrong move – one bad drop shot – and people read way too much into it.      It's not just them pushing their will on us. There's also the pressure we feel to maintain family unity. As soon as we suggest we need a moment alone, it's like we're rejecting them out of nowhere.      Exactly. And when I suggest I need more time in the evenings because of deadlines, it's always "You're not living the right way," or "You should be cooking or doing this or that instead of working." I've got to draw a line somewhere.      That's the lesson for you lads. Find your balance. I've been in the role of a manager too long to not know that flexibility and clear expectations are key – both in the office and at home. You've got to set boundaries, assert your needs, and still keep the peace.      So what would you say is the first step? Because I can go from really relaxed to really frustrated in about two sentences.      Start by expressing your needs clearly. You're not inflexible; you're just managing your own priorities.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, who decides that napkins need to look like undies? We’d got the turkey sorted and them buggers just ruined it!      Aw, it was a bit of fun, weren’t it? Lotta them uni friends o’ yers een Macclesfield brought ’em with they ridiculous nicknames and everything. Almost as bad as that time you tried to boogie to “All I Want for Christmas” and fell into the stew.      Naaa, that was ages ago! An’ it was  not  my fault... the rug was wet from Mary’s cat again. That cat’s the real menace round here.      Yeah, I remember you skidding left and taking half the tinsel with you. D’you know, I think Aunty Sharon had a nosebleed watching you do it.      Now, now, let’s be kind. The lad means well. An’ he’s not the only one who got the dance wrong. Remember that time I overstepped the ballroom floor and ended up in the hallway with the landlady’s best credit card?      Aye, that was proper chaos! Well, all got sorted in the end – especiall’ with the help of that wishbone Mary’s got up there. Binary choice-like.      Honestly, what I don’t get is how we manage to have such a great time every year. Even with the cats, the chaos and the odd oddly dressed napkin holder.      It’s the being here, innit? Family, food, laughs, and a few daft traditions. I mean, I know when I’m at uni, most of my housemates spend Christmas Eve watching that Downton Abbey and complaining about the Queen’s speech to the lot o’ us.      Aint it funny that America’s got a Thanksgiving turkey but we’ve got all the theatrics? I mean, I was in Florida last year an’ didn’t hear one person being asked to fetch the wishbone.      They’ve got the airpots for festive trips, though. Packed! I met folks queuing for weeks on end, if you ask me.      I’ll stick with our Stockport tradition, thank you very much. Pass the gravy will you, love? The weather’s been chilly enough, we’d best start wrapping up proper soon like.      Agreed. And if we start bickering like we did last time ‘bout the best music for films, we’ll end up in another dance contest.      Naa, that was Leon’s faul’ last year.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with Aisha anyway. We were meant to grab coffee last weekend and it got rained off.      That does sound a bit unfair, poppet. You do spend so much time being professional these days. But it’s only fair eeny if you  are  the one making the rounds and running people over on your agenda. Though I reckon that Aisha’s flat’s got one of those fancy Sky subs now? You ought to invite her over once. We’ve been meaning to go for months.      Told you I’d sort out the Sky! Not because I like telly—well, I still can do—but because now that Myra’s around, I’m not about to watch a documentary about Norse sea-charts for the fiftieth time.      Oh dear, sorry Myra. I hadn’t meant—      Don’t worry, love. People’s got different things! I used to absolutely love those Naval history programmes. Good ones, too, not Watergate with flannel and reading aloud from a script.      Right, but back to me—so I still might go in-country on Monday, or work from Westgate from the Bed & Breakfast. My client’s been barking about not having enough time to confirm equipment.      All that project co-ordinatin’ work—sounds like you’re keepin’ up the coffee intake.      Just trying to stay afloat, honestly. I do wonder what you did before this lot. Or you, Myra—prior to being an education head, are there any past lives about which I’m wholly ignorant?      Oh, luv. I used to work at Swindon Municipal school barely two streets away. Then up moved to that lovely place, ‘Walbrook Grammar’ for guest speaker weeks. Tutored sundry Sixth Formers on the finer points of A-levels. Blew it all, mind, when I convinced a lad to rebel against his parents. He’s doing a PhD now.      More importantly, have we yet decided who's taking veggie lasagne this week or if the chicken is still goin’ on the slab?      I made both last Sunday, but only if we’re goin’ by the usual rotation.      I made it special with korma in the mix. Properly cooked in the hob, not like some casserole ‘dumped in the oven and cleaned up while it bakes’ varieties.      Again, I’m the supreme suffering one always getting 'Leftover night'!      Love you, uncle, you’re as bad as a toddler in the veg department.

Rather annoying I had to take the cat in to the vet earlier. I was just starting on that new Marks and Spencer pizza I've been meaning to try.      Yeah, I remember you saying it was the £6 one with the caramelised onions and rosemary. Sounds a bit fancy for a pizza, but I'm not one to complain about good food if it's on the table. Though I suppose that thirteen-year-old wine would have matched it nicely.      It would have done, if I hadn't accidentally served the twelve-year-old during the appraisal meeting with my boss last week. Not sure how it went, honestly—Managed to get through the whole thing, only to find out the bottle had Mycroft on the label later!      Ten points for the sense of humour, at least. Made you memorable. Though I did hear you got a decent appraisal eventually. The blenders department must be recognising your skills.      Blooming thanks for that! No, you didn’t—it's the first time I've been properly noticed in years. Though tell me—why is it that blenders are forever full of toothpaste as if their users are entirely incapable of reading instructions?      You'd think in this day and age people might at least check the manual before mistaking it for a food processor. Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses my name. I know it's such a common first name, but I always correct them after the first mistake. I can't say I'm over it yet.      You know, I kind of admire that you keep pointing it out. I usually just let it go, unless it's an obvious   blunder  . I had one of those a while ago — a customer service rep called me  Stephen  for ten minutes. I just sat there, like,  who's Stephen?       That's the worst. You'd think in this day and age, people would be a bit more attuned to names. Still, I suppose they're busy. Just wish they'd   check the name against the order   more carefully.      I know what you mean. Sometimes I just take the coffee and say,  Not quite me  and walk out. It puts a bit of a damper on my routine, you know?      It’s the little things that add up, isn’t it? I do tell you this every morning, but it really impacts my mood — even if it’s just for five minutes.      Fair enough. You’ve got a rhythm in the mornings. You want your tea just right. I often wonder if people like that — the ones who take their routines seriously — are happier overall.      I think so. Routines bring comfort. Like those days in the 1920s when everything seemed to just  click  into place. I wonder what it was like to have a life with real structure and expectations — even if they  weren’t ours  to begin with.      You always do such interesting jumps in conversation. From tea mishaps to imagining living in another century.      Well, we were talking about names and expectations. It made me wonder if people in the past had a stronger sense of belonging — to a time, a place, a  role .      I sort of see what you mean. I sometimes dream of doing a party where everyone dresses as historical figures and wears the period clothing. Some people would no doubt be  uncomfortably  uncomfortable.      I’d rather get the costume right than risk standing out like a sore thumb. Still, I’m always wondering about the person with the same name from the same time. The idea of   a soul mate   really captures my attention in that context.      It's a beautiful thought — that someone from over a hundred years ago, who lived through completely different lives, might be the one for you.

Rather annoying when the air conditioning breaks down on a sweltering day, isn’t it, Sarah? We had to close our shop mid-morning this week, and I can already see the impact on our sales figures for the month. You wouldn’t have any experience with such things, would you?      I can imagine how stressful that must be, especially if you're running a small business on your own. I have about five sweaters from a previous crafting project, and the pattern had this intricate looking thistle on them. I think it adds a bit of heart you just can’t get from a shop-bought item. I remember being asked once whether it was the 'British thing' to do—knitting, I mean. The guy thought we all come with a pair of knitting needles in one hand and a map of the world in the other.      That’s the stereotyping I was thinking of earlier, by the way.

Rather annoying this new tax thing eh?      Aye, it's mental. I mean, we're students, not millionaires, and yet somehow we're being taxed like we're earning a buck for every sunbeam we catch. I’ve found that often the true value of education isn’t necessarily always in the immediate career boost. Rather a lot, I must say. You know what it's like out there in the countryside — so much to see and so little time. We stayed at that YHA by the lighthouse, where we volunteered. We had Cornwall behind us, and the lighthouse, and all them crabs. That’s something.      That it is. And I’ll tell you this — I’ve had a life, and over this one’s not bad at all.

Rather a lot, didn't we, love? That supermarket do everything they can to get us ‘normal folks’ to buy a bit more. You’d think with prices like they are, they’d want to make it easier on us, eh? Right, I’m just scribbling down what we need for tomorrow’s shop. Let’s see... We’ve got the big chilli from the weekend, so mince, tomatoes, onions, garlic, and probably some fresh herbs.
