Any chance they could’ve got in from the balcony again? We might about blocked the gap up a bit, but the wind still gets through.      Maybe. I’ll check that tomorrow. Now, while we’re all up for domestic action, how ‘bout that football? I heard Manchester United pulled off a last-minute goal against City. Lean on it, but it was nice to see.      You mad or what? Last-minute goals are  excellent . Also, Everton beat Brighton with a penalty right at the whistles. I took the shot in our set-up, I told ya!      Penalty goalds on your own living room floor mean about as much as air, lad. But fair play to ya team—bit of an upset.      So summin’ up: shop list, manage the insect issue, check bee sting fix, and dont’ let dad eat the last tin o’ spam again. Crickey! It’s a full team effort up ‘ere. Always forget somethin’.

Honestly, I just can't get through PE anymore — especially with Mr. Price. Do you remember when he made us do a mile run in the rain last week?      Oh my gosh, I nearly chucked up halfway round the field. It was freezing, like seriously, I felt like I was going to catch pneumonia. Did he say  anything  to the teachers about it? Or is he just one of those "good for you" type coaches?      No, he’s like that. Know what's even worse? He doesn't chase when people don't turn up. I saw like three of us just leg it when he wasn't looking. What a load of nonsense. I miss Mr. Mycroft, you know, the one who left last term? He was strict, but at least he cared about technique and not just our stamina.      Yeah, and he definitely had a sense of humour. I remember that one time when Jack in Year 10 tripped over and we all fell into a group deadlift? Mr. Mycroft sat on the edge of the mat, smoking his pipe and just said, "Pass the chalk, someone. We might need it for the floor." Classic.      Hilarious. Oh, and have you seen the new YouTube vid from Lauren Royal? She posted a clip of her doing this huge experiment with vinegar and baking soda for chemistry? Honestly, I've been stuck on one of the worksheets Mr. Dunbar gave in this week — the one about fizzy tablets and gas displacement? It just feels like so much jargon.      Ugh, I still haven't got round to analysing those results properly. I nearly flaked out doing it because the questions just kept talking about different ions and reacting masses. Honestly, who even knows what that means?      Exactly! No one in that class understands, but for some reason we'reexpected to do A-level work. I just wish teachers actually explained it before setting something bloody hard.      I know, right? My brother told me that at his school they use YouTube a lot to break it down. I think Mr. Dunbar should do the same. Anyway, let’s get off this and talk about the real drama — go onto Instagram and tell me if you've seen Anya's story.      Oh, don’t go there — that girl’s story today was  so  dramatic. She made it seem like the whole year knew she was being followed by someone in the art block.

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been chuckin’ m’head out for days ‘n it’s barely shiftin’. I thought m’cough was goin’ on the mend, but then this cold hit me with a right ol’ slap.      Aye, that een’t nice at all. Did the doc say it’s just a cold or somethin’ more? I’ve been readin’ up on that Grossman bloke again; y’know, the one with that ai project at CAA? They’re doin’ some right odd stuff with body language recognition now. Could even tell if you’ve got a sinus infection, apparently.      Oh yeah? My turkey still looks like bin chicken. I left it in the back o’ the larder, so maybe that was a bit iffy? But I’m more worried about the cold ‘nuffers. I’ve been dossed up in the house all week in me basewi’ and oversized jumper, makin’ soup for the fifth time.      Water and rest, you know the drill. Although—speakin’ of, did ye hear about that food poisoning case at Addenbrooke’s? It was linked to that local takeout, from what I read. They’re checkin’ cameras an’ stuff. Seems one bloke got really sick after a takeaway chicken korma.      Oi, don’t talk about chicken korma just now. Reminds me of the time I got sent a dodgy chicken parcel by a_coll— retch . Still, mind ye, I’d be more worried about the vaccination line-up in this country. We’re about five years behind the curve in some areas, right?      True. There was that report last month that cited some big disparities across the Midlands ‘n the North. My supervisor’s got me lookin’ at health inequities for my PhD. It’s a real concern—how something as essential as a jab gets patchy coverage based on where you’re born.      Right. It’s always been the same, innit? More cameras in the North ‘n no flu jabs, where as places like Birming— cough —Birmingham get plonked with every medical innovation under the sun.      And the telly doesn’t help, y’know. The way news about flu or hospitals is always shown with some poxy cheap camera, like someone stuck a phone to a tripod. It’s ‘ollywooded health, innit?      You lot in Cambridge are all moanin’ ‘bout the postcode premium, but where I’m from, we’re just stuck with cold, dirty winters ‘n no timely care before it’s too late.

Rather annoying that the gridlock at the shopping centre last week. I was trying to buy some fresh mackerel, and I ended up queueing for nearly half an hour! Honestly, it felt as if the whole town had flushed through the butcher’s shop at the same time.      Oh, I heard about that. I think one of the queue-liners was actually on her third trip around the same sausage counter before giving up! I managed to avoid it, but I had to go to some tiny place on the outskirts instead. The mackerel wasn’t half as fresh as the bloke at the main shop, mind you.      All this talk of queues and shopping centres is beginning to remind me of when I was headmistress and the students all tried to cram into the canteen during lunch! Always thought I’d be the administrator of the most orderly scene, but no — it was breakfast, lunch, then late afternoon tea all mingled into one chaotic hour!      You should have seen it at the weekends. One time, we had a musical matinee, and half the parents turned up for the play instead of the actual children! They said they were only there to take pictures for Facebook. These days, everyone's photographing everything, from the way the potatoes are placed on the plate to the Scrabble tiles scattered across the board!      It’s gotten out of hand, hasn’t it? Last weekend, I posted a photo of the family playing Scrabble in one of the retirement homes. A man commented saying, “You should definitely buy the deluxe edition,” and I thought, dear heavens, it’s not even a game show!      I daresay the deluxe edition of our lives! But speaking of games, let’s not be too distracted. Speaker_1, you’re up next. You managed to drop in that quite impressive 7-letter word the other time — “quarantined,” was it? Well, the letters are still on the wooden board, ready to be claimed.      Ha, good memory. I’ll try to outdo that one with something culinary. I’ve been reading the latest issue of a food magazine where they talk about pairing mackerel with mangetout and gochujang — it’s supposed to be a real fusion!      I suppose it could go with most things, depending what your taste buds resemble. I have to say, I’ve never been one for putting gochujang on anything that came from a fish farm.

Rather annoying the queue, isn't it? That man in front’s practically had her tea and a browse first... What was I saying? Oh yes, I remember now. I had this idea after seeing a type of printing press at an exhibition in Frankfurt, I believe—some sort of wooden contraption, but it gave me the idea for the dry transfer print system.   Frankly  , I had no idea of the machinery involved but I knew I could sketch the concept and show it to someone with a workshop.   Clever chap from East London took to it like a duck to water.        You were already involved in printing systems even back then, I believe.   I remember hearing you’d shown up at an exhibition in Düsseldorf dressed in that red velvet coat of yours, much to the surprise of the locals who probably thought they’d seen everything in machinery.   But then you did, didn’t you? You had a flair—still do—for pulling people’s attention.      Oh, I didn’t have any flair then, I had a vision. And I had to keep up appearances—being British, and being in Germany, one doesn’t want to seem out of one’s depth. I think the curator there, Herr Klaus, was watching for the usual trot through exhibits, but I stayed.   Stayed till they closed, sketched, and then asked for a demonstration of the ink transfer system. It was clunky, but the method was beautiful.   You don’t see much like that these days.      No, you don’t. And it just goes to show, doesn’t it? That at some exhibitions, the real magic comes not from the patent board but from people like you, who have about five ideas boiling in a single mind.   I still remember the time you brought a whole booth of your prints to Hanover and then barely left the venue. You said you preferred to talk with people ‘between the stalls rather than at them’. A very British way of putting it, to be sure.          I always thought you had to meet someone at their level to make a connection.   I’ve seen too many English firms walk into a new market with all the subtlety of a bull in a china shop. You don’t make the kind of impression I did with my dry transfers if you don’t understand the culture—and I meant to understand, not just superficially.

Rather annoying when the teacher’s goin’ on about gramma or whatever and it’s like ‘Yeah, I got it in primary’ innit? It’s not like I need a textbook to tell me a verb is a doin’ word. Although I s’pose some of the past tense stuff can be eeny weeny wobbly if yer tryin’ to write an essay.      Aye, I dinnae ken that too much, to be fair. Me education was all about 'fer’ and '’ere' an’ whatnot. But, don't forget, language grows with us, love. Like,  ye  used t' mean the same as  you , but now it feels old turkey, y’know? So universities got themselves all hot about that, ain't they?      I think I migh’ take English at uni, but Mummy says it doesn’t lead to nothin’. Like everyone goes mad for lawyers or medics, but ever looked at what muppets do for a qwick? Like, I’d love to learn why we spell 'through' like that, innit? I mean, what the heck does thro' mean? It's like, we’ve got French words for no reason!      You’re no’ wrong about that one, lass, and mind yer tongue—quinoa’s the same sort of thing. All right, it’s healthy an’ all, but you’d think we’d carry on with what someone at Spilsby Market sells! That stuff just wants to be expensive.      Yeah, but it's a holiday! Maybe we’ll find a decent quinoa dish in St Ives? I did daftly walk past the farmer’s market in the village, but I couldn’t be bothered. There was this old woman selling pork sausages and she said ‘Come back to the pig, ‘e’s just like your daft young man.’ Bit funny, wasn’t it?      Oh, I love talking to farm folk. Me gran was a pig farmer. She’d say words that weren’t in any dictionary. She’d call lightning a ‘flash whacker’ if it struck the shed. Still remember that.      I think I’d go squiffy if it rained or there was a proper storm.      I’d be soddin’ well scared too, lass. But innit nice that we can help? Like with the registration for organ donations—there was a bit of a to-do on the news about ‘opt out’ systems.      Yeah, I read up on it at school. My friend’s dad had a kidney transplant, an’ it did save his life.

Rather than chuck a bar of chocolate in the bin, ye could’ve sticks it in the lasagne!  laughs  That’s what me mam used to do when she were smugglin’ sweets past me gran! “Lasagne surprise,” we called it… like it’d grow arms an’ legs an’ crawl out een!      [chuckles] Dunno, reckon I’ve had enough excitement a’ day. Boss at work swore at me this mornin’ cos I used stewin’ apples as pears in me wine. I were like “ay, it’s fruit, innit?” An’ he went mad! Still,  laughs  nothin’ short of a full mental hospital admission for me now if I don’t keep inventions simple!      Ten o'clock, y’know what them hospitals is like: full o’ geezers with tins for heads, waitin’ for breakfast, no doubt. Look, while everyone here’s playing inedible posh, ever considered a simple fag packet puffin’? Real down to earth, real reliable—settle the tummy and the soul in one hit!      Puffin’ and fag packets? Tell that to me bowels, Jack! We’ve been out of sync since I tried pina coladas with espressos last night. Anyhoo, Anna’s the one who set this up—tell them what you said to Anna, Rhys! Smashing the principles of hospitality in five seconds flat!      Yeah man, rush to tell ’em. You what you did to your hostess? What’s next, you invite som’one for dinner and end up in a fist fight with their toaster?      She said, “Rhys, if you don’t take this pasta carbonara off the hob and handle it like a decent cook, I’m takin’ the ladle and puttin’ it up your bum.” And I told her, “Anna, any ladle I had up me bum would be for waiting on me spoon while I’m spoon-feeding that carb pile of yours.” Then she flipped lunches on me and whacked me with a lemon zester…  laughs       Oh man, I can go out tonight on that life if you don’t cut it out! You’re like a pirate without a plank. Honestly, Rhys, sometimes I think your survival rate’s only at 10% cos of how you eat.      Tell that to the dodgy stew I served at ‘dump day’ last week at the site. I’m not entirely sure what I did to that meat, but it kind of started moving of its own accord once it left the pan!

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be at the pub mucking around than crammed into a lecture hall with a bunch of chancers. I’m more of a practical kind of guy      Look, I get that, but I kind of enjoy it, you know? I mean, I'm working my way through a postgrad in linguistics and if it wasn’t for that, I’d probably just be listing to bands or reading in this café again.      To be fair, you always had the brains for it. I never got the hang of the coursework at uni. I like mixing drinks more.      Yeah, but I'm still thinking about bartending like that My lectures are fine, but I still get left with a bit of a rummy head at the end of the day. I think it's because I spend most of it breaking down grammar for students. I envy you a bit working in a place like this — in a café at least you get to people-watch without the pressure.      That is the blooming best part, tell you what. I can listen to the occasional raffle or even a squabble and carry on with my job. Have you ever worked something like that before, by the way?      Not really. I mostly taught at the school, but they had a huge schedule. I didn't quite have time to dabble at something like this. Although, I did catch the odd shift at a bar someone at the language centre recommended.      That's oddly sour. You out there getting the hang of a cosmopolitan as a language teacher? That must’ve been a bit of culture clash.      It was! I watched the barman take this man from Belgium and just walk him through ordering a pint using French and Dutch and it was bloody brilliant.      That must’ve been rather education for you. I mean, that’s more me than the whole education angle any bloody day.      It was surreal, honestly. I think hearing someone learning that much of the language in a functional bar situation was a new perspective for me. Now, I am trying to set some trips where I can travel and speak the local language away goenvironment of my classroom.      Show respect, I like how you think. You might be the only bloke I know who can get a barista at Costa to fluently quote Bakunin while ordering a flat white.

Rather annoying when the kettle’s still not boiled, isn’t it? I was just starting to think it was never going to go off at all. I’m more than a bit late for my break time, and this is the second time this week. Look, George—get over here. We haven’t got all day!      It was bloody   57 degrees   outside all last week, Graham. I don’t know if I ever managed a decent cup of tea. If I’d had a choice, I’d have gone to the Gambia for a month during that, don’t you think?      George! Not the Gambia references again. What’s next, another beach holiday and a well-padded donation box for the village fete? I’m not sure I need to hear about the Dunes Inn this very moment. Do you have a point with all this storytelling, or is it just breakfast conversation material for you?      The point’s the   coffee  , not bloody hides or sand bars. I say we get the kettle over, or I’ll be over with a hammer—personally knocking it into the next room if necessary. What did you say, Iris?      I said—it wasn't just the heat, was it? You ever notice how some days it's like the roads are shifted, Graham? You go off to the shops and come back home to find your postcode’s moved a mile. And the other day, the car wouldn’t start at all. Spent half the morning trying to get it going.      Some people still manage to find a way to start and be late at the same time! Look, are we talking about a breakdown situation or about your Munchausen Syndrome again, Iris? You had me worried a week ago when you said you were going to make a donation box out of upcycled materials. My, what   coding techniques   you were going to use!      George, it wasn't any bloody coding! I said I was going to make little ones with plastic containers. Daisy had a handmade project at school. It was meant to be a hobby!      Well, let’s drop it and get something around this table. I told the church bell goers I’d make it if they let me sample the cake they made at the fete. I had a banner in the corner last week displayed what your hobby was, Iris.

Okay, I just wanted to say, I am  so  sorry I was late for dinner. The bus got delayed and I thought I’d never get here. But I brought a few apps I think we could all try out. Not sure if they sound interesting, but they’re supposed to be really handy for planning holidays and things like that.      Oh yeah? I just got back from a holiday a week ago, actually. Went to the Lake District and got absolutely lost in a field. It would’ve been nice to have had one of those apps then. Didn’t even want to rely on my phone too much, to be honest. I mean, dead zone much? So what’s the app called again?      It’s called TripPlan. You can upload a specific itinerary, or just let the app suggest things based on how long you want the trip to be and your budget. And wait — it even has activities grouped by mood. So if you fancy a spooky vibe, it suggests haunted locations and places people say have, you know… spirits.      Oh, like ghost hunting places? I’ve always loved that. My cousin went to a supposedly haunted hotel in Suffolk and she said the atmosphere was terrifying. I’ve been meaning to go with her. Does it suggest horror-worthy hotels too?      True, I love scary stuff. Though I’m not much into haunted places — maybe because I already feel haunted at home. No, sorry, don’t get me wrong — the food was great at dinner. But also suspicious. Like why was the chicken so rubbery?      Also, I thought the mint chocolate cake was divine. That’s all I’m saying. Anyway, Speaker_1, are there any horror movie suggestions in the app too?      Honestly, yes. It has a whole ‘movie and meal’ pairing section. So for example, if you’re going to watch  Hereditary , it suggests making something dark and brooding — maybe a red wine stew or something. If it’s  Saw , you can go mad with your favourite sugary snacks as comfort. Though I’ve seen people go full with popcorn and a horror flick and then have nightmares all week. My sister once cried after  It Follows .      Honestly, I think it was more of a romantic element. Like, my ex and I used to joke about watching horror movies together as a bonding experience. Now it’s more like, ugh, I just want to eat popcorn and not get emotionally broken by some murderer in a mask.

Rather annoying this, I must say. You’d think in this day and age, it would be easier to get a decent bus from Norwich city centre than it is to charter a bloody limousine. I told yer I don’t need no fancy vehicle, but George—  Speaker_3  , bless his heart—insisted on splashing the cash so as you all get here safe.      Oh aye, I heard all about that tiff this morning. Yer know George, he gets it into 'is head and 'e won’t take no for an answer. But don’t be too hard on 'im, dear. Still, if I'd known me legs were to give way on me like that in the middle of Station Approach, I’d 'ave taken the good 'ousekeeper up on the lift back 'ome. But I thought I'd be the brave one—leading by example, as it were.      Come now, Alf. You did fine in your own way, planting the oaks in the garden to mark the milestones of our journey. I reckon those blooming things’ll outlast you and me, and George—perhaps I mean that with a twinkle in his eye.      Aye, and watching him sweat it out pacing in that stupid cap of 'is—he looked about as natural as a kangaroo in a drawing room. Still, I imagine he means well. All that money he spent at the yard when he ‘fixin’ that banger up for 'is self—but in 'is defence, I suppose it was a noble effort. I had a similar ambition in my day, before my legs and my back gave up on me.      Oy, I do miss those old beastly Morris Minor bangers! Y’know mine had more leaks than a sieve and more corroded parts than you could count. But it bloody  worked , that’s what counts. Burgled once by some cheeky young 'uns, but 'eck, they didn’t steal a thing ‘cept me hubcap.      Aye, I remember my first project. Designed a suspension bridge out 'ere by the 'ore. It was one of the first such structures in the county road system, I believe.      Oh George go on about it for weeks if you let 'im go. But I digress. Right now, I’m just glad we all arrived safe and sound. Now, you two—let me get the kettles on, we’ll stew those legs and maybe even stir up a pot of stew for dinner, ‘cause I reckon we’ve earned it!

Rather annoying this new traffic system on the M6, isn't it? I was trying to get up to Manchester last weekend and it took ages. I’m more used to Dublin roads, sure, where traffic's mad but at least it doesn’t try to make you think you’re motor racing every two miles.      I understand the frustration, but at least the new toll system isn't making a profit off us, right? At least that's a bit of progress. Oh, and by the way, you'll be wanting to hear the news—our laptops are being sent out today.      Right, because of the system upgrades, is it? All this digital nonsense, only to find out half of it crashes before it's even finished being used. Speaking of which, I overheard the news the other day. Some of these new features are meant to make journeys faster, but they’ve just made it complicated. I miss old-fashioned driving!      Aye, technology’s changed ever since I started driving, even back when I was working. Good ones, mind you—calculators and things, but nothing like this. Though I have to say, your health as a driver matters more than anything, especially as we get on in years. I've started pacing myself when driving these longer distances. My back?      Listen, I know you're trying to be the picture of retirement health, but you need to look after yourself. I remember you collapsed at your sister's house two years ago. Let me book you in for a check-up, shall I?      That’s something, at least. Health and machines both being unreliable as we age. I had to stop driving because of my balance. Not that I liked the technology anyway. I still remember watching the lads at BP doing things manually. Proper know-how, you know? Nothing like this modern engineering nonsense.      Aye, you always were the traditional one, Micky. Still, maybe there’s something to be said for all this newer development, even if you miss the old ways. We could talk about moving somewhere that’s more central, especially if you want to avoid flying and long car journeys. I’ve been thinking… maybe you remember that house near Birkenhead?      Mm, your aunt had that place, didn’t she? You’re not sure, are you, Mummy? That might be a bit near your brother’s place.

So did someone actually find it? Or was it just, like, dumped somewhere? Because I  still  can’t believe someone stole it from outside the college canteen! That was such a  genius  bike!      Oh, it turned up in a skip inDeerfield, apparently! A lady who was going through some bins with her little girl found it. Proper sad story, really.      Ay! What! In a skip?! Oh my gosh, did they get it cleaned up at all? I hope whoever took it had the decency to keep it safe rather than just trashing it! Still,  why  would they chuck it like that?      Seems like the turkey took it because they thought it was left behind, tried to sell bits on Facebook Marketplace, but when they couldn’t get a decent price, just gave up and threw it. Poor thing! Your breakfast, by the way — this happened  last week  in case you were wondering why I haven’t mentioned it sooner.      No way! So it was like a proper  scavenger  treasure? Oh, I hope it’s not broken! I’ve still got grief stickers on it and everything. Did they get it back to you? Or will it be coming home directly?      No, I got it, because the skip was near my mum’s place. It was muddy as heck and the chain was rusty, but the frame’s okay — just a bit of a wipe down and it should be back to normal. I’ll give it a full clean at the weekend and paint the letters back on the wheels.      Aw,  thank you so much  for doing that. I’m literally not even mad anymore, okay? Although, I  am  a bit mad that the college couldn’t do more to stop bike theft. Like, couldn’t they have just put up a proper rack?      I did actually speak to the head of the student services a few days ago. Turns out they tried to apply for grant funding for a bike shop security system, but the funds disappeared into a black hole somewhere with lunches and maintenance.      Ugh, no way!  That  is so annoying. I told my friend Eloise that I need to invest in a heavy-duty lock next time, and she said I could password-protect it with a box and bungee cords — yes,  joking  — I seriously might!      Well, now that I’ve got your old one back, we can have a little fixer’s day and get everything sorted.

Rather annoying when the train’s perpetually delayed, isn’t it? I was just trying to work out if it got us to destination on time after this last stop. I can’t say I’ve ever been a fan of transport schedules.      Ah yes, well, the timing relies on how far you are from Newton, don’t it? Having grown up in Cardiff, I’ve dealt with most of the Welsh rails in my day—none of this stuff follows a conventional timetable. Sometimes you’d get there quicker if you just took the bus.      That’s the worst. You spend ages frozen to your seat, brooding over every mile, hoping someone at the next junction has finally decided to let that signal go green. I remember being stuck between Wrexham and Tenby once on the charity train, shouted at the guard I think he turned round and gave me a biscuit instead.      Bucksy? Now that’s not a bad thing if you ask me. I always take a little bag to the station. Sandwich, maybe a few biscuits for mercy—never trust the guards, luv, they’ve got their own rations. Like a week’s worth of grief.      Honestly, watching the two of you rhythmically rage against the national rail is like – Mate, have you two considered, like, flying?      Flyin'? Mate, you know as well as I do that plane leaves you with more luggage, and the coffee feels someone else put it in a bucket.      That’s sour grapes talk—everyone’s got at least one flight horror story. But here’s the thing, I don’t mind trains because most people about them are civil. You don’t barge past the queue at the boarding gate and stuff like.      Speaking of which, have we managed to run out of the decaf in the kitchen? I swear it’s gone. I did put that box on the shelf the day before yesterday.      Yes, I think little ones might have discovered the coffee stash as well. Though to be fair, it’s their first time living in a place with mismatched chairs and a sink that you can hear the source of the water from the bathroom.      If you ask me, it’s practically a camping trip. Complete with no hot water and a Wi-Fi connection that periodically behaves like your ex.      Ah yes, and despite the questionable plumbing, we’ve all managed to belly up to the table on time.

Rather annoying when the beer’s warm, isn't it? I mean, you’d think by now in 2025, we’d have figured out more efficient ways to cool it, especially in a country where it's practically part of the national identity to sit outside on a sunny bank holiday with a nice pint and a barbie.      Yeah, I reckon it depends where you are. In London, we’re always under flat roofs and in tiny back gardens, so chilled beer is a luxury, not a right. We’ve gotten used to the idea that you chase it with ice.      Right, but here in Norfolk, when you're out in the garden, it's another world. You’ve got the birds, the sunset, you’re playing board games, you just want to sit back, relax, and not pick up a beer that’s screamed ‘flat’ in your face the moment you took the lid off.      Fair enough. I suppose part of the culture is about location and what's accessible to people. Like the games we play over here too, it’s not the same as back in the capital. We’ve got way more family-oriented stuff. We still play Catan sometimes, but more often it's something like Azul or Carcassonne. You get that national personality – calm, deliberate, fairly strategic, and not death-defyingly fast-paced.      Yeah, and it's partly because we live together and don’t want the kind of board games that someone at full volume shouting “I’ve won!” after a chaotic round. I mean, not that you don’t enjoy a bit of chaos sometimes… it’s just more considered here.      True, about the chaos. That said, you can still bring the heat with the right vibes. I remember you and your sister once had that massive Monopoly war that lasted three nights. You’re quite the board game generaless when you put your mind to it.      Oh, I was mainly trying to outmanoeuvre your sister, bless her. She’s the one who tried to hoard every railway line and always ended with a mortgage portfolio and no wherewithal to actually play the game.      Fair play! But it's one of the best conversations we’ve had in a while. Just two lecturers, a few beers, and figuring out why the box contents of "Twilight Imperium" keep changing with each retailer.      Yeah, I think those kinds of mornings—or afternoons—are exactly why we ended up where we are.

Rather annoying to be honest, we had our request in six weeks ago and they still haven’t even passed it to the right people, let alone sorted the bins yet. I can't believe how much time we’ve lost fighting with them over this.      Yeah, well, the timing was pretty awful on our part anyway, considering we moved out the week   ANON   was on annual leave. No wonder they’ve taken so long to get back to us.      I just wish it was someone local. Rather annoying this, isn't it? You think they'd do something about this stretch—the TLS came out first thing this morning and I haven't even got a chance to properly read it yet. Rather skip to the part where you two tried to build a tent in the hurly-burly in Yorkshire... What was the daft mistake you made this time?      Oh, that! Rather do a bit o’ wild winter camping, I say. A few people think it’s mad, but it’s the clearest way to see the stars, eh? Not a single light polluting the sky like it does in London. I’ve read somewhere that being close to the natural world helps slow the mind een if yer just sleepin’ in a tent with nothin’ but the wind dancin’ round you. A lot o’ research done in this area, incidentally; mind and body responses to elemental environments. Pity me back was never quite for this when I was younger, but now at my age... well, I reckon even older bones appreciate a bit o’ cold and firelight now and again.      Oh, I’ve done a wee bit o’ it back in the Borders – the moorland, the cold, the loneliness of it. It strips you bare, aye? Not in a negative way, mind you – just... ye feel everythin’. No technology, no modern comforts. No, you strip back to the basics, and once you’ve done that... you feel like a keener version o’ yerself. I find with patients who’ve lost their way, takin’ them out in nature helps remind them who they are. The air feels cleaner, thoughts clearer. Of course, it’s got to be done carefully, though. You cannae just chuck somethin’ like winter camping at everythin’ – it’s not a miracle cure, just a form o’ self-discovery.      Precisely. That’s the magic o’ it, isn’t it? It ain’t for the faint-hearted, but if you’ve got the will, it reshapes how you live yerself. I remember the first time I did it – mid thirties, and thought I was bein’ dramatic. But it taught me to be more mindful. My, I realized how much I’d been overlookin’ simple joys. The way the frost clings to your eyelashes when you wake up, the sound o’ distant birds at dawn. We get lost in our daily hustle so easily. Evenin’ by the fire, a thermos of tea, and the stars. That's where reflection happens.      I’ve taken some gooners on pond life surveys up in the Highlands – not quite camping, but in the spirit, I suppose. The further you get from everything, the better yer reconnect with summat deeper. I’ve been kina heartened to see those with stress or even mild depression find purpose in it.

Rather than just a DVD, eh?      Aye, it's such a classic. I got the Criterion Blu-ray with the extras and all. Proper box set, like a museum bit. Like, what was it, '81 or '82? Bit of a gap in the oeuvre.      Yeah, 1981—straight after  The Empire Strikes Back . That was a bold moveitunes that the turkey came out after such a big hit.      I ain't seen the Dune films, and I think I turned off Halfway through Star Wars VI. But you’re telling me it was good then? I mean, not a Gamechanger like the others, but decent?      Decent is one word. Good is another. It’s got its fans, you know. There’s a cult-like side to it. Like a bit of a guilty pleasure. Kind of like ... I dunno, watching  300  in the dark.      Mate, I love a bit of ridiculous action flick.  300  is somethin’ to me. But I dunno what to expect from Star Trek Beyond. Dunno if it was someone at Spock’s funeral or not. You seen it?      Oh yeah, had the kid for a birthday and then the cinema crowded up with teens all analysing it as if it were a thesis. Not bad though. Better than the Kakadua one, I’d say.      Yeah, that was grim. I mean, it’s Star Trek, right? My grandma read the books and treasured them. All that tragedy, philosophy ... and now it’s become a teenage shizzle show. I mean, I dunno how people can still take it serious.      Some of the old guard always comes with 'Oh, the golden days were better.' But the recent ones, you know, they’re trying t’do the visual bits right goenvironmental on the original vibes. It’s not so much about deep thinking as it is action and dialogue. But it’s bloomin’ fun what your lot do with the franchises these days.      Yeah, I think those days are gone. You don’t get the kind of books that shaped minds like Asimov and Clarke anymore. I’m not entirely sure if I like that or not. But where would we be without all the movie adaptations?

Right, so today I was helping Joshua with his Brownie Promise evening poster, and it made me think—what if we made it into a story? It could be about helping others, like a quest or a little adventure.      That sounds fun! Can the main character be a rabbit in a sweater? I like rabbits!           And a wheelchair rabbit! Cause I once had a rabbit called Puddles who wore a sweater when it rained.           Didn’t your Puddles also try to eat my keyboard once?           Yeah, that was funny! So that rabbit turkey, I mean rabbit, who wore a sweater, could be on a mission to fix things or help people, and the tools he uses? Lego bricks!           Can I use Lego to help build the story? Maybe I can draw it in my book, like a comic. Also, the rabbit could use a typewriter to write letters.      Oh, the typewriter! Remember your uncle’s old one from when he did his exams as a kid in the 90s? It was such a clunky thing. Made the most satisfying  clinks  with every keystroke.      Yeah! He had to hit the keys really hard. I once accidentally typed the whole word “Microsoft” in all caps just because I found it funny!           So the rabbit with the typewriter is going to type secret codes and be a spy?           Well, maybe not a spy. Maybe just the kind of adventurer who documents every part of a mission. But if you want that to be the case, it becomes a  super hero  secret agent rabbit. Go for it.      And what if his sidekick is a PlayStation? Or a telephone?           I don’t know if the sidekick can be a PlayStation, but if you want your computer or the PlayStation to be the invention he uses, maybe that works. But where do we fit Excel into the story?      Excel is where you type boring stuff like numbers, right? Is it like a magic spreadsheet?      Exactly! And your rabbit adventurer could use Excel to keep track of all his missions and roles in his mission log. Maybe even assign points, like a scorecard for doing good.      Or he can use it to count how many times he’s helped someone. Like a “kindness tracker” chart!      That’s a great idea, and it ties into the real-life mission you’re doing for your Brownie Promise. Maybe you can start writing it down in Excel for real too.

Rather skip the new coat till we've scrubbed up, I think. Like some mad tea party that never happened. It's a pity we don't have more adventurers walking those places—those ancient villages like that. You'd think someone'd build a B&B there. Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That phone of mine’s practically ancient. I keep thinkin' I ought to get a new one, but I just don’t fancy spendin' a fortune on a flashy thing. Honestly, I’m feeling your pain. Workload is pulling me under. We’ve had three copy edits and a new client literally halfway through the project. All that “shared kettles are the building blocks of community” talk. Anyway, what's this someone at work doing for the summer? That accountant friend of yours, Karen?      Karen is going to Prague and then volunteering with an NGO. I said I was going to save money and maybe do something sensible like finally take the trip to the Lake District my dad keeps suggesting. My parents think I should get a teaching certificate like my cousin.      They see you as a teacher or a therapist, innit? I think they see everyone's job in three types—educate, counsel, or service. It's like The Help 3.0 roles in their heads.      True, but we talk about that every over-egg breakfast or at Aunty Brenda’s homemade macaroni lasagna.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think when you get into the habit of running, it gets easier... but the weather always has to be against you. I only ran three miles last week — well, tried to — but it was beginning to hail, and I felt like an absolute   madwoman   out there in the wind with a bobble hat on.      Hmph, I've never been into running, personally. I do a bit of cycling, keep the stiffness out of the old bones. Still, I admire you lot, honestly. I couldn’t imagine doing it every day. What’s the point, really? You get older anyway, no matter how much you exercise!      Oh, you're just trying to avoid the guilt, love! But let's change the subject, since I'm feeling properly peckish now. How did your little project go, Mum? You were trying out that new recipe from the book club, weren't you? Some of the others at the meeting were less than impressed. Still, at least no one got food poisoning!      I prefer my bakes reliable, like a good Victoria sponge. Honestly, you try anything too fancy and it's barely a week before it goes up in smoke — quite literally, in some cases!      A tragedy, really. And while we're on the subject of disasters, have either of you seen the current house prices in our area? We barely live in a village and they've gone up by nearly ten percent this quarter! It's madness.      That's just it, isn't it? We think the market is cruising, then suddenly it's all about 'gentrification' and investors buying second homes in the countryside. I don’t know how long any of us can stay here without selling up at the first chance.      That’d suit me just fine — always liked the idea of downsizing and moving to somewhere quieter, further up the coast.

Rather annoying the new budget, eh?      Aye, it's mad they’re piling all the costs on to uni students now. Ever since I got into civil engineering after uni, I’ve thought we were £20k richer than we are! But you can’t even get student finance een if yer workin'?!      I reckon it depends where yer livin’. I’ve been transcription-blin’ documents all week from a social sciency project. One of the interviewees said it’s just impossi’le for her famil’ in Salford with a uni-age kiddle to even afford even part-time work. She’s workin’ six days a week and still in poverty.      That’s har’ to fathom. Ten years go, I’da been on yer books for that kind o’ research. Living with ma gran while doin’ ma PhD. She’d been nursing at Medway till she was 73 and e’d be bleedin’ hides if she didn’t have a bit of security. I dunno, I think the system just jumps round for some and leaves others dangling!      Here’s the thing: when you start dealin’ with language data—what people say and don’t say—it gives you a real lens into how economics shape lives. I mean, I worked on a project in York once, and the disparity between working-class families and their use of generational wealth was stark! Y’know, some people just get handed opportunities in dress-up boxes while others are climbing a ladder made of wet string.      Fair enough. So while I’m here, replying to site managers about drainage plans in Boreham about how we’re walkin’ gold round the area, you lot are deep in document queues in ty汥s of people telling you barely survived the housing crisis. No wonder we’re all just a bit over it!      Aye, it’s wild. Though to be fair, I was at the  Les Miserables  musical on Friday. I could see the parallels clear as day. You’ve got Jean Valjean with his jailed past and the poor folk in Montreuil-sur-mer—it’s a bit of a tellypiel version, but still goenvironmental on the soul if you ask me.      Oh I love that show! It always hits ‘ome—like when the revolutionaries sing  Do You Hear the People Sing ? Such a rallyin’ cry for justice, even if we don’t get to take it literally here.      Exactly.

Rather annoying this, innit? These gutters done me in. I was thinkin’ ‘ow much it’d cost to get a professional in, but then Blaire mentioned you, so I thought, “Ah, why not ask the man ‘oo’s got one hand on motor cars an’ t’other on concrete.”      [laughs] Aye, Blaire's all right for recommendations. I’ve ‘ad worse jobs in me life—like crawlin’ under a ‘ouse to fix a drain once. Know what I was thinkin’ when me trousers got soaked? That I’d rather be fetchin’ folk in me cab. At least I get t’listen to me radio!      My word, you seem to love your work. I’ve tried rallyin’ the lads at the uni, pushin’ em towards the arts. Film an’ acting, mostly. ‘Course, when I suggest it, I get a “But I’d be bad at it, you know?”      Aye, I get that too. A rooftop in Marseille, the light, the people about to fall in love... it brought a man down the street to tears.      Aye, I like that. I've only ever painted a ‘ouse in my entire life, ‘course. I like movies too. My missus dragged me into that play in Bootle. Didn't get ‘alf of it, I’ll be honest, but I liked the gist. Feels as if I were in the story for once.      That's the beauty of it, Johnny. Whether you’re delivering a line with style or fixin’ a gutter goin’ on your own, you’re creatin’ something, innit? I’ve got a student who bought a box of old films from a ‘and-me-down in Kirkby. The man was cleaning out his attic, and she said “They don’t cost much, but they worth the world, ‘cause they’re rare.”      Second-hand purchases—keeping the best for posterity, innit? Rather annoying the amount of traffic we're getting for a rural backwater like this. Don’t they know it’s got to be some quiet country road? Rather annoying this newfit lot o’ technologies, ay, Sarah? I was just trying t’message Hal when I crashed out ‘n shot it all across the room. Not a week goes by where I don’t hear o’ sommat new they want me t’get used to. And it’s not like eeny harm’s come t’me, but my son nearly had his tea cup all over me!      Oh, Nan, that was just a funny! You startled ‘im terribly, pulling that phone out and hurling it like a stone. Didn’t even get the chance t’catch it before it went clattering. Still, I can see it’s a struggle, all them apps and messages and whatnot.      Grandma! Don’t tell me you’re still on the phone with Darcy, is y’? Aunty Sharon says you’re far too old for ‘influencers’ and whatever that TikTok lot are up t’.      And why not! I fancies me a good laugh when I sees one.
