Let’s also nay forget why we are here, love. We’re clearin’ out the attic before your Nan wants to give it ‘er quilting museum make over. Found some precious stuff in about five old boxes—photos, letters, the lot. Some o’them dates back t’her youth! Proper olden days.      Aye, I’ll have y’ ‘cos I was rather bonkers in my youth, what with that business at the chemist. Got sent t’the institute once or twice for being too curious when I shouldn’t’ve been. Still, I’m here now, aren’t I? And I ain't allowin’ ‘mental illness’ t’stop me livin’.      That’s the spirit, love. I think it’s wonderful y’are so open about it. It’s far too rare in our age group, and far too many shy away from talkin’ about it. The kids today? They seem more in touch with those feelings, don’t y’ think?      ‘Course I do! We talk about everything in school. Like, my missus says we’re all pressure cooked and anxiously yucky all the time, so we might as well talk.

Right, lads, here we go — I’ve just bought this brand new laptop, and I thought it’d be a good idea to show it off properly. Blows! It's got a proper proper graphics card for editing photos and all that. Look at the hinge! Creaks a bit, but it’s all stylish now, yeah?      Blimey, that actually looks not too bad. I mean, I use one of those Chromebooks at work, and it’s alright for teaching, but it’s light-years away from decent software for editing. Do you want me to test some of the specs for you?      Aye, that'd be cracking, man. You know your stuff well. I still can’t get my head around why I can’t just plug my old camera memory card in. It's one of them newfangled USB-C ports again, innit? Probably better for gaming, but I’m more of a photography bloke.      Nah, it's USB-C, not flash-C. Should work with an adapter, or just buy a proper card reader, yeah? I’d say try the Wi-Fi next — your flat’s bound to be griefing off something old-school like a 2G dongle.      That’s a good idea – Mate, let me boot it up and try loading Blender for a second. Let’s see if it stutters or anything. Silly question, but is the fan working? Mine died and I spent a week not knowing.      Yeah, the fan just whirs like a proper beast when I start up some editing. I think the graphics card’s kicking in all right. Though, there is a bit about the battery... It dropped from 80% to 75% in 10 minutes and I wasn’t doing anything. Supposed to handle 8 hours, but that’s just nonsense, innit?      Aye, probably that screen’s eating it all. Those LED ones are all glary but power hogs. I remember my nan’s old laptop from 2007 being 12 years old with a pixelated screen but lasted all day. Some things, no matter how proper, never run.      Yeah, go back to the 80s or something. Just give it a memory upgrade in specs. Hopefully, it'll go further once that's done. Pass it here, I'll have a look.      Cheers, man. I really don’t want this thing to let me down like that ‘dreadful’ phone I bought from eBay last year.

Rather do this than sit at home, I suppose. Bit of a promising little place, don’t you think? What d’you think of the decor?      Yeah, it’s got a nice little vibe. Not quite as scruffy as the places round the corner. And it’s new, which is always exciting, isn’t it? You get that little sense of potential.      Aye, though I still can’t get this town to feel entirely like home. It was easier pulling someone to Cambridge and pretending to be normal. But this place… it’s quieter.      Not to worry, it does take a little getting used to. What I found strange first was the silence of the mornings. Back in Manchester, you could hear the world going by from ten paces back.      Hmm. The silence has its privileges. It gives you time to think properly. And when you’ve been nursing your mind through some mess... Well, silence isn’t bad. Only, sometimes that silence can be louder than anything else.      I know what you mean. I’ve had my own battles—nothing I’d call addiction quite yet, but still. I think for a while, I used work and others’ problems as a rhythm to keep from falling apart. It kept the cycle going: burnout, recovery, burnout again.      Doesn’t quite work that way for all, though. I’ve seen people chase after that cycle, and never quite reach someone who can catch them. And when you can’t even find your own identity outside of that—job, role, expectations—it can be real hard being yourself.      Yeah, identity is a funny thing. I try to remember the person I was when the world didn’t have so much a say in who I should be. Not that I mind the job, teaching English, but it’s just a job for now. I still dream of something more.      Dreams. Good. Even if it’s all it is. I tried once, long time ago, but I lost my way. Now I just try to live day to day with lunches like this and long walks to burn off the extra stress. You should try it—fitness.      Yeah, go on then. But it’s more of a habit now. Gotta look active in front of the kids. Although it does help—walking through the woods, keeping fit. It clears the head.      That’s the trick, isn’t it?

Rather skip the queue and just get us online tickets, innit. The Dorset Steam Fair’s been piling in the crowds, I heard. I’m more than happy to take a look online and sort it out for us. Not like I’ve got plans this weekend anyway — well, other than getting burgled by ticket prices, I mean.      I reckon prices are up as well. The last time I went, I think I paid more for a booth to squint at a steam engine wobbling about. We’ve no end of options for what the tickets even get us.      Right, but it’s mostly family stuff. I reckon it'd be nice for the grandkids to have a bit of a look around. Still, enough talk — I’m not sure if I’m going to be able to go if there’s not accessible entry for me. It’d be a shame if they’re not breakfasting with old engines and proper jam butties after all.      That is a thought, Mona. You always have the care for people, don’t you? I should do a bit of reading on what’s available — I can check online quite easily as it is. I’ve got a tablet, thank heavens for that. Makes me feel nearer to being with it.      Mate, I can just deal with it, it won’t be hard. Let me sort the tickets out and check what the disabled facilities are too. There’s a few things we’d have to consider, someone said there are ramps and accessible loos. Not bad for a bunch of oddly dressed folk pretending they’re still the 1800s and being powered by puff and puff.      Sounds good, doll. I was also thinking about our mam咪咪’s old cat, Tiddles — what if he fails to survive the weekend with barely a chair to curl up on? We’re thinking of shifting some things out of the living room for the fair anyway, perhaps that’s a chance to sort it out a bit too.      Ah, the cat. He’s a stubborn one, as we all know. But we can always set up a temporary roost for him in the garage if the living room's too much for the furniture.      Yeah, go for it. But let me get the tickets sorted so at least we’re not in the lurch when we get there.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘ere. I got the seats all out for the visit today, and I’ve had to wrestle ‘em inside three times already. Not to mention the daisies—  Lottie   tried to make a card on cardstock, and the thing curled like an accordion by the time it got in the envelope.      Aye, well, that’s Yorkshire weather for you; it’s got as many moods as a Sunday school preacher. I hope you didn’t chase the chairs too far with Mrs. Whates’ cat. That one does  not  like me, and the last time I grabbed her, she made a MySpace profile out of my new skivvies. But back to the visit—how are the rest of the arrangements?      Oh, dear, about the move—  Tommy’s   old dorm at Kendal’s still a bit in shambles, thanks to that Twitter argument he got embroiled in about the Oxford comma. I told him to stay out of it, but no, he had to prove I’m short-sighted.      It wasn’t that bad, mum. It was just… spirited. And it was all in good fun. Besides, it’s been a fairly quiet week in the literary world—more mundane than the usual. Now don’t go making mortal sin out of a typo. And we’ve found that the toilets in the old dorm work at full capacity now—after a trip to the local plumbers down Winn Plaza. Turns out you had to whisper a prayer in the sink and grovel at the pipework.      Not nearly as daft as the time the church choir from Thirsk had this “spiritual anthem” where they had to raise their hands like they were trying to juggle gremlins to the sky, ‘cos the rector got it in his head that it was active participation. I reckoned it looked a bit too much like the Birdman of Alvtuna waiting for a prize.      Oh, but  you young folk  with your tech and new-fangled ways. Now if you’ll excuse me for a minute—  Darren   , if you don’t mind sourcing one of those artisan cheese wheels, I’d like to give it a traditional Kendal Tom Kitten recipe. The latest version includes fermented walnuts and a ladle of metaphorical regret.      It’s a pity we can’t have a performing arts night while we’re at this.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to take both of you to the dentist this week—the hearing test passed first... got to pick James’ progress through the system yet?      I suppose so. I don’t really mind dental appointments, but I do frightened by the things that make funny noises. Hasn’t Margot had hers?      Who's Margot? An old friend of mine named Ashaad once told me that this lady he adores is named Margot. Is that someone you're talking about?      Didn’t even want to mention Ashaad right now... Not to ruin the mood, but speaking of appointments, did someone mention birthdays?      Oh yes My turkey and my brother Marco share a birthday. I find it quite fun, to be honest.      I think it's cool. Like you're both breaking the cake at the same breakfast, no doubt. Do you have some plans for it in mind?      I told you to think about that—and I still haven’t heard your answer—about the outdoor cinema, yes? But I’m not the one who needs attention quite yet. Did you know I'm currently designing colour cards for a project on Monet? Sounds extra rhythmical when put like that.      Only fairly recently, and I barely paid attention to the details. More pressing matters: I did have chocolate for easter. It was super lovely, but it made homework harder.      Remember when we went on that school trip to the gardening center and we got to plant something each? I planted a radish and it didn’t grow at all! It was so sad because it made about five days of conversation.      You had this chance to be a little farmer and fails—you know that was you barely gave the radish a chance? You’re quite similar, in that sense, to your guest speaker last month who did not speak up at all on the day of a event planned all through the year.      Well, I did my hearing tests and that math thing. Even if it’s not lunches, I think math is fun. Not if the questions are too hard, obviously.      Math is tricky because go so fast on your own if you don’t get something. But I find dentists are interesting, especially because they go on and on about bacteria and your teeth.      The lives we live, eh? Both of you pretending to know what you like, while I’ve got to plan for two over-enthusiastic mornings this week.

Rather skip the queue at the café today.      Ah, it’s mad in there, isn’t it? I saw it on my way down. Not a seat left      Honestly, £6 for a sandwich and no pesto on the menu? Madness      Yeah, I understand the menu choices, but I reckon it depends on where they source most of their ingredients.      Honestly, I’m so over it. It was easier back in uni. We’d just pop to the Morrison’s and chase it up with a pasty and crisps.      Oh, I remember that. We used to fight over the last blue cheese cracker      Ha! Yeah, and you’d always win because you’d sneak in while I was paying I think I turned round once and you’d vanished      I still can’t believe I hated blue cheese back then. My taste buds have developed, thank you very much      Well, that’s university for you, isn’t it? Small, chaotic living, and somehow, we got by      Yep. And I actually miss it. At least in halls, we didn’t have to worry about cleaning the kitchen. Now, who does it: me, my housemate, or the ghost of the previous tenant?      Honestly, I moved in with my flatmate Liam at the weekend, and he's just someone who lingers in the kitchen with his phone in a rush to clean up. I’m out in the hall, thinking: “Come on, be a bit more responsible.”      Sounds like about half the people I know.      Oh, but let’s not be too gloomy. Life’s better now. I mean, I’m working from home as a copywriter, for goodness’ sake. Geo., can I even believe it?      Unbelievable. You always had a bit of a way with words. I could see it from our GCSE project on the persuasive writing unit.      Thank you! That was such an interesting class. Still remember delivering the presentation with that dog in the background?      The Cavalier King Charles? That one that refused to line up? It was brutal.      And what your teacher said at the end: “Not bad, but the dog’s performance outshined yours.”      Ha! I still have a laugh over that. At least I landed a job in S&L therapy. I like helping people, especially in acute care. It's rewarding to see people make recovery, even small steps.      That’s brilliant. Being around it, seeing the small conversations, the first words after a long silence, it's personal.

Rather skip the new bar in town, if I were you. A promising sign for the community, but let’s be honest, it's no local dining room yet. I prefer a few glasses of wine with a close circle of friends over a trendy spot, even if it says 'rebranding'. Do you remember the beginning of my cycling adventures around the countryside when I was just a child? I used to ride for miles with just a map, no provisions, and a lot of courage. Oh, how far we've come as a journey!      Funny you should mention that, Jan. I remember riding my bike to Ramsgate pier with my father. That was before the roads got so wide and cars managed to fill the skies like clouds. Still, those were the good old days. As for the bar, yes, I too feel it's not quite the little local watering hole everyone was hoping for. Though better than when it was a bingo hall!      The bar at least brings some color to the grey, Ken. Still, the original plan for a community arts centre was far more interesting. My, those days in Manchester, when the regeneration began in the 80s and the whole city started to look like a different place… reminiscent of how it used to be when it was known for its mills – but with a new twist.      True, but the cheapest way to make a new friend is through their feet. Speaking of which, you heard about the jive event in the converted barn near here, didn’t you? Perfectly laid out, and oddly, the acoustics are very good for a barn. I thought being an oral surgeon removed all my musical ballet, but it seems I still have the rhythm in my bones!      I had heard about it. Maybe we could all go together. Speaking of which, have you managed to book in? I tried, but the show was fully booked by the time I called.      I know it sounds a bit ‘at sea', but I tried using them restricting waiting lists – just like the dental appointments back in the day. Rather amusing how the NHS would 'split a lecture' with your oral surgeon if the schedule was full for lectures, something akin to jiving!      That reminds me of a tale of a French real estate deal I once heard in Manchester. Rather quaint. He went with a violin and a bottle of brandy and made all the right moves!

Rather than going the traditional route of tutoring books or software, what if we focus on creating microlearning modules—basically, bite-sized educational videos—specifically designed for schools or even parents wanting to supplement their kids’ learning at home? We could call it something like "FrameLabs" or "SceneEd"—something visual and smart, yeah?      I like the direction you're going with it. A lot of parents I've spoken to in this house-sit have mentioned how tough it can be to keep kids engaged online. Maybe the videos could be short, action-packed, and based on real-world case studies like you mentioned earlier. Think  60 Seconds with Shakespeare  or  30 Minutes with Microbiology .      Exactly! The beauty is that we could team up with educators from schools or universities. We pick cool real-life projects—like a documentary team assembling a short film about climate change, or a history teacher explaining how to read primary sources via micro-docs. People’s eyes light up when they see learning in action. And the short format makes it perfect for mobile—parents and teachers can integrate it into PDHPE lessons or occasional home learning sessions.      And the real-time comments and embedded quizzes in each clip would help track engagement and understanding. We could even offer a subscription for teachers to get new content monthly, and maybe a basic version free for home use. Word of mouth spreads easily when you do something useful and beautiful. Have you ever heard of the principles they use in TED-Ed? That’s a good reference point.      Totally. I think what made TED-Ed work is the interactivity and accessibility—students aren’t just watching; they’re participating. We could do something similar but even smaller. Maybe start with 10 or 20 pilot videos on different subjects. Let’s meet up with some of the teachers from the Facebook group I mentioned. My idea is to put the development in their hands while we provide the platform. It’s open-source mentality meets business model. What do you think?      You’re getting your entrepreneurial spark back! I like that we’re doing something practical, creative, and not too flashy. If we do it well, it could become a meaningful supplement for teachers trying to manage class size and tech literacy. And really, for kids growing up in social media, this is how they learn best—chunks, stories, and screenshots of big ideas.

Rather annoying, though, isn't it? That Christopher keeps going on about his boat. I mean, he’s got the yacht, and all—_and he_ still_ talks about it like it's this grand adventure every time. Not to mention he likes to rope Simon in for weekend cruises. Do you remember the time we went out with them?      Oh, definitely. Classic Christopher. Though I suppose Simon doesn’t mind. He actually quite enjoys the social side of it all. It was quite interesting, though. We were out in the Solent when the wind picked up suddenly.      Yes, yes! And you'd made that awful meat pie—well, I still can't quite understand why you think turkey and apricot is a combination—but left it on the counter while we were below deck adjusting the sails, and of course, the wind screamed through the boat like it was a ghost gig. And when we finally got back up to the deck, the kitchen in his boat was looking more like a tornado had been stored inside it for a few hours!      I was tempted to tell him I had some sturdy apricot glaze that could keep the dishes in their place. Honestly, I think Christopher still remembers that. The funny thing is, we've been out sea-worthy enough since then—he’s upgraded the rigging fairly considerably, and Simon swears by his new autopilot system. Now he just needs to upgrade the kitchen facilities if he wants me back on deck.      Hah! Spoken like a true landlubber. But seriously, there’s something peaceful about being out at sea, isn’t there? I mean, despite the chaos of that day, it was nice, just being about nowhere. I think I prefer the Channel to the North Sea, though. There’s a certain lack of commotion in that smooth expanse. Doesn't it feel like time slows down a little?      Definitely. There’s something strangely restorative about the sea. I remember one summer I was docked at Weymouth for a few weeks waiting on a friend who was offshore. Those mornings, just being out there before the world kicked in—watching the first ferry come in, the light over the water... I think I caught a bit of the sea bug back then.      You always had a bit of a romantic streak about it, didn't you? I think it might have something to do with all those childhood holidays at the beach.

Rather annoying I thoughfit the pair o’ new trainers me nay sister hurled in me ‘owse... got heaps o’ good gear in the sale at D2, ay thought sure she’d have a fashion sense o’ £20!      Oh, like, who buys trainers when eeny boots are  thisclose  to the threshold     ? I mean, A listing by Phoebe Philo and a top by Rick Owens are  essentially couture , you can't just ignore that kind of stuff.      Mm, I saw the look yeh liked!  Obvs . That Rick Owens top is, like, totally edgy but still wearable, which is kinda genius     . I was thinking of trying to copy it, but I’ve not got the matching skinny jeans yet.      Yeah, I see what yeh mean, but everyone goes a bit in e-own’s direction ever so often, especially with the way telly folk shout it about. I mean, like, I do like the way it is, but I’d be ruddy struggle t’ve afford to dress like that      ... might go for something a little less... extra, iffen I got clothes from the High –?      High Street, yeah, but there’s a few indie stores in don’t know whereabouts     . There’s this one in Lewisham I go to. Takes in samples for a fraction o’ the price? It’s amazing.      Oh, is it a pop-up or a proper shop? If it’s  actually  affordable, I’m in about needing new skorts for the school fete     . I’ve been doing this failsafe “denim school rhoyalty” look, but  sletch , the kids laugh ‘cos they look like construction gear.      A proper shop, yeah. I’ll show yeh the Instagram once we’ve watched this advert break     . Yeh know what they say—look good, teach good. It’s essential to have a few extra oomph pieces beyond the uniform.      That is so goin’ on me own mission list. Iffen I don’t find a line in quality footwear, I might be goin’ barmy what with all them heels in summat o’ the tv shows we’re watching     .      Ugh, I  love  the way that show styles their characters. Like, so sophisticated and practical at the same time. I kind of want to model it but, y’know, on a teacher's budget and all.      Yeah, no wonder we’re all in conversations about fashion now— totally  influenced by TV, ay? It’s on yeh to look sharp when lectures are so visually inspiring.

So do you think I should go to college full-time, like proper photography college or just take it up as a course and see how it goes?      Hmm, what do you think about it first, hun? I mean, I know you've always loved taking photos. But it's also good to think about what exactly you want to do with it long term.      Well, I’ve been taking photos of the coast and sending them off to local newspapers and stuff. It gets published sometimes, which is nice. But I reckon college would help me chase it more seriously.      That’s brilliant, really! I remember when I used to work at the Hastings camera shop before I became a receptionist, and I’d always love showing off the photo weeklies. People go on about the big D.C.C. and things in London, but local journalism is actually really important, and you’re already getting your foot in the door!      Yeah, and my teacher said I could maybe try applying for the Hastings Photography and Media course. It’s full-time, like two years.      That sounds good. I mean, don’t let me pressure you, but I do think it could open a lot of doors. I remember working at a little café in Bexhill once – Matey’s, near the pier – and there was this guy who was into photojournalism. He did freelance assignments for the  Guardian  and the  Times , and he started out in a coastal town just like us!      That’s inspiring. I’d definitely prefer working freelance over, like, a 9 to 5 office job. Although I  do  like coming home most nights about now!      I get that. Honestly, you and I are alike that way. I hate staying up late. But photographing people, places, and things – that’s always been your thing. I think you’ve got more courage to go for it than any bloody comedian I watched with you yesterday!      Oh come on, didn’t  you  laugh your head off when we watched that stand-up on ITV4?      I did not laugh like that since the early 90s on the telly! It was brilliant – and yes, I do support you doing that. But serious talk, have you read anything about your course? What modules are they planning?      Yeah, I think it covers photojournalism, portraiture, and commercial photography, and there’s even a module about shooting natural disasters… which is kinda my fear of course, going into that.

Rather annoying this, I've got to say. That application form’s a bit of a muddle, like it was drawn up by a child with a compass and a passion for confusion. I nearly fell asleep trying to make sense of it all.      It were a bit much, weren’t it? Right mess of a form. I told the bloke down the shop I’m handing it over for a grandchild to complete, save me the stress! I got me hands full with problem children as it is—feral! One of the little terrors nearly pulled a plug out of the wall the other day!      Lakelands? Problem children? That's nothing, only this mornin' I 'ad a class where one of ‘em left a cockerel in the storeroom. Danged thing kept clucking away like the bell for break time. Nearly gave the librarian a heart attack when it fluttered out 'er window. Reminds me—did someone spot any baby birds in a nest near the back fence earlier?      Aye, I saw one or two, all perched there like tiny little noblemen in a treetop drawing room. Peculiar, ain't it? Watching something so small just... sitin' about all day. Not like kids – at least birds don’t sneak off with your cards or try to programme the telly themselves. All that 3D printing’s a load of nonsense if you ask me. Can't even print a decent kettle full of tea!      I wish I could sleep so peaceful. Some nights I’d swear I hear footsteps and whispers in here—though more like the house groaning, really. Not nearly about to fall apart though, not like some places I've seen. I had a cousin in Birmingham who lived in a place that looked like it were held up by a scrap of wallpaper and the smell of despair.      Aye, I've seen that sort of work. You can slap a lick ‘o paint on it, but it’s all shabby inside. We had to clear up after that building’s plaster came down like a thunderclap! Grateful I’m in education, ‘least I know where I am.      Still, I reckon goin' on birthdays is about the worst of it all. Givin’ out, “Happy Birthday” like it's a bad omen. Pass me a cuppa, love, I’ll manage the kettie. We 'ave to keep our strengths up, else we'll be talkin' ‘bout this lot when we're 100 and the grandkids all asleep!

Rather annoying, really, isn't it? That plane ticket price. I know her company would've paid if she'd taken a job here, but now she's on a sabbatical, so everything's a personal expense.      That is a bit of a cheek. But it was kind of you to offer to cover the accommodation while she's here. Still, it's not as if you're a million miles away from your own provisions, is it?      Well, what else could I do? She's been in that flat for nearly four years in Barcelona, and with the rent prices these days, I don't blame her for bringing it all to an end. Still, I do wonder whether she'll truly be happy here after living abroad for so long. It does change you, London life, or any city life, for that matter.      I was about the same age when I went out to Bucks. It does broaden your horizons, in a way. But you do miss certain things, you know, simple things—like the way the post comes in the morning over here, not at seven in the evening as it does in Spain. Or the way people still say 'ladies first', as we used to.      Indeed. She's got her eyes set on moving here permanently, but I fear it might not take her long to long for the tapas bars of La Rambla and the lazy Siesta afternoons.      There's also this question of work. She mentioned she's not looking to work full-time, but she's not out of the workforce either. It's a bit of a pickle. If she does find something, are there any prospects in Brighton for her field?      I've been watching the job listings. Tutoring, perhaps. Or some part-time school support. Nothing grand, but enough for her to do something, I suppose. I've got a few colleagues at the old staff network I could mention her to. She's got the qualifications, after all.      That's thoughtful of you, Margaret. You've always had a soft spot for her.      More than just a soft spot. That's my daughter, after all. I just want the best for her. Even if I'm not about to start working again or taking in lodgers to cover the costs, I’ll be damned if I let her land in London all alone and find her feet without any support.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh?      Aye, it's been a string of statements, and I'm not sure where this one will land. I mean, sure, the people there are doing their thing, but do they have the power?      Exactly. The Scottish een? I'm beginning to think it's one of those endless bandstands. They wanted their say, but with the Auld Reekie lot in Edinburgh and the top brass in Westminster, it's easier said than done. We've had the referendum before and what happened? Nothing, or at least not what they wanted.      Not to mention the chaos with the transition out of Europe. You know, like that wasn’t a doorstep enough for anyone who thought they were going to rally up independence.      But I digress. Talking politics is all fine and dandy, but I had a bit of a pickle the other week. Got an interview for a post at a university up in Newcastle. You know, you'd think I'd get a bit more respect after all these years of lecturing.      Oh, really? I thought you were quite settled in London. Do tell.      It was a Lecturer role. The salary was better, and it's a new challenge. But, fairly recently, I've had to pull back a bit. My daughter's in her final year at uni, and I've been helping her out with accommodation and homework and all sorts. So I'm waiting to see if they'll accept me deferring the start.      That's very much understandable. You can't be split in two, after all. My Janine started at St Andrew's last year. I've had to cut down the hours at the secondary school. I used to be head of department there.      You're up for more? Going back?      Not sure. I passed 60 last year, and I don't want to assume I've got the energy I once had. I'm looking into doing some part-time tutoring as well. Maybe online. Websites like Yellow or the Guardian Jobs keep popping up with these kinds of opportunities.      That does sound nice and flexible.      Mm, but life's getting busier. Just yesterday, I had to pick up Janine from a friend’s, and then I went to your place for that latest biology exhibit you showed me. You know, the one with the growth chambers.

Rather annoying when the box won't shut properly, isn't it? I've made it shut before when we had those weekend family gatherings at my place in Stratford. I can show you how we did it properly, if you fancy it.      It's been like that since I bought it on eBay. Thought I'd get a full set with proper instructions, but no. Classic. You know I've always found these British-made things far more infuriating than their American counterparts. Outrageous, really.      I remember once when I was in LA doing the exchange program, they had like, miniature mousetrap games made from bamboo and everything. It was wild. They had some kind of LED trap and a buzzing noise. Possibly illegal to possess in England.      Was the mouse cardboard or was it plastic? Because I made one with Ed for my Food Tech project once. I called it the 'Mousey Knock-Off'. It only worked if the gingerbread was warm.      Oh, that's why I like your attempts, Harry. Nostalgia for some of us is the occasional cardboard box with glue holding it all together. I tell you, when I was a child, watching American sitcoms and imagining a little boy building one of these at the kitchen table with his dad—it seemed like such a wholesome thing to do.      You know what amazed me about the American kids when we were at that weekend writing retreat in Maine? They all had an entrepreneurial spark. One of the teenagers designed a trap that oddly had a laser pointer and a jar at the bottom. Crazy as it sounds, it actually worked.      Sounds like about five Health and Safety violations all at once.      Honestly, I think we British kids need to be reminded that creativity isn’t about following a template. Remember that summer I found a way to rewire the guest room light into blinking when the trap was triggered?      That was  epic , Nan. Everyone else had to sort out who the mouse had hit and who hadn’t. Even Dad got involved with his terrible shots.      Wasn’t that where you got the idea for your first play, Gran? The gothic one with the life-sized mechanical mouse that destroyed the estate?      Oh, don’t go turning nostalgia into something dramatic, Jonathan. It was just a trap, after all.      Well, I think I’ll take your advice to heart, Josie, and overcomplicate the box a bit more.

Rather annoyingly, I've bought us a whole bunch of new pyjamas. We needed some new pjs, and I thought this was a nice opportunity to find something... a bit nicer than usual, you know?      Oh, right? You didn't say anything about it before. Got a bit of a passive-aggressive vibe with the 'we needed them' remark.      Ha! A bit, but serious, they were on a sale. And since we’ve had some time off work, and we might be moving house once this term is over, I thought it made sense to get some new things ready. I mean, pyjamas are pyjamas, right?      My point being, I’ve already got new pjs in the back of the wardrobe from the last time we went shopping and I bought a whole matching set—purple with seahorses. They’re waiting for me to actually wear them!      Oh yeah, the seahorse ones! That's you ordering them for the Instagram aesthetic. Good for you.      Come on—personality in pyjamas is important! You can't just expect everyone to dress the part, even while in bed. Speaking of, what kind of pjs did you get? Ordinary cotton or –?      No, actually, they were these really nice bamboo ones. Soft, breathable, and surprisingly affordable. You know what I hate about normal cotton pjs? They’re just so scratchy when they're slightly damp from a hot shower or something.      Fair point. Also, have you considered the possibility of being accused of matchy-matchy overkill? Because we both have about five pairs of pyjamas now. One red, one green... etc.      That's because we are academics! We live for categorisation and uniformity to some extent, don't we?      True enough. But maybe just have one matching set. It could be a nice touch. Imagine, curling up on the sofa with your favourite cup of tea and your matching partner in seahorse glory.      Well, I do have a red set as well—though mine are more red tigers than seahorses. There's room on the life-sized wall of pyjamas at home.      Hopefully, we'll outgrow this infatuation before we get a matching bathrobe stage. I can see it now: one in seahorse, the other in belly of the sea tiger.      You're not far off, love. I’m already imagining my bathrobe lined with tigers, drinking tea with you in your seahorse ones. It'll be very Narnia, and slightly inappropriate for our elderly housemates.

Rather a brilliant game we had last night, wasn’t it? That try by Kelleher came out of nowhere, and I’ll not lie—me heart nearly jumped out me chest when we held on for the win.      Did you see that as well on the stream? I was trying to get all the footage together for the card today for Uncle Colm’s birthday. He wanted to have a bit of a surprise presentation when he comes over this weekend.      Ah, now, that's thoughtful. We can put the highlights together and pop it in the frame with the signed cards from the others. It'll be a grand touch—those old lads love the glitz and glam of it all.      Oh, I’m just not sure he’ll be well enough to sit through the whole event, Frank. I think he turned 76 last week, and the old bones have been aching somewhat. But I do love the sentiment.      I’ll be making a card, of course. I managed to get the rest of the gang to help me over the phone, and we all wrote a few lines. I’m sorry I’ve not been around much—Oisin’s having such a rotten time at bedtimes these days. I swear, he got it from his father.      He got it from you, love, and you were a night owl in your youth as well. Silly woman.      And you’d better be careful what you say in front of the wee ones. He was a bit of a sports mad at school—keen to be captain of the rugby team and being told he was too small for it all. Oisin doesn’t understand yet that he’s not the same as the lads at secondary school.      Wait, he was that good then? I mean, if he wasn’t captain, do you think I could do something like that at school? I saw a poster for the Invitational Tournament the school is holding. I asked Dad about it.      You’ll have to crack on with that then. You’ve got a chance if you take it seriously. I’ll message your form coach if you like—get you set up with a training plan.      Frank, really, are we about to start turning him into one of those trophy-hungry lads?      Well, if what your husband says is to be believed, I’d say we might have one in the making.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand that they’re still trying to get settled, but piling all the kids' stuff onto  me  just because I’ve got an attic now is a bit unreasonable, don’t you think?      Yeah, well, you  did  promise eeny weeny  bop  that you'd look after the spare dusty cupboards… not that I blame you, though. Moving house  is  a bit of a faff, even if it’s just to a new flat in the same city. Oh, by the way, how's your little one?      Mary’s doing well. She’s starting to crawl, which is both terrifying and amazing in equal measure. Although I swear she crawls left and backwards much more than forwards. It’s as if she’s picky about destinations or something! But how about you, aren’t you working with Liam on the Thai language project at the Press now?      Yep, that’s right! We’re putting the final touches on the beginner phrasebook. Surprisingly, I’ve picked up a few phrases myself, and it’s really opened my eyes — quite a different way of expressing grief and warmth, for example. Liam says something about communal comfort, and it’s all pretty emotional compared to English.      Oh, absolutely. I’ve seen similar things in the Russian and Polish materials we've been collating for the Press. It's one of the reasons I love this job. Our co-ordination with language partners also means I often exchange clothes with the other admin staff. Funny thing—shared wardrobes have a way of making you feel closer as a team, right?      I about blocked you for ages for not mentioning your mammoth Russian-Ukrainian vibes. Honestly, you and your sister are such language scholars! I mean, how does  your  sister do with her  own  four little ones and her twin toddlers?      Oh man, it's a full-time job! But she’s brilliant — you know when I say “clothes swapping,” that  includes  being sent out laundry-traipsing lunches to keep the peace while balancing the various meltdowns. Still, it’s something I’d do for my family. Oh, go on then, spill it about Liam's new Thai work — is he into the language, or just into… you know, blooming something else?       Haha!  You’ve been reading the manifestos, haven’t you? Nah, truly, he’s been on it like a duck on a pronoun system.

Rather annoying when people can't get my accent right, innit. I was in Cambridge the other week and someone got completely confused with me saying "flat" like it were "flath"      Aye, we do differentiate the t and d at the end like that a lot in Eastern een, and it can catch folks out. I find it funny when people think I've got an RP accent just because I teach English.      Oh yeah, but you've clearly studied linguistics or something! You sound posh.      Nah, I just pay attention to detail, is all. I mean, I talk a bit more formally because I'm teaching people, but like you My accent still definitely shows I'm from Bedford.      I was at the pub last night and used the word "fart". Man, everyone was laughing harder than they shoulda. British people really love that word, innit?      Yeah, it's one of those words that's both so crude and yet so widely acceptable that it's kind of funny, like we're in on some weird inside joke.      It's funny how something as basic as a body function can have such a wide range of social acceptability depending on the context – works the same with verbosity, swearing and even food taboos.      Mate, you ever tried that new vegan chocolate bar? Near impossible to get the hang of. Like, someone said to me, “But you're a man, you just need to stop eating meat.”      That’s harsh. Meat’s meat! I mean, vegans are doing their best, I get that, but eating a chocolate bar doesn’t make you a vegetarian. Not really a mission for me.      I get it. There's a lot to do with diet personally for health, but for ethics or ideology? That takes more explanation and more time to become a habit.      I tried to explain to my girlfriend that I'd rather eat good-looking veggies that are properly grown than worry about trying to find organic mushrooms in Luton.      Still, I'd say if it's good enough for the cat goenvironment friendly on your own if you've got a cat.      It's funny because we were just talking earlier about protecting what your cat eats. So many people take flu seriously, but when it comes to poisons in food, people just don't think to question it.      Speaking of, I was down at the SPCA shop last week, helping out for a couple of mornings.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather spend the hour on the train just chilling with a book than listening to Radio 1 and cruising along at 5mph in my own car.      Yeah, I hear you. I’ve been meaning to get a train pass myself—it’s way cheaper in the long run anyway, especially with the fuel prices these days. Plus, I’m actually productive on the train.      Exactly! I was just thinking about that while I was stewing the mince for the bolognese. Every trip into the city adds another ten quid to my fuel bill, but I guess it does mean I can keep flexible with my start time, you know? On the train you’re bound by the schedule, even if it’s packed like sardines.      True, but I’ve been saving up for a second-hand car for about a year now. I know it sounds old-fashioned, but having a car after work lets me just unwind, you know?      I get that—and I still miss driving, too. I used to do it, before I sold my car to get into that short-term train fare. But I’ve been so busy at work as an administrator, I haven’t even considered driving again seriously. The cost of running a car – Servicing, insurance, mot, and now these crazy fuel prices—      It’s enough to make you want to cycle to work, honestly. Though that might not be the best idea in the rain. But anyway, maybe you can just consider buying second-hand when you’re ready—look for something with a good mileage and low emissions. Even better for savings in the future.      I’ll look into it. Although I’m the type who’s had three job roles and a house move in the last two years, so I’d feel like it’s a bit of a commitment buying a car for the long term. But maybe if I find a really affordable one? Like a 10-year-old Fiesta or something.      A little mad, but I get it. Just remember that even if you outgrow it, the parts could be sold or scrap—better than losing money. I’d be careful, though. My cousin bought a 2008 MIV on a whim, and after a few weeks of trying to fix the head gasket, it was cheaper to just keep driving the bus.

Rather annoying I though, the pair of yer, coming in with that lorry-load o’ ‘owse stuff, and not ‘even telling us! Me and Dows, we stared like we’d seen a Martian land in our front ‘ead!      Auntie Martha, it was a surprise! MUM said ye’d like it. ‘Ad to explain to me what a Martian was after that comment.      Ay, that was a spot on observation, young’un. We woz just comin’ from the market, full of leeks and pots, when the bloke came out fetchin’ things like it were a treasure hunt. I swear, the bins were still guid for thruppence that day!      Aye, and the smell of that polish they used on the floor! Roared o’ turps and lemon. I ‘ad a sneezin’ fit for breakfast, couldn’t stop till me tea went cold.      Stop bein’ dramatic, Harry, it’s just a bit of Polyf. We told that man to give it a reasonable coat, not enough to start up a ruddy garage!      And tellin’ ‘im we’ve got a ‘eadroom, not a spare room. He looked so confused, like we woz plannin’ a mind act or summat up there. I reckon ‘e thought we were ‘eaddin’ up to ‘ave a juggler in the house!      That’s a bit grim. Why’d Auntie Martha suggest we start a ‘eadroom project, anyway? It were just painting and a ‘ew shelves.      Oy, I did suggest ‘avin’ a proper ‘ead man! Someone dressed up in a box and stuff. But your Auntie said that was too dramatic. Typical!      Oh, come on ‘Arry, you always do that. You’re supposed to be restin’ on the day, not startin’ a showbbc.      I ‘avn’t ‘ad such a chuckle since the ‘ealth visitor tried to teach me Tai Chi in the ‘ospital. She kept callin’ it  Tie Chi . Pah! I told ‘er go back to the pond life if that’s wot she wanted.      It’s  Tai Chi , ‘Arry. And what ‘ospital was that in?      North ‘ull, where else? And I never ‘ead of that Tai Chi lark either. Look ‘ere, if we start doin’ that I’m goin’ to need a mace for when the crows come in, not a magic wand.      Oh for heaven’s sake, let’s just talk about the ‘eadroom, not Movit. We’ve enough to sort out before the solicitor's look. And that included the electricians and the plumbers.

Right, so today we've got Shakespeare week at the school, love it really. We're doing a workshop with some local kids from Stratford—oh, your brother and sister asked me about pirates over breakfast! Got to keep up with them! Did you know pirates use a lot of things in common with Shakespeare’s language? Like "Ahoy" is kind of like   " Ay"   in  Othello —I think it’s fun to mix in a bit of pirate-speak into our lessons to get the kids excited. We’ve even got a role-play activity where they dress up like characters from  The Tempest  but with a pirate twist.      What’s a  The Tempest  like? My turkey sandwich is being eaten by jelly!      And Oliver from the circus place said they’re doing magic acts with cloaks and rabbits this weekend at the big breakfast, and we might go watch! Mummy said I could throw confetti, like the Queen in that fairytale, but only if I don’t bleed my fingers!      Oh, the circus sounds amazing! I remember seeing a real one as a child in Devon when I was about your age—absolute chaos watching the tightrope walker in the rain. You two might enjoy the stop-motion animation show they’re doing with fake snakes and fiery hats. I’ve even got some of those books by Nick and Silly Billy that talk about pirates and jugglers. Maybe they can help you make your own pirate hat for the school show.      Pirates are  so  cool! Mom, can we do real magic with money and stuff like in  Aladdin ? Oliver said we can make coins disappear!      Only if you keep your promises and tidy up your room! Speaking of which, have you managed to photograph all your Easter scenes yet? I thought the treacle ones were absolutely brilliant—such a creative way to use sugar and biscuits! And if you ever wanted to go to Stratford for a little performance weekend, I could talk to my colleague. He’s doing a children’s festival with lunches and a little behind-the-scenes tour of the theatre.      Then can we learn sword fighting with the pirates goody? I want to be like Captain Hook, but with a pencil!      Well, you’re welcome to try with the chopsticks and spaghetti. It won’t cut, but it might manage a bit of a tickle!

Rather skipper a boat across the Red Sea to Cyprus, did you? That's quite the adventure! I’d be too daft to even dream of doing that after my first spell in Saudi. A bit much, don’t you think?      Oh, I wouldn't say it was daft at all. It was more of a misunderstanding than anything. I was sailing with a group of colleagues after a conference in Jeddah. We’d had too much socialising, and perhaps a few too many cups of that strong tea they serve in the Gulf. Next thing we knew, the coast guard was on to us like hounds on a scent. They weren't terribly pleased about the idea of unregistered vessels trying to cross international waters, I must say.      Well, I can imagine the look on their faces. I once tried to hand out dental magazines at a conference in Manchester — got told off by the bursar for 'cluttering up the education sector.' Though at least I didn’t end up in a cell in the Kingdom. Still, the memories I have from that time in Saudi!      I can believe it. I never did quite understand how they managed to operate the whole ban on alcohol in Saudi. I mean, how do you expect a dental surgeon to maintain good relationships at a conference without a decent glass of shiraz?      Oh, you're quite right there, Bill. I used to run English classes in the kingdom and we’d have these 'dry' social events. But everyone brought their own vittles — bottles tucked under coats or wrapped up in paperbacks. I once spent three hours looking at tea and dates trying to make polite conversation, while my students nearly about burst from secrets they couldn't verbalise from talking the whole time.      There was some good storytelling that went on! I remember one colleague who swore he once rowed 12 miles from the mainland to a floating dredger during a blackout. Said he feared he might vanish forever into the ‘azure abyss’ with nary a satellite to bless him with direction. Of course, as soon as he got off, he got picked up by the authorities and jailed over ‘violation of maritime boundaries’. Six hours behind bars after a day in the sun, no less!      And if that's not poetic, I don't know what is. It’s funny how we go from academic conferences to high-seas misadventure.

Rather annoying really, having to go through all that when you do everything properly anyway. But it's just like... got to follow the same format every time.      Yeah, I mean, it is a bit tedious. I know the rules are there for a reason. But it's still so draining, dealing with different people who don’t understand the system.      Yeah, I remember when I had to proof documents before sending them off. Everyone wants checks but don’t want to read through it. Especially when it was me sorting for schools or customer services, always the same things came up... like duplicate info, or wrong addresses.      Y’know, Ma, I had that at school yesterday. I had to write my left foot on the back of the form and then they sent it back because I wrote in red pen? That’s so annoying, why do they do that for?      Well, they do it in case they need to make copies or scan it, you see. Ink tends to smudge more than red or blue—especially red.      Oh, I always put in a biro as well. Did you tell your teacher?      Yeah, she laughed and said, “Jonny, no one else does it like that.” I didn’t mind because they gave me some stickers.      That’s the worst for proofreaders, though. Everything comes back wrong and then you just want to scream.      I reckon it helps building up resilience. You learn not to get too stressed over red pens and bad formatting.      Resilience? Not in about five minutes. That teacher does everything slow, talking to different kids at the same time and then expects us to know it all.      That’s not great to have to deal with for every lesson. What about your work experience? Did you get anything?      No, not yet. I applied to a few places, but I don't know if they even read them. Auntie Websites mentioned once trying with lunches, or babysitting? Would that help?      Babysitting’s good if you can get the parents go along with it. My cousin had a job doing that at a kids’ club in Birmingham. She had to referee the boxers one week when the proper people didn't turn up.      You’re joking!      No, honest to God. She ended up with a black eye, but at least she said it was the most fun job she ever had.

Rather skip the aul dum eh. D’ya lot fancy a bit o’ truffle ‘n pate or summat? I saw a real proper place down ‘te Istrian Way      Aww don’t start yon again love, you know well enough the two o’ us een’t used to eatin’ summat that fancy. But if it’s not too expensive...?      Mate, I’d go anywhere if it was truffles. My mate Dan’s dad said he once had truffles served to him on a gold spoon, but I reckon he’s lying... like most peoples      Nan, he ain’t lyin’ likkle lcuky. My turkey friend Jason, who I met in America once, said most American chefs ain’t even ‘eard o’ truffles. A bit sad really. But in Istria, you’re better off breakfast, no?      Haha, yeah, the states are ever so... uncultured in some ways. Though I suppose they do have their own chefs. Gordon Ramsay, yes? But I’ve never really got into that sort o’ thing to be honest.      Gordon who? Sounds like a proper egocentric, from what I’ve seen on the telly      Yeah, he’s a bit much. I reckon he don’t know how lucky ‘e’s been to have ‘is stem cell shizzle, huh? Like, someone at ‘is age should be more grateful.      Oh definitely. Some folks ‘ave more going for ‘em from the off ‘n most o’ us. Though, Prime, y’ about to finish yon education course, so the least y’ lot can do is be a bit nicer and not slag off people that know better      Maybe I will. Though, ‘eck, I’d still rather watch football than cook. Though I have me on a football strip fashioned after ‘at famous Istrian chef team      You what? There is no such thing. Let me guess... you picked the wrong one up on the internet      Nan, you don’t even know ‘ow cool it is. Yeah, go ‘ead on man, if you don’t think so. But I saw some real quality action last week.      Aww ‘e’s talkin’ aboot Bolton Wanderers again. Hazza been out      You don’t get it. I saw ‘em over in America too, at a proper arena. It’s where my cousin works, so I got in for free.      Mate, did you smoke yon cigarettes ‘fore we left? You swore to give up after yon cough last week      Not those ones! I had a bit o’ a sweet flavour on yon trip.

Rather annoying when the vending machine eats your penny, isn't it? I was just trying to get a sandwich... got the audible  click  and now I'm down a quid an' a snackless!      Tell me about it. Happened to me like a fortnight ago. I'm still haunted by the memory of that twitchy machine guzzling my coin without remorse. Though I reckon that coffee machine by the printers is more generous — but then again, it gives you lukewarm coffee that tastes like you've boiled damp socks for an hour.      Honestly, I'd rather skip a snack than have to endure that tannic brew. Still, if we can coordinate like that My turkey and cheese one's already made though left it in the back pocket of my coat for safety, in case the place catches on fire.      You’ve got to be joking breakfast, no doubt. Look, happened to me last week in the café next door. Put my sandwich in my bag to move it and when I went to pull it out, I was presented with a very confused chicken wrap and a slightly less confused falafel.      And then, what, did they launch into a mini war circle?      Not quite — just stared at one another fairly long, like, it was a standoff. Until the falafel picked up and sauntered off for a large portion of sourdough mexi wrap and never looked back.      I think my falafel just filed for sour-doughance and went off to some desert retreat with delicious layers and herbs. Can I borrow yours?      I mean, I was eating the same. But touch wood — this one hasn't turned into a walkabouts yet. Let me see. Okay, I'll split it up for both of you. But don't blame me if yours starts strolling off mid lunch.      Oh, I assume that's just the ambiance of this printing house — waiting for someone to stick out their thumb and yell hokey-cokey out of nowhere. Have lunches here been like this from the start?      Honestly, I think this entire building runs on a surreal set of protocols. I remember once I tried to open a drawer and it made a dent in the wall that had a faint hum, and then it disappeared.      That sounds like it's been kitted out after some mad tea party, maybe with marching parrots to match.      Might not be a bad idea.

Rather annoying that the satnav went off just now, isn't it? I was trying to follow it like a good passenger. But maps change, and roadworks don’t! Honestly, I think I might’ve been doing it all wrong to start with.      Yeah, the Sat Nav can be a bit iffy out here. I think the route updates haven't caught up with all the local roads. I’ve only done this drive twice before, from my flat to Tarnów, so I might not be the best one to give directions either. But what I do know is that the M34 turns into the A4 after around twenty miles—those signs are pretty clear once you get into Poland.      A4, yes, I saw that. I just hope we don't get sent back into Dąbrowa Gornicza by mistake. It's a lovely town and all, but I don't really fancy getting lost in some mini-metropolis when all I want is five minutes in Tarnów to meet Agata and have that hot lunch she promised me.      You know, I think Agata might actually be expecting us a bit earlier. Did you tell her we’d be late? Her friend is coming over for lunch, and from what she said earlier, it’s about preparing a new curriculum for her school. She really wants to pick my brain.      Ugh, I haven’t mentioned anything yet. When I spoke to her yesterday, she just said “enjoy your drive” and not to worry about time. But I can definitely manage with hotter food than what I had in the café this morning—some kind of sausages in a sweet sauce. Not about to live that down for the rest of the week.      I think what you had was actually quite traditional Polish breakfast fare. I remember when I was teaching in Kraków, a lot of the locals would eat something like that. Although, personally, I’m more of a blood sausage kind of person. Speaking of, I tried some once on your campervan trip. It didn’t go down well with the lady driver, by the way.      That was last year, and that road trip was something else. Remember stopping at the random roadside market in Miechów and buying that antler-shaped candle? Still have it on my shelf back in Cambridge. Honestly, it might be the only thing from all those trips that I have kept.

Just as long as they don’t try to put their logo on the side o’ them plastic bags now.

But my Nan says I shouldn’t be a prat and just go to the  work shop, you know, the one down Chatham way. Can I come with you one day?      Yeah, why not. I just can’t be blinking around this place looking like a no-hoper.   $   You’re the only one ‘cos everyone else thinks I got rich after Aunty Jan left them all her gold. I'm still paying bills, man.      Those  gas  and  electric bills  are the lunches of a new man with no savings.      Still, I’m happy with the George Foreman. Yeah, go ahead and get your own if you like, it’s got preheating and it’s got that green light. You just chuck the chips on and your steak and you don’t have to watch it all the time like a normal pan. And your mother never even belly-aches about the mess either.

Rather annoying when the sat nav goes wrong, isn’t it? I was driving up to Chester last week and it got me on some back lane—could’ve saved me a fortune in fuel if it’d just told me to follow the A6.      Yeah, well, I haven’t got a sat nav in my old Citroën. I just use Postcode Anywhere on Google Maps. Though I once missed a junction by five miles and ended up at a place where the only shop was a corner shop that sold more tins of beans than anything else. Didn’t even get a cuppa at the café there like I was expecting.      That reminds me the time I tried to drive to Cambridge and got completely turkeyed. I must’ve been about forty and thought I knew the roads off by heart. Drove past the very roundabout I meant to take—three times, by the looks of it. Turned around and then I noticed a notice for a drive in cinema at the side of the road! No, you didn’t—it had a plane crash once over that area, I think.      A plane crash? What happened?      Oh, back in the ’60s, there was a Boeing 377 over West Freckleton—I was just a girl then. It ploughed into a field, just missed a few houses. The farmer nearly had a heart attack, and the pilot was lucky to get out with a broken leg, they said in the paper at the time. But the crowd that turned up? It was like a fairground! Some folks had kettles on in their gardens and were passing out tea and buns to people waiting for news. I about wet myself laughing—poor pilot standing there talking to passersby with wings all over his trousers and not a care that he shouldn’t be standing up, if you know what I mean.      That’s brilliant. I can only imagine the explanation when he told his wife. “Damage was mainly confined to the left wing,” or something clinical like that!      Probably. I remember being sent out to wait by the gate to keep the pigs from running off—never seen a pig look so terrified in the whole of my eighty years.      That’s right funny if you like warts and odd stories.      I suppose it could’ve been worse—like getting lost due to a dodgy sat nav and then ending up on a plane’s path next time.

Honestly, I just can't get through our physics homework. Like, I know it's supposed to be hard, but the wave equations this week—how do you even  pronounce  some of those terms?      Chill, you’re not alone! I stared at the worksheet for like an hour last night. I ended up just drawing some scribbles and calling it an art project. The teacher said something about constructive and destructive interference, but I think I drew a kiwi bird by accident.      Classic! Wait, did you at least copy the diagram or just make things up? I like to think of it as  interpretive physics . Besides, the real drama only started this morning in English. My trainee teacher, Miss Caine, left her coffee thermos on her desk and then accidentally knocked it over while writing on the board. It went everywhere!      Oh no, breakfast on the desk gone? I mean, no one was in there at the time, were they?      Nah, the room was empty. But Sam from art snuck in just as it happened, and he says he dropped his pencil or something and slipped in the coffee. It was  viler  than it sounds—it wasn't just coffee, it was all the sugar she puts in it?      Ugh, that's  horrific . I reckon she gets way too much sugar in the morning. I saw her chewing gum at ten o'clock and then having a biscuit in between classes—her system must be like a rush-hour underground.      Honestly, at some point, I think the trainee teachers just forget where  they  are! I swear, about half of them walk into the same wall the second week of term. It's like a generational curse.      I mean, it is Cambridge, so I guess the architecture doesn’t help. Maybe they’re still confused if they’re supposed to be walking on the grounds or in Hogwarts.      Haha, accurate. Anyway, speaking of distractions—actually, did you hear that they're doing a sculpture project in art this term? It's supposed to be inspired by the recent work of Rebecca Salter.      Oh yeah! She's that really cool ceramic artist, right? I think her work is made of line-based pieces that almost look like drawings in three dimensions.      Exactly! So I’m planning to make something really kinaesthetic, like using those clay coils to make like, a winding trunk of a tree or something.

So nurseries, right? My teacher was talking about how they used to have nuns working in them. I got to see some old photos of this one school down in Bristol with these strict-looking ladies in long grey robes. But how come people don’t do that as much these days?      Well, dear, a lot has changed since they were around. Back when I was your age, most schools in places like London still had nuns teaching. I went to one school with a nun who would punish you with a ruler if you talked too much. Funny now, when I think about it. But you can’t expect young people these days to dress that way and live in the same way they did before.      Yeah, I guess they were just like teachers back then. But I heard from my friend Oliver that some of them were kind of controlling? Is that true?      It’s a complicated topic really. I mean, some were very strict in their beliefs and ways, and not always in a good way. But they also helped many people, especially those who couldn’t afford school.      Nana! I don’t like your face!  points at Speaker_2       laughs  Oh, don’t mind me, love. Let’s see… you must want a bit of cheecake, eh?      But seriously, after that, what about other religions? Like scientology or stuff like that? I looked it up once. It sounds a bit bonkers to me. Like a mix of sci-fi and religion? Some guy called David something?      That’s L. Ron Hubbard, your colleague. Some people think it’s cultish, while others think it’s just misunderstood. It’s quite strange looking at it from the outside. Like The Matrix, you know? It makes you question whether you’re real or just a computer program. I watched that film once with your dad, and it blew my head off!      Oh yeah, I haven’t seen The Matrix yet. I’m not sure my parents would like that. They say it’s got too much weird stuff in it.      Well, maybe when you’re a bit older. But if you do get the chance go for it. It’s about freedom of choice, real versus virtual—stuff like that, which is actually a bit like religion in some ways.      So are you saying scientology is like a fake religion?      I’ll say this: it’s not for everyone, and there are so many different beliefs out there.

Rather annoying when afit’s eh, innit? Eh, love, you think it would’ve passed by now, but I’m still gettin’ side-eyed by my mam for sayin’ ‘corpus’ instead o’ “a bóthar” or whatever!      A bóthar is Gaelic, innit? Not like that’s surprised me. I’ve been trying to resist the urge to correct your Slade lyrics since this morning, honestly. Oh, and you were meant to be listening to BBC Radio Four, not the.Fatalfanstayings when we said we’d drive up north...       laughs  Well, listen, the roads are still wetter than the south and My turkey still hasn’t finished defrostin’, so give me a break, yeah? Yeah, I noticed—your passion for metric, and your inappropriate amount of knowledge about Old English, puts quite a few people off. I mean, not that I mind—every good consultant engineer needs a partner who can outsmart them academically at some point.      Shut it, Haylie! I’ve seen your dance moves after that “Jimmy Choos” night out. Not exactly a case study in fluid movement. And just because I found an old TV show with a French title and tried to suggest we cosplay it doesn’t mean I’d ruin a holiday. Going to that charity football match instead of a fancy hotel was a calculated step. My idea of a romantic break is less about “staying” and more about just getting out o’ the hustle for a while. Speaking of, I tried to book a little trip down to see Casey’s kid—      Casey? The one who works in the hospital?      That's the one. You know, the nurse who told us about that go-to-place on the coast if we ever wanted to go somewhere without kids, dentists, or ageist bar staff breathing down our necks? Anyway, all the hotels online are booked through Lovefilm-style sites, and one of them was even called something like “The Metre House”. Just made me want to overcompensate by booking them a Airbnb that charges in Euros

Rather skip uni today an’ go playin’ cards with tha mogglin’ team tomorrow?      Ooh, tha sounds like more fun than lectures. That's cool, have you got an audience yet? I’ve only watched my cousin’s one. Ten views, loads of comments from gran.      Aye, it's tricky, but I've got a few friends helping out with editing and stuff.      That sounds like more work than uni, honestly, but if it's what you want to do, go for it! It's like that and more, I tell ya. Some of them are really detailed and have about five rule books.      Sounds complicated, but I’m always up for new things! True, I've thought about it. Might do it as a separate project.      Lot's of potential there. Just keep it real, y'know.      Aye, and before you know it, you'll have more fans than them Cambridge crumpet fanatics!      Haha, don’t jinx it, I’m still on tutorial mode.      But the dedication is inspirational.

Rather annoying this newfit sandwich policy, innit? Eh, Aislinn, d’yer like that new salad lot they put in the dining hall yet?      Oh, yeah! It is a bit funny, isn’t it? Rather annoying when half the students bring up social media when they should be referencing academic sources, innit? You wouldn't believe how much time it takes to filter out passive-aggressive posts from the 'library is out of date' brigade on Facebook. One chap last week posted a meme saying the internet was invented before the Dewey Decimal system. It's pulling teeth to convince people we're relevant.      Honestly, I still say some of the best use of LinkedIn is for older-than-dust academics to forget their Facebook passwords and still try to network in suits and MySpace-era confidence. I remember once at a conference, some oversized desktop hides my monitor to protect intellectual property—and then the guy over there directly shared the PowerPoint over LinkedIn, posted a screen shot of it, and I quote, “explains it all for you humanely.”      Sounds like watching a koala run rhythmically then fall off a tree. Pointless?      That’s a new one. You’re getting quite the flair for comic relief, Simon. Still, no one ever tells that joke on Twitter. People just someone at full volume for ten seconds with a conspiracy about a algorithm.      Some folks still equate profile likes with validation. Like that one about the guy who tiled his floor with library books. Unbelievable but all over Instagram.      You mustn’t knock the Instagram kid queens and their curated filters. Websites can always add a 'share this on social' button. Now if only our book drop returned faster via tweet…      That's the go, Ruth. They share about your antipodean ramble in New Zealand in the password recovery system. And the box might as well be enchanted due to how long it takes to arrive.      Must be tough starting those jokes, Ruth. You came from a land of talkback radio and overcooked meat pies—now here you're stringing together conversations so sarcastic they make a Channel 4 drama seem soft.

Rather skip ahead a moment, eh, David? I just want to make sure we get the  rationale  for the site choice down properly. Otherwise, when the consultation process comes around, we’ll have a mountain to climb. Not only explaining  why  Tunbridge Wells — well, obviously it’s in your patch, and that  helps  — but why   this   site specifically.      Aye, fair enough. I know the committee’s got their eye on a couple of options, including that old GP surgery avenue. But I keep coming back to the southern end of the Malling Road estate. That part of Tunbridge does  need  dedicated palliative support. The local health services have been stretched like wellies since the NHS reorganisation — you know what’s going on back there, Jan.      Oh, I do. And don’t even get me started about the lack of proper end-of-life nursing facilities. Look, the site has a certain  presence , doesn’t it? It’s spacious, near to the A21, and not over-exposed. You could get a subtle, low-key building there without clashing with the local vernacular.      And that  is  the idea: something unobtrusive. We’re not looking for a monument. We want calm. But also fairly accessible, and with that natural buffer of green space. The estate agents don’t love it, mind you. Still, I got the brokers at Rotherham’s offices to give someone a call. They’ll sort out the valuation once the business case is signed off.      Exactly. And the business case has to be  solid . That’s your key, David — your portfolio about how patient health is central to everything. You touch the hospices in Sevenoaks and Maidstone and make sure their heads are above water before laying it out. No one wants to feel bypassed. And the politics — well, well — Geography here is funny. Kent’s got its own priorities, but if you position it as a North Yorkshire initiative too, you might get some extra regional funding from the  joint  board.      Aye, and speaking of budgets. I’ve done a back-of-the-envelope cost for site prep and construction. The proposal is aimed at creating a 24-bed facility with a focus on dignity and care. If we go sustainable design — green roofs, low emissions — it’ll impress your lot at the consultation stage. Environmental credentials are all the buzz these days.      I’ll vouch for that. Just make sure the patient journey is at the heart of the design.

Rather skip the newfit slippers, innit? Seems like everything sticks to her chin, like when we all got the pictures done at Royal Ascot last year. Aye, it really does. I remember her telling you about the time the photographer accidentally burned the negatives, and we were left with the little ghost faces. Had us chuckling for weeks. Still, it was good of you to track them down after all this time.      Well, you didn’t spare a second thought for me when I told you I was going into the village today for some folders. You just dropped it in with your dinner as if you knew I'd be back with more than just paperwork. You always did have a rhythm about when people got home. We were laughing about it for weeks because Charlotte here commented on how it looked like something off of  MasterChef Goes Wrong .      Well, I took the liberty of applying for that communications manager position this morning. I told you I'd go for it, didn’t I? It’s based in London, though, so it’s not a done deal.      That your lot of confidence talking at the dinner table? If you get it, we’ll go for a proper meal in town, like we used to back in the ‘80s when we were younger and thought we knew everything.

Rather skip horror films, innit. You know what me mates call the one wi' the jump scares and all them creepy kids? They call it  The Hantu , cos it gives you the heebie-jeebies. Rather annoying when the tablet won't play anything, isn't it? I was just trying to order that Italian from the local place, but no luck. It keeps freezing on me. Rather skip ahead afit, eh, but I was just tellin' ye aboot that wee trip we’d got plan tin tae tak’ this year yet? Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you both anyway.      Well, I’ll let you sort this out, love. Just take your time      It probably won’t take too long, Mums. Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, having to talk about this just as it's warming up... What was I saying? Oh yes, maintenance. Blows me away what you can find behind a wall sometimes.
