Rather annoying to be honest, the NHS these days — six weeks to get a straightforward blood test booked. Mind you, I understand they're stretched after the pandemic, but I can't say I'm over the moon about it.      Oh I know what you mean, love. My cousin’s had a similar run-in with the hospital. She was waiting   ages   for a scan — nearly two months. She’s only in her mid-fifties too and has a family history of breast cancer. It’s worrying to be left hanging like that, don’t you agree?      Utterly disagree with the delay, even more so when it’s a matter of health. I only spoke to my mum about that the other day. You know my dad passed last year, God rest his soul. It was awful, the way the system treated him — turned him down for an MRI for far too long. He lost precious time.      That must’ve been so hard. When’s the funeral?      It’s next Saturday in Dorchester. I expect that’ll be one of the few times we’ll get to be up near home in a while. It’s still surreal grief, you know — still trying to process it all. My sister refuses to talk about it. You ever notice how some family members just shut themselves off, and others take the lead on everything?      All too aware. My Sil’s been the same — won’t cook, won't even look at food. She put on a stone in a month from just snacking all the time. I tried talking to her, but it's a minefield. Between grief and weight, it's such a sensitive area, eh?      Absolutely. I try to keep the conversation light at times. I mentioned doing some yoga classes to her — maybe that’d help get things moving a bit, both physically and emotionally.      That's thoughtful of you. My friend Beryl’s been on a sugar detox for the last month. Says it’s helping her clear her mind too. Odd how the body and mind are connected like that. Even if it’s just about nutrition, the emotional wherewithal is surely there.      Definitely. I’ve been reading up on some go-to diets for energy and mood. Not that I'm at all unhealthy, just trying to keep that headspace clean.      I can respect that. So, have you made it to the café in town yet?

Rather skip ahead a minute, eh? You've all had such a long day. How was work today, James?      Oh, you know the usual! Sorting out some logistics issues with a supplier in Germany. Not quite as exciting as I'd hoped! But nothing I can’t handle. Got a meeting tomorrow to hash it out properly. How 'bout you, Sue?      Quiet enough. A lot of proofing done this morning and a chat with a client about branding ideas. She's considering a rebrand and was very keen on what I proposed. It's always satisfying when the creative ideas land the right way. I’m still catching up a bit from the weekend, though!      My Saturday wasn’t bad either! The ski trip’s coming up, right, Dad?      That's the plan! A little break to the Lake District — not quite the snow-slicks of the Alps, but it’s still a good chance to clear the head. We’ll take the new car — the spare seats will come in handy for all your gear.      Yeah! I can’t wait — I’ve never really skied that much. It’ll be fun, even if we go in something of a rush.      That’s the spirit! Sue?      Yeah, I know, I’m not exactly the sportsy type. But I'll manage. Maybe I’ll borrow some of Mark’s gloves.      Haha — don’t get too jealous! That said, a good pair of gloves can definitely make all the difference.      Speaking of being cold — did I mention I got in a few bottles of that Catalan wine I told you about the other week? It really complements this cheese.      That sounds brilliant. I know I've only just finished dinner, but I'd quite fancy a glass for the story you always tell about your trip to Spain.      Ah yes, the time I nearly got stuck in a village because I stopped waiting for a tour guide. It didn't help that I couldn’t find the damn phone with me! Classic.      Some of us work far too hard, Sue. You're living the life with the holidays goin' on.      Oh, don't be daft! I’m just lucky to be in a job that sometimes gives the chance to travel. But I have to say, Mark — how’s the team at the start of the week?      Busy, but that's normal this time of year.

Rather skip ahead a bit here. So I've been flicking through the box of photos we took when we went to Japan. Never realized how many badger pics we snapped! Must be the most kitsch subject anyone's thrown cash at to shoot. Look at this one—Lola actually tried to make it look like a noble samurai!      That  was  one of my favorites! I remember she insisted on posing him in this ridiculous kimono we borrowed from a woman in Kyoto who sold it as a prop. She said the family used it during the festival season.      Right, and of course, Lola made sure the badger had the spiciest wasabi on the side. My God, I haven't laughed like that in ages. Remember when he sneezed right into the lens and the whole bubble of wasabi screamed down my shirt?      Oh, I still have that shirt! It's now buried in the back of a drawer, thanks to your camera hidespot, or rather, the wasabi. Good times, right?      Definitely—personally, I favored the one in Nara where we both stood still and tried to be as non-intrusive as possible watching the deer circle. Not that I mind—they were photogenic. I remember the deer lit up the frame with vibes of "sparkle and greed." One of them nearly took the whole sandwich, unashamedly.      And you passed it to him like it was dharma. I'm still not over the moment he dropped it in the grass ten seconds later, just so the squirrel could glide over and sprite himself off with it.      That was the cherry blossom moment, surely. But serious now—who knew a badger could be so go-to in the pond life? It's weird how so many of our best memories in Japan were moments between us and the wildlife.      Yeah... you know, I sometimes get lost looking at those pictures, thinking about where those badgers are now, or if that particular squirrel made it through the year.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get that they're part of her heritage, but when they're in the next room and you're trying to sleep?      Oh, yeah, that is rough. Not to mention they sound like a chainsaw on motor oil when it gets really loud. My friend went passive-aggressive on her flatmate by saying he was basically running a demolition site next door.      Fair enough! Honestly, I’ve had friends who used to   literally   snore and then chuckle like "Hey, that was kinda funny" the next day.      That sounds mostly mean—like a flexible jaw is the real weapon here. You know, like that My Name Is Earl bit with Cokie the horse’s lawyer. Ten seconds of nap music for the D-list citizens of Snoretopia.      For sure. But forget the snoring, have we actually discussed this zombie apocalypse plan yet? I mean, what’s the deal?      I have a few stock cans of spam, and that’s about it.      I’ve got the occasional tent in the garden.      And I, for the record, would live on coffee—and probably work at a bar all night. "Calling all aspiring poets, poets' therapists, and one experienced barista."      It's already been approved by my Instagram algorithm.      Okay, but I’m still waiting on all of you for the skinny dipping saga in Ireland.      That was definitely a low point for me. I swear the river used to be warmer, and before that, it was at least ethical to go topless.

Rather annoying when a bar in Cambridge finds a request for peanuts is a bit much, innit? I mean, we’re not exactly in the middle of nowhere here. Mate up the road’s got a Nintendo Switch with that new Mario Kart off-road map. Remind me to ask him if it’s any good when we’re home.      True, I’d still take that over these graphs any day. Gaming is better than spreadsheets any mortal minute. You know what I could kill for? A weekend at Alton Towers. Bet that Spinning Log fling is a proper ride. It just feels oddly therapeutic, innit? To her mind, it was all about the contrast between man-made structures and nature. I asked her once why it looked like a scene waiting for a thriller score. She didn’t like that.      Oh, right mate, speaking of films. I took the kids to that Tom Hardy one the other day, the jungle-based one. Bit gothic really, but it had some of that epic fight choreography he’s known for. It reminded me of watching the box set of "Peaky Blinders," you know how the camera sweeps and all?

Rather annoying the queue was taking so long. I suppose it’s Friday night and all—the university students must be having their weekend treat, same as us. I wonder if I can actually manage to stay dry this time. I’m finally going to start those rowing sessions as you recommended.      Oh, well if there’s anyone who can manage it, it’s you! I had to row in kayaking once—a nightmare in the wind last summer. Of course, it was absolutely pouring, so I ended up soaked to the bone and had to buy a waterproof jacket just for the occasion. Do you know what you’re wearing to your first lesson?      Honestly, the idea of getting wet again is beginning to worry me. I’ve got my old anorak from school, but I doubt it’s up to the job anymore. I’ve been thinking of picking up one of those proper GORE-TEX jackets. I see everyone in Cambridge has one these days! You’d be surprised at the number of rowers in hides, you know, near the river—like they expect to stay dry by will alone.      I hear you! I remember the first time I tried to teach my cousin to row, he looked like a drowned cat by the time we got back. He gave up after that. Ha! But it must be a beautiful place in the spring, don’t you think? I’ve been quite busy these days, actually. You know what it is—freelance tutoring, and all sorts of work at once.      That does sound chaotic, but oddly enviable. I’m still managing at the school, though I feel like I’m always trying to make up time. Anyway, it made me think—have you heard about what’s going on with my cousin Jane?      Jane! Has her mum been poorly again? I heard something a few weeks back—was she in hospital for quite some time?      Yes. My aunt’s health has taken a turn for the worse, I’m afraid. She had been fairly well till a year ago. It’s been really hard on the family. Her husband passed away recently, too. They had been married for fifty years. My sister went to see her last week and said it's been an emotional go.      Oh no, that’s terribly awful. I remember your cousin when she was a little girl, running around the garden at your family’s home in Dorset.

‘Mum said we’s better bring our swimmers ‘cause we’re ‘avin dinner by the mancester uni and dere’ll be them outdoor showers like at the festival!’      ‘Ah, right. Not sure I’ve seen one uv those since Bolton fair. But it’s nice they een mind uv holidays, innit? Lighten the mood on results day.’      ‘I don’t know. I tho’t this year was gonna be easier but na, me nan’s taken to textin me in full sentences. Gah! An when I mess with Mums glass bottle... like, I drop it once and now I’m not allowed near the fridge no more!’      ‘That’s madness, love. Oi’s a bottle, innit? It’ll survive if yer not pickin’ it up with your hands. But she’s got a point ‘bout mobiles, innit? I’ve been usin mine for eBay ever since me missus said I were hidesy, ordering them new shoes when I thought she wouldn’t see!’      ‘Oh, I shop loads too. I got me pens and stationery for sixth form last week, proper fancy. Bet me mates are reckonin it’s Vodafone then. D’ya think they remember?      ‘Likely. Oi’s been membin me somethin about student finance and Amazon deliveries. If yer donn’t specify, they might bring it to the Bolton branch again. Spent three hours in a queue once just because they thought I said 'Manchester’ with a ‘th’ instead of a ‘ch’!’      ‘No way! Blimey, da. I’m usin emojis now to clear stuff up. Y’know, like what yer said ‘bout me memory and school meals. Send it as a picture, can’t be bin read ‘wrong. Maybe Mum’ll start usin them too, cut down on all them letters she sends me... Proper ‘espresso’ with relish, them missives!’      ‘Hah! Right ‘ealthy’ with lunches, innit? But hear me out, love. Me nan used to deliver meals around this toun years back. No ‘phone’, no map, just a recipe and a hunch. Gave her a head for directions that’d outclass Google, I can tell ya. ‘Course, she dropped summat once in the rain and had to eat it herself!’      ‘Omg, classic! I’ve ‘ad this dream we’d be them modern street 60s food sellers. You know, those ones who sell stew and chilli, but always in ones that backs onto a curry shop for when they run out?’      ‘Now, now love, we’d go down them allotment roads, wouldna we?

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I needed to do everything online anyway for my essays and stuff like that, but I thought at least email would work more reliably. Not bloody likely, though. I’m getting ready to hit up the library tomorrow, I s’pose. Just can’t hack it in this eeny weeny flat of mine. It was bad enough just coming over here.      Aww, sorry mate. I know that this Wi-Fi here is easier said than done. I came back to my sister’s place just to get some reliable internet for the exam I’m prepping for too. Not to mention, even if it’s dead slow, at least the fridge works and I’ve got someone to cook for me, y’know? So it ain't all bad. I’ve planned a trip with a mates for next year, and Tokyo is the first stop. We’re thinking of hitting up Kyoto and Osaka next after that. If I could get a work visa while we’re at it, I'd be in Heaven. I’m seriously trying to get a job here before I start my masters—job’s looking better now than uni, honestly. Any solid plans for restaurants where you wanna eat when you make it over?      Oh you bet, I've got this list of vibes and stuff. There's this izakaya place that friends back home have told me about, close to the railway station. Burgers and yakitori galore. I heard it's top tier. And yeah, I'm told it's all about the ambiance and the way you interact when you’re out there. Feels like being in a full-blown cultural space. And I plan on bringing some English friends with me if the visa work out for us, you know? Plus, I’ve been looking into goin' on some tours if I end up settling there.

Rather skip Facebook entirely, if I'm honest. I post once or twice a week, mostly old family photos... got to show off my mother-in-law’s latest baking triumph! Honestly, it’s wild how much she likes it. “Grandma’s Apple Sponge” as if the world needs to know!      Oh, I understand the sentiment—and trust me, if it wasn’t for the group chats and the odd family update, I would’ve uninstalled it long ago. But you know what? Last time someone shared those photos from Buckfast Abbey—and what a lovely setting it was! That peaceful place really grows on you, doesn’t it?      Ah yes! I had the pleasure of visiting in my younger days, back when I was still an accountant. The tranquillity there, the old stone walls, the abbey and the view—unlike anything else in the southwest. I think we should all go back as a family, you know, for a bit of proper time away from the phones—settle into a nice little B&B and listen to the occasional bell instead of your phone buzzing every other minute!      A nice B&B—it would be lovely. I remember when we got stuck in that one near Totnes last summer. The water was lukewarm, and the kettle had a funny whistle. But somehow, we all ended up having the best laugh about it! Though, let’s be careful this time with booking. I remember the last trip my insurance wouldn’t cover car troubles because I failed to read the small print.      Ah, insurance! A minefield for those not fully aware. I about lost my hair after a health scare a few years ago. Turns out, most policies excluded what you least expected. Still, better to be informed and have it than to be in that boat with a ‘but hang on, no, this isn’t covered’ response.      Oh, I was just reading an article about David Cameron and how some big tax avoidance schemes were being highlighted. It’s unbelievable sometimes what people get away with! And honestly, I think it’s partly the system’s fault. Too many loopholes, not enough accountability.      Exactly. And then on the personal front, our own tax woes. Did I ever tell you, I had to go to the box office last week when my train broke down near Plymouth—it was chaos.

Rather annoying driving in Belgium, eh?      Aye, it's not like the motorways back home. Never mind lane discipline, I nearly got run over in this roundabout in Brussels! Got me thrown off me moorings, I can tell you.      You should een use the sat nav more, Dad. I 'ad me phone set up with Google Maps and it wos a life saver when I got lost in this little town, Waremme. It was quite easy 'til the roads got all tight and downhill and I 'ad a right scare.      Oh, I 'eard the markets there were lovely, though. I found a friend of mine in Harlow 'oo'd been there last summer. She said the cheese and chips were 'orrendous.      I'll be the first to say the food was far better than any chip shop breakfast, no doubt. I 'ad some moules marinières and fries, properly roasted, not that greasy stuff back 'ere. Real highlight of the whole trip, if you ask me.      Fries! I can still taste 'em. But I'll say the real tribulation wos cycling in-country. Told me wife I'd rather walk than get on a bike – but then I got a deal with me phone, and thought I'd see the sites 'fore it broke.      Oh what phone ‘ad you? I been meaning to upgrade mine, someone at the care home keeps putting me off with stories of 'orrendous new tech.      I got a Samsung Galaxy and it ‘ad this GPS thing  everywhere . Prime for cycling and about five days off the grid wos quite the adventure.      I didn’t fancy that! Going off the grid like! I ‘ad me old Nokia, but that’s just for ‘ands-free and playing solitaire. All that tech is more 'an I can handle.      Well I think talking it through, you two did brilliantly. My knees would’ve gone as soon as I seen the hills in Belgium.      Aye, the scenery took the oof out of it, though. All them windmills and the canals in Bruges wos absolutely stunning.      You’re right about that. đáng it's always the small things that stick with you — like that cake we 'ad in this little shop on the way back from the market. Sweet, crunchy and not as greasy as expected.      I bought me a souvenir from the market. Somen kind of chocolate wafer and they said it's.related to the region's history.

Rather annoying when the oven’s on and the whole place starts smellying like damp socks, isn’t it? What on earth are you putting in this dish, love? Not another shepherd’s pie, are you? It sounded a bit more gourmet, but now I’m thinking I may have overestimated my own cooking skills. You’re not serious about that old fancy stuff, are you? Bloke down the road sells logs from the local council park—he says it’s all Royal Oak, or something. Anyhoo, back to the dinner. Have you thought about making your rosemary tea afterwards? Or is that just for your Facebook friends who all take pictures of flowers in vases and tag you:  "Debra brought these from the Royal Horticultural Show in something or other."       Don’t be so crude! Look, it’s romantic to have about five vases of flowers all over the place. And my rosemary—yes, I  grew  it—has been doing well. Doesn’t it smell up the flat? A bit, like Burgundy baked into the guestroom walls. And yes, that  is  a real accent, thank you very much. Not some posh Received Pronunciation nonsense. I’m a proper Geordie.      Ah, yes, your accent. It’s one of the things I love about you, you know. You come from Middlesbrough, not Newcastle. So really, your life mission is trying to convince everyone you’re a Geordie, aren’t you?      You know what your problem is? You never have any perfume on, so you judge me for liking my cheap stuff from Boots. You don’t get to talk to me about ‘authentic pronunciations’ with that voice that sounds like it’s been lasered out of Channel Five.

Rather annoying when people from the South make assumptions about the North. I've had it plenty of times when I worked in Bristol. Never mind them thinking we're more down to earth— pah ! They probably thought we were all mooners or something like that.      Aye, it's all the same old, innit? I 'ad a time in Queensland where all them Southerners came through with all their posh telly boss looks, top hats and tailors. Makes me laugh 'til this day. I was down there for a short run when the firm sent me to manage a site in Brisbane.      Aye, Queensland's the real wild card, innit? Being from 'ere, I preferred living in Brisbane to Sheffield. It’s just more, well, I dunno,  far out , in the Australian way. Living in a sunburnt country is better than breakfast with a metal spoon and brussels sprouts.      I imagine the weather in Brisbane's a world apart from the rain in the West Country, isn’t it? I taught EFL in Bristol for thirty odd years and I can say with quite a bit of certainty, it only rains on Fridays. At least in the summer. Well, nearer twelve months when it got damp.      Don't I know it. I had to get a new suit the first winter there because the rain would seep through the fabric after three days in the office. And let’s be fair, someone in a business suit looking suspiciously like a mannequin just ain't doing a good job in Queensland heat. I borrowed a couple of singlets from the locals and called it a day, save my waistcoat about five times a week.      She’s right though—business men in Australia don’t take life quite so seriously. I noticed that while teaching a short course in Brisbane. My Sheffield ‘ard 'ead lot always got confused when I called a friend 'arvest me man'. They’d just assume I was shouting.      A little bit like when I told my students in Bristol that I "nicked" the cake with 'Arf the biscuits from the larder. They all gave me  such  looks.      Yeah, go on then, make life about rules and restrictions. Just give me a brash Sheffield language any day. It always means something, even if it scares your upper middle class southern classmates.      Oh aye, I'm with you there. Just like in Australia, everything is either  far out  or  cop it , innit?

Rather annoying, though, isn't it? That whole lot of social media people just jumping on every bandwagon... It's rather exhausting keeping up with all that nonsense. I prefer a good documentary now and then, or perhaps a podcast. You wouldn’t have any recommendations?      Honestly, yeah, I find it a bit of a circus too sometimes. But I reckon it depends on how self-aware you are with it. I still use it, but I keep tabs on what I'm seeing. As for podcasts, there’s one called  But Why: A Podcast for Curious Kids  that's great—it reminds you not to lose your sense of wonder. I mostly listen to it at the weekend when I’ve got time to relax.      Mmm, interesting. I tried listening to a couple of them once, but they all used quite a lot of jargon—too many assumptions about the listener’s knowledge. I suppose I'm more of a slow learner, or I prefer things unpacked, you know?      I get that—and I suppose not everyone wants to be spoon-fed, but sometimes you need a break from everything being too dense. If you like a bit more depth,  Serial  is good, but it's pretty intense. If it’s rhythm and light entertainment you’re after, maybe try  The Comedy Bang! Bang! Show . It's a comedy podcast but gets deep sometimes. It's got a quirky vibe, but I quite enjoy it.      There’s also this funny thing with the television—so much of it just wants to be edgy, or ironic, or something, and it's all over the top. Even the documentaries—I mean, some of it’s alright, but about half the time they want you to feel the right way about something instead of just learning a bit.      Oh, I know exactly what you mean! It's like the presenters are overcoding the whole thing. I can’t stand it when they make it sound like the most earth-shattering thing ever just to get a reaction. I miss the ones that just stick to the facts and let them speak for themselves. Although, I do find historical documentaries on Netflix decent—graphics are top-notch, and they tell stories in a more accessible way.      There's one on the life of suffragettes that was rather good—beautifully shot, too, with those illustrations of the time.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't got anything to do this weekend. I was just wondering if they’re planning to go to the pool or maybe do something with ANON? I need something fun after a long week of teaching.      Oh, we're going to Swim School again with ANON. I saw the butterfly fish!      I want to go on the climbing wall like on Blue Peter. A lot of people got badges doing that.      Oh, right, there's that. We can definitely do that. But before that, when can we visit ANON’s Travelling Circus again? It was brilliant last time. I love the horse and the clowns!      My turkey leg was eaten by ANON though. I thought it was funny, but I still missed my food!      They have pigs in clover, aren’t they amazing?      You need to behave better with ANON in future though. I know they looked after you, but ordering puffins and eating a turkey leg isn’t safe, even for fun.      I got a picture I can send to Blue Peter as well. Did I tell you, ANON gave me this photo to send with stickers? I黏住了 it properly.      That's wonderful! I helped you黏 it on the envelope. I imagine they’ll love it.      ANON is so old though. I keep asking, and they just say someone older in the village also works with them. I don’t quite understand.      They're not that old, love. Maybe being older is part of the show. Clowns do make a bit about age, don’t they? You just have to trust them, like you trust me.      They told us about China and how they eat old eggs for fertilisation. My science teacher said they do it for tradition.      Gross! I told them I would never want any of those eggs.      Well, I think it’s an interesting part of culture. Though I’m not getting anywhere near those lunches, I think.      We also want to go and get our photographs with Pippy! The one by the go-karts on pond life day!      Yes, I remember that, they had the green tie on with big gills.      We could have a big trip to the karts one day next week. I can ask ANON if they'll come too.      That’s ambitious, but if you both promise not to go over the height limits or forget our passports, then yes.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand it's normal and all, but it's been like... off and on lately. Like, one minute he's  absolutely fine , the next he's like, “Ahhh, I don't know, I just can't get in the mood or whatever.” And I'm  not  even one of 'those' girls who complains about everything, innit. I’ve just got a right clue what's goin' on.      Oh no, that sounds rough. Leeds weather mightn’t help either. It's  constantly  grim here. You know how it does. People can get a bit down and out, mental health-wise, and that  definitely  affects things like that. I think it's called... er, erectile dysfunction, or somethin'?      Yeah, that's it. My flatmate mentioned it when she was talkin’ to her boyfriend. Hated to ask outright what’s goin' on, obviously, ’cos it's so  personal . But I mean, I was worryin’ if it was somethin’ he might have to get looked at. He said he tried takin' probiotics or somethin’ for it, like it was a bug or somethin'.      Haha, no, that’s not gonna fix it, unless it’s a  very strange  kind of bug! I done a module at Cambridge about, well, human physiology. And there are  loads  of factors. Stress, tiredness, anxiety, or even what you eat—there's a fair stretch between the body and the brain, innit? If it’s not a physical issue, it’s probably psychosomatic.      So... he might just be  stressed ? I know he's worrying about uni stuff, like his finals comin’ up. And I dunno, maybe he's worried about performin’? Like, the pressure to be any good all the time? I dunno, I just wish I could help.      Yeah, but also, you've 've been thinkin' about it quite a bit, no? Like, are you feelin' like you're gettin' goin' on your own if you don’t get goin' with him? Because, innit, sex is a big thing in a relationship. But if it’s not happening, it can make ya question how you feel about things otherwise.      True. I mean, I’ve ‘ad this one thought like, "What if I’m not... enough for him?" But then again, maybe he just needs a bit of time to sort 'isself out. I suppose I could suggest he goes and sees someone professional, you know?

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That syrup is 0 calories but it's such an artificial flavour... got to be worse than sugar. I’m more than happy to take an extra syntholic if I can just have some real syrup with my tea.      Honestly, I don’t care if it’s  technically  free syns. I reckon it tastes like something that needs a medical disclaimer. A lot worse than just having one too many, honestly. Oh, and by the way, you said you were going to make that cauliflower cheese this week for the roast?      Yeah, I’ve even got the spice mix ready! Got the Quorn in the fridge. I managed to get the turkey mince for half price at Waitrose’s week-end offer – I’m calling it a success. But I’m sad not to have any of those double peas in the freezer. They’re so breakfast-adjacent if I just happened to have a bit in my soup.      Oh, I’m gutted about that. I had my eyes on those for one of my writer’s block days. Anyways, I’m saving my syn points as it is. I only used two for today’s dinner. I made us some lemon and herb mix with the veg box delivery. Super – saves me from having to deal with the shops again.      Same here. I did my shop through their app on the weekend and didn’t even have to pay tax. Our food budget is in one of those suspiciously generous government programmes? It just feels oddly sour.      I know, and I thought being freelance would mean I could  actually  spend money because I have about five tax years to file. But no, it still feels like I have to document every single soup and frylight usage. Honestly, I considered using Siri as a reminder for my calories. My phone  should  just keep track of how much I eat.      You know, I was thinking about it the other day. Maybe I’ll set my calendar for a ‘treat day’ next Saturday. Then I can go full with lunches and a little chocolate bar guilt-free. I just wish the scales weren’t so bloody temperamental. Sometimes I swear mine is set go up 1kg unless I stand on it for ten minutes pre-weighing.      I’ve noticed that too! I had to accept that the only time I can seriously trust it is when I weigh out my tea bags, never people.

Rather than going the traditional route, I was toying with the idea of writing our own book — you know, like a travel memoir or something. I’m more than capable of handling it, especially since I manage articles for the boss now.      That's a great idea, love. You always have that sort of eye for detail. I'd just enjoy watching you work on it — not that I’d let you do it alone. I’d be all, “You know, darlin’, I could help with the tech side or the formatting.”      Oh, well, don’t get too full of yourself. I'd still be the one with the words, and you’d probably make jokes about my MySpace-era tattoo being on the cover.      I’m not the one who got the dragon and said it was the sign of my "personal evolution." And let’s not forget when you thought it was “the early days of a new age.”      You didn’t say anything back then. Also, the dragon was fierce and majestic—unlike the time you tried to vote in a general election and put your cross in the wrong spot.      That was a clerical error, not a political one. Anyway, we’re talking about holidays – have we decided on the continent, or are we sticking to something closer to home like Cornwall or maybe the Lake District?      Well, you know how much I enjoy the countryside, but I also want to get outdoors more. Maybe a mix — like a countryside cottage with some kind of outdoor adventure nearby? Hiking, cycling… being active.      You’re romanticising it about now. I’m not the same biker I was thirty years ago. I can handle a walk and maybe a gentle ride, but I draw the line at unmarked trails in the rain.      Fair enough. Though I do think it would be nice for us to try something a little fresh, you know? I’ve been thinking about your job too. We could maybe even catch up with some of the clients you've been working with over a couple of days while we're there?      You mean while you're writing the bloody book? go ahead then, make it about me too — I'm practically a supporting character just waiting for a script.      You'd be your own subplot. The rugged, middle-aged IT guy battling conference calls while his wife writes a memoir that never gets published.

Rather annoying the wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp as a sponge all week. Never mind—what about that birthday tea we were going to arrange next Tuesday for Muriel? I don’t fancy her feeling overlooked this year.      I’ve sent the invitations and got a reply from most. I was wondering if we might use the conservatory this year—it’s been such a fine structure now, and this weather isn’t helping with garden plans. We’ll have to keep the doors open to air the place out later.      Sounds a good idea. Right, I’ve baked Mary’s madeira cake last week—well, I’d have had it ready now if Myra hadn’t called in with an urgent problem with her boiler. Probably her partner’s been fiddling with the settings again. A world of nonsense—gas is for heating, not for blowing things up, no doubt about that!      Ha! Well, I pity the poor engineer that goes out to deal with that one. As for the cake, that should be the showpiece, yes. Speaking of which—did I put that postcard of our trip to Tenerife on the table today? I was meaning to show you.      Wasn’t that lovely—those beaches looked better than I expected. I take it the photos came out well despite the cloud cover? I remember you saying the sun was rather unreliable toward the end.      Oh, someone at the resort fixed the blurs. You’d never know it was snapped through a patio umbrella. Though the real reason I mention the postcard is—would you mind mailing it to William? He’s still in about five decades behind in social media, so the good old post is his main channel.      Aye, that shouldn’t be a problem. I was meaning to go to the post office for the Gazette anyway. There’s been quite the editorial on that Scotland business, by the way—haven’t you read it?      Not yet. I did see the headlines from the  Times , of course. Rather grand statements with no plan attached, if you ask me. Some people still want separation for the sake of it.      Yeah, go on then—they’ll see if they don’t get a better deal out of it. Frankly, I don’t see how they can afford anything near what they’re threatening. It’s all politics and posturing, like always.

Right, so today at school we were talking about raising awareness for Syrian refugees, and the kids came up with a fantastic idea. James and Emily want to make drawings of chairs for a charity event we’re hosting next week. It’s called the 'Chairs of Hope' thing — you know the one I mean?      Yeah! The one where people write messages on chairs and donate to help kids who can't go to school anymore. James said that this week he drew a really big chair with a crown on it because he wants to give the Syrian kids "fancy seats when they get to school."      I drew one too! I did a red chair and the wheels go round and round on the floor like My Little Pony. I told Mummy it’s so the Syrian boys can go to playtime.      I love it — your imagination is brilliant, darling. And James is quite taken with the whole idea of 'fancy chairs for fancy schools.' He’s been telling me non-stop about how he saw a documentary where the refugees have to sleep on the floor, so his chair has both a pillow and a blanket inside it.      What did Emily draw, though? Her chair looks like it’s on fire on the outside, and it says, “Hot Bedlin!” at the top. I don’t think it’s actually spelled correctly.      Oh, don’t worry — she means ‘let’s bedlin together’ which I suppose is her version of 'let’s live in peace.' Honestly, I think it’s a beautiful message. I had a talk with the other parents at the meeting, and some of the older kids at school are making giant cardboard chairs for the foyer display about refugee experiences. Maybe we can show our drawings there too?      Can James put a picture of me on the chair? I want to be a ‘chair helper’ so the kids know that little girls can help too.      Can I have me on a green chair holding something shiny? I want to be a ‘sparkly helper’!      Of course you can both be helpers! What matters is that we keep the conversation going and make sure the kids understand that even small acts, like drawing a chair or writing a message, can go a really long way. I think this kind of work at home makes the school tests on history and art feel a bit more real — it’s what your teacher was talking about at the planning meeting.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't seen Sophie and Nathan in ages. I know her email address is out of date, and I've tried calling her mobile, but it goes straight to voicemail      Yeah, it's bizarre. They said they'd pop over for Sunday supper after the baby was born, and now she's six months old, and they haven't even sent a postcard.      I think they got side-tracked, honestly. You know how it is when you're trying to settle into a new job. Sophie's new role in conservation must keep her on her toes.      Conservation? I thought she was going to work in urban planning?      Yeah, I was surprised too. She’s working on a project involving London parks now—urban conservation, I guess you'd call it. Combining nature with city living. Rather fascinating if you’re into that sort of thing.      And what about Nathan? Still working in that computer modelling firm?      I think so, though I overheard her mention a new job in architecture—somebody in the building design department. They must be supplying Nathan with all the fancy design tools he needs to live the life of a modern domestic man.      Haha, fairly typical, I'd say. You'd think he'd be out there baby-proofing by now instead of trying to perfect the lighting in a virtual room.      Well, he is also teaching part-time at City Lit. He's been doing evening classes—3D design and some kind of urban design and sustainability module. That must be where he's picking up the extra income about which Sophie always complains.      Oh, City Lit. I used to take a weekend class there when I was barely out of university. Rather glamorous for evening classes. My, they've made it rather fashionable since.      I always wanted to go. Any chance any of those classes might have disappointed someone? I mean, I always thought they'd be good for learning something beyond being academically useful. Do people actually keep the models they make in class?      Some of them do, like a man I taught once. He really got obsessed with 3D house plans and now has made his own in painstaking detail, based on a 19th-century design. He told me proudly he could have sold it for 3000 pounds had he finished it sooner.      Is it like dolls' houses for grown-ups or something?

Rather annoying when a new tutorial pair finds out I'm a lecturer. I had this one bloke in first year, and I thought I'd lucked out with his essay, you know?      What do you mean? Did you not like what you read?      I read the essay, and I thought, "Oh good, he actually  read  the lectures." Normally you just get these generic regurgitations of titles and a sentence here or there. Imagine my surprise when he came up and asked me questions like "So what's your take on the class system in Jane Eyre?"      Oh, no! Did he think he was giving you a hard time or something?      No, not really. But I thought, "Oh right, I suppose they pick and choose who gives the tutorials. Blimey, I’ve been working with this guy, and I didn’t even notice he was a lecturer in his own right!" And the worst part was, he didn’t have a laptop in the staff room, and I did. I thought, "Tip-top, I can pretend I’m just a student."      And did you? Tell him you were a student?      For the first month. Ha – till one of his students sidled up to us and said, "Oh, weren’t you in Professor Bell’s lecture the other day? I thought you were a senior tutorial fellow, but then you just wandered into the room like it was nothing."      I can definitely picture that.      You know the worst thing? That I actually  was  a tutor for most people about then. I was fulfilling all the roles except talking to him. I had first-year undergrads, and I also had that guy doing tutorials beside me. And he was decent, to be fair, but for the first lesson he was like "Right, what's on the reading list?"      Wait, he didn’t even know what the theme was?      No. He literally asked me if it was the 'British Romanticism' one. I had to be like, "Yeah, that’s the one," like I was his co-teacher or something. But it was hilarious.      I like how you just went with it.      I had to. It made me look like I knew what I was doing, after all. And after that incident, we became fast friends. He made me a backup over the summer when he was on holiday. I’m not entirely sure if I did a better job or a worse job than he did, but I think I did alright.

Rather annoying I had to take out my mortgage to get a van. I know it's only a temporary thing... got to get some stuff from the old house sorted before I can take it all      Aye, we do know the van hire places charge a tidy penny nowadays. My arthritic hands couldn't drive the thing anyway, they'd be too stiff!      I remember that Aunty Phyllis had this old lorry van; it used steam to get pulling power. She always took it to the Great Dorset Steam Fair when it was still running. You'd fetch chips to go with it!      That's right, only trouble was, the van always caught fire on the drive home!      Ten to one the old shed's got some bits of machinery I could sell. I mean if you're up to selling old stuff online. I could set up an eBay store for you!      I'm no good with that computer lark, always managed to delete the cookies or something. It's a monumental pain, if you know what I mean.      What about the old electricals? You've got televisions from probably every decade. I've got a friend that deals in antiques.      I'm not giving up that fishing rod! It was the cheapest you can get from that shop in the high street. Still catches fish though, every now and again!      That fishing also cost me a mobile phone a while back. I left it on the table and the kid ran off with it. It was through my university social clubs!      I about lost me phone while I was trying to play those computer games with Charlie. Not much cop on them things!      I've been trying to get the family to meet up, but for the life of me, no one can make it. They all have jobs to go to or other commitments. Do you fancy coming with me to Basingstoke or somewhere?      I've been out of work all me life, I think it's been long enough! Was going to play the lottery, but I gave it up! The money's better goin' on petrol for the van or something else real.      I see your point. I hate blokes who live off your lotteries. It's like throwing it to the wind and hoping it lands where you want it to!      I've heard from your uncle Frank, he moved houses!

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? The council wants to knock down the library. I would've thought they’d be more sensible with heritage sites. I mean, it's not like it's a Victorian eyesore that's blocking progress. It's only from the fifties for goodness' sake.      I know, I understand the budget issue, but just bulldozing it without even trying to restore it? A shame really. I passed it this morning, and the old building still looks sturdy enough. You’d think they’d give it another go for funding from outside sources, or at least try some modernisation like retrofitting it with new tech.      What’s worrying is how many other places like that they’ll knock down under the guise of “modernisation”. I was reading earlier on the council’s website, they mention architectural conservation in the statement, but then you find out they’ve prioritised taller car parks and new retail spaces over community hubs. Honestly, I’m starting to wonder if they ever looked at what's actually useful to local people.      That’s exactly what I mean. I’ve had some of the staff at work raving about the children’s area and how it encouraged reading back when they were younger. It’s not just a building; it was a space that shaped people’s – well, minds, I suppose, in some cases.      Yeah, and don’t get me started on the council’s approach to maintaining old facades while the insides are in disrepair. Spent a grand amount making the front of a building look classy but left the wiring out of date and the heating inefficient. What’s the point?      It’s like they’re trying to fluff up history while neglecting everything else. Speaking of which, I had to choose a new fabric for the living room upholstery today. I considered something traditional, but in the end I went with a modern design. Maybe it’s symbolic. I thought, why not mix up the old and the new a bit? It seems more sustainable.      You always do have good taste, love. I’ll have to see it soon. In the meantime, I think I’m going to call the local branch of The Daily Telegraph and see if they're covering the library proposal. If the newspapers really get wind of this, maybe there’ll be more action.      Hopefully so.

Rather annoying when the Spotify Wrapped comes through and I only have 23 listens for the whole year. Seems I got too caught up in spreadsheets and emails to actually  listen  to music properly. What about you, Lucy? Do you still blast the same kind of pop tunes you did at university?      Yeah, I mean I still enjoy some good pop if it catches my ear, especially if a client’s coming in stressful. But I’ve also been getting into some chilled-out lo-fi beats while I dye hair. Makes me feel fancy, like I’m creating art when really I’m just plugging away with bleach. What about you, Ruth—still listening to that post-rock nonsense?      Oh come on, Jonathan, I’ve evolved. I left post-rock behind when I finally realized I’d never be shouted at by a sad acoustic guitar. These days it's either Radiohead’s Cats in the Cradle, or whatever Electronic Daisy Carnival happened to suggest last week in my “Mystery Vibes” playlist. You, Chris? Still slamming the classics in your car like it’s 1998?      Absolutely! I put on some Dire Straits or Fleetwood Mac when I’m driving, and there’s something about the gravel in the rhythm and the sea air that just fits the journey somehow. Plus, I’ve got a daughter who wants to be a DJ, and her saying “House music’s next” always makes me want to prove her wrong with a bit of good ol’ rock ‘n’ roll. Although I’ve had to buy a few Coldplay tracks to keep her from switching the radio herself.      Any chance I could persuade you to buy me a good set of Apple EarPods for Christmas? My old pair are broken beyond all recognition, and I can’t be doing with the corroded pickups that plug into the car while it snows. You’re the business analyst, surely you can justify the £20 as part of my productivity?      If you want to write it off as a business expense, fine—but I expect your hairdressing appointments to reach 100% efficiency. What about lunches, Chris and Chris? Any presents planned? We usually go for experience vouchers, something around TV or theatre.      I was thinking of booking a comedy night at the local Arts Centre—there's a new troupe doing a nostalgic 80s retrospective. Lift your glasses and you could be at the big night out of your youth, metaphorically speaking.

Rather annoying this new insurance thing eh, lad? I remember back in the day, it was ‘ave yer number plates and a clean reg shot and that was more or less it. Now it’s all gotta be this, that and £2000 quid as a deposit.      Yeah eenit, it’s mad. I got an 'insurance quote the other day for like… over £5k. A year? For just a bloody Fiesta?      Yeah, well, there's lots a factors at play here. Y’see, yer age, the car y’got, where y’live—it all plays into it. Malton’s got the roads, don’t think it’s like York where you’ve got all them young whippersnappers in fast cars. But still, the insurance companies don’t care. I think it’s all ‘bout making cash, to be honest.      Bucks yeah? I mean, I’m not in trouble or nothin’ and I’ve done my driving test ages ago. Shouldn’t I be like ‘calm driver’ or somethin’?      Aye, well ye’re bound to be a calmer driver by now, but they don’t reckon that. Insurer blokes are like examiners. They mark on the book, not on the chekin’. Anyway, if ye wanna drive, somethin’s got to be done. You could always go for a black box.      A what box?      A black box. It goes in yer car and tracks yer habits. How ye brake, accelerate, time of day ye drive—’nother panic ballet, really. But if ye drive sensible-like and not all night, the price eases up over time.      That sounds daft. Feels like they’re spyin’ on me.      Aye well, it’s a trade off. Less freedom and more money on the one hand, or ‘ve a bit of privacy but pay them schemers till the penny drops. It’s up to ye lad. But if ye want me take on it, the long run’s the way to go. Start with a cheaper car—somethin like a Ford Ka or even go electric. I ‘eard the insurance’s a bit better for those, even for us noobs.      Electric? A what?      Electric cars, lad. They’re all the rage now. No fumes, fewer belly aches to pay for parts. And ‘cause they’re newer tech, them companies like to offer the greenies a discount to make ‘em feel good about themselves.      Okay, I'll think on it. Thanks, gran.

Rather than going the entire conversation, I'll cut straight to it. So, as it is with work—what with the workplace stress and all—how do ye find managing stress at this age? It's a mad thing, isn't it?      Honestly, well, I haven’t really had eeny stress at  this  point. Not like   ye   have. I’ve only been at secondary school. A lot of stress tends to happen from exams, maybe. But it’s not   the same as   what grown-ups have to deal with.      Oh, well love, don’t underestimate stress. It follows you wherever you go. Even as someone who’s taken a step back from the workforce, the worry still creeps in—finances, childcare, you name it. Rather annoyingly, I just got through reading a study about cultured meat promising to revolutionise food production in like... ten years. Honestly, I think it depends on how it's made. I’ve been following a couple of small businesses from Brighton doing cultured meat experiments. They’ve done some interesting stuff with plant fiber to give it that "bite." Didn’t even taste like cardboard last week.      That sounds brilliant. I can see meat analogues evolving into something pretty decent. But have you ever tried turkey bacon? I swear it smells like left-over Christmas stuffing and tastes like wallpaper paste. And I say that as someone who eats wallpaper for a living—artistically, at least.      Oh yeah, I hated turkey bacon! Hated it hard. When I first went vegetarian 4 or 5 years ago, I was still horrified at the idea that I was eating something that, yes, is vegetarian, but still looked suspiciously like pork.      It took me ages to get used to tofu—it always reminded me of something in a lab. But once I found the right marination, it was, like, kind of tasty. Honestly, the real problem is vitamin B12 deficiency for vegetarians. I’m already taking a ton of pills, and now I’ve got to start doing this too? I skip most days.      Honestly, I think it's worrying that society is so focused on one form of oppression—say, animal rights—and less on systemic ones. Like, maybe we should spend less time debating if a pig was raised in an "ethical farm" and more time on getting fair wages for workers in abattoirs. They’re not getting the same consideration as the pigs.      That's a really valid point. I did a drawing series a while back called "Carnivore Studies" that was supposed to raise questions about human complicity in the system, not just individual food choices.      I saw some of them online—it was pretty confronting.      Thanks. Anyway, after that project, I started volunteering at a farm sanctuary in Norfolk where they let you meet the pigs and learn about their personalities.

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That queue for the talk—it was supposed to be ‘drop-in’ but turned out to be a full-on marathon press-up. Just last week I had to argue with goon of a man who had a disabled badge chained to his steering wheel, just in case.

Rather annoying to be honest, this whole VW mess. Seems like everything they said was a bit of a scam, if you ask me. Just went to see my son in Birkenhead the other day, and he was ranting about it. Poor lad, had one of those motor things in the driveway for years and now it’s  not worth the paint on the wheels , he says.      I’ve been transcription some stuff about it recently. From what I’ve read, it was a huge ordeal. Millions of cars affected, and the company practically admitting they manipulated emissions when no one was looking. Honestly reminds me of the sort of thing you'd only expect from a dodgy politician, not a car company.      Yeah, I remember hearing about it when it first came out. I had a mate who worked in the oil and gas sector—big on emissions compliance—and he was  terrified . He said if you couldn’t trust the numbers in one industry, what in God’s name were you ever going to trust? He even said it had a knock-on effect for companies regulated by the Water Framework Directive.      Oh, I’m not surprised. Like a domino effect, grief spreading everywhere. Honestly, we’ve got enough to worry about with prices where we are. Hunsonby's lovely – very quiet – but the real estate here, it just  does not  compare to what people in the south would pay for their council flats.      Absolutely. It’s kind of funny someone said to me last week that they’d rather live in the north for half the price and not worry about the housing market crashing. I mean, it’s obvious, but not  everyone  sees it that way.      I think you’re wrong talking about funny, Jane [Speaker 2]. There’s not a lot that is funny when you’re housing poor bloody £100,000 for a four-bedroom bungalow. I passed one for sale on the lane here yesterday. Cost you a bob or two, and with the state of the plumbing... frankly, I'd crack my back side over that one.      Oh, we’ve both cracked over things in our time, Johnny [Speaker_3]. You worked with cars once too, didn’t you go in for the oil industry? Something or other about planning.      Oh yeah, I was in the box for years – technical developments and all that jazz.

Rather annoying when a new housing estate’s raised to build, innit?      Oh aye, I’ll not lie—me poor back don’t fancy a site like that where me garden was. Though I don’t see as the young feller at the council can help it much. Got eeny plans to  not  do it, 'course.      Nonsense. They’ve only got too much policy in their heads and not enough common sense. Me old mate Bill’s place in Norwich—beautiful acres was, now it's concrete and council flats. That's progress for you... Right, I’ve sorted me  computer —still learning, but I found the pension web page and now I'm turkey on it. Still, who’d fancy filling in forms when you're on the breadline, eh?      Oh dear—Don’t mention computers to me. I’ve breakfasts and old lady magazines to worry about, not some inky keyboard. I pity the poor desktop hides, though. Still working at the weekends, isn’t he? Last I heard, he looked keener than a knife shop.      What did he say, grief? Hah! Tell 'im he’d better not mess with me rhythm in the B&B—I’ve no patience for cheek.      Oh, you were staying in York the other weekend, weren’t you?      Aye, gorgeous place that. Beautiful town hall, food that wasn’t just mucky toast. All my family wants is to pop up to a  B&B —silly me, I say  Yes  and now I’m  booked up .      I hear ya. I fancied York once too, but now I'm a homebody. No need to be upsetting folks or myself worrying about transport. Still, I'd do better sticking ‘em on the treble guest list if I had a friend that wasn’t me grandkids.      Oh, I tried once, but bless 'em, they just run about as if I’m a zoo keeper. Except me grand lunches, I think I’m more caretaker than grandma.      Then again, if you told 'em to go out of the pond, you’d risk  I  being in the brine.      Right, bloomin’ pensions—haven’t had a proper sum in me bank for 3 months and I’m blaming the form with the squiggles. True to say, it’s not ‘cause I asked the bank to lock it away.      You know, they said the state may raise the pensions, but always in 'next year' lingo.

So do you lot actually know what’s going to be in the AQA biology paper this week? I’ve been stressing out so much I can’t even sleep properly. I’ve asked my textbook, Google, and even Wikipedia, but honestly, nothing seems to make sense sometimes.      Honestly, it’s all the same old topics: photosynthesis, cell division, and probably some evolutionary stuff. You should ask your teacher—they always drop hints or at least hint at past papers. Oh, and don’t get me started on evolution! My brother was saying the other day that humans literally came from apes. Like, what even is that?      Well, technically we  did , right? Our bodies have like nine genes that are similar to chimpanzees. Evolution’s a bit of a controversial topic if you ask the wrong people, especially around here. My aunt’s super religious and was saying the other day that it doesn’t matter scientifically if we evolved—we were still created for a reason. Statements like that drive me nuts.      Yeah, I mean why do people still argue about stuff like that? If someone had proof of a god-like entity that created the universe, that’d be one thing. But as it is, there’s way more evidence for evolution. Still, it’s got way more to do with perception than science, right? Like, people take comfort in things that are simple.      Ugh, don't even get me started on people taking comfort in wrong things. Like this someone at our school who posted this ridiculous video saying that girls are just bad at science. I was like, “Well, no, you’re the one bad at science if you make a post like that.” He got about five thousand shares though, which honestly boggles my mind.      Honestly, the internet fails at giving facts. I barely even know if what I read on my timeline is real, like half the time it’s just random conspiracy theories or people giving their opinions on gender roles as if they’re gospel. Like, some people still think girls are just waiting to get married instead of pursuing actual careers.      Yuck! That’s not a new idea, though. It’s the same as when you look back in history. Women had no place in the sciences until the 20th century. It’s seriously so messed up.      I mean, we’ve come a long way with the feminist movement and all.

Rather annoying to be honest, I had to cancel a few meetings. But you know, it's better safe than sorry, right? I remember my nephew had an infection from a wound, and it escalated so fast—they had to hospitalise him for five days before they sorted it out.      Oh, infections are dreadful. Mate, you got to take care of yourself these days. I’ve seen too many folks not make it to 80 because they ignored what the doctor said. Still, we live and learn, eh?      Yes, and it helps a lot to have good friends or family—people who’ll nudge you in the right direction. Even if you're stubborn! Look at me, I still have about five friends I walk with every Sunday. Keeps me on my toes.      That’s good to know. I know I need to get out a bit more. I do enjoy rugby, for what it’s worth—but these days I sit on the sofa and strain my eyes watching it instead of any physical participation!      Haha, I used to rush down to the ground every Saturday. Took me by the lunches and a couple of whiskeys. Now I sit in the chair and grump around with the dog! Still, I can go skiing in my mind sometimes if I close my eyes real tight.      And he skis better than most young lads do! So, have you made the hospital appointment yet, dear?

Okay, luv, just before we start, I want to talk about this for a bit. The teacher showed us a video at work about the history of slavery and I thought it's probably time we had a little chat with you two. Just to answer any questions and make sure you understand the truth of what happened and how important it is to learn from it.      But mummy… what is slavery?      That's a good question, love. Slavery is when people were treated as property. A long time ago, people from Europe took people from Africa and forced them to work on plantations, without giving them freedom or fair treatment. That was completely wrong, and now we try to make sure that never happens again.      Like in the book about the sea journey?      Exactly, I think you're talking about the "Middle Passage." That's part of the transatlantic slave trade when millions of people were taken on ships across the ocean, packed tightly and treated very badly, to work for the rest of their lives. It was cruel and inhumane.      Why would people do that though, mummy? Why would they hurt others?      It's a sad part of history, love, but some people thought they were better than others because of the colour of their skin. That’s called racism. People used that idea to take and mistreat others. It was wrong then and still is wrong now. We have to make sure that we treat everyone equally and with kindness.      But mummy, isn't that something from the past? Why do we talk about it now?      Oh, because it affected how people live today. Families were separated, cultures were taken from people, and it caused a lot of pain. Some of that pain still affects people and it is important we remember it to do better.      What about war? I heard about it on the news too.      Oh, love. War is another way people have destroyed each other. We hope you didn't hear something too scary. War is when two sides fight, sometimes with big guns and even bombs, because of disagreements, money, power, or hatred.      Is that why people get hurt?      Yes. War makes people really sad, scared, and homeless. People fight for bad reasons most of the time. The good thing is that lots of people also work hard to stop wars and help the ones who are hurt, just like we try to be kind and help others.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh Harry? That Christopher Dean character’s back on telly, doing some panto in Brighton. Proper manic.      You're not in that, are you Harry? Healthcare?      Nah, self-employed. I’m into deliveries. Doing catering for event things, pottery, you name it. I just haven’t got time to get my head around healthcare. Though I’ve seen enough vaccine trailers with lunches to keep the whole of Kent fed.      Still, delivering something around Kemsing! I used to work in that bin on the edge of Wateringbury. Just rammed ladles full of tripe and green stuff down the box, then off to the next one. Now I just have toast and spam with Emma and Christopher’s chicken pox hours.      True to say, we've changed a lot over the years, haven't we? I’m still in my old job, at the clinic, taking people’s blood and giving them the cold shoulder once or twice.

Right, who’s ready for a story time with a bit of engineering thrown in? Let’s put the dishes away first and then I’ll tell you about poor old George Stephenson. I've been telling you about this for ages, haven’t I?      Yes, like when mummy’s writing on her laptop!  She pauses to think.  But who is he again?      Well, he was a proper hero from the old days—nothing to do with broomsticks and wands like Harry. He lived in the 1800s when everything changed with machines. You know those big trains that go  choo-choo ? That’s because of George!      My friend Oliver said trains are magic. He said they run on tracks and go to faraway places, like Hogwarts!      Oh! Like the Knight Bus?       Chuckles  Well, this happened  before  Hogwarts in real life. George Stephenson is actually called the “Father of Railways,” and he helped build the first proper train lines and engines. One of his most famous ones was the Rocket. You don’t need a wand for this sort of magic, just a brain full of ideas and buckets of hard work.      Does he wear a funny hat like Professor Flitwick?      No, he wore somethin’ called a top hat, but he didn’t turn people into frogs. He turned dust and steel into someone who could ride to Newcastle in a few hours instead of days.      That’s like Apparition without the magic bit?      Exactly! And it changed how people lived and worked. Before Steve and Alex here were even born! Anyway, while I finish stacking the plates, you two can ask me anything. What do you want to know?      Did he have a pet?      A proper one, like Harry? Well, there’s a story. He had a dog called Dobbins, who famously caused a bit of a mess one day when he followed the steam train and got caught with his tail stuck in the whistles. Not as exciting as Hedwig biting Filch, but nearly!      That’s so funny! Did he use spells or wands or anything?      Nah, he used levers, big wheels, and what your teacher would call “science.” But I promise, his stories are just as magical. And now, anyone for custard creams to fuel the talk about the Rocket? I’ve been promised silence from both of you if the cup gets dropped.       Giggles  Only accidentally, mummy!      No, I won the last custard cream last time!

Rather annoying when people just take ages to respond to moves in Words With Friends, innit? I know it’s got to be some sort of game, but come on, it’s not like we’re competing for the World Championship. Not like that scrabble I saw being played on  Bake Off  or whatever eeny-meeny-miny-mo they do over here.      Yeah, I mean I only play when I’m baking and too lazy to actually do something else. It's easier pulling out my phone and slapping down a "ZYMOX" when I get the letters. Honestly reminds me of the time I baked Mary Berry a "cannelloni" out of cornflakes for the supper club My nan dragged me to years ago. Funniest disaster ever. Ten minutes, gone.      Oh, I love supper clubs! We had an Italian one at the café the other weekend. Managed to get through three recipes in one meal... and only two people ordered the charcuterie wrong. You should’ve seen James. He got the instructions wrong, and ended up making minestrone into minestrone  x2 , I mean two different bowls.      It’s wild how much people go on about cooking shows these days. I remember when all we needed was a bottle of Mate’s Mate and a pot of beans, and now it’s like “You must have an apple cider vinegar-soaked quinoa salad or what are you doing with your life”?      Honestly, I think it’s mostly because everyone works a chaotic job nowadays. I do online courses and still get sidetracked by the admin and being told I’ve failed a  literacy quiz . You try being about to fall off the grid trying to prove the English lit major didn’t forget how to spell  oxymoron .      I handle it by sending people to my website with a ‘click here if you’re not cooking anything at 5pm’ button. Worked a charm last time. Pastry scientists relied solely on that link for their dinner. I told one bloke “never fear, sprite of the Websites陉”      That’s what I do at the café. My customers think I’m serious when I say “MENU Revised 3 seconds goenvironmentally.” They see improvements like "Optional Roast Disabled" and "Optional Ice Cream Optional." You don’t go further than that.      It’s all just part of the charm really, though. Like, my barista, Liam—he got in this legal trouble trying to say that ‘duty of care’ obligated them to give free espresso.

Rather skip the new salad bar today, aren't they? I've had one for three days in a row... got to my throat by now. I’m more after a bit of something warm, you know, like that chicken pie with proper gravy they have in the back corner. How about you?      To be honest, I’m still twitching from the breakfast I had this morning. My daughter threw a melon at my flatmate before school this morning, and somehow, it landed on me. She's three and a half and full of beans. I'm into painting landscapes, pottery, and I tried embroidery once... well, let’s stick to painting for now.      Ah, creative hobbies are great. I dabble in gardening—nothing fancy, but there's something calming about tending to a few herbs and veggies in the back of my pond life. It keeps me grounded.      I’ll have to try that. Thanks, I might actually head to one of those weekend gardening clubs you mentioned last week to get some tips.

So do you guys remember when we used to play that old internet game where you had to solve real-life mysteries with text and pictures? I just went back on it and I can't even remember how to start! It's thrown me into a bit of a mood, honestly.      Oh, that one! I remember  not  understanding half the clues. I think it fascinated you all because of the mystery element. A lot of those games were more about logic than anything else. If I'm not mistaken, someone once wrote a whole psychology essay about the addictive nature of chase games, don't you think? Any travel plans for after university? Because I’ve been thinking about moving about for a bit after I graduate. Maybe the Sciences museum in London? It vibes really well with my curiosity.      That’d be lovely. You could even both come. My sister’s planning on re-opening her guesthouse near Guildford, you know. She could sort the accommodation if you wanted to work it around.      You mean I could come out to stay as  well  as doing work? That’s the first plan I’ve heard of lately that doesn’t make me want to cry or immediately cancel.
