Okay, so today in class we were talking about different metals and fabrics, and it made me think — like, do you boys remember when we went on that trip to Comberton's old foundry last summer? I told you about the copper and the iron, and how they used to melt it down in big vats and pour it into shapes?      Yeah! Like Minecraft — crafting metal with a furnace. A lot of people just think of iron and gold, but you said there was a whole heap of metals. What’s the fancy ones called?      Oh, well in the real world, we’ve got things like brass, which is a mix of copper and zinc, or bronze, which is copper and tin. They were really important in the Bronze Age, you know. But in Minecraft, you’ve got special stuff like netherite — which is super strong and lets you do all sorts better than gold, no matter how flashy it looks. Although gold in real life isn’t usually for making tools! It's more for looking nice or trading.      Mummy, I like gold, but I like taking care of my body too! Remember when you gave us those vitamins and said they were like the "metals and metals for the insides"? Do they all help us grow?      That’s actually a really good comparison! Vitamins and minerals are like the "internal tools and resources" of the body. Just like in your world, Minecraft, you need all the right resources to build strong castles and survive the mobs, our bodies need the right bits — like calcium for bones, or vitamin D from being outside — otherwise we get  crabby , or we can't run as fast or walk properly. You can even get the odd "sickness creep" if you lack some.      Wait, but Mummy, we were also told the legend about the Burgess Axe — the one that can cut through anything. The teacher at nursery said the Saxons told it was made from some kind of stone-magic metal. Like a “cursed” material that only certain brave people could lift. He called it 'ore of the gods'! Is that true?      Oh, now that sounds like a proper invention of legend goings-on! But it might be based on real metals. Some ancient legends do that, they mix real facts with fantasy. Like the "Viking one-eyed god" — Odin — maybe made from special stuff, like a kind of steel that was really rare back then.

Rather annoying I tell ya, eh? You know what me Mam’s l’un like, always ‘yer typin’ on dere mobiles’—like she neva used one in ‘er life. An’ she ain’t pleased with us being ‘ere neiten—  Liam   an’   Jake   een’t even twenty yet!        Liam   just turned drite? No wun’s gonna realize, innit? An’ I mean, we ain’t even  drounkin’ . We’ve ‘ad like two pints. An’ if she wants us to not talk... like, wot even is  talkin’ ? That’s all we do!      My point   exactly  ,   Mitch  . She’s like, “You ain’t gonna focus on yer A-lev’l’s if yeh spend all yer time messin’ ‘bout with yer gitters.” Wah? I mean, guitar  is  me A-lev’l! Or is she thinking I’m takin’ a course in  derivatives  or sumfink? Hahah!      I know, innit. Me gran says grief. Says, “You should go on and be a nurse, lad.” Like, no. I want to be a sound engineer or something. I even mess ‘bout with bands on the side. I reckon she don’t even know what that means.      Nah! She thinks a band iz just a group of lads who “go ‘ad a lot an’ shout at people.” I tried explainin’—we got   Skip   from the   Echoes  , and ‘e plays in a few pubs most weekends. It’s kinda nice, playin’ the odd gig. We even had a kid cry once. Not ‘cause it were sad—no, ‘cause   Skip   dropped ‘is gitter.      Nuttins happenin’ in this country if we dinnit got talent like y’uns! But y’know, I dunno if I could stick being round such...  paddies  all the time. Kids that ain't even biggg ‘gainst such big, no respect for  nutthin’ . Pisses me off, innit goin’ on ‘bout if someone's  always  got respect.      I know. I were ‘university’ cafes the ‘ulr, see sum lad with biggg nose and kina creepy eyes, noddin’ ‘is ‘ead at a three-year-old. Feels like I should say somfin, nut I dinnat know ‘ow. Least ‘ere we got a decent crowd.      Yeah, innit. ‘Ere, cheers to the few places that ain’t full of ‘angers. As long as I can play me gitter an’ yeh can argue with yeh Mam, innit all good.      Cheers to that! An’ if she brings it up again, I’ll just tell ‘er I’m startin’ a new band. That’ll shut  ’er  up.

So do you guys reckon we’ve got anything to do this week or are we just gonna mope in like everyone else and waste half-term?      I dunno, I think Ama said she might be going to the Montenegro exhibition at the museum on Thursday. They’re showing all these old postcards and stuff from the Balkans. Not sure if I’m into that.      Aww Akeem, just come! It’s got to be easier than watching  Lord of the Rings  again! And besides, I heard they’ve got free coffee, or at least vegan oat latte substitutes. I’m trying to swap everything out for meat-free stuff now, you know?      My EPQ is madness, you lot though. I’m doing mine on how the education system in the UK treats poverty and I’m stuck. I went to an outreach event at uni and they kept talking about systemic bias and shit I don’t even know how to spell.      Yeah, but fair, right? I mean, I grew up near Wembley—there’s places just, like, minutes away from five-star hotels that are also like super deprived. You walk into the estate and it feels like a different universe. My cousin works in humanitarian aid, like gives clothes and food out – it’s wild how people deal with it, but they do.      Honestly, I did a thing for my EPQ too—about identity and how nationality isn't just passport stuff. My grandad was born in Nigeria and moved to Hammersmith in the ’60s—everyone had to fit in, or fake in. But now I feel like I  can  be fully British and Nigerian, without being told to choose. You guys know what I mean?      Yeah, and speaking of travel—I’m trying to convince my dad to let me do this teen summer camp in Spain for volunteering. It’s not like Club Med, it's more about helping with eco-villages and permaculture. Teaches you to cook too, which I need!      Oh that sounds better than me getting stuck trying to juggle three new A-levels and still do extra tutorials. My sister’s a med student and she’s like, 'You can go to uni on your own if you don’t get work experience,' and I’m like, no, I don’t want to be an alien.      So are you planning to go to uni, Haz?

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what they do with the money for the uni accommodation fund—basically nothing. I’m telling you, I paid good money for a double glazing system, and this is what I get. Just a bit of dodgy tape on the window again.      Yeah, I’ve been tryin’ to get a heating engineer out for weeks. They don’t even reply to your messages. I’m so fed up, honestly. And it’s not as if there ain't money floating around. My auntie works at the uni and says the finance blokes are sittin’ on millions. Lakelands is probably swimming in cash and we’re still stuck with dodgy boilers and pin-sized light bulbs.      I can feel the sympathy, mate, but you're in Lancaster, and I’m stuck back in Bolton with an even dodgier situation at home. I live with my uncle and auntie. They argue daily in Punjabi and English, and it's like, you can’t take a single step without being excluded from something. I mean, it’s not all bad, though. My cousin Faris moved out last year, so I got a little more room.      Y’know, I don’t get all the “uni is amazing – till it ain't” vibe, but I’ve seen some of the emails the uni sends out. All that “investment in the future” and “student-focused universities,” and yet, they don’t even fix the plug in my room. I had to buy a new one from Argos. That’s hotter than the shower.      Exactly what I’m sayin’. We get a Prime Minister talkin about how important university is for the economy, but when the building starts to f    off fall apart, they don’t care. Not like when I was a kid, we didn’t expect the uni to do much for us anyway. Now, young people are supposed to be paying rent for a palace. Doesn't matter how nice it sounds in the brochure, you know.      Speaking of brochures, have you seen the one from the lunches? I mean, whatevs happened to the omelette you used to get for £2.90? Now it's like £4 for a sad tomato and egg thing.      I’ve seen that. Honestly, it's bloomin’ extortion. Last time I was in there, I made it to the ketchup dispensers and my wallet was broken by then.

Rather annoying when half the turkey turns up missing, isn't it? I was just trying to carve it like... like the queen of shepherds, and yet somehow I ended up with less than half a leg and three Brussels sprouts. Where  did  you disappear off to, anyway?      Oh dear, I'm sorry about that, love. I got distracted by Moira in the next kitchen with that awful Christmas pudding recipe of hers that  always  catches fire. She was asking me about catering training courses. Knows nothing, of course, but insisted I'd want to reinvent my consultancy around... frozen festive appetizers. Honestly. I just had to keep her at bay, you know how she gets.      Oh yes, Moira left her last starter bottle of rum on the back step, didn’t she? I think the pigeons may have had a nose about it. Anyway, back to the main event. I've been thinking, after I finish teaching at the language school next year, maybe I should consider doing some work in Europe. Spain, maybe. The winters aren't so horrid and the Spanish take Christmas far too seriously for my taste.      Now that sounds like an adventure. You always did enjoy mixing fun with work. I remember all those years you spent at the language camp in France. I still can't pronounce the name of that village.  Something-on-lake , as you called it.      It was  Étang-sur-le-Lac , but yes, I did enjoy it. Children are easier to teach than some of the adults in this village who insist on speaking as though they're auditioning for a historical drama. Though, honestly, most people about here are lovely. Just not used to the English sense of... chaotic festive vibes.      Tell me about it. Last year, we had snow up to my ankles, and yet  some  of the local guesthouse owners thought it was a good idea to open a St. Nicholas parade. I nearly lost three of my boots trying to drag little Arlo out of the street when that handmade sleigh of his rolled off the platform.      Oh! That happened? Was Johnny there? Still trying to reinvent himself by dressing up the village carols goers in matching pond life sweaters?      You know him better than I do by now. Has a vision, bless him. Though if he ever gets me in a fluoro toad Christmas jumper again, I'm packing him off to visit his aunt in Denmark myself.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I used to do everything on my phone—the apps, the photos... but now I’m just using it for calls more than anything else. I've found myself actually picking up a book instead of reading things online, and it’s such a nice change. Sort of slowed things down, if you catch my drift.      Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. That’s good—personally, I’ve been dabbling in some customer service as a job. Not the most exciting by any means, but it’s stable enough. How’s Brighton then? You said you might be moving?      Yeah, actually, I’m considering it. The weather is better, and there’s more opportunity for work. I’ve already got a few contacts there, and the cost of living isn’t quite as bad as I thought it’d be. Besides, I’d love to be closer to the coast. It's been way too long since I’ve been to the beach in a relaxed way.      That makes sense. I know it can be hard living in the city if you're not used to it. Not that I've ever lived near the sea, but I do enjoy a good trip out. I went to Tanzania last year actually, with a few friends. It was something different for sure, quite an experience. I tried to remember to record everything on my phone, but honestly, halfway through I just gave up and started taking it in properly. It was one of the few times I let the phone be set aside.      That’s brilliant Dad. I really need to do something like that soon. Just give in and unplug for a while.

Rather skip the new PR seminar today. Found a few old records at the market instead—the vinyl section there has gone off lately. Gained some unique jazz stuff, actually. Not sure what specific we’d discuss there anyway, it all seems quite repetitive these days.      Oh, was it that market in Islington? I meant to pop along but kept saying to myself I’d get round to it. Did you pick up any decent Coltrane this time or are we just building up records we’ll never get to listen to?      Didn’t even get round to asking about Coltrane, but I did get these Art Blakey albums—some 60s stuff, really quite in good nick. Thought you might appreciate them more. Fun to reflect on what we were doing this time last year, buying up all these sad acoustic covers for little gigs.      True! That breakfast jazz gig was actually better than most of the PR stuff in London at the time. Still, I thought shopping, even for records, was a bit more erratic than your typical grocery shop—though, if we had to choose, I’d always take quirky record hunting over corporate speak.      Tell me about it! I reckon the market scene is a little PR-worthy in itself. People who find it often end up spreading the word, giving the place a bit more local cult status. It’s that whole thing about community branding—positivity through authenticity. Smashing the principles they teach in those PowerPoint presentations.      Precisely. Those meetings we had at the university last week—trying to teach postgrads the theory of public relations using case studies from fast-food chain rebrands—it about did me in. I prefer real stories, like the market or this place we visited in Birmingham where they had that retro synth store.      Oh, I remember the synth shop! Burgundy vinyl seats, guest spots every Saturday. Bit of a hidden gem. I think it was a PR success too—word of mouth, minimal marketing, cult following. Far better than launching with a slick Instagram campaign and 100 influencers with lunches delivered.      Exactly the point. Though you do have to admit, it’s a bit of a balance. We still need to reach more people. If we go too underground, even the best quality stuff becomes too niche.      True. But maybe that’s all part of the charm. I think we’ve been lucky with those kinds of experiences—shopping, hearing music, connecting it all loosely with PR theory.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You think they'd do something about that shower curtain by now. It’s got more holes than a sieve after the last time the wind caught it.      Oh, don’t start on that again, love. It frightened half the towels off the rack too when it all went flapping last weekend. But you’re right, we need something heavier next time.      I’m halfway through this new bean bag I’m knitting, you know. It’ll be just right to tuck in the corner of the bathroom when we’ve sorted the shower situation. You'd think the shop near the High Street had everything, but no, they sold out of the chunkier wool I like.      That’s a bit rich. It’s only January, and half the bolts of fabric they showed me were in Fair Isle patterns. I told them, “Look, I just want a basic shower curtain, not something that’s won a design competition!”      Well, we can’t have the spare bedroom looking like the entrance to a campsite—especially with the bean bag and everything. I’m not surprised, it was a riot of steam the other night. It took me longer than it should've to dry the trays after you left the kitchen, and the heat just wandered into the hallway. Honestly, I think my spectacles steamed up.      Just don’t forget to check the stew on the range. If I don’t get those potatoes fully defrosted, we’ll be lucky to have anything edible to go with the green beans. Not that I mind doing this, you know—I love cooking when I get it right. It’s more that the herbs are beginning to escape the jar again!      Well, I’ll open a window then before I go back to straightening up the paperwork. I’ve been persuading the office to switch from filing cabinets to cloud storage. It’s always trying with people to keep up with the pace.      You tell ’em something sensible once and they forget the next month. Just like when I tried to show you how to use the stitch markers properly. Still, I’m knitting the corner pouches with bean bag fillers already.

Rather a damp day, isn't it? That’s more like it for Norfolk. Don’t ‘member a drier July in Costessey since I was a boy. Not that I've been out much, mind, stuck inside with the telly the whole week.      Aye, it’s beginning to feel like the weather’s got one job and just can’t be bothered to do it efficiently. I’ve only done half-a-dozen of the children's foster items this week, what with the damp getting to the books and nothing drying properly. You’d never chase a tearaway toddler with a glass of custard, would you?      Honestly, sometimes the weather’s only another form of pension poverty if you don’t keep up with it. I left the workshop this morning and I had to clean the floor five times by lunch: every time the wind came in with a new deluge. Made a fortune when it was dry, I'll grant you, but I’m not looking to get soaked again so soon.      Aye, and why would you expect that? Water's the one thing we know we can rely on up here in the East. Got as much as water and potatoes in Norfolk. Tell you what, I’ve been reading up – it’s all these climate things. The kids – no, not ours, I mean younguns these days – they don’t know a proper summer. All that “global this” and “carbon that”.      It’s tragic, what someone said in one of the retirement newsletters: “We bred the climate for ourselves.” Funny thing, really. We used to moan about the rain being plentiful, but now it’s biblical in every way. Not that I’m one to walk about the Sunday baps without the umbrella, am I?      No, you’re not. I've known women your age who run in to the garden, barefoot and wet through, just for the thrill of it. Though I have no idea where it’d come from, really. Still, I tried gardening once, when I ran the business. Daisy didn’t like that much of the rain either.      Daisy? That your wife?      Still is, in a way. She left the garden to the goonhounds. But if you ask me, go on, ask her about the goonhounds. She’s got a story about each one.      I might just do that, though I won’t pretend those tales are never just bellyache material to us older folk.

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That Christopher, he’s promising one thing then dashing off like... Well, rather like a child, really.      Yeah, he said he’d pick up the ingredients we needed for the mince pies at half one. But it’s past two and he’s vanished off the face of the earth!      I’m actually tempted not to let him into the house when he turns up.      If he turns up, which is debatable! You might be better off going yourself. If it’s the Richmond store, they’re usually frozen to bits in winter, but the ones down near Ebbsfleet are decent enough.      I know Ebbsfleet! The new store’s got this ridiculous layout, makes you feel like you’re lost in a maze every single time. But the quality of the seasonal stuff? Good! And breakfasts—those sausages are top marks!      And the milk! That fella ordering the milk earlier was a proper grump, I noticed—settle for skim, didn’t he?      Funnily enough, I knew him. Old George from the bookshop in Rochester—it always does circle back, doesn’t it? You ever meet someone who works down there, he pops up elsewhere, it really is a small world.      Speaking of which, will he be coming over for Christmas?      Don’t think so. He mentioned something about his daughter having a big work event up North. Strange—never had the impression he liked the cold up there. Still, better safe than sorry, eh?      I’m just hoping the heating doesn’t go again. We were fumbling around with what felt like a corroded water tank plug last week and it took forever to sort out!      Po-faced engineer that came out passed judgment, said it wasn’t fixed properly the first time. Proper grump! But hey, at least you’ve got it sorted now?      Barely. It’s always something with this old place. At least we’ve got the extra cash in the savings jar for something fun this year.      Mm, I’ve already got our tree up at home, made my cousins in Canterbury do the lights. Sue’s boxset binging again, can’t tear herself away!      Oh gosh, I know those days all too well—after a long shift, it’s the only way I get through the silence at home.      I reckon we should get our tree up soon. With both of us working, it’s always last minute!

Rather lovely to sit out here on Sunday mornings, isn't it? The sun's just easing through the pines, and the coffee here is something else—way better than most places I've found in this part of the world. Not quite London standards, but it does the trick.      Oh, I couldn't agree more. It's one of the few things about this climate that doesn’t try my patience. A Sunday by the coast, no rush, no demands. And you, what brings you to Northern Cyprus? A teaching assignment, I presume?      Precisely. I'm teaching at a British international school in Larnaca. Bit of a whirlwind, actually. You know, swapping the chalky countryside around Dorchester for this—it's quite a change of pace, to say the least. It’s all very new to me. I came here thinking I’d just do a one-year contract, but now I’m thinking this place might have a bit more to offer long-term.      You'll find it's a curious place. I've spent more time here over the last few years than I’d care to admit. I used to live near Bushey and worked in administration for a while, but that was… well, before retirement. I sold most of what I had and started moving about. This place has become, in some strange way, a second home. Though I do miss the shops in London—especially on a Saturday. There's a certain comfort in knowing what you’re going to find in an English supermarket.      Oh, absolutely. I do buy out the English grocery shop near my apartment every Friday. But what I’m really interested in hearing from you is what it’s about Northern Cyprus that keeps drawing you back? I know the politics are a bit complicated and there’s always that undercurrent of uncertainty.      You're not wrong there. It is a peculiar place. I've had my fair share of shady encounters with people selling land, and the bureaucracy is a nightmare. But it's not the politics that do it. It's the people. There's a kind of simplicity to life out here. Locals are incredibly friendly and helpful—you don’t often find that in England anymore. Plus, the pace of life is just so much slower. I remember one time I ended up getting invited to a Greek-Cypriot wedding just by smiling at the wrong postman.

Rather annoying isn't it? The amount of pollution hanging in the air today. I swear it's been like this every weekend for the last few weeks now.      Yeah, it's a bit grim. I don't know how the locals cope with it on a daily basis. I mean, I saw a lady walking her dog the other day with   two dust masks on  , as if that's going to make a difference.      I felt so guilty watching her. We came here for the job and the experience, but occasionally I wish we had stayed in Norwich. The fresh air reminds you everything is real, even if it's cold.      That's true, and speaking of the job, did I hear you mention to someone earlier in the week you're planning to bring in Oliver for the student project?      Yes, he’s brilliant with the younger students. He has a way of making even the most complex literature topics accessible and enjoyable. And the way he hides behind his notes when he's about to tell a joke is priceless.      He always reminded me of Robin Williams when I used to teach drama as a side hustle in London.      Oh, did you really? I had no idea. So is that why the drama students adore you so much?      Could be. I reckon it's more to do with the whole charlatan vibe I emit during performances. But, in all seriousness, someone recently asked me to co-host a workshop on cultural integration with your students.      That is a   genius   idea. The students could really benefit from your experience as someone who grew up about five minutes from the Houses of Parliament.      [Laughs] I suppose you could say I know that place like the back of my hand.      Well, for the record, your guest speaker note passed off smoothly. The way you handled the question about colonialism was extremely well balanced.      You're too kind. I think we both have that middle professional academicky vibe that the students either love or tolerate depending on the day.      I think they love it. I mean, we're not bad looking on the outside if you don’t mind the odd preoccupied look on our faces when we're thinking about the course outlines or something equally boring.      [Laughs] Boring, eh? That’s high praise from the person who dresses as Alexander the Great on Movember for ‘educational purposes.’

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That phone camera quality. I was just trying to take a photo of those pancakes I made this morning—meant to send it to my mum, but they came out slightly flat in the middle. Still, the kids loved 'em. Just like the sausage baps again on toast and beans, I swear it's the only proper meal he'll eat.      Aye, I've seen worse, that's for sure. At least you're feeding 'im properly. I remember when we first got the flat and you tried to boil an egg—it went under the hot tap like three times! Still, you made a right go of it. I'm still waiting for you to let me cook turkey on Christmas Day, you know.      Probably safer to stick to what I know, eh? I'll let you have a go if you promise not to try and make chocolate breakfast buns again. I've never seen so much mess in my life! I'm ever so grateful we got you to do the wine list last week, actually. Saved me a right bother.      I can't believe I missed that, honestly! I’ve still got grief from uni, trying to decide what to cook on a Sunday. But I saw the photo you said was blurry—he looks absolutely content with his plate! So, what's for dinner tonight? I imagine it's not quite the same as what you normally serve at work, Sam.      We're having this pan-seared salmon my lad brought back from Iceland—claims it's top-notch. I said what you had to say about cameras, and he said it tastes better than it looks! We'll be having it with those mashed potatoes you always make, Lizzie. No talking the man out of it.      That sounds smashing. I'll make a green salad, keep it light. I do need to check on the bread though—it's in the oven now. Demo, you've been stressing about the meeting on Thursday, yeah?      Aye, I'm just going to run through the presentation again after dinner. It's always the same 'split the figures,' whinge about the budget, you know the set-up. You'd think by fifty you'd get the hang of it all, but life doesn’t hand you lemons unless it wants you to make a shithouse of juice.

Rather annoying this new bus route eh? D’ye think they’ve sorted it out yet ‘r it’s still all toorl? Looks so thick it might as well be in Russian. I swear, if I had to choose between Cambridge and t’Uni down t’south, I’d say   Cambridge wins   for the campus and the quads, but if it was all about transport I’d take – Mate, have you heard about that cheepsy protestor? Supposed the kid had a wind-upཀ喇嘛 and a ‘Revolution Poem’ or somethin’.      Sounds a bit   overblown  , to be fair. Dunno how long he’d been doing it. But good for   exposure  , I reckon. Well, he did manage t’ catch the attention o’ a few people. I mean, if you live in Cambridge, you know those museum steps are   geegaw toeristy spot   or summat. Might’ve had more tourists filing in        Aye, and they probably just thought it was part o’ the exhibit, right? ‘Museum of Climate Protest’ and all that.      Yeah. But while we’re on this subject, I have t’ say, ever since I came to Cambridge as a   first year  , I thought lectures were so much more chilled eus compare to Sunderland, that was real strict.

Rather annoying to be honest, how my social life seems to revolve around people's children now. But let’s be honest, it's no surprise, I've spent my whole life talking about their  scores  and their  angles  rather than their feelings and their futures! But enough about me, how’s that eeny friend of  yours  coming along,   Speaker_2  ?      Aww,   Speaker_1  , that was a bit personal. Oh but thanks for asking, Liam's coming up in April. We’re trying for early morning, when he's still manageable. You'd think at three months old, you'd get some sort of peace and quiet, but no, heavens no! So you’re meeting   Speaker_3   today though? I hope you haven't forgotten the usual orders.      I wouldn’t forget your sister if you paid me! And since you’re both breakfast, no doubt. I've been thinking, though — in all my years, you ever considered being a mummy to someone besides your own? I once had a pupil, brave girl, decided she wanted a baby immediately after finishing secondary school. I never did quite understand that.       Speaker_1 , if you say that one more time, I will put you on a diet of just toast. But to be fair, I think it's  adorable  that you’re getting in on the whole parent gig now. If I could blame someone for wanting to be a mother all day, someone who could teach my prospective daughter to solve a quadratic or two, it'd be you! Any plans to make a spectacle of it?      My,  very  much so. We’re going to Manchester Mummy and Kid’s event. You know, where any bloody parent can drink espresso and someone else will feed your child a spoonful of beige mush as if that were normal. And also, trying to find a  normal  English babble to teach the toddler. You think  that  would be easier than explaining the Pythagorean goings-on on day one of your math class.      Oh sure, let’s not mention math in a room full of cafes and your sister’s administrative jargon. I can already see the conference seminar roles we’d fill: “The Hypotenuse of Parenting”. Just don’t let   Speaker_3   start quoting the latest HR trends.

Rather annoying that the O2 is still just a big old steel structure to me. Don’t get me wrong, I watched a couple of concerts there once, music wise I had a good time, but that whole “riverfront building with a removable roof” thing just looks a bit... fake-standing, if you know what I mean.      Yeah, I know what you mean. It’s not got a bit of that old-world charm or anything. Proper landmark-wise, I’d rather have watched a comedy night or something under one of the bridges than go and get stuck outside when it suddenly starts raining under one of those clear domes.      Exactly! And we’ve been talking about going up there for like a year, but I’m not even sure it’d be worth the bottle of wine to look at the dome from the outside and say “ahh, isn’t that grand?”      Well, if we ever actually go, just remember to bring an umbrella — and a sense of style. You know, you can’t have a proper weekend in London without getting your outfit snapped by one of those street photographers under the stairs of the O2.      Oh, and I only live two stops from there, but I don’t even own a car. It’s got to be the most pretentious thing: living near a landmark and not owning the means to park outside it.      It’s the whole city, really. No car, no hills — just traffic. Our life is currently full of London buses and tubes. At least the buses have seats.      Yeah, and some mind-blowing ads being played at top volume all the time. But there we are.      I sometimes wonder if the lack of a car is making our holidays a bit more... domestic. This year we were barely out of the UK. Next time, maybe do something a bit bigger. Maybe America? I hear they have proper cups with centilitres on them. I’d love to see those American measurements in action.      I could see us visiting New York and ending up being asked what kind of cup we want for a cappuccino. “Large, with no foam.” “Do you mean American large or regular man’s large?”      Exactly! It’s not just measurements — it’s the whole system of things that Americans do differently.      Makes one wonder what’s really at the root of it all.

Rather annoying isn’t it, this weather? I mean, do we need this much rain every single week? It’s making my mobile phone absolutely barmy, keeping it dry in this house is becoming a full-time job!      Oh I know what you mean, love. It was the same during the children’s sports day last week. We had to move everything inside at the last minute. The kids didn’t mind though, they just wanted to splash about in puddles anyway. Mind you, it’s not as if they can go swimming much at the moment either — the water’s still gloriously not cold enough for anyone decent enough to go in.      What’s worse is that my daughter managed to lose one of her cuddly toys somewhere. She left it on the back of the car and I’m convinced it’s gone for good. A whole morning crying because Build a Bear was a failure — it’s breakfast, bedtime and then suddenly this happened. Honestly, I’m running on about two hours of sleep again, not that I’m complaining. Potty training isn’t helping much either.      Oh no, I feel awful for you! You don’t say! We still had grief with that, even as we were going on to secondary school. But it’s all good now. I’m spoilt really — I got to stay with my mam because our other kitchen appliances are totally knackered. All that rain and the whole house was flooded. Not that you can afford to live in a wet house, though — it’s madness. Just trying to keep a sense of normalcy.      Ah, it’s a wonder any of us stays sane with all this! Look, as for my lot, I’m at least lucky I don’t have to go out much — I’m looking after a house where they had a fall last week. I mean, it’s a tough job but someone’s got to do it. I like the people well enough. Although, honestly, I’m dreading the day they want something technical, like trying to fix a Wi-Fi router or something. My brain just switches off as soon as they say ‘mobile’ anything.      At least your job doesn’t require you to run after tiny humans who run with socks like it's their job to go missing every five minutes. I swear I’m losing mine at this rate!

Rather annoying this, but at least we’ve got the place to ourselves. You think it would be easier living in a country where people don't forget to lock the damn doors!      I suppose it's probably safer to leave it like that than lock it and risk things getting broken in. Anyway, aside from that, I meant to bring it up earlier—where do you see all this going? I mean, with the business and us? We’ve talked a lot about staying but not really what it’s supposed to look like.      Didn’t expect that question. I’ve been thinking... Yeah, I want to make it work. I love the idea of building a life here. It's like that old English saying, "Don't count the days, make the days count" or something like that, right? I used to hear it back in NZ. It stuck with me. But it better not be just me saying it and you nodding along.      I hear you. I want to, too. I’ve never been the type to chase deadlines, but I feel like we should set some, you know—goals. I’m not saying a baby timetable or anything like that, but maybe ... maybe a career move on my end. I’ve been offered a spot in a national professional development program. It’s fairly competitive, and I know you’d support it.      You know what? I will support it. And I don’t see why we can’t both make that effort. I’m looking into expanding the business to a new niche—eco-tourism—piece of the puzzle I haven’t finished painting. But look at this as an  us  opportunity, not just separate tracks.      That's good to hear. I was worried for a moment you’d say you couldn’t do that and I’d have to decide between the two of us. But I realized I need to ask you specifically if you’re in.      I'm in. And as for the development program, I’ll manage the kids or whatever while you're gone. We’ll arrange to see family more once things take off, too. They do miss the wedding bell-phase, no doubt.      They’ll just get to see goings-on on your well-curated Instagram feed again. But in all seriousness, I appreciate that. You don’t realize how big that feels when someone your age is used to being asked about  children  all the time, not  adult  plans.

Rather annoying when people can't get through simple request, innit. I was in Costa the other week and I got the barista to mistake m'order more than once! Kept callin’ me a “young lad” when I’m a grown woman in my twenties. Just like “Deer, that eeny weeny  After-Eight  one,   not   the biscuity sort.” An’ she kept bringin’ me flat whites with no cookies. Proper funny. Oh, and she had a dump of a posh accent. Leeds, maybe?      Oh, well at least you can handle stress decent enough. Lakelands? I reckon you'd last ten minutes before you'd bugger off and camp turkey on a hillside somewhere. Terry left once 'cause of a wasp – I still laugh at it, and I think he turned semi-professional photographer in the Lake District since.      Bucksy? He used to say “the only thing finer than a good cup o’ tea, is ordering puffin and expecting compliments.” Good one, Terry. I mean, it's not like we're in Iceland, innit? Anyway, what about that time you tried to tell off Gary for littering in the woods? Bloke tried to fight ya then walked off “cos he was –?      “Fit, but flight”, innit. Gary’s all “I’m not fightin’ you, I’m just ‘escaping’ the situation” like he’s in some kind of Spock routine. Gary's a dodger, really – he'd rather do an audit than talk to someone about feelings. What I want to know is why we all ended up in this pub when most o’ us are off to a camping trip next weekend?      Not much of a choice really. Going anywhere that smells like damp socks and handlebar moustaches in that tent. But ‘cos we all like arguing about Pokémon while passed out on the floor. I told Kath the other day I was thinking about getting a Fitbit to track how long I spend getting distracted by the app. Like, I just want to walk round the grounds with buddies, not act like a barmy pathfinder with no morals.      Pfft! Fitbit? That goody-two-shoes life-tracking nonsense. If I wanted to know how much I ate, I’d ask my mates – ‘cos let’s be real, if Mike’s in the shop, I’ll be downing sweets and after-eights like I’m running a belly-flopping buffet. I saw him ‘accidentally’ give Mums a fifth bag of them the other night when she was at the station.

Rather annoying the new council tax, isn't it, Joan? I've had to cut down on the potted plants and the Sunday roast now. Otherwise I shall find meself in trouble with the creditors!      Aw, don't worry George—get a bit of joy out o' life een! I've just been to the bakery in the village and got me some of that lovely fruit loaf. You should pop along, if only to have a chat with old Miss Ward. She remembers me from when I mind the kids at the nursery.      Honestly, Dad, you could afford a little splurge now and again. I've been meaning to plan the family get-together for the summer like we discussed. Just need to pick somewhere central between Norwich and London. Ten o'clock on a Saturday morning, with finger sandwiches and bubble tea—something modern for the younger lot, but still nice for the rest of us.      Aha! Bubble tea at a family meal? Sounds like we'll be ordering in pizza and chips again. Good for the waistline—terrible for the soul!      I mean, we did mention that to be flexible with the menu, Dad. As long as there are crisps, we're in. But yes, let's keep the venue something with a fairly large garden and maybe a firepit if the weather holds. Would be quite the experience, like something outta a film.      Poppycock, George. Let the children dress up in their posh clothes and have a decent conversation. I remember what you were saying at the meeting in the village hall last weekend—about the government tinkering with the education policy. I about lost me plate!      That’s right, Jo. It’s wild how much the system is changing. We barely have time to keep up as lecturers, let alone parents. And the funding cuts for education—they're going to hit the most vulnerable hardest.      Oh, I've seen it in the papers. You read them, Joan. It's as if they're trying to outdo themselves every week. One day it's the roads, the next the hospitals, and now it's the schools. Pah!      Yeah, but let's not end the night on a grumble. What about the match last weekend? That Spurs box-to-box player—you what your name was, mate?      Oh, Johnson! We was down to see ’im belly up a ’Ornsby in the third over yesterday at the cricket, and landed meself a cold cup of tea and a warm muffin at the canteen.

Rather skip uni today, innit. D’you ever feel like it's just not for you? Like... all the work, all the pressure, it's not  me  somehow.      I hear you. I’ve thought about it a lot too. Just can’t imagine how my mum would react if I  actually  did it, though. Still, it's not all roses for most people.      Fair dos. My dad used to say, “if you're gonna leave, leave with a plan, not just a.Fatalfanst.” Blimey, still say that word wrong... like, it's  badly  spelt regardless.      Huh? You mean  filepath ? Nah, that's an eccentric lefty saying. Ten to one your grandad said it. But anyway, I think school turned your brain to custard for a bit. How d’you even end up with that nickname?      Oh, that’s thanks to my Nan. She said whenever I’d say the wrong words, I would  babbled over it . Then someone said, “he’s really dabbling in words!” and it stuck. So I'm called  Dabbles  now… Sounds like fun, innit?      Haha – Mate, I got called  Smeggy  for  months  because the teacher couldn’t pronounce my surname right.  Smith-Gandy —and poor Liam at the back, they just called him ‘big Spag’—proper abuse. Ever had a weird name growing up?      Not really—only in the way of being ‘feeble’ all the time in Falmouth. I did once fall off the boat trying to win the lobster derby and had “crab-walk” for  weeks . Proper wipeout.      Lival? You’re lucky you didn’t break anything. I once got sent home from grammar school with  snot  on the football strip after the ‘important match’ cos I tried to stuff my face with a doughnut while running. Embarrassing beyond words.      Pfft, I once tried to do a cartwheel with muddy wellies on and  tore  the curtains on the classroom wall. Muddy map of life if you ask me.      Yeah, I’m still figuring out this mud thing. Me and Tom were due to do that ecology walk, but I lost both of my proper shoes in the park. Now I’m doing all this coursework with  rain boots  and a  jam jar  full o’ mud like I’m some weird farmer.      At least you still got both shoes, I always lose one or the other. Last time, I swear, I used the lighter to  match-ify  the left one in the bin— tossed  the whole thing away still on.

So, I just can't get over how long it's been. I was just reading through old texts and... oh my God, we haven't actually properly caught up since before lockdown, right? It's almost been three years. Do you remember when we went to that tiny little café near the university for our last coffee? I thought  this  felt like an age at the time.      Oh my God yes, I  do  remember that! I got a massive coffee there and watched the entire time someone played the Ukulele in the corner and didn't chase it out of the place. You were hell frozen over because it was mostly  traffic noise . That was the last real night out, wasn’t it? It’s wild how much has changed since then. I actually moved back up North, London was just getting too expensive, and then I started working for Pearson. It's actually brilliant — a lot of what we do is digital marketing aimed at students.      Oh wow! I didn't know you went back, I assumed you stayed in London. Good for you for starting something new — Pearson is big, right? I mean, I work in project coordination now, mostly with construction and urban development projects, based out of Bristol. It's not the most glamorous, but it gives me stability. Though I'm starting to get antsy about not pushing for more travel or something more global. I’ve been telling myself to apply for something with more international exposure.      That sounds amazing. I’ve always said you're too underrated. And regarding moving... I'm actually thinking about doing a sabbatical in the next few years. I want to travel through Central America and maybe volunteer with educational programs there. Kind of about planning it all while I'm still relatively young and still earning a bit. Honestly, I’ve been really bad about eating properly and exercising. I've been surviving on takeaways and squash. My sister  keeps  calling me out for it.      Come on, don't let your sister hear you say that. I tried cutting out sugar recently and I could barely function for a week. I’m being serious, though — trying to find a better balance between work and the things we love. My friends keep trying to get me to travel with them, but I can never fit it in. Maybe if you start planning your sabbatical, I can actually go with you somewhere.

Rather annoying isn’t it, eh, lad? These delivery times. I was just clicking ‘buy now’ for some nappies on Amazon—me poor back isn’t havin’ it after ye last mishap with the sofa. Remember that lorry said it’d arrive on a weekday an’ it turned up on a Saturday when I was out?      Ay, that was a blight, aye. A Sunday too. Fair enough, this lot isn’t so heavy but I’m not gettin’ it. What’s wrong with buyin’ stuff from the shops, like? Proper place to hold it before ye buy it.      That’s the beauty of eBay and Amazon, love. You can look at a hundred nappies an’ not bump into one of them, see? I mean, if I pick up a packet in the shop I spend an hour there, then wait at the checkout when it’s only gone up another halfpenny since I last bought. On the ‘net, I can compare, even read what other folk have said. That’s real helpful—especially when it’s something like… what was it again?      What was what?      The fancy brand—y’know, the hypoallergenic ones. The one that costs more but Matey here don’t sneeze, because he’s got a sensitive little mug.      Oh, Silka Nappies? Nah, I’m fine, they’re just a bit costly. But yeah, I don’t like buyin’ stuff online I can’t see—what if it don’t arrive or it’s the wrong size?      That’s where you read the about section, lad. Pay attention to the sizing guide, read the reviews—mainly the top ones and the ones at the bottom. The bottom ones are usually the ones who are fed up with a delivery problem or the item is not what they thought.      Right, so it’s a bit like word of mouth but online?      Exactly. We’re talkin’ strangers from over the world, but they’re tellin’ a real truth from their own experience. It’s not like you’re gettin’ this info from a man with a clipboard goin’ on your life if you don’t review properly.      Right, that’s a bit of a bloke on a clipboard?      Well, I suppose if ye live in a world full o’_ratings, maybe ye do, but to ye, it’s just ‘buy this, avoid that’. A bit like I tell the Year Elevens I mark.

Rather annoying this new council tax regime, isn't it, Love? I had to fill in a form like everyone got to declare what they earn. I’m retired and I’ve got a modest pension, but I see it's based on the property value, not the earnings!      Yeah, I saw that too, Dad. It doesn’t really make sense if you think about it. You don’t earn that much from your flat, but the tax is based on what the building is worth now, not back in 2004 like the old system.      Told you I like to keep it simple! Anyway, I don't get why the government’s always making things more complicated like that.      It is a bit over the top. I had to help Mummy with it last week. She’s confused by all the sections in the form. Cats, pets, breakfast, no breakfast—what does that mean for a kitchen in a basemen’s flat?      House prices have gone through the roof over the years, so of course the tax jumps up. But I still pay the same rate as when I bought that council flat back in the day, and still got a demand like I live in a mansion!      True, but at least you got a chance to speak to the council representative when you dropped the form off. It took me 20 phone calls to get through one day last month.      Who speaks to people anymore? Let me tell you about the time I did that. I called up the library to return some books, and I thought it would be easier if I had a colleague do it because he had about five calls to deal with the same nonsense the week before.      That's pretty bad. Have they not thought about the age of the person calling? You’re not 20 anymore. Maybe you need less time on the phone.      No siree. But I think it's very confusing for people like me when everything gets computer-ised. One time I tried to log in to pay the electricity with a machine, and it told me the wrong amount because it couldn't tell the difference between a ‘v’ and the number ’7’ in my address!      That doesn't sound very modern. Imagine making that mistake with a postcode box number or something. Anyway, if it’s too confusing, maybe I can help you with the next forms next month.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, who wants to fly on Christmas Day? Felt like everyone was upset or overly festive, or both. I’m more of a “stir up a storm, then curl up with Netflix” kind of person, not a “get on a plane in a nightgown and slippers at midnight” kind of gal.      I know! It was a bit of a nightmare actually. Like, the best kind of nightmare, where you eat loads of food, dump someone’s presents in the wrong bag, and then get pulled aside by airport security.      Right, because of the united  bacon sandwich  you smuggled into your jacket pocket? That wasn’t well done, love. You’ve got enough to deal with without making things more complicated.      But I thought I could get the little sandwich to Australia in one piece! Cats would have been breakfast, but Bucks Fizz and a bacon sandwich... I’m not a posh baker, I’m a messy, indulgent kind of woman.      It’s a combination of both, though. You can still be posh in shortbread tights. But let's not get off track. Have we all sorted out the Christmas fare for tomorrow night?      Not at my place. I got fairly sidetracked by a very large roadkill deer the other night. It was somehow larger than the whole car was wide. And we were literally ten minutes from town. Like, someone must have been juggling kangaroos before this thing came outta nowhere.      Also, have you seen the way the foxes in Margate have  attitudes now ? Not in about five decades have I seen the same pair of red foxes watching us from behind hedges like they own the place. One of them barely gave me a second glance as I exited to do bin day. Burglar-y little buggers.      I have no problem with it if they're giving my doorstep the once-over for crumbs. I am not convinced, however, that we should  feed  them. Websites say not to do it, mate.      Speaking of, I’ve set us a theme for this year. Festive food is going gothic. I mean, if you don’t mind sourcing organ meats.      I will. I can roast a duck on a stick one-handed with a smile. Fatback, entrails, and bone marrow are all fair game with the right spice mix. True, I did accidentally char the duck over the campfire last time, but that only made the mac ‘n’ cheese underneath all buttery.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand accents vary—me from Birmingham, it's not like everyone got the Queen's English—and I don’t judge people on their accent, sure. But this job, it's all over the place. Me and the lads on the shift talk like proper humans, and then we get passive-aggressive messages from the office lot saying we need to sound more "professional." I said to Aneesh, “Professional? Why’s a Manchester man being unprofessional for talking like a Manchester man?” We’ve all got jobs to do, right?      You know what? I actually sort of agree with the office types. I work in the editing department, and we get manuscripts from across the country, sometimes even further afield. When someone writes like they're talking to their mates in the pub, it's harder to get the tone right. It doesn't help when the grammar is all over the place either. I've been reworking a doc in which someone wrote, “We looked into the fookin’ sky and was like, why?” I mean, I get it’s casual, but it's supposed to be a written article.      Honestly, I think voices and accents are cool. I mean, we're making audio dialogue for games now, and it's amazing how adding a slight north-east vibe, or even a south London slang burst, totally brings characters to life. You know what gets me? If the script is poor, but the voice actor is great, you can polish the language to sound natural. Like my friend Lee, he's from Bristol, and he does this kid who's a hacker and sounds like a posh Oxford professor. I was like, "That doesn't fit," but he explained he's trying to sound reliable, professional, but secretly vibes off a Birmingham background—he fails at it. So you see, accent is key, depending on context.      True story. Me and Danny were at the pub last week and he told a tale of his mate who got asked to adjust his accent for an interview. You heard of “standard English” training? It's like being asked to pretend to be someone you ain't.      Some people genuinely want to be understood, though. Accent discrimination is a real issue, even in the 21st century. It’s not just about sounding "professional." I’ve seen people from Scottish or Northern Irish backgrounds face bias when what they say is actually perfectly comprehensible.

So do you lot reckon we’ve got anything to worry about for tomorrow’s physics test? I’ve been like... barely looking at the notes.      I know, right? Mr. Hargreaves is probably gonna hit us with the whole motion and energy section. I tried to make some revision cards, but honestly, I don’t think they’re doing me any good.      I reckon that A-level stuff is just gonna blow this all outta proportion anyway. I watched a clip about Newton’s laws and now I just feel like I’m gonna chase a black hole.      Yeah, but enough of school. Who wants to go listen to the new Indie band that went viral? I’m loving their mix of electro and melodic stuff.      I’m down for that, but I’d rather listen to something nostalgic like The 1975 or something. Remember when we all dressed up like them to go to house parties?      Honestly, nostalgia is amazing, but I’m kind of warming up to this new lo-fi hip-hop stuff. It just helps me chill, you know? Got one I’m obsessed with.      I tried that once, but I was like watching TikTok videos while it played, and got way too hyper. My nan would have rolled her eyes, and I barely paid attention to the music.      Okay, okay, but let’s not forget the real hit of our weekend was the movie marathon at my house. That new Marvel movie was solid, man. It had all the action and some funny moments.      I loved the twist at the end – I definitely did not see that coming. I about jumped outta my seat when the baddie lit up the whole scene.      Yeah, it wasn’t like the usual blockbusters. There was so much to take in, but for once, it wasn’t just action and explosions. They were showing more depth to the characters.      Definitely. I tried to read some of the comics before the movie to get a bit of context, though I ended up trying to draw the characters and looking more like the baddie with no powers.      Pfft! I tried to act out the movie on my own, like trying to sound like one of the sidekick kings, but I ended up with a box of popcorn on my face due to my dodgy timing.      Oh gosh, I remember that!

Rather annoying when the Balanceability results came back last week, Lucas scored a bit lower in the comprehension section. I got to go over some of the questions with him after I collected his work.      It was hard to do those timed questions, Mummy. The paragraphs were longer than we usually get.      It was tricky, I reckon. But you did better than most in your class, Lucas, which is impressive. Why don't we try going over one of the questions together? That way, you'll be ready for the next assessment.      Daddy specially helped me to understand it. He showed me how to break it down like a puzzle. That was quite fun.      Excellent! The goal is not just to finish the work, but to understand what you're reading and thinking critically. Oh, by the way, Tom at school told me his parents are renovating their house and even putting in a swimming pool in the garden. I imagine jumping in there will be tempting, especially for the two of you.      I do like jumps—proper ones, not just the dab I do with my feet. But you warned me last time, Mummy, about diving into shallow water.      That's right. We spoke about it in class the other week and even made cards for National Cat Day. You both helped make those, remember? Anyway, about the pool—only jumps with supervision and always check the water's deep enough first. Safety first, always.      Can we have a pool with a waterfall, like Tom's? I imagine the water would be nice and cold after a manmade waterfall.      That would be lovely, but it's expensive to keep running. And a waterfall means more filtering and cleaning. Not to mention the electricity it takes. Still, I bet the smell of chlorine and the wet hair would be well worth it on a hot summer's day.      Lucas, I noticed you haven't mentioned how your little conversation with your friend Casey went yesterday. What did she tell you at break?      She told me about chocolate and strawberry chip pizza. She said it was amazing with hot sauce! I told her no go, but I think it's nonsense.      I tried it once when we had a pizza night with Grandad—and it was one of those weird experiments. We only made it to the second bite before we had to start with something else.

Rather annoying I couldfit in a run on Sunday, me ankle’s still hurty from las week when I slipped off them cobblestones by the train station. Blows me how gym folk can just roll their ankle an’ carry on like nothing happened, I'd be layin’ flat on me back in an eeny coma!      Yeah mate, reckon it depends on yer self-discipline. I’ve only just started this new HIIT class, but honestly, I'm knackered by the third minute. We've to be doing burpees an' chase the ambulance or some bloke’s yelling... like, is that even exercise or a mental prank?      Huh, that’s well My turkey legs definitely couldn’t manage that! Me and Marc tried rally walking, see if I could get into some sort o’ shape before the summer. First week I was alright, eventually though it were breakfast, breakfast, then more breakfast while me legs burned like inedible steaks.      Oh, spare me the diet fails. I tried going raw once. I ate a big ball of cucumber and a feather for three days and thought I’d gone to heaven. Then I passed out by the loo on a Thursday. My flatmate came in, poked me with a bottle – Mate, you alright? I was like, barely, barely!      It’s laughin’ through the tears innit. Me and Liam tried that whole relationship deal for six months. Well, he said it was a 'trip', I said it was a 'mistake with floring consequences'. Still, he wants to talk it through over a brew, but I’ve got better stuff to do, like recycle old dating app profiles!      Aww mate, I get you. My sister is doing that Whole30 detox lark, but she's hooked up with a delivery driver from the local farm. Honestly, passed him in the shop and he winked at me like I was bloody Madonna! Bleedin’ ridiculous, I know. I told her stick to sprouts and not that sprite of a lad! He probably just likes her for the chips with supper.      Still, I’m happy for her. I mean, I wouldn’t have bin my best life if Liam had stayed. Just appreciated that he’s left me in peace, an’ we can laugh ’bout it now. Pass me them biscuits innit, I might fill me gap with something heart-attack inducing.      True to that. Here you go. Also, if we start running again this summer, maybe we can go up near Cambridge?

Rather than chuck afit in eh, lad? That lot o’ sticks hurled in t’ fire like it were nivver gunna budge owt. I’ve had t’ prod ‘em a coupla times meyself.      Grandad, can I ha’ another slice een? Me lot’s gone cold agin an’ I haven’t even got near as much as most a you’ve ‘ad.      Aw, naw, Tony, let it be. You ain’t a cwawin’ meyself when me slice was hot or cold. T’ meat’s still edible, innit?      Give ‘im another, Roberts. He’s in a growth spurt, bless ‘im. Besides, left’s no’ like t’ lot from t’ D Drive, is it? That’s the third week in a row now they’ve dropped ‘in Domino breakfasts—cuddy up mey blouse with a drive in me bascet, ever so grateful we ar, even if it is a bunch o’ overpaid council blokes tryin’ t’ get ‘in out of t’ office.      Did you lot get the ham and cheese today? I was on Domino for the lemon and herb chicken, but got left with nothin – Mate down t’ lane said he cheft it all in his burstin’ time.      Aww, fair play to ‘im, then! Though if y’ fancy, I ‘ave a spare receipt in me pocket. Pick up a couple of olly sourdoughs and something sweet at the checkout. You can add it ‘neath y’ nose when you come back in, eh?      Tony, you can help your grandad take the luggj out in the morning. Going into that frosty cold won’t do y’ any harm, eh. Rather annoying when the answer’s obvious, isn't it? Like we all know her—the one they’re talking about in the clue, she’s local, has a podcast. I mean, c’mon!      You wouldn’t have said that as a kid, now would you, Jess? I remember you being  so  good at this as teenagers.      Yeah, well, that was before I spent years in Africa! I got a little out of touch with what passes for pop culture in North Wales.      Oh, come on, it's not too bad. You’ve still got your  wit . I mean, look at Rhys—      My turkey leg must have dropped!      Ten more seconds on the buzzer, lads, and I’ll be the winner. I’m assembling a hand of Catscratching Domino breakfast, no doubt about it this time.      You’d be the Catscratching Domino, not the breakfast.      Let’s not get confused with metaphors—person, place, or thing. I’m with your mother. We still need human.      Oh, brilliant. I say "she," then. She’s local. She does podcasts.      Rhys, don’t burst the tension.      No, Silas,  he’s  the one that made the rules. Our collective someone who talks online. Let’s see: local, a podcaster, oddly literal.      I think it’s  Turbulent Toast . That’s  definitely  how it goes in about five seconds.      Oh, Jess, you’re trying to be funny again. That’s her actual name.      No, I don’t think that’s her. Maybe "Frittered Friday."      You’re all wrong. Let me tell you what happened last year—the way I played when I convinced Dad it was my grandad and that he’s doing a weekly space radio with lunches delivered.      That’s creative, but you  know  the buzzers don’t like metaphor-based answers.      It's not about poetry. It's about linearity, Silas.      You know what your problem is, Jess? You take this too seriously. Remember when we were kids and you’d earnestly try to define "apples" for like, five minutes before pronouncing it a "colored round fruit substance"?      Only when Clarice stalled so much she accidentally knocked over half the board game.      I want to make it fun, but there’s just  rules . I can’t go ignoring them now.      What if someone who talks weekly on the radio and has lectures in the morning?      That’s practically Chef’s Weekly Critique Circle.      If you didn’t overload the board with every clue under the sun, this would be easier.

Rather annoying when the moonlight shines through the window and creates such a promising view, don’t you think? It’s making my card shuffling slightly more dramatic than it ought to be.      Oh, don’t be daft, Karen. You’ve frightened half the set into hiding under the table during your intense shuffles last week. Light the fire again and we might actually stand a chance of playing a clean game.      If this isn’t top-notch entertainment already, what more would you like? Karen and her dramatic tendencies, us and this old run-down cottage in the middle of nowhere—we’ve everything we need right here.      Besides, the fire’s only going to make us sweat and Myfanwy will be back with enough eccentric anecdotes from the shop to fill the entire hour between now and midnight, anyway. I think it’s safe to say the rules of this game are negligible.      Come on, Michael. We can at least pretend to follow the rules of hearts! No, you didn’t take the last trick. That was me.      Honestly, I didn’t choose to start the game in the first place. It was you, Rhys, who insisted cards were the best way to pass the time. And yet, look at us. Karen’s already trying to figure out a loophole, and Myfanwy’s trying to remember the time her husband picked blackberries barefoot and ended up sentenced to three weeks in a hot room with a wet cloth for a dressing.      And God help me, I’ve already been told at least three variations of the blackberry tale in the space of an hour. Can we all make a pact, just for the remainder of this trip, to not mention blackberries?      Deal. And if you don’t mind, Rhys, you’re the only one not sweating up the board entirely. Myfanwy over here just trebled her score after making me believe the Queen of Spades was a joker.      Okay, but before you accuse your sister, Michael, just to clear up—I never said the Queen of Spades was a joker. That was your imagination. Now, can we all agree to remember that the rules are optional, and the points are even more so?      Fair enough. Just don’t expect me to not mention that I had a team of three against one—and still won your hand with a straight seven.

Okay, so I've just finished my first year at university. I can't believe it's real! It's been so weird, but also kind of amazing. I miss home a bit, though. I think what you said makes sense, Speaker_1. I’m lucky, too, because my apprenticeship is fully funded for the four years. I didn’t have to borrow anything. I’m actually planning a small family Christmas event at my nan’s place. Speakers, you’re all invited!      That’s such a nice idea, Speaker_2. Family is everything, especially over Christmas. And the boxset binging marathons after dinner. We could have a big TV special of whatever everyone’s been watching.

Rather annoying when the roads are all clogged up, ain't they? I was trying to get in from Essex last weekend and it took me nearly three hours more than I'd planned. Cycling would've been quicker, I expect. Not that I'd fancy it in those trousers — wouldn't be a patch on me on two wheels since I was thirty.      Honestly, I’ve given up on driving altogether. A lot less stress just walking or catching the bus, especially round Cambridge. It's easier to pop to the shops or meet mates if the weather's good. Although, don't get me started on the number of times bikes have fallen over because some muppet forgets the kerb's there.      Yeah, I cycled into town last week and skidded right off the path into a bin — landed right on my backside! Half the people in the queue at Matalan were laughing, the other half just walked past. Honestly, I’m thinking about getting a mobility scooter just to avoid any more embarrassment.      That does sound mercy-free! I do tell you, I used to cycle all the time in my day. Got as far as Windsor and back on a old penny-farthing… well, not quite a penny-farthing, but it looked like one!      I think it's really good that more people are getting out of cars and into active transport. It helps the environment and your health at the same time. Honestly, I'd love to get my parents to try walking to the local park more. I've got them out a few times, but they seem to think the bus is their only safe option!      I do like a bit of a walk, love the green spaces here. Course, I'm not doing five miles like you young 'uns. I've got me park near the house, that's just fine. Burgess's playing cricket there today — passed them by on me way in.      Cricket, eh? I haven't watched them for years. I did once get to a match and got so sunburned I looked like a lobster. I think I told the referee I took an oath not to set foot near a pitch again.      Haha, I remember you telling that story once. Honestly, it made my eyes water, I was laughing so hard. Anyway, speaking of getting out and about, you two fancy going for a walk to the river tomorrow?

Rather annoying when people think of the Basque Country as just another part of Spain, isn’t it? We were talking to a couple of alumni from the Faculty at lunch about it. I've been over there a few times on language surveys, and honestly, the culture and even the architecture feel world apart from the rest of Spain.      It was fascinating to see the divide for myself as well. Though I’ve only been through by train on the way from Santander to Biarritz. It was quite interesting that it felt like you suddenly weren’t in Spain at all. I remember the kids in the car seats screaming like they’d been dropped into  another planet . That’s when the real debate kicked off about whether it’s a region, a nation, or something else altogether.      I see what you mean, both of you. I spent a good chunk of my sabbatical at the University of the Basque Country—there’s a very real Anglo-Saxon drive in their language planning, you know, especially among younger professionals who still want to study in English. That divide between the Basque and the rest of Spain is very sturdy. Though I have to say, quite a few people still assume it’s just a mountain range in Catalonia. Preposterous, of course.      Exactly. And the funny part is, I’ve done presentations on it myself at academic circles in London, and people don’t even clock what the real political stakes are. There’s a real fear of linguistic erosion. Our co-ordination project in London also ran into similar issues with Cantonese and Mandarin speakers. It’s funny how something as simple as a word can carry so many historical and cultural meanings.      That makes me think of the time we pulled the Basque language into the office presentation on languages spoken in Europe. Everyone was like, “Wait, you mean they don’t speak Spanish up there?” I had to show them the map and explain the education system in detail.      Ah yes, it's a cautionary tale for the field linguists among you. You must always be ready to defend such things. I remember being asked once whether Basque was 'just a dialect of English’ in a pub near Rugby. The irony was, the man had a Chinese father and a Shropshire mother. I think he was trying to sound worldly.

Rather annoying to be honest. Loads of people just doing it for likes and ego. Don’t they know anything about MS?      Well, at least it raises awareness, right? A bit of fun for a good cause. I know the kids in our family loved watching their cousins getting drenched. Hasn’t everyone done it by now?      Honestly, I wanted to do it a year ago, but by the time I got around to it, half the people I knew had already done it. Plus, we had the heatwave and I was outside in the garden with the kids.      That’s mostly people doing it for attention, isn’t it? But okay, some bits of it are good. I did mine with my students last summer. I do think, though, the response has kind of died down. I haven’t seen anyone at my sister’s house do anything for MS all summer.      Not that I blame anyone who hasn’t had a go. Some of the people we've met with kids, or new parents, probably have more important things going on. Still, I did mine with Gemma and the baby was away in her room on the day-care blanket.      You’re just in the habit of being a team player, aren’t you? Anyway, all of that online stuff aside — I heard from your mum earlier, she was telling me about the birthday party for your half-brother.

Rather annoying this, putting the whole kitchen upside down for a coffee machine we barely use. I'd rather drink it off the lip of a mug than lug it up and down every time I've a cup.      Well, love, the place is being sold and we can't take it. Got a quote from a removals company last week—and trust me, if it costs more to move that thing than a new coffee machine, we're done. You can’t fix a broken country with more laws and less biscuits.      Fair cop, but there you go. After thirty years of Tory shenanigans and that middle finger to public services, people want a bit of new scenery. I’ve no faith in it, but you can't blame the voters for feeling fed up with the status go-to-rest-posh-village.      True, very true. Just don't imagine for a minute it'll be different when what your lot do is still all posturing in the grand picture and nothing’s genuine.

Rather annoying really, but at least it’s sorting itself out. I’ve had her in for a week already... got to go back Thursday. You know how it is. Not a huge amount of time with the little one before the festive season kicks off, but at least it's something.      That is a bit of a shame, isn’t it? I left her with my mum over the weekend – I had to go into the school open day. They’re expecting quite a lot for the upcoming term. The new breakfast club is really taking off this year.      That’s good to hear! You always did have a way with the kids. Good for you for starting up something like that. Might get you some extra cash as well, I suppose. A bit of a bonus for early December bonuses, maybe.      Well, extra cash is always nice. Though I’m not sure about the bonuses with the schools, they’ve been really tight on funding lately. More of an administrative nightmare to be honest. Silly really when it could just be common sense. Anyway, what about you? Any big plans for the holidays yet?      Nothing massive, just what you’d expect at our age, really. Maybe a weekend trip with the clubs I’m in, or a nice long walk with the boys. I might even try to get the grandchildren to visit for part of it. Maybe even take you both out to that new restaurant in Totnes.      That sounds lovely. Maybe we can do something like that too, with the rest of the family. I’d love something a bit different this year, something we can all remember. I’m going to talk to my sister about it as well.      That would be nice. It’s such an easy thing to lose touch with the family during the holidays if you don’t set go out of your way to keep it going. But you two have always had a good handle on that.

My turkey still hasn’t bin disturbed an’ left’s a wake of turbulence.      Aye, and I   thought   I ‘ad an astrolabe, wait ‘n see when it comes down to 'the bed linen cricket match'.      And ever looked in Waterfields, the bakers, when they’ve got Richmond sausages— proper  puddin’s for a pox—there I am in the queue, as if I were supplying the Ministry of Defences with gear.   Massive   queues. Absolutely  thrilled .      Oh aye, I know Waterfields. That’s a bit like the Royal Mint of sizzling fried onions and kippers for breakfast.
