Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That queue at the supermarket practically had me in a real mood. I got home so late I almost missed the start of the film I was looking forward to.      Aye, seems like the weekend winds up being one big race against time these days. Right mess at Newton Park Market last Saturday was, too. Full of blokes in their overalls chatting up the veg men, but I got in a decent load of squashes before they started going firm.      Oh, I heard about that! The council want to make it a car-free zone now, which is nice in theory, but I reckon it's the people who don’t do their shopping like that who’ll suffer. You know, like me.      I see your point, love. But I’d say every bit of green space we can protect is a step forward. Now, breakfast, what do you say? I’ve still got some of that muesli you like from last week, or we could pop into the farm shop once we get back?      Muesli is fine,老爷. I don’t fancy going out again to be honest. It’s deadly with the traffic on Sundays anyway—it always takes twice as long getting out of the village.      True enough. Though I did take the Hayfields up to the show last week. All that rolling fields and Silage was the talk of the barn! Laughed so much I nearly missed someone’s chicken doing a burnout on the way past the pig pens.      Oh yes! Someone told me about the chicken and it’s stuck with me all week. I can't make it up about how it ran off the verge sideways. Have you still got that photo?      Oh aye, that was on my mobile the whole way home. Maybe I’ll have a go at burning it onto a memory stick for you. I did manage to get some shots of the roses in bloom too, nice and full with the morning sun.      That would be good, thank you. Let me know if you fancy coming over to develop the pictures one evening. I’ve got a few things set up for the community garden and thought you might enjoy seeing it go together.      Aye, count me in. I do love a good design project. And it's bloomin’ marvellous to see you getting all that planning fluency from your day job, mind putting it to good local use.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't had a request yet for either of the French or Spanish pods. The first couple got taken rather quickly, though. I’m more than a bit disappointed by the lack of interest in this part of the village. I thought the community would respond a little better.      That is strange, isn't it? I'd have thought if people are living in the area with a fairly ambitious bunch of under-fives, they'd be looking to send the kids to something a bit interesting like that. We've had to cancel the Italian class at the school, but the Spanish GCSE ones... well, they're filling up fast.      I wonder if it's just word of mouth? Or perhaps parents are sceptical about the early immersion bit? I mean, the idea is brilliant, don’t get me wrong — babies absorbing languages just by being in a playful, musical environment. But when you're expecting to invest money in it, maybe some are just cautious.      Oh, absolutely. I had the same problem when I first started that after-school German club here, before we moved it to secondary. I remember telling my parents it would fill up in no time, and then ... nothing. Eventually, I had to circle up to a few of the local nurseries and just do pop-up demos. Once people saw, it really took off.      That's a good idea. Should I approach the local nurseries? I mean, they’re in different geographical clusters — one is in the north of the village, the other's oddly central.      I'd say the central one is probably better for visibility — but don't rule out the north one, just in case. I remember you mentioned the area has different demographics depending on where they live. Maybe the central part is more varied.      That's probably right. My sister had her first baby just last month. I passed by her flat on the weekend, and the whole place is covered in wooden toys and lullaby CDs. It's mad! My brother-in-law is obsessed with Montessori principles, which always comes with 'language sensitivity periods,' of course. He took the baby to that Welsh-speaking park twice last week by himself!      Oh my goodness, if that's not enthusiasm for language learning, I don’t know what is. Honestly, he's got the baby cooing all sorts of words at him — I seriously think the lad might one day outlearn both of us by just belly-laughing his way into linguistic gold.

Rather a lot of bluebirds’ve been visiting the garden this week. I've spotted 'em flitflyin’ to the feedin’ box I rigged up by the willow by the fence. Livens yer day a bit, don’t it, Albert? Especially wi’ the weather bein' so bright een recent times.      Aye, I reckon so. I’ve been making a bit of a nut cake too. Not the best this side of Harrow, mind, but it’ll do. Vicky always used to moan I made it too runny, but the bloomin' sugar... needs to go in gentle, gentle—mind yer diabetes, eh?      Oh Albert, that My turkey cake was such a melanger! All bursts in the oven! I had to rescue what I could and push it into a tin. But I suppose you lot’d far sooner have something better than breakfast, no doubt. I've been thinking of making some little puppets for the planting boxes as desktop hides, you know, for the birds? They might like the novelty, like.      Now, that sounds a proper dab of fun, Vicky. We might need to get off our old arses and give it a go tomorrow. We’ve been rather too much in the armchairs this Easter: sittin’ and thinkin’, starin’ out the window and not doin’ much else. Silly old people, eh?      There’s no harm in enjoyin' a rest every now and then, George. Besides, we’re doin' our fair share by weighin’ the world and being tea and cake servers. No one in the district feeds their birds about as well as we do. I've the touch for it, I have.      That you are, love. I've only just planted a new bush in that corner, found ‘cos the old trellis was saggin’ about. The birds have been takin’ to it something fierce. I watched a sparrow buildin’ a nest there yesterday while I was laying fresh leaves. Looked like a proper bit of industry 'pon a little bird!      Hmm, that’s proper good news. We need to feed the notion of more goin' on in life about here. If we can give the birds a line in quality meals, we might be givin’ ourselves one at the same time. So, tea, cake, birds, and puppet roles in the garden—should I fetch the old puppet boxes to give it a go?      Aye, that’d be a grand notion. The more to keep the brain working.

Rather skip the starters, don't you think? This grilling weather has me just wanting something hearty but light... What d'you fancy?      I'd say something with a bit of a kick to it. Not quite sure about the Turkish cuisine—do they do things differently from what we're used to? Still, I trust the menu they've handed over to me.      Oh yes, I love watching them roast the meats under those grills. It brings back memories of my grandparents’ barbecues in Dorchester. They always used the outside fire pit—they said it made the meat juicier somehow. Still, I never did like meat with the char on it.      Funny you mention fire. I was just recalling my niece’s accident last winter. She had gone back to Dungannon for the holidays and lights the fire up wrong, nearly singed the cat’s tail. Poor George—still limping slightly.      Oh George! I remember him as a kitten, always chasing puffballs. And now he’s older, too, like us? Time really jumps.      It does indeed. You know, as much as I like Turkey for its colour and people, it’s watching the elderly folks trotting about that gives me pause. I lost my Mate—is that what they call her in Cyprus? No,  mama , my mother-in-law—she passed in the winter. Still, it's strange to see old people so lively here.      Yes, I’ve often read about the healing energy of the Mediterranean. My friend Joan had a spiritual guide teach her dowsing here—say she felt all the ancestral spirits are stronger by the sea. I suppose I’m not the same age to touch the spiritual, but I find it intriguing. Have you thought about it?      Dowsing, you say? Hmm. I had a friend who trekked out toward the pine trees with his pendulum, believed the whole business of land memory. He once said I was meant for a life I hadn’t lived. As if you can control destiny!      Oh but what a thought! If we do have pathfinders in our lives, maybe it's not by stars or the pendulum, but the people who come and go. Like that couple at the next table—if you’d told me that pair would be in a restaurant in Cyprus arguing about counting to ten in Turkish at 1pm, I’d say you were after shaman tea.

Rather annoying to be honest. The living room needs a bit of love – you know, new wallpaper, maybe a couple of new sofas? Just to make it more... I don’t know, functional?      Oh, we do hear you, love. Your mum wouldn’t dream of spending money on eeny things like that, but if it was 'ere where we were still living – well, don’t get me started on your dad’s DIY mess from last summer.      Blimey, sounds a bit rough. If I were you, I’d just get the lot done at once – fetch the builder in, get it sorted. A bit o' redecorating never did anyone no harm. Though if it’s a Christmas list topic, best get the sums right before you mention it to the missus, eh?      Yeah, I suppose you're both right. But it’s not just about the look of things – half the socket sockets are in funny places and the Wi-Fi is dreadful in here, even with those extenders I bought. It would make such a difference for the kids, and for me working from home every now and again.      Oh, tell me, what are you up to at work now? You workin’ from home again? I remember when –?      Yeah and no. I’m project coordinating now, so I’m quite busy moving between assignments and phone calls. It’s less stressful than before, though, which is a bonus. I miss the office environment, to be fair.      Well, that’s a decent job at a young age, I’d say. Made a decent career for yourself in a blink o' an eye. Your old man would be proud.      I had to tell a few stories about you yesterday at the parents’ evening. One of the teachers was raving about the clever kids ‘cos they baked treacle sponges like proper bakers. I said, well, it must run in the family.      Oh, bless you! Honestly, the only good thing I can do in the kitchen is boil an egg. Or a pot of tea.      That's a proper skill, mind. Popping a decent cup of tea goeth unnoticed on most folk about these days.      I do love a good cuppa. And I’ve got the kettle on already. Now, you two, have you made any plans for Christmas? We were thinking of a bit of a garden party, if the weather is playing nicely, and maybe some walking up to the grandparents’ like we used to when we were younger.

Rather annoying when people just take off wi’out ay warning. My mam was on the Jeremy Kyle show once... got the shock of her life. That poor girl down the road ay hers was a total catfish. Didn’t even look like her picture, I bet!      Aye, it een't nice when someone pretending to be one person 'asn't really them. I’ve heard of a few of those scams online too. Ay cousin got swooned by someone on Facetime, thought he woz someone local. Turned out was from Algeria and just wanted 'is details. Ridiculous.      Catfishing is like a prank wi' teeth. I found out sommates on the Jeremy Kyle programme turkey a couple o’ years ago. The guy thought 'e woz in love wi' this lass, and then she turns up and ‘e couldn't even look at 'er. Horrible, innit?      Haha, yeah, the drama. I mean, we all follow the show for the qwick thrill, innit? It’s like reality telly, but for proper life mess-ups. I don’t think I’d have the guts to go on it, though. Imagine confronting ay face-to-face.      Nah, I wouldn’t do it either. Imagine meeting the real person and thinking, “Right, that’s the one?” Now don’t get me wrong, I’d watch the programme ‘til the end, though, just for the feels. It’s one o’ them things: everyone judges a bit, but we’re all fascinated.      It's like real life being played out under lights. I don't even know why it works about people being surprised. I mean, if the truth evers comes out, it ain't like you ain't gone know eventually.      Aye, but online it’s tricky, innit? Like ay person you’re messaging can be anyone. I had ay friend who said it was a nickname ‘es wanted to use, but then I found out he was doing all sorts to dodge reality.      That’s probably the saddest bit. They build these relationships with strangers and let it become too much, even though it ain't real. That's got go be really tough for them if it breaks down.      Yeah, I’m just glad I’ve not ‘ad that problem myself. Though, I wouldn’t be surprised if I meet someone on the Jeremy Kyle show next year. It’s like the big finish to a relationship gone wrong.

Rather annoying when a laptop won't play ball, ay gramma? I was just trying to work on that essay for uni and it just randomly went all crashy on me.      Yes, electronics is a fickle beast, dear. I had my old C64 do that once in '86 and it liked to make a dramatic scene about it. What were you working on? Sounds very academic.      Yeah, it's about social insects, bees basically. It's quite interesting, actually. We've been learning how their behaviour can teach us a lot about coexistence and communication. I like to think of them as nature's little engineers.      That's lovely to hear. It reminds me a bit of home — Vienna, not London, you know. I used to paint scenes of hives and buzzing gardens in the summer. But then you must speak German as well, right?      I do a bit, actually — in class at least. And ever since we started learning Latin in Classics I've been picking it up quite quickly too. I mean, it's not exactly practical, but it's fun!      Latin is still alive and well in Vienna, as we Austrians like to say. Though we speak a little differently from what is taught at your school. But I must admit, I've never seen a Londoner take so much interest in our old German ways.      I blame Dad for that. He loves telling me stories about his Berlin trip in '98. All my family are quite big on travel. I remember going to Paris with Mom a few years back. It was brilliant — museums, food, even ballet. Although I still have about five pictures of the Eiffel Tower from that trip.      Ah, Paris and Vienna — both cities are like living museums. But it does sound like your family has seen quite a bit of the world. I myself have passed through Italy more than once — mostly to visit my sister in Rome. Do you know much about Italian, then?      Not really, but I can manage "grazie" and "ciao" and occasionally ruin "dolce e caffè" beyond salvation.      Haha, that's Italian enough on most days if you ask me. Just don't go into Rome in the morning trying to order espresso in French, or you’ll get your head turned.      Speaking of which, have I told you about those beekeepers I met in Paris last year? This guy was from Perugia, believed he was the fifth in a line of beekeepers all descended from Roman apiarists.

Rather annoying when people drive like they're in a video game. I was trying to get out of the motorway off the A3 this morning and this poor chap thought I was going to swerve into him! It is just   so   disrespectful when people don't use indicators.      Oh een, I've met people who treat their driving like   it's 1912   with a Model T. I used to work in construction too and I saw so many building sites with   no planning  , it was just concrete and hope. They’d pour the foundations when it was still raining. No wonder half the houses collapsed!      That reminds me of the place I live. It's like everyone just threw a town together   backwards  . The roads are just tarmac on top of soil, and every time it rains, it turns into a brown river in the driveway. Cats would better off living in tents than that place.      Oh don’t get me started! I once told my professor about it and he was like, “Oh, that’s urban design for you, luv” — like it's some sort of academic term! I’ve still got grief from that university placement. I had to live three hours away because the only flat with an MOT passed car was in some dead estate in Brighton.      You should’ve stayed with us! We don’t do much, but at least the toaster still works and the phone doesn’t keep telling me to upgrade to Windows 8. Honestly, I still can't use Sat Nav — I had a map holder in my car   long before GPS   worked and it did just fine.      Windows 8 about did me in. I tried to call the solicitors to get it fixed and they said I needed to pay   £400 just to get it to speak English again  ! Joke, they said. I left the call. I passed my driving test on a Ford Fiesta mk2. This is not a joke.      Honestly, I think your car is older than my   degree  . But at least it knows the route to Dorset better than my phone ever did. Once it tried telling me to turn around after I had just started the trip because it updated the map. Talk about   stressing        I don’t see why they can’t just keep the map from changing your holiday plans. We all have enough to worry about with the traffic, the weather, and your mother never doing the dishes.

Rather a damp day, isn't it? That window's been open ages and it's still damp in here.      Oh love, I've closed it! You don't think I'm a madwoman, do you? I'll have the fumes from the motor cars coming in here. Got eenough to worry about without choking on exhaust fumes.      Oh, come on a bit. A draught never harmed no one! I mean, what are we, made of glass? 'Sides, you'd be surprised how good the air outside is, even with all those car fumes. It's like being outdoors, only safe.      Still don’t fancy it in this weather. I'd rather have the fire on and not worry about damp. And I ain't the only one. I seen Eunice Fairbanks with her curtains drawn in, and the old place looks like a crypt.      Well, she's in her eighties, for goodness' sake! She can indulg herself. We’re still got some spring in our step. I do tell you, being cooped up all the time don’t do no one any good. Did I tell you, I fancy taking a walk on the village green later? Might do a bit of birdwatching too – that duck's got fairly large, and I swan it’s nesting somewhere round there.      Birdwatching? If that's your idea of fun, then heaven help us. You'd spend the afternoon twitching in the grass trying to spot a blue tit when it's probably out hunting for dinner!      Hey, you know what I mean! Look, it’s not all about about sitting about doing nuffin'. I mean, the body needs a bit of exercise, what with us not being young no more. I've even started doing a bit of gardening again. My sister ‘eard me talking about it and said I'd be growing potatoes and grumbling by the time summer comes.      You always did have a green thumb, mind you. As good as your uncle Bill. Although I doubt you two would’ve got along on speaking terms! He was such an old tightwad, delivering sermons about tithes and all the time goin' on about his 'vegetables'.      Ha! I’ll bet he had green beans the size of bongos. But all jokes aside, I really do miss the feels of the soil, you know? Even with the aches and pains, there’s somethin' ‘bout bein’ connected to the natural world that keeps the bleakness at bay.

Rather annoying when the weather’s supposed to be so good an’ then it just dont’ show up, like... What was I supposed to be doin’ today agin?      Liv, yer meant to be putting the dahlias in the garden—yer picked them like a fortnight ago an’ left ’em waitin’ on the stoop. I reckon yer just wanted an excuse not to go out in the sun too much.      Haha, typical Rob. It weren’t like that. We’ve had three showers an’ a nor’wester come through. I don’t fancy frozen toads on my knees. Besides, I’ve been busy at work, sorting out this new research project on renewable energy frameworks. You know how it is.      I do, I do, don’t get me wrong. Fair enough. But if you don’t plant those blooms soon, they’re just gonna sit there lookin’ all forlorn in their pots. I might do it for you, you know, spare the flowers a sad end.      Naa, you don’t need to. Yer got that grant meeting t’day to prep for and all that PhD stuff. Listen, on another note, how are the lads from the old uni? I remember – Mateo was talkin’ last night, said they were gonna throw a little indie gig in Birmingham soon.      Oh yeah, ‘Lose the Rhythm, Find the Groove,’ at Spotted Cat on the King’s Heath side? It’s one I might make an effort for. Also, some of the lassies from our music DJ group are gonna be in, remember? Kinda about time I dusted off the decks again.      Yip, Nancy and Jo—that lass with the green hair and the bat handle. You remember? You’re not just sayin’ that just to make me smile, are you?      Nahhh, I really am. We haven’t all been together in ages. Makes me crack to think you and I DJed together at uni, trying to sound all deep and philosophical while people just danced and spilled beer over our setlists.      That goin’ on pond life if you ask me. But hey, if you do head down, see if they need a box number or something from the lads. I’ll message you the minute it settles down and I’ve planted them dahlias—right?      Do that. And for heaven’s sake, when you do, wear something that’ll keep you warm if the wind comes through.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, me being a research manager an' all, but even I got to admit it's been a hard road for young folks these days. Unemployment rates are still climbing higher than they should be.      Yeah, I can see it from my end een Cambridge as well, especially with the number o’ graduates just comin’ out all over the place. I’ve been helping a few younger tutees find jobs, an' it’s just brutal. They’re all doin’ their doctorates an' whatnot, but no real opportunities seem to pop up.      Lakelands is no’ much different. I’ve only got to ring in now and again to a cousin o’ mine who’s left university a couple of years back, and he’s still on the dole. The whole system feels broken to be frank, an’ with them new university fees, no doubt contributin’ to folk feelin’ like they're not bein' treated fairly.      Oh aye, I remember when that new fee regime came out, it sent shockwaves right through the Midlands. You don’t see as many young'uns takin' the degree route as they did back in the early noughties, from what I’ve seen at the uni. Plus, the cost of study, it just adds to the pressure. I reckon it’s gonna take a generation for the effects of that to really shake out.      True, someone at work was talkin’ ‘bout a friend of theirs who did a master's an' then had to work a bar shift while tryin’ to find somethin’ proper in their field. Sounds a bit daft really—invest all that time, money, and then end up sweepin’ floors.      Not to mention the mental toll it takes on people. I do enjoy a good chat 'bout all this, even if it’s a bit grim. Signals me to the day job a lot too, I mean, I am a PhD student in cultural research. We discuss these themes as part of our curriculum. Even looked into musicals recently to add some light relief to the darkness, an' it's interesting how they reflect these economic tides.      Mm, musicals are a good escape. Just the other day, me and the lads had a trip down t’ the Royal Exchange in Manchester to see  Hamilton —a real show to remember, despite the prices now! Even with all the inflation, it's worth it sometimes to feel that sense of community and passion again, y’know?

Rather annoying to be honest. My gran keeps sorting through old boxes. I was just reading [kids' book title], and I thought she might want to see more of my story. But sure, where are the old photos?      They’re in the attic — well, the box was in the eeny weeny shed behind the house. Not much organisation here if I'm honest. Though Nana Graham said something about listing your brother’s birth in this big photo album. Oh, and she mentioned some interesting stories about your grandfather’s brother in Glasgow. You might find it useful, or just fascinating. You know what she’s like with family histories.   Speaker_3 :   Alice and Sarah, what’s all the ruckus? I left the kettle on. And I see you’re still in my special books and photos mood, love? Good luck with assembling it — there’s photos from when I was a teacher, and plenty of stories with a bit too much detail. I might share the bit about Liam, the son I never had, and why I still call that man “Mr Stewart” if I see him in town. Got your stepdad, your brother as a child, and even photos from when I was a wee lassie in Glasgow. Absolutely no sense of modesty back then — just cheeky faces with no filters, like you kids!      That sounds amazing. I did sketch out a whole chapter about what it’s like growing up with two stepdads in Bristol. One in one house, the other in a different one. Trying to show it's not all chaos — it's just different. I think the photos might help with authenticity — like your grandmother, or my dad as a teenager. I want to show real stories from real people.      I like that. Maybe you could write about how different families are, not just how mine handled stepdads, but how Nana Graham ended up in Ireland after Glasgow, with that marriage that ended. You know, show strength and all that. We could even write you a little story or two if you need more content.      Ah, yes, that’s a good idea. I’ve got the story about the separation in Glasgow, where I had three kids under the age of seven goin’ on — life was wild. And your real dad, Alice, left in the middle of it. But he was bloomin’ marvellous after. Ticked all the boxes in the end.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather just leave it. I mean, it’s not like it’s... got to go anywhere or nothin’. It just grows back! Honestly, I feel like I’m doing it because I’m supposed to, not because I want to.      I een? I sort of do it because I like the way I look. But I’ve been thinking a lot lately that I should just stop. I mean, I don’t even know why I started in the first place. My sister used to do it when I was younger, so I guess I just followed suit.      Yeah, I can relate. All the lads at college always do it and like that it’s tidy, so I thought I should too. But honestly, by the time I’m done, I feel more dead than alive. Especially with this flakey razor I’ve got — it’s ancient, no doubt about that.      Oh don’t I know it! I used to use the same kind. I got fed up one day and just bought a proper one, you know? The ones with the little foamy bits — quite a step up! It’s only ten quid more, but it makes a world of difference.      Hmm, maybe I should splurge on a new one. My hands are always red and sore. I reckon it don’t help that I do it first thing in the mornin’ while I’m still bleedin’ freezing.      That’s probably a big part of it. I tend to do it before bed now. Soakin’ in a hot bath first helps a  lot . You know, it softens the hair up. I reckon you could do without the shaving cream if you really wanted — just water and a cloth.      Honestly, if I didn’t have to be at work for like eight hours, I might do that too. Demo at the hairdressing salon I do a few days a week. They don’t mind how I am, but I stick to the routine anyway. I dunno. It just feels like the 'proper thing' to do.      That’s what I’m saying. We shave because the world says so. But really, it’s about what  you  feel comfortable in. I just started leaving mine a bit longer. People haven’t batted an eye — if nothin’ else, it’s less to worry about in the morning.

Rather annoying when a bar’s got a "last order" sign and they still let people order pints like it’s nigh on midday. I’m more than a bit fed up with drinking where people think “last call” means they can shout the barman as if he’s not doing a night’s work eeny weeny  innit ?      Naw, I get it. It’s pubs that don’t know their policy, innit? I’ve seen it in Cambridge, as well. You go in wanting to wind down after a day at the uni or, y’know, watching the telly, and it just turns into a free-for-all with someone shouting “get the likker in” like it’s a boxing night. Honestly, who even got themselves primed back in the Sixties for this sort of shenanigans?      Haha, yeah, like we’re still waiting for the alphabet challenge to pop up again. Reminds me in Sunderland at the old King’s Arms when we used to play “A is for Alma” once we were properly in the stew. Nostalgia for daftness, really. I never did quite get “X is for Xouth”, but someone always remembers that odd one out, innit?      Oh, right – that’s one of the classics, innit? Though I imagine some of the lads in Birmingham would add “N is for Nuggets” or “Y is for Yearling” just to mess people up. Honestly, it’s madness. And boxing? That’s another one. I had a mate— matey —from the ’hood who used to box at the clubs back when it was all about proving who had da brawns. He used to say it was all about “cracking th’ jaw an’ not givin’ inch”.      Crikey, that’s heavy, innit? I’ve always preferred observational sport. I did catch that football match with the red card—y’know, the one with the black player? It was mad how quick the reaction was. Like, I’m not sayin’ it’s racism but there’s definitely whiffs of it. Some lad in the pub just said, “Git ‘em back on the pitch an’ go again”, like that wasn’t sufficin’ reason to question.      I’ve seen it too, bloke—and I’m not sayin’ it all the time, but when it lands like a punch to the gut, innit? You can’t help but notice it. I mean, I’m doin’ my PhD in social policy—got my fingers in that muck—and there’s patterns.

Rather annoying when the council’s got half a heart and a full budget elsewhere, isn’t it? The Halberton Place site could really use a boost, yet grants keep going to modernist projects over proper heritage conservation.      No argument there, Margaret. I’ve had the same conversation with three different Heritage Lottery reps over the last six months. It’s maddening. They all wax lyrical about "community engagement" when they just want flashy QR codes on top of period features. It’s all boxes ticking to get past the bureaucratic hurdle, not genuine connection.      Still, I think we’ve got a solid case with Halberton. That original 1632 timber framing is in relatively good condition, and if we can establish enough local support—school talks, volunteer plastering days—we might just tip the scales. I’ve already spoken to the head at Ashby Primary, and they’re delighted. The kids would love working on a real historic site for a term project.      That’s the way to go. People respond to stories, not spreadsheets—especially when it involves preservation. We need to make Halberton feel like a community asset rather than a high-end renovation for a private collector. Did you get the municipal engineering report? I saw a few structural weaknesses in the eastern gable wall that could be a liability in the bid if not addressed up front.      Yes, and it’s already in the budget breakdown we’ve drafted. Nothing we can’t fix with someone who knows what they’re doing. That stone pointing? It just needs a specialist. You’d think the council would have a grant section for that sort of thing, but no, it all goes into the "innovative design" pot.      Exactly my point. It’s all a game of influence and presentation. I remember working on the Dorton chapel a few years back—same problem, but we made the chapel into a shared cultural space. Mains were converted to open fires, minimal electricals. It became a hub for weddings and art exhibitions. The grant managers could see the value because it had that "blended heritage" angle.      That was clever. Could we do something similar? Maybe set up a community arts space or a reading room on the upper floors of Halberton if the costings are feasible. I could approach some of the local authors based in Stratford, might get them interested in a literary trail.

Rather annoying when people can't get their head round the way we talk back home, innit? I mean, proper "mitherin’" is more like "wichering" by the time it gets to Cambridge ears.      Yeah, I remember once you told me "Here een norf-east, we say 'we're 'avin 'ot tea', not 'I'm 'aving 'ot tea'". Slipped out in a lecture, and half the class looked like they'd seen a ghost. What's wrong wi' us for bein’ direct, eh?      Right, I said it mostly to show how dialect shapes perception. You know, when you do sociolinguistic research you look at how language reflects who people think they are. Ten minutes earlier, I’d called the kettle “the ketti’é” and someone from Essex nearly spilled theirs.      I still can’t get over how you say "genni" and not "jeeni". Makes me sound like I’m speaking gibberish. Good job I’m in a field where odd phrasing is acceptable, or I’d be written off in a heartbeat.      It’s not like you're the odd one out. My parents still confuse past tense from present. They’ll say – “Where you at?” not “Where were you?” It’s endearin’ somethin’, innit?      Absolutely. You ever notice how dialects carry all sorts of geographical storytelling in one word? Like me: my accent's from Brum, so I say "job" as more like "jowb" and people automatically assume I'm laid-back or a Scouser or something about football.      And I say things like “grand” for “fine” or “all right”, and people in Cambridge do that thing where they blink and ask if I mean anything more than what I’m saying. But I think it adds texture, no? Everyone’s got their own rhythm in the way they speak.      Definitely. It’s weird to think that behind every "innit" or "cheerio" is a whole history and identity wrapped up in sound. I bet when I finish my thesis on sociolect drift, I’ll never look at language the same again.      Time to head to your holiday research, innit? I mean seriously, why conference in Lisbon after all that tea and talk?      Oh, it’s for a European comparative dialect study—Palace of the Marquis of Pombal near the conference venue. My supervisor suggested it as a kind of romantic research retreat.      Oh, alright! So it’s not just work, it’s a bit of a love story with Lisbon as the sidekick.

Rather annoyingly, the school dinner service has changed again this term. I know it's supposed to save money... but honestly, some of the portions now are more like  teaspoonfuls  than proper portions for growing children. Have you two seen what they serve on Fridays?      Mm, we got  baked beans on toast  again. Ayden kept saying it "tastes like airport food". What  is  the point of that, Mummy?      I like it. We can eat it with the jam when we're in the mess.      Yes, but it's mostly  white toast . I asked the dinner lady, and she said "If you want more turkey, you have to pay extra." Which I can't do! I only bring five pounds in my lunchbox and I have to share between sandwich and pudding.      That’s breakfast, sweetheart. You need proper  lunch . I spoke to your teacher, Holly, and we thought maybe we can do group packed lunches a couple of days a week. You could bring something homemade, maybe even some of those homemade flapjacks I make on a Sunday.      Or shepherd's pie from Granny!      Oh yes, Granny gives us so much at the weekend. But at school, it’s  always  salad or something weird. I told Miss Patel I’d rather bring something from home if I could.      That’s the idea. We’re working on a system where you can pre-order a packed lunch for the week. It’s a bit of extra cost per week, but the money stays in the school to  improve the menu , not go to some company far away.      But what about the tennis tournament they mentioned on the notice board yesterday?      Oh right, the  annual school tennis tournament . Holly’s planning it again. It's in June. I think it's supposed to open to the whole school this time, not just the older kids.      I could stick out my thumb and  join , but I'm not very good with rackets...      It’s not about being  good , it’s about trying and having fun. They even said goody bags with pond life if you take part.      Is it like the circus?      Well, it might have some clowns. I heard Miss Tickle is helping and she’s into face painting.      It's a family-friendly event. I’ll help you both practice on the net this weekend. Now—on the topic of money for school...

Rather skip the new Disney one we saw weekend? Thought it was decent enough, but it lacked real heart. I got the kids to watch it after, and they were properly engaged, I've got to say.      Hmm, Disney have gone a bit soft in my day. Back when I was een Reading and holidays meant the weekend at the local 'oodie if yer were lucky! Though they don’t make films with real grit like they used to.      If grit was what you wanted, you'd have watched the war documentaries my company used me chase when training the kids in history marketing. Get the facts out of them! Not everything is a happy, shiny cartoon, after all.      My turkey, you’d probably agree with the left’s take on history teaching, wouldn’t you? D’you know there’s been a big debate up in Cambridge about it? Some say it’s been dummed down for kids and that we are not properly teaching our past — the good, the bad and the messy bits.      They might have a point, lass. When I were at reading, I got a proper dose of history — quite a few war stories from my dad, and that stood to me in good stead. These days, it’s all about ticks and boxes. My –?      curriculum and assessments these days seem to be more about conformity than critical thinking. Industry would love it if universities could churn out students who don’t question the status quo. Our degrees need more real-world exposure, more internships, apprenticeships — not just theory.      That is a concern in the schools I’ve taught in too. Far more focus on grades than actual understanding. I mean, I get the pressure of targets, but the kids miss out on so much.      Aye, you barely even get to know the history of your own country. Makes you wonder why the Tories always get votes — they’re supposed to be the leaders, but the education they’re handing over seems to be failing.      I think the problem is deeper than politics. The shift to academies and Ofsted with their ticklist expectations stifles creativity. I took an undergraduate class when I was a student — had a course on the history of advertising go hand in hand with British history. It was brilliant.      I’d love that in schools. Cross-curricular learning, linking what your doing with real-world applications.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, Doreen? I do miss the days when we'd sit on the verandah with a cup of tea and a good chat, not stuck inside like this!      Aw, don’t grumble so much, Harry. We haven’t been out on the verandah since we moved in ‘ere. Still, it  is  sodden most days these days. I remember when I was a young ‘un, summer used to last into August, not like now.      You lot never chase the sun these days. You should head down the village fair next week! Not much happening round here, is there? Still, wet or not, I reckon the turkey table will be going strong.      Probably, Lionel. I was just saying to Harry and Ida the other day about how you used to help us with the layout back when we moved in. I still can’t believe how much that old Regency sideboard cost!      Aye, that was a few bob back in the day, but it’s a fine piece of furniture. My Da brought it back from a market in Norwich. I tell you, he served in the war and brought back more than just souvenirs from the front.      True enough, Harry. My old man was in the Royal Engineers, and he reckoned that’s where you picked up a few bits ‘n bobs that made sense in civilian life. Though I must say, I’m glad we didn’t have to go through that.      Aw, mind, I worked in a tea room during the war! We were feeding the troops most nights about then. My Nan always said I had the touch of the old-time lass from Harrow where she was born. Proper London roots!      That’s right, Doreen. And I’ve always said your ability to keep a tea room humming at wartime pace is one of your best bloody achievements! Though I don’t reckon you’d say that yourself.      Oh, but we’re getting grand! I’ve told Ida more than once how I took the bus all the way from Costessey with three suitcases and a cat named goody-two-shoes! I couldn’t pronounce it properly at the time, but I was proud as punch.      A bit far from here, Harry! I’ve always said Norfolk’s pastoral charm’s in the mix of folk, though. You gave this place more character than some folks ‘ere realise.

Rather skip the new house’s viewing. You know I hate that. But you’d think it'd be exciting... Our last house, same thing. Remember how your mother kept knocking on the bathroom door, shouting, “Is it full yet?” Just to check the pipes?      She always feared the place would flood overnight. It was ridiculous. Still, moving is never easy. You don’t often get to swap your childhood home for one with a double garage and gardens that don’t smell like damp socks. Even if we do end up sorting through half the attic when it rains.      Right, but it’s mostly about the mortgage. I don’t like the way the interest rates are moving now. My lectures are fine, but you know my pay’s not much more than what you earn at the DSS, Dad. I’ll be the odd man out if I’m not careful.      You’re doing better than most. Less stress for you, at least, being the teacher. No felling to do or customer service shout-fests over late deliveries. I mean, it can’t get much tougher than listening to the occasional raving baron.      It doesn’t. Tell me about it… watching you during those call centre endurance games from the kitchen is no fun – Mate, you got a real job?      Doesn’t matter. You know what? I’d rather deal with complaints than what your old man had to put up with. Working full-time and looking after you and your sister? It counts for something.      It counts for a lot, Dad. But look at us – all I do is teach people how to say about five phrases in conversation classes. You’re the reliable one. We were never going to be wealthy, but maybe now it’s easier to make provision for things. Like sending your sister to the better school. She deserves the best, not just what passed for adequate when we were at her age.      She’s got her head on straight. Not unlike her brother. We’re not good at words… but as long as we always try with what we’ve got, that’s the main point.      I know. Just another course on the 'will' go or 'shall' we? Something's always got to give.      And the box of old films from your uncle goes with you. It’s about time someone asked why he’s never been seen in those 80s belly-dancer films.

Rather skip the salmon, isn't it rather expensive at the moment. I know her GP mentioned that dementia has... got worse in some ways. She forgets more than remembers these days, so we’d best avoid anything that might confuse her. Simpler the better, as you know.      Yeah, I noticed she doesn't seem to follow the conversation much longer at mealtimes. But what if she refuses something? What if she’s having one of those days when she's more alert?      Well, we’ll just have to decide on the menu when she's with us. Maybe start with cheese and crackers, then go gentle—roast chicken with mash and veggies, no surprises. I've made a note of the dietary restrictions too, you know what’s coming. And by the way, I've ordered some candles, and I think the purple ones would go nicely in the dining room. They’re not too bright—good mood lighting.      The purple ones are lovely, and yes, we can re-light them for the photograph session. Oh, I forgot to mention—I found some old photographs of Grandma in Grantham. I put them in the drawer as a keepsake for the table, maybe as we go on… watching her reaction.      That’s a nice touch – very heartwarming. I was thinking, though, about rearranging the table a bit. It might be better if the phone’s not visible. Last time, every ten minutes, she tried to call someone who isn’t alive anymore. Just trying to keep the room clear of clutter so it doesn’t fluster her more.      That’s a great idea. I hadn't thought of that. I did make a table plan for the catering staff to follow, though. I had to rearrange the seats last minute because Sarah suddenly got stuck at the office. The uncles are both coming, and, well, they don’t always get along.      Right, we'll go with your table plan but give it to them early so there’s no waiting at the last minute. As for the meal… I propose doing a vegetarian option as well. You never know what the digestive system might do these days. Even for someone in their 80s.      Mm, that works if we don’t make it too much of a choice-based conversation. I was thinking we could mention  The Great British Bake Off  recipes you made at the planning stage, to help bring her attention into the present.

Rather annoying to be honest. Me gran reckons they’re just part of the package, ‘cos everyone gets ‘em and it’s just pain temporarily, but honestly, I’d take a few extra bags of crisps over this. Not to mention they’ve gone and made a proper hole in the side of my cheek eenit. I swear I’ve been breathing through my   mouth  .      Oh no! That sounds   awful  ! I had mine out ages ago, but I was   nauseated   for a whole day after the op and couldn’t chase the ambulance or anything. Were yours specially bad like that?      A bit, yeah. The dentist said they were coming in sideways like posh turkey legs, so they   had to drill   a bit more. I’m glad I didn’t have to pick ‘em out meself like me mum did in the 80s. She used a teaspoon and a bit of carbolic! Haha, she’s a   hard one  .      Honestly, I wouldn’t wish that on anyone! I mean, it’s bad enough being awake and seeing the drill, let alone doing your own mouth with a spoon and   spirit  . Have you spoken to your folks about how it’s going?      Aye – Matey faces me fairly badly, and Ma’s just been trying to feed me like her grand baby again, giving me   bouillabaisse   and   mashy potatoes   in a baby bottle. It’s so   pathetic  ! But they just want to help, innit? Though, to be   fair  , I’d be grizzling too if I had a   hole in my face   about the size of a 20p.      Poor vibes. I suppose you’re not   thinking   of doing anything big while it heals?      Not really. Burgers and treacle sponges passed me by for a while. Though I am getting   bored   confined to the   flat  . I miss the madhouse of uni. How are you planning that again? Is it moving to a new place near the campus or whot?      Defo moving near the uni this time. Last place was so far go that I had to   cycle   or   taxi  , and neither is really in the budget. I’m sharing with three blokes – Tom, Jamie, and Lewis. It’s supposed to be all brand new and kitted out with those   IKEA cupboards   and a kettle on each side for ‘hot drinks at the same time.’ Is that not a   marvel   of modern design?      Haha, that's brilliant, innit?

Rather than going out and doing something extravagant for Chinese New Year, I thought we could do something a bit more... charitable, you know? Just something to make more people smile, maybe even someone we don't know. I've been reading quite a bit about random acts of kindness recently, actually—it's quite inspiring. Has anyone ever tried something like this?      Yeah! My teacher did one of those kindness challenges last year in class. We wrote sticky notes and left them on strangers' cars. It was so much fun. We had to be sneaky and not get caught when we stuck the notes under the wipers like we were delivering messages! One bloke even left a 50p on the dashboard for us like a reaction turkey, which was hilarious! So, what’s the plan?      That sounds brilliant, Harry. I think we could do something similar but in a way that feels special for Chinese New Year—like if we made a small batch of some cookies or a cake, using the milk alternatives we talked about ordering online earlier. We could wrap them up nicely and slip them under the doormat of a few houses in the village. Maybe even with a little note to let them know they're from someone who remembers the Year of the Dragon—and that we're celebrating in our humble way.      Can we put some Draughts pieces or Chess pieces in the bags like money-like tokens? Mrs. Grey in the library was saying the other day that her grandad used those for pocket money. She found one of the pieces in an old box and brought it to show us at school—looked very old and goldy!      That’s actually a lovely idea, Ruby. We could do something like that—maybe not gold, but small tokens of appreciation instead of real money. We can paint some Chess pieces with glitter or make little stickers for kindness points, so it still feels rewarding.      What about wearing matching hair colours for the week? I remember seeing a video where a girl got all her friends to dyed their hair pink or blue or something wild. It looked super cool. Maybe we could do something like that with temporary dye or glitter gels?      That's a fun thought, Harry. We could! Maybe pick a shade that's common in Chinese New Year decorations or something symbolic like red for good luck.

So do you remember that time we were walking to the post office and the car just sideswiped us like... off the pavement? And you went flying into that flowerbed?      Oh! You’re talking about when we were only about ten and twenty! I remember that—Deerfield Road, wasn’t it? I think the driver was on the phone and his car clipped your leg real hard. You’ve still got a little scar there, don’t you?      Yeah, there is. I always blame that photographer guy. But at the time it was the funniest thing ever—we both went crash-landed! And then I picked a daffodil out of that flowerbed and made you wear it on your head for the rest of the day like you were Alice in Wonderland.      [Laughing] A bit like a mad Alice in Wonderland, yes. Remember how we used to dress up then? I found some of your old costumes in the attic the other day—sheets covered in sparkles, those red gloves that went clank every time you moved.      Oh, I still have the one I used for your drama group’s production. I think it was called “The Caterpillar and the Clock.” You remember Mr. Beadle got so rattled when the clock part stopped working and I just read from the programme instead? Everyone was laughing.      We didn’t have much money back then, but you always loved the theatrics. Like this week at music camp, weren’t you auditioning for a play?      Yeah, something with singing and a red dress. It’s online music now—I’ve been uploading ballet songs onto my channel.      That’s lovely. Have you thought of posting your old recitals as well? Maybe some of your friends would like to see them again. You remember when we watched the old clips and realized we’d left your guest entrance note at the end of that one? The Internet’s a funny thing. It keeps it all.      You always gave the best guest notes. Like when that gull stole my hat during the finale. You rushed on stage with your scarf and took the mic like it was part of the script.      Oh, go on. I think it was more of a panic moment. But I did line it up with that green scarf we were given for the finale.   Speaker__1:   It looked like you were auditioning to be one of the queens of Hearts, though.

Rather annoying isn't it, how they just push these applications through. I was out in the garden this morning reading the local paper, and there it was—another wind turbine proposed in what was once a peaceful farming area near Cheltenham. No consultation, no consideration! I wouldn't be surprised if the site's practically in my  backyard  by the time it gets approved.      Oh aye, I know what you mean. We had a meeting last night with a group from over in Somerset—exactly the same issue. I gave them a few pointers from our experience with the solar farm proposal near Ramsgate. Still, it's a tough battle, isn't it? The council's on the side of the turkey, as the old saying goes. They’re all too keen to get the subsidies for their “green energy push” and not bothered about how it messes with the landscape—or the birds!      Look, while everyone's busy playing politics, we're not even setting foot in the real issue—storage. All the wind and solar they generate now, where does it go? If we had proper grid infrastructure and storage methods that weren't land-based eyesores themselves, we wouldn’t need to fight these bloody turbines and solar arrays just because they’re in the wrong spot. The Government pats itself on the back for throwing millions at renewables, but barely scratches the surface of  storing  the energy they promise will save us all.      Absolutely. It’s all very well someone at the Ministry of Energy talking about a low-carbon future, but when it's your village that's the test site, it doesn’t feel very “sustainable.” I remember when we spoke about the planning appeal about five years back—spent all that time collecting signatures, contacting MPs, but most of them just switched their votes once it suited their political agenda. It's not just wind turbines, it’s the entire  machinery  hiding behind them.      Aye, and don’t get me started on the alignment of the development companies with councils. It’s almost like the companies are funding the committees and then they propose the permits themselves. There’s a lack of real transparency—you hear the same consultants turn up in every meeting, delivering the same polished PPT presentation on how the project will “enhance the community.” It's all smoke and mirrors.

Rather annoying this, having to go through all that car insurance malarkey again. Felt like I was back in the ’70s when I first sorted out my own insurance after I left university.      Well, things are different now, Daddy! Car insurance is more complicated than it used to be. There’s more paperwork, more choices, and heaven knows what with all the digital stuff these days.      I know what you mean, love. And it’s not as if pulling someone to the side at the Motor Vehicles Office and saying “Crikey, don’t forget your green form!” like we used to will make it any easier. Now, we’ve got to fill out web forms and video checks and all sorts.      Yeah, and this is all while the lassie [gesturing at Speaker_2] is trying to get her driver’s license sorted. Made quite enough breakfasts and packed enough sandwiches to last a month after I went through learner driving myself.      Grandad, I’ve only got the provisional license, and I’ve only been out a few times. But I’m taking it seriously. You don’t just jump in and expect to be Hertz by the end of the weekend, do you?      That’s the spirit, my girl. But while you’re getting your feet wet, don’t forget we’re planning that family trip to Cornwall later next month. You know what it’s like with the hills and the traffic. Our nerves will be put to the test!      Oh, don’t remind me. Some years ago, I got stuck in the Whiteout near Bodmin with a cousin’s nephew in the back seat crying and about five bags of seaside candy all over the seats. Still got a photo somewhere.      That sounds like an adventure. I’d love to hear the full story sometime—maybe over a cup of tea?      As long as you’ve got more than a teaspoon of sugar for it, my dear. Speaking of which, what about your week plans, darling? You got that language camp sorted?      Yeah, I’ve got it all set. I’m taking a class of kids from a local community center and helping them with their French. I love it—it’s so rewarding.      Well, I just hope you don’t end up with a box of croissants and your head in the clouds all the time. You’ve got to manage the books around here too, after all!

Rather annoying really, Mate. I'm just sat at my laptop and the notifications just keep coming through. Mostly it's the Facebook app going mad. I’m more than happy to stop by the shop on my way to pick up some ingredients to bake those scones we talked about.      Got eeny harm outta that app if I'm honest. I reckon it's more trouble than it's worth with that constant buzzing. Like I said last week, social media is for kids and politicians. But scones, now you're talking me language. Those scones, the ones with raspberry jam specially... like to add a bit of clotted cream on top as well.      Yeah, clotted cream’s a must. I remember you telling me stories about the 50s – the café in your local, and the queues for the cream. Living in Brighton now, the scone shops aren’t even half as good as this.      Brighton’s a lovely place, is what I always say to people. But the parking? Good grief, it's like trying to move a tractor through a catwalk. Used to be much easier when land was unspoilt and houses only for families who could afford 'em.      Speaking of, how are you getting on with the rent? I know the food bank still needs it, but if you ever need a hand or want to come by and share a tea and biscuits or two, you know where to find me.      That’s so kind of you. Thank you. Besides, I can do the cooking and you’d better have a word with the local politicians about replying to all the concerns people are bringing up about healthy eating and fresh produce. Seems like they prefer to ignore the real issues instead of looking for a solution.      Not that I've got any influence, but I do my best. Makes you wonder if the lot of them even remember what it was like to struggle at all. You know, back in the 50s, no one had money or resources, but we knew how to survive.      That always comes with a story or two from your time. I do love hearing them, you know, even though I’m a regular student with my own goings on. But life, as always, keeps you on your toes. Still betting on the horses by the way?      Every weekend if I can.

So, I swear, my English teacher once told me that sarcastic remarks are her version of ‘breaking bad’. Like, she’ll start off normal, and then  bam! , something so cutting you wonder if she suddenly picked up a new hobby. And I was like, mate, you’re quoting  Hamlet  and then throwing passive-aggressive shade at the bloke who asked if he could call her “Professor” in the A-level ethics group. That’s Shakespeare meets social media drama, innit?      Haha, classic academic power moves. Reminds me when I tried to learn golf last year because my uncle insisted it was a  “necessary skill”  for the real world. Turns out, the only thing I mastered was how to yell “fore” like I was summoned back by the golf gods themselves.      I mean, golf is just elitist cricket, isn’t it? You wear all the posh gear and swing a stick for a decade in hopes that one day you’ll not hit the ball into the drink. And the surnames over there are even worse. I swear, if someone had a golf name, they might go full  Lord of the Rings  and start introducing themselves as “Sir Birdie of the Sublime Slice, Master of the Putting Green.” You ever try to remember all the rules while actually trying not to cry because the ball goes off into the woods?      Honestly, I considered nicknaming my cousin “Birdie” just to mess with him. He works in marketing and thinks he’s a real “winner” at life because he got promoted last week—based entirely on his ability to send a PowerPoint that looked like it had a midlife crisis. He nearly flinched when I pulled the nickname out the blue one day at the family dinner. I swear, he thought he was suddenly back at some primary school sports day.      My sister had that problem with someone once. She started calling him “Mr. Win at Work” as a joke after he got all smug talking about his new project. You could see the tension crackle in the air. He’s clearly out there now trying to find her a new nickname that rhymes with “nice” but means “nauseating” in Latin or something.      Yeah, man, if you start calling someone “bloated” at the family BBQ, that’s genuinely a blood feud opener. You gotta be careful with nicknames. It’s like Shakespeare lives in all this—tragedy, comedy, and maybe even a little sonnet involved.

Rather annoying I know, innit. Conference request forms are doin’ me nutts, ‘n like... got to pick between two speakers. Otherwise I’d be chuckin’ their emails into the bin! Got me stuck between sommat traditional or sommat... modern? Dunno.      Right, so  not  the one that 'speaks to his calculator’ as well? The guy with the A4 notes? Not the one from last year, innit?      Oh, cwore!  That  one. Didn’t even turn up. Left us holdin’ the mic for thirty mins!  Mate , I nearly lost my job, I’d lik’.      Yeah, I remember that. Terry left the room like Ten Commandments had gone wrong or somethin’. Made us all laugh though? But if you’re stuck between a dodgy choice, breakfast, innit? I’d just go with whoever I could wrangle a keynote out of.      I say get a comedian. That would at least keep everyone from dozin’ off.      I’m with you, as innit. But the uni, they fancy somethin' proper. They’re always like, “inspirational,” “industry leader,” “cutting edge.” Right lah, it just means someone who’s had a sommat of a CV and done a phone interview.      Truth. I mean, I just work at the factory, but even I can read between the lines of meetings.      Also, have you seen the canteen tea? That’s not  cutting edge . That’s nearly about to fall off the table.      Oh, fank th’ lord you mentioned the tea. I’m off cold turkey next week. Tryin’ཀ to do sommat ‘clean’ and ‘kickstart’ my system.      Are you sayin’ you’re give it up? I tried once, for a week, but I lost my hearing as well.      Git with it, mate. She tried ‘keto’ last month. Six days and a collapsed diaphragm.      It was my knees, if you must know.      Still, I reckon it's worth it, bloomin’ cafes what your lot get. We could have toast made for 3AM and someone to poach those eggs, innit?      I live with two roomies. We do mornings like a military operation. I get up lasaurus, and they’re already in the pan.      Right, you're cuttin’ up and pastin’ diaries again, you-? Meanwhile, I'm livin’ out of a van and last week had a tooth out. All free healthcare on the NHS and look what they've done to me.      Y’know, I used to live off a van, too. Delivered pizzas in Doncaster.

Rather annoying this new TV licence regime, innit? Seems they've gone and made it more ‘politically correct’ than ever. I mean, now they want everyone to declare whether their telly is on a wall or a shelf. What's next, a fanny-flicker?      Has it really got  that  bad? I 'aven't got me telly on for weeks, not with that eclipse passing by. Got the best seats in the garden, under the tree. It were a reasonable advert for light and dark, if you ask me.      Oh, I watched it on the BBC iPlayer! Not as good as being outside, but I couldn't go out with the gout acting up again. I was just skimming through the Cosmos documentary last night, the part about black holes. Rather fascinating how the universe starts and all. It makes you think about the old saying: "As above, so below."      That's right. When I was workin' as a civil engineer, I often thought how the universe and the earth shared a sort of architecture, if you know what I mean—mountains like craters, rivers as if they were human veins.      Aye, and speaking of workin', when are we gettin’ round to that garden tour you spoke about, Elsie? I were trying to grow some bamboo last week. All that talk about it takin’ over the world might be a bit much, but I 'ave someone at the end of the fence grumblin' already.      Oh, yes! Let's go now while the sun comes through. That owl box I put in the tree last spring has been rather successful. Two young ones took up the perch the other night. It's a bit like having your very own little programme manager.      Programme  manager ? That be a ‘cosmic’ development if you’re in charge of birds. Though I have me own tale. Last week, I was touring the garden with someone from Skype, bless 'em. We ended up talkin’ about moving to Norwich. Her grandkid were 'aving a new home built—course, he's a young lad with proper plans.      Moving’s a big go, especially on your own if you've not worked for ages. You ever think about shifting out, Elsie?      Only what your lot plant in the first place! I might manage a day walk, mind, but hours of travel?      Still, talk about the ‘plants’ in the garden and them modern trends—someby I read online suggested to water plants with music.

Rather skip the newfit in Manchester, innit? Seems a bit overpriced for what they’re servin’. I were with me mates the other week, and we all came away feelin’ a bit “meh”. Not to say they don’t do things proper — well, the place was nice an’ all — but I’d rather stick with the older spots where we know what we’re gettin’.      Ah, yeah, I’ve heard mixed reviews about it. It was meant to be that place where you get the full experience and whatnot — the kind of place blokes like me get asked to sort of sound smart at when they talk about restaurants. But honestly, I’d rather stick to the older places too, if I’m being truthful. The good old tried and tested spots ain’t half bad, are they?      No, an’ it’s not just ‘cos we’re stuck in old habits — I mean, some of those places around Sunderland are cookin’ up proper food, you know? I mean, have we not had that place near the Waterfront with the big windows? That place is just absolute bliss in shortbread land!      Haha, right — the Waterfront is always a proper option. I was just thinking about that the other day — it’s got a real nice vibe, and the views are something. Though, somethin’ tells me you can’t really get that same ‘fix’ when you’re drivin’ in from someone’s house in Harpenden. That’s like a good half-hour motor each way!      Aye, I’d be lookin’ at the clock like it’s Prime Minister Johnson in about five minutes. That trip does not bode well for my stamina on a Saturday. I’ve already got the sister’s place to pop in to and it’s a proper sprawl to do both, ‘cos she’s like 20 miles passed Harpenden somewhere.      Ah, bloody typical! First, I meet a decent gal who’s into cookin’, then we’re stuck in a grid of Websites and Yellow Pages with 'veg-friendly spots' to pick from, an’ no way of doin’ it with travel like a man. Don’t go there with my parents unless I’ve got a plan for at least two hours to myself, innit.      You know what your problem is? You were brought up in that leafy, posh bit of Hertfordshire where every bit of life is like a bloody sermon from ‘the good book of middle-class.’

Rather annoying this newfit alarm clock o’ mine, is. Keeps goin’ off ‘fore m’ ready, and I’ll often jolt up like a startled bairn an’ nearly spill me cup o’ tea. Not to mention, the bird outside me window — well, the song’s so bright eenin’ now, I swear it’s an alarm   clock   onto its own! Know what? I reckon it’s a chaffinch, but this one bird, it’s a touch more boisterous as normal. Know anythink abou’ that, Jan?      Aye, I like to think of it as nature’s version o’ a snooze button, only you can’t push it back. As for the bird, you’re probably not far off — chaffinches are right common, but they pick up little twangs in their melody depending on where they’re brought up. I’ve breakfasted to that same tune this past week, though I’m not at all sure. I’ve been tryin’ to train me whistle so I can mimic it, but that’s easier said than done, I know!      Aye, well, as to trainsin’ the beak — as we say in-country — it’s a work in progress, like the rest o’ us! Speaking of progress, I’ve started feedin’ the birds again up me garden. Got some of those peanuts in them little mesh feeders, and already the sparrows and the odd magpie turn up. Though, one mornin’, a cheeky squirrel tried to have a nosey! Some o’ the older birds mind the windchimes and tea tree stuff I’ve had put in, but it all seems about right. I hear a lot of our mammys still passin’ time in th’ garden, and not just because o’ the weather!      That rings true. My sister ‘eard someone mention Enid, down at the club. She’s been dancin’ round a few teeth troubles, and last I ‘eard, had a bit o’ a nosebleed and rushed off to the dentist. He knows the drill, I s’pose! They say if you let it go too long, it can lead t’ some weary business — even goin’ on to say if you don’t mind a hoarse voice or a tickly cough, it might be worth a peek by the docs. ‘As Mike’s latest summat about flu or throat cancer, and well, I’m startin’ to wonder.      Oh luv, over half o’ our circle has had something or other these days — all that stress, and they say the weather doesn’t help!

Rather skip the new book, eh? You know, ever since I had the twins, time’s been like... non-existent. But I have to say, your yoga blog’s a godsend. It’s a little slice of zen when the world seems like it’s crumbling at the seams.      That’s so sweet of you to say, Maria. I reckon people underestimate how easy self-care is these days. A lot of it’s just about hitting pause, honestly. Oh, and congrats again on the twins. Two at once was the full package, wasn’t it?      Oh, you have no idea! IVF is no joke, let me tell you. Months of injections and appointments that could’ve been documentaries. Still, worth it. The only downside is that I’m constantly on social media for work, and I’m beginning to feel like I’m either a helicopter parent or part social media post, myself.      Haha, I hear that. And ever since I started writing, even just for a few hours each week, it’s like I’ve found a new version of me. I mean, I always thought I was going to be in social work for the long haul, but life’s got a funny way of throwing curveballs.      Yeah – I remember when we first met, and you were just finishing your masters. You knew you wanted to work with kids and families, and I thought, ‘What a good job for someone who likes people.’ Who’d have thought we’d both end up in professions where we have to give so much of ourselves?      I think the key is balance. I mean, your ballet sessions or my writing have been like meditations. I’ve started using the weekends just to take a deep breath and not be switched-on all the time. Not that I’m not proud of my work, but I do need to ‘recharge.’      Same here. The only problem with yoga is it makes you want to write a book about it! I tried starting something once – just a few pages about single motherhood and being academically trained yet utterly clueless about the whole parenthood thing.      That’s something I’d read. I mean, we’re both in our 40s and our worlds are so different, but I think we’ve got that common thread – the ‘university brain’ versus ‘real life,’ you know?      Exactly. I’d love to write something real and raw, but to be honest, I’m still over here trying to not be a modern-day parenting faux pas!

Rather annoying isn't it, how some people think they can do what they like just because it's the weekend... Our next door neighbour had his barking dogs yet again last night. I've nearly lost my mind by now.      Oh I hear what you mean, love. Over here we had a bit of a different issue last week. One bloke tried to break into his own house thinking it was a stranger's property. Slammed the door too hard, shattered the lock. Turned out it was someone trying to help him out anyway. Rather annoying when the gym’s closed for weekend, ay? I was promising to lift today, ‘n it’s got turned out showering again. Rather skip the Easter eggs an’ just do a bit o’ gardenin’, if it comes t’ that... got heaps o’ daffodils needin’ diggin’ an’ replacin’. Rather skip to the front of the book, isn’t it? A few hurrahs for when the first one got the big boots on—that’s the one with the red football socks, sure himself. Now, where is that? Not quite sure where the film got lost on that one. But it was in Kinsale, holidays with the folks. God, didn’t I reckon his wee legs would never come clean again with that sand all over. Ay, that was a summer to remember, wasn't it?      Oh, yes, I remember that! Didn’t it rain sideways the next day? I had the baby in a sling, and I swear I nearly lost both the baby and the camera. I didn’t know what I was doing, and I think he turned round and gave me a funny look like, ‘What’s this, Ma?’      Haha, he’s so lucky you had that camera, Gran, or else I wouldn’t have that to show my mates. Oh aye, that was the year wee lad was celebrating his 5th birthday, wasn’t it, Mary? We went to the start line and had hot dogs and everything. Silly little rascal got so excited when the runners came past he climbed up someone’s back and started cheering. I swear my legs ached just holding him up. Mary was hotter than toast herself. I got photos of the fairground near the finish, too—didn’t like the Burgers and balls, but he absolutely adored the carousel. Still shows me that picture every time I pass him one of the memory sticks.      I did see the one from Iceland. That’s the one with the space helmets and the lava shots. Why was he in Iceland? Was it a holiday?      Oh, that was your dad's go—some work trip he had to take there. Told us he had to spend quality time with the lad. The boxset of films from the Road to Reykjavik is still in the cupboard.

Rather annoying when the sock’s pair finds its way into the washing machine and ends up in the ‘lost socks’ pile again. Never mind—how is that chicken curry I mentioned going on Sunday? It’ll be lovely to have you over, Mum. And I know what you were saying about the weather being too bright and sunny if we eat outdoors?!      I reckon it depends on how much sun cream I’ve got left from when I last went to this garden centre to visit friends. And speaking of curry, do you remember the night you first cooked it and made that My turkey curry sauce instead? Ha ha ha!      I do now I you mention it! Speaking of, I tried a new recipe from a cookbook I borrowed from the library last week—it was fairly simple, and actually worked quite well!      Now don’t go making everything taste like cumin and coriander, Annie! Give me something with a bit of bite in it. Although I do miss my knitting a bit lately. I had a lovely holder made for the grandchildren—only red and white and double-dipped at the corners! Looked as good as it was about to fall apart after a play date.      I remember looking at it once and wondering if you were practicing for crocheting socks! But honestly, it was charming. My sister knit for her children too, and her son passed it down. A few years ago, the whole family sent him a wooden set of hand puppets, you know the ones with the stick on the back—those yellow duckies or something like that.      Oh yes! They had such big, fluffy feathers too. I remember playing with them when I was four or so. Mummy used to let me sit by the fire and talk to them while she sewed.

Rather fine day today, isn't it love? Thought it’d be a bit damp, seeing as it pattered off and on all Thursday. Still, seems more summer than not at this rate. A bit of sun is always good for the garden, don't you think?      Oh, it’s delightful dear. I’ve been keeping one eye on the weather all week. Almost as if I thought a bit of brightness might cheer up the place more this year. The summer always brings back so many memories, you know. Especially with the children coming to visit when the season’s right.      Aye, I remember them mostly as when they were tiny, stomping around in the back garden with bits of wellington boot still on. Still, best to not reflect on time flew by, ain't it? D’you know, I think the world might be changing faster than it used to. All the mobile phones, the laptops, and this newfangled net — I’ll never catch up, and I don’t suppose I want to either. There was something nicely slow about the old days.      Oh, I hear you. I don’t need no fancy gadgets to be happy, love. A good sandwich, a bit of watching the children, and a chat such as this one is all I want. Sometimes I wonder whether we’re still needed these days, being as we’re both retired and don’t go out much. But then I remember the tea parties with the old buggers at the village hall — full house for a suspicious crowd of my age, if you catch my drift.      Haha, aye, and being accused of plotting something all the time. Best not argue, I suppose. I always say: let them think the worst, as long as they’re thinking of you. At any rate, that shepherd’s pie I made it yesterday does sound promising, if you fancy a bite for lunch?      As if I need convincing! I could eat a whole plate of it, as it happens. I’ve been helping myself to the biscuits while you weren’t looking as well. You being the only one left who’ll feed me a proper meal with vegetables in it, love. My knees tell me I’m getting too old to chase the kids around as I did when I was a childminder, but at least I made a dent in the world that way.

Rather annoying I had to take the bus in to work this morning. My car's decided it doesn't like the weather and conked out on the way outta Bristol. Not a good start to the week!      Oh no, I heard rain yesterday and thought about you getting stuck in it. That sounds awful, I feel for you. Which bus did you manage to catch?      A lot of people have been talking this week about how much easier it would be to get a reasonable car. We've been meaning to go for a drive outside of London but the decision has not happened yet.      I can imagine! Having a car is such a blessing for getting about now that the weather is getting changeable. So what are you going to do about the car problem then, Speakers_1?      I'm thinking of taking it into Catsfield Autos near breakfast, but I'm nervous about the costs. Hoped to spend a bit on planting some new desktop hides, you know, for the classroom?      Oh, I do like the way you think, Speaker_1. I remember when your classroom did that last time and the children were so delighted. Did they get to choose the stickers?      Yeah, they did! Teachers: always having a rush of love from children at school with meaningful gifts! Going into that office area! I mean, it does sound strange but to have something like hand cream is just treasured nowadays.      I have been to a few weddings where people got quite quirky gifts. I once received a rather cute beetle farm. We had to feed it and that was as constant as watering indoor plants with lunches. I think it lasted about three weeks before the glass lid exploded for some unknown reason.      Oh no go, really? That is about as dramatic as losing a vase in a very active toddler’s room. I genuinely cannot go further than that.      So how have things been for you all this week? I had a long weekend, went with friends to nearby to Kent on a road trip where we found this lovely little b&b near the coast.

Rather annoying this new bar across the road innit? Seems like everything sticks out in this ‘hood these days... got to be some sort of local investment scheme, eh? I mean, sure, where we are in L8, Liverpool, it seems like the city centre’s expanding bit by bit. I’ve only een here a few months, but even I’ve noticed more folk coming in.      Aye, I know what yer mean Mark. Proper changed since me dad were a lad. It weren’t like that. We used to ken everyone. Not no more. Yer get kids running ’bout on their phones, folk in brand new flats, and no one really knows the real history of these streets. It’s like the city’s trying to forget its soul to make money. It sells ‘Potter’ books — y’know, Harry Potter — full sets for collectors. I reckon my gran read those to me when I was seven.      Harry Potter, eh? I’m a big fan —  Professor Snape, Prime Example of a Man with Layers . That film scene where he drops the potions book? I still get chills.
