Though I suppose not many people round here think o’ it like that. ‘Course, some folk seem to think about far darker stuff...      Like what?      Heh, recently there was a news story about some fiend from a no-good group calling themselves something like ‘ISIS’ — the ones spreading hate goin’ on in far-off places. I wonder how much it affects us here in the scheme of daily life. People box things up sometimes.      Aye, I’ve heard about that. Hazards in every generation. I just think people like to talk ’bout it more than live with it proper.

Rather skip the new sausages at the Farm Shop, they talk about gluten free diets now — which is all very well if you're allergic, but I think it's all a bit over the top, don’t you think? Not like the old days, when we just ate what we were given — proper meat and two veg! I remember my mother feeding me steak and kidney puddings when I was young — most people didn’t have all these choices back then.      Oh, I’ve had some interesting gluten-free options! My husband was doing the school meals system during the lockdown, and he made some meatballs that were entirely gluten free, just made sure no breadcrumbs were used. It’s not as hard as people like to think, but definitely not as cheap. I think it’s much more expensive, to be honest.      I think it’s just a trend most of the time. Cats at the Village Shop, no doubt about that — real Anglo-Saxon stuff in there. When I was on holiday in Nepal, you didn’t have to think about that sort of thing. The food was simple, just lentils, rice and dumplings — I don’t think anyone said “gluten free” there.      Oh, I’d love to go to Nepal, but I don’t think I can cycle it like your daughter does, Specky! She’s doing an Iron Man, isn’t she? That’s something else entirely. I remember when we were at that weekend, and the Tour of Britain was in the village — the crowd was out in force. Those bikes came so fast, it made my legs tingle just watching! Last time, I asked my sister-in-law if she wanted to give any baby advice to the new grandbaby and she just said, “Make sure they take lunches to school — it’s not the same as the good old days.”      My husband works the dinner table now, so he does most of the cooking. He’s quite good at it, really.

Rather annoying I had to take the 6 am train in from Sheffield today, dontcha think? But typin’ and emailin’ from the dining table isn’t exactly profitable, innit? Meetings start proper at ten o’clock proper.      Yeah, well, you know how it is een Cambridge. Everyone thinks they're the one making the coffee and running the show at all times of the day. I swear half the people I know in this town never sleep. Oh, and congrats on pulling off that conference last month, by the way. Massive hit, innit? That's a big deal for a new co-ordinator, honestly.      What’s it like, working on conference stuff? I’m just curious if coordinating events is more exciting than waiting for spreadsheets to load.      Well, there’s the excitement, and then there’s the panic ordering more croissants cos the delegate numbers changed at the last minute. But yeah, it’s proper busy, innit? Like, today I was panicking cos one of the machines wouldn’t read the correct code, and we had a production run due in six hours. It's like Russian roulette with money and deadlines.      Oy, I about lost it last week cos the coffee machine broke down and my boss wanted triple espresso for a visiting client and I had to explain that we barely had grounds left. I could’ve handled that. My day job gives me the "poor man’s panic," if you know what I mean.      Oh, I know. I tried to calm my boss down last time one of my sponsors messed up the funds. Said, “It’s not the end of the world, Jan. It’s just a bit of money and a couple of nice banners.” He looked at me as if I’d just insulted his entire life’s work.      That’s the thing, innit—no one ever feels like what your job is actually matters at the right time.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh? You know what, I've been thinking about it all week. We really ought to start some sort of petition to stop the council from knocking the library down. It's a proper shame—how long have we not seen a decent children's book programme like the one they had at the Plumstead branch? I don't think they've got one of those anywhere near here now.      I agree entirely. I've had a spot of trouble with my shift pattern as it is—my Admin role at the local office makes for long hours during the week, and I often don’t get the chance to even think about community stuff until the weekend. That said, I’d help with the petition if you’re starting one. You’ve got a head for organisation, you know—from transcribing and all.      I’ll be the first to say, I’m far from perfect at it, but I do know a bit about pulling things like this off in a clear and coherent way. I remember we talked about building a kind of timeline—dates, meetings, deadlines, all that—during the village fete committee a few years back. I think we even used a mnemonic to keep it all in order. Tell me, was it SAMT? Something like that?      Oh, for heaven’s sake, I thought I was the one with the memories! No, I think it was more like “Schedule and Manage Timeline” or “See All Members Tasks.” Either way, the point is someone’s gotta take the lead. And you know what? It just goes to show how the local borough’s decision-making feels a bit disconnected from the community—prioritising shiny new buildings over a library that most people about our age actually walk to.      Exactly. I had to document a borough meeting last month—you know that new school they’re building up near the cemetery? The architect’s just a twerp. They didn’t even sit down with the residents. They just handed them a glossy leaflet and said ‘get it or get lost.’ Honestly, it’s mad. Makes me wonder if we should combine the petitions—library and school space both suffer from the same kind of poor consultation.      That’s a good thought. You know, I started watching a few brain-training videos on the train about mnemonics again.

Rather annoying lot, them Jehovah's Witnesses. I used to get 'em knocking on the door when I first retired, and I told 'em straight, "I don’t have time for your pamphlets." Mind you, they were persistent, wouldn’t give up easily—some of them'll talk your ear off 'til you're dizzy, I swear. But they’re good folk if you think about it, just a bit fanatical, wouldn’t you say, old chap?      Oh, aye, 'course. We've had the same here. Funny thing is, my wife used to speak to one of 'em for weeks. Mary thought he was charming, always called the poor lad "dear"—but no, 'e still couldn’t convince 'er to change her views. Tenacity, I give 'em that. But I’d say they’re the least of my worries in this village. Cats ‘n’ clutter, now that’s what keeps me up at night.      Clutter is dreadful, especially in the back lanes. I took the grandkids to the park by Watercress Fields, and we nearly got lost—somebody left two fridges outside as if they were supplying the whole town with cold beer. Honestly, it’s a proper eyesore. Speaking of which, have you all tried that new café at the edge of Horsham Lane yet? Anna’s the one running it. All that clatter and clink of china—heartwarming! Though the toilets are tiny, just someone’s chicken coop turned into a loo. Quite a character, Anna.      Aye, I've been once or twice. The shepherd’s pie’s not bad, and there’s a bit about voting on the walls—Anna’s quite the political one. She says “we must take responsibility for this country” and that we shouldn’t take the voting rights lightly. Maybe she’s got a point. Taxes 'ave trebled since I was at work, and 'ave you seen the price of a decent filling at the dentist now? I tried to get my molar looked at last week, and they quoted me over a hundred pounds for a filling with 'hope I survive it first.'      That's just  unfair . You're a dear man, James, go on. I remember your teeth being perfect when we went to the pub at the old Crown. Now it's like you’ve got rocks in your mouth. And don’t even get me started on the parking down at the coast in the summer.

Rather annoying the new restaurant’s smoke finds its way in, isn’t it? I mean, they’re  next door  and it’s starting to smell like a smoked salmon factory in here.      Honestly, it’s alright when the wind’s not directly on us. But it was a real issue last week when  someone  decided to deep-fry something at 10 in the morning. I swear I could smell it halfway up the road!      Oh, well, there you go. We’ve nothing to complain about here. Didn’t even get the scent last week when we had the three of you over! Not when we were cooking  real  food, like proper mashed potato and fudge My, but I did enjoy that.      Yes, well, I’m not a fan of these sorts of modern businesses creeping up. It used to be a nice place. Quiet. When I was a schoolmaster, everyone knew everyone for miles around. People went out of their way to keep things tidy, for heaven’s sake.      Ah yes, nostalgia, Dad. But I’m not convinced I want to legislate your youth to be my present. Anyway, what do we do with the logs now? We have quite a stash from the winter.      True. I was thinking, maybe store them in the shed. Though I’m not sure if they’ll all fit. If we’re going to outsource our furniture repair to some business out of London, which is what I’ve been told about the new plan for the office, then what use are the logs?      Don’t be so crude! We can continue using the log burner about half the year. It does keep the room warm, especially with this cold wind from over in Scotland coming down.      I don’t even remember the last time the logs were  not  wet. Unless you’re expressing them in a different way. I remember trying to burn some a few months ago and it just fell apart mid-process. You’d think the antique shop down the road had something better to say about log preservation!      Ah yes, the antique shop. My, you remember when it used to sell proper things, not just cat ornaments and dog collars. I do miss the days when one could find a decent head of a Roman bust instead of plastic boxers for pets.      It’s all gone bespoke now. Even the roles in education are being made to sound like belly-dancing to third-level bureaucrats.

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, isn’t it? I was just reading ‘bout it on the Parish Council site, and it seems like they want another ten quid a year off us for some “community improvement fund”. Chuffed if I know what they’re improving exactly. We haven’t even had a new bus stop yet!      Aye, it’s not as if they don’t already take enough from us. With the council tax and the national insurance, it’s like we get paid just to be alive! I was down at the depot the other day, and the bloke there was muttering about buying a house now. Says he’s been looking round the outlying villages, but with the stamp duty what it is, it’s near enough impossible unless you’ve got a pot of money from the pension or something special.      Oh dear, you lot and your taxes and houses! I was just watching a documentary earlier this week about rural areas and how hard it is for people to move in or even get planning permission for a second dwelling. One chap had built a bungalow over twenty years, and it still wasn’t up to code because of some land use rules from the early 2000s. It was like watching a war documentary!      You’re not far off, Lorna. I remember, when I was still working on some of the road schemes around here, there were houses that couldn’t even be connected to mains drainage because of the way they were built. Waste of good property, if you ask me. Now, with all the remote places getting more popular, you’d think they’d grant more flexibility. But no, it’s all red tape and red ink, most likely about nowhere at all.      And the Sat Navs now—juggling what you can do and where you can plug in. I nearly drove into a lake in Lowestoft last month ‘cos the route showed up as “permitted” when it was just a gravel track. Thought I’d achieved something, I did, but ended up with a wheel half off!      Oh that’s nothing. I once got lost with a builder mate on one of those remote lanes near the Broads, and we ended up in this tangle of hedges so dense, you couldn’t see your hat off. He said he got it from the planning office, but that was thirty quid wasted and two hours arguing at the garage.

Rather annoying this new laptop’s being. You’d think for what we paid, it’d be a bit more... robust, wouldn’t ya? Been glitchin’ since I got it, sure enough. An’ this is after I had to leave the old one in warranty!      Ba’t eeny harm now, I suppose. It was well good while it lasted. Almost as good as the fajita sauce from the weekend!      Oh, that was alright! I know you said you were going to Leeds to the rugby this evening, though, but the lad has been specially poorly the past couple of days, so—      I'm not sure we can make it. My poor little one’s ears have been so sticky and he’s just not behaving well at all. D’you think we could maybe get the evening off? It’d be far better for everyone if we’re all well and healthy, wouldn’t it?      Aye, of course we can, don’t you worry about a thing. I’ll give the lads a ring and see if we can arrange a separate catch-up. Bah, rugby’s as much for the company as for the game, anyway. Ba’teeny fun, sure it is.      – Mate, I got a chance, I think I really  can  fix the laptop. We don’t have to go through the warranty hassle again. There’s a few things we can try before giving up.      Ah, that’d be helpful, love. I do appreciate it. Just don’t want to break the thing more. Still, if you’ve had your head in there, then I suppose you know what you’re about!      I had to look it up online and everything. This model is well known for the overheating problem, so I just have to rebalance the fan and replace the thermal compound.      Aye, the technical stuff never was my strong side. I fell for it because it came with a year’s free warranty! Like I thought that would save me from all problems with computers altogether!      Well, let’s hope you don’t have to be swimming in warranty claims for the next go-round. I remember your old one surviving until it was practically prehistoric!      Honestly, it was bloomin’ ancient. But it worked!      And it was good while it lasted!      It was alright for emails and Netflix, sure enough. Might give it to the young fella for the weekend so he can pretend to do homework while watching videos.

Rather than share a text-based response, I request a voice message. I know it's silly, but I’d love to hear your voice properly after this week. Blows! I haven’t slept since we came to stay at your parents’ place. Look at the children—they’re  still  pretending it’s a “Jam and Jelly palace,” and the dog keeps stealing   your auntie’s slippers  .      Lo! I got to draw Nessie last week in art! She’s got long neck and was living in very cold water. Mummy said the monster under the bed is like Nessie, but smaller. Can I wear my sparkly dress to dinner? Grandpa said we are going to visit a monster under the duvet!      Oh, well if the monsters under your duvet and the duvet slippers are all making friends, then let’s just roll with breakfast, bedtime and then dinner dressed up. Maybe a bit of spaghetti and meatballs for the oversized desktop hides, you know? I say we make the most of it and have a proper laugh.      I two, no three! Pie is one and the other two pieces is two plus one… plus… GIRL? Where is the boy who said he loves Lady –?      Slow down, tiger! The fairies have been quite busy these days. Seems their tea party supplies ran out and they stormed your Pikachu homework again. Our little someone here found one of the bulbs from the fairy garden a bit too shiny.      They’d better not be in the way of my handstand! I did  two  last night! Not nearly about Lady Leggings though—she brought a man! She said he is from far away and is very good at making her laugh.      Well if we run out of celebration food, I say we just lay out guest settings for the fairies. Bunting? Check. Pizza? Unspecified. Duvet monsters? Foundation stone. I’ll make a menu out of the cereal boxes as we go. Let’s just see how many sides of toast a little one can eat in half an hour. But serious now—who wants to go on a real-life go-kart on pond life if we ever meet a real one in Scotland? Fish in the pond, Nessie in the box, pizza on the dock?      I want to hold her tail and give her pizza! She can wear my dress and then we’ll both be monsters!

Rather annoying the queue at immigration eh, lad? Thought we’d get sorted before it turned dark.      Nah, no worries, I like queues. Mate, I've been thinkin’ about doing a report on new inventions at school and I bet you lot wouldn't be against a bit of eeny-time holidays, eh?      Ay, I’m all for that, but you’ve got to factor in policy changes and air travel logistics, right? If Steve Jobs was still about, maybe he could’ve solved the queue problem for us!      Tch, leave Steve to sort it out! In my line of work, we rely on supply chains liker than politicians rely on policies. Speaking of inventions, did you hear what’s coming out of food technology now – I read about some new stuff and I think it could be a game-changer for nutrition, even for pregnant mothers.      Mate, you alright? That’s a bit heavy for the first night abroad, innit? Let's get a drink and talk about something more like the weather or the food round here. I heard this place specialises in seafood – not as much as back home in Bolton, but still, there’s something to it!      I love it here! My nan said I should take some photos and upload it to my project blog. She’s all about telling people to travel and see the world. Somewhere like Switzerland, maybe?      Who said anything about Switzerland? Let's not get ahead of ourselves – we're still figuring out what to do with this swimming pool in the accommodation and being able to jump in straight after a curry, eh? Not many about Bolton who’d walk a mile for a pie and chips and then chuck in a swim!      Properly grim! I mean it is a holiday, but I do miss a good Burgundy baked potato from Manchester.      And I do miss the biscuits round here. Oh, I once brought some ginger cookies for a little one I was tending to back in Bolton. He’s doing alright now, by the way. I think it helps to have things from home.      Right, but back on the points we were goin’ on before – if you had a choice, what country would you choose to go to that you haven’t seen yet? Me, I’m thinking about Romania.      Me? I'd go to Canada! I heard it gets real cold there but there’s massive games and stuff.

Rather annoying this new debt collectors, isn't it? Seems they've got forms for everything now. The other day got a letter 'bout some PPI I paid for years ago. I've nearly forgotten about it by now!      Oh, George, you mustn't ignore it. I read een article in the  Sunday Times  about it 'bout a month back. They said thousands of folks got their money back through these claims. Got one from my son, gave me a few records to go through 'bout his mortgage. It was quite a task, but well worth it in the end. You'd fetch the documents from the attic, dear?      What I found strange is how some of these companies set you up in the first place. My niece’s lawyer tried to help her with one back in '12, and I think he turned down a chunk of cash for his troubles. He said it was too much of a headache to chase everyone down after all these years. People’s lives moves on, but these bits of paper stick around!      Well, I suppose I could give the company a ring and listen to their side of it. Like a week to organise the paperwork. Never liked having to deal with banks much—it always ends up in a mix-up. Mind you, I remember my father once borrowed ten guineas and paid it back in a few years. That sort of thing would be unimaginable nowadays, wouldn’t it?      For sure, George. These days it's all emails and forms. That said, I had to sort out a magazine subscription earlier this week—had a mind of its own and kept renewing even after I cancelled it. Staggering how many people are taken in by marketing speak these days.      It's a whole new world for us oldies. Not that I mind staying up to date, mind you—being on a computer gives you the world in your hands. I even did some seeds and plants ordering online the other week. Proper easy, once you get the hang of it!      That’s good, Dorothy. You've always had a green thumb with 'orticultural things. More importantly, have we organised whose turn it is to sing in the church choir next Sunday? They've got go-to pieces on the menu, and our Abbey choir was invited for the Easter line-up, remember?

Rather annoying the new changes in the court procedures, isn't it, Ethel? I always think it's a bit too rigid with all the tick-box stuff these days. Not sure what they think is going to make it more efficient.      Oh yes, well, you know how it is, Margaret. Every time I attend the bench they add   another form   or rule to follow. It seems like they’re complicating things just to have a show of control. Still, I suppose   the intention is to keep things fair and standardised  , for what that’s worth.      I suppose, but it does make things rather slow. I've been grading language exams all week and found myself thinking how the courts are not unlike exams — you follow the rules, you tick the boxes, and the human side can feel a bit lost in the process.      Aye, well, I've often thought of that myself. When I was younger in my early career, you had more room to, you know,   react to people the way they were  . Now it's like, if a person is late, they get written up regardless — even if it was their train breaking down for two hours.      Exactly! And it’s such a shame. I’m at the college preparing new students for ESOL and sometimes it really strikes me how much the system is set up for people already comfortable within it. If someone is already lost, the more rules, the harder it feels.      I suppose that's a problem not just here, then. Some years back, I visited my sisters in   Edinburgh   and even the public transport over there is better, at times, with consideration for delays and the like.      It's true — I’ve been to   Barcelona   twice and the organisation there is unbelieveable to some of our standards over here. But, you know, I'm not sure that's always about expenditure. I think a lot of it is about   attitude and how people understand service  . We could learn from others.      Perhaps. And I suppose a little more investment wouldn't go amiss. My grandchild is going to university this year and it's all hands to go in various directions — loans, savings, and   beggars can’t be choosers  .      Oh, what a relief it must be at your age to be helping out, though. I’d love to be able to   do that easily   myself, but I have two young ones at home still and the education costs add up.

Rather than money, Mateo, I think happiness comes from moments like these—us being together, having a cup of tea and some quiet time after the kids run around like they’ve been chased by a dragon! What do you think, Georgia?      I think happy is when mummy gives me eenie meenie miney mo to sing—and when I get to draw with the dolly that’s a prince. A prince is like a king but not a king, right, Mummy?      Yeah! And happy is when I don’t fall off the bike or the swing. Daddy says I’m getting good enough not to fall anymore. Can I get a marble out of the jar for being brave like that?      Later, darling. But you know what? I was just thinking, the more I think about money and happiness—like if we had a million pounds or something—it’s not really about that. It’s more about what money  allows  us to do. Like, if we had more spare time to do the things we like, that would make us happy.      Like going to the park every day?      And getting real ice cream, not just on special days!      Exactly. But even without lots of money, we can still be happy, and sometimes it’s the small things. For example, Georgia loves rhyme and rhythm—why don’t you make up a rhyme about happiness while we sip our tea?      Okay—here goes: “Happy is smiling, happy is fun, happy’s a teddy, happy’s a sun. Happy comes when you sing and rhyme, happy is when there’s not a line!”      I can do better than that! “Happy vibes and shiny coins, happy rides and jelly moons. Happy days and treats for kings, happy hearts in happy strings!”      Oh, that’s quite good, Mateo. And it rhymes perfectly. You two have such nice rhythm. I always tell your teachers how lucky I am to see the world through you.      Mummy knows the best songs too.      Well, let’s keep singing and laughing—and maybe dream a bit too. Because even if we don’t have millions, if we have each other and these little bits of joy, we’re already pretty rich. What do you say?      Yeah! We have the best lives!      We are rich with happiness!      Exactly. And isn’t that something worth singing about? Or rhyming about? Or just giggling over like we’re doing now?

So do you reckon I should go into engineering or software stuff? My dad keeps on about it ‘cos he worked in design and all that.      I think you’d be good at engineering, like, building stuff with computers or robots or something. But you gotta get good at math for that. I'm thinking more about investment and stuff with the markets. I reckon people are going to need that with how China’s taking off.      Investment? Like, financial stuff? Man, I wouldn’t know where to start. Maths is my weakness. Didn’t even want to do A-level maths.      Nah, it’s not all about heavy maths at first, you can do some courses like business studies or economics. You learn how money flows around the world. And China, mate – they’re building massive hospitals, schools, tech firms. They’re investing in everything, and sooner or later, we’re going to have to invest in them if we want to be part of the big picture.      Wait, you mean the UK should invest money into China?      Not exactly the UK as a whole, I mean people, companies, even students like us. It’s like with the internet – in ten years, the top tech firms will probably all be Chinese. So if we invest early, maybe we can make something out of it.      But how do you even start investing? Do you need a lot of money?      No, not really. There are apps and platforms you can use to invest small amounts. I’ve got an account with something called robo-investing. It’s like an AI that does the hard work for you. Kinda about how I’m thinking about the future. Instead of just building something, I want to be part of the ideas that are going to make money globally.      You’re so confident, mate. I just like the idea of inventions. I did this project last term on patents. I’d love to make something that people use worldwide.      That’s cool. You could even combine that with what I'm talking about – invent something, patent it, and then do tech-focused investing. Like, you don’t even have to pick one or the other. There's so much overlap now.      Maybe. But I dunno how anyone gets that far. I mean, I can barely balance what little pocket money I get.      It starts small, man.

Rather skip the new bar at base of the resort, too smoky for me. Felt like a pub in the snow, really. You tried it yet?      Oh, yeah! It is a bit over the top, the acoustics were dreadful, like shouting to make yourself heard. Right mess when there’s more drinks involved than conversation. But the people there were all so nice, a proper community vibe from what I could tell.      Oh aye, I caught a bit of that atmosphere when I was served. Still, I’d rather get the kids warmed up with hot chocolate before we head back up the slopes.Managed to book onto the half-day session with Rob for tomorrow, you fancy joining? He’s got that new skier group starting at 10, works well for the kids.      That sounds grand. I did actually pop by the ski school yesterday and asked about private tuition if need be, but with a group in the morning being half-price, it might as well suit the lads. Should save the wallet, too.      Definitely, and it’s less pressure for the wee ones if they’re not one to one. I only thought, since Rob’s from here and speaks English, it may be a little more relaxed. I’m hoping the twins won’t get skintired and actually take to the equipment today. One of them nearly faced planted into a pine tree at first attempt.      Laughed so hard I nearly missed someone going full wipe-out on the chairlift! Children are resilient, give ’em a chance with hotter cocoa, and they’ll skiddle down the slopes like Olympians next thing! We should take the camera out today, make sure to capture a proper gold medal run.      Oh yes, definitely. We could cap it with that dip in the pool later, the one with the view. My sister texted earlier—had no idea she’d passed here last year. Said it was a bit of slap-up event but insisted I ought to come meet her for a little chat if time permits. She’s in some yellow cabin at the side of the hotel with lunches delivered right to the door—course I took the liberty of bringing you along, of course.      Oh, goody! I’d love to see her again. Always appreciated your family, even in the snow, it's like being back in the Midlands with the proper conversation and cake.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, love? These old strings—no sooner have we strung up the racket, and they're slipping out of the frame like minnows from a fishing net. I told you we shouldn’t have gone for those cheaper tennis-string substitutes at the pound shop again.      Aye, I understand the budget issue, but if we're going to pitch this racket repair business—what with all the retired folk in this area and primary schools needing affordable replacements—the string stability is worth the extra. We can't be having the children playing with rackets that come undone every five minutes.      Still, I made a note last week—try using cable ties around the stressed corners like that Mycroft chap did on Dragons’ Den. Tighten the knots just behind the shuttlecock impact zones, and they seem to hold. A bit heavy-handed for secondary school, but the younger ones won’t mind, no doubt. I've been thinking, though—what if we angled the strings ever so slightly more, like the way those ships in a fleet align? Tighten that diagonal tension and it might hold.      You're using 'fleet' as in warships, I assume? Or is that another idiom I’ve not caught up with?      Oh, come now! You must know the meaning, Horace. Like a line of ships sailing in tight formation. All moving as one through the Pacific. It's a metaphor for consistency and control, which are just what we need in racket stringing. And regarding the secondary schools, maybe suggest we use a lighter gauge string for the top half and a thicker one for the lower third—compromise between durability and flexibility.      Interesting... though marketing the idea will need clear terminology. We can’t be standing there in the staff room at St. Wilfrid's and have the untrained eye mixing up the tension zones. And speaking of marketing, what about the pricing? We can offer a discount for schools if it's a bulk order, can't we? Slide pricing down from 5 quid per repair to 3.50 if they commit to 20 rackets a term.      Perfect. That's where the profit comes in. Now, dear man— careful with the scissors! —let me tidy that cut you just did.      Sorry, Darlin'. That blooming lobe caught your hair and you felt it before I did. There we are—tidy now.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracin’ the garden, it makes a body think... got me rather nostalgic, I must say.      Oh, Alistair, it always suns like that when the cherry trees are in bloom, like the one by the old chapel. I rememb' when the lads 'ad me painting it for the village arts group, aye? A right laugh we had, sticky brushes and all.      It's interesting you mentioned art, Nana. I was just going through some of your old paintings last week – you did a brilliant miniature of the brook near Costessey, didn't you, Dad?      My word, you did find that one! Had it tucked away in the wardrobe, I reckon. D'you know, I used to paint little watercolours of the farmland and the old church when I was younger. Not much happened in Costessey in them days, but you learned to find beauty in the quiet bits.      That you did, love. I do tell you, being a childminder, I put that theory into practice. Taught the little ones to draw what they saw in the garden – not just stickers and little animals, but the way the light filtered through the trees. True art, not just noise and colour.      That's quite inspiring, honestly. In my lectures on visual culture, we don't talk enough about those kind of personal, almost therapeutic approaches to art. Most of my students are obsessed with trends and galleries. You lot made something meaningful out of your surroundings and your lives.       Sips his tea thoughtfully.  I daresay art isn't about standing on pedestals and watching the world from thar. It's about cap'n that beauty you see in the day-to-day, like the way the herbs dance in the wind or the quiet look in your dog’s eyes. A true artist, they don't need a salary or a degree.      I couldn't agree more, Dad. One of the things I try to pass onto my students is that idea of grounding art in personal history and location – it makes it more meaningful, something they can connect with.      Mm, that's right. It wasn’t so long ago I saw a young boy making a little clay statue of his puppy by the fire. No training, no lessons, just pure emotion and love. That’s the kind of art that comes from the heart.      Aye, and that’s the kind we should all remember.

Honestly, I swear some of the girls I work with are like glue sticks—sticky, and they just  stick  to everything, including problems they don’t need to be part of. I mean, last week, I was trying to process some project timelines and Sarah—  the one who can’t make a sandwich without asking if it’s the “right” way  —decided to basically analyse all my desk choices. Like, I had a coffee cup next to a pen, and suddenly, it was a   crisis of organisational moral integrity  .      Oh, don’t even get me started. I’ve literally had patients who  managed  to seem worse in the morning because they knew how stressed I looked. My colleague, Rachel, had meltdowns left and right this week over how the clinic coffee machine wasn’t “warm enough.”   Warm enough?   It’s either hot enough to burn you or it doesn’t count.      Haha, yeah, and I’m not saying I don’t get stressed, but the amount of energy people put into nonsense that doesn’t matter… Like, today I cleaned my kitchen—properly—then sat down for 20 minutes and   joked with my cat   on the floor. Then, by 7, it looked like a war zone again.      Oh, that’s  exactly  the issue! We don’t clean to  stay  clean. We clean to   procrastinate the homework or the email we actually don’t want to write.   Like, I cleaned the entire bathroom last night, then sat scrolling through the internet for   two hours   and still didn’t finish that patient feedback form.      Ugh, I know! I’m the   queen of starting a job and then immediately doing 100 other things that shouldn’t take time but do.   Maybe I’ll do something productive  next  week.      Yeah, that’s always the plan. I’m going to make my famous procrastination schedule this weekend. It starts with cleaning the kettle.      Let me know if it works. I’ll add   bitching about girls who overcomplicate things   and delivering a rant about how the adjective “girl” can go from empowering to infantilising in   five seconds flat depending on context.        Honestly, maybe I’ll start a support group. “Women in Service Professions Tired of Being Thought of as Organisational Incompetent by Default.” It’ll start right here in this kitchen with overcooked pasta and venting about everything else that’s not work.        Count me in.   Water's on.

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses my name. I know it's not that hard— Claudia , not  Cassandra  or  Claire .      You’re lucky they don’t miss  Steve . I bet you half the townspeople call me Stu or Dave depending on the day. Or just ‘Sir’ if they're being polite.      At least you don’t have to deal with my caffeine addiction. Oh, and don’t get me started on my late-night wine habit. I swear when the working day is done, I just  need  that glass of red even if I only had two meetings.      That’s what I like about you, love. You’ve got enough common sense not to wake up early, but you still manage to get everything done and look presentable. Some of us take longer for coffee just to forget what we breakfast on.      And here I thought I was just being lazy. Honestly, I thought being qualified gave me some sort of intelligence bonus. But I still can’t work out the printer, and I can barely instal software without needing you.      You’re human. You’ve got more brainpower in your little finger than I have in my whole head. You just apply it – at work, at home, with me. I just follow the step-by-step guides and hope I don’t delete anything vital.      You don’t seem to live in fear of modern life though. I get so anxious when my phone dies or the Internet goes down. I wonder what it’s like to have a life without screens and being ‘always connected’?      You know, I did live like that for a few years. Spent time in Morocco—mainly cooking for some remote research team. No data, barely a signal. The most ‘connected’ I was was to the generator and the chickens. To be honest, I think it did me more good than harm. It gave me a different perspective.      That sounds mad. I can barely live 24 hours without being irritated by someone else’s take on Feminism on social media. I’m not even going to start telling you what I read this week.      go on then. But let me warn you—I’m still hungover.      Hopefully not because of the boxset binging again. Okay, fine—for instance, have you noticed how some people think calling someone ‘independent’ is the moral high ground, but to me, it just sounds like overcompensation when they’re actually alone all the time?

Rather skip the queue at the café, love. Thought we could do a bit of a picnic with the sandwiches I got out of the fridge earlier. Otherwise poor Em and Freddie will be stared at by the queue behind us for far too long.      Yeah, well, the café was full when we came in anyway, Mum. The one they had at the other end of the farm… not this one with the cow sculpture by the entrance. We waited like ten minutes and then Freddie screamed because a cow came walking past.      It hit me in the leg! That cow made me spill my chips, Mum!      Oh, no! You poor thing. You must have had a My turkey leg must have dropped everywhere. I left it on the back seat, didn’t I? D’you pick it up in the car? Or was it in the handbag?      He doesn’t have a handbag, Mom. And he was licking the remains of his sausages on the spare wrapping when we came to the car. It was revolting, if I’m honest.      Well, it’s their first time at a real working farm, Em. Let them be a bit messy. I remember when I got to come here at – what was it, five? – and I swam in a huge mud bath and cried because of the ticks later.      Oh, don’t talk about ticks now. Our trousers have got chicken feathers and hay in them. And unfortunately a bit of cow slobber on the hems. Also, I think the tramp from near the pig pens used our bag to sleep on.      Right. So the picnic it is. I found this lovely mix of thyme and mozzarella slices yesterday. Em, you’re a big girl, you could probably cope with the herbs, yes? And I’ve got some tomato slices ready too.      Can I have a bag of those microwave chips we always get at home? The ones with the stick on the side you twist.      Not with lunches, Freddie. They ruin your appetite for proper food. You know you don’t get any nice bits like roast chicken or crumpets in them. But if you promise to eat your picnic first, I might just tickle you into it.      And what about after? The DVD at home? The one with the koi pond in the garden? I know Freddie always belly-laughed at the guy in the speedo doing the diver award at the end.

Rather annoying I could've got better wool fer cheaper at the craft shop in town, but nooo —  had  to go with this fluffier stuff off the internet! Honestly, it’s overpriced and it’s probably £20 more than I needed to spend on a pair o’ baby booties een!      [laughs]   But Ay, they’re  beautiful , don’t you think? That lilac’s got that  sheen  to it — makes it look bespoke or summat. You’ve outdone yerself this time. Y’know, Mummy’s friend saw the pic yeh posted and  insisted  her niece is the spittin’ image of Ellie Goulding.      Oh, left’s a right laugh! I ain’t knittin’ these for no celebrity twerp — just ‘cause the little darling’s got a giggle like breakfast, no doubt about it.      Well, e’s prob’ly gonna be famous, given the lot she’s got round ’er. Half that family’s got talent, if y’ask me. Y’heard that shortlisted dramme as their uncles and aunties were performin’ fer the local arts festival? Mate, it was bawling material.      True enough. Though I think it was the comedy sketch — the one where the Olympics were run by ducks and e’s was the opening ceremony! That had me in roars. Our bleedin’ Prime Minister dress’d as a mallard!      [laughs] Yeh’d better not say that too loud in here — Paul’s mum’s  obsessed  with the Olympics and about to knit up a whole team of bobbies in the same green as the vibes they showed on TV last summer.      Doesn’t sound uncommendable, to be fair, ‘cos they look like bobbies. Though I’d sooner stick with the baby booties. I’d told Paul ‘get me some art print for the wall’ when I redecoratin’, and e suggested  alphabet art  — y’know, with proper paintings of the letters?      That sounds like  that  kind of telly shop the bloke with goenvironment goes on — all about ersatz art and real ceramics!      Exactly! It’s the telly that gave it to ‘im. Now e wants me to get bespoke 3D letters, in some high-end finish, like… like  glass  or somethin’. ‘Posh and modern’, e says!      Fair play to ‘im — yer flat  does  need a little romantic magic, even if e is gettin’ a bit of the telly sheen on ’im! But wot’s the plan fer Easter? Still them egg hunts last year, with the personalised chocolate eggs with names carved on ‘em?

Rather than going up The phố Museum today, I was thinking we could catch one of them 3D films at the IMAX, eh love?      Hmm, I've seen a few of them 3D films, truth be told. Some of ’em are alright, but I don’t eeny mind a bit of culture every now an’ again. What about the museum in Trafalgar Square?      That one's a bit posh, ain't it? I know you don’t mind me saying, but the last time you called it "boring as a dead squirrel". Besides, I’ve heard they’ve got a new cinema with 4D effects now, where you can feel the wind and all sorts. It might be a bit of a different experience.      D’you think it’s worth the money? We had an alright pension this month, but if we’re going to splash it about, I’d like a bit in return. And I hear the trains aren’t running on time at all. We could be stuck for hours.      Come on, love, it’s a Sunday afternoon! If we miss a train to Waterloo, we’ll be on the next one. It’s not like we’re workin’ then. And I’ve looked at the buses as well, just in case. If it really is a pain, we can always catch the black taxi—dear God, I haven’t done that since I was a girl in Liverpool in the ‘70s!      That sounds romantic, but I’d preferably not get flummoxed about transport. What time does it start? If we leave now, we can be there before it about five. I hear the film’s a bit of a space adventure—cracking for a sunny Sunday and not too bogged down with kids.      That’s right. My sister ‘phoned me last week and said it's perfect for folk our age. She reckons it gives you something to think about. And I dunno about you, but I could stick a few hours looking at stars again. Liverpool’s skies always been a bit cloudy, and I do miss the stars.      Aye, I can agree with that. That an’ goin’ on them old Liverpool trams again. But I think I’ll line in for the 3D cinema today, long as we don’t get strung up in London traffic again. I’ve been there once, and I’m not keen to repeat it.

Rather annoying, though—right? I mean, I remember back in London, it felt like real Christmas spirit kicked off the moment November ended. You’d see the decorations go up in the shops, and everyone was getting into it. Not to mention those big, busy pubs at the weekend. But out here in China, aside from a few glittery shopping malls, it’s just quiet.      Oh aye, I know what you mean. Manchester was always a proper Christmas town. The Grand was packed, you couldn’t light a fire in the pubs for the amount of people, and the Christmas lights came on with a big fair in the square. Here? Well, it's the same every year. You get the odd Westerner turkey dinner, and that's about it.      I’m half tempted to just chuck some decorations and a bit of mulled wine in an Airbnb for us and a few mates. I mean, we’ve got this pool table here... I could throw a bit of a non-traditional, slightly indulgent kind of festive do. What do you reckon?      Sounds a laugh, mate. Might be one of the most Christmassy things I've done in ten years abroad. As long as you don’t play carols over a karaoke machine—I still cringe at that one-off Royal Caribs gig I did with the other lecturers back in 2013.      Oh, I remember that! You did the  When I’m 64  one, right? And you nailed it. It just felt oddly appropriate at the time, what with the tropical setting and all.      Aye, best man, best song. I about wet myself laughing after I finished. But the thing is, I was thinking—would Nancy be up for coming? She’s got that new movie out, right?      Oh,  Revive the Moments ? Yeah, passed it around with the rest of the group. I saw a few snippets, it’s very intense. Strong stuff for a debut. She’s crackling good as Mei. Though I’m not sure how many of us will be able to sit through the full thing over Christmas night—it’s  two and a half hours .      Fair enough. But it would be good to catch up with her properly. She’s been out in Canada for filming since, I dunno, what, April?      Something like that. Mind you, we could mix it with the dinner. You know, start off with the film, then over to the dinner—just like a little screening.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, who reads a 200-word rant about a £2 coffee and thinks they’ll get anywhere?      Honestly, I've had people scream about “slushy £2 coffee” like I personally grind the beans with my bare hands. I’m just glad the place  I  work at isn’t open on weekends.      Oh I’ve had worse online stuff. Once, this woman wrote a full story about how she watched me trip over someone’s leg and blame it on me. It was me chase a hot cake.      Right, because of course you  chose  to drop someone's almond milk croissant onto their cardigan that day, no?      Yeah well, you try working 14 hours and keeping your feet beneath you when every single customer is a drama magnet looking for a free latte. Wait, does Margate actually need this many coffee shops?      I hear the new place that opened near the beach is dead posh. All marble tables and that—vibe’s just, like, inappropriate for a place where I can see the sea.      It’s wild how much design stuff they put on TikTok. I mean, yeah, got to make it look good for the ‘gram, but not least, because the  sea view  is enough.      Honestly, I considered putting up some ‘gram boards at my place, but then I was like, “Why dress this up when it’s just a place to buy oddly sour pastries and hotter than hell tea?”      But look at Margate now! It’s not just the surfers and the old people anymore. It’s a whole Renaissance of artsy kids and vibes.      Yeah, that place you told me about—what’s it called? The one with the ‘industrial-chic’ vibe. I passed it last weekend. It’s open on a Thursday? That was bloody nice.      I mean, I sort of want to open one as well. Maybe as a side business. Not with lunches, keep it simple—you know, like, grab a coffee, skip the theatrical.      Maybe you can set go for a map of cafes if you start one. Just don’t expect me to not tripping over your bench.      And what your croissants would be missing out on.      Oh I'm cheap with the butter anyway.      Same with your ‘Signature’ pronoun croissant.      I miss when I could make a buttercream mushroom and get applause.      I did not need to know that.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't grown anything at all in that garden yet, just a few failed attempts. I got the raspberry bushes in first, but they're not doing much at all.      Why? Do we not water them enough?      No, we do, but the soil doesn't seem to be very good. I reckon it's not as productive as most. Maybe I should test it.      Maybe we can plant some vegetables as well, like carrots. We can give the ones we grow to the gerbils or the garden birds.      That's a lovely idea. I've got the seeds, actually, in the shed. But what do you think, Marco?      I think I'd like to try growing them, but I don't know the first thing about planting them, to be honest.      Maybe I can help. I did some in school at the cookery club.      Oh, so did we once, yes. It was loads of fun, if I remember rightly. We had to write it up, too.      Hmmm, I might go on a walk down the trail by the river then tomorrow. It's so lovely – very peaceful – and I can check and see if the bird eggs have hatched yet.      You always find the most interesting things in the garden. What kind of bird is it?      I think it's a whitethroat. I definitely need to identify them properly, though. So I can give it back to the nest if I need to, or make sure I don't meddle.      That’s very kind of you. I like stories about baby animals.      Yeah, I remember when we had the gerbil. That was the best time ever.      And it was a bit of a mess, too, I might add. All over the floor when he ran out one day. Marco, you’ll remember being sent out to chase him with a broom and a whiske-broom!      I did run with it like a maniac!      Anyway, enough of that. Just one question before I finish my meal. How was your exam today, Daniel?      It was all right, I suppose. I think I messed up on the algebra part, though.      Oh no, not over this one. We spent ages on it last week. I can go over it with you again, if you like.      Thanks, but I think I just need to accept it and move on. Still, it won’t count for much in the end, I don't think.

Rather annoying when the supermarket’s out of stock, isn’t it? I was just trying to get some pears for the crumble this weekend. I’m hosting Claire and her daughter, you know. Thought I’d make it fancy with a nice dessert.      Oh, that sounds lovely. Got plans for the holidays? I meant to ask you earlier. I reckon it’s about time we all chilled a bit. A Sunday lunch or something? If you’ve got details sorted, I’ll make sure to leave work early. We can even pop to the shops before.      That’d be brilliant, Sharon. I’ve even got a voucher for a nice pub in the area, only twenty quid for two courses. Thought it’d be a nice treat after the usual takeaways. And I’m picking up the tab, too, since I’m the hostess. Might even invite Amanda — do you remember her?      Oh yes! She still smokes, does she not? And ever since her operation, she’s looking for a bit of help once in a while. I’ve been giving her hand with the shopping and a few bits about the house — quite a nice soul, really.      Oh dear, smoking again, is it? I remember when all the young ones used to knock on the door with their fags and ask if they could have a smoke. I’d nearly had a heart attack! Anyway, enough of that. Last night, I had the grimmest time at the hairdressers. They gave me a snip a bit too close, left me looking like a cartoon character — a pink cartoon at that. And what’s this I hear about your eyebrows, Laura? Not plucked out, I hope?      No, don’t worry, they’re doing fine. I’ve been doing them myself now, really it is a lot easier in the privacy of your own home. I watched a YouTube tutorial — much better than some person with bad eyesight and minimal talent holding scissors too close to the skin.      I reckon your mum would’ve had a go at you for doing that! Used to do lunches for a couple of the elderly in the village too, back when she was still about. Said it was a nice way to keep in touch with the community and help those who couldn’t go out much.      Oh, she always had a big heart, your mum.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, weaning’s a bit of a faff when you're trying to balance everything else. I remember when your mother weaned  me , she’d have a mad schedule of pureeing veg and timing the feeds. But at least you can get those handy pouches these days if you're stuck for time.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve only just started with Milo, so every meal feels like a new experiment. It was easier planning the childminder’s schedule than navigating the timing of mealtimes, but the formula has been specially chosen like, I had to make  sure  it was iron-fortified and hippo-proof.      Ha, "hippo-proof" — I like that. Probably holds up against the occasional floor-feed too, which I think is the norm at this stage, darling. What about you’re thinking breakfast, lunch and then... well, dinner with a bit of repurposed lunch. Don’t tell the fussy ones, though. Also, the grandparents offered to help out this week with the twins, which is a massive relief. They might take two or three DVDs as childcare and credit and expect a thank-you note in braille.      Oh, that’s brilliant. I’m so grateful. I’m meeting a few mums for a playgroup on Thursday — the baby café at St Mary’s? You know the one. It's got that gorgeous outside area where we can all sit out with babies in prams and coffee in mugs, like it's a bloody conference or something.      Yes, I remember the place well. That used to be your ballet club’s venue before it was refurbed. Do you think you’re going to the sign language classes this week? I’ve been meaning to ask you. I know you mentioned you signed up a few weeks back to do basic communication for parents and toddlers?      I did actually book onto the class on the Thursday afternoons — you know the sessions start soon, I think it’s a small taster course first, and then a full 12-week course with lunches and a little certificate at the end. I thought it would be easier trying to communicate with Milo and helping him express his needs even before he really gets speech started.      Oh, brilliant! That’s a clever move. It'll help with empathy as well when he can say “I’m upset” with fluency instead of crying like the sky is falling down every time he drops his rattle.

Rather skip the new bar in Norwich. You know what I mean. I was just reading about it in  The Norfolk Chronicle —something about it being more gadgets than ambiance, if you ask me. No, this is far more peaceful. Just us, the fens, and the hills in the distance. Got a bit of a view from this path today, didn’t we?      Yeah, I’ve been meaning to say. The walk out this way has taken on a new kind of charm, hasn’t it? Especially with the way the sun catches the fields during autumn. The hills aren’t really hills, like, in the grand scheme of things—certainly no comparisons to the Lake District or anywhere in Wales—but they do look rather dignified from up here.      I think part of their magic is precisely that. I mean, the history of these hills is far older than our country. They’re just there—quiet and watchful. Reminds me a bit of the Roman roads and settlements in the area, didn’t they use the natural contours to their advantage?      Definitely, yes. There’s a place up near Thetford called the Weg to Walsoken. It was an ancient trackway, and it follows the natural high ground of the fens. I remember reading about it in one of your lecture notes last year. Thought it was fascinating. You weren’t the only one, by the way—students were quite taken with the concept of hills as both geographic and historical waypoints.      Oh, I read about a recent dig near here, a Bronze Age flint scatter at a site in the parish of West Row. Not much has been excavated, but it highlights how even our little corner of the world has stories to tell. It makes you think—every village in Norfolk has layers beneath it that we know barely a fraction of. These hills aren’t just the backdrop, they’re part of the narrative.      It does make you consider how the landscape is a living archive, doesn’t it? With every field, every tumulus, every brook, you’re standing on centuries of human interaction. And with that, a kind of responsibility to understand and respect the land. Even just walking through it now with you, I feel a bit more in tune with it.      That’s one of the reasons I love being out here. It’s not just a walk—it’s a conversation with history.

Rather skip the new Marvel one eh? I've seen six already. I know who's gonna kill 'em... got the big villain reveal all sussed already, eh? Not saying I've seen all of 'em, but… you can see it coming like a lorry on the motorway.      Aye, I understand the sentiment. But mate, if it's not all self-serving, a bit of popcorn fluff once in a while helps. I’ve barely seen a film since last year’s lockdown. Work’s been grinding hard, mate. Funny how being a consultant suddenly means you’re responsible for everything like, literally, from teleportation to tractor transformers.      That’s Pete for you, always one turkey short of a dinner! The lad got put on this ridiculous project, some environmental impact assessment for a new housing estate. The funny bit? Half the team is cyclists, uni types who think they’re saving the world by biking to work. They all get in each other’s way, and then blame the local roads for not having a cycle lane. Good for a laugh, though.      Oh, I’ve dealt with impacts assessments in the land remediation world. It’s all numbers, graphs, and bloody consultants charging three quid for a cup of tea. Tell him to take a knife to it: cut the waffle and get it done. But yeah, the cycling lot… don’t get me started. Silly daft lads wearing lycra like it’s some kind of super suit. I saw one the other day weaving past a delivery van like it was a race—piece of toast is what he looked like.      Aye! Look, as someone who manages a corpus of transcribed conversation for a living, the thing that’s fascinating is how most of it is just filler. Like “erm”, “ah,” and “you know?” Maybe we’re all just making up for the fact we’ve got nothin’ interesting to say. Bit depressing, innit?      Sounds like a bit of a dead-eyed job. I could stick being technical, but words… they feel like they’re always trying to catch up with the thoughts you had five minutes ago. Still, at least you get something tangible out of it.      Mm, usually. I like patterns though. Speech patterns, word usage. It’s interesting, really. Although the other bloke on the team said to me the other day, “You must’ve been obsessed with dictionaries as a kid,” and I said yeah,

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The daffodils in the hedgerows... It's rather heartening how quickly the countryside comes back to life in spring.      Yes, I can't help but smile at the sight of them. They’re a sign that it’s beginning to thaw mentally as well as physically, you know? Makes me think about all the work on cash crops that I read about this morning before we left.      Oh, what did you think of the one we discussed in the lecture last week? The one about shifting from subsistence to commercial farming in East Africa. I couldn’t help but think about how important the local supply chains are for both the economy and the environment.      Exactly. I was going back over some examples from the Guardian Economics section too, and I think it's fascinating how even in cash-crop economies, traditional agricultural knowledge plays such a vital role. It’s not just about yield figures — it’s about planting the right crop at the right time based on seasonal rhythms that have been learned over generations.      Oh yes, I’d say that takes special appreciation if you’re not from that region. I’ve actually been reading more in German on this topic for my own work — it feels like the way languages shape how we think about economic systems is something people still underestimate.      You mean like the German term  Gemeinschaft ? It's got a very different meaning from, say, 'community' in English. It reflects a deeper sense of shared responsibility and identity. I can definitely see how that would influence how a society approaches economics.      Precisely. Though, there's also a balance to be struck. I sometimes wonder if the English tendency to take efficiency to an almost religious level can lead to devaluing that interconnected way of thinking. But then again, I suppose the market here in the UK does create its own kind of resilience.      Well, as long as we don’t lose sight of sustainability, I suppose. Speaking of resilience, did I tell you about that time I followed a group of young farmers trying to introduce organic legumes into traditional cash crops? Some of them were resistant at first, but once they saw the environmental and long-term economic benefits, it was like a lightbulb went off.      That’s interesting, I might need to look into that for my upcoming paper.

Rather annoying I couldfit in the Angel o’ the North on me day off. D’ye know how many parking nutternancies they’ve got around there?      Oh, yeah, it is a bit chaotic. Got stuck in a lay-by off the A1 for an hour, like it was a private car-park or somfink!      Sounds right grim! I’ve bin lookin’ at flats nearby, tho’. But if you’re moving about, you’re better off gettin’ a prime location than a top view if you spend half your day looking for the bloody road in, you know?      Good point, love. I was thinkin’ if I book one of them viewing appointments I can sort out the flat as well as the early start for the Angel today. Would probably save on bailin’ up at a B&B.      Mate, I can pop along with thee, take the other vehicle. I’ve got sommat of a testin’ schedule at work today anyway. ‘Sides, might be a good chance to kill someone at tennis in your spare time!      Hahaha, yeah, let’s not make it awkward for me again like that Cheltenham match — I  thought  I’d seen it all about ref calls until you pulled the "umpire touch the grass" card on me!      Guilty as charged. I've got it down to a dark art now. My sister ‘ardly speaks to me since. All I said was "Good luck at the new job" before she mentioned how my comments had brought shame to the family!      Blooming good as. D'you fancy a quick game later? 'S a new club near the flat I’m lookin’ at — proper green grass, not tark! Maybe get the lads in too?      If it ain’t too far, yeah. Just let me finish this report on the client site — I’ve had to modify the specs at the last minute for a conservation unit in one of them old industrial builds, like some sort of architect/designer crossover horror!      Right, well, if you can’t make it, I’ll be at the viewing today.

Rather annoying the new developments in Peterborough aren't they, Sarah? I was just reading about that case involving that celebrity and the geese. You remember that music star? Some kind of dispute over where the geese were landing. Not quite sure why the bird got involved!      Yeah, I saw that on TV last week. It was ridiculous really. Someone had to report them because they apparently scared a few children in a park or something. Honestly, I thought wildlife was supposed to be a good thing.      Geese and people never did get on too well in Peterborough. I remember when I was a girl, the geese would come down the river in flocks. It was like a carpet of grey. You could hear them a mile off, honking away, just like they do now. But nowadays, I think the world is upside down with rules for everything. Cats on leads, breakfasts at 6am – next thing you know, the geese might get permits to fly!      Well, I suppose people do get wound up about their spaces these days, don’t they? Particularly around the parks. Anyway, speaking of geese, did I tell you, my kids set up this tiny watching thing during lockdown? They started keeping track of local birds. Geese weren’t really on the list, but one swan turned up and created the biggest commotion.      Swans are iconic, aren’t they? And so proud. Our garden here at the house is also filled with birds. Magpies, blue tits, and occasionally a starling. But the geese? No luck.      I used to feed the birds most mornings about forty years ago. Just a few breadcrumbs from the buttered loaf. The geese would come down and take it all. Not like now, everything is plastic and fluff-like to the wildlife, they say. Maybe they’d come for something more real.      You know, I was thinking about migration the other day. How do the little ones know where to go? Like, do they just follow the old ones?      They do! They have this instinct, passed down through generations, something to do with stars and the Earth's magnetic field. But I think it's getting more difficult with so many lights and high-rises in their path.      Oh yes, your lot with the latest developments have blocked out the stars. We had one in our backyard once, a strange goose that came from Denmark I expect.

Rather annoying when a kid’s got a cold and they grumble everything they eat. We had that with Hal... got to the point she’d reject even apple puree. I swear, someone would have had to offer it in cash value to get her to take a bite!      Yeah, I'm assuming she liked the chicken. It was the first time he tried it.      Oh, right, but he's so fussy isn’t he? Like, bless him, he's just a baby, but you can practically set your watch by when he turns his nose up at meat... like, literally, even if it's chicken. I swear he's out to make my life hell in terms of what he'll eat. Still, his mummy’s a qualified nutritionist, so I’d assumed things would be easier. I think he turned down a piece of banana once by the way...      Oh I know! He has a bit in his face when he refuses anything. You can just see the drama happening. Also, the grizzling is immense. I mean, it's not loud per se, but it takes forever to sort out anything. It’s like trying to get a grumpy toddler to go on a walk. Doesn’t work unless it feels like the best idea.      I feel you. My sister had a similar thing with the baby. Now don’t get me wrong, I find her helpful in general, but every time we’d go out for food someone would have an opinion on the recipe or the temperature of the yogurt. I had a point where I had to whisper things like, “Can’t be arsed with the dietary education today, thanks.”      Ahh I love your bluntness. We were at our wits' end last weekend. Hal wasn’t eating and I was trying to decide whether to cook or not. But I realized I just didn’t want her expressing herself on food. The battle at mealtimes would strip a grown woman of all happiness. I ended up just giving in and getting her some shop-bought custard creams. Let the toddler have space!      At least the chocolate took the edge off. Still, I’m a bit worried. I told my sister that go-to plan on snacks wasn’t going to hold up for long, and obviously dentists would not enjoy it. But it was either that or arguing about taste all night.

So do you ever just lie awake at night and think, like, what the hell am I even doing with my life?      All the time. I’ve had these moments where I wonder if this is it. Just cranking out emails and sorting paperclips for the rest of my days. I mean, I  am  a full-time admin assistant and if someone had told me that at 23 I'd be sorting stationery in West Sussex I'd have said, “So what?”      Know what you mean. I do this production control job, but honestly, half the time I just wander around the warehouse trying to convince people that a missing widget is not, in fact, a catastrophe.      You’ve got to be kidding. It’s like working in chaos half the time, isn’t it? I think I’d lose my mind if I was surrounded by manufacturing gigabytes of breakfast cereal boxes every day.      I’m lucky at least I’m not tracking desktop hides, you know? I mean, I still feel like I’m walking a tightrope, but at least I can say I’ve got a postgrad degree.      Me too, by the way. I did a masters in communications. Now I write meeting minutes. It's absurd – but it's also fairly real, isn’t it? You study for years, and boom – here you are, making sure the tea machine is working and the meeting room isn’t booked double.      It’s also weird because you read articles like, “20 Things You Should Be Doing by 29”, and you think, “Oh no, I’ve  definitely  done none of those.”      And you’re the only one? I once had a mentor who said, “If you are doing anything you’re passionate about by 25, you’re the exception, not the rule.”      I wish someone had told me that. I felt totally sidelined for years, thinking I was failing.      I think the pressure is from our parents and that middle-class dream they had. They want us to be the big whizz-kid CEOs and inventors, you know?      Total pressure points. My go-to is I just tell myself that surviving  is  a full-time job on its own. And I genuinely mean it.      Yeah, and you know what? I’m seriously toying with starting a side business. Maybe with something I actually like, like making candles or something. It sounds over-romantic but at least it's  mine .

Rather annoying to be honest. He’s always checking his phone. I’m trying to have a real conversation and...  beep , gotta go check messages. It’s like, ay, c’mon!      Aw, don’t I know it!
