Aye eenough, now eat up. Kids, you all right with what you’ve got?      Aye, this roast tho— this is spot on.      Yeah, it’s nice. Not sommat I’d get me nan to make but still…      That’s because you'd rather be grabbin' a takeaway, son. Still, Alice managed to cook it turkey style, bless her!      Ten out of ten from the lad, alright! So, I hear there was a hockey match today, Tom? Win?      Yeah, we won 4-2! Broke a bit of leg and looked like we might concede in the final ten min, but Emily nailed it at the death. Total hero!      Yer always winning in the land of youth leagues! Did you tell Marnie today? She was on about it at break.      Who's Marnie?      Mates from school, new girl. Real sporty.      Aye, well, don’t bring your mates along and expect her to walk forty in heels to the café! That way she’ll have to run to catch a bus outta here!      Hey, she’s still young, but she’s got good legs. I about blocked the kettle while I was screenshotting the touchline pass.      You and your photos are mental. Speaking of which, have you managed packing for Barcelona?      I’ve got guest speaker Friday morning, so probably late tonight. Still, the flight is a midnighter, so better get it done.      We’re talkin’ about travel again as though we’re always off somewhere.      Cos you do love going places, you and Jack.      That we do. Though really I just loathe being sat there for so long in airports.      Aye, bloomin’ cafes near your gate will be charging summat like ten quid for a sandwich.      I’ll take that as a pity laugh. But, Jack, I asked earlier— are we fitting in that game near Belfast? The dad’s got a friend who plays in a Sunday league.      Aye, I reckoned that’s the kind of trip worth making, you know? A game and then a walk in the countryside— now  that  would be a proper adventure.      Can we come?      Please? A bit of grass and real people? Please, don’t forget us.

Rather annoying when the GPS keeps changing its mind, isn't it? I was just reading about redwoods—did you know they can live for over 2,000 years? It's wild, isn't it? You think we'll see the giant sequoias on this route?      Honestly, I could do without the GPS making ridiculous U-turns. But yes—2,000 years is insane. Like, walking around this car, smiling at your friends,  untouched by time . If only we trees could do the same. Didn’t your mum get the address mixed up again?      Ha! She did. I swear, the last text she sent was "If you get to the sign saying 'Don't Go Here,' go the other way." I had to Google what the actual correct entrance was. She’s good for a laugh most of the time, really.      I love that about her. Reminds me of my aunt Violet, planting five different gardens every year, then forgetting where each one is. One time she told me I could stay with her, and I found out she had the guest room full with potted asparagus and a grief stricken guinea pig.      Oh, poor little thing. Asparagus? That's absurd. Mate, I often wonder if people like us, just zigzagging through the States, are quite mad to outsiders. You have to know what to look for, right? Like, those tiny coffee shops someone mentioned in an obscure blog. Or trying to spot a red-tailed hawk doing a lazy swoop over the treetops.      I mean, I  would  be there for the coffee, tiger. But while I love the travel, I can't deny this job temping in the office has been corroding my love of spreadsheets. Every time I press "print," I just feel like burning the whole lot. Paper. All that tree-killing nonsense.      Unhh. I think I once used a redwood-based document as a coaster. We should rebel. Like, next time we print out anything, we print 'Save a Forest,' and leave the document in the air. Defiance via polite request.      That's genius. Though I get the impression if you start lecturing people at your office, you'll just end up being handed a new box of staples and a sideways glance from Management. So, have you made peace with your conference call job yet?      Semi-routine life: I translate for a company where over half the time nobody knows who they're talking to.

Rather than share a text-based conversation, I request a visual depiction of the scenario. Is it possible to display a related image instead? Maybe something representing the described dinner conversation? This allows for a more immersive interpretation of the described activities.      An image would be great. But could it also include some visual references to the topics we were talking about? Like a chicken Kiev on the plate, maybe a rugby ball nearby, and a picture of your Granny from Dropbox or Flickr?      Oh, that sounds lovely! Put in the biscuits too and maybe a hedgehog wandering into the garden in the background... like we were mentioning earlier! And maybe show me with a headache and a cup of tea beside me?      Alright, I’m on it. I’ll try to include the essentials – the chicken Kiev on the plate, the rugby ball on the table, an image of my mother , a picture frame from Flickr or Dropbox, some biscuits in a jar, and a hedgehog peeking in from the garden. Also, a tea cup for you, Partner.      Fab, Dad! Make sure it looks like I’m giving backchat a bit to you and Mam. It’d be more realistic that way!      Absolutely, then it gives it that real family – very close ones – vibe. Make sure our expressions are clear: yours are the raised eyebrows of concern, and mine are the tired tea-sipping looks.      Got it all in mind. Let me generate this image. Just a moment...         So, after dinner, I was thinking about wallies in the garden last night. I mean, I know it's supposed to be good for them, but man, they can be annoying when they shuffle into the flower beds!      Maybe we should do something about them over the weekend. Enlist Dad’s help? He's quite the gardener when the biscuits are on the table.      I’ll be right there when the biscuits come out, and I’ll also help out with the wallies. Provided I survive the whining about rugby and the complaining over chicken kievs.      Haha, classic go-to plan. But seriously, that's what makes evenings at home so much fun in Ballincollig. Family, good food, and arguing about your team winning the latest match.      And the occasional headache from tea and biscuits. Just like your life, right?      Precisely, Ma! It's a perfect recipe for a great family dinner and evenings at the house.

Rather annoying that the vintage cups and saucers I bought off eBay came with just the one chip in them... Well, I’ll not be sending them back, not after all the trouble I had tracking them down. I was quite taken with that 1940s floral one.      Right, I liked the eggshell one you posted about on Facebook. But did they actually come with a missing saucer? I thought they said in the description it was a full set.      Well, you know what online sellers do. Didn’t even look too closely at the photos — just went for it when I saw  1930s  and  collectable  in bold letters like that. Anyway, I’m not too cross about it. It’s just a minor setback. I’m already planning to pick up some buckwheat flour from the market tomorrow for a weekend bake — better things to worry about than chipped china.      Aye, you and your buckwheat bread — it’s the only time I’ve actually fancied that kind of thing. My mum always had some in the house when I was a boy, said it was good for grief. Hated it, but there we go. Anyway, speaking of baked goods, are we cooking together Sunday or just sharing it at lunchtime?      Oh, we’re cooking together — don’t be daft. Silly question. I already invited Liam and Natasha — they said yes, just someone said chicken and sage again. I said no, a bit of a change. I’m thinking nutty buckwheat with a drizzle of apple honey. Can you manage the veggie side or would you prefer I handle that?      No, you take the main dish. I’ll chop and stir. Just don’t let me near the handle of the knife for more than two minutes, ‘cos I’m bound to lose a finger. And while you’re at the market tomorrow, would you pick up a nice bottle of red? For the leaving do on Thursday. Sarah’s being such good friends and taking over as admin lead before she heads off.      Of course, love. I’ll be calling in on the way home. I’ll get the Cabernet that goes with your own cheeseboard — everyone always raves about it at your leave-ins. And by the way, did I tell you Tom at your office is coming to the leaving do as well?      No, that’s a surprise — he’s usually more of the ‘formal over tea at the function room’ sort.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what they do with the fines for money laundering? The first time me and Claire were chucked a warning, more or less, but then the second time we got buckled up. £2k seems like a fanny at first, but when it’s chunked on top of holidays and uni fees?      Ay, I know all too well, love. Running a business, you’re always one step behind the rules. And it’s not as if pulling someone to the bank and saying, “I swear this is clean money, mate,” helps. You gotta get everything tickety boo. I mean, imagine if me customers got the idea I’d washed money from the cafe? My turkey sarnies would be skint within the week. Tenpence on the back.      I think the whole banking system’s mental, really. My old gig was waiting breakfast, and even then I noticed people trying to slide cash in funny ways. I remember one lad tried to fawn to the manager and get a deposit made over £5k—nearly got me suspended for being suspicious. Bloody joke really.      Here’s the thing, son—banks ain’t in the business of watching for fun. They’re in it for the risk. And if the FCA come knockin’, you and I know they don’t care if the money came from donkey work or dodgy work. If the bookin’s don’t stack up, they don’t ask. I had one job in the construction game, man, and once a bloke tried to give me a crate of cash for a skip hire. I told him no and called the feds. Guess what? I did earn me respect after that. You can’t touch the kids with this lark either.      Oh that’s right! I mean, if the kids see it as the norm, they’re going to grow up thinking it’s okay to be sneaky. Max is a right bloody gremlin, but I dunno how long he’d take before he started to think,  “Well Auntie Zoe did it,”  and then he’s off whippin’ money through a sink.      You're spot on, love. That goon of a son of mine is seven and already trying to sell "services" in the garden, like lawnmowing, bloomin’ hell. Last time he tried to take £10 in 50p’s from his nana—imagine!

Rather annoying this wet weather isn't it? I mean, do we need this much grey every morning? We haven't even seen the sun properly since January!      It does seem a bit relentless, doesn’t it? I was outside gardening this morning and half the things I planted just disappeared under a downpour. But I suppose it’s better than   dust  , eh?      I don’t know. I think this weather’s messing with my toddler’s routine. Last week, she started napping at different times, and now she’s rung out the toy horses under the living room like they're jousting. I swear she's learning from the   TV   or   spies   on the internet.      Yeah, she’s just picking bits up from the world, innit? I’ve been trying to sign ‘More milk’ for her, and she just goes "Moo!" then throws her sippy cup... I’m thinking about signing up for the local sign language class, to be truthful.      That’d be lovely for her, and maybe for you both. My cousin went to one with her daughter, and they’re now doing whole stories with cards and hands. It’s not just for the little ones, it gives you a new lens – especiallly with deaf friends, and stuff.      I reckon it’s a brilliant idea. You always hear people say “I wish I had more” – and this is just someone giving back in a new way. Fundraising has a rush, but oddly, I think working with kids has more patience. Or less money and more tea.      Oh, you know I about to ask about your trip to Sutton Coldfield next week. We were thinking of coming over for sandwiches and maybe a coffee. Not that I need an excuse, but we do want to talk about the ‘baby party’ you’re guest speaker at. Are we giving blankets and baby hats to the guests or just stamps on their hand?      You’ll be making   minibokies   and baby hats as well as edible cupcakes topped with 'OMG' writing from mini pens. Some people paint the faces of the babies after they’ve slept or feed the baby first. go with the flow. The point is to raise money for Disabled Children's Charity.      And the box for the babies? what comes inside? you know I have a big brother to help, and he's notorious for packing batteries, Rubik's cubes and tattoos supplies into the box for ‘fun’ – we need to lock this down.

Rather annoying when the proof copies don't arrive on time, isn't it? I mean, they know we're working to a tight deadline with the academic conference press. I’ve had to call the printer three times this week.      Oh I know what you mean. I had to make coordinates again on Tuesday because there was a typo in one of the author bios. Honestly, it all feels like a game of whack-a-mole sometimes. What's the title again?       "Phonetic Variation in East Anglian Youth Speak: A Sociolinguistic Analysis."  Sounds rather dry, but actually very enlightening once you get into it. All the slang, the vowel shifts... quite fascinating.      You must love this though, Anna, right? As a language coordinator, you're probably the only one who reads the whole thing from cover to cover for fun. I’d have been breakfast, no doubt.      Haha, fair point. I do love it! I mean, even if I have to skip the methodology sections, I still like reading the personal stories the contributors include. Gives it a really human feel.      I didn't even know we were handling anything sociolinguistic. I've just been in the backroom renumbering pages – very precise work, I assure you – but it's all a bit head-scratching. What's the takeaway?      Well, the core argument is about dialect shift in young speakers. The study found that even in South-Eastern regions like Aylesbury, which we tend to think of as more traditional, young people are pulling away from their regional dialects more than in previous generations.      Exactly. It's not just the accent fading – it's the whole linguistic identity. There's even a chapter that looks at how social media and globalisation are affecting localised speech. Makes you wonder whether the "correct" English will ever even be based on regional dialects again.      Do you think that’s a shame? I mean, I grew up in Malaysia hearing queens and commoners being academically dissected with lunches delivered separately and speaking English with the same rhythm as a Manchester derby.      Pardon?      Sorry, I mean it was bizarrely multicultural. But I think I picked up a language without really figuring out where it was from until I moved to London. Now I speak with something that’s... vaguely Southeast, but not in any pure form.      True to life, really. Language is always shifting, especially among young people.

Right, I just wanted to go through the to-do list for the charity rally again, ‘cos there’s a lotta stuff to sort out before we even think about applying for a visa.      Aye, we’ve only got a few weeks before the deadline. We better make sure we eeny every single thing. Passport photos, the application fee, and then there's all them ads on Gumtree we promised to post.      Yer, I think we should get the photos done asap. I was meanderin’ past the Boots in Wigan last week and they do like three for a tenner. Cheaper than a shop in the centre, I reckon.      Yeah, I’ve already got my left photo taken. Tenner was well worth it. D’you wanna meet up in Wigan? We can take photos for each other and do it for breakfast, save time.      That’d be a good shout. Only as long as we don’t wind up takin’ an hour over it, cos I’ve got to tell you—personally I’ve never trusted people who wear a hat in their passport photo. I dunno, seems like dodgy business to me.      Haha, fair point. My nan once wore a fairly large headscarf because she thought her hair was too wispy. It took three goes and the phone’s memory card was already full. Still, we got through it in the end.      That’s just a photo, imagine tryin’ to sort out a visa at the embassy in London. I’ve got an appointment next week but I’ve not filled in the form about our intended activities yet.      Oh right, you need to be clear that this is for charity. Not like some random backpackin’ holiday up the side of some mountain, ‘cos they look like they do.      Aye, well the rally is a proper event, it’s fully registered with the Warrington Youth Foundation. We’ve already got a few sponsors onboard as well.      Yeah, speaking of—did you get the reply back from Tom at Peak Electrical?      Yeah, go on then. They said if we promise not to go over budget and provide a log of expenses, they’ll be in with a modest contribution. Lift your arms cause you might be lucky enough to get a donation, eh?      Haha, that’s a right laugh. But that’s good, at least we can finalise the ad description now.

Rather annoying really, I've got this cough and I can't sleep properly. I think it's that cold weather we had the other week.      I know how that is! It's a proper hooly £20 viag and it winds you up, innit? I’ve had eeny weeny sleep the last couple o’ nights. Still reckon it's worse than hangovers most a' the time.      Honestly, I’m so bleedin' tired as well. University is a proper arse-punch. You're up early, lectures all day, then trying to get everything done at night. I’m like dead inside some days.      You know, like that one turkey night we went out? The one where I accidently flew over the chair and landed on the table, and then I hurt me arm? That was an absolute scene.      Yeah, and then we 'ad to go to the doc in the early hours, you poor thing! That fella didn’t take no nonsense, he were like, “Off to hospital with ye, you’ve got a buckle.”      Felt a bit like a drama queen when they poked me with all those sticks and scanned me, but it were a relief once I knew it weren’t broken. Still, I’ve got a bit of slap on there now.      Mate, you look like you've been attacked by a grumpy juggler. It’s all in good fun though. That night weren’t boring at least.      No, not with you chuckin’ yourself over furniture and then pulling a look at the bloke in the ballet boots! You two nearly did me in with your daft faces.      I'm just saying, what's this lark with that new lad in the next room? You're always in there, bin goin’ on?      Aww, nuffink much. He’s alright, a bit awkward, but he brought me ginger tea once I came back from the hos. Feels a bit odd being looked after, but it’s nice 'cause I haven't told my mam yet.      Don’t tell me you're like a proper proper softie goin' on now! I knew it!      Come on, let’s see what's in the box in the kitchen. Lift your legs and come with us. I’m seriously needing a kip, and I'm startin' to plot murder over this toffee on the counter.      C'mon! It's a proper bleak night outside and I’ve got me pills in me bag.

Rather do I! The granda’s 60th do was a bit of a squawkin’ affair, don’t you think? Y’know, down at Malton by the old Red Lion?      Aw, yeah, I had a good time, like. A few too many cheese scones, but hey. It was nice to see auntie Julie's twins, they don’t often come up from Leeds.      Aye, and rightly so. It were interesting, mind. We had to move the trestle tables outside when it started drizzle. You'd have thought someone'd 'a brought a weather app!      Yeah, Grandpa was in good form though, wasn’t he? Still cracking the jokes. That one about the leaky tap an’ the bin, I thought I'd die!      Oh, aye, better than breakfast, innit? I've been marked enough GCSE papers to know what’s funny and what's just mawkish puffin nonsense—and that weren’t puffin nonsense, son.      Yeah, I mean, he looked happy though. Like, really happy. Did you tell him, like, we’ve got something to tell him soon? Or did we just spring it on him at the table?      No, it weren’t sprung. We had a private chat before the speeches. He was tickled pink when I said we were thinking of having a family holiday in the Lake District. That’s more his crowd: hills, a good walk, and a preferably empty bus shelter.      Haha, being crowded out by moor birds. Yeah, I reckon he'd about die. But serious now, you think the Lake District’s a good place to be? I mean, not that it’s not brilliant and all, it is, but it's just so... quiet. Burgled by badgers, like.      Aye, well, it's a chance to think, innit? For once you can hear yourself think. We could take the opportunity to discuss your GCSE prep—though from the lunches we’ve shared together, I’ve got a fairly good idea of where you are.      ...Fair ’nuff. I've got a few more mocks left, so I reckon I'm on track, but I will need your help with surds and quadratic whatnots. Shawty doesn’t understand flu.      Oh, come on now, don’t bellyache. I’ve been talkin’ ‘quatrics’ longer than you’ve been talkin’—which is all of about five minutes. Anyway, you get it done, and I’ll see you on the other side of the holidays with some decent cake and a cuppa, you hear?

Rather annoying when a water bottle freezes up in your car, innit? Me an' nan ‘ad to chisel the ice off one of the ones I put down in the bottom by the gear lever last week. I was chucked out of the house I was so frightened I wouldn't be able to get it een!      Aye, that’s the thing with not having central heating most a' the car these days. If you’re too far back, you don’t notice how cold it gets. I remember one time when we were stuck for hours in the Pennines in the winter. Had to fetch frozen tea from a brand new  Holland & Barrett  bottle and it spilled all over me trousers and made a Mycenean mess. Still smells like bergamot on ‘em!      Aww, and I bought a whole bottle of green tea in the  Amazon  gigant shop when we moved in. It said  Nitro HiiCha Protected by the Sky Japanese style  an' I stored it in the boot so I thought it’d be safe, but I opened it this morning and it was gone all fizzy and rancid. What did it do to it?      Sounds like it wasn't sealed right. Maybe it was got left in the back – Mate, I got a sneaking suspicion sometimes these big shops don’t test the chill cabinets in the car journeys they deliver through. Should’ve bin in ‘Balby’s’ if you wanted the good stuff.      That stuff was a nightmare, remember when nan got  Irritable Bowel Syndrome  after trying some strange liquorice-looking stuff in the  post  she got? Took nearly about five days off her eating routine! I swear it looked like something outta Japan. All sparkly and not at all like the school pen I got for Christmas.      Aye, and I still got that pen in me diary. Still works. I remember trying to write in Latin once ‘atque’ or something and nan said I was mad. “You’re not gonna impress  examiners  with that,” she said.      That’s funny ‘cos I tried to remember a Latin saying once and said  “magni govis”  which ended up being  “I go to the loos” . Then the cat went to the  flap  an’ nan thought it was me. So I said I was learning to speak like Romans and she said, “Well, don’t forget your loo roll.”      That’s typical, innit?

Rather annoying when the recording’s all crackly, isn’t it? I had to pause it about five times just to rewind and replay a vowel. I’m more than a bit tired by the time I get to “rho”… “rho” indeed, I swear sometimes it just sounds like a cat was in the room!      It was raining that day he gave the speech as well. The microphones were constantly picking up the wind and the swoosh of the drizzle. I watched it myself; you couldn’t see anything past the first few rows. Didn’t even get the full effect of the presentation because the speaker was right at the back—literally!      That was quite the event, My dear. I remember being disturbed by the weather myself. I had a young student who insisted the speaker shouted, but no, in the world of clarity—particularly in academia—storms and speeches do not get on well.      Haha, you sound like I’ve ever spent a lot of time in lecture halls. I mean, once I finish building that new shop over the road, maybe I’ll start listening to things I don’t struggle to understand. But for now, I tend to let the radio go on in the background while I work. If it’s got “rho” or crackles, I just mistook it for noise from the other room.      All that aside, the content itself was quite remarkable. The young woman who made the keynote speech, what was her name again, Emily or Edith?      Emma. Emma Ward. Though judging by some of the questions she got at the end, I don’t think she spoke in a way people were prepared for. She talked about technology quite theologically, which confused quite a few. I suppose you could say she was answering to a rho of expectations!      That she did. And quite bravely, too. Though I noticed a few people drifting off into their screens. It was probably too much for the average listener. I transcribe all day, but reading her talk back as words… it’s like a different language!      More likely the same language but with no pictures for once. You know, it’s funny, my dad used go to lectures on pond life if you can believe it. Showed me once on a camera reel that had green splotches all over it from the tape getting old. So I know what I’m up against when it’s just static and hours of earnest talking!

Rather than going out, we thought we'd spend the day together. The kids have already made cards, and I got them to practice some Mother’s Day rhymes. I know it's cheesy, but Liv's been doing a lot with the class about the meaning of things like 'flowers for the mother' or 'love letters from the heart'.      Can we have pancakes for breakfast? Like, a big stack with strawberries?      Well, pancakes are a definite yes. But not as breakfast. We can have them for brunch later when your uncle comes over. Let's try not to get everything mixed up, even if  somebody  forgot to clean the plates after Forest School last week.      You told us to clean up after ourselves, and we did, but the cat knocked them over again and I think he turned into a mermaid in the dishwasher.      Oh for goodness’ sake, he didn’t turn into a mermaid, you two! You both saw the cat’s fur go all sopping wet, yes, but mermaids aren’t real, and the cat is very definitely still a cat.      But we only live once, right?      And we should seize the day!      Oh, you two! Right, now that the  drama  is over, let’s get to making your Mother’s Day card beautiful. And we can talk about the homework from Forest School too. The one about animals and their homes. You had a fun time building that little ‘bug hotel’ with the sticks and bark, didn’t you?      We did, but we had a competition with the boys to see who could make the best one. We won, obviously.      Definitely. Not that I’d tell if it wasn’t true.      Well, you’d tell even if it wasn’t true. Both of you suffer from the glorious affliction of thinking you’re very, very accurate about your performance at everything.      But we are. It’s not called the 'British disease' for nothing!      Oh you cheeky little ones. Now, can the two of you go and get the craft bits from the drawer while I go and preheat the oven for the muffins I’m making with oats and banana? And what your teacher taught you in class, about  idioms , how’s that going?      Oh, I’ve been practising. I told my friend at the park that my brother is  full of hot air , and he said, “are we having a tea party or are we throwing things?”

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's such a mither when you don’t get a call through, especially when it could be something serious.      I was just speaking to my brother the other day—  Liam  —Deirdre’s youngest—well, he’s been having some twitching in his arm.      Oh Lord, that sounds worrying. Like he's had a bit of a stroke or something?      Oh, no, nothing like that. But when you're in his position, with a young family... like, he's only thirty-five, and he's got two children, and only Rob working full time now that Myra had her heart scare last year.      That must be hell for the family. I know how I'd be if anything happened to Jamie—he was at uni and working part-time when my dad passed away suddenly. It’s still a shock in some ways.      Exactly, you never think it's going to happen to  your  lot—especially when it's someone who seems healthy enough. My mum always said if we looked after ourselves, and didn't smoke or drink too much, we'd live to a ripe old age. Well, look at Rob. He's always on the go, fairly healthy, and now he's having his own health scare.      It’s the whole unpredictability of it, isn’t it? And with cancer being in so many families now. My aunt in Liverpool had bowel cancer a few years back, and then her sister had something with the lungs. It just seems to be everywhere.      Yeah, there's a feeling about it at the moment. My sister Carol's talking about having her own tests done—she’s only fifty-two, but with that family history, she's not taking any chances.      That's the smart thing to do. Early detection is everything. I always remember my gran saying, 'Bless you for looking after yourself.' It’s funny when you’re older and the advice makes more sense. You think of all the things you've done to keep the whole whirring machine going.      I know. It made me think the other day—when's the last time I had a check-up? Probably over a year. It's easy to ignore it when you don’t feel ill.      Aye, but sometimes flu or fatigue can be symptoms of something more. And with all the stress we have now with everything—work, family, bills—it's hard not to feel like you're living on adrenalin.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you anyway.      Oh, come on. You're telling me you're more annoyed about missing a lecture than missing time with me?      I'm not annoyed about missing the lecture per se—it's more the fact I'm stuck at home pretending to do some research on   Old English phonology   all day.      Ugh. That sounds so dry. I remember you saying it was going to be interesting, but now I can tell you're lying to keep me entertained when really it's glorified boredom.      No, honestly—Old English is pretty cool once you get into it. There's like these remnants of   Ingvaeonic nasalizaton   in specific verbs. I’m trying to write a paper on how these subtleties turned into   Anglo-French influences   during the Middle English period, but I’m getting stuck trying to map the   diglossic   shifts properly.      Do I even want to understand that? I'm still trying to wrap my head around the way   Chinese tones   work.      You’ll pick it up. It’s not like you're starting from scratch—it's just a whole rhythm of sounds. Look, languages all build on each other:   phonology, grammar, syntax  —it’s like the puzzle of human communication.      You know what I find interesting? The way in   South Korea   food is not just about taste but   tradition  —for example, how they use   kimchi   in every meal.      That’s actually a great point. It's   ethnolinguistic   as much as cultural. I remember the   Chuseok   [mid-autumn harvest festival] I saw photos of last year—how Koreans preserve   ancestral rituals   around food is fascinating. And the way men and women sit in different spaces during traditional meals reflects   social structure  . It's not just lunch.      I miss when we went out to the market in   Gillingham   to get veggies. There were these amazing mushrooms and peppers from South America—way cheaper than in   Sussex  .      Yeah, supermarkets here go overboard on cost per gram sometimes. If I go vegetarian for another week like this, I’m going to be buying a   lamb chop   just to reassure my system I’m not made of leafy greens and lentils.      Just because your university canteen made you a vegetarian over the last month doesn’t mean everything else should suffer. I can teach you to make   something decent  , you know.

Rather skip uni today just cos we're all sat here with pizza. I know it's only Tuesday but like... come on. Someone had to bring this spicy chicken box. This is what happens when you live with three other people. Not all of us like jalapeños!      Okay, but it is Margherita Week at the flat, right? So it's not all their fault? I mean I only had a little bit of that box and I’m feeling like a firework now.      Oh, I got the numbness in the fingers too. Still, not as bad as the time we tried Laksa during that week last term. No one washed the pan for weeks and now that MyKitchenRules mistress is living with us and left’s a vegan. Probably crying everyday watching the ghosts of pasta past haunt her sad little Fairtrade tofu.      Cats would have been breakfast, no doubt. I mean, she still thinks micro-waving a pan’s the same as cleaning it, you know?      Yeah, but that’s Waterfalled out, luv. Shout out to the people at Sugarhouse last weekend. Honestly, they were like, “We’ve run out of shots.” And you had the grace to say, “Okay then, tea and biscuits?”      That was a fluke! I was not trying to win the prize for Most Chic at 2am. But thanks for not rolling your eyes at me when I accidentally replied to a Facebook message in my sleeps.      Speaking of which, passed out on the sofa and slept through a knock. Unlucky mate, it was a delivery for your timetables. I told you about my 9am lecture on Cloud Atlas, right? Sorry, but we were doing Heads Up on campus the other day and you tried to play it in the 3rd seminar room after someone asked you to explain Newton’s Laws of Motion to a seven-year-old and you replied, “His laws are: everything pushes back and the universe buys all the crisps.”

Rather annoying when the council’s got us on read only, innit?      Yeah... What d’ya mean by read only?      Y’know, when yer tryin’ to process changes or upload data and it says access denied. We can’t do anything een it.      So like, the system’s basically not lettin’ you do your job?      That’s right, yeah. And nae one seems to know why. We’ve been stuck like that for nearly a week. It’s like they’ve forgotten we exist.      That can’t be helpful. What’s the deadline lik’e for the project? My turkey still hasn’t finished defrostin’, so I feel like I’m on the back end of a Roald Dahl book.      Sounds like you’ve got worse problems than a database crash.      Haha, nae long’s you’re not tellin’ my project manager I said that. They’d deduct my eyes and sell ’em for coffee, maybe.      I’m with you on that. So, I dunno, maybe today we go in and try and fight it. I’m sick of just sitlin’ at my desk taplin’ the same error message. It’s like a typing companion.      A mortal enemy, more like. What’s the emergency contact for the IT team? Our last callout in Sheffield, the system went wonky just like that and it took three days to fix.      I think the number’s in the shared drive but it’s also read only at the minute. I’m walkin’ on fumes trying to find a way around it.      Have you tried pluggin’ in a backup drive or runnin’ the system offline ‘til they fix it? Sometimes the dirty work pays off.      I did a few things, yeah. I don’t wanna lose my overtime hours or risk a data compromise. Those words can’t be said out loud without a health inspector appearing.      Some people believe in ghosts for chrissake.      Yeah, go talk to my database backup if you don’t. And that was the line in the sand that divided professionals from the box tickers.      So sum it up for me, innit?      Corbin’s bellyache is a locked database and I’ve got over a week’s worth o’ data like it’s the ghost of Christmas Present.      I can tell you’re romanticin’ it, but yeah. Just make sure when ye call IT they’re real human, and not just some automated left-hand turn of doom.

Rather nippy today, ain't it? That wind off the fen sticks to your bones, it does. I got the electric fire on in the dining room, and I still need me bobble hat on! Got me tea? Not too sweet, mind, I’ve cut down on the sugar after the doc’s een sayin’ I’ve got a bad ticker.      Oh Frank, you don’t need that bobble hat if you put more layers on, love. And you don’t need to dump that hat in front of the fire like a currant bun — it’s childish.      Right, but it  does  look cosy. I swear, the fire’s only on for show half the time — you know, for the atmosphere. I left mine off this morning; I’m trying to reduce the electric bill, and I’ve been walking more. Living in Norwich, you’ve got to if you’re stuck in the dorm during term time. Less car, more exercise — helps with the back ache.      I hear you, Kate. I walk too, but I get distracted by the lads’ match on telly sometimes. You don’t miss that, Frank and Iris? Woodham Market today — they’re playing Lowestoft, I believe. West Norfolk all the way. Though I can’t understand half what the chap on commentry says, all his East Anglian twang — don’t know if he’s saying  goal  or  Balham .      Aye, luv, that’s me lad from Costessey, he’s got a proper accent — still, better him than a Londoner talkin’ about our match. I saw one last week, said Norfolk about like it’s “Noff-ark” — proper daft. Course I ain’t watching the match today — me back is killing me. Been taking more painkillers than I ought. The ‘ealth centre here says it’s degenerative — what's that supposed to mean, eh?      Sounds like they don’t know what else to call it. We had to rush off to Aldershot once with a back spasm — cost a pretty penny with the taxi fare and the ointments you don’t even use.      Yeah, go for regular check-ups, if you can afford them. I know some college friends in the NHS that had to queue for three months just to get a proper MRI. It’s all postcodes, really.      Well, you can’t argue with the new tech, right? I saw a documentary over the weekend — they’re using these tiny robots to go into the body and fix things up.

Okay, I just wanted to say sorry for canceling last week’s catch-up. I had that admin training all weekend and my laptop died on me, so I completely forgot! How are you all?      No worries, love! Look, we’ve all been busy. Hell, I’ve had a total whirlwind with the new sales manager role—I handed over to someone last week and have been on a break. A  much  needed one!      Oh, congrats, Speaker_2. You’ve worked hard for that. Speaker_4 and I have been swamped too—we’ve been juggling a brand new project for a luxury brand, and the client’s only shown up stressed and made everyone else turkey on it. Honestly, enough to make you want to just throw the Mac out the window!     Ha ha, I can relate. Work’s a bit of a nightmare when it comes to training and this new system they’ve thrown in. But hey, thanks for not being too fazed by the cancel. Anyway, we were actually thinking we’d do something over the weekend, maybe book a cozy dinner place up near you two, somewhere not as fancy as the place we went to for my sister’s wedding… although that was  so  glamourous. Remember how Speaker_4 spilled that red wine on the table, and we all panicked?      Oh God don’t remind me! I couldn’t even see the dress underneath the table—it was a disaster. Our group just laughed our heads off while the rest of the wedding party tried not to.      Yeah, and I thought the DJ was the be-all and end-all, but he played a pop song at a wedding with violin covers— so  not the vibe.      Honestly though, your sister’s wedding was beautiful. I mean, it helped that she got engaged to the most kind-hearted guy. I still can’t believe how much he did for his in-laws to get it sorted. Proper romantic, right?      Oh 100%, and to think, he proposed after being together for just 7 months. I keep thinking “hmm do I want marriage so young?” Still, I’m single with three cats and the dream of having go-karts on the kids if and when I ever settled. Ha.      I know! I think marriage might be something I’m just not ready for. I’m planning to live 30% of my life alone, 50% of it with a cat, and 20% doing art.

Rather annoying this newfit lot eh, love? I couldn't get the telly to_work properly_last night... got to press twenty buttons jist to see_what I'd already paid for! It's a mad hatter's box, that remote.      Oh, dear, I don’t een want to touch_nothing like that. I 'ad me son set it up_last Christmas. Now I just sit down and it's on, so long as I don't move a single penny. But, 'elp, one time I was watching the soaps and 'e came in with 'is 'ands full of wires and said I couldn’t 'ave no pudding until it was fixed! Spoilsport, the lot of 'em, if you ask me.      Tenr, I was at the school yesterday, and one of the kids asked me what a "personal computer" was. I nearly fell off me chair. You 'ave to remember, these kids in 'Olts Heath today play games on sticks, thinking they're working out the problems. One time, I took a class out for observational drawing—personally, I'd_rather teach 'ammerth —but they were grief. One kid kept asking if there was a_game for it.      That reminds me. My grandboy—is twenty_four, I think—'e wants to put up a stable and 'ave ponies to rent out for parties. I said to ‘im, 'Why not teach them to 'andle ‘orses in the village? Let ‘em know what a 'orse's been doing all its life, not jist some flashy laser show in a cinema!      Well, as long as he 'asn't got to walk us all up a field in the rain, I'm all for it. My Jane—granddaughter that is—once 'ad a pony called Thunder, galloped_all over ‘er 'ead. Got a black eye and a broken sundae. Still, she’s a farmer now, ‘eself.      Aye, I envied her that. At least she had dreams. I 'ad me 'ead in a book writing exams for the state, but_teacher work's_dead these days. Money’s tighter than a man’s waistband goin' on ‘is twentieth birthday.      You’re_telling me. Last week I had the council bloke round to fix your 'eating system—it cost me_twenty pounds down and said the rest’d come in_ratings, never mind that I 'aven’t got a penny for ‘oliday meat.      It's a悲惨 show all over, dear. We were drinking tea and biscuits in the old days_overtime 'is backs, and now you ‘ave to line up for the food bank like you’re at the movies.

Rather annoying when the kettle’s on the blink, isn’t it? I had to pop across the road and borrow Mrs. Hargreaves’ one today. Blows my cool, self-sufficient teacher image to pieces.      That Mrs. Hargreaves—what a character. She once tried to teach me how to knit a hat and handed me a pair of knitting needles like they were a swords. A real force of nature, that woman.      Oh she was, wasn’t she. We had to teach her granddaughter for a while during the lockdown. Funny how things came full circle like that. She even helped  us  out a bit when the school supply chain was in chaos.      Touching really, how people step up in tough times. I remember back in the '70s, I used to head down to Canary Wharf for work every day. The place looked nothing like it does now. Just dockyards and derelict warehouses. I’d never have imagined that shopping arcades would take over the whole area.      I was there just the other day, taking a weekend walk. I showed my A-Level students the site back in the day, when the cranes were still watching over the construction. Now it feels like we’re in a different city entirely. Speaking of weekends, what have you got planned?      Truth be told, not much. I might pop over to the village fete at Chelmsley Wood. They've got music and a bouncy castle. A man of my age playing hangman at the fair—it’s all downhill from there, I suppose. Any weekend plans for you?      Actually, I’m helping out at the local community centre. One of the volunteers had to pull out and I’ve volunteered to take over her language taster class. Adults, mostly. English for speakers of other languages, you know the drill. It's always nice to help people feel at home here.      You’ve always had the gift with words, Clara. You must take after your mum, hearing her talk. Though I’ve never quite got the hang of French myself.      Some people just aren’t wired that way, I think. But I remember you taught me go in my early teens. I still keep a couple of stones in the shed just in case I ever manage to jog the memory back up.      Aye, go it’s a special game—played one in Cambridge once that took all afternoon and we hadn’t finished by sunset.

So did you go out for dinner on Valentine's or what? My sister was on my case about it like...  shh , she keeps shipping us silently, don’t ask. I've been over that since uni started.      Oh I did! Went to this little French place in Milton Keynes eeny weeny out of the way, you know the one? Kitchen Garden's doppelgänger. The wine was all right but I ordered the steak and it was like rubber stretchies.     . We had to send it back and when the chase-up came out it was underdone to hell like, literally like baked inside. My date was a bit awkward the whole night.      Oh My God, I’m living for this! Did you take Scott back there or someone from the café or?      A lad from down the housing estate, Nick. Met at the Domino breakfast, he was nursing a cappuccino... I thought he was cute, you know, bit rough around the edges, kind of a working-class heartthrob.      Like, a proper East Midlands man, innit? You don’t get that in London. I only ever meet uni boys in gear: bow ties, MacBooks, rhythm in their speech like “I’m gonna –  ha  – just let you go, because the  hypo  the  the  sis is,” y’know?      Ha! That sounds exactly like those Stem people at our uni. I tried so hard to not read into him, just thought we’d do dinner and maybe a movie, but when the bill came and it split it evenly – no hesitation – I was like, right, about this guy... is he trying to win the Renaissance Man of the Year?      Wait! Did you split it then or were you like, uncool?      Split for the chicken and the guest speaker bill. I did feel a bit awkward, to be honest. I was holding my hand behind my back like, is it 50-50 or 70-30 or what? He probably thought I was a complete psycho with my head like this the whole night.   .        I get it, sometimes it’s just so weird trying to read the vibe, innit. I mean, with blokes sometimes it’s your fault cause you don’t have the fluency to read their micro-expressions against the cheap lighting and wine. You don’t get to expect them to have ‘signals’ like we do, innit.      Fair point. Maybe I should’ve just gone with my original plan of romantic movie night in, but then again, someone said adventure

Honestly, I just find it so exhausting these days when anyone talks about politics without even glancing at the roots of the problem. Like, how can we even begin to fix housing in this country if we don’t first address the role capitalism plays in pushing people out of places they used to afford?      Right? I  completely  agree—and it’s not even about just building more houses. It’s about who gets to own them and  how much they cost to live in , you know? Like, someone buys a flat in Croydon for £150k, but the second they rent it out, the rent skyrockets. People can’t afford to live anywhere near where they work anymore.      Yeah, I’ve seen it so much in my work. I was on a project in Dagenham last year, and the council just didn’t want to build enough affordable homes. The big developers, they’re all about profit margins. They don’t care if people are being priced out of their communities.      And that’s why I think we need to talk more about  who’s being priced out —which impacts minority groups the most. Racism still exists in the housing market too. I’ve read so many reports about it. Like, when people from certain ethnic backgrounds try to rent or buy, they’re either discriminated against or get charged more. It’s not just about numbers and policies; it’s about people.      Absolutely. It’s all linked. If you don’t have a system that actively protects people from racism and economic inequality, then housing— and all the other things tied to it —will just keep being a battleground for those lower down the ladder.      I think you’re the only one of my friends who still actually  eats your noodles  instead of using them as a platform for political ranting. You’re quite impressive, honestly.      [laughs] Well, I did just have my first mouthful before you mentioned housing again! But hey, if we’re gonna eat together, we might as well talk about  everything , right? Even if it’s with chopsticks in hand.      Exactly. My chicken katsu ramen is nice and spicy—which makes me even more goaded to talk about how corrupt our housing policies are.      Then let’s continue. I’ve got more broth than opinions.      Great. So, I’ve been thinking—what’s your take on those so-called ‘affordable housing’ schemes?

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, me going back to work next week and Emily having to start nursery full time. I’ve been dreading it for months, to be honest. She’s a little anxious at the thought of being away from me, and you know how things can be — if they get off on the wrong foot, it can make everything harder.      Yeah, I can imagine that. I mean, I know how close you two are. But it’s gotta be easier in the long run, right? She’s got to get used to it, and you’ve got your headspace back to sort of get back into the swing. I remember when I was at uni, working part-time made a massive difference, helped me focus more on my studies. It’s just a short-term sacrifice for the future.      Aye, I suppose you’re right about that. Though it’s breakfast, bedtime and then suddenly I’m at my desk for nine hours and she’s off exploring with someone else, you know? I keep thinking I’ll miss things, or that I won’t do things the way I used to. But I guess it’s necessary.      And think about all the ways you can make it up for her. We’ve been talking about our “big holiday” – that’s been bugging me, like, it’s supposed to be a trip to Cornwall or maybe even somewhere out of the UK. If we book it now, maybe that’ll give Emily something to look forward to. It could also be a way to bond a bit more before we’re both wrapped up in other things again.      That’s a great idea, sweetheart. I’ve been meaning to have about five conversations about travel plans with you anyway. Cornwall sounds lovely this time of year. I’ve already started the weaning process easier than I expected, it helped a lot when she started having meals with her nursery friends. It gives her a bit more confidence, you know?      Ohhh, I wish I had thought of that when I was little. I could’ve avoided my kid-stage rebellion of only eating cheesy pasta every night! Do they let her watch any of those kids’ shows yet, or do you set a time limit? I remember you told me the last go-round with my cousins ended up with our house destroyed by one of those brash robotic pirate characters that had a siren alarm.

Rather annoying to be honest, the EE phone bill turned up with a hefty increase. Don’t think I've even got the data plan they’re charging now for. Blows it out of the water, that's what it does. Not sure I'll have much choice—get on the phone to them tomorrow or else I'm stuck with a bill I can't justify.      I’ve had that with a couple of our suppliers too. Not that I’m one to carp on about it, but as a fundraiser, it’s always tight. You’ve got to keep your chase when it comes to these things. Sort it like you mean it. Otherwise, they just keep riding you. What’s the deadline again for the charity’s next deadline? Just so I don’t get caught short myself.      I know what you mean, Speaker_1. A bit of pushback never goes amiss. But forget the phone bill, have you actually heard about the police visit this afternoon in the high street shop? Mega confusing! No one saw anything, apparently. Just a statement to give, but that’s bound to gum things up a bit for the shop staff next week. Poor thing, it’s their busiest time and all.      Yeah, I reckon the police have it in for all of us small business owners – just looking for statements and interferin'. Honestly, if it weren’t for the community support, half of these places would pack their bags and run. Not that I’m shirking responsibility, but this statement business sounds like a right headache. Is it just a formality, do you think? Some nutcase walking up and down the road smoking and being ‘suspicious,’ but that’s it?      From what Anna said, it’s the same old: something seen but nothing much out of the ordinary. Still, that’s the way the bat goes, I suppose. You’re the director, so you must know the ropes better than most. How did you deal with it in your store?      Bare bones, I tried to make it as quick as could be. As long as we can’t put a name to it, the police move on and it gets closed as “no further action”. The hard part is getting around the tedium of the forms and the go-sees on your own time. Not everyone’s got a PA.      I suppose.

Rather annoying when a TV show you're watching gets axed. I was just watching this Roman history doc—basically, a bloke with a massive beard waxing lyrical about superstitions and how people used to believe in all sorts of things. Was like watching Spartacus on drugs.      Right? I liked the farming ones more, the ones where he showed how they used to make herbs and stuff. A lot of those would actually work too. I’ve got this pestle and mortar in my place that my sister brought back from Cyprus. You can literally chase the spirit of the past with some tea and a good crush of coriander or something.      That’s cool. You like that My Name Is Earl type vibe with the eccentric stuff. It reminds me of how my grandad used to chuck oranges and lemon into every single dish he made—like, even his chips. He once told me, “if it’s not bitter, it’s not British,” and he’s dead now so I can’t even argue back.      Mate, that man was one with the wisdom of the ages. Anyways, I mean, seriously, the way people still die early nowadays for something like malarials in foreign country holidays? You'd think a little sea salt and olive oil would do the trick. But no, people still think it's a good idea to bath in seaweed and not wear sandals. Sea lice? That's no joke.      Oh, someone at my sister’s wedding dropped dead because they ate a nut cake and they had a chickpea allergy—silly mind, tragic way to go through bread. I mean, China’s got better stuff out there about how you source your ingredients. You can just touch the chilli and boom—death or madness.      Speaking of which, have you managed to wear that sweatshirt I gave you for your wedding? The one with the big Cyprus flag on it and all them strange symbols.      Oh, I tried, mate. The lining started coming out the first time I wore it. I’ve taken to calling it the 'British-Garden-of-Dead-Ole-Friends' jumper. Still, I wore it once and nearly got the 'best dressed goon of the day' if you ask me.      That’s the only award you need in life, tbh. Anyway, if we ever go back to Cyprus, I’ve been meaning to take you to where those mines are—my gran gave me a souvenir stone made from that ‘dreadful’ Cypriot gold.

Honestly, I’m just  dreading  the English test on Friday. I still haven’t revised properly. I got so caught up with French homework and art prep for the display next week.      I know what you mean! I panicked and stayed up until half one revising modal verbs for French on Tuesday and now I’ve got a massive headache. At least we’ve got the wind band practice after school today. A bit of a distraction, eh?      Oh, yeah! I  love  the wind band. We’re doing that new piece called “Morning Light,” aren’t we? I reckon we’ve got a brilliant chance at winning the regional competition. What’s your instrument again? Clarinet?      Nope, you’re thinking of Anna. I play the flute. I reckon you're on the flute and I’m the flautist—Don’t get us mixed up at the next breakfast, or whatever. I swear half the band thinks I’m the oboe player!      Ha, I told the conductor the same thing once and he almost dropped his coffee. Honestly, I loved music class today. I mean, we did a bit of sight-reading, which was stressful as hell, but Marcus—remember the new percussion guy? He dropped the cymbal at the most important bit and the whole class cracked up.      Oh my God, don’t remind me! I couldn’t stop laughing. And poor Liam had to finish the whole rhythm by himself. Honestly, he’s so good with everything. I reckon he’ll be the future leader of the band.      Yeah, and being head boy is just the  beginning . He’s practically a legend now. I hear he’s doing a solo in the assembly this term—something from Elgar, I think.      I’m jealous. I’d love to step up and do something like that. But no, I’m more of a quiet-on-the-side kind of person. Although I was thinking about doing the art club exhibition next month. You know I did that painting of the queens and that?      Oh, that one with the big crown! My nan took a photo of it for her phone background. Said it was like the real thing or something. But I think it was more of a Roald Dahl kind of look.      Well, it was  sort  of what your nan described. So I’m planning to redo it with more realism, maybe next term.

Rather annoying the new barista eh, love? Keep calling us 'you lot' like we're some poncey lot o' toffs dining at Fortnum's!      Aye, proper disrespectful if you ask me—shoulda been told to smarten up 'er tone if she wants to stay employed 'ere 'mong decent folk!      I reckon that coffee machine is broken or sumfink. I had to tell 'er what a flat white 'asn't got anything to do with the colour. Didn’t even want to make it properly.      Still, at least we've got a proper cup o’ tea first thing in the mornin’. Just 'cos they're young and got themselves a fancy certificate doesn't mean they know their Darcy from their Elex in the world o' cups an' additives about the north east!      'Magine if they tried to teach like she works the bar. Proper disaster that'd be!      Good job I still keep me head over there, if I didn't I'd be up t' Wellington with a face as blank as a grief stricken penguin.      I asked 'er about the ingredients again and she looked at me like I spoke in Latin!      Oh, she gets a new set of orders and starts making things up for fun! She probably thinks a 'bunny' is some 'sort of latte' now—proper lost in the world of branding and trends that barista! Give me that and plug me in and switch me brain up for something that works with a ‘flat white’!      Mummy, I have told her the sugar is on the ‘sugar shelf’. I will, cause you see I have been here for 30 minutes and it was starting to affect the quality of my revision time to do my history studies for ‘the Great War’—ain’t even near that exciting. Rather annoying when the car won't play ball, isn't it? I had to get it booked in first thing tomorrow and I've got no luck getting an appointment until Friday.      That's mad, isn't it? I had the same kind of thing last month. ECDe was booked out for two weeks. I had to take it to some mate of mine who's got a garage not far from here. A lot cheaper than those main dealers too.      Yeah, I'd know someone like that! You just pop the bonnet when you're in, don't you? You show 'em the engine and they mostly figure it out. I've been doing it for forty years. Never managed to get the turkey on Christmas Day, mind—you know what I mean? Still, I ain't obsessed with money. But I used to think I could fix anything with an Allen key and a hammer.      I always say this happened because of the genes in his family. Our old dog looked like that, you know, always had a thick stomach. I reckon it's like that with people, if your parents were sturdy, then you might take after them no matter what.      That's interesting, but isn't it also the lifestyle? I remember when we got together last Sunday at the Baptists' place. I was looking at that lovely jigsaw of theirs, and I nearly had a heart attack when the phone rang. It was my GP—had to tell me they're thinking about starting surgery in May for a suspicious lump. Makes me consider time and health oddly.      That is worrying. I can imagine the stress. I had a cousin with a bad operation in her youth and about five allergic reactions after. Poor thing, the doctor didn't take it seriously first off.      Life's got its ups and downs, hasn't it? You're all thinking, ‘How do I avoid problems?’ But you can’t fix genes. I always told my lass—well, she's sleeping now—that I tried to make her understand the value of a hard day's graft and that money’s not everything. Heh.      More importantly, it’s the love in the family and friends that counts. We had a man over the week go out of his mind because his partners were moving. Just one of those phases you can't predict, really.

Rather annoyingly, I've got to update the Moodle module for my computer software design class tomorrow. The university is pushing for a 'blended learning' approach more than ever, and I've been dreading having to make it all visually appealing with those interactive elements.      Honestly, if it's beginning to grind your gears already, I'm not surprised. I tried doing that for my systems architecture module last week, and by halfway through, I was just crying out for easier access to Excel. It’s supposed to be interactive, but it's practically like dragging your class through a spreadsheet.      Right, I get it! And when I talk to the support team, they only help with the most basic issues. It’s like they expect you to be fluent in Moodle by now. I’m half tempted to just chuck everything into a PDF and be done with it—my students could at least read something!      I know! And with the assignments in there too. I had to rework the whole rubric into those tiny tables, and once I realized I couldn’t even adjust the column widths—personally, I want to write to the developer and ask why they made it like that.      Honestly, sometimes I feel like we're both spending more time re-learning tech than actually designing content. But I guess, in some bizarre way, it is part of the job description now—being both lecturers and IT experts.      Absolutely. Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what I mean. I was just reading an old article on Tony Blair and how New Labour came about, and honestly, I can't say I miss it that much. And your views on that connect with the rise in populism? I see parallels in culture and politics — a hunger for authenticity, perhaps?      Per'aps.

Rather annoying when a new movie releases and all the relevant debates have already happened online. I feel like I missed half of the fun, you know?      Oh, I know exactly what you mean. Rather annoying when the petrol’s up, innit? Me an’ the lads had t’camp on a roundabout in Carlisle once. Nuttered cars were, blind as stuffed bats. An’ yer think y’can get some scrumpin'?      Aye, it een’t the first time I’ve bin stuck on a roundabout. When I were callor than most a you lot, I used to deliver tellys all ov’r Greater Manchester. It was wintery once, and me car was stuck in Salford for hours, but the bloke up t’tavern brought me a baked potato. Proper tasty.      I’d rather not get stuck like that. I still get a bit panicky if the tank’s below a quarter, to be honest. Drove from Bristol to Portsmouth in a rodeo of Range Rovers once — nearly died of boredom. I could’ve slept if I’d been allowed to.      I know the feelin’. Proper claustrophobic. Should’ve bunked over, or took a book. Nutter, though — we’d listen t’top forty two or three times as we circled and circled, waiting for someone bloody well smart to move.      Top forty? I used t’tune into Vera Lynn fairly often, still do sometimes on the long wave. When I were in the service, they played it at tea-time every day. Near enough every house had a wireless. Our food wasn’t full on, but the tellys were a rush.      Vera Lynn? Never heard of her. I grew up with The 1975 and Kaiser Chiefs — you know, about five decades off. My dad used to play Renaissance, which is even worse.      That’s proper posher then! I grew up listening t’Coldplay and the Arctic Monkeys. Then again, I was brought up near the Tyne — nothin’ fancy there. Still, any bloody music was better than the radio programmes I had t’record for me corpus work one time.      Corpus? What’s that then? Sounds bigggish.      Oh you know, it's where y’map the English language as goin' on — dialects, patterns, all that. Fun innit? I’ve got a gap in me data from North Wales though.      So y're collecting words? Like down ‘ere, we’d say 'chud' for belly, but up north we talk about the ‘barran’s’. Or them lads up in Salford all call it ‘wobbly bits’ if it's them women, always ruddy flapping about.      That’s gold. I’ve got to admit, me job’s better on paper than in practice, but it keeps me employed and I could do with that.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be at my flat. But anyway, it’s only temporary. I got the email from the association about the maintenance schedule this morning.      Yes, dear, we all have to do our bit. Be glad you’re staying with us while it’s sorted. Right, now, I’ve made a list of things you’ll need for your own place once it’s ready. A lot of this tends to get lost in the details, don’t you think?      Definitely. It was me sorting through the boxes during the move that I remembered things I'd forgotten like duplicate mugs and half-used seasoning packets. I swear someone must have taken the good ones.      Oh, I remember you saying something like that on the phone. I’m glad I asked Daphne to keep the old dining set for you. It’ll be far more useful than the modern breakfast bar you had before.      That means a lot, Mum. Honestly, I thought I'd have to buy a whole new set. I miss your Sunday roasts, by the way—personally, nothing beats the smell of rosemary and garlic as it bakes.      Aye, and watching you mess it up before getting it right. You’re a good cook now though. But I’m not sure how you ended up teaching language skills. You were always quite the analytic mind.      I blame Dad for the grammar obsession, and the coffee obsession. He always said language shapes the way you see the world. Besides, I travel a fair bit for work—there's a fair stretch between Bedford and Berlin.      Oh, how romantic it must be—meeting people from all over the globe. Do the different time zones get to you? Ron always found the jet lag brutal.      It does, a bit—being on a different rhythm every few weeks is hard. Though I strangely sleep best on the trains. Probably the rhythm of the land being different from the sea.      You always did stick out from the rest of us. Even as a young lad trying to catch weaver fish by the pond. Now, the kettle’s boiled—should I pour us some tea or do you want the American go-to of coffee again?      Tea, please—ginger this time. I had a cup the other day that tasted like what your cat left behind. It was a real mood kill.

Rather annoying the new A-Level system, innit? Seems like they’re trying to simplify it ‘n all, but I reckon it's jist makin’ it harder for the lads      Aye, we were talkin’ aboot it in our uni meetin’s. Got eeny PhD students wiv younger folks, an’ they were reckonin’ it all needs a clean-up.      Tha's a fair point. Oh, ‘ave yeh seen that new hairstyle Lucy’s got? I were like “blimey, that’s bold” – reminds me o’ yeh back in uni when yeh razored yon sides, only shorter.      Ha, I liked that. Fun to mix it up, innit? Different look each week. But I’d say stick wiv yeh roots if yeh’re a PhD student – makes breakfasts easier wiv the bristles.      Bloomin’ bleedin’ lot, innit? I’ve still got the clippings from that time I went for that Bob Dylan ‘do in Sunderland. Got laughed out o’ the shop.      That’ll be th’ shop on High Street, eh? I remember when it got rebranded as – what wos it called? “New Wave”      Yeah, an’ the staff were like they couldna even cut hair ‘til they passed an exam, innit? They wanted hair consultant accreditation. Honestly, I’d read books than faff wiv that.      Aye, and then the politicians ‘ave been tinkering wiv the NHS again. Not sure about this privatisation malarkey they’re trying.      Tha’s somethin’ else that needs plugghin’ up quick. No one in their right mind should ‘ave to queue like National Trust entrance if they’re unwell. I were dossin’ round a few ‘ospital wards last week, meetin’ some folks who’d been waitin’ for weeks.      He knows wha’t a crisis it is, but Parliament’s too busy takin’ selfies for the telly t’ fix the system.      Talk about sufficin’ – at this rate, dentists’ll be runnin’ hospitals in three bloomin’ minutes. Pass th’ remote. I wanna skip this news special on the petrol crisis. We’ve seen enough o’ that bellyache this week.      Yeah, why not? I were like “Andre, I’ve been fed oatcake and custard the whole week and yeh come home wiv 'cosy caravan'”      Still, it’s not like we’re in a warzone, innit? I think it's just media babe. Irrelevant. Television, innit. Makes me feel somethin’.      Aye, it’s practically minderzing the whole country. Remember when we bought that cute little fennel? What wos its name?

Rather annoying I could've got a scholarship fer uni, but they 'ad me on the list an' puffed off wi' it. Just luck, I guess. I'd murder fer a fag, though. Dunno what I'd do without 'em when things get stressful.      Oh een, I tried smoking once and felt like I 'ad a pigeon nesting in ma throat. Nae a fan. A lot o' me mates have stubbed em out an' said they’d rather get a job to pay fo’ rent anyway. Fer once, me parents were right about stuff lik’ that.      Still, uni’s dead expensive regardless, innit? I’d lik’e to think about doing My turkey, but I’ve already got overdraft anxiety. Y’r gonner hear the term “loan” more than you’ll ever want to. Blimey, I’ve even ‘eard breakfast, no universities teach 'ow tuh budget.      I know, innit? I’m stuck looking for part-time work whilst applying for full-time courses—sounds ery funny, if yer know what I mean. My Nan says if we’d’ve lived through the Black Plague, we’d still be chucking around like we’ve got extra coin spare, but I ain’t feelin’ that one.      Yeah, slap’s on the back of us all-like. All that history and still, here we are—messin’ 'bout wi' our degrees 'n someone else people's money. At least feminism made me a bit more aware o' the sh-t that goes on at uni. Still, sometimes I feel like I’m trying to make a dent in a dam wi' about five eggs.      Oh, come on, we’re trying th’ best we can! An’ that feminist sh-t? It's helped a lot, specially in the uni context. Burgled me like twice already. All that equality rubbish actually works. Just me on the outside, I was ‘ad to adjust how I looked an’ dressed when I started doing me GCSEs—don't even get me started on how people act 'cause I walked in with my head fiеr oon.      You're like a bloody activist now, goin' on aboot about suffrage and stuff. But yeah, I do agree, innit. It’s的好处, blokes sometimes don’t ‘ave a clue. I’ve been in classes where the lad’s think they're the head of the project just because they're born male. Rote, ‘tis mad.      I tell ya, my cousin near Cambridge said if they don’t sort out their finance department, the whole university 'll be out of business.

Rather annoying isn't it, how grown-ups just expect you to glue sticks and all—the friendships that once felt... you know, effortless? Just sort of stick around forever. I mean, sure, some last a lifetime, but others don't. No one ever tells you how to tactfully step back from people when you don’t want to be friends anymore. Not like ending a relationship, where people actually acknowledge that it ends.      Honestly, that's one of the most emotionally confusing transitions. It's not like it’s a business deal where you can just hit “end of contract.” You say you don’t want to see your old friend, and suddenly you're a villain. What’s worse, you feel guilty for needing that space. I’ve definitely had moments where I left someone hanging for months by the dumbest small talk, just too afraid to say, “I’m just not interested in spending time together anymore.”      Exactly. I've been thinking about this for a while. When I moved to London again after my year in Geneva working as a freelance translator, I realized I’d lost touch with half my old university classmates. Not out of malice, just life changes. But their messages were like, “Have you forgotten me?” It felt so immature—and it wasn't about them; it was about my own ability to let go gracefully. I almost became defensive because they were trying to cling on.      It’s so funny, because when I was younger, I used to live in the countryside just outside Enfield. I remember once phoning my friend Lynne just to cancel our evening plans—she had the kid flu and was miserable. I told her I understood and genuinely  meant it . But then I did it twice more after that with other people, and the pattern became “untrustworthy.” Like, “if you are suddenly not available, you’re avoiding me!” No one mentioned that some days, you just don’t have the energy for anything social.      Right. You can't expect people to give you space when you yourself are too polite to ask for your own. It’s almost like that middle stage of a friendship where you've outgrown a shared phase—you don’t have the same goals, you rarely laugh at the same jokes anymore. But the worst is still go along with it for politeness’ sake.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get it — everything's online now, and they’re trying to update the syllabuses and stuff, but honestly, I miss going into the library and just picking up a book. Not to sound nostalgic, but it felt less... well,  pressured .      I understand that, dear. I feel the same when I paint now. I used to work with oil, but now I have this new watercolour set, and I’m trying to get used to it. It feels almost like starting from scratch. Do you want to see it sometime? I’ve been sketching a bit since I made that sculpture last year.      That’d be lovely. I still remember when you did that sculpture for the school exhibition back in, what was it, 2012? The one shaped like a tree with glass leaves — it was amazing. Mum used to take photos of it constantly.      Oh yes, you were so little then, you didn’t even go to that exhibition. I think your uncle Derek was the one who truly appreciated it. He still keeps up with that sort of thing, as do you, I suppose, with reading so many books on art history.      Yeah, I’ve been reading –  Monet and the Impressionists  – really interesting stuff. I’ve even considered applying for an art history course after my degree. I’m already planning a trip to Paris, maybe the next time someone books a group tour. I’ve not been there properly since I was 15.      That would be delicious. I’m planning a trip to Vienna myself in the fall. Not nearly as exciting as Paris, I know, but the museums there — especially the Belvedere — they have some pieces that are close to my heart. I even met a few people in that museum years ago.      Vienna? As in Austria? That’s where you used to live before you moved here, right?      Yes, Vienna. We lived there for almost ten years after I finished my studies. It was a beautiful place, but it had its challenges too. Still, there are parts of it I miss — like the café culture, or the sound of the cobbled streets beneath our feet.      I’d love that — maybe we can travel together one day soon. Pass some of that art history on to me!      Well, you’ve always been quite the sponge for knowledge. Just don’t fall asleep over museum guidebooks like your cousin Lily does.

Rather skip the gym, if I'm honest. I mean, I've had my workout for the week—what with the walking around campervans and stretching my legs between wars and superstitions. It's a little thing we call “getting old,” you know. But you go on. You'll make mince meat of the place, I reckon. Light it up like a campfire.      I said I'd go if I had the energy this morning, which I don’t. It was one of those nights. We had wine and cards—and then when the chase started, I thought I’d won. Only I hadn’t! Still, I made sure I ate before we set off, only grabbed a few bits of that sausage you had left over from yesterday. Hope you don’t mind?      You're stealing pastry, and I'm sitting here like a good English host, hand on heart saying it's breakfast, no doubt about it. Should’ve given you some eggs or something. I know the milk's gone, but the eggs are still edible—just not quite full on English—settle for poached.      Yeah, I know, your idea of breakfast is a full English, and mine is granola in a country where the shops run out of toasties by 9. Ha – but it's all fairly nuts, isn't it? You and me, driving a campervan halfway to Tarnow at 8 am. Last night you were telling me, “this is what someone forty-something-year-old would do.” Yet here I am, twenty-five, preferably wrapped up in something warm at 8 in the morning and being told I should be out there doing ballet, or whatever it is about your gym.      No, no, listen. It's not a generational thing. It's that I know when I'm worn out. At my age, the idea of ‘gym time’ is less about vanity and more about keeping active. I remember when the gym was a badge of beauty—back when I tried to lose ten stone. Now, I just shuffle into a class that doesn’t say “hi” very often. Feminism and gym culture—terrible mix when you reach 40, I find.      Yeah, go on then. But it's more than that, isn’t it? I mean, in England, it's always the box ticking—what’s what your gender is supposed to be. Even in the gym.

Rather annoying power cuts we've had this week, ay? I was halfway through internet marking and  poof —dark as a midgie’s bottom.      Oh aye, I was tryin’ to boil a cuppa and the kettle just stopped sputterin’. Ruined eeny plans I had of drinkin’ me brewed tea with milk! My cup all warm an’ no milk. A right proper scandal if you ask me.      Imagine! I know someone said their lightin’ was flickerin’ when the power was out. That bloke up the road, Bill—he said it scared the life out of his cat. Of course, then the cat knocked over a hand-thrown mug I’d bin sent. Terry left it on the side by the kettle, an’ the cat, bless it, just gave the little push. It shattered like a thunderclap!      Oi! Brian told me that in his garden he’s planting some lavender an’ fennel to attract the bees. Course he did, but that man’s got no idea, no! He’s dug up the side of the path an’ now it’s lookin’ like a proper grave site.      Eh, I’d like to give him a hand – but it’s Terry’s deal, and I’ve just started on some new chrysanthemums for the front border. Silly things are all leggy, but I’m hopeful they’ll bloom out. The weather’s been so suspicious—up an’ down like a badger’s back.      Aye, I thought it poured yesterday, but today’s a bit of sun, eh? I did see Steve walkin’ past with the wife the other day. Both looking a bit worse for wear! Going to that festival by the park, Terry told me, but I bet the lot of ‘em came back with no less than five bags of rubbish.      Oh they told me ‘at it was a bit of a shambles. People dropped all sorts, an’ then of course the power outages meant the bar lunches were a complete disaster. Terry said someone took an omelette for a fried egg. Said it was a man with a blue goatee bin on the loo wall. If it was anyone I know, it sure was no one I’d like to meet in the loo.      Oi, I’ve been tidyin’ up me shed. Found a jar full of spiders’ legs I had forgotten about, and over half of ‘em were still alive! I’m not entirely sure what I did with ‘em, but I’m sure I let ‘em go in the woods somewhere.

Rather skip the hotel and just go to a campsite, innit? It’d be cheaper ‘n all... got heaps o’ mates who went last year, and I fancy a few days away where me phone can actually switch off.
