Oh, love, I were thinking more o’ een hotel with een bar and proper meals. Not sure about sleepin’ on een pitch… not after a recent back ‘ur. An’ I’d hate for you to be stuck with nae hot watter or nothin’.      Oh, come on, don’t be daft, Ma! It’s a holiday! Not a hotel week! Besides, the lads I go with, we like een good fire, singin’ songs an’ telling stories. Remember when we used to play back home in Widnes? Easier in campsites for that sort o’ thing.      I know, love, but you were younger... I’m just worried about the state o’ you lot, you know? I mean, I want to support you all, but I need comfort, if I’m going on a trip too. I’m not quite your age no more.      Aww, Ma, we can find a good mix then. Like one that has een – what’s it called – een mixed site, where you can have a tent or a cabin-like thing? I remember my mates saying somethin’ ‘bout a campsite in Dorset that's got ‘big improvements’ now. More like een seaside hotel than een pitch.      Yeah, that sounds a right plan. Chilled weekend in the sun, but with nae faff. I’d even bring een guitar an’ show you the lads my old rifts. Bet it’ll be good fun.      Yeah! And if we do that, I can bring ‘cosy up’ stuff, like blankets and proper sleepin’ bags? Like a sort o’ posh ‘roughin’ it’ vibe. Everyone can pitch in – me an’ Da can sort out the tents, Ma can cook us up some lunches, and Granda can spin the tunes?      Oh, come on, dear! I don’t even go spinning anything except the loo roll. If I go, it has to be in a proper cabin with a kettle in it, or I’ll be one sad receptionist.      Well, you heard the gal! You might have to learn a new lark ‘n this one’s not singin’ like I’m goin’ down the mines.      Honestly, both of you can take it or leave it. Just make a decision and then we can get booking it,

Honestly, I could've done without the whole ‘visiting parents on the weekend’ plot in  10 Things I Hate About You . Like, is that even relevant anymore?      I know, right? But I quite liked Mia, even if she was a bit naive. And Heath Ledger’s eeny weeny bit of screen time was sorely   missed  . Almost as much as the sequel.      Ayup! Why'd they even kill off Patience? It would’ve been so much better if she was like the school headmistress in the second film. Anyway… what did you think of the prom sequence?      That was fire, don’t get me wrong. But what’s up with the fact that Aaron and Bianca are like… destined, but then they’re not. Like, was I supposed to ship that? Or was I meant to be team ‘influencer meets posh girl’?      Honestly, at GCSE, I looked at that film, and I just thought, “I wish I had a guy like Patrick defending me when the lads in Y10 ragged me in the playground.” Still, I think it only works as like, a throwback… watching it now, it’s a little silly.      Mate, I got misty-eyed at the lyrics to  Hand in My Pocket . But seriously, after that, what did you think of the film’s relevance to education? Like, they’re in this super strict school and everything.      Yeah, it's oddly literal. Like, you had the letters and whatever, and then the whole ‘fee structure’ thing with Kat’s dad. You know, about how rich people walk a different path round the school system?      Honestly, that was kind of obvious. But then again, the film is a  Romeo and Juliet  retelling dressed up like 90s teen tragedy. Still, I reckon we'll all be discussing this in media studies next year. I tried to get my teacher to let me base an essay on it.      No way! What’d she say?      She said, “Okay for extra credit, but you're going to have to compare it gothic themes.” But I’m like, “I'm not even sure if Patrick is gothic, I’m just in love with his leather jacket and ‘I’m not like other guys’ act.”      Well, you're not wrong. But anyway, to switch gears—what about our trip to London next term? I’m already counting down the days so I can go to the National Gallery.

Rather annoying this new Facebook lot, isn't it? Seems they've changed it again—the buttons ‘ave all gone off and I ‘appen to be one o’ them that can’t get ‘old where me pictures are s’posed to go. No, I ain’t frightened by it like some, I just want eeny weeny  simple  buttons with ‘Post’ on them.      Oh I feel that, love. I nearly lost one o’ me best photos of young Brian when me mouse slipped—absolutely tiddy-winked me for a minute. But, don't you worry ’bout it like I did, George! It’ll come. I've got the patience of Job, really I have.      Honestly, you two, it’s not that complicated! I made you both safety folders on your computers and I explained it step by step. But I’m not surprised you forget. You’re still using laptops from the 80s!      I know what you mean, Sarah, even some of the students I teach struggle with it. It’s generational, really, and it’s not just tech. I mean, did you know that some still carry grief from childhood illnesses like chicken pox? It’s not considered a big deal these days, but I had a student who missed three weeks with it—she still limps on one leg from the complications.      Aye, I ‘ad that myself when I were a boy. Me and the lads ‘ad chickenpox and ringworm at the same time. Ruddy miserable it was. Some o’ the nuns at the school would give it their own way if they saw your head looked unclean. I about blocked me face up with all that balm and eau de cologne.      That’s because they were trying to be pious, George! Those nuns were just trying ‘ard. I treasured them. My Brian used to play with them at me house. They’d give him ‘sugar plums’ and read ‘The Bible’ with him while the rest o’ us rushed off to feed the children.      That’s what interests me—how people still cling to religion or a routine as a cure-all. I met a woman in my lectures who had OCD about opening doors left-handed or right-handed—no one in the room could explain it. She said it calmed her. But some of you older generations have that in spades!      Well, I don’t ‘ave OCD, I’ve got common sense, ‘as I always said.

Rather annoying when the oven’s on the blink, Christopher grumbled. I was just trying to rustle up a proper Sunday lunch, but no luck. It switched off on me mid-roast      Aye, we've had the same sort of dramas over here. We've been using the eeny weeny toaster oven more times than I'd care to reckon. Not much call for making a whole roast that way though, if you know what I mean.      It's interesting you mentioned the oven, Eleanor. I were once called out by a customer whose oven had packed up too... Right, I had to make do with a microwave and a sandwich to keep us going that evening. Not exactly posh      Ha! Microwaved sandwiches and calling it dinner – I've been there too, and I think it turned me off takeaways for a while. But forget the oven, I was actually thinking earlier this week about returning to Germany in the summer. I've got an old pal, you know, working out there in the publishing business      Christopher, you're always talking about other countries. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like the idea, but as someone who's got three kids at home – it’s rather difficult just escaping the country at the best of times, let along with school holidays and all      Truth be told, I've been through that too. Travelling with the young 'uns isn't exactly a stroll in the park. But my lass Alice, my youngest, absolutely adores Germany. Funny thing with the kids, is it not? You can’t be sure what will grip their fancy      I do miss the old days a bit, when the kids were smaller and we had more time for what you might call proper holidays. Not that I’d want it back unconditionally, but there was something, I don't know, rather nice about being passed off to sundry grandparents at me daughter’s age      Oh, I hear you, Eleanor. I sort of miss being able to sit and chat over a cuppa for hours without the 'phone going off or the computer pinging      Aye, I'd say that's the true luxury – goin' on holidays wasn't it. If I'm at home and I just chuck in a DVD, it's the boxset or something equally questionable. But still, I suppose it's better than nothing      From where I'm sat in the kitchen, I’ve been talkin' to Esther this morning.

Rather skip the new The Chemical Brothers album, to be honest. A bit too samey for me. Haven’t got the time or attention for it now anyway, what with all this internship prep      Aye, I heard that one and kind of zoned out. But it was alright. I'm more into live stuff these days. You know, just the energy of it all. You ever go with that Amon Tobin gig in Manchester this year?      No, not that one. Know some people who did go though. Didn’t seem to be the most rocking of gigs, like, more of a brooding vibe. I much prefer live bands, full drum kits and all that. It’s a bit more exciting, you know?      I totally hear you. Droning electronics and headbanging don’t really go together in the way a live gig with skin on skin action does. I've been messing with a kitchen in Exeter more than anything lately, but every now and then I drag the sticks out.      Ah yeah, tell me about it. I listen to the occasional drum solo, even if I’ve still got no sense of rhythm. Have you ever properly taught others how to play?      Not really, just helped out mates with their basics, like, making sure they weren’t totally out of time during our jam sessions. You?      No, not that much, but I did this work experience in an arts centre back in Nottingham. Worked with kids doing workshops. Funny stuff—more paint all over things than actual rhythm worked out. Still, it was good exposure for my CV.      That does sound useful. I mean, the arts centre angle gives vibes of a mission-driven vibe, you know? Not like some of the stuff I’m up against in catering. My sister’s planning on doing something similar, actually.      Cool, well, it's a different angle, I guess. I dunno how long waiting on tables could stick. Feels like it could get to you after a while. Do lunches and keep the chips from falling over?      Most of the time. But like I told my sister, go in with the right mindset, and it does get you appreciated in some circles. I’ve got a buddy who just started a gig as a sous-chef after doing some casual stuff. Minds made up to jump in and take it professionally.      That’s a contrast to me.

Rather skip the new drive-through café near the station, ain't it? That Domino Drives lot—what with the queues and all them bobbies skinnin' their ears on the tills, I'd sooner pop into somewhere proper with a bit o' character.      This is eeny mucky, I'll say. Not 'alf noisy out there today either—sounds like a whole gang o' teenagers by the looks o' this lot. Still, we're used to a bit o' noise. We've had our fair share of that in class when them lads kick off.      Still, I like this place, Mum. It’s got tables, proper chairs and they do the turkey sandwiches. You don't get them in the takeaways back home, do you? And the lemon cakes are good too.      Aye, the waiters here aren’t too bad neither. I've been here with a few o' me colleagues from the school over the years, you know. I told 'em the other day, I said—“You know, if I had me own shop, I'd put in a loyalty card as well and give extra slices o' cake as points go on.”      Well, if you opened one, I'd invest. I want to become an entrepreneur, you know. Got some ideas about a new kind of phone app—like for tracking homework or something.      Oh, well, just make sure to put your name in the app title, love. Make it like, “James' Homework Helper,” and it'll get downloaded by all the mums at school.      Not funny, Mum. I was being serious! But the problem is my dad says I should get a proper job and not mess around with apps. Says I should handle real things, like transport routes.      Aye, well your dad’s a traditional sod. He probably reckons it's a waste o’ time trying to grow nothin’ from nothin’. But stick with it, as long as you've got a plan.      So what are we gonna do next, anyway? Still set for the trip to Durham next week?      I think so, love. If it don’t rain too much. I’ve got the beds and sleeping bags box’d up in the shed. Got a couple o’ tents as well, if we need 'em. We’ll start off Saturday morning and take the old car. Just don’t fall asleep over the wheel, like last time!      Fair enough.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you lads than jumping through hoops for university... What's been going on with you, Tom? Still doing all that IT testing stuff?      Yeah, can't knock the job, mind you — bonus schemes and all — but it's beginning to grind a bit. Heard you've gone into teaching? English?      Yeah, I taught a few classes last term in this community college place. Not bad, alright. Got interesting folk coming in wanting to learn the lingo for when they're moving out or stuff. You know — "How to talk like a West Midlander" sort of thing. What with supply chains and all, bits of that My grammar still gets me sometimes — who am I to tell someone their accent is "wrong"? You're from near Birmingham, I think? Bronsgrove?      Mm, yeah. Just near the border up that way. Mum always said in my accent the word for "bath" sounds like "bath", so I still say it like that, even though I know it should maybe sound like "bath" written in short words. Got one friend still back home who calls "village" "viklage" for fun.      That's so typical of the Mate. I often tell my class that understanding these differences is key to understanding the culture. Now don't get me started on phone use in the classroom — one young lad comes in, says he's just starting at the language centre and expects me not to mention a phone once week.      Mate, is it me or is money and being able to live decently slipping away daily? Prime cost of living about daft. Couple I know had a baby last week — had to skip most of the baby things and just gone for that basic plug and play baby kit. You up for anything like that?      Nah, not for a while yet. Still got my sights on a bit of a fling in Spain I think. I hear there are some little villages there where you can live good and not end up being broke out of the blue with lunches and all.      Sounds spot on. You think you'd get around with your Spanish?      Mm, scratchy if you ask me. Just got hold of my line in language learning, between Spanish and the boxset binges.      So, have you made it to any conference or something in education?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh?      Aye, it's such a mither when you don’t get a call through, especially when it's important. I've been trying to reach my GP again about that blood test they promised I'd get after the scan. Honestly, it's taking eenough time as it is.      I reckon it's not easy on the other end of the phone either, but I know that from my lass. Oh, she started having some niggles with her tummy and she's been dragging her heels about getting it checked out. You'd think the signs would be enough, but no—she's as stubborn as a mule!      My son's been the same with his back. His teacher mentioned he's been off-kilter in class, and he's just been brushing it off. I told him, 'Look, you better not ignore it—your back’s not going to heal itself.' But he’s a bit of a lad when it comes to health, always says he'll tough it out.      That's the way of it, isn’t it? I suppose we all think we're made of stronger stuff than we are. I’ve been thinking a lot about my mum lately. She was just 60 when the cancer took her, and I can still remember that day—how long ago that seems. Now don’t get me wrong, I've been lucky. Me and you—we’ve been healthy up to now, someone said the other day—'health is a treasure' and all that.      They're not wrong. I think sometimes we take things for granted until it's taken from us. You know, about five years ago, I went through a real rough patch. My job had me frazzled, and I wasn't sleeping. I barely noticed the weight loss until one of my friends said something. I realized then I didn't look well at all.      That’s the mental side of it too, isn’t it? Mentally you can be shot to pieces while the body acts as if it's fine. I mentioned it to the doctor, and they were astonished I'd made do the way I had for so long.      I owe my family go bad really. They didn't let me hide it for long. My partner just said, 'No more excuses. You’re going in on Monday'.

Rather annoying the new changes at the school aren't they, Lucas? I know it's supposed to save costs, but the kids are often left hanging about for more than an hour at the end of the day.      Yeah, I've missed a couple of trainings. We've got this new eeny weeny block of coaches at the tennis club. I reckon it's not as good as most. I’ve only had one decent session where they actually taught us to play, instead of just running drills.      That's the thing, when you run a business or manage an operation, you can't just hand it over to people because they've got a short course under their belt. You need real experience and the right qualifications. I’ve met enough interns left and right who just weren't ready.      Dad used to take me to watch local football matches in Durham — the old place had character. But now it seems like everything’s all about the slick academy systems and GCSE grades over passion.      I want to do the apprenticeship, but Mumsays I should just stick with A-levels. She doesn't get that some of the best people I've met only started after an apprenticeship.      I work closely with a few apprentices now. Some of the marketing people I've hired straight from school, because they had a bit of drive and were hands-on. You don’t always have to go the university route.      There are pros and cons either way. But personally, I think knowing what a business actually needs is just as important — maybe more — than a degree in theory.      I agree with your dad, Lucas. Real-world experience is invaluable. That’s why I’m thinking about investing in this proofing and document management business idea. It's quite niche, but I've got the background and contacts for it to work.      If you do go for it, Mums, I might actually be the one to help you out with it. I could do some stuff on the IT side. We did a bit of coding at school.      Coding? That’s new. I thought you were all about football and tennis?      Pfft! I still am. I just really get into it if it's something I can turn into a side line in the future, you know?      That’s your mindset. It's all about planning ahead.

Rather annoying that the train’s a bit delayed, isn’t it? But at least it’s a nice first stop off to visit some old uni friends now they're down in Lancaster. I've heard they've got this little seaside town nearby, do they have somewhere decent for fish and chips yet?      Oh, you  have  to try the chip shop on Ayton Beach when we get there — I’ve been told it’s the best in the area. I’m so excited to be going back, actually. I’ve just moved to Leeds after my masters at the uni in Lincoln, and it's been ages since I went down that way.      Oh, the Lincoln uni still has such a strong reputation in the postgrad departments. I remember you were working on a specific comparative lit thesis, was it? Dostoevsky vs. modern British authors? Or did I get that mixed up?      Close enough — I did Anglo-Soviet in the early 20th century! That sounds more indulgent than it was, but I actually found it fascinating. Eventually I decided academia wasn’t for me, though. Got made redundant two years ago.      Oh no, that still sounds bloody awful. I can't imagine working on a thesis all those hours just to end up on the side of the curb, like, because the funding ran out. Did you have to pivot into something else?      I went back into education support — which is kind of what someone at my level is expected to do. I'm a language research admin now, which isn’t hotter than the job I had, but I get to travel and still speak to students about their career paths, so I suppose it's useful. You’re still working the co-ordinator role at the uni?      Yeah, that keeps me barely afloat. The unis are all investing so much in ‘digital transformation’ now, it’s like we’re all expected to rewrite the whole language testing system in a year instead of decades. At least my family is fairly settled. I still live in my parents’ converted cottage just outside of Aylesbury.      That’s lucky. I took the plunge and moved out after uni, but my sister still lives at home — she's still figuring it out, if you know what I mean. Did you ever think about doing a study-to-work trip along the coast like this when you were younger?

Rather skip uni today an’ go see The 1975 – they’re in Chester ‘ere. Dunno what I’m doin’ this week yet. I’ve bin stuck in the library studyin’ for them exams all week, feel like I bin brain-fried.      Got eeny plans fer wibben? Cos if you’re feelin’ like escapin’, I’m a-likey up fer a drive or summat too. I’ve bin listenin’ to their new album like ev’ry time I was stuck in the digs studyin’. It’s nutten like their first stuff, but I like it none the less.      Y’know somethin’, like that Mylo Xyloto album by them new kids ‘at tried to be Coldplay – I’m not a fan of all that twinkle twinkle nonsense. But nah, The 1975’re proper good live. I went once in Leeds a few years back – the crowd was mental, an’ they played all the old tunes so I still got through it.      Yeah, I know what you mean. Got Izzie with me a while back and she tried tellin’ me they were some deep intellectual bunch, but I’m more of a rock n’ roll kinda guy – Matey: Royal Blood, Cage the Elephant, summat with some real volume.      Aye, I dun’ mind them ‘ither. I’ve been into those lads too. Got in an argument with Mikey last week about whether they’ve run out of ideas – he said ‘they’re evolving,’ an’ I said they’re just runnin’.  laughs  But hey, it’s about taste, innit?      Exactly. We were lads th’ same age and not a care in the world. I mean, it’s all good fun to have debates, ‘cos we all like stuff that’s different. Izzie’s int’rsted in photography – told me ‘at I should get a better lens for my little compact. You still crackin’ on with that sprite of yours?      Oi, whaddya mean “crackin’ on” – I’m a connoisseur! I met this lass at a camera shop in Barnsley, an’ she recommended this lens an’ camera body that I might be goin’ for. She were proper nice, you know summat? I might’ve been blushin’ after I asked her about the shutter speeds fer photos in low light.      Yeah, why not? Aint like we’re not all goin’ to be stuck in our flats in sixthform, watchin’ memes an’ listenin’ to music. Might as well try an’ find somethin’ ‘at means summat long term.

Rather annoying that the red plague is spreading so fast, isn't it? I think it's because we've all got too big for our boots and tried to run this game solo. I've played pandemic with a group before in Barcelona with a few South African friends, and it's far calmer when you coordinate properly.      Aye, you’re right. Someone needs to be in charge of the teams. I don’t know if we’ve got too many chefs here. Oh wait,  there is a chef among us!       Haha, very funny Jerry. But seriously, I can handle logistics because of my kitchen experience—prepping, setting up the tables, getting stuff where it needs to go. Maybe I should be the logistics expert in the game, you know? I’m good at organisation, even if I’m not in school like you teachers.      Cats, better logistics breakfast, no doubt. I've been playing with a group in Cardiff at a social club and it's amazing how some games devolve into chaos when no one actually wants to communicate—especially when it involves concepts like 'event cards'. Y’know I’m decent with a poker face and bluffing when it comes to cards.      Ah, now that’s a skill. I’ve run countless workshops at charity events with fairly motley groups, and the trick is often to balance enthusiasm and strategy. All these dinars and players trying to win—messy. We might need a leader. Like, someone who can call shots and keep things on track.      Well,  I  did my master's on collaborative group dynamics and here we are—clearly  not  collaborating! We need a balance of strengths. Anna , take this [hands over a clipboard]. Sam, you are the data cruncher. Jerry, you're logistics. You’re the motivators. And Lew—Lew, sit down and stop arguing with the rules. We'll go one round where we don’t comment on each other's actions, just focus on getting the outbreaks under control.      Is that right? Well, I taught a couple of teens to do team building exercises with no verbal communication once, after a bullying incident. Total mess—had to go back to basics. Maybe if you all had to work in teams of two? Then, no one individual thinks they can ‘run the show’. Lift your eyes from the table and look around you.      That could work.

Rather than going out for dinner this summer weekend, what if we do something a bit different for Emily’s birthday? I was thinking, CBeebies is doing a pantomime special on Sunday afternoons this month, and I thought we could film the one with "Peppa Pig" or "In the Night Garden" and have a little movie night at home. Then we can make cupcake pops or something a bit ambitious with the kids. What do you think?      Ooh, CBeebies panto! I remember the one where Lady Zayka sings, but the Mudda monster steals the sparkly onions. I  always  sing along with the puppet people, don’t you, George?      I liked the jelly! When’s the one about the jelly? I want to be a jelly dragon and bubble in the world like Ruby. It goes  gloop-gloop-gloop !      Well, here’s the thing — if we do the movie day plan, we can even do some activities inspired by the show. I’ve got a Water Quest outdoor adventure story I wrote for World Book Day last year that we could shorten a bit to read to them. It’s based on dragons and knights… plus, I can work in a little sea jelly theme if that’s the one they pick, George.      That sounds fun. Let’s have some apple juice and finger sandwiches while you read. I’ll get the colorful paper and stickers so they can make their own story covers. Emily also loves making sayings like “GOSH!” and “OH LALA!” like the characters do. She wants to be a “sayings dragon!”      I can say about five dragon speeches. I’ll show you the best one:  “You shall not pass! Unless you have a jelly!”  That one I made up yesterday after we watched the sea episode.      George, that’s actually quite dramatic for a seven-year-old. I think it’s time we got those Dragon Speech cards I made for them printed out. I could stick them to the side of the sprite bottles. And if they’re lucky, we can wrap it all up with chocolate birthday stars. I’ve set a budget of around £20 for the treats — no goody bags, just a nice little keepsake box for each of them, like the pirate ones I bought for Mother’s Day last year.      That sounds perfect. I can make special emoji cups with messages in them.

Rather annoying the wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp week after week. You'd think by now it would at least warm up! Mind, I think I might be moving out of my flat soon. No space and the landlady’s gotten a cat — can’t een sleep at night with the thing dashing about like it’s got ADHD.      Oh no! A cat? That’s  so  much more trouble than people give it credit for. I think it’s just me and the flat for now. Didn’t even want to start internet dating after what my sister went through last year! Honestly, I don’t need someone to outsource my life to — and now that MySpace is obsolete, I’m not even left with a timeline of embarrassment, which is the only upside.      Fair enough. But if you're moving out, you’re welcome to plant your details in my address book. My house is spare in parts at the moment. Only thing wrong is, you’d have to be okay with the clatter of spanners and drills over the weekend, and maybe some DIY fumes — I’m engineerin’ a shed to go with the garden.      Sounds… domestic. I tried workin’ from home the other day. My partner Mateo brought in a pot of beans, and the room smelled like a sauna and somethin’ fried by seven o'clock. If I could just find a proper job where I wouldn’t have to work forty hours and still smell suspiciously of my own cooking, I’d be a happy girl.      You shouldn’t have to be apologizin’ for beans! Most people are lucky if their home-cooked meals don’t smell like turmeric and regret.      Turmeric is practically holy! Going back to the moving conversation — I have to decide whether relocation is healthier. My back’s been out again since I guest-taught at a primary school and had to tote a year six child across the playground during an inspection.      Arche!       Cough cough  Yeah... always trying to do the right thing and ruin your posture.      Still, I’m around if anyone wants a man with a drill goin’ on in their living room or a shed full of questionable air quality. I’ll even throw in a cup of strong bloomin’ tea and your choice of cake. Brought it in for lunch.      As long as it ain’t that rhubarb crumble you made last time...

Rather annoying when the book club meeting finds its way into post-work chatter about childhood, isn’t it? But honestly, I rather like discussing those old toys from your box we all had lying around. It transports you, doesn’t it? Remember that ceramic rabbit I had as a child—my nan bought it for me during a market day in Boston. It got broken and handed down to me like it was some sort of heirloom. A lot of childhood memories are tied up in objects, aren’t they?      Oh, absolutely! It was the same for me. We didn't get toy shops often in Peterborough back then, so even a cheap plastic tractor was a treasure. What I found fascinating was how some of us had toys our parents made themselves, you know, like homemade spinning tops or puzzles. My mum would involve me in these little projects: hand-stitching felt animals with bits of old clothes. Made better memories than, say, buying them online now. Less shiny but far more emotional value, you know?      I have to say, the memories I have are more about food and comfort, if I’m honest. My nan would always make shortbread cookies every time I visited. I think she got the recipe book from some local library in Southend. She’d write it out herself in her lovely script on pieces of paper I still keep in my kitchen drawer. Funny thing is, despite her basic kitchen and that recipe, the cookies were better than anything you can buy at Marks & Spencer now.      That’s so beautifully said. Makes me consider how much our language and dialects affect the way we talk about these things too. Take you, Pauline—I hear the slight twang in your speech when you talk about your roots in the south-east. And the different areas we come from affect not just how we speak but how we value things. I mean, growing up in Boston in Lincolnshire, there’s that flat, open feel that’s quite different from Peterborough or even Essex.      And work—oh, I shouldn’t even mention it at a book club. But hearing you talk about being in admin and HR always gives me a different lens on management versus sales. I do love working in sales—it’s a thrill, trying to close a deal, the psychology of it all.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand that they love the mountains and the peace and quiet—my grandparents and I were often reminded of how lucky we are to have a few days away from the hustle and bustle. But honestly, they have to bring up the weather  every five minutes .       laughs  Yeah, they’re good on that. My parents used to say the same thing when I was a kid—like every rainy day back home was easier or something. It's not like it poured every time they were gone. Still, I guess when you get older, you just start appreciating the little things even more.      That's just it, love. On our trip up to the Lake District, I remember saying to your dad one day, “Right, if I never see a single cloud for the rest of the year, I won’t complain.” And you’d better believe I meant it. But I hated myself for moaning straight afterwards when the next day was clear as a bell.      Well, that’s just life for you—always one weather complaint, one missed opportunity, one bad meal. I never did quite get that trip to the coast when we were in Skegness. The kids were excited, and I remember arguing all the way down about whether the hotel had been overpriced, and then it ended up being the best trip I’d had in years.      Oh, I remember that! We rode the donkey for ages, someone got stuck in the sand pit—your dad was a prat, Grandad.      Ah, now that's the real memory being dragged out! I was  trying  to save money at the ice cream van, and I ended up standing there talking to a donkey for二十minutes.      You were telling that exact same story to the hotel receptionist, if I’m not mistaken. Then she laughed so hard her colleagues passed out.       grins  Classic. I think it was funny because no one really knew what else to do with themselves. Like, what do you do with a retired grandad with a donkey and five whingeing kids? Probably play Bingo, you think?      I think the real magic of that trip was that it was supposed to be about “escaping the kids” and it just ended up being filled with the kids anyway.      Exactly. So I’m not sure if we ever had a grown-up moment the whole trip, apart from when your gran bought three pounds of lollipops from the shop on the way back.

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That phone lot. My Wi-Fi's been playing up ever since I got the new mobile plan. You'd think more bands would improve coverage, but I dunno, probably it's just £20 a month down the toilet.      Honestly, it's all the same with me. I use an older model and reckon it catches signals better than these fancy smartphones. I taught my class this week about signal strength and frequencies, but honestly, none of them gave a toss. They just want to scroll TikTok and get free games when they should be learning grammar.      Honestly, who  chooses  TikTok over the real world? Still, I can't blame 'em entirely. When I was at uni, I lived off of messages, memes, and Guardian articles. But anyway, I think the real issue is network reliability in the North. Birmingham's better than some, but still—not up to scratch. I was in a café in the city last week and had to switch providers to get coverage. Madness.      It's not just the phones, luv. I’ve been up half the night trying to diagnose why the boiler's supplying lukewarm water. I’ve read something on municipal engineering forums and it says it could be a faulty thermostat or a blockage in the system. But I swear it's one of these modern systems that no one understands anymore.      If I weren't so hopeless at DIY, I'd help you out. Honestly, I think I dropped a spanner in a pipe once and it's probably still rolling around in the wall.      Any chance I could swing by after work and take a look? I did an electrical course years back. Not a pro, but I might spot something. And if not, I could at least be your plug-man extraordinaire. You up for that? I need a good distraction from the news, honestly. All that tragedy about the wildfires and the economic slowdown. I'm going mad reading all that.      Aye, that'd be crackin'. Just let me know what time you're free. And thanks, mate.      Speaking of going mad, you remember that time I tried growing herbs on the windowsill? I overwatered them and killed three basil plants. Just one of those small plant-based crimes no one will ever know about.      Oh yes, you made me feel guilty for giving mine a little extra attention after I saw those viral videos of gardeners singing to their tomatoes.

Honestly, I still can't get my head around how Reg ended up working in Saudi Arabia for two years. I mean, I get it's a massive opportunity, but I can't imagine living there. The rules are so strict. Do they even let you go out at night?      Yeah, I'm kind of curious myself. I think they do have expat zones where people can hang out after dark. From what I've heard, the best part is the salary. You're practically bankrolling yourself there just to do a regular job. Reg said once he could afford a decent house with what he was paid each month.     Mate, I wouldn’t last the weekend in Saudi. You can't even get a pint after 10! The most interesting thing is the food – I heard the kebabs are next level. I think he even managed to take us all for a trip down memory lane last summer, remember that?      Haha, yeah, he’s got the taste for that, right enough. I told him I’d pack the tent and walking boots for one of those big desert treks they do, but I don’t think he was as keen as me. Still, two years is nothing in life… but it's a hell of a long time when you’re apart from the ones you love, eh?      Totally, Anna’s going to miss him like crazy. We’ve all started trying to make plans already so he doesn’t feel like he’s just disappears. I’m still trying to sort out his old flat. It needs painting, so I’m going to paint the living room a bold grey. It’s going to look amazing!      You know I love interiors, so any tips for the living room area? I’ve been thinking about redoing mine too. Satnavs and Google Maps barely gave me any idea where to run my wires. My sister had to show me how to do her light fixtures.      Honestly man, it's a minefield. I once tried to patch a wall myself and ended up making a crack run from side to side. Let’s just say, trying to find the right ladders and tools in B&Q is no easy feat either.      Aye, I’ve gooked up my fair share of walls trying to cut corners. But if you're in, stick with the professionals.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, ever since I moved to瑞典, I've been struggling with this dry skin. Maybe it’s the weather up here? Not like Wellington, where you always had this sea air. Not to mention those long winters in Stockholm!      Yeah, I'm telling you, I used to think I was just overreacting. But then Sarah here, she said something that stuck with me—she got this prescription treatment after a GP appointment. It was costing a fortune, but it worked wonders. I wish I could just chase it up but the bloke at the clinic said to wait a couple months.      What’s strange is that both Alice and I had the same symptoms, but only she got the prescription. It makes me wonder if the clinic here is underfunded or something. The lights turned off at 5 in the morning the other day!      I've been thinking about this for a while. When I was back in Dorchester, you didn’t have to prescribe a treatment to actually help your skin—there was this shop, a bit like a pharmacy, where I bought this balm. It was made from calendula and something called ... I’ve forgotten the name. Doesn’t work quite as well as the prescription one, mind you.      Oh, that does sound familiar. I remember my mother using something similar when I was a kid. If I could just find out the brand name, maybe I could order someone to get it for me. Alice, can you check the Internet for that balm? Some cal something—maybe calendula?      Can you believe I hadn't even thought of it until about five minutes ago? I mean, it's such a typical New Zealand thing to be obsessed with herbal and plant-based stuff. Not that I mind, it just feels a bit strange to have to go back for basic things like balm.      I have no idea. I'm just glad I brought it up. I tried using some of the ones sold here in Stockholm, but they were way overpriced and didn’t help with the itching. It was just—ugh—way too thin. Defo not delivering the results.      Exactly. Look, I think it's more of a cultural thing. In New Zealand, we're surrounded by greenery. People use plants for almost everything. Medicinal, you know—like treating flu or skin irritation.

Rather annoying when the devices don't understand our accents, isn't it? I was trying to use the voice assistant last weekend and it just kept mishearing me. I said "Replay the song", and it thought I said "Rocket the stone"!      Oh aye, it's all the same with these newfangled gadgets 'ere. They're all trained on posh voices. You’ve got to speak slow and clear like a human textbook, right? If I try to speak like 'ow I normally do, it's like talking to a wall.      I can't even get it to make a cuppa. I said "Make a cup of tea" and it made a cup of  tree ! I swear it left it on the back steps, just standin’ there. But anyway, I think it's funny. Living with accents, aren’t we? I remember when I was younger, I hated my Essex twang — thought it sounded posh, and looked down on my own family’s way of speaking.      I mean, it's not all bad, is it? Our accents make us who we are. They carry stories and roots. My old man had a Kent-country burr, proper working-class lad, from Chatham. He used to say it: “When I was young, we had to cycle miles to the pub 'fore parents thought to pick us up.” You know what I mean?      Honestly, I've been thinking about my granddad's voice a lot lately. He was from Gillingham — you know the type? Straight-talking, no-nonsense. He used to make such a point of speaking clearly in public meetings. But at home, he'd just talk proper fast, like “we ain’t got all day!”, and that was that.      Maybe that’s the tension, ‘cos we all have different ones. My wife used to say that I drank too much and it made me shout too much at the telly. I said, “Well, you stick to talkin’ and I’ll stick to shoutin’,” and that was a long row over "Eastenders".      I’ve seen it too. My best friend's parents go at it on the kids about whose accent is better or inferior, and it just makes the kids confused. It’s like, bloomin’ hell, your accent isn’t the sum of you.      That’s where those issues crop up with children, especially with custody stuff. I’ve heard of cases where one parent insists the child talks like them, and the courts get involved.

Rather skip the new kid’s party entirely if I were you. A few people her age would be better. Besides, the boys are old enough to be more selective now. Not that I've got time to be holding their hand through it all.      It's not like that, I promise. She’s nice. We’ve been in a few classes together and we’ve played Minecraft all last summer. I reckon we’re gonna start working on the science project together, too. You said I could pick some interesting people to do it with.      Didn’t say I don’t trust her – just means I trust your abilities even less. Last time I left you to it, I found out about some kind of Halloween party you were planning with Marco and his mates. I’m not sure I want to hear the story, but go on then.      It was just for dress-up and cakes! Domino breakfast, Marco said. I said no. Honestly.      Yes, and then you thought, “What’s the harm in a baked Alaska?” Or was that me?      That was you, but I liked it! You even grated the cheese for the grief of it, remember?      Because I wanted to see it explode from the heat. Not ideal – but it made for a good story and, let’s be honest, you boys weren’t going to clean that mess up after yourselves.      You cook like that on purpose just to make someone else clean up. Honestly. And you know what? It worked every time.      Also, it's a Programme Director’s prerogative to occasionally mess up your kitchen as part of your character development. Not that you've all grown up to be proper adults or anything. Not yet.      You’re not that old. I mean, you're not my stepdad.      Oh yes, well if I recall, he did once have me on the carpet over a grilled cheese sandwich comment he thought I approved of. Not that I ever did. Not my words, and certainly not what I raised you to believe.      Grilled cheese sandwiches do not discriminate, Ma.      Enough of that. That's one go-to argument I never wanted to hear directed at me – and definitely not from you. Just remember that between choosing friends, doing your homework, and what your age of consent legally doesn’t allow you to question yet, there’s still some boundaries you need to think about.

Rather skip the toast an’ go for porridge, mebbe. I had me fill o’ sausages last weekend an’ me bowels be skinnin’ like a dog’s after a rabbit! Got me tea? Not the green stuff, I mean—get a pot o’ proper leaf in it een? I cannae understand folks today an’ their fancy brews.      Aye, I dinnae ken that! I got me mug o’ darrrk coffee, like it’s a cup o’ motor oil and warm! An’ don’t start with me ’bout my porridge—put some Lakelands flapjacks in it the other night, likkered it like a MySpace profile. You’ve met enough eccentric folks in Japan to know I go aboot the place like a fox in a chicken shop!      Aye, aye, better than breakfast, no doubt. I’ve been thinking, after I’m done at the uni today, I’m givin’ them flying lessons a shout. Oi, I’ve fancied one o’ them Cessnas since we flew up t’Edinburgh t’see meself back in the day, remember?      Blooming hell, Jan, you want t’be takin’ off like a Royal Air Force, and I barely stay awake on the plane unless I’ve got me phone to TikTok through! You know what I got mailin’ me the other day? A request someone said I looked like a suspicious relative in a family tree algorithm. That’s not a compliment— mate , that’s a red flag!      Aye, social media, eh? Not nearly about people any more—more about what your mam likes for breakfast and who had vibes th’ weekend you skipped! Anyway, that New York trip I’m taking—booked for June—think I’m going for the jazz and the skyline. Though I heard rubbish about the refuse collection—they leave the bins out for three bloody days! Bleedin’ rude!      Aye, you’d miss the yellow-sponsor lampposts here with your nuanced sensitivity to municipal whines. I took the kids there once—swore the lift had t’have the number of floors go up  twice , if you ken wuh I mean! You ever think about goin’ back to Japan? That bloomin’ place has your soul embroidered on the sumo helmets!      I think I’m startin’ to miss the rice boxes ’n the talk o’ ‘isching’ when I say fish! It’s a world apart from all this oatcake nonsense. Speaking o’ which, y’got any plans t’day apart from y’usual routine o’ eyebrows-twitchin’ at Facebook and scribblin’ love letters to me?

Rather annoying when people text saying they're "late", but they end up turning up hours after they said they’d be "after". I mean, is there a term I can use that actually means  truly  late?      Look, it’s called "lying about your timing", but seriously, you use "late" and then just say,   "I mean it this time!"   with a funny voice. It never works, but it helps show you’re running out of patience.      If you're into the Scrabble angle, you could literally just use the word  delinquent . It means "failing to do something required," so depending on the circumstances, you can dock someone’s minutes and hit them with "You're a time delinquent."      I had a A Level exam and I turned up late because of traffic, and the invigilator literally said "You're practically British late this time!" like a joke in bad taste. I didn’t get extra time, of course, but the phrase stuck. What does "British late" mean? Like, if we're late in a place where people take time seriously, are we  especially  late?      Good on you for not risking it. I remember when I got to uni late for my first lecture because I mistook the timetable, and the prof said something like, "I see you're still clocking in at 12.30 for a 9 o’clock lecture. Who taught you how to read?" I said my mum, and half the class cracked up. Some things don’t need explaining.      Anyway, speaking of university courses, did you know the word "scrabble" comes from a type of noise? Like the kind birds make—rough and jumbled. It kind of fits that game you’re playing where it's all letters and chaos.      True story. And that’s why I always aim for that triple word score with the most awkward letters. I think it's a chef thing, you know? I sort of see the board like a tray of ingredients being messed with—try to make lunches of letters.      Some people play it like you’re delivering a poetry slam by snack time. That's how go for it on your own if you're confident. Just don't expect me to not pirate out that  Word Genius  boxset or something.      So, have you made it to the Chelsea Flower Show yet this year? I heard it had like, a virtual tour on the app or something over this past weekend.

Rather a damp day, isn't it? That’s the weather for you—just when you'd think it’d be bright and sunny, it decides to chuck more than a droplet on the nose. I told yer yesterday we should’ve pinned up those daffodils before the rain set in.      Aye, I was just thinking the same. I reckon Bill at the post office said most of the flowers will hold out if they’re in a dry spot, but we’d best inspect them later. You know, just to be sure. They do get a bit drooping when the wind's up too.      Aye, and don't forget the ones out back near the wall. They like that bit of sun, bless 'em. I left the watering can inside by the back door, so if we feel sprightly enough in the morn', we can give 'em a brisk top-up. I've no doubt Winnie'll want to see a bit of colour in the garden for the Easter morning walk, you know how she is about that.      Oh yes, Winnie, and she does take such delight in them flowers. Remember when she planted that marigold last summer, and how proud she was when it bloomed? She kept telling all the old ladies at the club – “It's got the same golden cheery look as my Jim used to have when he pinched those toffs’ pastries at the war!”      Ha! Now there was someone with a cheek to spare. I often doubted whether he really did it, mind. Mary—what's the time? It's been ages and still tea unbrewed!      You know I do like me tea after a nice long bicker! But you're quite right. I'll be right there. Going to be frosty cold by the time it does arrive, but that’s just a ‘proper’ cuppa for you. All the others, you know, have gone soft on sugar these days. ‘Blast the taste, just give them sweet,’ they say!      Aye, but we’re old-fashioned types with proper palates and spots of digestive biscuits to match the tea. Reminiscent of the ones my Mummy used to get from the goody shop on the high street. Not that it was fancy, nor very far in quality, but it filled the belly, and that was the main thing.      I can still remember the day we first went together—fresh off the bus and belly as empty as a church on sermon day.

Rather annoying this new train station delay, isn't it? I've been trying to get down to Exeter for ages and the thought of having to wait even more is wearing thin. I've been over this with my nephew in Exeter, and he says the local paper says it'll open sooner now than previously expected. Do you believe that, Annie?      Oh Bill, I've heard that too. The community group in Wellington has been pressuring the council, and it seems it's started to work. Honestly, it’s high time the line got modernised. The services are so erratic compared to how they used to be when we were growing up.      It’s taken long enough, isn’t it? My train journey here from Bristol last week had left so late that I missed the dinner hour. And what with the recent array of local news — like the plans for the new housing estate near the station — I can understand why it’s delayed.      Yes, yes, you're not wrong there, Jo. Still, the delay isn't why I brought it up—actually, it reminded me of the lovely meal we had up here in Wellington yesterday. What did you call that herb you used, Annie?      Thyme, dear. Well, from the window box. We planted it last spring with the help of young Mitchell, the lad next door. He’s quite the little herb expert now.      I could try growing thyme too, maybe for salads this summer. Oh, and also, I downloaded a new fitness app recently—bits of a discovery out there in the digital world. It’s called  HealthPath , and it does meal plans in tandem with workout schedules.      Fitness apps, eh? I've seen those on the telly a fair bit. My sister Sarah tried one that told her to do squats every time she watched the news, and she nearly took the telly out!      That’s not far from the truth. But Jo, I think it’s a marvellous idea. I could stick to one too—don’t know if I’d manage the workouts with this old back, but the meals do sound doable. I’d be set for the year with tinned tomatoes, brown rice, goji berries, and a few strategically placed thyme sprigs.      It really individualises your needs, Bill. You can change your dietary restrictions and goals—it even asks for allergies to build safe recipes.

Rather skip uni today, haven't even opened my books since last week.      Yeah, got to be honest, I went to that seminar on European politics and stared at the clock for about three hours. Nothing but theory and charts, I felt like I was watching paint dry.      Same, I sat through one on Shakespeare and tried to sleep basically. Classic literary genius? Maybe. Held together by Velcro and wishful thinking? Definitely.      Honestly, someone should do a doc or something like "Shakespeare Didn’t Eat Pasta" and make it bingeable... like, without the soliloquies.      Yeah, I'd watch that like a documentary turkey on Christmas. Still, enough about uni. You going to the Nottingham game this weekend? Oliver said they might actually beat Manchester City this time.      Cats are better than breakfast, no doubt. I've been playing Fifa for hours each night trying to get the tactics right, thinking, maybe if I train the virtual team, I'll somehow transfer the skill over to real life.      I don't think your Fifa insight counts as grief when real football let's you down. Speaking of, how's work at the bar doing? You still booking stag weekends?      Yeah, actually it's bonkers. Some of them have been quite odd journeys—like the one who booked the stag went full Liam Neeson in London and then spent the rest of the week trying to avoid the police.      No way! Some nutty ones out there. So, have you and Georgia split up yet? I heard she spent the weekend crying in about five different pubs.      She’s watching “The Theory of Everything” again and crying at the fact that Stephen Hawking only had motor neurone disease. I'm just here like, 'mate, he was still high on knowledge, probably' and she's like, 'yes but it was all tragic'.      You mustn't stick to such emotionally damaging films. You should’ve taken her to see the latest horror or something dystopian—less tears, same vibes.      You're a gem sometimes. Yeah, go out more on your own if you don’t want to be alone in the line of sob stories. You're always dragging course mates off to cafes and your house. How's all that working out for you?      Honestly, it's just easier than hearing about third-year breakup dramas or exams over text. They say silence is golden, I’m just... busy earning that gold.

So did you really just take a 4 am train from Oxford to Cambridge just for this coffee?      Pretty much! I figured I’d surprise my mam with a visit after uni, and this is the only £20 train the day allows—get on at 4, make it in by 6.  Totally  worth it, though. Haven’t seen you in… what? A year? A year and a half?      Oh my god, yeah, time’s flying. We need to be better at scheduling catch-ups. So, how’s Oxford treating you? Still frozen to your bones even in  this  weather?      Still? It’s like that all year, isn’t it? The chill goes straight through you. But I’m loving the job, honestly, even if I do get the odd ‘Oxford is for dreaming, not working’ look when I’m in the marketing office in town. Haha. And don’t get me started on my ex, Ken—don’t say the name.      Oh no, tell me—person inappropriate email? Cheating? Background obsession with landlines as décor?      Nothing quite as hysterical—it wasn't  that  bad, thank you. Just relentless communication – texts at 3am, hovering in my flat,  insisting  on my new flatmate learning to knit. I couldn't even work. And then he basically assumed we’d be cohabiting by now. Ugh. But you won’t believe the upside – he moved out a week later and sent me this adorable letter saying he realises being ‘prioritised all the time is a special requirement.’ I about choked on my muesli bar.      [Laughs.] Honestly, you and your exes—I’m still barely over the guy who unironically mentioned to the entire pub ‘she must be hiding stuff since her phone passed 50% and I haven’t seen it drop!’ But okay, moving on. I tried something new for dinner last night—couscous as a side to salmon. Websites said it’s  easy , right? Well, I must have added extra cinnamon… or water… or something.      Oh no go—did it come out like sand or like… sauce?      It was between a gritty mud box and an aggressively sweet dish. My brother’s in Paris, visiting fluency classes and writing posts like “Bread crusts are moral in France.” True to life?      That’s honestly better than this guy I’m subletting from near Cambridge. Claims Channel 4 drama is softening the English, like it's a language battle.

Rather annoying when the new seedlings don't take, innit? I've got this basil that's potted up and everything, but no luck yet.      Yeah, sometimes they just don't pop. Not to worry, the mint in our kitchen window thrived after a few failed attempts. Right mess at first, truth be told. 'Course, if it's not tropical, they don’t need that much sun, but I know that from my nan, so don’t take it as gospel!      Aye, and what about repotting? Do you reckon I need to shift it into a bigger container soon? I don't want it to outgrow its pot before it's even well rooted.      Nah, better to give it a little time. I've been following these tutorials and I think the first sign is when you can see the roots coming out the bottom. Or when the soil dries quicker. Plants are kinda in tune with their own needs, as odd as that sounds.      Good to know. It's just one of those things—my nan always said, 'You don’t grow plants, you grow with plants.' And she’d always say that while baking something—usually shortbread.      Hmm, baking – that’s a new hobby I’ve gotten into because of the long evenings. One time I nearly set off the smoke alarm trying to make a soufflé!      Honestly, I'd stick to simple things—breads or biscuits. When I was younger, I made Mary Berry’s Victoria sponge and it was a mess. It collapsed like a deflated balloon!      I about did the same with a Christmas cake. But talking of baking, I had my nan over for Sunday roast not long ago. She still makes the best Yorkshire pudding—so light, it’s just,  fluffy !      Agh, I wish I could replicate it! I always end up with something more like a pancake. You must’ve inherited all the good genes, then.      Aye, well I think it's partly the patience, partly the ingredients. Still, I’m happy with what I can do. Oh, go on then, tell me about your parents—were they at your brother’s wedding in July?      Oh yeah, nan and your dad went. Mum was planting tomatoes in the garden all day and refused to take any pictures with the guests. Typical, innit?      Yeah, classic Mums. But I mean, the garden’s been great to her, right?

Rather skip the queue at the café, I've made us a decent coffee and brought it in with me. I got the rather fetching one with the cardamom and whole milk—remember how we’d joke about that back in our university days?      A touch of nostalgia in a polythene cup, eh? That’s more of a treat than I deserved after marking that blasted module on British literature. I’ve only got three left to grade, and I swear, half of them think Chaucer’s just a brand of bread.      Ah yes, the kids these days. Though I suppose we shouldn’t be too hard on them. I was reading the other night about how many footballers now are bringing their young kids to training sessions. Terry left his son at the pitch, and the lad nearly got shouted at by one of the physios for playing with the cones. You’ve got to wonder, when does the child actually just get to be a kid for a bit?      That’s the downside of celebrity culture—and I suppose not just in football. I was over at my sister’s the other day, and she mentioned that two of her snooker-playing cousins are only ten and twelve, yet they’re already watching live tournaments and mimicking shots. She got worried it might be a bit much for them.      You know, I had a cousin nearly sixty years ago who started as a boy policeman in Cairo. His son’s now in the armed forces in this country. Spent his gap year sailing around the world, and here he is, a military man in his thirties. Makes you wonder if being ‘military’ runs in some people’s blood, or if we just make our kids want it.      I had a lecture today on civil service entry requirements. One of the students asked me if it’s harder to get into the police force than to become a barrister. Honestly, I had to check that. I told him the minimal uniformed strength was quite an issue, but that attitude is changing. I think people see the security in it.      Perhaps. While people chase a new kind of security in various ways, I’ve been taking proper care of my garden this weekend. The magnolia tree in the back has finally started blossoming after I cut back the hedges. Thought I’d let that serve as a metaphor for academic discipline sometimes—prune gently and you’ll be rewarded.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what happens when everything goes on her own schedule. The first mince pies are always out by the weekend, yet somehow I’m stuck prepping the rest of the lot for the full £20 spread the week before as if I wouldn’t be busy myself. Got a meeting on Monday, of course. It was supposed to be on Friday, but they moved it on a Thursday. A real proper Thursday! Got so much going on, I swear it’s like they just dump these things onto people’s lives and expect us to keep up.      Honestly, I just don’t get how you  managed  to plan everything round the baby’s christening. I mean, that’s a proper full-on thing with enough eccentricities for a sitcom. And I’m not even married, for goodness’ sake. If I turned up at my nan’s for a Sunday dinner saying I hadn’t even washed my hair that week, everyone would’ve taken in me and ordered me to the salon!      Milk!      Tea—yes, dear, you get the milk and we’ll get the tea sorted. Right, as to this weekend—lunch on Saturday as we’ve got… well, the usual. And I was just thinking, is Sunday too much?      No, actually, I was thinking of heading into Manchester for the afternoon after that big lecture I have first thing. I could pick up a couple of presents and then swing by someone’s house in Wilmslow. That way, I can just pop over to yours on the way back—unless it’s too much to ask being crowded in with the baby  and  the guests?      No, not at all, love. Actually, I was going to ask you if you could remind Sarah that she promised to bring the handle-thingie for the cake. My sister  absolutely  refuses to guest her own recipes if they can’t be presented with a certain amount of flambées and theatrics.      Mine!      Yes, love, all yours. Just trying to find the right balance between what we’ve got and the schedule. The christening’s on a Tuesday and if we rush into the actual goings-on on the following weekend, it’ll be like one of those shows where the camera just cuts between events with no background music or explanation.      So are you planning to make special sums and lists again, then?

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was looking forward to getting the garden in order over the weekend... What d'ya think Anna?      Honestly, I've been over that! It's thrown my plans all over the place. We'd even picked out things to do for the day on Saturday and now I'm stuck at home twitching about on the sofa. I wanted to get a few things done at the store but I know that's just not happening unless we're rushing into things.      You and the store. You're never off your feet when the place is open. Get some rest love, even if it's dead week. Have you and Dan taken the weekend off yet?      We did actually! The kids left for a sleepover with their cousins and I thought I'd maybe pick up a bit of shopping? But then the rain just about drowned the place! Wait, you're not going out this weekend are you?      I'm not, not unless I can convince Heather to go to that new place over in Lichfield Water with me. Might get a proper coffee and maybe even have a short walk around.      It'd be nice. Listen, on another note, how's work on the New York trip coming along?      Oh right! Heather and I had our deposits in ages back. I think she's just wrapping up her schedule at work so we can go in June. She's so excited. Our wedding someone said was one of the best they'd ever seen, and here we are, already planning something hotter and busier.       Squeaks  I  wannaget  there!      That's the spirit, sweetheart! She said something about the Empire State Building and hotdogs! Going to be fun.      You're going to have the most awesome time! I just wish I could go with you.      Well, the next time you and Dan take the kids anywhere, just let them know. I'm sure they'd love hearing about your shopping trips as well!      Ha! That's what I do with the staff. Announce where I am after a day of errands. They laugh away go.      You've always got a sense of humor, even in the deepest moments. Darlings, maybe we can all plan a little holiday together at some point. Even closer.      That’d be something! I think even the little one here might start tracking down dolls from over there.

Rather annoying to be honest. I've barely touched it since I got back from my fieldwork last week. I got heaps of raw data from the interviews I did down in Lancaster, and I need to start categorising it before the deadline. I’ve read the marking criteria at least three times now, trying to make sure I hit the right key points. It’s all about theory and how it's applied in real-life cases.      Fair enough. I’ve got to be honest, I’m not quite there yet with mine. I'm still stuck trying to get the intro properly lined up. The more I read, the more I think I’m going the wrong way with it. What’s your deadline again? I think mine is the same, but I’ve lost count between the dozens of assignments I’ve got on the go.      I think mine is due in four weeks, yeah. Look, forget the intro for a second—maybe I can just run you through some of my early analysis, you know, in case it helps to see how I'm structuring it. I’ve split the data into three broad themes—personality traits, environmental influences, and interpersonal conflicts. It’s all based on human geography and social theory, which is probably why it feels a bit heavy at times, but the way it's presented in the essays is supposed to justify it.      Yeah, that makes sense. It’s just when you’re dealing with theory, it can feel a bit abstract if you don’t ground it properly in the data. I’m trying not to just quote the textbook; I want it to actually reflect something meaningful. I did a couple of primary interviews myself recently—do you think your key themes might fit most people I spoke to?      Interesting. Could you tell me a bit more about what you found? Like, were the people you spoke to broadly supportive of the hypotheses in the module, or did they challenge it?      Honestly, it was a bit of a mix. A couple mentioned how their experiences relied heavily on personal motivation, but most seemed convinced by situational pressures. Like, they talked about how their environments really affected their decisions, sometimes more than what they "should do." So maybe that third theme, the interpersonal one, could fit the context of how people negotiate those pressures.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be up than down. But anyway, it’s real when you... What was I saying? Oh yeah, I had this dream last night that I won the lottery and built this massive dog kennel with 100 golden retrievers.      Oh come on, you  always  say that you want a dog if you suddenly had all that money. I’ve been telling you for years now that one dog is more than enough, but 100 golden retrievers? That’s just madness.      Retrievers are big dogs. Get like three miniature ones. Like… like poodles, or something.      Yeah! And they could wear little hats! Golden retrievers are too big for this house anyway, Dad.      Okay, I’ll concede the point. 100 was a bit much. Maybe five, no more than that. Just some big, friendly dogs running around the garden. Imagine it! No mowing the lawn for once—and I could train them to chase away pigeons.      You’d still be up half the night with your dogs as if you were humanely waking them up. You’ve got a terrible memory for getting up at a reasonable hour.      Mate, I got five hours last night, barely had a wink. I had a dream that I was trying to walk all the dogs at once. There was a bridge that collapsed, and I fell into someone’s chicken coop. Honestly, I woke up covered in hay just from the dream. That’s the weird thing with dreams, right?      That’s called  dream logic . Some of your dreams about the lottery are worse than the bridge story. I still haven’t forgiven you for the one where you turned the whole village into shareholders.      Were we shareholders in that dream?      Oh yes, you were. And you were on the board. Wearing a really long coat and all business-like. I tried to buy a little bakery with your shares. It didn’t go well. The baker was a space alien with a Yorkshire accent.      That sounds like it  could  have been a dream by a 10-year-old goon rather than your own dream.      Well, I like to think I’m creative. And it was a successful bakery.      So all this dream nonsense aside, what do you think we’d do if we really won the lottery, realistically?      Buy a proper house. Maybe in the countryside. I’m not entirely set on the dogs, but they’d definitely love the countryside.

Rather annoying I had t’go through all that at A&E. I was just trying t’sort out a twisted ankle an’ they treated it like I’d fallen off Mars.      Oh, hun, that doesn’t sound like much fun. Did they at least patch it up proper? I mean, you  did  say it was bleedin’ out like mad when it happened.      Aye, t’was a bit of a bleeder, alright. But t’doctor clowned arroond with me for what felt like forever, asking the most basic questions as if I were some sort of dodgy character. "Describe the pain," bleedin’ obvious. "Were you doing anything?" Yeah, I was walking an’ left foot went one way an’ ankle the other—flash news, innit?      Sounds like one o’ those new lads straight outta college who need to feel all fancy in their little scrubs. I had the same when I got that deep burn near the elbow a couple o’ months back. Kept gettin’ asked if I used a microwave—like I’d be stupid enough not t’know what hot things do, innit?      You got it right then. I swear it takes more time to wait for a plaster than it does to walk on it again. An’ I didn’t even ask to be referred for scans or nothin’. ‘Balances?’, they said—well, what do you think? I’m standin’ here like a prat, one foot in the air, floring the kid with a clipboard and all.       laughs  You’re a right character about pain, y’know. I’d have been howlin’. Anyway, how’s it feel now? Still stiff?      Yeah, a bit, but I’m stretchin’ it out. I’ve got laces ready if it flares up at work again. I can’t have bloody collapsed at the admin booth again, them boys waiting on me data all day. Manager was  pissed  last time.      Aye, do you need an ice pack? Still got a couple around from t’last time. Don’t go wasting binliners again if you don’t need to.      Nah, I’m alright—bit bloated though. Lift your legs up at the end o’ the day, innit?      Aye, that might help. Still, talk about a day over complication. Only had to go once y’self—most folk I know go at least once a month, an’ that’s not includin’ flu season.      It’s not somethin’ I’d be rushin’ to again, let me tell ya.

Rather annoying this new tax on small business profits, isn't it, James? I read it in The Guardian over breakfast and thought of you straight away.      Oh, you think  that's  annoying? Wait till we start paying the same rate as the big corporations. Ten percent was bad enough, but now it’s creeping up to fifteen percent. I haven't sleep well for a week thinking about how I'm going to balance this new nonsense in next year's budget.      I know, it’s just so frustrating to see the government dragging its heels when it comes to supporting local businesses. You lot are the ones keeping these towns alive. I tell you, the High Street only still has some kind of soul because of people like you, not those big store chains.      I appreciate that, Vivian, and I think it's ironic given how many of the customers are tourists from abroad. I've noticed a lot more Germans and Dutch folk coming in in recent months. I even had a couple from Norway, ordering puffins. Well, not  real  puffins—there's no way I’d serve one of those—just puffin-shaped chocolates, a bit of a joke I tell.      Oh, I imagine you've got quite a little story attached to that. You always have. Remember that time you told me about that Belgium man who claimed he once knew your supplier in the 90s?      Ha! That might be a tall tale, but someone believed it and bought ten boxes! That's business for you, isn't it? You give them something to laugh about and then you can charge double. I still don't get how people are so romantic about ugly souvenirs.      It's the charm, James. Not everyone can be into minimalist Danish design. Some people like things a bit quirky. Besides, it's not just business, it's part of the local identity. Now, are you going to the village fete on Saturday? I assume you’ll be there with a stall, even if your profit margin is razor-thin.      You know me too well. I plan on bringing the whistles and bells, the plastic crown, you remember that? Then again, if I started with the actual goings-on on the High Street, I’d probably go out of business very quickly. Imagine trying to serve food with the council trucks knocking down cafes left and right.

Rather skip the chips and meat pies, innit? Seems like everything sticks to my hips these days. We could try the vegan chilli instead—heard they switched the recipe last month.      You’re not that bad, love. Look at you—still rocking those curves. And I don’t want to hear about  their  recipes. I had enough theory at university. I wanted practice, not a textbook. A real life. Not lectures on this and social theory on that. Sometimes, I swear, someone should invent a degree in just doing the dishes.      Oh, don’t start with the university rant again. I  promised  you, no comparisons to my hippo of a first-year roommate. Anyway, you seem to have enough to occupy your week—what with the administration and the cat, Vivian, and I think you even screamed at the telly again about Happy Valley.      Heh, well, everyone has a hobby. Vivian’s got me on edge enough as it is—she’s been knocking over the chandeliers and walking over the keys like she owns the place. I swear, if I don’t get out of that flat for ten minutes of real, non-mouse-related action… I’d probably go feral myself. But yes, that Cottam girl—isn't she brilliant, though? Far more interesting than some of the people I deal with at work.      I watched one episode last week while transcribing those medical records. God, the way they filmed the moors made me consider buying a coat like hers. You think you could get one of these red and black tartan numbers in a decent size for a woman who’s never quite made about five foot four?      You can  always  get something decent if you walk into the right shop. Not like Woolwich is exactly Paris, but I still like the smell here. Burgundy and treacle and tobacco. A proper pub. The décor’s better than the one round the corner too—with those neon lights and that hideous plastic waiting staff station. We could live in a place that smelled like this instead of always trying to find a place that doesn't smell like someone took the kettle off boil too late.      Now you’re just cruising gothic nostalgia on me again. You trying to romanticise our flat? With the leaky shower and the cat who’s more bloke than Tom Jones?      Well, I am a romantic, and I do stand by those virtues, even with the drip overhead.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh?      Aye, it's been damp as a cobbler's workshop this week. I’m more used to it being this wet in March than April, to be honest. Chucked my hiking plans in the bin for the week again.      Aye, I was tryin’ to get up to the Pentland Hills last Saturday, but with that downpour, I just tacked a film night on instead. Might have watched a couple of documentaries on journeyman photographers. You ever take any photography trips outside of Scotland?      Aye, I’ve been mostly to places like Iceland and Norway. The light in those places is mad for photos. My postgrad thesis was on environmental photography, so I’ve tried to combine work and play, you might say. Always packing the camera, even when I'm just wanderin’ the streets of Oslo for breakfast.      That’s fancy alright. I’ve just been snapping stuff around Edinburgh for the mugs -- the old tenement blocks, the canal, the view from Water of Leith Walk at dusk. I’ve got a wee collection of photos now.      It sounds grand. Have you ever thought about showin’ it off anywhere?      Not really – I'm more of a snapshot guy. My laddie’s got me into film photography though. Gifted me an old Nikon for my birthday. Bit fiddly, mind, but the photos are someone else when they're on film.      That's the magic of it—more about the experience than just the finished image. Any weekend plans for using that new toy?      I was plannin' on taking a journey down the east coast this weekend. Maybe a stop in Dunbar or North Berwick. Supposed to dry out a bit, and I heard the sun might peak out just enough for a decent light.      Aye, the further east you go, the more the sea gets that golden light. You’ll need your layers though, even if it's sunny. Ch Websites mentioned it’s going to be a little cooler with breezy conditions.      Aye, I’ve tacked a couple of jumpers in the bin with me tripod. If I’m lucky, I might even get some clouds in the frame to break up the background.      Aye, clouds are grand for photography. They add depth and interest. I'm always after that atmospheric shot.      Sounds like poetry from you, Professor. Maybe I’ll try and string a few clouds and castles together for a theme this weekend.

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That Christopher, he’s promising one thing then dawdling like... Well, I don’t know. I’m more than a bit tired of having to micromanage this whole nursery situation. You wouldn’t have thought it’d be simpler with three kids already under the roof and all the experience, but no. It’s like starting over every time.      I get that, love. Honestly, I do. I mean, I’m only used to dealing with a dozen little tykes at once in the classroom and dragging that whole process out of the past has been gruelling. I just wish they'd made it easier, you know? Like, just a web portal and a bit more turkey on offer for the latecomers.      I’m not obsessed with the food, I’m just not bothered to queue up for an hour for mushy peas and carrots. I could feed the child better than that. Honestly, I’m thinking about asking if we can cater for ourselves, you know, have a bit of involvement. That would give me something to do with my week apart from chasing Christopher and tidying up that room with the toys as if I didn't have enough on my plate already.      You'd love it, being the “relevant parent” – that’s what they called us last time, because they thought we didn’t care enough. Now don’t get me started on their rhetoric. I watched one programme last week that made me want to roll out someone’s eyes. It was all about nurturing creativity through chaos. As if we haven’t got enough chaos in the real world.
