Oh yes, I caught that one too. Prime time at 8 on a Thursday. I don’t know the network still dares show it. It made me want to write to someone. Not that I’d get a response. No one in that lot has a ‘proper’ telephone number, do they? Just emails and portals that no one checks on a Thursday before Christmas. I think I might have to meet Christopher’s team in person, just so I can tell someone  properly  how I feel.      That might do wonders. I took the kids out for a proper lunch after a day of arguing with the system the other go. They need to see real people. If nothing else, it gave me a chance to breathe and actually think about the week ahead rather than getting lost in all that technology.

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me n mine lads just cranked through a pheasant and a couple of rabbits after the conference run down in Leeds. I've been overworked this week, it were hectic to say the least.      Nah, I get it een, we were  not  expecting ye anyway 'cos of that thing with the daffodil competition in Cambridgeshire. Fair dos, too much social eventin' goin' on, innit? Worked me off in the warehouse forfay, literally, I bent a back trying to fetch crates of paint. Still, it’ll be good t'catch up, supply you with proper food and ale like the turkey on Christmas.      Oh, I  hated  the daffodils this year. The lights turned off at 5 in the arse and it was pitch black, no one could find me partner. Honestly, I’m thinking about moving outta the London area — not that the daffodils are the problem, but I just want fresher air, you know?      Aye, well ye can always come back and visit me, innit? Try on a pair of my old work boots and then tell me how that fresh air does?      Haha, nah, I'd end up tripin' on my own two feet and sprain somethin’. Besides, don’t be too cocky, Lee, someone at the daffodils saw you trying on a dress just to try it on. Some guy had a laugh about it, and you looked livid.      Oh bugger off, about daft Steve innit — he fancied me sister and thought this was a jib. Gave him a proper telling off. Still, I looked cruel unwell in that dress. My sister ‘ad to pry it off o’ me. Said it was 'fashion-challenged'. Unlucky mate, I had to relapse into paint schemin’ that night instead.      Right, but moving to somewhere with 'better air' sounds whanky. I do love a good fresh set of lungs after a day in a conference room with ten blokes in binliners and cheap aftershave.      I know innit, but serious talk, bloke — I might try to get a job at the planning office in Bournemouth, sounds more chilled out. And heck, maybe even find someone better to date than the bloke I’m with at the moment, who only talks about CPUs and nichts.      Mate, love is weird innit, but always remember — don’t fall for a bloke that can’t tell a motherboard from a motherboard.

Rather annoying this new tea bags they bring in the shops, they’ve gone and made 'em ‘ard like... like old socks, they have. I’m more used to the old style, the ones that proper brewed, don’t you know?      Oh, yes, dear, I’ve noticed it too. I liked the loose leaf one they used to sell at Billington's in town. Though I reckon that was before your time, Charles.      Haha, well, not as old as he thinks! But I'll say this for the new tea bags, they’re not too expensive. Though I prefer my Lakelands builder’s blend, no qualms, no complaints. It goes like that old turkey on Christmas Day, you know! .      Roht, I think the world has gone mad with tea now. My old school children would breakfast on tea and toast and this happened! They’d get in at eight and I’d give ‘em a mug, didn’t matter the size, the colour, or the strength—so long as it was hot! But I’ve noticed the last few years, even the builders in Newport, they only drink something called ... Green Tea, or Yerba Mate. Fancy names, all.      Mate? Mate with a “mate”! It's all getting too much. I reckon the doctor told me to switch to green tea for the cholesterol, didn’t I? And I said: “Doctor, I come in for a cholesterol reading not a bloody tea tasting!”      Oh Charles, don’t be so huffy! It’s not as if we all  have  to drink it. I do like a bit of Earl Grey now and then. Though my cups keep getting vibes from it. Maybe they think I've been drinking perfume!      Ah, nonsense. Burgundy cup with Earl Grey, that's proper British. Though I have dabbled in Rooibos once, it was very North African, you know. I was doing a GCSE kid as part of a cultural diversity module—had me sampling lunches from Leeds to Lagos!      Hmm, well you remember, Leslie, teaching and all that, whereas the rest of us were on the loo with our cups of builder’s blend.      I had a cup of something called Darjeeling once. It was like drinking air. I made it to the kipper in two sips! Darjeeling or not, I prefer my tea like I prefer my meat—on the strong side! Stronger than the butcher’s dog!

Rather skip the hotel stay and go to The King’s Arms. I've had my fill of B&Bs with damp and dodgy continental breakfasts this week. Blows my mind how someone can charge ten quid for a sun-dried tomato spread the size of a matchstick.      Oh come on, Natalie, the place we stayed was lovely. I reckon it depends on where you are on a map. A lot of pubs now serve proper meals and even have parking. If you go to some of the ones in North Norfolk, the food's very decent.      Mithose sorts of places, I prefer just to grab a pie and a pint. No need for tables or reservations in my opinion. My uncle still runs a little place near Caerphilly—what do they call it now? Dine-in, no-reservations, just queue up. It's brilliant, honestly. Real atmosphere. I mean, yeah, the place has seen better days, but there’s a charm to it.      Pie and pint culture isn't exactly widespread in London, I can tell you that, but I get what you mean. I remember one bar in Bethnal Green where you could get real ales and homemade mushroom pasties—it wasn't five-star, but it was humble and good. Back to the point: any of you done CRB checks recently? I'm brushing up on background checks before I start my next course at UCL next term.      Oh God, those things. I did one for a summer camp job a few years ago and thought I’d definitely failed out due to the drink license fine in ’07. Still got no answer for  weeks . Staggering how long they take. I was half-terrified the thing had been lost in the ether.      Going back to the pubs—Nancy, have you noticed the way some of them, especially near Norwich, have started guest beers from local breweries? It's wild how into craft ales they've become. Not just the lager crowd anymore.      We had one such pub in Caerphilly, but it was run by a mate of mine from uni. He took the concept a step further and opened a gallery in the back! The owners believed in gothic art, which wasn't my taste, but it got respect.      I had a student last year who wrote about protest art emerging from pubs and galleries—it was fascinating. Her focus was how public venues fostered debates that spilled into political action.

:  [currently in the kitchen, making tea]  You're back! I was just wondering when you’d get in. You've been on holiday for a week, and I’ve had to fend off the cat and this flat on my own. How was the trip?     :  [enters the kitchen and leans against the counter]  It was good, honestly. The weather was actually better than most people expected. A lot of people got rained out, but me and Alice had a right laugh. She's that au pair we met in the pub last month. We literally just explored the coast every day—we saw like three miniature horses. One of them tried to steal my sandwich at the pub on the last night.     : Oh my God, are you telling me you were out on the coast with a stealing micro-horse? That’s the most British holiday you’ve ever described. Cats, incompetent wildlife breakfasts—this is getting familiar.     : Says the woman who once challenged a raccoon to fetch in London. Also, the raccoon won.     : Okay, but that raccoon had the advantage of two hands and a very distracting granola bar. Anyway, what are we having for dinner tonight? I tried to make a stir-fry last night, and the veggies won. Resoundingly, and with barely a flicker of garlic.     : Honestly? Maybe just order something. There's this new mexican place up the road. I got the email for the 10% off a week ago, and it's probably expired by now, but I'm still trying to convince myself it's still valid.     : I did technically recycle 50 empty coffee cups from the office, so I have vibes. Let’s go for it anyway. But before that—how's work? You sound like you're still on holiday time.     : It’s been hectic. I’m rotating between the day wards and the crisis support team again. I ended up helping a colleague with a transfer who had to rush back to Bristol last minute. It’s always something with this job. But it's good. I do love it. Even when it’s a mess.     : That's so you. Always chasing chaos and calling it meaningful work. I swear, you’d go into a war zone with a box of tissues and call it your calling. How's your ex, James? Still haunting your emails?     : Ugh, don’t remind me. He messaged me over the weekend.

Rather annoying really, isn't it? You know what happens with these sorts of properties—the owners think it's a fantastic idea to sell mid-renovation, like people are just going to ignore the toilet in the hallway and the floorboards that look like they've seen better days.      I get it, but if they  are  making an offer,   we   need to be aware of what's going on. A listing just appeared on the village website for Old Mill Cottage; it's right by the stream. That place always looked lovely in the summer, when the light comes through the trees.      It is a nice property. I can see why people would want to move there, especially with the village being what it is. Quiet, community-minded, not too far from the train station. But I still don’t see why they couldn’t wait a little longer to put it up for sale. They’re only halfway through the loft conversion.      I suppose they must be needing the cash. Or maybe they’re planning to buy somewhere bigger? They might not be directly related—village life can feel a bit isolating after a while. I know Adrian says it’s beautiful and peaceful, but for someone with kids, there isn’t much for them.      That’s true. Looking back at it, maybe they should have sold before they started the project. Anyway, enough about houses. How did you manage the phone call with Derek this morning?      He said it was someone at the hospice who rang him. He was a bit shaken, oddly. I think they’re talking about more invasive treatment now, but the prognosis is still…complicated.      I dread to think. I know he's kept such a good sense of humour this whole time. To be honest, I worry it’s going to get the better of him soon. Maybe he deserves some peace, you know. Maybe it’s not about how much time he has left, but how well he can spend it.      I agree. I just don’t think anyone’s ready to accept that. I know I’m not. He’s been a part of both of our lives for so long. Remember when he took us to the South Bank by train for the weekend when we were still students?      God, how did we even afford the tickets? It cost practically a month’s rent, but we went anyway.

Rather annoying when the bar’s out o’ order, innit. I was just in t’campus bar last nigh, asks for a pint o’ lager, comes back with a pint o’ bitter I don’t even like. No, I likes lager — well, when it’s in stock eenyways. Seems like we’re always one step behind on everything.      Oh aye, I know what you mean. I was just doing rounds in the building last night and some dump pulled a prank and tipped wine all o’er the corridor outside the elevators. Mucked up t’elevator, mucked up t’floor, mucked up t’mats, and now we’re stuck mopping it up like it’s our fault. Fun stuff.      Aye, and what with these student accommodations: every day you find summat broken in one o’ the rooms. Last breakfast, I was doing a security sweep and nearly dropped me coffee when a pipe’s cracked and water was everywhere, floor to ceiling. Sorted it out, but I swear I’ve seen more disasters than any of us had in uni. Y’know I never did go.      It’s deadly stressful, innit. Me job, I’m expected to be all nice and “supportive” – but then I’ve got students coming in, barely educated, and some are just a nuisance. It’s not like them all, but I swear some ‘ave no bloody idea what a responsibility looks like. Waste of a degree for some. Just trying to live a chaotic lifestyle and we’re stuck cleaning up after ‘em.      Hey, look at it this way — we get a good story out o’ it. I told a lad the other day that the building had “crashed and burned” thanks to some kid leaving the kettle plug in the sink overnight. Nearly electrocuted himself. My day’s over when I’ve got that in my log.      Aye, it is a laugh ‘til it’s not. I mean, I understand they’re young and they make mistakes, but sometimes they cross the line. Just trying to do our jobs and not die of exhaustion by the end o’ the week. I swear, if another kid knocks the keg machine over, I’m just gonna throw the whole thing down the stairs.      Haha, don’t go doing nuffink stupid. ‘As to keep the professionalism, right? Still, sums say we’re in t’wrong jobs, eh?      Tell me about it. But I mean, we’re here now.

Rather annoying to be honest, meeting so many other English folk in Antwerp this time last year. I was there with uni friends, and it felt like half the people I bumped into spoke with a UK accent! It is mad, don’t you think?      Oh, I know what you mean, love. When I took a coach package tour to Kraków in 1996, most people I met were from these group holidays. Such a contrast to solo backpacking. The differences in age and expectations were pretty stark.      Funny you should mention that, dear. I went to a Christmas market in Bruges last year—also saw a lot of English people, only they were mostly in couples and families. Just wandering around with cups of mulled wine, you know? I made a right attempt at speaking some basic Dutch, but it turned out most people were actually from Cardiff!      I tried learning a bit of Dutch before visiting Antwerp in case I needed to, but I never quite got the hang of it. Still, it’s always nice when you can speak the same language, don’t you think? Though I guess it’s also quite a rude shock for locals when they’re overrun by tourists.      Overrun? Absolutely. When I got back from Kraków – Mateusz showed me the city, and he said they were trying to restrict the number of coach trips allowed to ease the traffic. You know what it’s like with all that package tour traffic. Our roads here at home are bad enough!      It just goes to show how international some of our habits have become. Whether it’s Christmas markets, seaside resorts like Brighton Seafront, or even Herne Bay about this time of year for Christmas shopping. I went last Saturday, and had to jostle past quite a few young mums trying to find outfits for their children's birthdays in January.      Oh yes, I can see that. Parents are always at it to sort it out early. I think I once met someone from Germany who was waiting at station here who lost their grandparent over the festive season. It was very sad, but we ended up speaking English the whole time he waited. That's how it goes.      I remember when my go-to was my son's birthday. Always had to go overboard with posters and cakes, even if it was just the three of us.

So do you know what the "equality vote" is, like, what does it mean for real? We had some big news on the telly about it in school today, and I was confused.      Oh, love, the equality vote—some people call it the marriage referendum. It’s all about whether  anyone  can get married, no matter if they’re a man and a woman or two men or two women. Ireland had this big vote on it a few years ago.      Oh! Wait, so like, you don’t need to be with a girl to get married? That sounds mad! In our class, me and my mates were joking about how we would have like  fake  weddings if that was allowed.      [Laughs] I know what you mean, silly. I remember when the government first talked about it, there were massive protests. Some people called it unnatural or said it would destroy "traditional values." But a lot of people also marched for it, you know, for love and equality. And actually, the majority voted yes—about 62 per cent of people said they wanted same-sex marriage.      Wol-oh! That’s a lot! I reckon if it happened here in the UK, more people would say yes. Or at least I hope so. My friend Sienna’s mums had a civil partnership before, and they said it wasn’t the same. Her gran used to say creepy stuff about them in public.      Yeah, my mum wasn’t big on it either. She was all like, “What if the neighbours find out? They’ll think I’m  weird !” and then I about died from embarrassment. I told her “you’re the one watching this [British LGBT anthem] on the telly last night!” She barely noticed me!      That is classic! I bet she watched the whole thing after I left the room. But honestly, I don’t get why any grown-up can’t get married if they want to. Like, your birthday is allowed to be  any  day of the year, so why can’t a wedding be whomever you want?      You’re not wrong. I think it’s one of those things that’ll take a while for everyone to get comfortable with—especially in places where people are really set in their ways. But the younger generation tends to be more open-minded.      For sure. I think it’s really cool people can love whoever they like.

Rather annoying this, putting the hamster in the microwave. I’ve heard people do it, but it’s a proper nutter, mind you. I’m more of a gardener, you know, me and old Ivy—my wife—used to have a few things going on the kitchen window sill.       Laughs dryly  Yeah, puts me right off my cuppa, that sort a thing. A hamster in a microwave! Why not a parrot in a blender while we’re at it? My sister’s lad was messing about once with the toaster when he was ten. Tore the hell out of it, trying to fix the toast. Now, speaking of toast, I can do with a bit of what you call doorstep madness, you know, left over cheese sandwiches.      D’you know, I think the world’s gone mad with rules now about pets and appliances. I used to run reviews of school curriculums, for goodness’ sake! It’s like they don’t trust you to do simple things anymore. As for appliances, I still like me a good set of lathes. My老爷 takes special care of his old one. He still uses it when the grandkids fancy making a wooden spoon—it’s fun for them, and then it gives him a reason to remember the good ol’ days.      Oh, I’ve a lathe in the shed, but it’s been a while. Last time I used it, I made a little lantern frame out of an old carrot. Just a bit o' fun, really. Ivy always said it made the best firewood later, though she’d be grinning at the mess I made in the garden.      That’s the spirit! Now talking of tools, I had a neighbor a few streets over—grand old woman she was—who gave me a proper old carving knife in exchange for helping her up the stairs. Still got it in my kitchen drawer, sharp as a pin.      Ah, I once had a knife like that from when I was a lad. It got lost in the middle of the war—don’t want to think about it. More importantly, have we fed the cat yet?       Chuckles  Yeah, go on then, get it sorted. I’m more interested in discussing microwave safety nowadays. Imagine baking a potato and ending up with a charnal stink due to dodgy appliances.      Oh, I’ve seen worse. One time I had a new microwave that kept on playing ‘Happy Birthday’ every time the food was done!

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, the whole charging for plastic bags thing? I mean, it's a good idea in principle, but honestly, now I've got to rummage through my purse every time I go to the cash register. I’ve seen some people just carrying a spare carrier in their car. Got eeny idea where  I’ll  put one of those? My car's already full of cat fur and paperbacks.      Honestly, I’ve started using a couple of old rucksacks to do the weekly shop. I got so fed up paying when I don't even use the damn things. It's enough to make you write your shopping list in mirror to outwit the system. On that note, what’s with all the mirror-writing obsession in the papers these days? Probably some nutcase who wrote a note and thought it said "attack the palace".      Cats, shops, breakfast, no doubt. I've been reading about a scandal in America at the moment, the politics are quite something, to say the least. But that’s beside the point. I was just thinking, if all of this debt and house price nonsense carries on, quite a few people might be choosing to live with their parents for a while longer—very 1950s. Mind you, most of my grandchildren are already with their respective partners and none happier for it. Marriage is the cheapest insurance policy in the long run, after all.      I’d been tempted to follow in your footsteps at one point, but I’ve not got your flair for crossword puzzles, let's put it that way. Still, mind you, I've been through some sodding impossible  cryptics  in my time transcribing them from old newsprint. You’d think the Government could take this debt crisis and solve it like a good crossword. One smooth plug and away you go.      My sister had to put the cat up for adoption last month because she was moving and couldn't take the creature. I was bloody gutted. Imagine, someone breeding them for little ones, then shipping them to good homes. I swear to God, if there’s one thing we need more of in this world, it's more fluffy things for people to love unconditionally.      There's a touching report in the  Times  about a stray that made its home in a bank, between the vaults, I believe.

Right, I just wanted to bring up something I noticed earlier. I saw you two were really into your computer and building with Legos after school, which is totally fine. But honestly, I’ve seen the books you picked out for your reading time still stacked on your shelves. I’m just a bit worried you’re not getting as much reading in as you should. You’ve both got so much imagination, so this isn’t to kill your fun, but to get you using it in a different way, you know?      But the new Minecraft world update is like, epic! There's this new castle with a dragon and the fire works are so cool when you craft them. It takes forever to get all the materials though. It’s like a puzzle game now, Mummy!      Fair enough, I can see how it’s a bit of a challenge. But have you thought about trying to write down a bit of your adventures? I remember when I was your age, I used to keep a journal. One time, I even wrote a story about a village guarded by treasure-hunting ghosts. I mean, that probably sounds as silly as your Minecraft dragons, but it still gave me something to be proud of.      I don’t like Minecraft – I prefer Ninjago. I’m building a giant Hayato today. His sword is nearly as big as my Legos! You know what I could try, Mummy? Maybe inventing my own Ninjago story. Maybe the next book read could be about me building the ultimate dragon tamer ninja. That could be a cool book.      That’s  exactly  the kind of thing I mean! You’re both already storytelling gods in your minds – why not put it down a little more and maybe even draw it? I’m more than happy to listen to you both talk it out, read over your ideas, or even sit down and help you type it up if you want. I used to do that all the time with my students when I was your age – making reading and writing part of your fun world instead of something separate.      Could we do a collaboration? Like, you work on the writing, I come with the adventures and the Minecraft bits, and Tom adds the ninja action.      I’d love that – a team-up. And what your team creates will be all yours, I promise.

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That plane delay. I was trying to get us through to Luton and ended up stranded in Heathrow for two hours. Not a single bit of toast, mind you, just cashews and bottled water the airline fobbed us with. But it was worth it once we got there, I reckon. Venice was lovely this time of year.      I remember that trip from when we were younger! The gelato, the canals, Grandmother nearly got pulled into the water by that gondolier when she chase after her dropped handbag. You'd fetch frozen fish sticks and brandy shots when we were kids, and now we’re choosing organic brunch places and needing apps to book ferries. Still, I suppose we’re getting fancy with age, ain't we?      I think it's just about having the cash for once, and you’re not breakfasting alone with your 'fancy' plans this time. Joanne and I charmed a discount from the hotel to spread it between the two of you. Speaking of which—Joanne, tell them what we discussed this morning—what are your plans for your shift-free tomorrow?      Honestly, I’ve got a meeting for my thesis work at Ten, but I might come over after for lunch. I want to help with sorting out that photo album you’ve been scanning, Mum. It's got all the snaps from Venice and the rest of the holidays! Though, let’s be fair, someone at the hotel probably spiked the coffee because my memory of the second day is a bit patchy.      Oh, let’s be fair, Joanne,  you  are the one who nearly flammable-danced your dress on fire trying to touch the ceiling at the bar. And I suppose you found some local cabaret manager to fix it for you, didn't you?      Oh, I like that one. Though I'm not sure 'flammable-danced' is a verb any dictionary's ever heard of.      I make up what I need to as I go on. Rather than 'spam email' lunches, I think it fits! So, if Joanne arrives, you remember to fetch the aprons. I told her we're goin' on a DIY mission today. If not, I’ll ask her to bring the password for the Wi-Fi—still haven’t changed it since your dad passed, and I’m feeling nostalgic.      Poor dad.

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode about the military thing was wild, innit? Like... I don’t know, maybe it was because my cousin joined the army last summer, and he told us it wasn’t that glamorous.      Yeah, I saw that episode too. It made me kind of curious about how the military actually works. I reckon it depends on where you come from too—like, my mate Hassan’s cousin is in the army, and he said they train a lot harder in the Middle East. But anyway, how was your cousin’s experience, Jerry?      Honestly, it was tough, apparently. He had to get up at six, do laps before breakfast and everything. My mum keeps saying "poor dear" like it’s the most dramatic thing ever, but he says it’s all good. The funny bit is he had to move out of the house and into barracks. He said the dorm rooms are like... mini bootcamps. No privacy, you know?      Ew, so restrictive. Imagine living like that for years. I wouldn’t survive a day. I’d start a riot in two minutes. What about school stuff, though? Did he get more time off for holidays?      Well, he got Christmas off, and some days in summer, but not much. My cousin said the best bit was the people he met. All backgrounds, ages, you name it. He said it helped him understand the world better. Like, someone in his unit was from Pakistan, and they’d never met someone like that before. Turns out they had a lot in common, though.      That’s actually quite cool, in a way. I mean, I know not all of it's good, especially with war and all. I’ve seen some pics from Afghanistan that are just... I dunno, unbelivable.      Yeah, I watched a documentary about that once. It made me think more about how the media only tells certain stories. Speaking of, I tried to get into that new series your brother told us about— The Sandpit , or something like that?      Oh!  The Sandpit ? The one set in the 90s with the kids and the go-karts? It’s about racism and family dynamics, right? My cousin sent it to me, and it’s kinda deep, but it’s still really funny. The older I get, the more I notice how complicated grown-ups’ lives can be.

Honestly, I just can't stand Mr. Patel any more. I mean, he's supposed to be like...  really  good at physics, right? But he talks so fast, I can’t even write down half the stuff he says before he moves on to the next topic.      Oh I  totally  get that. It’s like he’s got his own language in lessons. The other day he was listing all these equations and one of us just whispered, “what planet are we on?” and it was just me and the guy next to me cracking up the whole time.      That’s literally happened to me too—last week! And then the worst part is when he tries to mark you on things you definitely couldn’t have heard. Like I got marked down for not knowing the right symbol for centripetal force and I was like, “did you actually mention that in the lecture?” And he just said, “You should have been paying attention.” Ugh.      Yeah, he’s not the only one being a bit unfair, though. Our form tutor, Miss Rivers, is being so annoying too—she keeps giving us these “progress updates” and she  lives  off of points system. I lost 30 points last week for being five minutes late to registration – even though I got held up in the queue because someone’s phone dropped and the teacher helped pick it up.      Oh, I got into trouble for that too, but I just said someone bumped into me and I dropped my book. Thank God none of the rules are written  clearly —we just have to guess what’s acceptable!      Look, it’s not all bad, though. I finally watched the "17 Again" film he made us do for English. It was kind of cheesy but Andy Lau was funny and it helped a bit for the essay. My sister had to do it like six years ago and passed it down to me.      Ohhh, was it  any  good? I tried to read the summary before watching it to prep for the questions. Let me know if it’s worth watching—because I’ve got to do it next lesson. My teacher set it for something to do with character growth or whatever.      It wasn’t amazing or anything, but at least it wasn’t boring, unlike that  one  person from last year who read the whole book instead.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you lads. Felt real stuffy in there and the surgeon had no sense of humor at all. Not a single joke the whole time! Got me wound up more than anything. Was like, "get on with it" after twenty minutes of eeny-meeny-miny-mo.      My goodness! Sounds like a bit of a nightmare ordeal. At least you got this sorted, yeah? Oh, and congratz, by the way. Know you’ve been dreading it for ages. So, how’s the vision? Still a bit blurry?      A bit, yeah. Docs told us not to do anything stressful like reading the turkey shop menu for at least a week. Can’t be bothered to go to the Post Office, can I? Made me think—remember when we all did that dodgy night out at the Domino Club, and I almost stepped on a pigeon with a blurry eye? Feels like yesterday!      Ah, spare a thought for the poor bird, mate. I mean, it looked like it had one eye missing—probably your left one, judging by that dodgy flick you did off its wing. Reminds me… watching the footy tomorrow night in Mel from the local café. Looking for cheeky ones with a sneaky cheeps because they’re trying to meet the cheapest price on apple pie and turkey. Seems like a lost cause to me.      There’s also this someone at the bakery who keeps suspiciously trying to buy a half-share in the sourdough starter. Just looking out for a red flag, really. Anyway, changing the subject—Transylvania, anyone? Tom and I are actually off to Transylvania next week to visit the orchids at the Carpathians. Have you lads done that before?      No, not in that neck of the woods for quite some time. Heard it can get real misty there and all them castles. Real fairytale vibe, sounds. I tried to get my little ones convinced it’s the same place as Dracula’s castle. Got them all spooked last night.      Some people still go there for that, you know. Popping into the castle expecting to go vampy on them. I’d say “I feel ya,” but I just ticked out a full weekend behind the counter arranging buns.      So how have things been for you down at the café, Claire? Still holding it down?      Just about. Keep ‘em coming in the summer, them students like iced lattes all day long.

Right, so the photoshoot is on Saturday at 10. I've just double-checked with the photographer... got to pick some good music to play in the background. I was thinking maybe a bit of classic rock for the fun bits, and then the kids' album at the end. What do you two think?      I want my party music on! The one with the bouncy bears!      I want “Alice in Wonderland” songs! Timmy said they sing while dancing in the woods. We can dance around the tree like that.      That could be brilliant, actually. We can do a mini dance-off in the garden, then go for Alice in Wonderland at the end when you change into your best outfits. The lawyer said backdrops need to be clean, so we can pick one of the lights ones for the fairy tale photos.      Wait, does Alice live in a place where everyone has a hoop in the sky? I saw the aerial hoop once, you were doing those moves so high!      Oh yeah, the hoop, right! That was a few years ago. You don’t need that to be in the photos, unless you fancy trying it properly… although it does require a little endurance, and probably no mud. Ha – speaking of which, I heard there was a muddy obstacle course on the telly last night. It looked exhausting.      I could do that! I could run, and then jump, someone said there are bags of sand to carry. I like carrying big things.      Just don’t fall into the mud puddles and ruin your clothes – photos  and  obstacle courses might not go so well together unless you want the "After the Party" shot, which I’m not convincing the photographer to take.      I’m hungry. Can we eat before? I want a biscuit and some juice. Do we have cookies?      Let me see… there are some chocolate chip cookies left from when I brought your favourite. There’s also some fruit yogurt in the fridge if you two want something healthier. Go on, grab the chocolate if you like it, just remember to brush your teeth later.      I want a biscuit and juice! Can I have two?      Just two, okay. And no spilling the juice on the photoshoot clothes. We all have to look our best. Oh, one more thing – can you two please try not to fight over the dress-up box when we get to the outfits?

Rather annoying this, having to type up these notes when I could be out walking the dog or ‘aving a cup of tea and a quiet read. Still, at least I can take a break after this bit.      Aw, don’t grumble so! You wouldn’t be out walking if it een weren’t for me nagging you every Sunday. Give me that roulade — chocolate and cream? Sounds just like my grandmum made in the old days.      It is interesting, though. We’ve been talking about the children at the school when discussing the kids’ exams. Did you hear, young Daisy from Mary’s group nailed her maths paper — the teachers are still going on about it like it’s a bloody marvel. Still, best to not put too much pressure on the lads and lasses.      Yeah, but what if you don’t do as well as you think? I was really worried about this results day, but I only got a GCSE grade five in English — not bad, not brilliant. Still, it’s just the start, right?      I got a six, but I don’t think it matters as much as my teachers say it does. I’m just going to be a nurse or something. Well, unless I decide to be a –  ha!  – a football manager like dad does on the weekend. We’ve got loads of time.      You know what I ‘ate? This talk about exams and all that pressure. As if one paper decides your whole future. I never had to do that sort of thing — you had to work it out for yourself. Chained down in a factory all week, come ‘ome and eat a tin of beans and walk back the same road the next week.      Honestly Ron, your factory days are such fun to listen to. But it does sound so awfully exhausting. At least now the children have laptops and GCSEs — not that that’s much better.      ‘Course it sounds fun, but there’s a little bit more reality in the real world than in that sprite of academies and grand statements.      At least the kids today aren’t as far lost as we were. You know, I started my teaching career goin’ on twenty years ago and I’ve seen so many different kids, some in the same shoes as you were in, bloke.      Mr. Worrill, seriously, why did you become a teacher?

Rather annoying the new recording system we've got at the care home. I was just trying to play some old records last weekend and it didn't want to pick up any of them properly. The volume kept jumping about like it was half-deaf or something.      That does sound a bit frustrating. I'm assuming it’s digital now?      Ay, they've all gone digital these days. I remember my first flat had one of these big cassette recorders; you used to press play and you’d hear a whole heap of hiss and pop before the actual tune started.      Yeah, I guess even older-than-old technologies like reel-to-reel tapes had their own charm. But now everyone just uses a phone to stream music. Fun to reflect on, really—from cassettes to Cell D.      Aye, I suppose you're right about that. Though I'll stick with breakfast cereal and a proper cup of tea after playing a few games of Chinese chess with my dad every morning, even if it's the weekend. Good for the mind, keeping it sharp.      I’ve noticed the berries in the garden are ripening nicely. Did you say anything to the lads from the local allotment group about swapping some of our ingredients?      Mate, I got a pot of beans from Brian just last week. We had a proper chat about black-eyed ones versus the haricot varieties. Brian said they're good for the soil and the people too. Takes in one for the body and one for the garden, he said.      That’d be a fine idea if you want to bring some green vegetables into the future kitchen, especially when most people about our age worry about eating the same bangers and chips all the time.      Another thought—you know that new school Brian mentioned? They’re doing up a lot to the curriculum, focusing on linguistics and communication with animals.      I have actually been thinking about animal communication. It's an interesting field, blending psychology, linguistics, and even some neuroscience to understand how animals perceive and use forms of communication.      That’s whistles and barks and whatnot, you say? Mind you, it's a bit different from human goings-on, but it's still pretty fascinating. Just don't expect a cat to give you a full explanation of its day, that's for sure.

Rather annoying the new testing regime they're imposing at the school. My students are just children, they don’t need to咄咄逼促 them like this.      Yeah, I mean, it is a bit over the top. Look, I’ve taught in a couple of places in Poland and I saw the same thing — more testing, bigger pressure. I reckon it's not all bad, but I feel for the kids. At least your side of things isn’t so busy since you're part-time.      Well, I do what I can when I get the chance. Honestly, I like to keep it gentle, just because I don't want to overload people, you know? On the other hand, you look pretty busy these days. Still got that school in Krakow, or is it two places now?      Oh, it's actually both — Krakow and Nowa Huta. I teach at both in the week, and in the evenings I usually pick up an extra class or two online. I have to, the student loans are still hanging around like a bad smell, and being a full-time teacher doesn't make you rich.      It doesn’t for me either, if I’m honest. I used to rely on the state pension — but now who knows? I hear they’re not giving out the same sort of benefits as they used to. It worries me, quite frankly. You're young, but you’ve at least been lucky enough to get out of the full-time grind and into something solid.      I do manage, but it's tight. And speaking of money and being solid — did I tell you about my friend’s car? She about blocked the whole main road trying to do the MOT last week because she had no idea what to do. I mean, that was a dramatic way to handle it.      That’s for sure. I always tell her if she needs a friend to explain it, I’m here. I assume you all still use Netflix? I haven't touched it since I moved here.      Oh yeah, we've all got it. I think it's probably the only thing keeping our class together — we have a group chat and every week someone points out a go-to movie on the platform if anyone needs something to chill with after class. It's a bit daft but it helps with team bonding sometimes.

So, I just got my A-level results last week, and I’m thinking of applying for Human Sciences at Oxford or maybe Cambridge. I know it’s a bit of a gamble with their specific requirements, but I like the idea of combining psychology with a bit of biology and anthropology. What about you?      That sounds interesting, honestly. I was actually wondering if I should go for something more mathsy. Maybe a Maths degree? I just love the logic and problem-solving. But I’m not sure if I should stick with just numbers or maybe do an engineering course instead. Have you done much decision tree thinking?      Honestly, I made a table last week—pros and cons column for each course like a MyUniChat mistress. I’m still waiting to chat with one of the tutors to hear what their lectures are actually like and if they get the human angle. But enough about that—how’s the rugby going, mate? You playing this season?      Aye, thanks for asking! We’re starting to train for the first games in October. Coach says we’ve got one or two big matches lined up in November—probably one against Wellington or somewhere near as brutal. You coming along for training? I might buy us a couple of pints after if it doesn’t cost too much. We can’t afford a bottle of real ale like normal these days.      Would love to! I miss watching you at the scrum. Last time you almost flipped the ball carrier over in mid-air. Spent half the weekend with a sore neck. Oh, and I brought a recipe with me from my nan—she says if I want to be a university student, I need to stop eating processed snacks and about five eggs a day. Her "One Pan Spaghetti Bolognese" takes like twenty minutes and fails to explode like that school canteen stuff. Want to try it after the pint?      Definitely. I’m more of a pizza person, but I'll try it if you promise it's edible. Speaking of which, you know when I started making pasta the other day, and I ended up with a mess thicker than the lunches we had in reception? I’ve got to be more consistent, you know, for when we're living in the same halls or go to parties on weekends.      Just don’t microwave it like in the packet, will you?

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, love? That lot in Westminster promising one thing and then they go and... Well, they don’t even finish the road yet down by the canal, do they? Tax rates are higher than they were when I was your age, and you're spending more on a loaf of bread than I ever did, I’ll say that for it. Still, it's not all roses on my end either. A chap my age tends to have a few more fingers in the pot, what with pensions and all that. Know what I mean?      It's just so bewildering, Dad. I mean, even you'd think that if you earn more you'd get to keep more of it, right? But no, the tax takes an even bigger slice the more you earn, and I still end up with less take-home pay in the end than I expected. It’s enough to make you want to plant your own vegetables and never step a foot outside Horsforth ever again.      Oh, I bloody well tried the vegetable idea once, back when I fancied myself a farmer, and it nearly killed me. Digging that plot with your mother as my audience and supplying only comments on my backside the whole time—it wasn't exactly a financial success, but I got good at root crops.      You were never much of a gardener. But to be serious, I just don’t understand how we can afford to pay so much in taxes and someone forty miles away is still paying less because they live in a different town. How do they even decide what the rate should be? It sounds like politicians tossing dice under a table!      Aye, well, they've got these “revenue forecasts” and “economic models”, as they call them. But it all boils down to who's voting. You're not in Birmingham, and you're not part of the same ward. They passed that rubbish cut on the education budget to the north because a few tossers said it’d grow the economy, but when it started affecting kids' school uniforms and books… Well, they had to backtrack.      But surely the National Government should set the standard for  that , not just letting every council man their own rules go? It's bloody confusing if you're not born into it, and I just started earning enough that I need to know where my gong’s being spent properly.

So do you know how long they're going to be delaying the training session? I mean, they said first thing in the morning, but no one's even turned up yet! Honestly, it's becoming a bit of a joke. Not to be dramatic, but we’ve got a project deadline in two days and it’s all falling apart because of this last-minute faff.      Oh come on, you’ve only got yourself to blame, love! I mean, you know how they are in those corporate environments. Admin gets mixed up, directions go missing, someone called in sick or something. You can’t get everything to go perfectly. I mean, I used to manage exams and people would still turn up hours late or bring the wrong forms. You learn to breathe and not lose your rag about it, truly.      I’m trying not to lose my rag! It's just that when you’re a project co-ordinator and your team starts relying on you to keep everything running, it’s awfully hard when you can't even get training. And I’m not exaggerating when I say I feel like I’m holding it all together with bailing twine and a strong cup of tea. It’s exhausting.      Oh honey, I know it’s exhausting. When I got promoted to manager at the school, I thought I was done with organisational hell, but oh my God, you think parents are bad? Try sorting out exam timetables and getting universities to understand the principles of form filling. Honestly, sometimes I think I need to audition for some kind of office survival show. It’s funny in a very tragic sort of way.      That’s actually  exactly  how I feel. I mean, I walk into the office every day and the first thought is “are they expecting me to fix the universe today?” Not that I mind the work, but the chaos level? It just hits different for someone who likes things to be neat and on time. I just wish they’d sort it out a little more quickly instead of reacting to problems as they pop up.      Well, maybe that’s what they’re paying you for? Joke’s on them, really. Now, do you want to tell me what the team’s head of HR told you when you go in later on? You know your mum’s cousin’s nephew is working in line management?

Rather annoying this new recycling schedule eh, love? Thought they’d get the bin out on time ‘n all... got the white one out by half ten like they said I did, an’ now where’s it gone?      No, I saw it! They picked it up at twenty past. I saw the van go past me window with it on the back. You reckon it all went in? I’ve been sorting things by the hour this week! I got a whole bin lid full of glass, cans, paper. We’ve been doing it properly for once.      Aye, specially with the three o’clock system. Last time I left it out the bins, they came at eight in the mornin’ an’ bin lid still closed. Left it all back! I’m not the only one bin they pick and I’m not the only one with an opinion, far as I’m concerned. I called the council last week to complain. They said I’d be “contacted soon” as if that’s some great answer for a folk who want to do the right thing by their bin.      Yeah, I’ve written in two or three times as well. It’s only ten paces from my mum’s house to the kerb. I can’t fathom why it takes them – surely they can knock the lid down and take it off the back of the van like somethin’ that’s done through the will of the wind ‘n’ water.      Aye, but they're also suspicious o’ my lot. It's one o' those things—job applications, letters about recycling, and then the politicians ‘sayin’ all the right things, but when it comes about to actually doing somethin’ round the area, well, I'm looking at a clipboard full of fails.      I mean it is a bit strange, to be honest, ‘cos we’ve all got education. All passed our exams. Me and Jon here worked hard. Even you, Billy, you had a proper job once. So when I see these forms being sent back as unalphabetised or poorly written... it’s just sad, really.      Some of the applications look like they were sent from the 90s. No formatting, bad grammar, no formatting if you like. Any real professional would expect at least a decent template, let alone a cover letter.      Aye, I've been helping Tasha with her writing and formatting. We go through the bits step by step, type it up on the ‘puter ‘n’ all.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be at a beach or something.      Oh, come on Claire, it’s only one more day. I can’t say I’m over the moon either, but at least we’re finally getting somewhere with those resources.      Yeah, I suppose the conference  is  useful, if you can get past the migraine of all the powerpoint slides everyone seems to love so much.      Ugh, I know what you mean. Honestly, it’s like nobody was taught how to keep a presentation interesting, or maybe they just don’t care.      It’s so bizarre, isn’t it? I only trained for two years and that one of my tutors drilled into us how to not put a paragraph of text onto a slide.      Right? If only the people up here today had taken that advice. I nearly fell asleep when David from Manchester started monologuing about Hattie’s meta-analysis for an hour.      I couldn’t believe it. One time, I thought I was dreaming and looked at my watch, and it was still 10 minutes into it. Did you see how the other teachers were reacting? Some of them watching like they were waiting for a light to change.      Oh yes, I was sitting in the front and I swear some woman had her eyes nearly closed the whole time. Honestly, if I’d been one of the teachers that came along and paid for this, I would have been so suspicious they were trying to sell us something.      Exactly. Also, have you noticed the way they’ve split up the workshops? I was in the EMI one today about how to incorporate conversation skills in monolingual English lit classes, and it was completely out of my league.      EMI? Yeah, I was in that one. Honestly, I felt like the only person there who didn’t know what VLSs were. I don’t mind a bit of jargon once in a while, but some of these abbreviations they throw around are as mysterious as a code.      I think I walked out with more questions than I came with. The guy was delivering it as if it was a TED Talk, but nobody in the room seemed to be getting it.      I just started smiling politely and hoped they’d go away, but sometimes I think your training as a teacher doesn’t prepare you for all of this seminar stuff.

Rather annoying driving a campervan through these Polish roads, isn’t it? I mean, they’re  fine , don’t get me wrong—just not as nicely laid out as I remember the A12 being back in Cambridge. Charming country, though.      Yeah, it’s a bit different to Newton-le-Willows, that’s for sure! But I actually like it. Quiet, peaceful, not too many people rushing around. I’m trying to listen out for differences in the Polish dialects as we go along. I read once that the further east you get, the more the accent changes. It’s like noticing Lakelander variations, only with more consonants, you know?      Oh, I’ve never really taken much interest in accents beyond the standard London drawl or the stereotypical Geordie twang. But I suppose you’d notice far more being a teacher. I envy you that actually working in a field you enjoy. I’ve been scraping by for the last few years, dabbling in TEFL when I feel like it, and that’s about it.      I know, I sometimes wonder if I land a job abroad for a few years, maybe I could save up properly and retire early, or something. Have you read much about that? I remember reading a book while I was in school, it was  The Long Haul —expat life and all that. Silly really, because I didn’t even know what expat meant at the time.      I haven’t read a lot lately, oddly. I tend to flit from one genre to another—sometimes a historical novel, then a thriller, then ballet back into romantic fiction. I did try reading something about health and fitness the other week, but I had to stop because I felt judged! Like it was telling me I’d let myself go a bit, and that’s just not fair. Life happens, you know.      Yeah, I think we all go through phases. I’ve been trying to get back into cycling, especially since I’m working out less in the city. Though being out here also helps—walking lunches, campervan parking breaks. Not that I’ve managed to find a parking spot around this bend yet!      Tell me about it! It’s like wherever you turn, camping is off-limits without a permit. I tried asking a guy on the street earlier, and you could tell he didn’t speak much English, and I certainly don’t speak much Polish.

Rather than trying to find an ideal length for a conversation, perhaps we could focus on the purpose it serves. From what I understand, this is about crafting a more natural and engaging exchange by taking into account the personas and context involved. So we wouldn’t have to fixate on a specific length in advance — we’d just create the most coherent and meaningful dialogue that reflects the   metadata attributes   you provided — like age, origin, education, relationship, topics, etc.      Right, right. I know you said you can generate a   detailed and realistic conversation  , even if it begins  mid-discussion . So, as long as you  faithfully reflect  the   traits of both speakers   and the   topics listed  , you’ll cover all requirements — including the rich mix of   history  ,   gerontology  ,   anti-ageing  , and even   comets  . It's actually a great combination — very diverse and doesn’t feel forced if you use a continuous, conversational tone.      Exactly. That’s the key:   continuity  . Imagine they’re sat in a relaxing room in   Cork   — partners or close friends, perhaps two mugs of tea to their side and   ANON  , as you’ve called it, becoming the intermediary. The mix of   historical references   — the Vikings, pyramids, tectonics — and   modern concerns   like   telomeres  ,   immortality  , and   global warming   could create a very interesting flow, even if it feels spontaneous at times.      "Ah, here's that sour-dog expression you get when you weigh up a risk versus a reward. I was just watching  Cosmos  last night and it was on about   tectonics   and   comets  , and it hit me — what if the very   pyramids   were built by people who had a  higher life expectancy  and, dare I say, a better understanding of   telomeres   than we have today?"      "Okay, but don't start introducing schematics on how the   Vikings   had immortality tech. Even if they were the first to reach the New World, do you think the   ice cores   remember that? I’m not saying it's all nonsense — go ahead, map your own theories — but I’m still waiting for the   weekend away   plan. We could go   kayaking   near your parents' place. It’s low risk, high reward, and doesn’t involve   global warming   or   geothermal shifts  ."      "A fair point, and I admit the    viking time machine  theory is a bit of a stretch — kind of like trying to romanticize an   anti-ageing protocol  . But when we look at   geriatrics   and how far   life expectancy   has stretched in some countries, it’s worth thinking about how people's personal beliefs and behaviours affect that.

Rather annoying I could've got a voucher for the café in town. I was just there las week with Nan... got the big cake an' all, but paid full price! Any idea how we’d get a discount again?      Oh, I think you need to download the app for the café on Queen Street. I’ve got a loyalty one, and I reckon it’s got all sorts of offers. Maybe that’s how you get vouchers? I’ll show you on my phone if you like?      Aye, and I were thinking about the coffee maker, too. Mithat thing fetchin’ out of order again? Last time it go chuckin the spout, Rob had to run out and buy a new one. Still, best to have it prim’ and proper, ain’t right?      I think Aunty Sharon gave us one for a present? ‘Cos she doesn’t really drink coffee... but she’s still got one in her kitchen. I might ask her later, if you want?      Good idea, and actually—speaking of coffee, maybe we can pop in to the supermarket later and pick up a few things for the baby? We need that fancy chair they got on offer. I saw a voucher in the mail today—I’ll call them and check it’s valid first.      Aye, we’ve enough vouchers around here to start a shop ourselves! Though I’m still trying to figure out that referendum business they had in Parliament. Seems to me like a lot o’ trouble just for a bit more cash. I dunno, but the chickens have been skinnier this year—ain’t like they had enough to eat or nothin.      I don’t get the referendum stuff either, but my mate at school said somethin’ abou’ European Union and how it helped unival people get jobs. My teacher ‘as like four PhDs and explained it like ten times. Still no better me...      Oh, it can get confusing. But you know what else I could use? A good pair of sunglasses. The ones I’ve got are cracked again, and the light from the sea today was murder. I’d be lost without something to protect my eyes.      Aye, an’ if you’re thinkin’ of spendin’ on glasses, maybe see if they’ve go a bloomin’ offer at one o’ them shops at the beach. I’ve seen ‘em do deals on vouchers for fruit trees too—Andrew might appreciate a new one for the garden.

Rather annoying the new neighbours, eh? You know, the ones who came in just down the road? They had some big white van with German plates, parked up and I thought, oh sure, another Airbnb type probably doing a cash-in. But seems like they're proper people — well, at least from what old Mrs. Hedges, the postwoman, says.      Anyway, wanted to talk to you about something else before I lose track of it. I got a call in from work today — some interesting case came up. You remember the guy I told you about during your last visit? The one with the... frozen shoulder?      A bit, yeah. You said he’d been working on a farm and it’s been giving him trouble for ages. Is it getting worse?      You're spot on, and I think he's managed to make it worse again by overdoing it with some DIY, no doubt. I've been thinking about a bit in his medical history, you know, when we talked about Germany’s farming culture during our German history class, or was it during one of those quiz nights we used to do? Anyway, I remember that land is as much their heritage as food.      Oh yeah, we laughed so much over the sausages and pretzels – Mateo nearly choked on one, and I had to help him up. Anyway, what's the connection to your patient?      Well, you know how Germany's winter can be just freezing — full on. He said they often tough it out without central heating in some of the outlying barns and things. So I started thinking, their approaches to health, especially with muscles and joints, might have about five decades more history than our own. Interesting talking points when explaining this to our young med students.      So you’re telling me it helped you understand him more? That he wasn’t overdoing it just for fun, but passed it down as 'manly'.      Exactly. You can see how it's ingrained in them. I told one of my colleagues, and he just laughed. Websites and all things digital can’t keep up with that sort of human connection and history.      You know, by the way, your boyfriend asked about you when I saw him about your birthday plans.      Oh, did he now? He’s planned a weekend in Brighton, your suggestion was that we could have a Christmas tree up early and start the festive season.

Rather skip the newfit tutorial eh?      Aye, internet's working through the first floor, and I've had no luck on the gadgets down here! Any idea how we're going to connect it permanently? A lot of flat provisions done so far though, top marks for storage space. Just need a reasonable amount of shelf stuff and the kitchen'll be set. You know I’m not much good in the kitchen – I’m terrified I’ll end up with pickles and eggs again.      Well, let’s do grocery shopping breakfast, Saturday morning then? We can allow it to settle in gradually, but let’s do it after delivering the furniture.      Yeah, go ahead then on your own if you like. I'm going to finish reading the Wi-Fi manual, and maybe give the box a soft pat.      So I have the fluency to speak and manage roles in two languages, so I think I’m alright at following manuals.

So did you go back to Manchester after the break, or did you stay here for a bit?      No, I went back for a few days, had to visit the parents, you know how it is. But I only stayed like a week before heading back. What about you? Got plans for the holidays?      I just chilled at home for the most part, a bit of family stuff, but not too much excitement. I actually went for a short trip to Cornwall with my cousin. We stayed in this tiny cottage and just lazed about, explored the beaches. You'd have loved it.      Ooh, sounds idyllic. I’ve never managed to get down there, but I’ve always wanted to. I did spend a few days in York back in December with some friends and I think I turned into a human scone for about a week — all those breakfasts and afternoon teas...      Ha! No wonder, you look as if you survived some indulgent holiday. How was the placement over the summer, by the way?      It was up and down, honestly. Got some insight into how human resources departments actually work, which is probably something I would never have appreciated without getting stuck into the detail. How's the project coordinating been going? I know you were swamped before Christmas.      It did pick up a bit, yeah. I got stuck into a massive logistics project which kept me out of the house and barely looking at my phone. Thank God it's winding down. I’m actually hoping to get out a bit more and see more people now. Work has been  literally  consuming my time and about half my soul.      That’s rough. I get it — I was pretty much glued to that office too. I’m actually thinking about sending out some invites for a weekend trip over Easter. If you're free, I'd love you to come along.      That sounds great. Easter’s always a bit of a madhouse at home. There are queens and uncles and cousins whose names always escape me. I'd much rather do something low-key with you. Where's it going to be?      I was thinking maybe a little B&B in the Cotswolds or somewhere nearby. We can spend the day exploring, maybe a bit of shopping or something? Just your standard girl’s weekend with tea, cake, and plenty of champagne.

Rather annoying when people think the whole of the North East is just Newcastle and Sunderland. We’ve got so much more going on beyond that, innit? I mean, I’m from Sunderland sure, but we’ve got Hadrian’s Wall up near Carlisle and the Lake District on our doorstep!      Right, I  am  a southerner really, bred in Birmingham, but I’ve spent a fair few summers up by the coast in Tyneside. The vibe there is totally different to what’s going on round here in Cambridge. I mean, this place is all about the uni blokes and the smart suits, but up North, people still dress like they've got the day off work!      My nan still says "bletherin’" and "’eck" everyday – I swear, if I pick that up in the office, I’ll get in trouble again. But you’re not wrong, the fashion up North is a bit more... I don’t know, authentic. Everyone looked like they just came from a gig or the working men’s club, whereas round here everyone’s into subtle tailoring and inappropriate socks with sandals.      Fair one. I’ve tried to fit in with the Cambridge gear, but I reckon I still look like a Geography dropout who tries too hard at being posh. Still, I’m working on it. My supervisor says I’ve got promise – don’t know if he means the work or the outfits!      Ha! Honestly, I work at the university too, as a research manager, and it just cracks me up when people out the North hear me talking and immediately think I sound posh. Can’t speak for your Birmingham accent, but most people about here reckon I’m a Swede or from the South East because I use my ths properly.      Not you! I know it’s a North East gal to the core, ‘cos you still refer to tea as "a brew" and sods as "pop." I remember going to a nice café once with you and trying to order a macchiato while the bloke behind the counter just stared at me like I was speaking Gibberish.      That's our Manchester grandad trying to make a latte machine do the work of a go-kart on your life if you ask him for something fancy! Speaking of, d’you see that Mancunian bloke on TikTok who goes by  Drizzle FatStack ? He sums it all up in two minutes.

Rather annoying the new lot in power, innit? Seems they’s promising one lot then doin' another... Like wi' the roads 'round here—always buildin’ a by-pass then sayin’ “Nah, we can’t afford it.” Proper confusing!      Aye een, dear. I’ve seen it all before 'n I reckon it’ll carry on. Politics is a funny old ‘un, but I think they do it more to keep the lid on than to help folk like us. We’ve had governments that promised gold an’ served up rust!      Right you are! Still, I reckon we could do worse. At least they’re tryin’ ta sort things out, even if they mess it up most the time. Remember when they told us the Post Office would all be privatized? That was a right panic—my gran was near to tears ‘cos she thought she couldn’t send a letter without payin’ for a goat and a shed.      Oh, I remembere that. I were still in Darlington then, shopin’ for my Nellie up t’ Wellington. Aye, it made quite a stink, it did. Good thing they stopped it before it got out of hand. Mind you, most of the policies they come out wi’ these days, it feels like they’ve been written by som’un in London who’s never lived their lives.      Truthfully, they should take more someone like you an’ me into account. You’ve seen it all, an’ I’m out there survivin’ it fresh. What worked in the ‘70s might not work in the ‘20s, innit?      Oh, you're quite right. I wish they listened more to folks wi’ experience. I were only a young un in the war, but I saw ‘ow the hard work of everyday folk kep’ the country runnin’. They could learn a lot if they stopped ‘earing their own press and stared at what people really need.      Yeah. Though I’ve seen young folk trying their 'ands too. At school we’ve got PPE, politics, economics and philosophy—som’un told us it's all about how govs really work. But if you ask me, they give us books, but not the real talk between folk like us ‘n the ones in power.      Aye, but that’s the heart of it, innit? Talks and books don’t mean much if they don’t ‘elp poorer folk up or at least try. I tell you, my missus used to say politics was a bit like tea—unless you stir it, it don’t do much!

We can talk about old times and the changes we’ve seen over the decades.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh?      Aye, it's been on the telly nonstop. Never thought I'd be watching yet another debate about whether Scotland wants to split from us lot again.      Look, I’ve taught kids for thirty-two years — thirty-two years! — and I’ve seen a lot, but   this   divide is getting tiresome. The younger ones talk about it too. Not that they'd be voting, but they're very into it, pulling out facts and wanting to argue both sides. It's fascinating, in a sad sort of way.      That's mostly because the media keep fanning the flames, in my opinion. On the telly one minute, you get one side saying it's all doom and gloom, the next you've got them saying independence is the only way forward. Half the country must be confused!      I couldn’t agree more. My Brian has a job in Edinburgh at the moment, and he says the atmosphere is polarised. People he works with — colleagues, real nice sorts — just don’t see eye to eye on it. It impacts the workplace, quite a bit. He's worried about moving back for good.      My Linda – she’s only just got herself employed as a receptionist down at Royal Pavilion Hospital, and mind you, she’s been brushing the issue under the carpet. She says if you don't bring it up, you don't get the job. She's just someone who wants to get on with things. Makes me a bit proud, oddly.      That is a fine attitude, I’d say. My Margot —  our  Margot, your nearly about daft niece — she's off to the university of St Andrews this September. I dread what she’ll make of it all. She barely left Brighton till she got up for university interviews. My wife’s over the moon, of course. All that tragedy about the weather up there, but the girl's a fighter.      She always was. You must be doing all the proud grandparent things. You bloke with the grandkid with lunches and bedtime stories and whatnot.      You think  that’s  not tiring! I get called away in the middle of pond life improvements to tidy her room or give a "story line." I’m only a pensioner; I’m not paid to be your unpaid housekeeper. It's all in the name of kowtowing to my wife, really.

Rather annoying driving though, isn't it? That Christopher, he’s always hurrying off somewhere. But he’s got to pick up some gear for the new flat. I can't say I blame him, though. Getting a new place can be a bit of a faff.      Yeah, I'm just thinking about the mess we've got to sort out at his old place. He couldn’t resist buying that coffee table when he was done in. I mean, what are you gonna do with it now? Throw it in the bin?      If it was me, I’d just squirrel it in the garage. Still, it’s his choice. Christopher's the only one who can do something about it. My point is, I’ve met enough people left high and dry when moving, and Christopher’s lucky he can afford this place. But he’s got that tuition fee bursary or whatever, and being an instructor helps—bit more dosh puts your head above water.      Honestly, we’ve got to be grateful it's not something like, I dunno, national insurance – that’s a total skunk, and none of us are getting much back out.      Speaking of which, Dad was meant to get that tax return sorted. It’s been ages, someone should give HMRC a nudge. They just like to sit on it, don’t they?      Or maybe he doesn’t want to see the mess he’s in. Hello, most people about our age are worrying about the gold standard of their pensions. We were lucky to get a house, and even luckier that it's barely a time bomb.      Yeah, but I for one don’t miss that cooking mess. I did manage once to make porridge the right way – not too greasy. But I tried to make a lasagna once, and the water turned as orange as sprite.      Family stories! I’ve told you the one about the omelette Christopher once tried to make with tinned tomatoes? That was one go bad. I think it was rated in the world records of culinary disaster.      You don’t say, blokes. I’ve had some dodgy meals at the retailer I work at. Thought we were saving dosh, but honestly?

Rather annoying when afit’s goin’ so slow, innit?      Oh aye, an’ often no luck gettin’ outta first gear, either      Aye, we do see the same kind of things on motorways all the time. Got eeny friend who liked tryin’ start ‘irends on hills an’ ended up stuck completely      I once got stuck in this big hill here Timperley, right by some farm. This cow just wandered past the bonnet and starred me in the eye like it was my fault      Oh! Sounds like a proper drama, then      On farms like that, you’ve got sheep, cows—you name it. One time I was goin’ through the Dales, this whole flock of sheep turned round an’ stared at the car like waitin’ for breakfast, innit      Haha, yeah, they’s awlways starein’ you down, those critters      It’s terrifyin’, though, isn’t it—these big animals in the middle of the road      Honestly, we’ve got rules on municipal engineering standards for it. Be ideal if more folk took them into account though      I never really thought about it much. More worried ‘bout not losin’ the phone’s signal when I’m stuck in the hills      That’s the same for me. Just trying to stay afloat technologically when stuck on the outskirs      I’d be lookin’ at the birds, really, or the sheep, about now. My main issue is usually trying to keep the car cool on these vibes. Heat builds up fast if you are stuck in the traffic      Maybe I’ll have to invest in a better car. My little car’s passed its time. Aint’ handled well the past few winters      I dunno how people manage with such old tech. Feels like we’re stuck in 1987 with some of these machines      Yeah, but there’s a beauty in these old cars. I mean, the classic goenvironmental routes usually work if you know what you're doin’      I don’t know ‘bout that, son. Passin' on to summat newer might be a smarter choice      I agree. Just like, better to invest in something more durable ‘nstead o’ fannin’ about fixin’ it all up      Totally. I’ve done both, an’ it's definitely more stable in the long run to switch up completely      Hmm, sounds good to me, but I’ve yet to find my last car’s replacement      Oi, just lookin’ on Autotrader once you finish messing about—end of.

Rather annoying when people keep showing up late for dinner, isn't it? I mean, it's not like it's the weekend or anything. We've already paid for the food, haven't we?      I completely get that. Look, I promise you — I'll be timing myself this time. My friend Margot had to leave her choir practice   5 minutes earlier   so as not to be a bother. A lot of people just think that punctuality isn't important these days, don't they?      It was different when I was teaching. If a student was late more than once... well, let's just say they made sure to get here on the dot after the first warning.      Ha, I remember you saying something like that last week when we were talking about the school Oliver goes to. Now I think he turned out alright. But I was about to say something about the breakfast clubs and whatever funding they've been given for after-school tutors — all that’s thanks to some charitable trust, you know?      Oh yes, those sorts of foundations give it a nice little boost, don’t they? I mean, we all know that local government alone can only do so much. At least they're watching out for the kids who need it most.      Exactly. Speaking of which, have you decided what exercises you'd like to do this weekend during our family gathering? I know Silas was hoping to go for a proper hike — he’s been in the frame at work and is looking for a break from all the rush.      That does sound lovely, a family hike and some good home-cooked food afterwards. I was thinking, maybe we invite Nia and her boys? They’re always asking to come for dinner, and it'd be a nice opportunity for the kids to be together.      That could be fun. I just wish they realized punctuality isn't always optional — passed 7 o'clock and all, they might as well just join us as it is.      You're getting your stick out already, aren't you?      Well, someone has to keep things from running like a slapstick play every time we get together.      I'll make sure go talk to my parents and check if they're free for Saturday. You know they started going to that local food group in town — they say it helps your cholesterol and you learn how to make proper stews.

Right, thanks for coming in today. You know, I do love the chance to discuss how they’re getting on, and I’ll be honest—both Holly and Ethan are lovely in class.      Oh, thank goodness! We’ve been kind of frightened our little ones might be falling behind again.      Yeah, they didn’t enjoy the maths test much.      A lot of the class didn’t! I mean, we've moved on from simple addition into multiplication, and some of the kids are struggling. Ethan’s working through it but still takes a bit of time.      Oh, no pressure, we just want them to feel confident. You know that MyMaths homework thing? He still bites the pen like it’s a personal attack if he gets a question wrong.      That’s not unusual, far from it. Kids can get really frustrated when something suddenly starts feeling more complicated after playing in their heads they’d cracked it.      I told him that the numbers had just gone on strike against him and wouldn’t play nice anymore.      Oh, brilliant! That might be a better idea than me just saying “it’s hard for everyone, work harder.” Be creative, that works so much better with their age group. I’ve had some kids really get into World Book Day and base their characters off their struggles in maths!      Oh! That sounds like something he might like.      Yeah, they design a character to represent their strengths or struggles—quite therapeutic, actually. It gives them space to be imaginative and still tie it back to learning.      I’m disappointed he didn’t win the prize last time, though. He turned into a very fierce pirate with a crown that scorched the side of his head from the glue gun.      That’s not unusual either. I did warn parents about glue guns on the day—well, mainly about microwave glue sticks, but… you know little ones.      Anyway, thank you. And also, we were wondering—do you have any suggestions about dinner? We’ve been stuck for ages, something around this week.      Mm, usually it’s something hearty—I go for stir-fries or shepherd’s pies, really. Although the other day I accidentally burnt what I thought was lasagne—it just tasted like... disappointment.      Och, I had that once. Smelled like forgotten dreams or something.      Is it true that— I read online that cooked human flesh smells like?

Rather annoying this new tax on rented houses, isn’t it? I mean, it's one thing when you're working and trying to plan for the kids' future, but now landlords are getting hit where it hurts. But isn’t he the one who said his brother is treasurer of a garages group now? I’d ask him for some help if the turkey still cost the same price as it did last week. I near dropped my chalk. But you know what? It made for good banter between the students. Also, have we discussed the exact arrangements for his birthday yet?      Oisin said we were going to bring the cake to the rugby match. But what match is it? And will Ronan and Jackie be there with the twins? I spoke to the manager earlier and he said they can set out a space by the side of the pitch. If we do it before the match, that should be good.      I’ll make sure goody bags get sorted and if you don’t mind sourcing one of those posters off the printing shop, I’ll be done with arranging the rest.      So nice to see you俩 manage all this despite the stresses of the usual stuff, like tax or not hearing from some unsavory charities every other day.

Rather annoying word today, innit? You know when you get that feeling you've seen it before but can't quite咄 out what it is?      Yeah, what was it? Rather skip the queue an’ go through the side door, innit? That’d save us ‘alf an hour, don’t it?      I know, I know! It’s a madhouse in ‘ere. I’ve seen t’ same queue for three songs now an’ we ain’t even got a pint yet. You think they’d get more staff on a Friday night? Nutter a chance. A lot o’ us lot in this town, innit?      Aye. We’ve been stuck like this once before last month when Beth come with ‘er mates from uni. It was like some kind o’ pop concert, with more shoutin’ an’ fewer guitars.      Oh, you mean the left photo on ‘er snap, the one where you're all wearing hats and I’m holding the bottle upside down an’ it’s flipped?      Bucks yeah that one!
