Nah, you’d be takin’ it easy with a long, warm, post-nap cup o’ tea, somethin’ to calm them tensions down.      Smashing. Nappin's what someone said in one o’ them American films. Rather annoying that the council planning meeting’s on a Wednesday this week. I know it's supposed to save time having it on a weekday, but half the committee tends to miss it because their day jobs interfere. The old utility buildings near the canal?      Right, those ones with the problematic permits. Let me check the latest draft of the brochure you sent me. I think we might need a more reassuring tone in the 'legal considerations' section. It’s putting off a few of the potential buyers.      Exactly. Also, have you seen the architectural proposal being floated? That new rooftop extension over the main hall would be a selling point if we can get the height limit waived. But we're depending on the planning committee to fast-track that approval.      I'll mention it at the committee meeting. My vote counts for the architectural development subcommittee. Though I might have to speak up more clearly to ensure it's on the agenda. We can't afford another deferred proposal.      This one’s straightforward. Just a safety upgrade and expansion space. If we don't act soon, we risk losing the buyer. I’ve set up a call with them for Friday—would you be up for joining? I think their finance director needs a bit more convincing personally.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand grilling everything they know her, but they’re like... stalking her on Insta now. Like, what are we, teenagers again?      Honestly? Not to start a topic but I think it's  so  weird how we always een beginning to talk about the neighbour. It was like that when we were at uni as well.      I know! I mean this isn't even Ohio, it's just a flat in London. If anything we should be moving to somewhere like the outside of town or the countryside. You'd think like, moving in with your  girlfriend  would make someone less nosy.      My turkey curry definitely needs some more spice though. I've tried adding more ginger and garlic, but I don't know. I think it needs something. Or maybe I just need a better sauce.      I've been wanting to go for a walk at the park, maybe by the river, you know, just somewhere to get the fresh air. But that requires me to leave the flat and actually do something other than Netflix and take two-hour naps.      That sounds amazing. We haven't been for a proper day out in such a long time. Maybe we can even pop into that café opposite the library, you know the one with the sweet chilli waffles?      Oh, I remember that place! The waiters looked like they'd just stepped out of a TV show. Like, unfortunately a very old one.      Also, have you heard from Sarah and Rob lately? I feel like I haven't spoke to them in forever about our old university days.      Actually, Sarah messaged me a few days ago! She was telling me that Rob's trying to get a promotion, but to be honest, I think he just wants to look like he's doing something with his life at 29.      Ugh, that's exactly him. I always thought he was such a clever guy but he’s doing nothing but waitressing with lunches delivered right on time from the café.      Honestly, I find it tiring that the news is so go bad all the time. I sometimes just switch it off. But then I feel guilty, like I should be paying attention, you know?      I feel the same. I’ve been reading a lot about mental health lately, and I just find it so worrying how much it’s hidden and over-looked.

Rather annoying advert just popped up on iPlayer, ay? Like talkin’ about how ‘healthy’ pizazza is with some mad claims about wholewheat dough an’ whatnot      Aye, honestly I’ve seen those kind of things before, like the ads make it sound eeny weeny bit better than it is an’ you feel like you  have  to buy it.      Ay yeah, this one got me so interested I even watched the whole ad like it was a doc or sommat. S’pose it was quite clever the way they used lighting an’ all that      I reckon, but the real question is, do you think they use the same NLP techniques as they do in like marketing or psychology courses? I’m doin’ a bit o’ work on that at the uni.      Mm, I know, innit? I’ve been workin’ on teachin’ GCSE English and it's amazing how some kids struggle with reading so much. One of them told me he was dyslexic, and it reminded me of ANON I had in my class a while back      Oh right, go on…      Well, he got so frustrated most of the time. But with a bit of extra support, he really came up. One time he wrote this amazing short story about a phone that was too smart and drove its owner mad. It was daft, but it was one of the best pieces of writing I've read from a GCSE student      Oi, that sounds brilliant. Did he get it published or anything?      Dunno, but I reckon he could have been a writer had he had more confidence. Anyway, this weekend I was thinking of doing some online shopping for the car boot sale      Oh yeah? What for?      A few bits n’ bobs really – probably got some vintage records, some kitchenware stuff. You mad I’m sellin’ such stuff?      No, I’ve been keepin’ an eye out for some cool glassware myself for the house. Then again, if you see a chance to go out of the house and about it's always a good one      Yep, I need to go further than the pub most days. Speaking of which, I’ve been noticing more people smoking outside than before, which is a bit weird      I expect it’s the ‘open-air crime’ lot, them that like to smoke near the shop doorways to avoid cameras. My job’s kind of started me noticing it more, I suppose      Ah, the dirty lot.

Rather annoying, though, isn't it? That phone app for everything – you’d think it'd know  what  to play based on your moods, yet somehow I ended up on Survivor themes when I was craving Kate Bush. Not quite the vibe, I can tell you.      Honestly, I'm with you there, Charlotte. It's like these apps think we all wear the same socks on a Tuesday. A lot of this AI jazz is too much, if you ask me. It's easier pulling out a record and choosing based on the crack and pop.      Right, because nothing says  hip  like a crackling static and a supply of headphones. On the other hand, you know, I’ve been revisiting leftfield jazz this week – I’m half obsessed with Darcy James Argue’s latest. Pretty heavy stuff if you're not used to it.      Heaviness aside, are we alright for food? I ordered the Japanese takeaway as usual, but you didn’t say anything about a group decision over dinner.      My apologies, Julia, I forgot to mention I planned on sharing a casserole with you all. Eggplant with harissa and some local ale. Doesn’t sound quite West Midlands, but I promise it's –?      Dead good, if the photo is anything to go by. You know I'm all for anything less processed than the usual BBC editorial meetings. Our food here at Anon’s should be legendary. Ever had a plum cake, Charlotte?      You mean the infamous ‘sinker’ plum cake your grandmother, Anon? I about choked on mine last time. Decent, though.      And I suppose you found some local cabernet to dip it in?      Should we discuss the new National Theatre play? I heard about it on the radio. Sounds like it's going to be all about the grey areas of media – oh, right, could be a touch too close to home for some of us.      Radio has been tough lately. Too many tweaks and a lack of support for investigative pieces. They want content go viral rather than report well.      Not much has changed really in the media landscape between us. Storytelling is getting glossed up to be click bait instead of enduring journalism.      And while we bellyache about work, let's not forget where we are – we've got plum cake, ale, homemade music playlists, and one of the best views of Birmingham from here. That's the real feast.

Rather do share a drink and bring us all up to speed. I confess, it's been a string of lively reminiscences, hasn't it? It's strange how all these memories resurface over a glass of wine.      Look at us—half our anecdotes now centre around how we found eeny residences when we first moved into this very area. I reckon it was about '63? I came here with a suitcase and just one dental appointment booked, funny enough. Prior to that, I was teaching history in Ramsgate, of all places. Didn’t even own a dental handpiece.      Oh, you mean when I was still learning teeth at the Manchester dental school? That was wild. My postgrad mistress nearly dropped her scalpel when I blurted out I had gone for a week in Athens for a course in the first days of the Greek dictatorship, thinking the jets would better me breakfast, no doubt. I swear time zones still mess with me.      Good lord, I remember ordering a taxi and the man thought I was heading directly to Crete over the Thames, not Birmingham, of all places! I left London with quite a determination to be a dentist. Hired by the council in this area—it wasn't exactly a towering postcode then. Mind you, negotiating mortgages – that’s been another fairly long, chequered journey.      Truth be told, when I started as an EFL teacher, no one ever explained that the principles of bilingualism could someone allow full discussions to also suspiciously morph from past to present, depending oddly on the subject—job histories, housing, meeting the spouses.      Aha! We all spoke of romantic encouters about our spouses. Anna and I had our first touch here at this very place. It was absolutely cliché! Going for that first school staff meal and it began snowing, both of us with our ‘warm hand’ hiding ice waters under desks.      Come on, the meeting was a library event, I had brought a gingerbread for my waiting wife, but I lost my way as soon as I entered the building—then ended with lunches and a new dental chair! Per various path, our paths crossed.      Pah! I met my intended in the room I rented—the landlord had a cat.large cat. I made her line in the garden, between bench and mud box, until she stopped what she was doing and offered me tea.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracing the windows just as it would through the pines in the garden, back home in Somerset.      It does make me feel like I've stepped into a painting. That view from your window — well, it's quite picturesque. I'm assuming you designed the place to look this lovely.      Oh, most certainly. I ran a little gallery just before I retired — back in Bistol. Art was always my livelihood, though the antiques and the occasional dealership kept the coffers considerably heavier when the paint was not selling quite like it should. Still, it made for a nice enough life.      You sound well-acquainted with the art of living! I myself spent much of my career helping others communicate their thoughts. Rather different, I think, but equally fulfilling.      How very interesting! What exactly was your role?      I specialised in speech and language therapy for quite a few years, working mostly with children. One of my proudest moments was when a child who had never spoken a full sentence looked me in the eye and said, "Thank you," for something as simple as a colouring book.      That gives one pause, doesn’t it? I often tell my friends and, sometimes myself, that life is the truest of canvases and every conversation a stroke of paint.      What a poetic way to put it. Spoken like someone who's not only seen a lot of life but also captured its essence in paint and stone.      Well, I suppose I had to learn as I went along. I was born and raised in Somerset, quite the green and tranquil lot we had there. I remember my mother often said, “Life shouldn’t be lived like it’s running out.” Quite the mantra, really.      How lovely — a sentiment that reflects both her and your appreciation for a life well lived. I, on the other hand, was born in Sydney, Australia, and as you can imagine, the oceans and the scent of eucalyptus trees were the first memories I carried. Though I’m British by nationality, growing up in the sun was something I always cherished.      Oh, I imagine it very well. I remember a boyhood trip to the Australian coast — marvellous place. The people were warm, much like yourself, and the skies seemed to go on forever. I always liked that about your land.      That’s very kind of you to say.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand why they do it, but it’s like, couldn’t they have waited a bit longer after the service? Blows all your superstitions out the wind, see?      No, I kind of agree. People like to rush in and rush out, like they can't bear the thought of missing out on the best bits of Christmas. Honestly, I reckon half of them just want to get their cookies and drinks taken so they can start planning what to do next. Christmas is magical, but sometimes the pressure gets a bit much, don't you think?      Oh yeah, it's so intense. All the planning, the decorations, the presents. And then the turkey, you have to make sure it's not over or underdone, the sides... You're a pastry pusher, not a world-class chef. It's a miracle we've managed to survive breakfast, let alone a full Christmas dinner. Honestly, I reckon if someone invites me for Christmas lunch again, I’m ordering a pizza and sending a sock puppet to represent.      Come off it, you’d still want the side of shortbread cookies your Auntie made. And the real deadly gift is the brussels sprouts. My parents used to make such a big deal out of them – no one knew what they were, least of all us kids trying to get the mint sauce on our tongues to cover them up. Honestly, I’d rather eat a shoe.      Haha, fair one. Although I’ve got my own traditions. My brother’s massive into candy canes now, and he insists on draping the whole house in green and red candy decorations. He’s like a kid about it. I walk in the door and the place smells like melted fizzy drinks and a thousand different scents of “traditional Christmas.”      That does sound fun to be honest, like a party baked into your guest room. As long as he doesn't start dishing the biscuits out alongside any presents, I might have to start using them for my bakery. Customers always crack up when I hand them sprite of festive cookies with festive ribbons. Especially when the ribbon gets caught in the filling and you reach for it and get a face full.      That's the best one! My customers sometimes come in with their own pre-packaged decorations in separate bags, like they’ve done box sets or something.

Rather skip the new developments in Trumpington. That place is going mental with all the cranes and the piling in. I prefer somewhere with a bit more... character. Maybe Grantchester or one of the older parts near the river. Charming stone cottages and whatnot. Just like the books make it out to be.      It’s all good and dashing, I suppose, but don’t you think you should settle for something more... practical first? You’ve just finished your degree and, well, it’s one thing to romanticise the countryside when you're in your twenties.      Right, because thirty is  so  the new twenty, is it? I’d rather live somewhere that’s going to make me fall in love with life every morning. It doesn’t have to be wildly expensive—rent in these older areas is not out the roof. Plus, I’m about to start working freelance for a couple of universities. I can commute. Not everyone needs to be in the city, you know.      I suppose so. I remember when I was starting out after Oxford, I thought I had to be surrounded by the prestige of London or somewhere equally as grand. But grief, how wrong I was. There was something so stable—and uninspiring—about that whole lifestyle. I’m proud of you for thinking differently. I know you’ve worked really hard on that thesis of yours.      Thanks, Mum. I spent three years chewing over every bloody sentence, and I’m just starting to feel like it actually means something. I’d like to write more, maybe a proper book one day—something about how young people these days still want to live decent lives but don’t know how because all we’re told is to “climb the ladder” without the tools to do it.      That sounds very... academic. But I’m not cruel—I think it’s powerful. My, you really do look like your father when you get that spark in your eye. He used to say the same things before all the editing meetings and deadlines took him over.      I didn’t know that. He always seemed so... functional with his work. I mean, I’ve got respect for what he does for a living.      Oh, he still goads me on with his deadlines sometimes. If he was here, he’d be chuckling at that joke. But he’s proud of you, I can tell.

Rather annoying when a speaker’s accent is so difficult to catch. I mean, it's understandable they’re from... where was it, Lincoln? Or is that more of a surname than a place? Anyway, I was totally thrown off when we were speaking about the Chinese dialects in the Lower Yangtze Region. I'm used to passive voice and reduced relative clauses, but I reckon his use of all that “that” stuff might be from a different area altogether.      Oh, you mean Dr. Hargraves? He was born in Oswestry, in Shropshire. Probably not too many people talk like that around these parts anymore. I found it charming to be honest. He was quite animated about that Mycenaean excavation site he worked on last year. Remember when he told the story about the amphora they found and the translation he did? That was an excellent anecdote, really highlighted how language doesn’t just sit in books but in the mud.      Yes, the amphora was a key turning point for the study of the period. I remember that excavation myself—though I preferred the village sites in the lower regions. I used to lecture quite a bit on early human settlement movements, especially as we moved from the Sublime Porte towards the West Asian cultures. You young people might remember that as the Silk Road era, but actually it was far more complex. The Arab traders weren’t just moving goods—they were moving ideas, words, and entire cultural frameworks.      That’s actually what I’m looking into for my current project. It's amazing how much language can evolve alongside trade routes. I've spent the last two months looking at loanwords in Chinese dialects, especially in the context of Arab influence through the port cities of the South. It’s fascinating to see how much of what we consider “traditional” might actually be millennia in the making.      My, you're quite the insatiable researcher. As I did with my work at Oxford, mapping the linguistic shifts was a bit like trying to preserve a way of life that was always already changing. You have to remember that rural dialects, especially in areas with a long agricultural tradition, survive partly because of their insularity. Even in places like Aylesbury, where you're from, there's still a smattering of old English patterns that persist.      I think that’s part of why the alumni day is so important.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get that they're trying to raise awareness, but when it interferes with my job or my studies, it's not exactly helpful. I've been struggling with a lot of class stuff anyway.      Yeah, I can see that. It’s one thing if you  want  to be an artist or something creative, but when your career path is a bit more concrete, stuff like that can mess with your head. I mean, I started as a catering assistant years ago and now I'm running my own bakery. It wasn't always easy.      That’s really impressive, Maisie. I opened my café six months ago, and some days I still think, "What if I’m not cut out for this?" I did Sixth Form and then straight into work, so I’ve never really had someone push me to aim for anything bigger.      I actually find this conversation interesting. You know, when I was younger, no one in my family even thought about going to university. They were like, “Sounds like a waste of time if you're going to end up in something that doesn't land a job.” But I went anyway, and it changed my life. I’m now a film producer, and yeah, I get that most kids – especially working ones – just want to be normal these days.      Oh don’t get me started on that. If I could blame one thing for younger people not wanting to 'aim high', it would be TikTok. All my younger cousins post these videos like, “I’m happy just resting at home with my dog,” and it’s so underwhelming. I don’t even know what most people do with their time these days.      Honestly, I get it a bit. At the start of the pandemic, I felt the same. Like, who cares if the world melts down if I just have toast and sit in bed all day. But eventually, you start thinking – is this it? Do I want to grow or just exist?      That’s a really common sentiment these days. People always talk about 'finding a new normal,' but the truth is, some young people just don’t  want  it. I think it's partly because the world has changed so fast that trying to keep up is exhausting.      I don’t know, bloke. I’ve had to work my tail off just to get where I am, and I think that's the truth for most people like me.

Rather annoying, though, isn't it? That whole NHS funding debate—it's just the same old song and dance every year. Someone always needs to be saved, and I'm getting a bit sick of it.      You're not the only one—  L  . Honestly, it's like politicians think we're  simple . You know they'll just dip into something else's budget to make it look like they’re helping, but in the end, nobody wins.        Yes!   That’s why we need to change the structure. Didn’t your cousin get admitted last week? I saw the message from your mum.      Yeah, the cancer ward at that new hospital in south London. It was full to bursting, and they left her in the corridor for hours. It's not just a funding issue anymore—it's a system-wide problem. It's like they’ve prioritized efficiency over care, and that doesn’t even mean better outcomes.      I know. I remember we talked about this back when we first got together. That whole  ‘national service’  thing, right? But it’s not really national anymore if you land up in a different postcode and get a totally different level of care. It’s not fair.      Tell me about it. My colleague down at Royal Free said last night, it's  personal now —you know, because of their kids and all. You get the feeling no one’s thinking beyond the headlines and the next election. Honestly, it’s madness.      It just makes you wonder,  should  something like this be a political issue at all? The NHS was meant to  remove  the political element. I mean, who’s even listening to the clinicians anymore?      Not much. But thanks for not rolling your eyes when I brought up the housing crisis after we moved in together. That,  that  was the perfect guest speaker note at the pub.      You know me too well. At least the new flat in Cambridge is sorted financially. I just hope the market doesn’t  plummet  out of nowhere.      Don't talk about it—  L  . Still remember when you got so tense about rent the first month in gothic room on Regent's Walk.      You’re just picking on the only month we had a boxset bender.      So  we  made it to the end of  House of the Dragon , but never even got started on  The Bear . I still say you’re sabotaging our entertainment choices now you’re a  grown-up academic .

Rather skip the new season of  The Great British Bake Off  then—it was just crumb and no pizazz last time, if you ask me.      Don’t say that, Clara, it were £20 and the cherry scones were well near gone by half past two on a Saturday!      Honestly, I think it depends on your expectations. The competition is just more subtle these days—like science! I mean, baking is chemistry, right?      Nonsense, Ann. You can’t chase a soufflé with a calculator. I like to see a bit of  character —a bit of drama, perhaps, or a stressed-out contestant biting the turkey leg.      Well, you haven’t seen the episode I’m talking about! They used a new kind of sugar substitute—something with a  chemical name longer than my breakfast cereal— and I swear half the judges didn’t even taste it!      You young folk do take the fun out of everything, don’t you—Ann and her "science"!      I’m sorry, Steve, it is  science ! Recipe ratios, fermentation times, even the temperature of the oven is a precise thing. You can’t just slap it in and hope for the best like you used to do!      It was slap it in and trust your gut—and it worked just fine!      Hah! Spoken like a man who once made a custard cream cake that sour enough to out-rival vinegar at a vinegar fair.      That’s  hilarious . You two have about as much baking skill as the average boulder!      And you’ve only lived thirty summers, child. We’ve weathered storms, snow, and more than our fair share of overcooked stonings!      Baking? Stonings? I meant cakes.      Slide your sarcasm into the oven, darling. It’s as overdone as Aunt Mabel’s mincemeat.      Now, Ann, I do think you have a point with the chemistry—every good recipe is goin’ on some level about  change , isn’t it? You start off with separate things, and they become— unified  through heat and time.      Exactly! It’s like the molecular bonding— interactions  even! It’s not just about the outcome, it’s about the process.      S’all so posh to say, but when the ring goes and the loaf looks like a half-deflated balloon, we’re not in the lab, we’re in the kitchen, and that remains plain, simple, and preferably edible.      And ever so personal. You see, on my mother’s birthday, she always made a vanilla slice with a soft centre—never iced, mind, and the crumb was specifically ground not too fine.

Rather than playing a new game on my phone, what are you doing these days, Fergal? We’d got the boys together often when you were younger, and I can tell by the look on your face that it's probably something quite different these days.      Erm, yeah, I'm mostly on  Fortnite  with some mates. But if it's not all digital, I do enjoy that board game stuff. Got this one from my cousin, Tim; it’s called   Catan   or something. You build settlements, trade resources—cool strategy kinda thing.      Right, I’ve heard of  Catan . That’s clever. I haven’t played it, but my older friends do a bit. Still, I suppose it’s a much better alternative to just watching TV or scrolling on the phone for hours. Do you find playing with others is more fun, or do you prefer gaming solo?      Honestly, playing in a team is usually more fun. There’s team chat in  Fortnite , and we usually play with four of us. I do like the satisfaction of working together, especially if I can help someone land a win. But  Catan  is more like... a board game version of that, I guess.       Me too…       All that talk of games and building things reminds me, Mark, I might bring Ben out for a walk tomorrow at the park. He loves playing chase with the other kids and building oddly-tossed-together piles of soft toys. It's like his unofficial career is repurposing items into giant, squishy towers.      That sounds typical of a laddie like Ben. Our lads are always building something—whether it's out of lego, sand, or, in his case, treacherous stacks of teddy bears. A few years ago, the whole family turned into ‘builders general’ after I tried to tidy up his creations. Didn't go down too well.      He’s lucky he gets a little more latitude with the chaos he creates. Me, if I tried something like that in a class room, I’d go straight to the head teacher’s office.      Well, in fairness, that’s because we know how precious his imagination is. But all of you older lads—you might be lucky that he’s not in full bloom of your logic yet. You might find your dad on the receiving end of something very similar when he begins to understand cause and effect.

Rather annoying the new roads here, finds I've done. Used to get to her nan in Bury St Edmunds and it were just a bumpy road with potholes, now it's tarmacked and it's full of bloody lorries, I tells yer! Mind you, the mince pies at eeny shop there, I don't think they 'av been the same since the nineties.      Oh, but dear, that's just because it's easier to get into town now! 'And you! You and the mince pies! Didn’t you eat the lot last year? I saw the wrappers in the bin!  laughs )      I'm still thinking about the car needing a service before the Christmas drive back to Norfolk. Had a bit of a rattle on the M1 the other day, and I don’t fancy bursting a tyre with two teenagers in the back giggin’ about on their laptops. I've been thinking of taking the old Deirdre’s horse out as a break, you know, just a bit of fresh air and dirt under the wheels instead of tarmac, maybe clear my head a touch.      What did you say your horse is called, Mr. White? Sounds like a proper war horse!      Deirdre, actually. Borrowed her from my sister in Worcester. She’s a bit of a nutter with ponies, but them things have a strange way of calming you down after your been grilling the kids about someone called ‘Ethan’ in the diary they keep hidden behind the wardrobe.      Ethan's not a   boyfriend  ! He’s just a friend!      Oh, I don’t believe that for a second! I know when the eyes light up, and they do  every time  you mention that ‘Ethan’.      Maybe he’s the one, ‘cos she’s hiding stuff now. I passed her room yesterday and I heard her saying the word ‘no’ a lot. Probably talking to someone about Ethan!      Ha! Girls and their secrets! Let ‘em be, let ‘em be! I was told I was seeing a man with no knees for  weeks  before my Mavis knew the truth!      But let’s get our heads back on straight, kids! We’ve got to think about Christmas. Who’s cooking the main course again?      That’s the problem with having five girls in the family—someone always brings dessert and forgets the legs of lamb!      I bought Mavis a painting the other day—got it online for like five quid!

Rather annoying I know, isn't it? That Christopher, he’s promising himself for our garden party but he’s got to go to some jazzy conference up North. Not that I've heard where exactly, but it's probably £2000 flights and continental hotels for him.      Right, now  that’s  one for the   INFORMAL   bucket — self-serving laziness with a side of ethics. Not that I'd be doing it, but I could  understand  someone trying. Christopher’s always been the "light on principle" type, isn't he?      Honestly, who  chooses  to work at the weekend, let alone go on holiday like that?      Oh, he’s one of those types, isn’t he? Darcy, he used to make me the   BRAVE IN   comment when I’d leave early when I was working nursing shifts to drop the kids off for football. “Brave, ever so brave,” he'd say, like I was a hero. Then he’d be taking himself off for a week in the Algarve.      You know, I had a   CLEAR TRANSGRESSION   from my head of department last week. Absolutely lit into me for “poor communication – failure to inform senior stakeholders about last-minute organisational delays.” Sounds huge, right? But the truth? I sent them a phone call at 7:45 am that the toilets overflowed in the west wing. That’s what   POOR PROFESSIONALISM   is to a pointy-haired chucklehead now.      Okay, but that  is  a bit of a transgression. I mean, not informing about a flooded area sounds like it could have been a hazard. Maybe they had good reason to pull you up?      You’re not wrong, Lucy. Turns out the person who was supposed to attend was giving a presentation at 10 am, and was stuck in the building with no access to his room. I sort of see the technical side of it. Though being shouted at by Simon from the lunches team over the fact that I "should’ve known better than to think flooding would happen around senior management" left the points a little goopy.      If it was anyone else, I’d be smiling. But it's always the box-tickers who get what they want. Christopher could be planting bombs in the water supply and still wear his blazer like it’s moral altitude.      I’ve got a client at the moment who wants everything   WELL INTENTIONED   but vague. “We want a campaign with soft, powerful energy, but not too trendy.”

Rather annoying this, having the power off all day, isn't it? Me radio's been playing up like mad, and I've had no luck getting through to the council! These modern days, you'd think they'd have some backup plan for emergencies, like the good old days.      Oh, don’t you worry, George. It was the same here yesterday. My cup of tea couldn’t even boil. A lot worse than just the radio! I went to Timmy’s mum for a while; she said she wasn’t even perturbed. Still playing cards outside in the garden. Not quite sure if it's a phase or just one of those weird little quirks he’s picked up from the kids.      Honestly, I’ve given up on trying to figure out what’s in that brain of his sometimes. The important thing is, he hasn't upset the little ones. You'd be amazed how tolerant they are. Although, I caught Mollie grinning like a Cheshire cat the other day and asking me, “Mummy, are pants for grown-ups like wellies?" Just typical.      Well, at least the kids are adaptable. Oliver on the other hand – every night the little man goes to bed in his bear onesie. And when it comes off, he puts it under his pillow for safekeeping. Blooming mad, if you ask me, but it’s adorable.      It’s their own little world, isn’t it? Anyways, I don’t want to dwell on their bedtime routines. I thought we were meant to be discussing something far more fun... like where we’d put the utility room.      Oh, right – the house extension. Good thing we’re not actually building it, otherwise you’d be the first to run out and measure everything with your teacher's ruler. Our living room currently full of dress-up boxes and a half-painted room counts for oddly precise architectural plans, you know.      Hey, you try fitting a desk  and  a fully functioning coffee bar into the space without any walls. I’m just trying to imagine how we can cram everything in comfortably. We could convert the old shepherd's hut out the back. You could run your accounts from there, and I could just pop in with a tray of tea.      You would do that? Bringing my tea and talking about lesson plans? I am madly in love. As long as we can still have the dining table space – with proper chairs, not those wobbly things we brought with us.      Pfft! The kids would end up eating off the pond-side if we don’t get real furniture in here. Still, let’s see what they say in the morning. If Oliver wants to draw architectural diagrams with his crayons, then perhaps we can start a family business.

Rather annoying the new water company charges, isn't it, Tom? I had my bill today — up by over ten quid! And I haven't even run the shower! Mind, I think they might be holding it until they can charge us for the Hadron Collider somehow — you can't trust particle physics not to find a way to bleed dry the British budget, eh?      Ha! No doubt you’ve got a leak they’re charging you for somewhere unseen, Tim. My cousin down in Aberystwyth had a phantom increase and turned out his loo cistern was dribbling all over the place like a miniature waterfall. Though honestly, I don't blame the bloke, water companies do make it sound like the turkey on Christmas Day — you get it whether you like it or not.      Aye, and I think the world might be ending if I’m expected to wait any longer for breakfast, but I digress. Speaking of water... I've just finished redecorating the kitchen tile — felling the lads at the hardware shop, I reckon I’ve spent more over there this month than on fuel and food combined! I stuck with a bold pattern as well, nothing like the off-the-shelf hideousness they sell for "modern" tastes these days. Mind you, I found some Italian-style ones at a chap in Horsham, keen on the Mediterranean vibe.      Always fancied a jaunt down to Italy myself, but with the university’s grant business this term — full on. Adjacent to insanity, unfortunately. It took them three months to approve what boils down to a simple study into urban water consumption trends, and now I’m told we need a "pitch" in about five days. Honestly, it’s like the Renaissance of bureaucracy — we’re going back a few centuries and not in the way that's profitable or elegant.      That’s just standard university procedure for you. Grant writing’s an art form now. Though I have been to the meeting they told us was essential for the funding pitch yesterday — you know when they expect your schedule to bend to their mysterious whims. Let me tell you, trying to find conference space on a Monday morning with half the building still in Zoom meeting limbo is a farce.      I bet it was! If I could just meet them properly over a decent coffee instead of in a meeting room filled with the scent of bad air freshener and bad ideas, I’d have sold the bloody thing on day one.

Right, I just wanted to go through all these Lego sets with you both before it's time for bed. It's taking forever to sort them after the party, and I can't find the Hogwarts kits anywhere! You two were building with them earlier, weren't you?      We weren't building on purpose! We just wanted to see what the castle looked like if it rained ninjas.      Yeah, we added the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles into the broomstick tower. It was a magical-mutant battle for like half an hour, and the Death Star came too... like, from Star Wars.      That's very creative, but that My Little Pony definitely did   not   belong in the Ministry of Magic! I’m going to need you both to pick and choose what goes back into the boxes. I’m about to put them into storage when we move in July.      We can’t just sort them out and not have a sleepover to test out the final designs!      Yeah! We could tell you a story, like in The Simpsons special they showed yesterday about Bart as a Time Traveler. Kind of like how we’ve got Doctor Who and LEGO overlapping!      You want to build a time machine with Legos and then film your own slapstick comedy? I imagine that would be quite the disaster, like when Silly Billy tries to reboot the universe with a hairdryer.      That’s also what happened at Granny’s the other day. I left a toaster out and something melted and now her skirting board is being replaced. Can we all go over in a few days and help about with the renovations? I think you mentioned the builders are doing something chaotic with the garden.      Oh that was brilliant! I saw it on the news last night—there was a time someone put their whole garden on wheels and passed it down the road. I told them the day before I was coming, so they could wheel it over for me when I visit!      Right… just as long as we don’t take lunches to Granny and it arrives by the end of the week in some road-side parking lot. Now, back to the Legos— go and bin the Harry Potter if you don’t think you’ll use it, otherwise it’s going into storage. And don’t forget—after we finish your Easter chocolate you’ll be going to The Cinema to see the new one about magical turtles pretending to be monkeys in belly of a whale.

So did you watch the Euros last night? That match with Italy was bonkers. I stayed up till like 2 and I’m still paying for it today.      Yeah, I caught a little of it. Not quite as exciting as I'd hoped, but at least the weather was nice for once! I went out for a runner with some mates at the park. My goodness, have you seen how hot it is? I think I lost three pounds just sweating.      No way! That sounds brutal. I'm still recovering from my holiday in Spain though, so the heat has won. I went to Malaga with my sister—Managed to get a short break out of work somehow. It was amazing, the food, the sunset walks by the beach...      I’m jealous! You're lucky, I was stuck in night shifts for weeks straight. I was about to drop something heavy on a patient—relaxation is a myth for a week in my job. I missed the chance to go on that trip to Brighton. Also, the cookies I made for that—set them out, you know?—cat ate them all!      Ugh, my grief. At least it wasn't a launch pad for disastrous exes. Remember when we all got way too drunk at the Brighton bar last year and I almost became engaged to someone’s ex?      What? Nooo! You have to tell me this one again. I might have missed the best story this year.      Okay fine. So, we were at that bar on the seafront, and this guy was buying everyone gin and tonics. He said his ex was in the group, and I about did a Steve from marketing trying to win the broken record prize. Anyway, I didn’t actually propose—he thought he was proposing to me! I nearly fell off the stool laughing.      Oh my god! That's priceless. I remember Steve. The guy was worse than a spreadsheet at a surf competition. Speaking of, I tried to update my waiting list system at work. It didn't go well. Let’s just say, trying to 'improve' things with my limited tech skills is a no-go for HR.      I told you not to go there. I tried it with our project management software once. I made my line manager go into a full-blown panic. I'm learning from your mistakes, obviously. So, have you made plans to see your parents this weekend?

Rather annoying I though, the pair of yer sat there grumbling 'bout the internet like it's some ponce off the telly! Just bellowed at the router, "Reckon ye might be buckled in?" Not a peep from either of yer!      Right, eeny weeny, I’ll chuck some more logs on the fire. Narst as it is, a clean day, but still. Ay, best too keep warm, eh love?      Oh, Mrs Cooper, was me n grandad talking 'bout them pipes agin? 'Cos I like to think of it more like—      Oh, don’t go on about that posh turkey again, bless yer! The lad left bursts in the backr, didn’t he? D’you know how I used to patch 'em with an old sock?      Hmm—well actually I've been thinking, maybe I could repurpose the old leg of mutton hides, you know, for the laptop?      Oh, I do tell you—personally I think this new-fangled luv is a bit much for the likes of us, what with the gear on and watching shows without getting up!      Oh pish! I tell yer, I wouldn’t mind one myself, but these lads and lasses don’t know their mortal arse from a large pot ‘o frier!      Grandad, I think what you're trying to say is that technologists have made a lemon outta something that could have been a lemon scone.      Look, as far as I'm about, I'm off to the bridge club to touch the base, but mind ye thim pies in the larder be frosty!      Maybe we could have a laugh ‘cos the lad left bursts in the backr, did he? I reckon me grandad would have told him ‘at it was a bit of a howler waiting to happen.      Oh, as if I’d allow such a 'orendous idea! I’ve got enough ‘eadache with you trying to rig the fridge door like a man-trap!      Well, math does get real odd when you’re line in, but that’s because we were solving for X on a rainy day and it was like summin' was missing!      Well, I never! Just because I was born ’fore the war, ‘asn’t mean I can’t tell a gadget when I see one! Unless of course it's got legs?      And always remember love, patience is a virtue. ‘Ere, want a bob or two for it? Yeah, we're long in the tooth but we aren’t green on the job!

Rather than going directly from point A to point B, let's talk about why her dress would be red first... What do you think she wore red for?      I've seen Red Riding Hood and it was probably because she had a red hood.      Spot on, Tom! The red is a symbol of danger or warning, like   "Beware the wolf!"   But with   Red Rose   , it adds warmth and love, as it’s also the colour of love. But what if we flipped it? Let's imagine a different version of the story where she wears  white . What would that mean to you, Nancy?      My turkey was dressed in white! So it could mean she’s pretending to be a princess like in Darcy and the Secret Tree.      Wow, that’s a really great observation. Princess, purity—maybe innocence. So if Red Rose wore white, she might not be the same character we know, right? She might not have the same  function  in the story.      But then the wolf would be confused! He’d think he was safe and then   BOOM!   Surprise!      Like in Peter Pan when Tinker Bell is okay at first?      Good comparison! In some films, like   Pan  —the 2015 version—you actually see Tinker Bell as the villain’s sister in a way. So yes, the   function   of characters can really change depending on how a director wants to paint the story.      But she’s still the same  person  as in the book.      Exactly! Different stories can   function   the same but be portrayed so differently. Another good example is   Great Ormond Street Hospital  . They use superhero-like symbols, just like Peter Pan. They create colour and hope in what are otherwise really tough situations.      So is being a teacher like being a superher—?      In a way, yes. You help people, especially when they're sad or stuck. Like Wendy helps the Lost Boys, teachers help students learn and grow.      Can I be a goody bin on your desk if I help everyone?      I suppose you could be a   sort   of goody bin. A helper bin. A  Tom-the-Helper-Bin .      And I can be a  Nancy-the-Noticer-Bin !      Or the  Nancy-the-Confident-Bin !      Right on, team! Now, when we read the next story, maybe we can think about what  function  each of you would play if you were characters. Would Tom be the mechanic? Or would he lead the gang?

Rather annoying driving up from Southend to Devon to see you off. But I’d do it for any family... got to admit, I miss the old house more than I thought. Still, we found a proper little flat in Exeter. Very convenient, and the garden’s a bonus.      That sounds lovely, Dad. You both deserve some peace after all this time in that… well, let’s just say not so quiet area before.      Oh, it was quite interesting living in Taunton before, I'll give you that. But, don't get me wrong—we saw the signs. Too much property inflation, and no space for the children to grow. Still, we managed to get what we could. You remember how you used to drive us to Tenbury, didn't you, love?      Aye, I do. Had a cottage there for years. Wait breakfast, no television, and plenty of cold water... but in a good sort of way. Good for the soul, even if it did mess up the sleep rhythm.      My, yes, sleeping patterns are not really your strong suit, Dad. Still end up in early hours reading, don’t you?      He always did, from what I’ve heard—he just never cared for bed-time! Though I think it's slightly affected my sleep too, being around him for so long.      Well, you teachers seem to live and die by the school calendar. That’s what I’ve heard from your Aunt Lucy, at least. Funny thing—time’s very odd now. So much faster and more crowded. Can’t even get a train without crowding out in about five minutes.      Oh, definitely. I had to get a lift into work some days because of that. I mean, it is a short drive, to the school, but for the time it takes… well, at least it gives me something to think on the way in.      I always thought you found waiting on station platforms a sort of good opportunity to read over lessons or something. Except you've recently mentioned a new plan—you're staying with friends near the school, you said, for a while.      That's right. I'm trying to get some more regular hours. And yes, the accommodation’s not bad at all. The box might be modest, but your mother’s coming to the house-warming, and we’re all quite excited about it.      True, I expect it’s going to be very lively.

Rather annoying this, having to stand in the cold when you do get a bit of a kink in your back, don’t you think? Been doing that press-up stretch they told me about after a Swedish massage last week—proper £60 knock, I had—get a bit of relief, mind. Got eeny use outta the stiff-backed one they 'ave here at the hospice.      Oh Aye, I knoo that too well. Me Missis had one of them massages when she were in one of the Leeds ones. Not cheap nor lasting when it come to pain relief, specially with the spine. But I won’t argue with no pain, eh? Y’know, we were in that nursery the other day, bit near here. Fun wee place, though I can't see the point in 'aving special chairs and cushions in the corners for crying—like it was a bloody therapy gig! Wait, you said hospice earlier?      Aye, the one at the end of the lane, the Blossomwood one? They've got a real nice outlook on things there, if aperson is sturdy enough to take it in. Funnily enough, their staff are all real deadly smart, but they speak like they live in a trotting gallop from the 80s – very precise with words. I asked ’em one day about equality, and the poor woman nearly had a heart attack. Seems like she was sure I meant equality for the hills versus the valleys!      Equality for landscapes! Haha! Y'know, them women are a changin’ the world, I suppose. I worked in housing for thirty years – all the talking in the world would not have about half the jobs been handed to women. But now, well, I mind me th’ou’er th’ other day, you barely find a housing office managed by a man anymore. My, they've made their mark, haven’t they?      Aye, and it's a positive mark too, if you don't mind them restricting your mad ideas. We had to clear up words at our last ME event—’cause with 'aving a new generation of women in charge, the old terms like "head of the room" are like a man with a bow goin' on a lake in a rowing boat – wrong metaphor.      Oh I don’t go on ’bout it myself, but some of the older lads I used to play cards with still grumble about it.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you both anyway. But it’s been like... non-stop snow, hasn't it? I just don’t fancy being stuck on a mountain with a bunch of people I don’t know. And I mean—  Lola  —Deerfield is een plek in  Colorado , not somewhere you want to be if you hate the cold. You don’t even have central heating at your flat, so this is a step down, basically.      Well, you said you wanted us to do something outside of the UK, Mollie. I thought you’d like it! And I’ve been flexible with the holiday dates, only asking for two weeks of advance notice since I’ve got that new consultancy work coming up in January. And I’m not the one who flies off to Paris every other month for teacher training conferences, dear, while I wait for you to get your priorities sorted.      I’m not a spring chicken, Mum. I thought, you know, maybe somewhere less... harsh? I would’ve thought Crete would do just fine—personally I’d rather be sunning myself with a good book than dragging my grief across icy trails with someone’s gear on my back.      You got that from my email –  ha . But I’ve done my research, and Deerfield is a proper ski lodge set up for beginners like you and Silas. It looks lovely, with hot tubs, and the chalet someone recommended has wireless. Honestly, you won’t miss a thing, and I can do some work between the snowsports. It's not as if it’s Everest.      I suppose it could be fun. I mean, the photos look nice. But what about Charlie? I thought he wanted to go to Kyoto this year to see the snow and temples.      Charlie,  Charles —I’ve told you before. And yes, his work conflicted with the timings. I mentioned Kyoto as an option, but he couldn’t take the leave. Besides, this is good for  us , as a family. He knows the kids like a little snow anyway—didn’t he say Johnny’s been taking ski trips with his boarding school every year? They’ll enjoy go-karting in the snow and sipping hot chocolate at the lodge.      Well, he hasn’t said "yes" yet. He’s still at the planning stage for the week, and he’s been swamped with that project in Edinburgh.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what me Mam’s like with her books and ‘normal pricing’. Got to pay full price for a copy o’  Harry Potter  by accident the other day! Got it thrown at me proper hard too, like it was worth a bob. But it was in good een, mind.      Haha yeah,родители из старой гвардии. A lot o’ parents tho, from anywhere, really. But listen, what was it worth? Full price books can be somethin’ else nowadays.      Nah, I went to this secondhand shop in Grantham, you know the one, only twenty quid and like brand new. Just hadn’t bin priced. My Mam’s like, “rubbish, I won’t risk it, and I’ll get the official site price.” Had to hand over thirty quid for a secondhand book. I swear, if she saw me in Tesco buyin’ five o’ the same, she’s have a fit.      I mean, it’s not a crime, though. Y’know I never really read a lot like that. I tell ya, when I were younger in Barbados, books were a little different, but we got by. My brother Mateo—he got fairly radical, readin’ all these political copies. One time he nearly had a heart attack ‘cos he found a signed book by Obama in a market. Like, daft, someone just put Obama’s name in a book.      Oh I dunno, Mateo is a bit of a legend. Anyways, still—I missed the sale in the library because o’ about five misread dates. And then I watched the whole of the “Fantastic Beasts 4” and thought, “well that was barely a film.”      Yeah, I ‘eard the response wasn’t hot. I saw it with me niece at me sister’s. She told me ‘at it was very confusing. But you know little ones, they stick to Daisy Ridley as some sort o’ constant.      Yeah, speaking of—my nan took the kids over there for a couple of days. Picked ’em up yesterday and goin’ on about how Daisy looks like “the real Lily Potter” or some rubbish. It’s like they’ve seen three films max and already got ‘em obsessed.      Haha, sounds like my sis. She watches all the Marvel stuff, draws ’em on the walls, ‘at’s one’s Mums, this one’s me—got so much crayon on the walls, the renter now says she wants it like that 'cos it gives the house character.

Rather annoying this newfit Skype eh?      Aye, it's such a muddle when we don’t ‘ave no luck, poor things down ‘ere in Harrow can’t get a proper signal at times. We do try, though, as you know.      Course een, dear. I’ve been tryin’ to get on to Bill yesterday to show 'im this aardvark map I got from the globes project back when I were a lad. It were interesting 'ow the lines 'ave changed since the war. Didn’t even know the kids still made 'em these days.      Oh, I remember that school projects thing, only my sixthform class made 'em turkey on 'ow the world ‘as got so flat. Tenr, the Yorkshire lads 'ad these great stories about sleepin’ in youth hostels in the dales. Made it sound like it were practically Winnie the Pooh with a bit o’ concrete!      That sounds smashing! I always wanted to do that once, but never did—‘elp with the childminders, and then—well, I never did quite make it to the high fells.      A good country walk would do you good, then. Mind you, my leg – it’s been bellowin’ like a trumpet since the fall in the garden. Got me trying not to wander off through the allotment when it ‘urts too much. Still, the old garden ‘ere in Costessey is me patch. Used to grow me own veg, ‘elp out the missus at times.      Still, at least you 'ave one, eh? Not many about with gardens these days. My missus 'ad the telly on last night—this new underground line! Going to be easier to get 'round, if you're not in pain. My, ‘ow times change.      I did see that. Rather exciting, the modern world. But ‘ard to adjust to, no? I miss when relationships ‘eld on the telephone and you had time to think of what to say.      Aye, the old days ‘ad class, for certain. Mind you, it’s a wonder 'ow some go out of their way to be partners or not. Just don’t ‘appen to be in tune, I s’pose.      Pass me the cake tin, dear. The missus made this mornin’, and tea with a bit o’ sponge is just right on a rainy arse of a day. We ‘ave this old globe up the stairs; been in the family since the forties. Funny to think of all the places it 'as pointed out.

Rather annoying when the booking’s gone through on the phone, but then they email you the schedule ‘n it’s got the wrong destination code on it, innit?      Oh no! I mean, that’s £200 gone out the window if you don’t catch it before check-in, innit? I had that last year when I booked a holiday to Malaga—pressed send on a typo and only noticed when I got to the airport and got told I was booked to Marseille instead.      Naaa, that sounds like a nightmare. I just called the bloke back—we sorted it, but now I’m stuck with a flight at 6 a.m. on a Saturday. You want to come with me? I’ve already got the left-over pie from last night, so if I’m gonna risk getting pickled I might as well have a mate with me, innit?      Only if you’re brining coffee with you for the road. And maybe some of that chocolate hides, you know, for the long drive down to Cambridge. I’d help you get there, but I’ve got this meeting with the production team in the morning.      Sure thing, love. I’ve got a couple of those stickers left over from when we got married. The bride – Mate’s sister – insisted on custom ones, so they’re everywhere now. One time her flat was blacked out and the phone’s going off—someone left a banner that said, “Congratulations!” just someone at the door shouting it. Typical of my lot, innit?      Only you’d get a surprise banner at 1 a.m. That’s wild! We had a Prime Minister speech in about five minutes and suddenly a mating call bellowing out of the hallway. Honestly, I’ve lost the plot since starting that job. I’ve got to be logical  all  the time. Makes me want to just burn the guest list every time I have to book something now.      Aye, I know how it is. I’ve had to sort out a regional event for a client that wanted to know what kind of cake the lunches matched with and what the digestive mismatch would do to the attendees. Still, I’m happy with it. I mean, Doncaster goon really doesn’t match up with scones and jam, innit?      Honestly, I’ve got no idea where to begin with that.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, love? These supermarket prices. I was in the Asda in Walsall the other day—good luck getting more'n a couple of tins for a tenner! It's gone right over the top since the weather got so bad last winter.      That's true, Dad. It's one of those things that affects everyone now—regardless of age. I was in a Tesco the other day and a loaf of bread cost more than what I used to pay for a whole pack of six. It's just... it's childish.      I’ve noticed it even more at the cash counters, dear. The people who work there seem stressed and like they’re not being paid enough either. The queues are so long you'd think everyone had gone shopping at the same time. It's not just the goods that are expensive—it's the whole experience.      And then you've got all these mobile phone contracts tied in with your shopping. I tried to switch providers to get a better deal and the customer service is practically non-existent. I spoke to three different people, and none of 'em could sort me out.      It's not just mobile phones either. The country's going through a financial squeeze, from what I hear. People are even thinking of moving their savings, and not because they're trying to be fancy. I had a student last week who was worried about her pension—she's barely in her 30s for God's sake.      That's just a disgrace, isn't it? You think you're looking out for your future and then the politicians go and mess it all up. I spoke to my cousin in about the justice system—poor thing had to go through all this red tape trying to get justice for a bad landlord. Proper hassle.      It's staggering how much has changed, isn't it? I mean, even in the last ten years. I have students who don't remember a time before all this. They grow up with climate worries and price worries. We had to worry as well, but at least we didn’t have the internet to keep reminding us of it.      The weather's a menace these days too. Last week it was snowing in Birmingham on Good Friday! It's not natural—that's what I say.

Rather annoying I know, innit. You know what me Mam’s like—she’s always ‘yer paws off the lamb shank!’—like I’d actually  want  to eat it. I’m more of a… £2 kebab kinda bird, truth be told.      Got eeny idea!  I’ll  bring the mint sauce and we’ll just… call it ‘Sharing a roast but only eating the potatoes and the yorkshire’, yeah? No shame in that. It’s not like it’s a  proper  roast if no one’s touchin’ the meat anyway. My grannie’s still got a habit of  not  cooking meat enough—well, I don’t rightly know why she still serves turkey when it’s only gonna be grey.      I’m with you both, honestly, but I’ve been tryin’ to spend more cash for holiday feasts at home. I mean, I love a proper meat dinner, alright—but in Ireland, the holidays are all stews and colcannon, innit? Real down to earth, real hearty—nobody’s jokin’ about what they put on the plate. You don’t turn down food made with grief and warmth, innit?      Well, we don’t do all the same in Wales, but I swear I could fairly devour a warm, creamy leek and potato soup at  any  time of year. And when it’s holiday time, my grannie’s sherry trifle is the real work of the Lord. Honestly, I’d die for a bit of that.      Yeah, but have you  seen  the price of spirits at supermarkets? I did a bit of a comparison last week and I’m walkin’ out fatter in cash than I am in vibes. Honestly, you could take that cabby to the city centre and have yourself a  full  £50 less ‘cos of the treacle waters. All passed me by when I wasn’t looking.      Oh, I know, I tried that too! You’d think the prices would come down as we get closer to Christmas, but it’s the opposite—£70 for a dozen mince pies, no less!  Unless , of course, course you just get the actual goody boxes on the web from somewhere like Germany or Poland. I swear, the Germans are out here  winning  with their gingersnaps and strudel. Real craftsmen, seriously.      I’m startin’ to wonder if it’s just more worth it to have a holiday in宜昌, or whatever them big cities in China are called?

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get that art’s all about expression and such, but like... some of the stuff they’re making us do just feels a bit  pretentious , you know?      Aw, don’t worry about it! I get where you’re coming from. I saw the brief last week and thought, “Right, I’m gonna die of boredom.” But honestly, once I started playing with the materials, it was like, “Oh, actually, this is kinda interesting.”      Really? Because for me it’s just, like, “Today’s lesson... experimental multimedia collage.” And I’m like, “Is that even the real name of it? It sounds like a MySpace blog.”      Honestly, I know the vibe, but what I’m getting out of it is the creative process—like, it’s not about making something  good,  it’s about thinking differently. And honestly... I’m thinking a lot, thanks to this bloody essay on abstract expressionism I have to finish by Monday.      Ugh, you get it done? Because I’ve written three short paragraphs and a very long rant about Pollock.      No, not done—and I have to say, it got way worse when I tried to connect it with the lecture last week, because the prof goes off on these deep philosophical tangents about  nothingness  and  ageing . Rather annoying this new speaker’s consent form innit? Seems like we need to list our qualifications  twice  in the bloody thing—once under academic and once under ‘teaching credentials’.      Aye, honestly I’ve seen better forms—some simpler, some more vague. But it een’t the sort o’ thing we can faff about with if we want the funding confirmed.      I think they’re doing this to make sure every speaker is fully vetted, especially as it’s an international audience. I read through the seminar abstract again, and the title is “Global Business Communication: Bridging Cultural Gaps.” We need to make sure the content reflects that clearly.      Oh definitely. I suggest we split the seminar into sections. Maybe start off with the main principles of communication, then delve into cultural differences and how they affect business practices.      That sounds good. I’d add some practical examples for the audience to take back to their own regions. Case studies or real-life scenarios can make the session more relatable.      What about including tips on non-verbal communication? A lot of misunderstandings come from misinterpreting body language, especially in multicultural settings.      Aye, that's a good point. Maybe we can dedicate a segment to that.      I reckon we should also touch on the role of technology in global communication. Video conferencing tools, emails, all sorts. How they help and how they can hinder.      I agree. That’s a modern twist on an old topic and would add value to the seminar.      We need to balance theoretical content with actionable advice. Don’t want it to be just a lecture. Maybe a Q&A session at the end would let the audience engage and get specific advice.      Should we put that in the guest speaker note? I think the funding committee will want to know it's a dynamic event, not just talking heads.      Definitely. And maybe we can include speaker ratings as well. That always comes with lunches and networking sessions. More people come if they think there’s something for them after the talk.      That goon of a man from finance is always wanting to know what the "audience gain" is, so we’d better box all that in the notes.      I can handle the tech and tools section—I’ve done those kinds of talks before. It’ll help to have someone with that understanding over this part.      And the cultural differences—how about we do that together?

Honestly, I don't know how we're meant to plan anything when the building hours keep changing every week. I got to my seminar five minutes after the maintenance crew shut off all the power.      It's honestly ridiculous. Did the technical advisor respond at all to your email about it?      I haven't got an answer yet. I gave up and just map-walk from here. If I go two blocks west, left at the gate, it's always the right route. You'd think your phone would remember.

I made noodles on toast, no joke.      Well, thank God your research isn’t in biology. I made the lentils and rice last night, and those babies are bubbling away in this pot right now.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of a break ‘ere. I got the lightweight coat out from the airing cupboard, and I can tell by the smell where me gran put it in. Not quite the fresh sea air like we used to get near the coast.      Oh, I understand completely, dear. I haven’t been out for a proper walk since the last drizzle started. I would love to go and see the sea; it used to be such a comfort to watch the waves. My dear husband and I used to take our grandchildren there every summer.      That sounds brilliant. I’ve been stuck indoors more than I care to admit. Between the teaching and the turkey on toast for dinner, you get left with precious little energy. I’m thinking I need to get out more and do something—volunteer somewhere, perhaps?      Now there's a good idea if I've ever heard one. I used to help out at the local library when we lived near the old chapel. Volunteering kept me grounded when things were...well, when the weight of life became too much. I don’t say nothin’, meself, grief and worry can sneak up on anyone.      That’s a lovely thought. I’ve been struggling a bit lately with burnout, between school and home life. That’s when I picked the baby blue tits to keep an eye on in the garden. It gave me that little bit o’ joy and helped the loneliness wear off.      Aye, nature always does that. I used to walk up to me sister’s place by the coast when the weather was nice. Her little house is all whitewashed with the shutters, and that view of the sea... always gives me a bit of peace.      Was it money that set you back, though? I know I sometimes get so caught up in worrying about the future, savings or house prices—that one’s always a dent in the spirit, between you and me.

Now don't laugh, but it's stayed on for three hours in a row and not a budge in sweat. So sum it up, it's a day where we can transform ourselves into complimentary bundles of   geekdom   without a single sermon or sudsy hair product.

Rather annoying when a step-parent tries to do too much, isn't it? I mean, they’re like... trying to play the same role as the biological parent, but they're not sure where the line is. I keep telling my partner that he doesn't need to correct our son like that. My son is 11 now, and we’ve got to trust that I can manage him.      I’ve only had a little experience with that from my sister, but yes, she was quite involved in her daughter’s life after the divorce. Her new husband tried to take charge of the school things and homework, like he was the dad who'd made sure she studied hard. But the girl only listened to her real dad and My sister, obviously. Still, I suppose it’s a bit of a minefield – who you are in these roles and how you earn the child’s respect.      Exactly! And when you're separated or divorced, people tend to forget that the child needs routine, not five opinions on what's best for them. I think a lot of it is based on insecurity. Like, "I need to prove I matter." But I don’t think your worth as a step-parent is measured by how much you try to demand something from the child.      That’s so true. My sister’s ex often complained that her new husband was too passive, but I thought he was doing quite well to just be kind and not push too hard. Children don’t need another boss in the house. They just need someone who offers stability and support. At the end of the day, it’s all about connection, not control.      I agree. And I think your own parenting style is key in how you mediate these things. I try to keep the lines of communication open with my partner. Maybe that helps prevent unnecessary clashes. We’re both trying to do the best for the child, just in different ways. I’ve always told him: respect my boundaries with our son, and I will try to support any input you can give.      You must be doing a good job, then. I know being a teacher helps with patience and empathy, right? At least, that’s what people always say when you tell them you’re in education.      There's a grain of truth in that.
