Rather annoying when a recording of the game gets messed up, isn't it? I mean, if we wanted to update the version, we'd probably be playing more than we are now anyway.      Aye, we do try, but half the time half the group gets distracted by the alcohol and chocolate and forgets the actual instructions. Not helping that someone always uses the wrong map.      Honestly, if only someone had a better memory for names and places. It was quite interesting last night when one of the older players got Genghis Khan completely wrong. Laughed about it for ages.      Oh, I remember that. We were all still thinking about whether we like that type of music. You know, Aaron always got so competitive when it came to the placement of armies, risk and all. I think he turned 30 last week, by the way.      You don’t say. Time flies for us older lads, doesn’t it? I mean, even thinking about having a child these days seems like something that only happens in the movies, and being honest, some of us are way past that point. Still, I credit grief when it comes to such things.      For what it's worth, I still think about children sometimes. Not often, mind, and certainly not with the current climate. Abortion is such a hot topic, and the whole ethics of what it is we're doing with our bodies is never far from someone's thoughts. Faith in doctors is not always there, is it? I had a friend with a negative pregnancy test who thought Chinese medicine would clear it up. Can you imagine?      I did not know about that. Although I can see where the mispronunciation of most place names in the game fails us. Having your own child is worrying enough, without considering the laws that have changed, like child policies and sterilization laws.      And honestly, meeting the right people these days is quite an act. I meet way too many waiting for someone or something. As for happiness, I reckon being young once again would help with that, right? At least for the chocolate and the glass of wine you remember so fondly.      That's the spirit! But let's get our heads back into this game before we all head out for that party. I think the last one we went to your mother was threatening to move the Christmas decorations in if we didn’t wrap it up.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I get it, we’re all supposed to be ‘changing the world’ and all that claptrap, but honestly, sometimes I just wanna be left alone in my flatmates flat in Lancaster with a nice cuppa and a biscuit. Just like the good old days when I didn’t care if I was a barrista or a barista.      Oh aye, I know what you mean love. Proper confused I am. One minute I’m all, “I wanna be a social worker and change the world cause that’s what the leaflet told me,” the next I’m thinking, “Do I even like kids?” All I’ve seen are hippo-sized toddlers in my mates MySpace photos. Honestly, I swear my left arm is allergic to babies.      Aww, no I think babies are little delights. When I was at uni open day, I saw this tiny tot crawling up to a professor with a beard like he’s been licking beards for 40 years and puffing out the professor like he was full of hot air. I nearly cried, it was so sweet. Though I might have cried from the smell as well, to be fair.      Honestly, watching other people's babies is a little like watching other people's dogs – cute from a distance but I wouldn’t mind it myself. But back to the real question – don’t you just feel like you're stuck in some big career maze with no exit? There’s also this someone called Emma Watson who also got me thinking. First a child star, now advocating for equality with hotter eyebrows than is humanly possible.      Can you imagine! Look at her now, all Apple about sustainability and doing walkabouts with Prince William. I swear she had this whole life mapped out in her cot! Going back to university halls and thinking I have to decide on a future that’s just, like, part-time processing chickens and part-time being called Maisey.      Ahh, but think of the positives, lass. Imagine your kids getting your sense of sarcasm and your flatmates being academically-traumatized by your bedtime stories. At least the chickens path will let you cuddle exotic fowl. Just make sure you don’t end up goin' on some life mission like trying to get Taylor Swift to open her line in the Lake District.      Time to lay off your caffeine and actually pick a subject that’s seriously going to get you a job, otherwise you'll end up doing belly dancing on a Northern Ireland talkshow for ‘dancing with the stars and tourists’ like that

So do you think we should base our project on the impact of consumerism on poverty in the UK? I mean, it's kind of relevant, right?      Yeah, I dunno, it sounds a bit heavy. I was thinking maybe we could link it to things like fast fashion or how companies market junk to kids. That might be easier to get info on.      Fair point. But I feel like if we tackle the bigger stuff, like poverty and how big businesses affect it, it'll be more interesting. Plus, the teacher said she wanted it to be thought-provoking.      Still, it’s tricky. I don’t want to accidentally make it sound like we’re blaming the poor for their problems, you know? Like, saying they just need to "make better choices" or whatever.      Oh, right, I was thinking the same thing. We need to make sure we include stuff about systemic issues—like how low wages and lack of support from the government contribute to it. Maybe even mention Universal Credit? That’s something that’s actually affecting people here, like my cousin in Slough.      Yeah, that might work. And then we could contrast it with how companies spend millions on ads. Like, when people struggle to afford food, fast-food chains are out there trying to sell them burgers for £5. It’s a bit messed up.      Definitely. I could add some stats from that BBC article I read. They said forty per cent of low-income families in the UK are in "food poverty." That’s outta control.      So… you’re saying we combine all that with scientific research or something? I don’t even know what that means. Like, do we talk about how stress from financial stuff affects health?      Yeah! I mean, it’s kind of mentioned in the curriculum, like linking mental and physical health to socioeconomic status. I think it would make the project deeper. Plus, you mentioned friendship before—maybe we could add something about how having stable friends or a good support system can help people cope.      Oh, right! That’s a good angle. Some people don’t even have proper friends to talk to, like my man Jake. He goin' through stuff and no one's there for him. It makes you think how, like, individual problems tie in with big structural stuff.      So we're planning to make it personal and factual, kind of mix both.

Rather annoying really, the way he finds things to say. Like the other day, he comes over pretending he’d got lost and asked me for directions, and yet he hadn’t even stared at the right road! It is rather sweet, honestly, he likes to chat—  Lori   you haven’t been writing on your blog at all this month. Is it the   recorder   again?      A bit, but I think I’m more just stuck. The whole idea is due for   rework  , to be honest. It was me trying to be deeper than I can be.      Right, well, even Mary is still doing hers, with two children and all. Still, I understand needing time. Now, you haven’t   lost   any weight, have you? I see you’re still in your black trousers and I think they look   lovely  , dear, but do try something better for breakfast, no doubt?      Haha, thanks. I went for the oversized burger instead, you know, for the nostalgia? Bad idea, yes.      My, yes. Try and listen to the doctor. You don’t want to end up needing   physiotherapy  , like I’ve been doing—it wasn't fun. My   joints   have been playing up for years. I often wish I hadn’t spent so many nights dancing in my twenties.      Ugh, I will. I’m already foreseeing needing that. Anyway, what's this someone said about the neighbor? I heard you mentioning it earlier.      Oh, yes. That is a   different   world. Lives through music, plays all night, ballet, jazz, and I about   crack  ! He used to play   cello  , I believe. And I suppose he found some   peace   in that. I mean it is a kind of peace to have something, even for the odd hours of sleep.      That is surprising. I don’t mind a bit of music, but   eleven at night   when I need to sleep is my limit.      And also, trying with lunches, I think it helps to have   friends  . My physiotherapist even gave me a snack idea the other day— go-to lunch on day three if you don’t get so tired.      I see. Well, I’ve been working on getting what your suggestion was—  move more  , eat better, but it’s easier in theory. And with all the   changes   life brings right now it’s a bit over-whelming.      I tell you, my dear, it's all those little bits and bobs. And, it always helps to talk.

Rather than chuck a bar of chocolate in the bin, I just raided the larder and came up with...  this ! Look at it, it's not even droppin'! A proper Yorkie cake!      Look at that—  Larder Queen   strikes again! I'm impressed. I mean, I've seen some   Frankensteins of leftovers   come out a' that oven before, but this one's a showstopper. Oh, and congrats on pulling that bar out just in time, I nearly threw it away myself when I don't know what came over me like, "Ye gods, is this dead?"      Aye, well, I like to think of it as "chef du cupboard." When’s the last time you fried up the back of the fridge, anyway? I think it turned   Biblical   in there a while ago! Wait, does it even turn up to a dinner like this unless you throw in a bit of   baked potato muck-in-the-middle  ?       laughs  Oh yeah, tell me about it, I’ve had the occasional falafel land a week later still trying to tell me something. But honestly, this… this is the circle of baked goods, right? You’re giving new life to something that was fairly doomed, and now it's starin' back at us like it was meant to be done all along.      Exactly! And the cherry on top is this here — full Premier Blend and   euphoric crunch  , just like we’re at the Trafford Centre’s cafe and not my shoebox-sized kitchen here!      Look at you! You’ve made about five square feet of chaos taste like a million bucks. Although, I have to be a little bit selfish here — are we telling   Grans   it's a classic Yorkie cake, or are we letting her in on the little   unleavened miracle   we've just worked?      Do I look like I'm takin' that risk with your Gran? She'll either   adopt   me or   test   me with a nuanced question on chocolate production! No, we go with the standard:  brownie , with a bit of   structure   and goody-two-shoes-via-the-freezer.      Fair call, mate. You're savin' your modesty from what your Gran might call "an act o' culinary ignorance." Smart woman’s choice. Move those plates, I’ll stir the sauce to life, and we’re cookin' with fire again!      You really are a   star  ! Only you would say "cookin' with fire" like it’s a battle cry!

Rather skip the new horror flick everyone’s on about, honestly. I’d much rather watch something old-fashioned like...  The Others , or maybe  The Sixth Sense  again. There's something about those proper jump scares, y’know?      Ah, come on now!  The Others  een’t even that scary, more atmospheric. I’d rather watch something fresh. I’ve heard  The Quiet Girl  is real good. Not a horror, though, if you don’t fancy it.      We’ve been through this before, Speaker_1. You always say that. You watched  Hereditary  last week!  That  was a proper horror and I still don’t wash my hands now.      Okay, fair! Yeah,  Hereditary  was scary – I didn’t sleep for a week. But I still like the classics most of the time. They’re better crafted. New horrors are more about jump scares and not a lot else.      I agree with Speaker_1, kind of. I liked  Hereditary  and  Midsommar , but I loved  The Others , I mean, that ending twists everything. But I’ve also seen  A昔 White Girl , and it wasn't bad – it’s about identity and stuff. Not horror – but it made me think.      You all need to give indie films a chance! I saw  Bridging the Gap  last night – it’s been around a while, but someone at uni recommended it. It's not a horror, but it's oddly captivating. Low budget, yes, but it tells a story real good.       Bridging the Gap ? I haven’t heard of that. What’s the plot? I like films with vibes and stuff. Maybe that’s my kind of thing.      Quick up, Speaker_5. Indie films for the win! Although, if you want proper vibes with a bit more colour, go for  Damage  or  Unstoppable . Proper accurate too, unlike most stuff out there.      You being from County Durham, Speaker_2, I think “proper accurate” is code for “we know how people talk where I’m from.”      go on then, Speaker_3! You're from Northern Ireland, what’s your pick? I reckon you like gritty stuff, bloke films.      You could say that. I’ve been obsessed with  In the Land of Blood and Honey . It’s a war drama, made in the ‘80s, but it captured everything about that period. I read up on it for a history class. Gave me the shudders.      That one’s a power film, yeah. It’s real, you know? Not glorying in the war, but showing how it destroys people.

Rather annoying to be honest. The metro was so packed, I swear I was herded like a sheep. I got to my hostel and my ribs were already hurting from being squashed by someone’s bags!      Aw, love, I bet! Travel can be like that, especially in rush hour. Was it  that  busy on the metro system on a Saturday? I’ve only been on a train that full once when I was stuck in a storm back in '98. It was quite a chaotic night.      Oh no! Do your ribs feel okay? You won’t get through three days of baked goods if you can’t tuck in properly, will you?      Thanks, Mum. I’m fine though. The pain is just a minor inconvenience compared to the  amazing  Eiffel Tower views and the croissants, by the way — better than breakfast, no doubt. I’ve been taking so many videos in there, they’d be perfect for showing Sarah, you know, my friend from uni.      Ah yes, tell me more about her — you mentioned she might be moving back from Manchester.      Yeah! She’s finally got a job offer at that theatre company in the north. So she’ll be back by October. We could all meet up, it’ll be like old times. Sarah and I used to go out every weekend before work was too much of a chore!      That sounds nice. It’s also good you had a break. It must have been so therapeutic after what you went through at work. How’s your back being now?      Oh, it’s nearly about right. I was a bit sore when the lift wasn’t working at the hostel and I had to carry my stuff up four flights. I think I strained it a little, but it’s better now.      You young ones are all resilience — up flights of stairs and then off shopping? I give it to you, but I wouldn’t have done that at your age!      Well, I always knew the lunches would keep me going anyway! They had this amazing omelette place near my hostel — not too dear either, for the capital. Maman, shall I show you some of the photos I took?      You do that, love, but let’s finish your soup first. You can’t take in too much Paris and then leave your lentil soup untouched, can you? It’s healthy for your back and your budget over there, anyway!

Hey Laura! How've you been? You look like you've had a bit of a week.      James! Oh, I’m just exhausted. This weekend I had to cover two extra shifts for someone who called in sick. Was not fun what with the heat. But it was also good; I finally got to go to Chichester with my sister for the weekend. You know how she loves the theatre.      Oh, cool! Is there a new show there? I might suggest it to my students. I occasionally bring them out for a day trip—it's a nice break from the books.      Yeah, there's this new musical they’re putting on. Being a My Fair Lady fan, I’m always up for a bit of theatre! I had to drag her out of the house and I think she turned 11 phone photos for every 2 minutes we were there, but whatever. It was worth it.      I hear you. I'm always taking photos myself for the British National Corpus. I'm currently exploring variations of the passive voice, and reading through social media posts takes forever! Anyway, your turn as a photographer. Do tell more.      You always find interesting work stuff in mundane places. So what about you – anything fun this weekend? I know you were swamped with grading.      All I did was finish marking the upcoming students’ creative writing assignments. It made me want to write a novel at full speed. Honestly, I might actually do it this time. I've got an idea about a kid who moves from Bedford and realises being an English teacher is more complicated than it looked!      That does sound like you. Interesting! But you're not settling down and starting a family and all that are you? Still single?      You're not getting a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ out of me that easily. I just have no time. I'm working on my MA part time, I teach, I'm waiting on my student loan refund to clear... and I have to pay off my tuition fees with lunches and a little bit of magic.      Still, I bet someone nice is creeping up on you somewhere. I remember when my ex-boyfriend proposed after a romantic weekend at Greece—still hard not to think that was genuinely beautiful. That bloke really pulled out all the stops.      Romantically, sounds Greek to me! In all earnest though, I might go to Croydon sometime for a coffee this week.

Okay, so, like, first you just put the rice in the pan and pour in the water, like... got to make sure it’s the right ratio, right? I mean, you can’t have a rice cake explosion. Not again.      For God’s sake, Liam, it’s just rice and water, not rocket science. Though, considering what you tried last week— jellyfish with curry ? I still can’t unsee that.      It was an  experiment , Mum! You said to try new things. Didn’t even look like jellyfish under the meat... like, literally, it looked  meaty . Then it went weird, like, gelatinous and... well, you know. You dropped everything. Twice.      I had a toddler in my arms, Liam. I wasn’t prepared for a food-induced nose kaleidoscope. Anyway, back to the rice—maybe include this voucher you got from the takeaway place? The one you printed out 10,000 times so I’d stop driving to collect food like some over-40 woman being inappropriate on a motorbike.      It’s not  just  a voucher. It’s a voucher  with conditions . You have to mix Asian ingredients. So no meat, just veggies. Plus, I’m not old, I just  look  old. You’re the one dressed as a mortal and pretending to know what looks ‘toned’.      Oh, someone’s full of themselves today. Just because you watched a chef documentary at 1 a.m. doesn’t mean you’re a culinary genius. Hey, while you’re at it, try cooking without adding jalapenos to everything. My lungs remember the curry fiasco where the neighbor had to call an ambulance.      They were allergic to chillies? Or just unprepared for my  flavor revolution ? Anyway, the voucher says “stir-fried with spices and rice.” So, it’s a chance to make it... healthy-ish. No meat, no mad salt. We could talk about  food content , like how much fat is in takeaways and how rice can ruin your day if it’s not fluffy.      You know rice can go off if you go out of the room for five minutes. If it sits at room temperature, you’ll be cleaning that up with a mop, not your face.      So I have to cook it all? Just like last time with the chicken and the strange skin tone it developed after sitting on the bench for five seconds?      You said that was the  marinating magic . Don’t forget, the only chemical reactions you’ve seen were from things going off.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what me Mam’s like—she’s always ‘where’s Robbie got to now, has he sorted himself out yet?’ I can take it, but sometimes I feel like I’m 12 again and answerin' back at her.      She’s just worried, Rob. You’ve got a degree and haven’t even applied for anything… not that I blame you, mind. Some of the jobs out there are daft. Like, what kind o’ job advert do you need to be six foot and under? Looks like they don’t trust underheighted workers not to drop things.      That’s the weird thing, right? You get these daft criteria and then you wonder if you’re just not good enough. I mean, I’ve been applying for A-level support and I think I turned in a CV with grammar mistakes by accident. How embarrassing.      Look, I’ve been a support worker for a few years, and it’s rough, but it’s good. There’s always work, especially now with the funding cuts and everything, but it’s tiring. You have to be thick skinned as well as thick blood. You two’ll do fine though. Just don’t give up. I remember when I got rejected so much I just about gave up, but I kept pushing, because I thought if I stopped, I’d regret it.      You know what the real problem is? It isn't even the jobs—it’s the money. I’ve got me emergency fund, but it’s runnin’ low, and I’d rather not ask me Mam for more. Even if she offered, I don’t want to make it a habit. I’m not a bad lad, but I just haven’t found the right path yet.      Don’t you get the JobCentre support or whatever? I mean, I’m not on it, but if you’re claiming, they give you a bit more, don’t they?      Yeah, I tried, but I’m not getting out much. Feels like they expect you to jump out every week and take any job. I’ve told ‘em I’m doing some work volunteering for the library, but they don’t care. They just want govt buzzwords: “productivity” and “economic contribution.” Sods line.      Honestly, it feels like everyone’s already one step ahead. You watch uni students fluently quote statistics and manage roles in two languages, and I’m just like, “What’s a spreadsheet even for?”

Rather annoying I had to cancel last Sunday’s gym buddy plan. My sister was in Doncaster ‘n wanted to see the grandparents ‘fore she went back to uni down south.      Aye, fair enough. Not like I’ve got plans anyway—get up, watch the telly, maybe eeny weeny bit of walking if I feel like it. Retired life's easy, innit?      Like I said in the message, maybe we can meet up later in the week or something. We’ve been mates long enough for me to chase you out of the house for some fresh air like you need it.      That’s the idea, innit? You know I like you best of all my lot of mates who are left. Most of them moved, some gone back to work, and the rest I lost touch with somehow. Living in Cambridge, far as it is from Cuckfield—still, I appreciate the company, alright.      And I appreciate you lot, you know. With the gig I’ve got now, conferences and all that—basically, I book hotels, assign rooms, make sure people don’t turn up to the wrong event. It's non-stop, but it’s brilliant for the CV. Still, when I got home from work yesterday, I swear I could sleep for a week, it was so long.      It’s that professional-y type work, innit? Me, I never made the grade—left school at sixteen, full stop. Didn’t seem worth my while at the time. But I do wonder what it’s all for now. Being retired and all… Still got mates like you, which is more than I can say about most people I know.      Look, listen to me. You might be doing your larkin’ about at home, but it’s a choice, not a failure. And ‘course we look after each other. Friday next week, you up for a morning cycle? I'm told the paths along the river are stunning this time of year.      Sounds good as long as you don’t outpace me. I’ve not been on a bike since the fiesta ran outta petrol last year, and I had t’push the sod the last go’l on the road.      Aww, don’t be silly. I’ll go easy on you, promise. And what your legs lack in speed, you make up for in navigation—got one heck of a head for remembering directions.

Rather do the dishes myself, eh, love? Or would you like a hand in there, Jamie? We can’t all adjourn to the living room unless things are cleared up a bit.      I’m not doing the washing-up, Sarah. You lot picked the messiest night — chicken in a sticky sauce!  I’ll  be the one handed over to the plumber's call-out next week if I’ve got oil under my nails again.      Oh come on, Dad, who needs to do dishes when you can hit a tennis ball instead? I want to test that new racket you bought, Dad.      A week without a racquet, Jamie, and now you want to use it? Just wait until you’ve remembered to store it properly. Ten more bits of clutter like you, and we’d be sad in landfill world.      Wait, wait — why did breakfast, um… Hitler suddenly show up in Mum’s videos on Instagram? When’s she ever looked like that? Looks like Grandpa dressed up in the attic for her.      Oh, don’t start that, Robin! I put that costume out a week ago and didn’t tell you, and as for Hitler, that was just a Halloween selfie! Ten out of ten for dramatic angles, but no one needs to be seeing it still, least of all your history teacher. Delete her comments before she sees again.      She’s got a proper fancy girl, huh? Like what someone at our school would call a ‘pillow friend’? That one with the flowy clothes and the long hair? Her name again?      Her name  doesn’t  matter, Jamie, about half the time. Just don’t try to touch the remote while I’m looking at her pictures again. That’s her boyfriend she’s currently ‘taking a break’ from, in case you were wondering. And put the treacle back in the bowl — not on the floor.      Let him have the treacle, Sarah. It’s just sugar. I could stick to my administrative tasks and let Jamie have his feast if it comes with treacle shots.      I bet you two  had  a serious talk with Jamie once about the importance of facial goop. I remember he had that antiseptic stuff on his face once like it was gelatin.      Time to lay off your brother’s skin-care regime, Robin. That was a conference seminar’s after-effects. And yes, I had to have a talk with Jamie — about the ‘dreadful’ grooming and the sporting remoteness.

Rather annoying I though, taking ma gran’s old sofa an’ everything.      Oh I got the new one she gave us, it’s actually quite nice. Bit plasticky, but better than that old chintzy one.      Oh now love, I don’t een want to be passive aggressive, but that one was handed down to me by ma own gran. It saw a few generations through, if you kno’ what I mean.      She said it was just taking up space, Nan. Like you said when we moved the garden shed last year... like, literally said it took  too much space .      That was a shed, that one’s a bit more personal!      Tenr, I was the one who shouted, “Blimey, this is a piece of history!” at the tip when we chucked it. Buckshee bit of a laugh, though.      Honestly, Nan, I didn’t even take the one from the house. My friend’s family had one and she, like, begged me to take it. I thought, well, as long as it’s got real stuffing...      But what if someone else washes it? You ever wash someone else’s clothes and end up ruining them and then it just builds this huge tension. I’ve seen it happen with my cousin and their sister.      Aye, and then you’ve someone going full "mum mode" on yeh like they own the bloody cycle.      I just chuck mine into the communal bin at university and call it a day. Honestly, most people about just recycle yeh socks.      Oh I had a present from Ron’s sister once that was so tasteless I gave it to the charity shop. You’re not supposed to give someone else someone else’s guest soap, passed on by dementia.      Unhh. That’s just wrong. I tried once to give my niece a spoon I found from our grandparents and she just laughed. Kids these days!      At least the new building the university’s building for beaver scouts looks nice. They said the Network Scouts can go there too on weekends.      Oh, I remember the old building. I had a beaver box in the ceiling when I were 10. It held all ma lost earrings and kina’s hair clips.      It was a right laugh back in the day, this one lad—big Alistair—used to sneak in all the boys at primary school to collect them.      You know, I met him the other week when I dropped off a present for my mum and he was just, like, in the shop giving advice about what my partner  should  have given me for Christmas.

Rather annoying to be honest, I’d rather be at the gym. But anyway, it’s only temporary. I got the email from work yesterday—unbelievably, I’ve been made redundant      Oh no! What do you mean? You’ve only started there like a year ago. They’re not even halfway through the fiscal year      Yeah, I know. They’re restructuring the whole department and cutting back on the more junior project co-ordinators. I’m not sure who else it’s affected yet. They’re sorting out what roles are still needed or if they’re going to reassign people      Right. That’s short-sighted, don’t you think? Being a project co-ordinator, you must have developed a good structure by now      I suppose, but I’ve been handling the interns mostly. It doesn’t help that I’m still waiting on my postgrad placement agreement to go through. I was in talks at the beginning of the year      I see. But that’s over, now, isn’t it? Have you spoken to your dad about it yet? I know he’s not as quick with the grief as I am, but he might have something to add      No, not yet. I just told Gran last night. I didn’t want it to get back to him too fast. He gets quite combative when things don’t go his way      True, he does. Though at his age, he doesn’t have to be a prat all the time. I remember what you were saying at the weekend, though—about being able to come over to the house on Sunday for lunch? I did offer you a chance to redeem your standing with your grandad      I know—he fails to know that I know. I’m thinking of doing up the side extension. My contractor’s got the plans ready, and he said I could start with groundwork within the next two weeks. It’ll give me something to do until I meet with Jobsfair or start getting headhunted      That’s a positive attitude. Do you plan on keeping it? I’ve got some extra paint in the garage you could borrow      That would be goon really. But let me see. If I go over this weekend, do we need to do some food shopping ahead of time? I’ve been skipping meals lately, and I know that’s terrible to admit, but I’ve been using those instant noodles again      For goodness’ sake!

Rather annoying to be honest. He’s on at six o’clock and I just get home ‘n’ all.      Well, maybe ye could ask Eamon if he’d wind the programme for ye? Not like he’s doing much else—           Yeah, but I’ve only got so much of Eamon these days. Still, easier watching it backward than not watching it at all.      That’s called a compromise, love. Rather than going the usual route of making a request, how do you suggest we approach it differently?      I often start by understanding the underlying needs first, you see.      Aha, quite right. That way, we address the root problem rather than just the symptom.      Exactly. So, first step is always to listen actively.      What if they're not clear about their needs themselves?      In that case, one might need to ask the right questions to help them reflect or articulate what they truly need.      And how do you go about asking the right questions?      My approach involves open-ended questions that encourage exploration. For instance, asking them, "What would you like to achieve through this?"      Interesting, it definitely sounds more engaging than direct questioning, which can seem intrusive.      Absolutely. People usually respond better when they feel heard, not interrogated. Also, maintaining a non-judgmental attitude is key here, don't you think?      Definitely. It requires a high level of empathy and professionalism.      Precisely. And then, once you have a clearer picture of their needs, the proposal or solution needs to align perfectly with those needs.      It seems like you've developed quite the methodology over time!      A combination of experience and continuous learning. I often read up on negotiation techniques and try to apply them with a personal touch.      Any recommendations on books or resources you'd trust?      I'm currently reading "The Art of Possibility," and I'd recommend it wholeheartedly. It's quite philosophical but incredibly insightful.      I'll have to check that out. I've always found psychology quite fascinating, especially when it comes to understanding motivation.      Speaking of motivation, another way I've found success is by involving the person in the planning. Once they contribute, they feel a sense of ownership over the process and are more committed to the outcome.      Smart idea. That's the crux of collaborative problem-solving, really. It's not about taking over, but guiding and supporting.      That's the mindset I try to adopt. It's all about building relationships and trust.      And with that solid foundation of trust, requests or changes can be perceived as more of a partnership effort rather than an imposition.      You said it exactly right. It shifts the dynamic of the interaction from transactional to relational, which can make a world of difference in outcomes.      That's quite profound, really. I've always tried my best, but it's refreshing to see someone who's taken the time to study the subtleties of this process.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be at home with my cats anyway.      What, rather than teach French to a room full of teenagers? That gives me a headache just thinking about it.      I mean, it's fine. But it was my day off! I went out of my way to make sure I had time to actually read without feeling guilty for not being productive.      Why'd you promise to watch my son then?      Because you were doing the school fair and called me at the last minute. You know I like to help, even if it messes with me. Only one – and it looked like it was last year's batch. Honestly, some people just overdo it.      You know what I found interesting today? She's been doing a lot with beauty products—trying out different skincare routines and she wanted to read labels in Korean or Japanese or something. I about lost it.      Oh come on, she had to be joking.      Not at all. She looked genuinely unbothered that the idea of learning for reading beauty labels rather than for expressing herself was a big deal. I told her the minimal amount of any language you can learn to read labels is about ten words. I could see the light dawning.      That always comes with a cost, right? More product, more language barriers. My sister just started delivering something around town and she’s told me she can go straight to the pond unless she learns some Hindi.      I suppose it’s inevitable. But it's amusing how something as simple as reading a label could inspire someone to fluency. Or, in this case, at least ten words.      Tell me about it.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand the history and the cultural significance, but when you’re sat there for like, five hours sipping four cups of wine and listening to the same songs over and over...      Look, it’s traditional for a reason. It’s not just a dinner, it’s the Seder. You can’t just fast-track it. Proper Jews have been doing it that way for centuries. Plus, the food’s amazing, right? Matzah ball soup’s like comfort food in cup form. I mean, when you're in the oven.      Yes, but it's also  meaningful . That’s the whole point, isn’t it? You contemplate slavery, freedom, bitterness, and redemption. And not just in one sitting – through the entire meal.      I know, I know. It's just, by the end of it, I'm more focused on when I can finally eat a proper sandwich or at least get out of my seat without my back cracking. I mean, I still liked it, don’t get me wrong.      I think it takes time to appreciate the Seder as it is. I remember when  I  was younger, I groaned just as much. But then, the more I studied the history – the Ma Nishtana, the Exodus, the Four Questions – the more I saw it as a living conversation through time.      That’s true. Same with me when I tried making latkes. My Aunt Rachel nearly fainted trying not to laugh when I flipped one into the air and missed the plate completely.      Pfft! I’ve done that in the oven with casserole dishes. If it hits the microwave by accident, it’s a science experiment. But yeah, I get it – the Passover recipes you learn at home, you pass them down, and they kind of become part of the family fabric.      Exactly.

I've been trying to plan for the week in advance at work, you know, sorting out team rosters, setting up the virtual check-ins, but it's like trying to do jigsaws with one hand behind my back. I told her it'd have to wait until Monday unless I get discharged early, but she's barely 18, bless her.      Aye, I hear you're not one for sentiment at that age, huh? Our Ethel was in and out of detention last term. Thank God it's not like it was when  we  were at school. Back then, the teachers would make you stand in the corner in silence for an hour and about half the school would hear about it. Now it's all about “pastoral support” and “emotional welfare.” Don’t know if I’m laughing or crying.      That  does  sound like quite the leap toward modern parenting, doesn't it? Honestly, the only thing holding any of us together is talking it out, I suppose. I sort of miss the good old straightforward lectures. Anyway, speaking of which, you've been coming over on Thursdays to do the deep clean, but when you're delivering the bucket with the cleaning products, could you pop in the bin on your way if you don’t mind?

Rather do this than sweep leaves out o’ a pub, innit? Although, it’s real busy first thing in the week, mind. Y’know, stag do wars and whatnot      Aww, honestly, I would not wish being a barmaid on my biggest enemy. Got eeny friend at uni who does it full-time and she looks like death warmed up all the time      Nah, I knooooow. I’m facin’ it, innit. But it’s just me and the auntie for now. Hers a right pain, but at least I get the three o’clock shift.      What’s she like, then? This auntie of turkey?      Yeah, she’s from Birmingham, works the five to seven on Friday, and I think she turned 60 last week, but still goes ‘in character’ when the Bucks Fizz starts in.      Blooming mad, is she?      Mad? No, I reckon she’s like Watergate or somethin'. Keeps folders of spreadsheets I don’t even wanna see. But still, I dunno, it pays the bills. Me and her split it – I mix, she gives customers sarcastic comments – works for us, fairly.      Sounds like a proper nightmare, but maybe not as bad as this whole library scene. I could kill for a job where I didn’t hafta read full essays for ten hours.      That’s sour grapes talk, you know! You’re a science student, innit? Get a decent degree and your world will open up. I about did med school after uni but then I just wanted the easy life, innit.      Oh my god, barely survived A Levels, let alone university. I do just wanna get over this year alive, honestly.      Aye, well, it’ll fly. ‘Ere, have I told you about my customer last weekend? We had this kid, like 19, whose nan always comes with 'im. Grumpy little buggar took the glass out o’ my hand after I gave it to 'im. I was goin' on for life about it.      Oh my god, no! You don’t go on for life about anything, your face is like a comedy act sometimes.      Oh I know, innit. Just like stand-up to myself sometimes. But that ‘dreadful’ glass o’ lager I served— I reckons I got it wrong. My nan would’ve hit me upside the head.      Just make sure to keep the dirty pint jokes to yourself, you won’t get a career long in customer service like that, you know.

Rather annoying really, but at least it gave us a bit of glue sticks and markers in bulk.      Never mind them. I’m more interested in where you’re escaping to over the long weekend, David? Not to some beach, I hope—get a bit of tan, make the rest of us feel ancient?         Oh aye, I love a bit of tanning too. I’m off to County Clare for a while, just to sit and read in the sun. You lot never chase the sun long enough.      Clare, really? Sounds lovely. I was actually thinking of heading up to Manchester for a visit with my sister’s family. You know, standard Brummy bursts of humidity and overpriced pies, but family time, eh? I’ll be back by Tuesday—Donna, you’ve got the weekend off?      Well spotted, David. I’ve earned a bit of rest, and I told you last week I’m going to the Lake District with Sam and the kids. Supposed to get some proper rain, which I guess is the point. You know, wash away grief and all that. Have you ever been, John?      No, but I’m thinking of doing something completely daft this year. My wife wants to go to York or something civilised like that, but I’ve convinced her to let me take the kids to that weekend coding camp for eight-year-olds at the science museum in London. All my professional life, and I want to brag that I made a kid write a loop in Python over the holidays. What nonsense.      You know, I did that once—well not Python, but touch-typing on an Apple IIe in 1982. Not that I’d tell it to a youngster these days; they probably laugh at us. Maybe you’ll get promoted after that parenting achievement.      I’d say something technical, but I’ve never tried to teach my little niece anything. We just run around looking for yellow sprite stickers. She’s always trying to draw pixel art on the floor with the stickers and the play dough. Still, I’m happy with it.      Honestly, I think life improvements start with not using real play dough and risking carpets. David, enjoy your Manchester trip—just don’t spend too long watching people try to find yellow polka dots in 3D mazes in the park.      True to life, Donna. I’ll be reading crime fiction on a deck chair near the Cliffs of Moher and pretending to be Channel Five.

Rather annoying when the ref’s got no idea what’s goin’ on, innit? ‘S like... got the lot of us in the dining room here agitated! Ee, we saw that long-hand it was offside, but he didn’t see it!      Yeah, I saw that too, yeah. It’s one o’ them days when the ref’s like completely on a different wavelength. Disgustin’, really! I mean, we've had enough of it, pulling reasonable penalties as well!      Didn’t even want to watch it at first, I had to sort of get united shots made and everything, but once the match kicked off, we were in like well set turkey, couldn’t tear our gaze away. The tension, innit, the drama! You love hating it and I think it turned out alright in the end, at least.      Yeah, I mean, it goes alright for us, but the first half was so poor we were thinking to ourselves we might have to grab a few snacks or something—settle the nerves, maybe? But then, mid-way through it kicked off quite a storm.      Oh, we’ve got a couple of bites in. We ordered a few humble burgers from that place – Mate’s been raving about, and, let me tell you, we were like somethin’ fried outta the phone for a large portion and we were at it in two minutes flat! They arrive at full speed, and the portions: my word, they’ve gone up so much since the last time!      Hey, cheers. That’s good! We’ve been there a few times about late nights, innit. I prefer the chicken one myself, but the vibes from burgers is always good! Going anywhere that gives you barely a taste of home, but decent enough to have with a pint on the sofa.      Yeah, that’s true. I don’t mind a few ‘proper’ chips with it though, you know what I mean? We crack one up as soon as we get the parcel and always trying to catch the game on ITV4 or the BBC if the match isn’t too exotic, something around us, like!      Yeah, that’s about it. If it ain’t action, it just tickles no one. Never could go for blokes on the telly all shoutin’ at each other in the rain. We like our live match, tea with bits of spice, innit.      Sounds good, anyway.

Rather annoying the new model of Land Rover, isn’t it? I’ve had it in for work, and it’s alright for city roads, but I’m more used to the old ruggedness of the Defender. Got it thrown at me to drive up the motorway as a project bonus.      Bless you, lad, we didn’t have all that when I were your age! My Brian, rest his soul, had a flatbed truck that was all but falling to pieces but could go anywhere, pulling building supplies. We lived out in the sticks for a while. Nothing fancy but it’d plough through a frozen ditch without a thought!      That’s real stark, Nanna. You made that old turkey look fine with your melon! . But back to the cars – I’m thinking of getting a used van. Toyota Hilux. Something that can survive my job and giggle through breakfast, no doubt. I’ve been doing so much drive in rep basements, you ever looked in one, Ken? Smells like old socks and memories.      Naaa, I try to keep it clean up here in the north land! But to be fair, the real treat for today is this: did you reckon how proper we’ve been making scones? Not one – three batches of scones, and none of the self-raising lot. Binary choice of apple jam and clotted cream at tea-time!      And let’s be fair, someone had to teach us how. I made my own bread and cake for forty years. Mary’s hotter than the oven now mind, and I helped her through it! I remember when your grandmother, there, couldn’t even make a soufflé without it collapsing the second the oven door opened. Not much cooking skill in this family, sorry to say.      No, but that’s just grandma for you. Poetic soul, lumpy fruit crumble. The rest of us suffer the consequences. Speaking of suffering, I had to relive your tales about your school days today again. The one where you got chased out of a classroom by a goat?      That goat took the bull by the horn and charged after me with a bit of the dinner lady in go-between! I didn’t know what hit me.      I’ll bet that was a sight to see! Time to lay off your legs and enjoy the warmth.      You lot are full of those tales, never had belly laughs hearing ’em on the telly.

Rather annoying when half the class bring in penny cakes and grumble about the milk. James got to the front of the queue and said, "I prefer them soggy..." and everyone's like, "James, we're not allowed to bring things home!"      But seriously, it's been  such  a good assembly this week. They celebrated Pancake Day in style with a paper hat competition and prizes. The kids got a bit excited, but overall it was great to see their enthusiasm. Today one of the girls brought in a short story called "The Pancake Mummy," which... needs to go on the school blog, imo.      Mummy, turkey pancakes are not real! The teacher said so. But Harry said they're real because he saw them on the internet.      Harry's assembling a world of his very own, I see. He doesn't need a Science Museum trip for that! But yes, you're right—turkey pancakes are not for breakfast. Real pancakes, like with eggs and flour, are the way to go.      I don't like pancakes.      Me neither, Harry. They go in your mouth and then... they're in your throat.      Mate, you got to deal with it, because tomorrow’s Friday and we’re going to the beach! If the weather stays okay, at least. Poppy said she’s bringing her castanets—her very first seaside concert? It will be oddly literal.      I want to go to Paris like in  Green Knowe . We had a about children who don’t eat all their food the other week. One of them lives in a house where they grow vegetables because their parents can barely afford food. The teacher said it's to do with kids living in poverty. I didn't understand most of it, but it made me feel sad.      That was a very intense lesson, I know. I think your teacher was trying to explain how different lives can be out there. It’s sad to think about, but sometimes the world needs people who want to make changes, even as kids.      Mummy, do I get to be one of those kinds of people?      Absolutely, love. And the first thing you can do is your part here at home—like brushing your teeth, washing your hands, and putting your vegetables on your plate even if they're turkeys on a Friday.      Mums, can we go to the Festival Hall when we go to Paris?

Rather annoyingly, the dumplings were all cold when we opened the box. I mean, they said  home delivery within an hour , but it was more like 70 minutes by the time we got a lift home.      That is kind of a bodge. But it was Bob the Builder all the way, yeah? The one that builds   and   burns things.      Ha! A lot worse than just burning things this time, honestly. Oh my god,   the dump was full of dry pork and wasabi mayonnaise  . I can’t even say what that was supposed to be.      I don’t get why the takeaway supply chain is so dodgy like that. I mean, I’ve met enough agronomists in India who can get perfectly timed shipments of DMC cotton, and I’m sitting here with a soggy prawn pizza.      Because no one actually studies this stuff. Agronomy for food production and logistics, you ever looked into that? They didn’t teach that in sixth form, did they?      My postgrad classmates used to say that crop rotation is like a well-managed timetable. You know, real-life project co-ordination in farming—very different to Bob the Builder, of course.      I’m sorry I laughed, but I had to—Speaker 1, you were saying about the funeral you went to at the weekend?      Yeah, it was for my cousin. Aged 25. Just a tragic case of heart disease. I had a housemate at the time who got me into cricket as a kid—prior to that I had no idea it existed. He made about five referrals to every game. I batted once, got out on 2. To be fair—he got out on 1.      That’s not cricket to have claimed that. That must’ve been awkward at the funeral. I mean, people just have no idea what to do when something like that happens.      It’s mad how awkward all the small talk is. I remember being asked at a funeral by some random person I didn’t even know if I took the M&Ms or the sweets.      I think the M&Ms were supposed to be about positivity or something. Maybe optimism in black? Anyway, after that, I genuinely stopped eating box foods until someone explained what your actual allergic response to wasabi mayonnaise feels like.      And now, I just make my own dumplings. I saw a documentary over the weekend—it had a guy from the cricket team—got so inspired I got out the flour, the chopsticks.

Rather annoying isn't it, eh, the whole Scan As You Go thing at supermarkets? I walked in like everyone else and nearly left with no luck, because I thought I'd need a specific trolley with a built-in barcode scanner. Charming idea, but it's such a faff when it relies on good Wi-Fi and everyone wants to haggle for the spots where the actual tills actually work.      Ah, but they'll get used to it, Miss Alice. In my day, pulling a barrow and balancing tins of beans and corned beef in equal measure was the weekly pilgrimage. I still vividly recall my Mary humming "Ave Maria" as we trudged up the turkey aisle. You’ve got luck though, nowadays, you don't need to tote five shopping bags on the push and hope not to spill your milk all over everyone’s shoes!      Mary—yes, I've heard stories! Hattie mentioned at dinner the other evening that you once fainted ordering puff pastry. Should have been a Christmas miracle instead, but instead it became a queue crisis! Speaking of shop trolleys, though, quite a different world altogether from supplying food for a household today. Between the rice krispy cakes and the banana bread from the local church bake sales – it’s been a fairly sugary summer, let's say!      Now don't start comparing sugar grams at me, Dinah. You’ve had your finger in those krispy cake mixers longer than I've had a lesson plan. It's amazing how sourdough baking and bake-offs have turned into a community sport. But back to scanning – I had to get a second opinion at Apple about how the barcode worked for the gold-pressed English thyme. Very polite, they said. Maybe they thought I was drunk.      You're not drunk, Alice. You're  civilised ! Remember that time you passed out after giving that geography presentation on erosion? I was told it was quite inspirational.      Inspirational? I could barely crack my own pronunciation of Mantle of the Earth! Except by the lunches we keep on the fridge shelves now, I wonder if it's easier just delivering something around with a drone! I mean, even go-karts on wheels can be more efficient than me trying to navigate Sainsbury’s after work.      You can say that again. And with the latest Google tax deal, it feels like we’re moving into some high-tech world, don’t you agree?

Right, so today we're doing something special to celebrate Chinese New Year – and it's dragon colouring first! What do you think, shall we start with your dragon, Lucy, or Harry’s?      I wanna draw my dragon like the one from  Barbie and the Great Adventure ! Hasn’t she met a cool green one?      But I wanted a rainbow dragon. Maybe we can all draw different ones and then compare?      That sounds brilliant, Harry. We could each give our dragons different powers and names. Let me get the crayons out – I’ve got some nice ones from school. Oh, before I forget, the fire dragons only come out during Chinese New Year, you know. That’s why today is extra special.      Why would they only come out today and not every day?      Well, the legend says the dragon doesn’t come out if you’re mean. So if you’ve been kind and shared your toys, then you might get to see it. Also, the colour red is really important today because red scares the dragons away from cities and protects people.      What about the other planets and the stars, Mummy? Did they protect people too?      That’s a good question, Harry. Astronauts protect people in a way because they study space and tell us how to live here on Earth better. But the dragon was the protector of old China! Though, let’s be careful what we scare with red. If we’re not kind, the dragon might run away and we won’t see it!      So if I’m nice today, I  definitely  get to see a dragon?      Definitely. And when the dragon dances at the parade later, you can help me wave your red paper scarf! I made it yesterday after packing away your school books. Speaking of, Harry, you’ve got drum lessons next week, right?      Yeah! I was thinking maybe I can play the drums when you dance your dragon, Lucy?      Oh, but  I  want to do the hoop flying like Aunty Helen. She does it every year for the parade.      Maybe next year, go together? You could do drum and hoop while Harry hits the drums.      I wanna learn the piano, actually. You know what your teacher said at school, Mummy? She said I have good rhythm!      I’ll take that as a hint to talk to your piano teacher this week. We can add another instrument to our homemade parade band.

Rather annoying really, but at least it’s not pouring down like it was this morning. I think it picked up some vibes from Rome—too romantic for its own good.      Haha, fair point. Not quite as dramatic as I imagined, but I wouldn’t say it was a letdown. I mean, I was expecting everyone to be handed a vintage camera and a gelato on arrival. Maybe that only happens if you speak Italian fluently and don’t look like you’re on a student’s budget.      Speak for yourself! The Airbnb was lovely. Proper central, not too far from Piazza Navona. I can see why people choose to stay here instead of hotels. It’s got that home-from-home thing going on.      Oh, I hear you. I stayed near the Colosseum and screamed at my phone for the first 24 hours waiting for the Wi-Fi to load. But it was worth it in the end. I even roasted some stale sourdough to impress my brother when he came to visit. He thought I was trying to tell him off for something.      You’re a gem, Jess. I only wish we’d all been there together. I reckon we would have rhythm and blues’d our way through most of the city.      Let’s just confirm tonight’s dinner first, yeah? It’s not like we can phone in a reservation or anything—unless someone fancies learning Italian for 36 hours straight.      I tried already, love. I got one out of six sentences out before my Mandarin interferences kicked in. I still say  ciao  as  chee-oh .      Haha! That’s why I had to document it all in my failsafe iPhone voice memo. I’ve got it categorised as ‘Jess’s Italian Accent vs. Jess’s Poetic Enthusiasm’ ready for your next poem.      Let’s just all agree to get a table near the Trastevere. We could compromise on a decent wine list as well as edible pizza.      If we do manage to grab a spot, you’ll have to come with me to Santa Maria in Trastevere later on. The light filtering through there at sunset is unreal—no line of poetry could do it justice.      I can picture it. You with your camera, lost in your own head, while I’m pretending to know anyone in the photos I’ve been snapped in.      We should all try to string a few conversations together without the help of Google Translate.

Okay, so the hen do is still on for the weekend? I just had to book the Airbnb in Yorkshire... got the confirmation, but I’m now panicking because I can’t remember if we’d sorted the travel for Lucy? She can’t afford the flights, as you know.      Oh een! I thought  I  was bad for forgetting stuff. Lucy’s travel's all sorted. I chatted to Aimee this morning and she’s helping her out with the flights. It was a bit of a scramble, but we’re all covered for that. Phew, don’t want to have to cancel like we did last time!  Shudder . That was awkward.      Yeah, like that MyFav mistress bit back! So embarrassing. I still feel bad about dragging the bride through the Denny’s in Manchester. She was good about it—laughed about the waitron dropping her breakfast, no doubt about that!      Okay, at least we’re not getting loaded and causing drama this time. Casper and the rest of the grooms are coming over for the dinner—personally, I want to make it a bit chic.      And that's where I come in! I’ve been planning it. We’re doing a humble “dessert at the table” kind of evening—mini cakes, cupcakes, all that jazz. Let’s be real, no one remembers what the venue’s like after three splits and a photobooth, they just want food someone else made and to remember the photos. Trust me, I’ve run  way  more out-of-control events than I’d care to count.      That  does  sound good, actually. I’ve also been baking a bit of biccies for the hens’ vibes. I made some Speculoos because that was like... the only digestive biscuit we ever mentioned to the bride, so that made the list. Geo’s been helping me test them. He’s into cookies as much as he is into my microwave.      Aww, that’s so sweet! So you and that sprite of yours are getting along? I’ve not seen you two in weeks. Not since the pottery class when you set a wheel on fire by stopping it the wrong way.      Ugh, don’t remind me. I made her apologize in pirate lingo to the group of three-year-olds who were watching. It was  brutal .      Yeah, okay, those three-year-olds had  standards . I had to promise them a jellybean pronouncement on the wheel’s ashes.

Rather annoying I caught flu just before my weekend trip away, innit?      Oh no, what a bummer! You was supposed to go to France with that art exhibition, yeah?      Yeah, the one in Avignon — well, the timing was kinda good eeny way since I had to leave my flat 'cos I reckon it might be full of germs.      Fair enough. Did you ring up the hotel?      Oh aye, and was like "Hey, I've got flu" and they was all "Come on, is it even serious?"—like I'm making it up or something. Still, they managed to shift the booking, so I’m gonna go to Barcelona instead.      Oh, Barcelona! Roight place to go if you're unfit—beach, relaxation, and giggle at breakfast, innit?      Yeah, apparently Spain is easier for the syst— err, you know, for the immune system. And I reckon I’ll be better by the time I get there, I hope.      What did the doc say when you called in?      Bloke in the surgery said, "Flu is no joke – especiall' with your art, you've got to rest."      What? You told them you were an artworker?      Yeah, said I was someone who needed "mental and physical peace" to create properly. He thought I was a bit funny, but he dropped some paracetamol and told me to stay off the subway for a bit.      You know he's not a man of the arts, is he? He probably thought you was being posh.      Probably. Still, I've got your sister cooking for me while I'm guest in my brother's kitchen. Bazzinga!      Well I can cook, but I'm not your sister. My brother's visiting from Lagos and I'm stuck doing dishes and acting like a proper chef.      That's a proper far cry from delivering something amazing with tongs and the ladle, go on then.      Roight, I made this mediterranean stew last night. Added a bit of paprika from what your brother brought back. It was alright, if I say so myself.      Sounds better than your usual attempt to recreate pizza in the oven over here. Remember the time the smoke alarm destroyed a Searing?      Hey, I thought it was Italian fusion, innit? Right, you're fit to cook when you're back?      Yeah, I said I'll give some fresh Spanish paella a try when I get back, once I recover. You can oversee the pan boiling.

Rather skip the new jelly tots, do you think, or do we stick with the old ones? We’d got the tin half full from the last lot, and I can’t say they’ve improved with age, ha!      Oh, heavens, let's  definitely  go for the old kind. I  remember  the one they gave me on my 12th… “Centred on a central theme, but tends to wobble off track.” No idea who signed it now, but someone once wrote in green ink, “Don’t forget the broccoli when it melts,” whatever  that  means! It was a rather fetching card, though. I've got the pen I’d always use for card writing still—blue fountain pen, cappy-place—it left bursts on the back of the card if I didn’t careful, but very dramatic.      Oh dear, yes, and do we remember when we made those calendar fobs in Mrs. Henshaw’s class, using the oversized desktop hides? They didn’t fit the laptop calendars we got now, mind, but I kept mine, you know. Rather sturdy, for all I put in it. What did they teach back then? Woodwork for the boys, art and craft for the girls. I remember making a humble “reading nook – nook of silence” out of old comics and cards—now that was the start of an obsession with design, if you like.      And the hockey boots, those bright green things someone donated to the dress-up box! God, I tried to walk across the room on them—looked very smart, mind, and I thought being able to leap across the plains of ballet, but no. I about face-planted. I think you tripped over the music stand once during our performance of  Peter and the Wolf  that year.      Indeed! Those were tales. My, time for the story has moved on. Now I'm about to speak with Max, a university student studying sound recording. Do you know, I tried to follow him when he started out? Not to such an extent that I disappeared from view—though I've recently passed a couple of prehistoric mainframe computers to a small computing museum. Volunteers there run with it like it's their baby project. It really does make life more rooted.      You simply do not stop, do you? And he's exploring the societal history angle, yes? How computing changed the ordinary fluency of life, and roles in education?

Rather annoying the new neighbours, eh, love? I mean, I can’t rightly say I’ve seen much of them yet beyond the odd nod through the fence, but I’ve heard their terrier howling long enough to know they don’t do silence, not in the traditional Southend fashion anyway.      Oh, I’ve met the woman next door. Very nice actually—brought round a plate of scones from a local bakery in Holsworthy. She said they’d only just moved in a fortnight ago and were still unpacking. She doesn’t chase the dog or anything, at least not that I’ve noticed. Still, I’ll be honest, terriers are a world of their own when it comes to the turkey on Christmas Day mentality!      Yes, I agree with Anna. Darcy, their dog I mean, turned up at my evening walk near the village green the other day. She was practically dancing at me through the mud after some crow she’d spotted, bless her. I thought, you poor lass, stuck in the mud like that. The man was out with her, a pleasant enough fellow, waved and I waved back. A bit awkward to be honest, but welcome all the same.      Well, I’m not sure about the “welcome” bit just yet. I’ve been meaning to speak to the man about his noise levels. I’ve been trying to catch him in the mornings for a chat—about the extension at the back, mind. Our builder says the cast iron drain runs suspiciously close to their garden. I thought I’d ask him what he’s done with his drain, just to get a feel. Can’t have the future in the hands of a barking terrier and a man with gold-embossed wall paper, can we?      That sounds very diplomatic of you! I mean, if you’re not in to the idea, I’m happy to go over with you if you'd like. A bit more open-ended conversation would do you both the world of good. I tried gardening groups for a bit, but I found my thumb as un-green as the chalk hills round here.      A garden group must have been the perfect place for you, dear. Then again, dear, the notion of gardening goads rather than cures if you ask me.      I’ll stick with the scones, thanks.      Now that I have to agree with.

Rather annoying this, innit? I tried to order me some glue sticks online for the photo album maw’s got me startin’ for Christmas, but the box I wanted was £14.99 and it wouldn’t come to Cumbria owt as says Cumbria on it.       laughs  Yeah, they all do that if yer not careful. Most of ’em reckon we’re all still in Northumbria from what I’ve seen. If yer go to Amazon, just add a note at the bottom saying "Courtenay chase, Egremont, under code CA2"—I’ve had it work a few times.      That’s a faight good idea. I’ll give that a go. Oi, while I’m on, d’ya fancy gettin’ a new game or somethin’? It’s Black Friday, and they’re doin’ all sorts of bargin deals.      Blooming hell, is it that time of the year already? I got the Xbox one off eBay for like £120, and it still works properly—probably better than if we’d bought one from a shop and only used it for half an hour.      That’s a proper good find. I’ve just about had it with the chap down the shops, really. Got up me the wrong somethin’ and then tried to phone me up after I already left. Smerte.      Aye, they should sort out their stuff before a rush of customers come in. Anyway, you still looking at jobs online or just stewing being ‘prioritised’ for future roles as Prime Minister?       laughs  Na, I just found this job fookin’ doing admin for some local cab firm. Could barely be arsed to unplug the landline. My sister ‘ad to do it for me. All I heard was "advanced communication skills required". Luvver me.      Nah, you’d be mad not to apply. It’s proper employin’ as well, innit? And proper payin’ whack—better than doin’ nothin’.      Aye, points taken. I’ll bin my pond life if I don’t get a reply in a week. Finally, I’d be doin’ somethin’ other than watching all them Netflix shows at 10 am.      Which one you watching now anyway?      Got that ‘Stranger Thangs’ series again. It’s a proper bleak go down near to somethin’. Totally fookin’ upside down, like somethin’ out of a newspaper in Whitehaven, except they’re real people and it actually ha’ppens.       laughs  That does sound barmy. Rather annoying this new condenser, really isn't doing much. I've had it installed for a week and it's still audible, same with the boiler. I've been thinking, after the walk along the coast, maybe we can plan a shopping day to get those new curtains and the table for the kitchen. Rather annoying to be honest. The stress levels among the postgrads I’m working with are through the roof... It's been tough keeping them motivated while they're dealing with all this burnout      That does sound quite tough. I had to see a couple of health psychologists who helped me manage it. It was quite the experience. Didn’t expect to be the one working in the field like this      Wow, I didn't know that, honestly. I’m looking into how healthcare professionals cope with long working hours and the emotional load that comes with it... That one boy who always started his tests with goop on his hands? I still don’t get how he pulled it off      Oh god, of course I do!
