Rather annoying when the cat’s been scratching the sofa again, isn’t it? I swear, that moggie thinks the furniture’s some giant scratching post.      Don’t look at me, I’m not the one who left the cat flap wide open last night. But honestly, if it’s beginning to scratch  this  much, you might want to think about getting it used to a proper post. I remember my mate once swore by putting a bit of double-sided tape on the furniture to deter it—absolutely hates that stuff.      Oh, I read online that some people use frozen peas or onions around the furniture—apparently cats don’t like the smell. Although, I have to say, I still prefer the idea of a proper post. It’s just more practical.      I used to have a cat when I was younger in Rochester, and she’d leave little breakfasts—rats, mostly—for us. Not a bit romantic, though. I remember the vet saying that feral cats do it out of instinct. Good job we never actually  ate  the things, though!      I never had a cat as a kid, but I did once redecorate a room that a cat had wrecked. Tricky business. You want to match the furniture, but also protect it, and none of the homeowners wanted to spend the money. Now I tell my customers: expect at least a 10% hit on your furniture budget if you’ve got someone at home with sharp claws.      That’s oddly practical, isn’t it? Also, have you seen the way the cat moves? Left-handed, definitely. Clumsy when it tries to climb up things. My dad used to say it was because he was left-handed and it just inherited that.      I’m left-handed too, so I kind of get that. Funny thing—had problems at school in Rochester because they wouldn’t let me use a left-handed uniform for something. Not that it matters now, but I always remember it.      Left-handedness being controversial at school? That’s sad. I think it was more common in the older generation not to be supportive, honestly. My head of department told me when I go back to my parents’ place sometimes, there are still forks in the wrong line in the drawer.      Time to educate the masses, then. So, have you made the special dinner, Haz?      I had to, since your dad is here.

Rather annoying I couldnae get through wi’ the grater. I was just gonna do a bit o’ stir-fry, but no luck. It’s stuck fast! Any ideas, Grandad?      A stir-fry, is it? Naughty fancy affair. We used t’stir-fry when I were younger—wi’ lard an’ onions an’ all sorts of root vegetables. Not ‘proper’ stir-fry, mind. I used t’call it stew-fry, as it simmed away low an’ slow for hours.      That’s like three peoples’ worth o’ effort. I just chuck in the noodles, some veg, some bits an’ bobs an’ hope fer the best! Oi, Dad, I was thinking we could take a little trip—somewhere up North, maybe near Sunderland, since it’s been a while.      Up North? I’m thinking Spain next week. I’ve got a flight sorted to Seville. Client needs the infrastructure review, and that’s the one with the, er, aggressive pigeons—everyone I’ve sent before says it’s like herding grief with beaks.      Spain, eh? We went in ‘63. Excellent trip. My Mate Harry borrowed his cousin’s motorbike, swank thing, and we rode all over the sierras and down to the Costa. Still got the photo o’ me wi’ a screwdriver in me hand at the campsite—thought I were a real adventurer. Turns out I’d preferably buy me hotter meals than contend wi’ a broken carb.      That’s dedication, though! You two have about forty decades o’ travel between you. I’m still clinging to “holiday vibes” as doing nothing and not corroding the washing machine. I mean, it does sound like fun to do something, but planning feels like treacherous territory after the last time I tiled up the loo.      Ah, plumbing hobbies. I could stick the grater as we speak. Let me out fetch the pliers from the shed and whack it free. Some tools, no doubt lost in a box somewhere with three errant Allen keys an’ gooseneck fittings.      Just don’t go slipping off the ladder like that boy Darby in ‘59. A bit o’ ingenuity goes a long way, but ya also need a heart that knows when to pause.      Thanks, Grandad. Very sound advice—possibly the only time I’ve heard that description apply to my floorboards. Maybe if we do a trip, it could be less Grandad, more granadacino?      Granadacino? Ah, now that sounds like a good start.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't had time to get my lectures ready yet this week. I've been preparing a workshop and adjourning with the dining hall more than I'd like, honestly. How are you getting on with your physics classes?      It's been chaotic again, much like it usually is. I met with the students today for the first practical and it was clear they're not entirely afloat. A lot of them just panic when the equations don't immediately make sense. It was quite interesting, to be honest.      Oh, typical first-year jitters. You know what I like to do is start with a group activity. That way, the students get to tackle problems together and bounce ideas off each other. You don't have to do all the explaining upfront; they start picking up patterns as they go.      That’s not a bad idea at all. I suppose I get too caught up in demonstrating step-by-step problem solving for them. Maybe letting them try it first would benefit them more in the long run—and reduce the number of panicked eyes that follow me around.      Absolutely. And if I can be honest, it also gives you time to observe how they're handling the material. You can always swoop in where it feels most needed. I’m thinking of adding something like that to my curriculum next week.      Would you mind sharing that model next time you use it? I could really do with that. It’s kind of funny, though. Since we moved here to China, I've noticed how different the students are compared to our UK ones. They study a lot harder and take their classes more seriously, but sometimes they are quite reluctant to ask about things they don’t understand.      Oh, I’ve noticed that as well. Our classes here are so compliant you barely need to handle the univalve side of the process, but for the creative engagement stuff, well, that takes a bit more work. Speaking of, would you like any advice on how to get them to interact more?      Actually, that would be brilliant. I’ve been trying to add some lunches to keep the conversation going outside the classroom, but it’s been hard to get the students to relax. I think dinner is more go-to in this culture, if you know what I mean.

Rather annoying this new coffee machine of yours, isn’t it? I tried to set it for a moka pot last weekend and it just shot half the grounds down the side! Kept me up all night cleaning it out.      Oh, sorry about that, Deirdre. I didn’t think it would be  that  difficult. I read good reviews before getting it. Must have been a faulty one. A shame, but I think it's just a question of getting used to it.      Know what you mean, love. Those newfangled gadgets always act up at the worst time. Reminded me of when I still worked. Machines would short the whole supply line if you blinked wrong.      Honestly, I’m thinking of putting the storage box by the garden shed for now, if it's not too heavy. I don't fancy lugging it about every time something goes wrong. What do you think? I mean, with the removal costs these days, I might as well bury it.      Well, the box is fairly heavy, but I can help wheel it out for you if you want. I don’t mind. You can put it in theouthouse, by the garden gear. It’ll be out of the way and then we can decide if we replace it?      That’s kind of you, Dawn. I imagine it’ll be quite a job to sort through the tea and supplies. And Mark, I suppose you’d have the old coffee someone at work gave us—what was it called again? A Rovers?      Yeah, that one. Rusty as hell and poured out more water than coffee, but it got the job done about half the time. Still, I prefer the good old thermos and an espresso from a café.      Not that I mind the new machine, but it's just the cost, isn’t it? If we put it in storage now, it might as well be a freezer. Any chance any of you can afford a new one before you pack it off?      Not really. You know how it is with us. I’m a retired math whiz with no income and Mark over there lost his job after the latest budget cuts.      Look on the bright side, Deirdre. At least it gave us a chance to discuss that Labour candidate again—what bloke was it, your lot’s idealistic new leader?      You mean Keir Starmer?

Rather annoying to be called pseudonyms, innit? Seems like everything's got an alias these days. Like... shit, I don't even want to start with the river names round here.      Aye, honestly, I've lost count of how many rivers near us have names like 'Beachy Head' or 'Little Cogstone'—it's like they wanted to make it a bloody riddle before erecting a sign.      If only they were easier to spell. My sister nearly got lost navigating the canals last summer when she tried to board a boat in Oxford. It was like some kind of postcode lottery.      That's nothing. You haven’t tried figuring out if a boat you're passing is kosher certified or not. I swear half the vans in Birmingham have some kind of certification sticker you don't even know what it means.      True—though I've never met someone who actually checks if a product’s kosher. I remember once, in this club near the canal, the bouncer asked for ID like it was some kind of initiation ritual. I still don’t know if that was just a way to keep the griefers off, or if it was properly licensed.      Speaking of clubs—I still can’t get over how much better the Italian food in East London is these days. I had this risotto in Shoreditch last week that’s stuck with me. Near enough as good as Nona’s in Balsall Heath. Though personally, I’d die for a good condiment situation. I buy out hotter sauces each week now.      I know what you mean. My customers love it when I let them customise their toast with whatever condiment they fancy. We even had someone ask if we could microwave some capers for extra zing. Honestly, it’s madness.      Microwaves. What was life before them? Still, I get it—they’re the modern version of something being quick and easy. I tried using them for defrosting dough once. It didn’t go well. Let’s just say it ended with a sticky mess and a whiff that made the entire flat smell like a failed experiment.      That's classic go-to-plan on your own if you don’t follow the rules, innit? I’ve seen people try to microwave everything from blooming tomatoes to what must have been some kind of pesto protein bar. It never ends well.      Anyway, enough about dodgy kitchen tech.

Rather skip uni today, innit. Me and Fran were doin' this internet cringe real-time. I got matched on Tinder with some lad who said he plays guitar! Pfft, I dunno, where do they all come up with this stuff?      Oh, I’ve had eeny weeny wobbles on that one as well. Ay, yesterday I matched with this bloke from Wirral and he said he's got this dog, a beagle or summat. I’s like, do beagles even like us? Like me chase em, but they chase me car? Get the difference.      Ay, forget the dogs, I’d rather find some calm like that My turkey on Tinder said he likes The Kiff’s, you know? I’m from Derby and I don’t even know who The Kiff’s are! It’s like dating a Manc! Wait, na—relax I said that incorrectly, innit.      I tell you, Kenzie’s got a bit of the clout, she’s like bangin’ it off with some lad from Leeds. Got three messages in a minute! I’ve still got grief from uni, innit. Tryin' to live with five housemates in Wakefield. It's like takin' pop-up tents and sleepin’ on the floor for a laugh.      Oh, you poor thing. I’m still in the donkey hills—Wakefield as well—but someone at uni gave me a blu. He was a chef, thought I’d fancy him cos he had the collywobbles real good. Anyway, I said no, he took it in his stride, about five days later he sent me photos of the broken chips machine at his job. Classic stuff.      So you’re sayin’ it’s all a load of bobbins ‘cos we just want calm waters. All I want is some sod who’s into board games and can keep it frosty during the night. Me flat is so cold I dream about a crackin good fire and that lad being warm.      I tell you wha’, if he's playin' guitar and delivering the rods with style like that, he's got goin’s on. But if he's not got a clue what "ginger" is, then I’m out. That bloke said I looked ‘gingerbread’ summat. I lost me welly there, innit.      It's alright lass, I’ve ‘ad this one lad from Macclesfield that thought the River Trent runs near to Manc. I was like, "nowt's romantic like a geographer".

Rather annoying this new eligibility criteria for universal credit, isn't it? I was just reading it ‘ere—basically, they’ll take away half of y’benefits if y’earn a quid over yer personalised earnings threshold. Chuffing nonsense, in me opinion. People like us who’ve been out een work f'r a long time shouldn’t ‘ave to jump through hoops just to get basic support.      I entirely agree, Arthur! I mean, what are we meant to do, dump jobs to keep getting our benefits? I heard one woman who had to turn down a well-paid carer’s job because it’d pushed ‘er over the earnings limit. That’s harsh, don’t y’think? It’s like they’re punishing people for wanting to work themselves outta hardship.      D’you know, I think the whole government’s got an agenda, far as I’m concerned. I see it every prime-time show they run here after the 9 o’clock news. All politics, politics, politics. I told the missus, I reckon ‘tis all one big show, like a political soap opera—everyone shouting and shouting, no one actually doin’ nothin’.      It’s not just the soap opera rhythm of it all, Harry. It’s the policies they’re pushin’. Listen, I worked on infrastructure projects for years. I’ve seen how things are done. This whole benefit system is a bit like a bridge that isn't up to code—it’s patched up one end and collapsed at the other. And they just keep tryin’ to fix it without looking at the foundations.      I still don’t get why people are surprised when it all about faces. I mean, the same arguments are repeated week after week on the news. "We need to make welfare fit for the future," they say, but all they do is cut the funding, ‘cos they think it’s less expensive that way.      Well, the TV ain't any ‘elp either. I don't watch them schemey ones with the telly personality types—don't care to see whose face is highlighted with special lighting while they whine ‘bout “the public” takin’ ‘em serious. ‘Ow many of 'em even go out of their ‘omes if they don’t ‘ave to? Sits me in the chair, it does.      Aye, well, you could at least take in the special on how Romans built roads and bridges. Much more interesting than all that political to-ing and fro-ing, ‘cos let’s face it, them modern ones would fall down if they wasn’t held up with concrete and a bit of engineering.

Rather skip the newfit lasses entirely tonight, Christopher. I've had one of them setbacks with m'elbow again an' it's buggin' me properly.      Aye, I don’t blame ya. That shoulder o' yer’s been a problem all summer, eh? I saw the doc about the bicycle fundin’ yesterday. Still got me head full as it is, but I’ve got a meeting with some folk in Sutton next week.      That’s not far from where yer grew up was it? Suttin’ Coldfield or somethink.      Sutton Coldfield. Aye. Bit posh now, but still got a few good folk that remember me by name. Listen, enough talk of work. What about the lass? I saw Oliver on the picket today in school uniform, pushin’ a pram like he’d better been breakfast, no doubt.      Haha, he’s a right charmer, Oliver is, even if he’s a bit thick-headed. I reckon Sami’s terrified of tellin’ 'im what’s what most days. Anyway, what d’you think of the food on offer tonight?      Not bad, not bad. Be nice if we had a bottle –?      – and some decent pudding, yes. I said I’d make apple pie, but then the phone rang an’ it went back out the door. Lost the will for it all.      Typical. You always get distracted half-way through. I remember what you were like at uni. Always sketchin’ and day-dreamin’. Still, I’ve never seen a better about-turn from y’ou when you lose the touch of what you were doing.      That’s because I was trying to draw you while you were busy lecturing me. My, time for the baked apples, will you?      Aye, go on then. Let's have the microwave chips with relish instead. Not waiting till I get a crack at the pie.      Next time you've lunches to keep you busy while I do the pie an' no interruptions.      Pudding man’s negotiations done go bad then I suppose. I do miss those days – proper drawings.      I suppose. But I’ve got the telly on your side. The latest summat about flu or something. Thought you wanted to see it.      It's alright for a Saturday night, I suppose. Might give me a few more ideas for fundraising. I reckoned I'd make a theme out of it. Bring in them old CB radio things from the backs of lorrys.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You know, I do love the mountains around here, Tarnów... but the constant showering is wearing on me more than I'd like to admit. It's not like it's sun all the time in the UK, mind you — well, at least not in Cambridge during October.      It was lovely enough when we were out walking in the morning, but yes, I can't wait for the clouds to break. Still, easier said than done in Poland’s damp autumn. Speaking of which, I heard from my cousin — his wife's been poorly. Had to fetch the doctor twice already. I mean, I don't envy someone who's taken ill when they’re in a foreign country, no access to proper care. It must be awful.      I know what you mean. I’ve been thinking about going back to the UK for a few weeks — not for a holiday, but actually need to attend a funeral... for my niece’s grandfather, you know. There’s no way to do it properly from here. One of those occasions that forces you to leave, even if being home is... not really home anymore.      I get that. For me, as much as I love Tarnów, work is in Manchester. I mean, I teach – it’s not glamorous, but it pays the bills and gives me some sense of purpose. Now don’t get me wrong — I  am  enjoying this trip out of the routine, but I also wonder if I’m just avoiding something. Or trying to find a sense of peace.      That rings true. After a while of being here, I’ve considered staying — cheaper, quieter, and most people about are nice. But I don’t quite know where I’m placed in the lives of other people. At home, it’s easier to feel ignored, but it’s  your  home. Here, I’m like someone hiding from something. Though I suppose it's better than being surrounded by the sirens and telephone calls all day.      I’ve been doing some reading about therapy lately... not that I’ve  gone , mind you, but I keep thinking maybe talking to someone would do the world of good for people like you — not that I’m calling you broken or whatever. But I think life gets suffocating when you don’t open up.      Well, I’ve had moments where I’ve thought about it.

Rather annoying I know, isn't it?      That her team would be so  elitist  with me—that’s the word, isn’t it? I've been applying for jobs since I finished my physics PhD and honestly, I just—  Lori  —Deirdre’s een total mess when  not  drunk. Not that   either   of us are all that great most days.      That’s Deirdre, yeah. She used to be quite interesting as a student—went to Leeds, did philosophy. Didn’t finish, but still… She came to Oxford like three times last year,  promising  me she'd start penning her first novel. You know that MySpace still exists, right?      Ten thousand, everyday English, yes, I’m picky I know. But I just—Don’t get me started on grammar. Wait, does Deirdre still use MySpace for... I don’t know, social media?      Still does. Also uses the term  eaten  like it's the beginning of a book quote or something. She once wrote in a letter, “I read this article last week, it said we’ve been   eaten   by society.”      Does she—?      Yeah, Deirdre’s a bit much. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I  like  her, we’ve known each other since university. Our group’s not full of geniuses or anything, just a mix of odd people doing weird things with their lives—  like me,   trying to get a job as a copywriter  anywhere .      I’m lucky I have you round the corner, otherwise I’d have to document my own lack of fails. This last data plug-in I coded looked   exactly   like that astronomy app,  but —I ended up swapping out the pigment code. The customer? A man named Terry who sent me a nice pottery mug with a question mark on it when he got the wrong shade of green as  earth .      Oh no, I feel for you! That happened to me with a charity client once. I gave them a campaign title that sounded eerily gothic rather than uplifting. I got a  very  polite email—still on my draft folder, by the way—titled “Misguided Marketing?”      I  think  I'm still employed after that. And now I’m doing this new survey analysis for a tech startup, where over half the interviews are silence and awkward breathing. It’s bleak. The only one that was useful was a guy in Bournemouth who accidentally recorded 20 minutes of his cat coughing into the mic.

Rather annoying to be woken up by the clatter of little hands and hurrying feet, isn't it? What on earth are you two after now?      We've found your keys! We thought we could go to that circus skills workshop in town today. Remember, the one by the park?      Oh, that one! I completely forgot about it. Is it not on a Saturday?      That's this Saturday, Mummy. We promised Grandpa we'd meet him early! And we  really  like the trapeze, don't we, Elise?      Yes! And I saw a sign about the Neon Moon event in the park too. It's a light display with music! The circus is having a special team up with the event for safety, so they pick and drop us off.      Well, that’s handy. Wait, you said ‘We need to go now, or we'll miss the bus’, didn’t you?      Yes. Also, we made pancakes, and Elise taught me the Australian phrase—ah, what is it again?      “Aussie battler,” Daddy! Elise says it means someone who works really hard, and then we got “G’day mate” down pat too. I even tried to act like a kangaroo while the pancakes were cooking. Mummy laughed.      She did not laugh at your acting, she laughed because you someone bumped the pan off the table! That was unfortunately a very dramatic pancake incident. Now—what about the key? Are we leaving as planned?      Yes, we are! We cleaned up about five minutes ago. We’re all ready to go.      Okay, okay, calm down—you know that rush to get out the door is unwise when both of you are involved. Burgers for breakfast, not pancakes next time.      But Mummy, burgers are for dinner, and the circus is for daytime. Also, Elise pointed out the light-up signs and posters on the fence out there. She said 'that’s the “Neon Moon” path,' and it's where we get the trapeze instructors.      Mm, right—the sign is pretty bright. Just don’t expect me to run after you if you disappear behind the box of old jumpers again today, understood?      Yes, but we’re not going to! We’re staying right with Grandpa this time. And we saw that ‘battler’s award ribbon’ on the window. You have to be great to get one of those, Daddy.      Yeah, and Elise said we can make a wish and wave at the neon moon when we do the trapeze.

Rather annoying this new tax policy, isn't it? Seems like everything's getting more expensive by the week. I got the bill from my accountant the other day, and I swear it's like we're paying for Brexit again in cash instalments.      It's a shambles, if you ask me. I met with a few colleagues the other day over tea, and not a single one of us could figure out what the government’s  actual  plan is. We've had three changes in direction in as many years! You’d think after the mess of the last decade, someone might’ve gained a little... clarity.      Honestly, I don’t see the point in getting worked up about politicians like that. They’ll keep changing things until something sticks. I mean, most of the time I just try not to think about it too hard. If I did spend all my time worrying about policy, I’d never get my essays done.      I suppose there’s a difference being the one in power, or the one working out the cost of living. I mean, I was raised with the belief that reading the papers and voting was part of being a responsible adult. But lately, it all feels like such a farce. Still—it wasn't always like this, was it?      Mate, when I was a lad in Nantyglo, the only political arguments were about union positions and coal mine safety. You know what I mean? It was more about principles and fair treatment. Now it feels like everything’s wrapped in a conspiracy or a hashtag.      That does seem very old school. Or maybe I just grew up in a different time altogether. My nan used to talk about about how excited people were back in the fifties and sixties—when things were changing for the better. Like her family voting for the first time, or the NHS being created.      Oh, I remember that well. My father was a London transport officer, worked the tube before retirement. He always said he believed in the Labour Party for most of his life. Not sure if that’s something I've picked up—though I do find it a little baffling to see such deep divides now.      Then again, some things never change. My go-to argument on the lecture circuit is always that identity politics today is merely the modern version of class struggles between 1910 and 1945.

Rather than share a text-based version of the request, I recommend watching the video for full engagement with the typewriter text and audible storytelling elements. The visual and auditory aspects are integral to the experience. If you'd like, we can discuss the video afterward!      Oh, it was so good! The way the narrator brought the story to life with just typing and his voice made it feel like it was happening in real time. Like, I could  see  every sentence appearing on the screen as it was spoken.      Isn’t that brilliant? It really heightened the drama. You don’t often get that kind of synchronisation in storytelling. I felt like the typewriter was another character in the story itself.      The suspense levels were through the roof! I didn’t know what was going to happen next. The slow build-up of the typing added so much tension.      Exactly. It forced you to focus solely on the language and the pacing. No distractions. No flashy effects to detract from the narrative. Everything was streamlined directly to the imagination.      I wonder if the typewriter sound was rhythmic as well. Did it match the story’s tempo?      You’re absolutely right. The tempo of the typing changed – faster during action, slower during reflection – which made the story feel dynamic. Using a typewriter in this digital world made it feel  authentic , like the story was being created as the narrator told it. Like it  needed  to be there at that exact moment.      Interesting observation. It tapped into an almost documentarian or diary-like feel. The typewriter added a layer of immediacy.      Yeah, for me, it made it feel personal. Like someone was literally  writing  their life as they told it.      Precisely. The blend of sound, pacing, and voice made for a compelling, immersive experience. And honestly, I think it’s a powerful reminder of the strength of voice and text in storytelling.      Yeah, go ahead and watch the video if you haven’t yet – it’s worth the full sensory engagement. đáng trải nghiệm.      Fully agree. Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I understand where they’re coming from, but it’s not like everyone got to pick what they’re served now, is it? I mean, sure, you gotta be careful with meat… but honestly?      Yeah, well, you know how my mum is—she’s  not  a fan of 'weird' stuff. I’ve been trying for a while to get her to try some of that plant-based burgers, but she says they “taste like someone sat on them.” It was me trying to be helpful, though, because the bloke next door fetches three times a week! Not because he’s a heavy person but because he only eats meat.      Yeah, I’ve met him once. His belly sort of wobbles if he laughs too loud, but I mean, he probably has a good heart in there somewhere. Cats giggle and breakfast, no doubt about that!      Anyway, back to the meatless thing. I mean, even if you’re not a vegetarian, I reckon we should all try eating less meat, right? I saw a documentary the other day that puts your face as the guy in it. All these abattoirs—just… watching it, it’s quite a dark look. You ever seen one of those videos of how they deal with animals, Speaker_3? It’s not like somethin’ that would be on Curb Your Enthusiasm.      God, no. Curb Your Enthusiasm is bad enough. At least with that show, you can point out the ridiculousness and have a laugh over it. But when it’s real animals, it’s not funny. I have about five friends who are illustrators who do the kind of work where they draw vibes and stuff like that—that kind of art that supports small businesses and environmental stuff. They all went vegetarian to some degree, ‘cos they just felt like it was right.      I remember Speaker_3 used to go hunting with his grandad, didn’t you?      Yeah, but that was… rural Scotland. It was always respectful with lunches and shots and stuff—you know the routine? It’s not like you’re delivering something to animals by trucks and chains and lots of goings-on on your own farm. It’s… different. But I don’t support factory farming, not even a bit.      Yeah, and you don’t have to be completely vegetarian to live a more ethical lifestyle.

Rather annoying I thought, the washing machine went off again. I swear it does it just when I’m  not  in the room to empty it. It's getting on my nerves, really it is.      Aye, seems like it likes being a drama queen. But it was doing that on New Year’s Eve as well, remember when we were just settling down for our film? You had a clean shirt on from when we went out, too.      Oh bless me, that's right. We had to go change halfway through. Didn’t even get to watch the end of the film properly. I still don’t know what happened!      Nor do I. Never managed to get the turkey properly cooked either, did you? All that faffing about, and then the internet cut out too. Made things even more difficult trying to watch the countdown.      Wait, you couldn’t stream the New Year’s Eve countdown? I watched it on social media and it was fine, apart from the load of spam messages. One aunt of mine thought I was one of her old university classmates, and she started asking about PhDs or something.      And did you let her know the truth?      Absolutely not, I just said I was too busy working. I got a commission last night, so I  was  busy. Though honestly, I wish I'd been out at a party rather than sat typing away at my laptop, huh?      That’s the life you chose! Working a bit harder for the future. Now what about you, Mark? You went out to the pub, I assume?      Aye, we did. Club Steve finally pulled the plug on the broken bar stool he’s had for years — what was that, ten years? Not that I noticed really, just managed to sprawl my leg on the floor for the majority of the guest speaker’s tale.      Oh, the one about his surf holiday in Portugal again? I swear, you’ve heard it a thousand times.      You think  that’s  bad? Try explaining a new budget process to the team when the kettle’s spitted and you’ve run out of tea.      Honestly, I think it was more of a excuse for him to flirt with the barmaid. I saw him give her three blooming tomatoes.      So I’m not the only one? Thought I was going mad. And now I’ve got bellyache from that cheap steak and ale pie.

Rather annoying isn't it, those butterfly forks? I remember when we first had her—the little madam—home from the big city she insisted we dining like duchesses! Kept complaining the forks were too “clumsy” to do those fancy things with asparagus and sugar. Honestly, I don’t see the harm in a normal fork. It was all   Vicky  ’s idea, of course. She’s got a thing for continental knick-knacks.      Nan, who needs forks to do anything to asparagus? You just stab it and eat it.      Yeah, I mean even school dinners don’t use them, unless the teachers are being posh for something like that My turkey dinner Christmas madness thing.      Well, well, well—  Oliver  , you pick and choose what school food is worth your while, darling, but try telling Vicky when she comes for tea and starts conducting some sort of kitchen experiment with a dinner fork. She looked like she was going to patent it. Also, the two minutes silence on Sunday—did you both manage to get through?      I sort of spaced out. We were walking past the park and listened to the bugle… but then I saw a pigeon on the bench and I just started thinking – Mate, is that a pigeon, and is it going to fall off?      I did better than that! I was at the service in the village hall. Poppy gave me this funny look when I crossed myself. I said sorry, but it just felt oddly appropriate. You ever think about the people who   used   to live here, Nan?      Frequently, my dear. I mean, this house has been around since the 18th century—there’s a whole family buried not ten miles from here. I once met a   Russian   gentleman in the local market, selling   vodka   he made in his garden shed. Complete madman, but lovely man. Used a nickname for everyone—called   me   “Suffolk Sofia.” Odd stick.      You met a Russian in   Bury St Edmunds  ?      Wasn’t that where Gorbachev had a snack once? That was in the 90s, if you can believe it.      Wait, no, that was in the   palace  .      So, have you made the special birthday cake yet, Nan?        Andrew’s   birthday is on the 4th, not mine. I’m just catering the   surprise   so he doesn’t muck it up. Though I doubt he’ll forget, given it’s only two days from now.

Rather skip ahead a bit here, shall I? So, I was promising you two the Adventure Island episodes first... Well, I thought we could mix it up a bit. This year, instead of just watching a DVD, we could actually go somewhere a bit like the show! I remember Cornwall had a few places that reminded me of holidays  I’ve  watched on screen. Anywhere you'd fancy going? Or should I just book Abersoch like last time?      Cornwall sounds  proper  interesting! We could go to that beach where the sand's pink? Is that real? Mummy won’t let me go near it if it  is  real, though.      Yeah! And that Mylor Creek place where they did jelly-making last time we tried to go, didn’t they? D’you think we could go there again? Or even take a trip to the Catscrath Caves, like in that one adventure where everyone goes mad in the dark and finds treasure.      Oh, I love the caves idea. That would be fantastically spooky and outdoor-y, yes! But I’m not sure I can guarantee we find a treasure chest with coins and everything. Although... I might’ve read something on the V&A website last week about a new exhibition on national parks – it’s got loads of interactive stuff and even a section on mining and cave exploration. Would you two want to check that out before we head down to Cornwall?      The V&A? Who cares about an exhibition? Let’s not read books or have museum tours when we could be out in the real woods with a torch and real rocks being split in two – like  proper  treasure hunters!      Actually... the exhibition  does  sound cool. I mean, they showed what the caves looked like in that Adventure Island episode we watched. And if we went first to the museum, we could be proper treacherous in the woods knowing what to look for? Like a sort of... educational holiday?      That’s exactly the spirit! I was going to mention how you two could use what you learned to impress me with your cave knowledge on the trip! Of course, the V&A thing is  not  a day by the sea, though. Then go straight to Cornwall for your real coastal adventure. But – one pre-trip condition. I’m only doing this if you promise not to say anything about your recent allergic reactions to all the things I packed for dinner last week.

Honestly, I don't know how we're meant to revise for five different exams in the space of a week. It's so chaotic—Mr. Patel keeps giving us extra worksheets like it's going out of style.      I know, right? It's like he expects us to be humans with infinite time and energy. I swear if one more assignment gets added to the list, I'm just going to sit in A-level maths and start humming until the examiners throw me out.      Haha, maybe you'll be the one to cause a revolution in the education system. But seriously, I like maths more than some other teachers—like Miss Jenkins, who's just… relentless. You know she made everyone re-do the biology essay because she found spelling mistakes?      Yeah, I had to re-read mine and I think I turned into a human highlighter for about 20 minutes. I still can't believe I missed "diaphragm" in there. And I'm the one who hides my dictionary in the spare sock drawer in case I'm caught checking words—so embarrassing.      I feel for you. I never thought spelling would be the thing to end me in A-levels. Anyway, did you hear the news? Mr. Harris from the year above is becoming a school prefect next term. He's like, barely ever in school, but the teachers all adore him.      Ugh, typical. I don't even know why they trust people like that with authority. What if he's trying to sneak a phone into his tie during assemblies? Some guy's got to have a plan.      That’s actually not a bad idea… we should have about five people doing walk-throughs every day to check the hallways for rule-breakers.      Definitely. Not that I’d be caught cheating or anything—I'm just the guy who once tried to rewire the guest speaker’s mic during DT. Accidentally, obviously.      Oh yeah, the one who ended up shouting about  "power surges and the ethics of electric toasters."  That was epic.      It was legendary! They still took extra points off, though. But hey, at least we can talk about lighter stuff. You coming on Friday to Sofia's party? She said it's going to be in the garden, and she's promised themed drinks—vodka-free, of course—for us.      Count me in. Just don’t bring your cousin Liam—he eats half the snacks before we even start, and then demands seconds when we're halfway through the movie.

Rather annoying when the roads in this neck o’ the woods get closed off for no reason, innit? I got stuck in some construction site traffic this mornin’. Lost ten minutes, nearly missed me train to work.      That’s the same on our motorway out near Herts. I saw a van spilled lorry of paint the other day and traffic was tail lights all the way to Luton. Seems like every other week there's a reason to be.Gridlocked. It's costing me overtime to get in time to meet clients. You’d think they’d get the planning done better.      Aye, I’ll give you that. Mind you, I’d rather have some blockage on the roads than fall off me bike. Oi, did you catch the cricket on the telly last night? Yorkshire and Somerset in the first round. Livingstone cracked a six wide of the lights. I was shouting from me flat!      I did watch a bit, yeah. Kept getting called to answer emails. Client in the Netherlands had a problem with a seismic project and wouldn’t wait for Europe’s daylight saving shuffle. I’m knackered as it is. But tell me, who do you fancy in the Ashes? You got a team then?      Oh Mate, I’m fairly rooted with Surrey, but the Ashes is a biggie. Still don’t reckon they’ll beat Australia. If Warner or Finch fails early, that sets the tone. Our lads just gotta hold up in the field. Ever watched a Test match at the Oval? Atmosphere hotter than the summer sun.      Sounds intense. I’ve only been to a few county games in about five years. Bit too much of standing on broken concrete and watching someone fumble for a catch. But I do know that bikes shouldn’t be left on parkin’ spaces in town. My sister got hers nicked last month by some young git who took it for a joyride. You would think a few ‘no bikes’ signs would do something.      That’s rough. I had that happen to me a couple years ago with me old fixie. Took me weeks to save up for a new set-up. Mind you, it was a proper good chance to go out and get something fancy. Gonna be gettin' a new Salicy in the next few months. Fancy the boxset frame and Shimano Ultegra gears.

Okay, I just called the usual Chinese place we go to, and they said they’re shut for renovations. I’m  this  close to ordering sushi because I don’t fancy cooking again.      Ugh, honestly, they should’ve given us advance notice. I had a night planned with noodles and that sweet and sour chicken that’s just spicy enough.      Yeah, I remember that one from when we first moved in this area. They gave me a free dumpling once because someone said the chicken wasn’t sweet enough.      Wait, what Chinese place are we even talking about again? I’m still new to this part of the town, and my memory is like a sieve at the best of times.      It’s the one on High Street, Dunguahton Road. Very difficult to pronounce if you’re not German, obviously.      Wah? I mean, no... I’m just British. I have no idea what that sounds like to anyone besides a native speaker.      Okay, forget the name—what options do we have now? I’m not going to walk to the high street tonight in these shoes.      Well, we could try that new spot off Elm View. My colleague’s been raving about it. She swears the duck is “like velvet and dance music.”      If that means it’s chewy and sets the whole plate in ambient mode, then yes, please.      Haha, so do they take deliveries? Also, have they got the real stuff? The kind with vegetables that  actually  are there because someone put about five percent of them in the bin?      Alright, they deliver. And they do have stir fries and that cold sesame noodles we all liked at the first place. My colleague  did  say the veg was “plentiful,” so probably that’s more honest than the first joint.      I tried cold sesame noodles when I was in Shanghai. It was...  interesting . They gave me a side of peanuts that were  literally  rocks.      Oh, I’m not trying anything like that. That was one go-to-place on your life if you don’t mind walking two blocks and slipping on something greasy that definitely isn’t in the menu picture.      So are we planning delivery or not? I’m voting we give Elm View Chinese a try. I’ll call to order.      I’m in, just don’t forget to ask for my order to be extra spicy.

Rather annoying the new chappie living next to me, do you get that in your neck o' woods? Always playin' cricket with the kids at 6 in the mornin'.      Aye, we do sometimes, but generally things are a bit calmer where I am. I'm in a different part of the city, near Sefton Park. Less noisy, more leafy.      Fair dos. I'd say it's easier being a nurse in a calmer environment. We've had sommat the opposite here. The council want to build sommat up on the green, near enough. Residents are losing the plot, as you might well say.      It's a real shame when they try an’ redevelop without consultin’ the folk who actually live there. But I suppose I should be grateful for what we’ve got, considering the state of the NHS. I’ve been nursing for fifteen years now, and I've seen it go from strength to strength in some areas, to near collapse in others.      It's a monumental system, the NHS. I can only imagine the pressure you two puts up with as a lecturer. I tell me students that today’s pass marks are yesterday’s standards.      Tell me about it! My shift last Tuesday, I was with a patient who had been waiting nearly six months for sommat as simple as a routine scan. You know what it is, don’t you? Funding’s all in the wrong places. Private clinics get the cash, and the ones who really need it are left waiting out in the cold.      It’s an unenviable task for the policymakers, but it seems to me like the grassroots suffer the most. I’ve spent the past decade teaching literature and language — what you say often becomes evident in the way people express their ailments. There's a lot to be said for language and mental health being intertwined, even if I'm not a nurse.      Aye, I think it does help, hearing people express their fears and frustrations. We get to know their story. You being academically trained probably helps you to keep the big picture in mind.      Still, I wouldn't trade travel for anythin’. I spent goonie on time in Finland a few summers back workin’ as a guest lecturer in Helsinki. You might say it was a balm for the soul after a year in this old city.      Must’ve been a change of pace.

Rather annoying this new eligibility cap they've set for welfare, innit? Me an' a few m'colleagues were havin' a word 'bout it at the uni today.      Aye, can see where you’re comin’ from, lad. Seems t’me eeny time y’catch y’foot they want t’squeeze yer benefits tighter as if they're a pair o' cortège. Not t'mention all the red tape now.      Truth. We've had som'one from the psychology department who's bein' made t'doc everything, even 'aving t'prove his landlord's takin' out bins on schedule. It's like 'ere’s no trust anymore, you know?      I ain't seen times like them, me and I'm 86. Back in the '60s, if y'were ill for more 'n a week, a doc in a bowler’d be knockin’ on yer door to give y’knees the once over, now it's all over the shop, lads in white gloves want receipts written in Bahasa Indonesia!      Hah! Tell me 'bout it—It's getting so it’s a full-time job just applyin' for part-time support. I wouldn’t mind work myself, but these part-time teachin' gigs are few and far between.      Work? Aye, they all want this ‘big full-time job’ but they won’t let a man work more ’n a few hours without chuckin’ him off the dole and sayin’ he’s ‘got a job now’. You try and about earn a bit to buy a Sunday banger without the state watching like an eagle.      Definitely. Not to mention the wind-ups with the police these days—seen som’ ‘sting operations’ in Toxteth last week, all flash and no class.      Aye, I ain't takin' no sticks off the stickmen, but you can't blame blokes whose houses've been broken 'nto and their whiskeys poured down the sink. Even if they are foreign.      Yeah, go easy on the immigrants, if you ask me. They're trying to get on in the world, same as we were. I had a nephew what married an Eastern European lass, bit of a to-do with the neighbours at first, but now they're garden friends, better to ’ave them ‘ere ‘n poorer crime stats, innit?      Fair point lad. Always forget som' people come 'ere just to survive like we once did. My lassie now, she’s wantin’ to work, but before that, she needs help, just like me. Not easy for old people, ever's lookin’ for a way to cut back on som’ or other.

Rather annoying this new eligibility criteria eh?      Aye, it's mad they suddenly limited who can volunteer for transcription projects. I was already sorted for next month’s corpus update.      Honestly, it doesn’t make sense. We’ve all got the qualifications and experience — or at least, we thought we did.      I reckon it’s about resource management. The department’s probably being pressured by funding cuts again. From what I’ve heard, Cambridge are scaling back some linguistics budgets. We’ve had to axe a couple of pilot research projects, myself.      That’s a right bummer. I’ve been working with the phonology department on that new accent classification system — what’s it called now? CULP , I think.      I think it turned into COLLAPS — Cambridge Open Language Linguistic Analysis Platform Suite. Or was that just a nickname?      Oh don’t get me started. There was a day where it had eleven names and still no acronym that worked. I mean, do we even get told what changes are coming next?      Probably not. Most of the real decisions get made in those boardrooms we can't access. All we see are the “new methodologies” – which tend to mean more boxes to tick, more forms to fill, and less time actually doing the work.      If we’re already doing the work that the principles say should be outsourced — but aren’t — it's a bit of a mess, isn't it?      Exactly. It's like we’re being told to run the marathon but given ballet shoes and no training.      I’ve had a couple of e-mails asking if I’m interested in doing some “streamlined research pickups”. Sounds like they’re trying to fast-track people without investing the time.      And here’s the kicker — they’re pushing all this without acknowledging the existing talent on-site. Do they think we haven’t evolved with the tech?      Look, I’m not being cynical, but it’s the reality of a tight budget and a mismatch between management and the work floor. I get where they’re coming from.      But really, it's about more than just budgets. It’s about valuing the language work that actually produces the data, not the dashboards and reports people assume will speak for themselves.      You’re not wrong. In publishing, I had to fight for inclusion of dialect authenticity in our content over client complaints.

Rather annoying when a new series comes out and you only catch it on the plane or in some foreign country. I got to see half of “The Sandbaggers” on a flight to Spain a few years back and it was… excellent. Very 70s, you know.      Oh, you mean that  spook  one? Yeah, I remember it. Ulsterman in MI5 with that awful grey sweaters and the side parting. Still, cracking tension. It was quite a cult hit. We had to watch it in the archives when I was training as a researcher at the BBC.      Exactly! I’ve been meaning to rewatch it, only now it's nowhere to be found. All the streaming services either skimp on the old stuff or overprice the restored editions.      I hear you. It’s all about cash now, isn’t it? You’re lucky—your PhD probably keeps you busy enough not to be obsessing over missing out on decade-old spy dramas, though.      Good one, Sam. I’ve been into more, er… academic pursuits than telly recently. But don’t think I’ve forgotten my early love for  Doctor Who  and  Midsomer Murders . Still a guilty pleasure.      Mate, I binged three series of  Midsomer  in a weekend once. Now don’t go making me feel lazy for catching up on American shows. I’ve been into those  historical period dramas —you know the ones: everyone in a corset, oddly sour at one another, and the plot about a shoe falling into a well.      You mean Downton Abbey? I did actually try to watch the first series the other week. My sister had me at "sparkling," as you know. But then I noticed the series is unashamedly British. My, they talk like baked scones. All that proper English with that  soft  sort of accent—no wonder I nearly fell asleep.      You mustn’t knock the accent! Those words are meant to  soar ! Besides, you can't fault the cultural value. Some people, like Americans for example, get obsessed with British TV and the English language because of that very thing.      Oh, I know—there's a fascination out there. I’ve seen Yank students in cafes near the university with Shaw and Yeats books open, all trying to sound posh. As if Oxford educated them just because they read a third of  Dubliners . It reminds me of that guy from Texas I once taught in my online language course.

Rather annoying I though, the pair of yer, coming in with that lorry-load o’ ‘owsehoith and not ‘even telling us beforehand.      Oh, ‘ullo there, Janice. Not quite complaining are you? We’ve frightened the life out o’ us in that eeny weeny boot of yours.      Naw, not complainin’, just a bit o’ a napple would be best! I mean, where are we to put all this junk?      I liked the animal print cushions though, Grandma. Mithose ones... like, very seventies!      That’s the spirit, lad. Janice’s always been a bit too clean-cut for me taste. Bit prim, innit? We’ve brought you what we feel is a bit of character.      And the cat’s better for breakfast, no doubt about that. Found some fancy Hovis there and a bag of cat milk!      Oh aye, well, she’s more like a matresser, really. Comes in, eats up half the room, and leaves as much mess as a barn cat on heat.      Doesn’t bother me a jot. I’ve had worse than a cheeky moggie sneaking in, that’s for sure.      All that aside, you couldn’t even call it ‘living’ with that empty room up top. So someone’s gotta go up and sort out the attic boxes. It’s been cluttered up since what? Nineteen??      Ninety-five, Margaret! We’ve only moved in two years about.      I can do the attic, I s’pose. I need to write that essay for tomorrow anyway. I mean, it’s not like I’ve got better things to do.      Aye, lad. And if you find the old photo albums, ‘ve got a story or two to tell about when I was your age.      Let’s not go there, love. Janice and I tried to do a few ‘reminiscing’ sessions, and I nearly caused a heart attack with the tales goin’ on!      Just don’t find my dentures, Margaret, I’m serious. That’d be the end of your holiday here!      Oh, and we’ve brought some stew for dinner, dear. Thought we’d help out on the ‘ouse ‘oith. Only fair, innit?      Arry, well that’s the spirit. I was just wondering how to shoik the kid out of the flat for a few minutes anyway.      Yeah, Grandma, you’ve got some major grandma powers.      Aye, better than ‘youth’ I can tell you that!      Just so long as you don’t end up telling us all your life stories again.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't brought anything to drink with us. I was just going to say that once we got to the park, but I've already forgotten. I can't believe how hot it's getting this time of year. We do miss the spring in England at the moment.      Yeah, it  is  a bit relentless, but I reckon it's not as bad as most people here make out. I think they expect more from us because we're new. Still, I'd dump the damn coffee and go for something like a smoothie instead. Although, I agree with you about the weather — but I guess even London can be blistering in July.      Oh yes, that one sweltering day back in 2018 when we were walking to the pub and Oliver shouted, "Blimey, this is hotter than most of the Mediterranean!" and you nearly dropped your pint. Remember that? I happened to have a photo in my phone of both of us looked absolutely parched, and showed it to the group the next time we met.       [Laughs]  Yeah, I remember I looked like a freshly dressed beef tartare. And I thought  he  was the best at watching for the sun. Honestly, when it got to that point, the three of us looked fairly motley in our little group. But that was the photo you set as your wallpaper for like two whole weeks.      Absolutely — it’s the perfect combination of awkward and memorable. Honestly, I think my mom still has it filed oddly in a folder with all the ones from our trip to Barcelona. It’s got some great photos —  that  day excluded, most of them are amazing.      Oh, speaking of Barcelona — I meant to ask you this earlier. Sarah mentioned she's coming over next month. Would we be up to do something, like maybe show her the local guest spots? I know she's been tagging along with us a bit in the beginning but seems to have dropped off the radar since we came here.      Yeah, she’s doing a short placement in the north of China and can't settle in yet, but she’s insisting on coming for a weekend. I say we do the simple thing — maybe a relaxed day trip if the weather cools down. I could even line up a couple of nice photo spots along the way — something with the lake and maybe a temple or two.

But you were halfway into your "nose陉      Oh my  god , I tried to stop him when he started doing that. But you were halfway into your "nose job selfie map" thing where you'd hold your glasses at different angles. You started smiling into the gap. Honestly, it might have been the best one all night.      I was clearly drunk and manifesting poise. I just want someone to send me a compiled reel of the entire night over text so I can relive it like I’m the main character of a Sally Rooney book.

Rather annoying to be honest, the weather. I mean, do we need this damp in April? But anyway... Our dear Mary is coming to visit this week, isn’t she? I've been humming and ahhing about what to cook for her, but I think a good pot of stew would make her day. Do we have enough root vegetables?      Oh, definitely! I picked up a few extra sacks at the market this morning. Such a bargain, honestly. Oh, and she mentioned bringing a treacle tart! Classic Mary, she makes the best. Do you want me to remind her not to fetch the three miniature spaniels with her? I still haven't forgiven the damage they did to the garden last time.      Ha! I left the primrose patch flattened, didn’t I? D’you know, I think the world might end if those dogs aren’t there. They’re almost breakfast guests now. But I digress. Mary arriving is a reprieve, honestly. She always manages to fill the room with life. Still, the Fifa match last night—did I tell you, Speaker_2? Absolutely deranged. I thought we were going to end up in grief when that player from Manchester United deliberately tripped the other fellow.      Was that the lad with the ginger hair who got a red card and then made the gesture to the fan? I couldn’t quite tell if it was a phone call or a threat toward the referee! Absolutely hilarious, though. Our viewing group at the pub is practically suspicious of him now—claims he counts down the minutes until the worst possible crime.      I thought it was obvious! The boy had a bullying complex! You can't let people misbehave like that on the field without consequence. We were brought up properly, you know—that kind of culpability is simply not acceptable.      Come on, come on. Everyone knows football has always been a bit of a free-for-all. Just me saying. I used to work on those massive oil rigs, and there you learn when to let things slide. As long as the project doesn’t explode, right? But with Fifa... well, that’s another world altogether.      I’m more concerned by how Mary's going to react to the room I painted. I wanted to give it a bit of a country cottage vibe, but I might have gone a bit over the top with the chintz.

Rather annoying when a laptop’s brakes—as in, when they stop working properly, right? I've been trying to update the software, but it keeps glitching. Blows! Any of you fixed anything recently?      Aw, don’t worry, things like that always happen when it’s raining again. My friend had a blackout last week with her laptop and just got it sorted with some basic diagnostics on a clean install. What model is it? If it’s a Windows one, you might just need to dump it to a USB drive and start fresh. But what are we even discussing today? Still tea?      Oh, I'd rather not talk about technology. What’s that drinkable water? You know that one you mix with tablets? I saw it left out on the counter by the sink and I nearly drank it, thought it was just tap. Dangerous nonsense if you ask me.      You mean alkaline water? The one everyone goes mad for in health circles? I tried it once and thought, “What’s the point when I can just fizz my own with Soda Water and do it cheaper?” Mind, I’ve not really dipped into that wellness scene.      It’s not for me either. I much prefer municipal water, even if it feels like we’re being bled for it. Speaking of, I heard Horsham Water’s on strike again. Bin collections are bad enough, now we can’t even rely on clean tap water.      Honestly, this all reminds me of my grandad. He read books like they were gardening journals. He said he made a point of going for a walk around the town hill at least twice a week. Something about "clearing the flack", he used to say. I can’t help but miss those days.      That’s quite poetic. Speaking of which, have you managed packing for Brighton? I recommended using a voice recognition app to keep guest lists updated. I installed one on my phone, worked a charm—no more messy notes.      I miss when I had a SAT NAV to tell me which way to go. These young folk are all about GPS on their phones, but the old map-case with the voice telling you, "Turn left in fifty metres" had a charm. Though I do remember it nearly got me killed once.      Oh, I remember that. You were driving past the main high street and went straight into the car park behind the post office!

Rather annoying that the barista was making a mess of grinds. But the coffee's still decent, don’t you think?      It's not bad, no. I think where we are probably helps — sun came out after a bit, and those big overhead windows really lighten it up. Got a bit of a passive-aggressive message from an old mate saying he expected me to call last weekend — I didn’t, obviously, but he's got this idea I’m suddenly interested in seeing him now I’ve got a job and can afford to buy him a drink.      Mm, reminds me of someone I had as a student when I was teaching part-time at the British Council in Prague — immensely likeable lad, but terrified of exams. The fear got so bad I had to talk to him for half the lesson, pick and choose what he wanted to study. It made it far harder for me, honestly. When you're responsible for someone else’s results... I used to live on ginger biscuits and oversized desktop hides, you know, those Swedish ones? They were like, £20 each and came out of a bookshop in Fenchurch Street.      Oh, I remember those! They look like hideous fabric bowlers. I tried working on a farm once just after uni. My partner at the time got a job, and I thought, “Right, I’ll be her handyperson,” but within two days I was covered in muck and had no idea which animal gave birth at what time. It was also suspiciously often raining, and none of them had boots or an umbrella you could call your own.      Still, at least you had your colleague, Laura, right? I remember you told me she was reliable, efficient — the kind of person you trust to take charge of your classes if you suddenly got ill and left the room. I remember one time I was just,  mentally  exhausted, not even physically. I took the afternoon off, told them the day before, and relied on Laura again. I think she even played a bit of cricket with the students outside as part of a cultural angle. Her idea.      She was incredible. I took the kids out there for a couple of hours once and had a student from Eritrea who really loved pond life. We sat there for ages just discussing tadpoles in separate stages, between Spanish and Polish, while the rest of the class drank tea and made shelters.

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me event’s gone a bit pear-shaped ‘n I’m stuck on conference call till ten. Otherwise I’d’ve popped over for a proper meal. Livin’ out o’ £20 lasagne and a tin of baked beans.      Right, yeah, I understand. It’s all good. Ay, I’m dancin’ a bit but I’m just working tomorrow, so this is a top night in. Got chips and some curry sauce to do a bit of sommat. Not sure me oven even works but we’ll see.      Honestly, you  promised  me you'd bring out that lasagne. I've made a MyFridgeFood list for seven days and lasagne is like the holy grail. I’m in a bit of a sad place because the only edible thing in my apartment is a dodgy jar of breakfast cereal and a bottle of wine that’s been opened for a month.      Nah, you didn’t have to rely on me. I would’ve shared— if  the oven didn’t break mid-chip. I mean, seriously, it’s like this electrical grief only started once I put in a bag of frozen ones.      Speak for yerself, Steve. I’m with Sam, lasagne needs to be  exchanged  not  theft . All that effort and you couldn't even  warm it up ?      I mean, full marks for trying. But Steve, your oven is literally a ghost. I remember you said something about smoke coming out the back of it last weekend. That’s not  trying —that’s waving a white flag. Steve— literally , the oven lit on fire once. Not metaphorically.      Not  once —once is a  mistake . Twice is a  problem . I’ve got guest speaker status at the Cambridge fire station now. They leave a biscuits box for me ‘at the door’. I dunno how I haven’t been banned yet.      Right, but moving on from the ashes of a fireball oven—how're yeh with dates, Steve? I heard somethin’ about the lovely Esh goin’ on with someone from your worksite again? Not that I'm meddlin’, just wondering.      Aye, well... you could say she’s  interested ? Not confirmed, mind. More like “there’s banter, and she’s on the same shift every day”. Might meet up at the bar near the depot—got my fingers crossed like sommat.      That's romantic. Concentrate on not spontaneously combusting the venue when you ask her out, yeah?

Rather annoying lot, chuggers. You know, the ones outside the cafes here in Gordon Square? They’d be better off working at a local coffee stand, don’t you think? I nearly dropped my coconut cake doing a double-take when one ambled up as if he hadn’t a care in the world during my morning walk.      Yeah, I reckon it depends on your mood. Though I’ve been known to slip them a couple of pounds if I’m feeling particularly generous. It's easier than getting involved in a whole debate, especially when you're short on time, or the bloke looks as if he’s genuinely struggling. Still, I can see why it'd grate on someone's nerves. On the other hand, you'd be proud to know how my last research trip to China went, albeit via the safety of a Zoom call and a translation aid. I taught English online in a small village near Sichuan. Felt a bit like I was playing cricket in a panda’s back garden, you know?      You always say the most diverting things, Sam. I mean, do tell, what was the educational system like up there?      Contrary to the popular image, the kids there are delightfully curious—and not just about West Ham United. Though I must confess – trying to teach while the students, in between conjugating verbs, burst into the latest Chinese dance challenge was a spectacle in itself. You know what struck me the most? The teacher, she never once used PowerPoint. Spent half the lesson making a coconut-flavour cake just to show us the word for nutty—silly me, I bit into it through my Zoom lens!      Blimey, I must try to get hold of such a thing the next time I'm looking for a PhD supervision break! Going back to London, I noticed the lime trees near the lake in Gordon Square. Makes me think of the treacherous roads in Devon I took when I last visited my sister. I'm told it was quite famous for its intense hedges you can’t see through!      Oh that rural driving, a real game of trust your GPS or perish. At least the lime trees aren’t as obstructive as those hedges. Pity I missed the chance to go there with you. If I had gone, I might have taken some WeChat-based language tips from your cousin.

Rather annoying I could've just phoned innit, but they've gone and made it mandatory for everyone to have a face-facer with them. Otherwise I’d have been in bed by now      Aye, we'll knock the meeting quick as we can, then you can lie in 'til all hours like a normal person.      Cheers luv. Though they don’t seem to be listing any starting times on the website anywhere, funny enough. Might have to turn up and just see. Know how they are with the minutiae.      Probably won’t get the full details 'til you’re already there. That’s their idea of supplyin’ information innit? Just what you need, not what you actually want.      Aye, and if I’m late and I’m the only one there then I'm just about as useful as a chocolate breakfast, innit? I'll just be awkwardly tapping in my car.      You can always pop out and get a brew. That would at least help you stay awake, if nothing else. I mean, if I can survive a ten-hour site inspection without water and only ten coffees, then anyone can…      Ten coffees? You’re loony – Mate, I got a job arranging and organisin’, not being a caffeine casualty. But yeah, maybe that would be something at least. Somewhere closeby with a mexican, maybe? Like this someone called Spicy Tales? I seem to read about it everywhere these days oddly.      Aye, heard of them. Bit pricey perhaps but decent food if you can stomach the heat. I about melted the last time I went but it was good. Might take Jane there next week if I can drag her out of that new plug and play chair of hers.      That ‘cos she’s treble guest points toward that sofa, innit. Just trying to become one with it.      Guess so. So when are we headin' to this shindig then? 9 o’ clock? 'Cause I’ve got that report do today if I don’t drop it like a hot sparrow by like 10:00.      Aye, so give it an hour? Then, no matter what they say, we can say we gave it due time and make our escape. I can seriously cope with no more roles in my life that demand earnestness and belly laughs at the same time.      Sounds like a plan. One hour. Then I reckons I'm out and into that report, and you're back to your peaceful, undisturbed, very British madness.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what grumbles do – they just get louder when you’re lying in bed trying to sleep. Been like that since Friday I think. I've nearly got me a temp, but me and the vet agreed the best thing would be to give him a few more days of rest and see if he bounces back on his own. Still, his tail's as straight as a tie so that's a good sign, yeah?      Aye, me nan’s horse once had one of them fancy jobs where his back legs wouldn't work no more. Tore her heart out, but it sorted itself out in a week. All he needed was a few days of peace and quiet and the odd bit of sweet feed. So, if your one’s just grumpy, give him the time. But if it keeps goin’ on, then you’d best get him checked properly. You’re still working the weekend gig this Saturday, aren’t you?      Aye, that's the plan. I told the client we’d pull off something blooming bonkers with canapés under the stars and all the rest of it. Like a dream to organise, but only if you’ve still got the energy to dream. I've got rhythm in me from the way I bounce at the tiller of me planning, but I swear it's wearing on me. Though, honestly, don’t get me started on the client. Bit much for me, eh?      Who is she again? If she's trying to run a five-star event out of a shoebox and still wants sparkle, then fair play to you being able to smile through all that. I’ve seen it all in about five minutes. That said, you’re the reliable one of the lot of us. I’ve already skipped out on another meet-up with friends because I couldn't unplug from my project. My boss is over the moon with the guest speaker stats I cranked out, but I'm over the moon with a surf ‘n’ turf night in.      I could stick out one good night in. Though as of last week, me with 'in' and not whippin' up the kettle in the road is a serious feat. Picked up the cold early in the week and I'm still plodding through it like one of them brambles in the field between Darlington and Yarmouth.

Honestly, I just can't get through the day without grumbling about the people in my project team. We had another "status update meeting" today, and more than half of them stared at their screens like they were doing a photoshoot. I don't even know what they were  supposed  to be presenting on!      Ugh, that’s honestly exhausting. I get it completely — I’ve been working in a mental health ward this week and I’ve had so many people just not show up or cancel last-minute. It’s like the entire NHS is run on hot air and well-meaning intentions these days.      Right? I swear someone once told me only 10% of people who say they’re "on top of it" actually are. Ten per cent, Em! And I’m not even halfway through the month.      Honestly, I’m better off when I just pretend no one else matters. I just keep doing my rounds and remind myself that not everyone hides behind a spreadsheet looking for a way out. Good news is, that new girl I trained this week—personable, consistent—she might actually be decent.      That’s something. Have you heard from Anna lately?      No, not really. We –  ha!  – had a bit of a messy break-up again. I thought we were on the same page, but she just moved out last week and didn’t even say goodbye properly. Honestly, I just don’t get how someone can seem fine one minute and chaotic the next.      That is so frustrating. I mean, being split up is hard enough but when people are emotionally inconsistent it’s about five times worse. I don’t even know how we all cope with it.      Yeah, that’s why I take the day off if I can. I do something like read for six hours or go for a long walk — anything to get away from the emotional whiplash.      I tried that once — read a whole book while wearing my fluffy pyjamas. Let me tell you, it was weird to keep seeing “hurried” and “deadlines” in the same chapter.      Oh no go there! I remember your last presentation — everyone was so confused when you read line-by-line out of  Jane Eyre  while explaining the budget.      That was  not  on, was it? I think those were the tears doing the talking. But honestly, it was the only way I could express/project/whatever modern work jargon they want now.
