Rather annoying that the school’s got this filming trip tomorrow, isn’t it? I mean, they’re asking everyone to turn up bright and early—seven o'clock sharp. Not sure what they think we are, Olympic athletes.      Well, it’s a cultural day. They said it’s for a documentary about rural schools. I think it was some local education trust thing. They wanted to show off a bit. A lot of the parents are doing this stuff, helping out backstage or whatever. It’ll be interesting to watch in the end, I suppose.      I’m scared. I don’t like cameras pointing at me.      Don’t worry, love. You’ll probably be too busy drawing smiley faces on your face—you know what’s coming. Ten minutes of fame.      I want a doughnut. When’s the last time we had a doughnut?      You had one just last week after the football match at the park. But yes, we can get some soon. After the trip, why don’t we pop to Waterstones and get you a book?      I’m with you on that. But back to the real issue—have we sorted out the filming thing? I remember something about a warm night clothes note. They said it might get chilly outside, even in the afternoon.      Yeah, the teacher sent that out. Seems like they’re doing some outdoor footage near the hills. It’s all very picturesque. I told her to打包 two extra jumpers just in case.      My leg still hurts, Daddy. I think I hit it when I was trying to make a ballet move in the living room about an hour ago.      Oh come on, not again. You said you were going to be careful. Let me check it again. Does it hurt when I press here?      A little. But I can still run. A bit.      Let it be. We don’t want another strain. I’ve got a gym membership. Maybe we should go later on this week. The running machines would do you a world of good—stayed in the simulation but gave you proper legs.      Don’t push it. We both need to get more exercise. If we go together, maybe we can support each other. You know we的好处 of endorphins.      So I have to get fit to help my daughter’s dance career? Typical.      I want to come too. Can I use the slide on the running machine?

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, isn’t it, James? I mean, they’re calling it a "green levy," but it’s just more pressure on small businesses, like yours. I read about it in the local paper over breakfast this morning.      Oh aye, it’s beginning to bite, I’ll say that for 'im. My shop just outside Hove needs a bit of a revamp, but now I’ve this extra burden to consider. Green ideas are all well and good, mind—don’t get me wrong—but when you run a small business, blooming green policies can often look more like red ink. I’ve been watching the Green Party’s debate on the telly and they talk about boot sales, if you believe it! Boot sales, for heaven’s sake!      Boot sales and bubblewrap! They seem very green in theory, but do they ever think of breakfast, James? You need to run your business, for goodness’ sake! I hear the council is also mulling over changes to the job centre. Something about streamlined applications and less paperwork for the young, maybe encouraging them into self-employment. I suppose that’s a step in the right direction.      Good on 'em for that, if it’s genuine. Mind you, most of the young folk I know are struggling, and not because they don’t want to work. Too many of 'em have been through the system and are still picking up the pieces. And let’s not even talk about relationships in this age—my Alice says my tongue is as old-fashioned as a magazine wrapped with ribbon. But hey, mind your own tongue and mouths will follow, as my old mam used to say.      Ah yes, the ties that bind! She’s right, mind. And it’s not all bad—you know that new school I mentioned? They’re doing a pilot in green technologies and found ‘em quite the response from pupils. A few are even thinking of self-employment by the time they’re seventeen. Do you think there’s a way you might get involved, perhaps supply some materials or advice?      That’s a grand idea, Tom. Might do ‘im a world of good. The kids these days—mind you, some of the ones I see go in with one pond and come out with a fountain! But it could open some doors, no doubt.

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses me a pastie and just gives me a croissant... What was I thinking? I went in at 6 in the mornin’ bleedin’ knackered. Not proper start to the day, innit?      Yeah, I saw that place, looked like a proper nice café. But if it's not dishing up a decent pie and mash along with your pasty, what’s the point, eh? Out here in Cambridgeshire, pasties are sacred. They don’t call it the Home of the Pasty for nothin'!      Oh, no, it's the real deal only for me. You like that Mynt t shirt I was wearing last week? The one with the Norse runes on the back?      I did, the cut of it an' all — very sharp. You lookin’ to start a new wardrobe trend or something? I’m thinking about getting me one of them for uni, you know, to go with me boots and jeans.      Naa, it was just a one-off I got in Manchester. Like a week to go and I'm off on holiday, might buy me something proper for the sun. I been reading all these articles about how much fashion marketing is borrowed from the political sphere these days — really interesting stuff, if you like that kind of thing.      Oh, I could try to follow that — I mean, politics is all I ever read. Although I’ve not read anything properly good lately. I had a rant with my supervisor the other day over his obsession with the politicians ‘prioritizing crude financial reform’.      I know! I was watching the news the other day and it had this whole vibes of a Ronseal advertisement gone wrong. ‘Does exactly what it says on the tin’ but to the detriment of ‘all the tin’ rather than improving it. I mean, Donald Trump? The man’s a walking PR disaster, innit.      Aye, I could see the bloke as some sort of bloke out of a comedy with his hair a little more whispy and wearing an oxford shirt for some reason.      Haha, yeah go on then, make a film out of him. Just give it a proper line in the credits that it's completely fiction, might save the director from a libel case. I have to get back to the conference in the morning, otherwise those jokes are never going to stop.      Oh, you're in the big one at the science museum?

Rather annoyingly, I've got to mark those essays from the first-year undergrads this week. Honestly, I got to the end of one and thought, “This could have been written by a Victorian steam engine.”      No, I bet some of them wouldn't know a well-structured argument if it tripped over its own feet. Which topic were they on again?      It was about postmodernism in art—such a funny topic for a 20-year-old to try and grapple with. I remember once when I was teaching, I had a guy argue that Banksy’s graffiti was just property damage made acceptable by a clever marketing ploy.      [laughs] That's not entirely wrong. I think I remember you mentioned that, didn’t you? Darcy, the one I met at the Blue Peter badge evening in Norwich? His wife is into tactical breakfasts—like she has this entire spreadsheet for which foods optimise brain cells, you know?      Yes, the Darcys. Their house is like a museum for vintage Bob Ross Christmas cards and cat-shaped bread knives. Anyway, going back to the undergrads—some of them write as if they’re composing a tweet, not an academic essay.      –And they get upset when you dock marks for it. You'd think after the first lot of failed tests and re-submissions, they’d learn. Last night, I was watching a documentary about killer whales. Did you know they have these social structures that are like advanced human societies?      No, I didn’t. I thought they were just big, loud dolphins with ballet shoes.      [laughs] Not quite. But it really got me thinking—how much of what we call “wildness” is just barely informed instinct? And does that change how we treat them, especially for TV? There’s that BBC nature programme that humanises them endlessly.      You know, I watched a bit of that too. The way they narrate the footage makes you  feel  as though you’re right there with the seal. It’s almost unethical how persuasive it is. My students would  kill  for that kind of presentation. They hate essays, love documentaries.      That’s one of the reasons I started showing films in my lectures. People forget how effective films are at communicating complex ideas. But I have to watch the violence on TV these days—I had my mother in last week and she was watching some horror channel and ended up sound asleep before bed.

Rather annoying this new hostel they’ve set up down the high street. I was just reading in  The Norfolk Chronicle , and they say they’re having all sorts of trouble managing it. I remember when we had a little shop in Costessey run by the Marshalls—very strict, but you could count on them always having fresh butter and eggs.      I reckon it depends on the people running it. A few years back, I looked after one of their boys, Timmy. He was quite a handful, truth be told. But anyway, the hostels nowadays chase money, don’t they? You don’t hear much about character education these days—just jobs and qualifications. What’s all that got to do with being a decent human being?      Yeah, it’s just more about the bottom line now, isn’t it? I used to teach history at Handsworth Grammar, and the kids would come back when the weather was bad and just sit about with a cup of tea and a biscuit. Proper people, not some glorified boarding house with a profit motive. Speaking of which—did I show you the photos of my Mum in hospital the other day? She’s quite taken to the food there. They serve shepherd’s pie every third evening—it’s the proper kind, not that healthy rubbish.      Pictures of your mum? I still have one of my sister in her wedding dress—taken in ’59, when the war was still fresh in people’s minds. She’d have never dreamed of someone not working in a shop or a factory. Her and my old man were so hardworking—opened a grocery at the end of the village and kept their accounts under the counter! We’d have starved if it wasn’t for them.      Oh, my poor Charlie—always thumped on the head if he forgot to deliver the newspapers or left a ledger unbalanced. I remember the smell of the abattoir next door to his shop. Said it was his way of earning a living. Unpopular, but essential, he used to say. I miss the way things were then. There was a bit of pride in doing a job well.      At least your parents had purpose. Mine were teachers—strict, of course. My Dad once told me that if I wanted to get ahead, I’d have to think like an engineer. I just wanted to read science fiction and build go-karts in the shed.

Rather annoying to be honest, how some lecturers expect postgrad students to know conventions off the bat when they haven’t even been introduced to them. I’m more lenient, you know, I think we should support their academic literacy properly rather than assume they already have it.      I get that. My undergrad students liked the clear frameworks I gave them. I think it depends on how self-directed the students are. A lot of them just panic when they see a 3,000-word essay dump on them. Especially when they’re coming from very practical fields — it can be a complete culture shock.      Exactly! And speaking of culture shock, I was just reflecting on how different your background is from what’s typical around here. I read in your profile that you used to work in recruitment back in Australia. How did that even go alongside the academic side of things?      Yeah, I did recruitment for a couple of years. Mainly for startups — tech and social ventures. It was quite a shift to move into the academic world. One second I’m negotiating salaries and project timelines, the next I’m marking reflective practice essays written in two different tenses. But I found it incredibly useful, actually. Recruitment taught me how to read people, how to assess potential from humble beginnings — skills that come in handy when you’re trying to pick up on subtle strengths in student writing or presentations.      That’s interesting. I suppose it’s a similar kind of critical judgment, just applied in someone else’s language. Evaluation in academia often relies on a very specific vocabulary that can trip people up if they’re not used to it. I’ve seen students use great logical reasoning but panic when it comes to quoting or about how to articulate their arguments in formal academic language.      Oh yes — academic literacy is not literacy in the traditional school sense. It’s more about knowing the hidden rules. My sister once tried applying for a law course in the UK and was really confused about how open-ended the assignments were.
